## 12. Iddhividhaniddesa: Description of the Kinds of Supernormal Power
## Explanation of Direct Knowledge

[1] 365. I have stated (in the Description of Concentration, p. 644) that this development of concentration has the benefit of the direct knowledges (abhiññā) through the power of those mundane direct knowledges. To bring those mundane direct knowledges to fulfillment, a meditator who has attained the fourth jhāna in the earth kasiṇa and so on should apply effort. The specific benefit is that, by doing so, the meditator's development of concentration will both have its benefit and become firmer. Being endowed with a development of concentration that is both beneficial and firmer, the meditator will be able to bring the development of wisdom (paññā-bhāvanā) to fulfillment easily and pleasantly. Therefore (although it is time to describe the development of wisdom), I shall first set forth the explanation of direct knowledge (abhiññā-kathā).

For the purpose of showing the benefit of the development of concentration to those clansmen who have attained the fourth jhāna, and for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma in higher and higher stages, the Blessed One said: 'When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the various kinds of supernormal power. He experiences the various kinds of supernormal power in many ways: having been one, he becomes many,' and so on. In this manner, He taught the five mundane direct knowledges: (1) Iddhividha-abhiññā (Direct knowledge of the kinds of supernormal power), (2) Dibbasota-abhiññā (Direct knowledge of the divine ear), (3) Cetopariya-abhiññā (Direct knowledge of others' minds), (4) Pubbenivāsa-abhiññā (Direct knowledge of recollection of past lives), and (5) Cutūpapāta-abhiññā, also known as Dibbacakkhu-abhiññā (Direct knowledge of the divine eye).

[2] Among those five, a beginner meditator who wishes to perform the supernormal power (iddhi) and the transformation (vikubbanā) described as 'having been one, he becomes many,' and so on, should produce the eight attainments in each of the eight kasiṇas ending with the white kasiṇa. Then, the mind should be disciplined in these fourteen ways:

(1) In the forward order of kasiṇas (kasiṇānuloma),
(2) In the reverse order of kasiṇas (kasiṇapaṭiloma),
(3) In the forward and reverse order of kasiṇas (kasiṇānulomapaṭiloma),
(4) In the forward order of jhānas (jhānānuloma),
(5) In the reverse order of jhānas (jhānapaṭiloma),
(6) In the forward and reverse order of jhānas (jhānānulomapaṭiloma),
(7) In the skipping of jhānas (jhānukkantika),
(8) In the skipping of kasiṇas (kasiṇukkantika),
(9) In the skipping of jhānas and kasiṇas (jhānakasiṇukkantika),
(10) In the transposing of factors (aṅgasaṅkantika),
3:
(11) By shifting the object;
(12) By shifting the factors and the object;
(13) By defining the factors;
(14) By defining the object;
By these fourteen ways, the mind should be previously trained (to make it pliant and workable).1

366. Among these fourteen, what is kasiṇa-anuloma (successive order of kasiṇas)? What is kasiṇa-paṭiloma (reverse order of kasiṇas)? ... What is defining the object? This is the question.

(1) In this Dispensation, a monk enters into jhāna in the earth kasiṇa (pathavī-kasiṇa), then in the water kasiṇa (āpo-kasiṇa); in this way, he enters into them in successive order through the eight kasiṇas, even a hundred times or a thousand times. This is called kasiṇa-anuloma (successive order of kasiṇas).

Note
1. In this context, "previously trained" means practicing beforehand in the manner of preliminary work (parikamma) to achieve mastery as desired.

(2) Starting from the white kasiṇa (odāta-kasiṇa) and entering in reverse order in the same way,1 this is called kasiṇa-paṭiloma (reverse order of kasiṇas).

(3) Entering repeatedly in both successive and reverse order, from the earth kasiṇa to the white kasiṇa, and from the white kasiṇa back to the earth kasiṇa, this is called kasiṇa-anuloma-paṭiloma.

(4) Entering repeatedly in successive order from the first jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), this is called jhāna-anuloma.

(5) Entering repeatedly in reverse order from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception down to the first jhāna, this is called jhāna-paṭiloma.

(6) Entering repeatedly in both successive and reverse order, from the first jhāna to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception back to the first jhāna, this is called jhāna-anuloma-paṭiloma.

(7) Having entered the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, he enters the third jhāna in that same earth kasiṇa. Then, having removed that earth kasiṇa sign, he enters the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana). Then, he enters the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). In this way, skipping the jhānas by one interval without skipping the kasiṇas is called jhānukkantika (skipping jhānas). Similarly, applications should be made starting with the water kasiṇa, etc.

Note
1. The phrase "in the same way" indicates the meaning of entering the eight kasiṇas in reverse order a hundred or a thousand times. (Ṭīkā)

(8) Having entered the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, he enters that same first jhāna in the fire kasiṇa (tejo-kasiṇa), then in the blue kasiṇa (nīla-kasiṇa), then in the red kasiṇa (lohita-kasiṇa). In this way, skipping the kasiṇas by one interval without skipping the jhānas is called kasiṇukkantika (skipping kasiṇas).1

(9) Having entered the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, he then enters the third jhāna in the fire kasiṇa. Then, removing the blue kasiṇa sign, he enters the base of infinite space. Then, from the red kasiṇa, he enters the base of nothingness.2 In this way, skipping both the jhānas and the kasiṇas is called jhāna-kasiṇukkantika (skipping jhānas and kasiṇas).

Note
1. In this context, skipping objects starting from the second jhāna, etc., should be understood in the same way.
2. Regarding "from the red kasiṇa, he enters the base of nothingness," it means after contemplating and attending to the red kasiṇa, he does not enter the base of infinite space by not attending to the space revealed by removing the kasiṇa sign (the Ṭīkā notes that while the text says 'entering', 'not entering' would be more appropriate), but instead enters the base of nothingness by taking as object the absence of the previous consciousness of the base of infinite space in that space. (Ṭīkā)

(10) Having entered the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, entering the other jhānas in that same earth kasiṇa is called aṅgasaṅkantika (shifting factors).

(11) Having entered the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, entering that same first jhāna in the water kasiṇa, the fire kasiṇa... up to the white kasiṇa. In this way, entering only one single jhāna in all the kasiṇas1 is called ārammaṇasaṅkantika (shifting objects).

(12) Having entered the first jhāna in the earth kasiṇa, he enters the second jhāna in the water kasiṇa, the third jhāna in the fire kasiṇa, the fourth jhāna in the air kasiṇa (vāyo-kasiṇa). Having removed the blue kasiṇa sign, he enters the base of infinite space. From the yellow kasiṇa (pīta-kasiṇa), he enters the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana).1

Note
1. "In all kasiṇas"—this phrase should not be taken to include the space kasiṇa and consciousness kasiṇa, because only the eight kasiṇas (ending with white) are applicable here. Similarly, the four immaterial jhānas should not be called "one single jhāna," but since the goal is to train the mind through the eight attainments, shifting factors and objects through immaterial jhānas is said figuratively. Because it is figurative, it says "from the yellow kasiṇa, he enters the base of infinite consciousness," referring to the consciousness of the first immaterial jhāna which has as its object the space revealed by removing the yellow kasiṇa. In this way, the rest (from the red kasiṇa...)

From the red kasiṇa, he enters the base of nothingness. From the white kasiṇa, he enters the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. In this way, shifting the factors and the objects by skipping one is called aṅgārammaṇasaṅkantika (shifting factors and objects).

(13) Having defined the first jhāna as having five factors, the second jhāna as having three factors, the third jhāna as having two factors, and likewise the fourth jhāna, the base of infinite space... up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (as having two factors), in this way, defining only the jhāna factors is called aṅgavavatthāpana (defining factors).

(14) Likewise, having defined "this is the earth kasiṇa," "this is the water kasiṇa"... "this is the white kasiṇa," in this way, defining only the object is called ārammaṇavavatthāpana (defining objects).
4:
(14) Similarly, having noted, "This is the earth kasina," "This is the water kasina," ... "This is the white kasina," such noting of the object alone is called "defining the object" (ārammaṇa-vavatthāpana). [4] Some teachers also desire "defining the factors and the object" (aṅgārammaṇa-vavatthāpana). However, because it does not appear in the Commentaries (Atthakathā), that defining of factors and the object is certainly not a basis for meditation (bhāvanā).

367. It is not possible for a beginner yogi, who has not previously developed meditation and has not first tamed the mind (to be gentle and pliant) through these fourteen ways, to achieve psychic transformation (iddhi-vikubbana).

Note 1: The meaning to be shown here is already included in Note 1 on page 7.
Note 2: Connect with "...will be able to complete."

Indeed, for a beginner, even performing the preliminary work (parikamma) for a kasina is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it. For one who has performed the preliminary work, producing the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it. When the counterpart sign has arisen, developing it and attaining absorption (appanā) is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it. For one who has attained absorption, taming the mind through the fourteen ways is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it. For one who has tamed the mind through the fourteen ways, psychic transformation is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand can do it. For one who has reached the stage of transformation, quickness in reviewing and attaining (khippa-nisanti) is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand is quick in reviewing and attaining.

Note 1: Regarding "even performing the preliminary work for a kasina is a burden"—it means that practicing on the kasina disk until the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) arises through the procedure of avoiding faults, etc., is itself a burden; how much more so for psychic transformation? (Commentary)
Note 2: "Developing it" means developing both that counterpart sign and the meditation. Indeed, it is not possible to develop the sign alone without meditation. (Commentary)
Note 3: Some yogis, after attaining access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), are unable to attain absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi); such persons are many. Therefore, it is said, "attaining absorption is a burden." (Commentary)

(How is this so?) It is like the Elder Rakkhita, who had eight years of seniority since his higher ordination, among the thirty thousand possessors of psychic power who came to attend to the illness of the Elder Mahārohaṇagutta at Therambatthalaka. His power was already described in the "Description of the Earth Kasina" (Pathavī-kasiṇa-niddesa, Visuddhimagga Vol. 1, p. 478 etc.). Seeing his power, the Elder said, "Friends, if Rakkhita had not been here, we would all have been blamed, saying, 'They could not protect the Naga king.' Therefore, a weapon that one carries with oneself should be carried only after it has been cleaned of its stains." Abiding by the Elder's advice, those thirty thousand monks also became quick in reviewing and attaining.

Note 1: Thera (Elders like Mahinda) + Amba (Mango trees) + Thala (Hill) = Therambatthalaka, the hill with mango trees where Elders like Mahinda descended. (Commentary)
Note 2: In the Pathavī-kasiṇa-niddesa, the name is Buddharakkhita; here it is abbreviated as Rakkhita.

Furthermore, even if there is quickness in reviewing and attaining, being a refuge and support for others is a burden; only one in a hundred or a thousand can be a refuge for others. (How is this so?) It is like the Elder who, during the Giribhaṇḍavāhana festival, when Mara caused a rain of coals to fall, created earth in the sky and protected against the rain of coals.

Note 1: The Giribhaṇḍavāhana festival is a grand lamp offering (dīpa-pūjā) starting from Cetiyapabbata (now called Mihintale in Sinhala, where Elder Mahinda first stayed) throughout the whole island and up to one league into the ocean.

However, for those of great past merit (pubbayoga) such as the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Chief Disciples, this psychic transformation [5] and other special qualities like the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are perfected through the mere attainment of Arahatship, even without this stated sequence of meditation development. Therefore, just as a goldsmith who wishes to make a special ornament by blowing with fire...
5:
During the celebration of that great offering, Māra caused a rain of burning embers to fall, but even within that moment, a piece of earth was created in the sky (for protection) so that not even a spark reached the people. (Sub-commentary) The detailed account of this matter is no longer clearly found at present.

2- Connect with: "...and are accomplished even without the sequence of meditation practice."

3- It means that only for those endowed with the cause of powerful effort in past lives are the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) accomplished without the sequence of meditation practice shown here; for others, they are not accomplished. (Sub-commentary)

Just as a goldsmith, wishing to craft a particular ornament, first makes the gold soft and wieldy (fit for the desired work) by blowing with fire and so on, and just as a potter, wishing to craft a particular vessel, first makes the clay well-kneaded and soft, even so, a beginner yogi should first tame the mind through these fourteen ways. Then, by means of attaining through the heading of desire (chanda), the heading of mind (citta), the heading of energy (vīriya), or the heading of investigation (vīmaṃsā), and by means of mastery (vasībhāva) such as adverting (āvajjana) and so on, having made the mind soft and wieldy for the required work, he should apply himself to the various modes of psychic power (iddhividha). However, a person endowed with past causes who has attained mastery even in just the fourth jhāna of the kasinas may also perform (psychic transformations). Furthermore, wishing to show the method of practice that accomplishes psychic power in this context, the Blessed One said: "When the mind is thus concentrated..." and so forth.

368. In this passage, the following explanation is a decision made strictly according to the method of the Pali.

Note:
1- This refers to the words shown with quotation marks on page 2, paragraph 2, line 3, etc.

In those words of the Buddha, "He" (so) means that yogi monk who has attained the fourth jhāna. The word "thus" (evaṃ) is a term showing the sequence of attaining the fourth jhāna. By this, it means "having attained the fourth jhāna through the sequence beginning with the attainment of the first jhāna." "Concentrated" (samāhite) means concentrated by this fourth jhāna concentration. "The mind" (citte) means the fine-material sphere mind (rūpāvacara citta). In the terms such as "purified" (parisuddhe), it means purified by the state of purity of mindfulness due to equanimity (upekkhā-sati-pārisuddhi). Because it is purified, it is said to be "bright" (pariyodāte) and radiant.

Because the blemishes (angaṇa) such as lust and so on have been removed by striking down the causes such as pleasure and so forth, it is "unblemished" (anangaṇe). Because it is unblemished, it is "free from imperfections" (vigatūpakkilese). Indeed, the mind becomes imperfect because of blemishes. Because it is well-developed, it has "become soft" (mudubhūte), meaning it has reached mastery. Indeed, a mind that stays under control is called soft. Because it is soft, it is "wieldy" (kammaññe), meaning it is fit for work and suitable for work. For a soft mind is wieldy like well-refined gold, and both of these qualities are due to being well-developed. As it was said:

"Monks, I do not see even one other thing that, when developed and cultivated, becomes so soft and wieldy as this mind." (Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.22).

Because it stands in these states of purity and so on, it is "steady" (thite). Because it is steady, it is said to have "attained imperturbability" (āneñjappatte), meaning it is unmoving and without wavering. Alternatively, because it stands under one's own control by being soft and wieldy, it is "steady." It has attained imperturbability because it is grasped by faith and so on. Indeed, a mind grasped by faith does not waver through faithlessness. Grasped by energy, it does not waver through laziness. Grasped by mindfulness, it does not waver through negligence. Grasped by concentration, it does not waver through restlessness.

Note:
"The state of purity..."—It is said that equanimity causes the purity of mindfulness.
1- In the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta, it is explained that "one who does not want others to know his faults, one who does not want to be questioned about his faults in public, one who wants to be a leader, one who wants abundant gains, one who wants to be respected and honored—such a person tends to get angry and displeased because things do not happen as he wishes. In such cases, these evil states of greed (lobha), anger (dosa), displeasure (domanassa), and delusion (moha) associated with that greed, etc., are called blemishes (angaṇa)."
2- Although the word upakkilesa is explained in the Commentaries as "that which causes burning or oppression," it is translated here as "imperfection" for ease of understanding.

Note:
1- This explains the term "steady" (thite) from page 3, line 3; it means standing in states such as purity.
2- Being "grasped by faith, etc." means that they support the mind by occurring intensely in the mode of faith, etc.
6:
The mind supported by faith (saddhā) is not shaken by lack of faith.1 The mind supported by energy (viriya) is not shaken by laziness. The mind supported by mindfulness (sati) is not shaken by forgetfulness. The mind supported by concentration (samādhi) is not shaken by restlessness (uddhacca). The mind supported by wisdom (paññā) is not shaken by the darkness of defilements. The mind supported by these six factors reaches imperturbability (āneñja). Thus, the mind endowed with eight factors2 is fit for directing towards the realization and personal experience of those things that are to be realized through higher knowledge (abhiññā).

Notes:
1. It is said to be 'unshaken' because, through the power of faith, the state of lack of faith or turbidity does not arise, and the mind remains only in a state of clear and confident faith.
2. It should be understood as being endowed with these eight factors: (1) being concentrated through the fourth jhāna (samāhita), (2) being thoroughly purified (parisuddha), (3) being thoroughly bright (pariyodāta), (4) being unblemished (anaṅgaṇa), (5) being free from defilements (vigatūpakkilesa), (6) becoming malleable (mudubhūta), (7) being wieldy (kammaniya), and (8) being steady and imperturbable (ṭhita āneñjappatta). Alternatively, since it describes the factors of a concentrated mind, the term 'concentrated' (samāhite) is excluded, and the eight factors are counted from the remaining eight terms. (This is based on the Sub-commentary/Ṭīkā).

An alternative explanation from the ancient commentaries: When the mind is concentrated through the fourth jhāna; when it is thoroughly purified by being distant from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa);1 when it is thoroughly bright by transcending thought-conception (vitakka) and so on; when it is unblemished (anaṅgaṇa) due to the absence of low and evil desires that tend to arise based on the attainment of jhāna;2 when it is free from defilements (vigatūpakkilesa) due to the absence of covetousness (abhijjhā) and so on which defile the mind. This pair—being unblemished and being free from defilements—should be understood according to the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta and the Vattha Sutta.3 When it becomes malleable by reaching mastery (vasībhāva); when it is wieldy by reaching the state of the bases of power (iddhipāda) which are the means of success;4 when it is steady and imperturbable by reaching the most sublime state through the fulfillment of mental development (bhāvanā). 'Steady and imperturbable' means it remains steady until it reaches imperturbability. According to this explanation also:

Notes:
1. Being distant from the hindrances is itself called 'thoroughly purified'.
2. Evil desires refer to unwholesome states such as conceit (māna), deceit (māyā), and hypocrisy (sāṭheyya), such as wishing 'May they ask only me to preach the Dhamma'. (Based on the Ṭīkā).
3. By saying 'according to', the Ṭīkā explains that the coarse unwholesome states directly taught in those Suttas are not taken here; only the subtle unwholesome states are meant.
4. This refers to reaching the state of the basis jhāna (pādakajjhāna), which is the proximate cause for supernormal transformations. (Ṭīkā).

The mind, being endowed with these eight factors, is fit for directing towards the realization and personal experience of those things to be realized through higher knowledge; it is the foundation (pādaka) and the proximate cause (for supernormal transformations, etc.).

## Explanation of the Ten Kinds of Success (Iddhi)

369. In the phrase 'He directs and inclines the mind to the various kinds of supernormal power (iddhi)', it is called 'iddhi' in the sense of succeeding (ijjhata), in the sense of accomplishment (nipphatti), and in the sense of attainment (paṭilābha). Indeed, that which is accomplished and attained is said to 'succeed' (ijjhata). As it is said:

'If, for one desiring sensual pleasures, that desire is fulfilled (samijjhati).'
(Sutta Nipāta 772)

Likewise: 'Renunciation (nekkhamma) is a success (iddhi) because it succeeds (ijjhata) and is attained; it is a miracle (pāṭihāriya) because it removes [the opposite]. ... The path of Arahantship is a success (iddhi) because it succeeds and is attained; it is a miracle (pāṭihāriya) because it removes [the opposite].' (Paṭisambhidāmagga).

Another way: It is called 'iddhi' in the sense of causing success. This is a designation for the perfection of means (upāyasampadā). Indeed, the perfection of means causes success because it produces the desired fruit. As it is said: 'This Citta the Householder is virtuous and of good character. If he should make a wish, "In the future, may I become a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti)," this heart's desire of that virtuous one will succeed because of its purity.' (Saṃyutta Nikāya).

Another way: It is called 'iddhi' because by this, beings succeed. 'They succeed' means they are prosperous (iddhā), grown (vuddhā), and have reached excellence (ukkaṃsagatā).1

Notes:
1. By this first explanation, 'iddhi' refers to the state of success or fulfillment itself.
2. By this second explanation, 'iddhi' refers to the correct and good cause that brings about success.
3. By this third explanation, 'iddhi' refers to the cause of prosperity and progress.

That supernormal power called 'iddhi' is of ten kinds. As it is said: 'How many kinds of iddhi are there? There are ten kinds of iddhi.' Furthermore, it is explained: 'What are the ten kinds of iddhi? (1) Adhiṭṭhāniddhi—success by determination (transformation)...'
7:
(2) Vikubbana-iddhi: The power of transformation by discarding one's natural form and creating various other forms. (3) Manomaya-iddhi: The power of creating a mind-made body (identical to oneself). (4) Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi: Success achieved through the diffusion of knowledge. (5) Samādhivipphāra-iddhi: Success achieved through the diffusion of concentration. (6) Ariya-iddhi: Success attained by the Noble Ones. (7) Kammavipākaja-iddhi: Success achieved depending on the result of kamma. (8) Puññavato-iddhi: Success achieved by those of exceptional merit. (9) Vijjāmaya-iddhi: Success achieved through magical arts or spells. (10) Tattha tattha sammāpayogapaccayā-iddhi: Success achieved through right effort in various circumstances. These are the ten.

370. Therein, "While being naturally one, he reflects on becoming many; having reflected on a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand, he determines with knowledge, 'Let me be many'"—the success shown through such analysis is called Adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi (Success by Determination) because it is accomplished by the power of determination. (1)

371. "That person, discarding his natural appearance, shows the appearance of a youth, or the appearance of a serpent (nāga), the appearance of a garuḍa, the appearance of an ogre (yakkha), the appearance of Sakka, the appearance of a deity, the appearance of a Brahmā, the appearance of an ocean, the appearance of a mountain, the appearance of a lion, the appearance of a tiger, the appearance of a leopard, the appearance of an elephant, the appearance of a horse, the appearance of a chariot, the appearance of an infantryman, or shows various arrays of armies"—the creation of success described in this way is called Vikubbana-iddhi (Success by Transformation) because it proceeds by the power of changing and discarding the natural appearance. (2)

372. "Here, a monk creates from this body another body, mind-made, having form"—the success described in this manner is called Manomaya-iddhi (Mind-made Success) because it proceeds by the power of producing another mind-made body within the physical body. (3)

373. The distinction produced by the power of knowledge, whether before, after, or at the moment of the arising of knowledge, is called Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi (Success by Diffusion of Knowledge). Indeed, it is said: "The state of abandoning the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence is successful; therefore, it is called Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi... The state of abandoning all defilements through the Path of Arahantship is successful; therefore, it is called Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi. The Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi of the Venerable Bakkula, the Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi of the Venerable Saṅkicca, and the Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi of the Venerable Bhūtapāla (should be understood)."

Note 1: Translated with a different phrasing for smoothness in Burmese; literally, it means "as it comes thus."
Note 2: It can also be translated as "because the state of abandoning is successful (it is called Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi)."

Therein, the Venerable Bakkula, as a five-day-old infant on an auspicious day, fell into the current of a river due to the negligence of his nurse while being bathed. A large fish swallowed him and went to the landing place at Bārāṇasī. There, a fisherman caught the fish and sold it to a treasurer's wife. Having developed an affection for the fish, she thought, "I will prepare and cook it myself." Upon splitting it open, she saw a child as beautiful as a golden image in the belly of the fish and was filled with joy, thinking, "I have gained a son." [8] Thus, the health and freedom from harm of the Venerable Bakkula, who was in his final existence (pacchimabhavika), while in the belly of the fish, is called Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi because it was produced by the power of the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship that he was to attain in that very body.
8:
The story should be told in detail (as shown in the Commentary to the Uparipaṇṇāsa, p. 135, and the Etadagga-vagga of the Aṅguttara Commentary).

Furthermore, the mother of the Elder Saṅkicca died while he was still in her womb. When her corpse was placed on a pyre, pierced with stakes, and burned, the tip of a stake struck the corner of the infant's eye, and he made a sound. Realizing the child was still alive, they took the body down from the pyre, split the womb, removed the child, and handed him to his grandmother. When he grew up under his grandmother's care, he went forth as a monk and attained Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). (See Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 1, p. 426). In the same manner as mentioned, the health of the Venerable Saṅkicca on the burning pyre is called Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi.

Note 1: Here, since it is a narrative, some parts are translated with adjustments for smoothness; the same should be noted for similar instances hereafter.

Furthermore, the father of the boy named Bhūtapāla was a poor man (who sold firewood) in the city of Rājagaha. He went to the forest with a cart for wood, loaded it, and returned near the city in the evening. Then his oxen slipped their yoke and entered the city. He made the young son sit near the cart and followed the oxen, entering the city himself. Before he could come out, the city gates were closed. The boy's safety for the three watches of the night outside the city, even in a place frequented by fierce yakkhas, is called Ñāṇavipphāra-iddhi in the same manner as mentioned. The story should be understood in detail (as described in the Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 284). (4)

374. The distinction produced by the power of serenity (samatha), whether before, after, or at the moment of concentration, is called Samādhivipphāra-iddhi (Success by Diffusion of Concentration). Indeed, it is said: "The state of abandoning the hindrances through the first jhāna is successful; therefore, it is called Samādhivipphāra-iddhi...

Note 1: Here too, it can be translated as "because the state of abandoning is successful (it is called Samādhivipphāra-iddhi)."

The state of abandoning the perception of the sphere of nothingness through the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is successful; therefore, it is called Samādhivipphāra-iddhi. The Samādhivipphāra-iddhi of the Venerable Sāriputta, the Samādhivipphāra-iddhi of the Venerable Sañjīva, the Samādhivipphāra-iddhi of the Venerable Khāṇu-Koṇḍañña, the Samādhivipphāra-iddhi of the female lay follower Uttarā, and the Samādhivipphāra-iddhi of the female lay follower Sāmāvatī (should be understood)."

Therein, on one occasion, while the Venerable Sāriputta was staying with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna at the Kapota Ravine, he was sitting in the open air on a moonlit night with his head newly shaven. A wicked yakkha, despite being warned by his companion yakkha, struck the Elder's head violently. The sound of that blow was like a thunderclap. [9] At that moment, while being struck by the yakkha, the Venerable Sāriputta entered into a meditative attainment. Consequently, the Venerable Sāriputta felt no pain whatsoever from the yakkha's blow. This absence of pain in the Venerable Sāriputta is Samādhivipphāra-iddhi.
9:
The detailed story is found in the Udāna Pāḷi (p. 123).

Furthermore, while the Elder Sañjīva was in the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), cowherds and others, thinking he was dead, piled grass, wood, cow dung, etc., and set them on fire. However, not even a single thread of the Elder’s robe was burnt. This lack of burning for the Elder Sañjīva is psychic power through the diffusion of concentration (samādhivipphāra-iddhi), produced by the power of serenity (samatha) occurring through successive attainments [Note 1]. The detailed story appears in the Māratajjanīya Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa (409).

Furthermore, the Venerable Khāṇukoṇḍañña was naturally frequent in entering meditative attainments. One night in a certain forest, he sat having entered an attainment [Note 2]. Five hundred thieves, having stolen goods and fleeing (from the village), realized that "no one is following us now" and wished to rest. When they were putting down their stolen bundles, they mistook the Elder for a tree stump (khāṇu) and placed all their goods on top of him. When those thieves were about to leave after resting, at the time they were picking up the first bundle placed, the Elder emerged from the attainment according to the pre-determined time limit. Seeing the Elder’s movement, they were terrified and cried out. The Elder said, "Do not be afraid, lay devotees (upāsakas), I am a monk." They came and paid homage, and through the faith inspired by the Elder, they went forth as monks and attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). In this story, the absence of injury to the Venerable Khāṇukoṇḍañña, who was pressed down by five hundred bundles, is psychic power through the diffusion of concentration (samādhivipphāra-iddhi).

Furthermore, the laywoman named Uttarā was the daughter of the Treasurer Puṇṇa. The courtesan Sirimā (whom Uttarā had hired to attend to her husband), out of jealousy, poured a cauldron of boiling oil over the head of Uttarā. At that very moment, Uttarā entered into the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (mettā-jhāna) [reflecting on Sirimā's kindness]. The oil rolled off like drops of water from a lotus leaf. This lack of burning by the boiling oil for the laywoman Uttarā is psychic power through the diffusion of concentration (samādhivipphāra-iddhi). The story should be understood in detail (as shown in the Dhammapada Commentary, Chapter 17, and the Aṅguttara Commentary, Etadagga Chapter).

Sāmāvatī was the chief queen of King Udena. The Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, desiring the position of chief queen for his (adopted) daughter Māgaṇḍiya [Note 3], placed a poisonous snake inside Sāmāvatī’s lute [10] and told King Udena, "Great King, Sāmāvatī wishes you dead, therefore..."

2. Although "attainment" (samāpatti) is mentioned generally, it should be taken as the attainment of the fourth jhāna or the attainment of cessation; taking it as the attainment of cessation is more appropriate.

When Māgaṇḍiyā's parents went to ordain, they left their daughter Māgaṇḍiyā with her uncle, the Brahmin Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya, as stated in the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* and other texts. Therefore, she is not a biological daughter but a niece. Thus, the term *dhītā* is used as a metaphorical derivative (*upamātaddhita*), meaning 'like a daughter.'

'She carries a poisonous snake inside the lute,' she slandered¹. King Utena, seeing the snake, became angry and, intending to kill Sāmāvatī, drew his bow and fitted a poisoned arrow. Sāmāvatī, along with her five hundred attendants, suffused King Utena with loving-kindness (*mettā*). The King stood trembling, unable to shoot the arrow or lower it. Then Queen Sāmāvatī asked, 'Are you weary, Great King?' 'Yes, I am weary,' the King replied. 'Then put down the bow,' said Sāmāvatī. The arrow fell right at the King's feet. Then Queen Sāmāvatī admonished him, 'Great King, one should not wrong those who are harmless.' In this story, King Utena's inability to release the arrow is the psychic power of the expansion of concentration (*samādhivipphāriddhi*) of the laywoman Sāmāvatī.

375. Furthermore, the power of accomplishment such as dwelling with the perception of the unrepulsive in the repulsive, etc., is called Noble Power (*ariyā iddhi*). In accordance with this, it is said:

'What is the Noble Power? Here, a monk, if he so desires, "May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive," he dwells perceiving the unrepulsive therein... [pe] ...he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.' (*Paṭisambhidāmagga* 3.17). This is called Noble Power because it occurs only to the Noble Ones (*ariyas*) who have attained mastery over the mind.

Note
1. In the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* (Appamāda-vagga, Sāmāvatī-vatthu) and the *Aṅguttara-aṭṭhakathā* (Etadagga-vagga, Khujjuttarā-Sāmāvatī-vatthu), it is mentioned that Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, who held a grudge against the Buddha, also held a grudge against Sāmāvatī, who was a devotee of the Buddha. She placed a snake inside the lute and slandered her.

Indeed, an Arahant monk endowed with this Noble Power, when faced with a repulsive, disagreeable object, dwells perceiving it as unrepulsive by suffusing it with loving-kindness¹ or by attending to it as elements (*dhātu*)². 

Note
1-2. Toward a disagreeable living being, he suffuses with loving-kindness or attends to them as elements. Toward a disagreeable object like excrement, he attends to it as elements. This should be applied accordingly. (Ṭīkā)

When faced with an unrepulsive, agreeable object, he dwells perceiving it as repulsive by suffusing it with the perception of foulness (*asubha*)¹ or by attending to it as impermanent (*anicca*)². Likewise, in both repulsive and unrepulsive objects, he dwells perceiving them as unrepulsive by suffusing them with that same loving-kindness or by attending to them as elements. And in both unrepulsive and repulsive objects, he dwells perceiving them as repulsive by suffusing them with that same perception of foulness or by attending to them as impermanent.

Note
1-2. Toward an agreeable object such as a relative or friend, he should attend to foulness such as hair, etc. Toward an agreeable physical phenomenon, he should attend to it as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and subject to change. In the word 'anicca' (impermanent), the word 'iti' implies 'and so on'; therefore, attending to it as suffering, etc., is also included in perceiving it as repulsive. (Based on the Ṭīkā)
3. Six-factored equanimity (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) means equanimity regarding the six sense objects, being neither attracted nor repelled. Since this mostly occurs in Noble Ones and Arahants, it is called Noble Power (*ariyā iddhi*). To a lesser extent, it can also occur in noble worldlings (*kalyāṇa-puthujjana*) who are practitioners of Insight (*vipassanā*).

By exercising the six-factored equanimity described in the manner beginning with 'Having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad,' he avoids both the repulsive and the unrepulsive and dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. For in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, this very meaning is analyzed: 'How does he dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive? Toward a disagreeable object, he either suffuses it with loving-kindness or applies the attention to elements,' and so on. This is called Noble Power because it occurs only to the Noble Ones who have attained mastery over the mind.

"One contemplates also by way of elements," and so on; the meaning already shown is analyzed in this manner. Because such accomplishment according to one's will should only occur for Noble Ones (Ariyas) who have attained mastery over the mind, it is called Ariya-iddhi (Noble Success). (6)

[11] 376. Furthermore, the success of birds and others, such as traveling through the air, is called Kammavipākaja-iddhi (success born of the ripening of kamma). In accordance with this, it is stated:

"What is success born of the ripening of kamma? That success of all birds, of all devas, of some [primordial] humans, and of some fallen beings (vinipātika) [is success born of the ripening of kamma]."

Note:
That six-factored equanimity (saḷaṅgupekkhā) indeed occurs. Therefore, in the Aṅguttara Commentary (Vol. 3, 52), it is stated: "One who has begun insight (vipassanā) is able to do that." Furthermore, in the Mūlapaṇṇāsa Commentary (Vol. 2, 130), it is stated: "But this bhikkhu, by the power of energy and the perfection of development, establishes his insight in the place of the six-factored equanimity of an Arahant; thus, insight itself is called six-factored equanimity." Regarding how six-factored equanimity occurs for a practitioner of insight, see the Manual of Insight (Vipassanā Shu Nee Kyan), Vol. 1, p. 265, etc.

(The power such as being able to travel through the air exists); this power is called Kammavipākaja-iddhi—thus says the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

Indeed, among these beings, the traveling through the air of all birds without the need for [supranormal] absorption (jhāna) or insight (vipassanā) [is Kammavipākaja-iddhi]. Likewise, the traveling through the air of all devas and some primordial humans without jhāna or insight [is Kammavipākaja-iddhi]. Similarly, the traveling through the air of certain fallen beings (vinipātika) known as earth-bound spirits, such as the yakkhiṇī who was the mother of Piyaṅkara, the yakkhiṇī who was the mother of Uttara, and those named Phussamittā and Dhammaguttā, is called Kammavipākaja-iddhi. (7)

377. Furthermore, the success of Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti) and others, such as traveling through the air, is called Puññavato-iddhi (success of one possessing merit). In accordance with this, it is stated:

"What is the success of one possessing merit? A Universal Monarch travels through the air with his fourfold army, including even his horse-grooms and ox-herds. The [prosperity] of the financier Jotika is the success of one possessing merit. The [prosperity] of the financier Jaṭila is the success of one possessing merit.

Note:
1. Insight accompanied by uplifting joy (ubbegā-pīti) can cause one to rise into the air; this indicates that even such insight is not present [in the case of birds, etc.]. (Explanation based on the Ṭīkā).

The [prosperity] of the financier Ghosita is the success of one possessing merit. The [prosperity] of the financier Meṇḍaka is the success of one possessing merit. The [extraordinary prosperity] of the Five of Great Merit is the success of one possessing merit"—thus says the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

In brief, however, the special distinction of accomplishment due to a store of merit that has reached maturity is called Puññavato-iddhi. To give a few examples among these persons of great merit: for the financier Jotika, a palace made of gems emerged, breaking through the earth; sixty-four wish-fulfilling trees (kapparukkha) also appeared. This distinction is the Puññavato-iddhi of that Jotika. For the financier Jaṭila, a golden mountain eighty cubits high emerged. For the financier Ghosita, although attempts were made to kill him in seven different places, his remaining free from illness and danger is Puññavato-iddhi. For the financier Meṇḍaka, the appearance of golden rams (known as 'goat-sheep') made of the seven gems in an area of one karīsa is Puññavato-iddhi.

The Five of Great Merit are: (1) the financier Meṇḍaka, (2) his wife Candapadumasirī, (3) their son the financier Dhanañjaya, (4) their daughter-in-law Sumanādevī, and (5) their slave named Puṇṇa. Among these five, when the financier Meṇḍaka, having washed his head, looked up at the sky, red hill-paddy fell from the sky and filled twelve thousand five hundred granaries. When his wife Candapadumasirī served the inhabitants of the entire Jambudīpa, even if she took only a small measure of rice [with her own hand], the food was never exhausted.

When the son Dhanañjaya took a bag of a thousand [coins] and gave to the inhabitants of the entire Jambudīpa, the coins were never exhausted.
12:
The daughter-in-law, Sumana Devī, [12] holding a single measure of grain, distributed it to all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, yet the grain was not exhausted. When the servant named Puṇṇa plowed with a single plow, fourteen furrows appeared—seven on this side and seven on that side. Such extraordinary accomplishment is the 'Success of the Meritorious' (Puññavato Iddhi) of those five people. (8)

378. Furthermore, the accomplishment of wizards (Vijjādharas) and others, such as traveling through the air, is called 'Success through Knowledge' (Vijjāmayā Iddhi). In accordance with this, it is stated:
'What is Success through Knowledge? Wizards, having recited mantras such as the Gandhārī science, travel through the air. In the trackless sky, they display elephant forces... they display various military arrays.' This is from the Paṭisambhidāmagga. (9)
Note 1: Vijjā (knowledge/mantra) + dhara (bearer) = Vijjādhara (one who possesses knowledge or mantras).
Note 2: Vijjā (knowledge) + maya (made of) + iddhi (success/power) = Vijjāmayā Iddhi (success accomplished through the power of knowledge).
Note 3: Since the term 'infantry' (pattimpi) will be mentioned later, the term 'elephant' (hatthimpi) here does not refer to a single elephant but to an elephant corps. The same applies to the translations of cavalry and chariot corps.

379. Furthermore, the accomplishment of various tasks through the right application of appropriate means is called 'Success through Right Application' (Sammāpayogapaccayā Iddhi). In accordance with this, it is stated:
'Through renunciation (nekkhamma), the abandoning of sensual desire is accomplished. Such accomplishment is "Success through Right Application" in the sense of being achieved through right application in various instances... Through the Path of Arahatship, the abandoning of all defilements is accomplished. Such accomplishment is "Success through Right Application" in the sense of being achieved through right application in various instances.' This is from the Paṭisambhidāmagga.
Note 1: In this context, 'nekkhamma' should be understood as non-greed (alobha) or wholesome mental states characterized by non-greed, which are the opposites of sensual desire. This is also known as a factor included in access concentration (upacāra-jhāna). Therefore, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Commentary (Part 1, p. 96), it is stated: 'The seven answers beginning with nekkhamma are shown by way of access concentration. Nekkhamma is non-greed, the opposite of sensual desire.' The Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā (Vol. 1, p. 78) also states: 'By nekkhamma means by wholesome mental states characterized by non-greed. Indeed, wholesome states that are the opposite of sensuality are intended here as nekkhamma.' Since the first jhāna and others will be mentioned separately later, the term nekkhamma in this context should not be translated as the first jhāna.

Through non-ill-will (metta), the opposite of malice, the abandoning of ill-will is accomplished. Such accomplishment is 'Success through Right Application' in the sense of being achieved through right application in various instances... Through the first jhāna, the abandoning of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) is accomplished... Through the Path of Arahatship, the abandoning of all defilements is accomplished. Such accomplishment is 'Success through Right Application' in the sense of being achieved through right application in various instances.' This is from the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

In the detailed explanation of this last type of success, the Pāḷi text is similar to the previous ones (such as Success through Concentration) by showing only the right application known as practice (paṭipatti). However, in the Commentary, it is stated that 'Success through Right Application' includes any craft or art such as military formations (wagon array [sakaṭabyūha], wheel array [cakkabyūha], lotus array [padumabyūha], etc.), any medical work (such as surgery), the learning of the three Vedas, the learning of the three Piṭakas, or even down to the specific results arising from plowing and sowing. (10)

Among these ten types of success (iddhi) just described, in the phrase 'for the varieties of success' (iddhividhāya), only 'Success through Determination' (Adhiṭṭhānā Iddhi) is explicitly mentioned. Nevertheless, in this context (of the benefits of higher knowledge), 'Success through Transformation' (Vikubbanā Iddhi) and 'Mind-made Success' (Manomayā Iddhi) should also be understood.

380. Iddhividhāya means for the parts of success, or for the varieties of success. 'Directs the mind, inclines the mind' means:
That monk, when the mind has become the basis for higher knowledge in the manner described, directs the preliminary-work mind (parikamma-citta) for the sake of attaining the varieties of success. He draws it away from the kasina object and sends it towards the varieties of success. 'Inclines the mind' means he makes the mind lean and slope towards the success to be attained. 'He' refers to that monk who has thus directed his mind. 'Aneka-vihitaṃ' means of many kinds, of various sorts. 'Iddhividhaṃ' means the parts of success (or the varieties of success). 'Paccanubhoti' means he experiences [13], 'he meets, realizes, reaches'—this is the meaning of 'experiences'. Now, regarding the [varieties of success]...

4- The meaning within these parentheses relies on the explanation of *iddhivikappāya* shown previously.

To show the state of being manifold (multiplicity), he said the words beginning with "*Ekopi hutvā*—Being one, he becomes many." In that passage, "Being one" means being one by nature prior to performing the feat of psychic power. "He becomes many" means that, wishing to walk to and fro, or to recite, or to ask a question in the presence of many, he becomes a hundred or a thousand. How does this possessor of psychic power become so? By fulfilling the four bases (*bhūmi*), the four feet (*pāda*), the eight steps (*pada*), and the sixteen roots (*mūla*) of psychic power (*iddhi*), and by resolving with knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

Notes:
1. In the phrase "Being one," the word "also/even" (*api*) implies the meaning "Being many, he becomes one" as well, as stated in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*).
2. The sub-commentary explains this as walking near or together with the many created (*nimmita*) persons.
3. Both *pāda* and *pada* mean "foot" or "cause." However, in this context, *pāda* refers to the collective general cause, while *pada* refers to the detailed causes within that collective. Therefore, the original Pali terms are shown as (pāda) cause and (pada) detailed cause.

381. Therein, the "four bases" should be understood as the four jhānas. Indeed, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, said:
"What are the four bases of psychic power? The first jhāna is the base born of seclusion (*vivekaja*) due to being secluded from the hindrances. The second jhāna is the base of rapture and pleasure (*pītisukha*), or the base born of rapture and pleasure. The third jhāna is the base of equanimity and pleasure (*upekkhāsukha*), or the base born of equanimity and pleasure. The fourth jhāna is the base of neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*adukkhamasukha*), or the base born of equanimity which is neither pain nor pleasure. These four are the bases of psychic power; these bases lead to the attainment of psychic power, to the repeated attainment of psychic power, to the various transformations of psychic power, to the various scopes of psychic power, to mastery in psychic power, and to intrepidity in psychic power."

Notes:
1. Translated in accordance with the sub-commentary which explains *pītisukhabhūtā* as "being rapture and pleasure." It should be understood that this is said because rapture and pleasure are predominant in the second jhāna. The latter meaning follows the sub-commentary's explanation as *pītisukhasañjātañca*.
2. In the term *upekkhāsukha*, equanimity refers to *tatramajjhattatā-upekkhā*.
3. Here, equanimity refers to the feeling (*vedanā*).

To explain further: Among these four jhānas, the first three jhānas are known as "preparatory bases" (*sambhārabhūmi*) because the practitioner, by pervading with rapture and pleasure, enters the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness, and having a body that is light, soft, and wieldy, attains psychic power. The fourth jhāna, however, is the "natural base" (*pakatibhūmi*) for the attainment of psychic power.

382. The four bases of power (*iddhipāda*) should be understood as the four feet (*pāda*). Indeed:
"What are the four feet of psychic power? Here, a bhikkhu develops the base of power endowed with concentration due to desire (*chanda*) and volitional formations of striving (*padhānasaṅkhāra*). ...energy (*viriya*)... ...mind (*citta*)... ...investigation (*vīmaṃsā*)... These four are the feet of psychic power; these feet lead to the attainment of psychic power... to intrepidity in psychic power."

Notes:
1. The first three jhānas... should be understood as preparatory bases.
2. (The possessor of power)... having entered... having become... attains psychic power.
3. Because of that (attainment)... because of occurring for the sake of obtaining... take it as a connected sequence.

To explain further: In this text, concentration that has desire as its cause, or where desire is predominant, is called "concentration due to desire" (*chandasamādhi*). This is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the desire to act (*kattukamyatā-chanda*) the dominant factor. Volitional formations that are the principal ones are "volitional formations of striving" (*padhānasaṅkhāra*). This is a designation for the right effort (*sammappadhāna-viriya*) that accomplishes the four functions. "Endowed with" means occurring together with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving. "Base of power" (*iddhipāda*): it is called *iddhi* in the sense of "succeeding" (*ijjhana*), which is a synonym for "accomplishment" (*nipphatti*). Alternatively, it is called *iddhi* because it is the cause of growth and excellence for beings.

Notes:
1. Two ways of explaining *chandasamādhi*: concentration obtained through effort relying on desire, or concentration associated with predominant desire (Sub-commentary).
2. *Padhāna* refers to the four right efforts (*sammappadhāna-viriya*) that accomplish the four functions; *saṅkhāra* refers to the volitional effort. It is used in the plural because it refers to the four right efforts.
3. *Nipphatti* (accomplishment) and *ijjhana* (succeeding) have the same meaning.

(Alternatively) The collection of the remaining mental factors and consciousness, which act as the foundation (*pāda*) for the concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving associated with the higher-knowledge mind (*abhiññā-citta*), which are called *iddhi* because they are the cause of growth and excellence, is called the "base of power" (*iddhipāda*). Indeed...
14:
Through this Dhamma, beings prosper and attain nobility; because of this figurative expression, or because they are the basis (pāda) in the sense of being the foundation for the concentration of intention and volitional efforts (chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhāra) which are associated with the supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) that has reached the state of being reckoned as 'iddhi' (success/power)—the remaining group of consciousness (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) is the meaning of 'iddhipāda'. This is very difficult to understand. The meaning is: concentration characterized by predominant intention and the energy called volitional effort (padhānasaṅkhāra) are called 'iddhi' because they constitute completion or accomplishment. Alternatively, they are called 'iddhi' because they are the cause of growth and nobility for beings. The group of consciousness and mental factors associated with that concentration and energy is called 'pāda' because it is the supporting cause for that concentration and energy. Therefore, 'iddhipāda' means the group of associated consciousness and mental factors which is the supporting cause for the concentration characterized by predominant intention and the energy called volitional effort, which are the means of accomplishment or the cause of growth and nobility.

This statement has been taught in the Vibhaṅga: "The base of power (iddhipāda) is the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness of one who has become thus (attained such success)."

Alternatively, it is called 'pāda' because it is the means of reaching [a goal] (1). That which is the means of reaching accomplishment, or the cause of accomplishment, is called 'iddhipāda' (2). This is a designation for intention (chanda) and the others. In accordance with this, it was taught:

"Monks, if a bhikkhu, depending on intention (chanda), gains concentration, gains one-pointedness of mind, this is called concentration of intention. He generates desire, makes effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states... [etc.]... these are called volitional efforts (padhānasaṅkhāra). Thus, this intention, this concentration of intention, and these volitional efforts—this, monks, is called the base of power endowed with concentration of intention and volitional effort (chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgata iddhipāda)." The meaning of the remaining bases of power should be understood in the same way.

Notes:
1. Translated using an easy-to-understand method.
2. The means of reaching accomplishment is the same as the cause of accomplishment; therefore, both meanings are essentially the same.

383. The eight factors starting with intention (chanda) should be understood as the "eight steps (pada)." Indeed, it was taught: "What are the eight steps for power (iddhi)? If a bhikkhu, depending on intention, gains concentration, gains one-pointedness of mind: intention is not concentration, concentration is not intention. Intention is one thing, concentration is another. If a bhikkhu, depending on energy... depending on consciousness... depending on investigation (vīmaṃsā), gains concentration, gains one-pointedness of mind: investigation is not concentration, concentration is not investigation. Investigation is one thing, concentration is another. These eight steps for power lead to the attainment of power... to confidence in power."

Indeed, among these, the intention—the desire to produce accomplishment or power—leads to the attainment of power only when it is combined with concentration. The same applies to energy and the others. Therefore, it should be understood that these eight steps (pada) were taught.

384. Regarding the "sixteen roots (mūla)," the imperturbability (āneñjata) of the mind should be understood through sixteen aspects. Indeed, it was taught: "How many are the roots of power? There are sixteen roots: 

(1) The mind that is not sinking or shrinking does not waver due to sloth; therefore, it is called imperturbable (āneñja) (1). 
(2) The mind that is not elated or distracted does not waver due to restlessness; therefore, it is called imperturbable (2). 
(3) The mind that is not leaning (anabhinata) by way of attachment does not waver due to lust (rāga); therefore, it is called imperturbable (3). 
(4) The mind that is not turning away (anapanata) (not averting the face in hatred) does not waver due to ill-will (byāpāda); therefore, it is called imperturbable (4). 
(5) The mind that is not dependent on the notion of a 'self' does not waver due to wrong view (diṭṭhi); therefore, it is called imperturbable (5). 
(6) The mind that is not bound by delight and attachment does not waver due to desire and lust (chandarāga); therefore, it is called imperturbable (6). 
(7) The mind that is liberated from sensual desire does not waver due to sensual lust; therefore, it is called imperturbable (7). 
(8) The mind that is detached from defilements does not waver due to defilements (kilesa); therefore, it is called imperturbable (8). 
(9) The mind that has been made boundless regarding defilements (4) does not waver due to the boundaries of defilements; therefore, it is called imperturbable (9). 
(10) The mind that has attained oneness, not relying on the companionship of defilements, does not waver due to various defilements; therefore, it is called imperturbable (10). 
(11) The mind supported by faith (saddhā) does not waver due to lack of faith; therefore, it is called imperturbable (11). 
(12) The mind supported by energy (viriya) does not waver due to laziness; therefore, it is called imperturbable (12). 
(13) The mind supported by mindfulness (sati) does not waver due to forgetfulness; therefore, it is called imperturbable (13).

Notes:
1. It means the mind that is not sinking or shrinking is called imperturbable because it does not waver.
2. This is the meaning of the term 'anabhinata'. Abhisanga (attachment) + nata (leaning) + ana (not) = anabhinata (a mind not leaning by way of attachment). Alternatively, abhi (excessive) + nata (leaning) + ana (not) = anabhinata (a mind that does not lean excessively).
3. This is the meaning of the term 'anapanata'. It could also be translated as 'not turning away excessively'.
4. If defiled thoughts arise in between meditative thoughts, it is said to have the 'boundary of defilements'. This refers to a mind developed so that defiled thoughts cannot intervene.
15:
Therefore, it is called 'unperturbed' (13). The mind supported by concentration is not perturbed by agitation; therefore, it is called 'unperturbed' (14). The mind supported by wisdom is not perturbed by ignorance (avijjā); therefore, it is called 'unperturbed' (15). The mind accompanied by the light of wisdom (i.e., knowing clearly and distinctly) is not perturbed by the darkness of ignorance; therefore, it is called 'unperturbed' (16). These sixteen are the roots of psychic power (iddhi); these roots lead to the attainment of psychic power... to courage in the exercise of psychic power."

Note:
1. Although it appears identical to the first 'unperturbed' (āneñja), it is stated here to show imperturbability through the power of energy (vīriya). In number (14), it is stated again to show imperturbability through the power of concentration (samādhi).

To explain further: This meaning (that the fourth jhāna mind is not perturbed by laziness, etc.) is already established by the words "When the mind is thus concentrated" (as shown on page 2). However, it is stated again to show the ground (bhūmi), footing (pāda), step (pada), and root (mūla) of the psychic powers of the first jhāna, etc. Alternatively, the former method is the one found in the Suttas, while this method is from the Paṭisambhidāmagga. Thus, it is repeated for the sake of non-confusion in both places.

385. "Resolving by knowledge": This means that the monk, having fulfilled these qualities which are the ground, footing, and step of psychic power, enters the basic jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) for direct knowledge. Emerging from it, if he wishes for a hundred, he performs the preliminary work (parikamma) by thinking, "May I be a hundred, may I be a hundred." Then he re-enters the basic jhāna, emerges, and resolves. Simultaneously with the resolution mind, he becomes a hundred. The same applies to a thousand, etc. If it does not succeed as described, he should perform the preliminary work again, enter the jhāna a second time, emerge, and resolve. Indeed, it is stated in the Saṃyutta Commentary that it is proper to enter once or twice. In this process, the basic jhāna mind has the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) as its object. The preliminary minds have the hundred or thousand as their object, specifically by way of appearance (color), not by way of mere concept (paññatti). The resolution mind likewise has the hundred or thousand as its object. That resolution mind, like the absorption mind (appanā) mentioned earlier, arises only once immediately after the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) mind, associated with the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere.

386. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "Being naturally one, he adverts to many—a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand. Having adverted, he resolves by knowledge: 'May I be many.' He becomes many, just like the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka." In this passage, "adverts" is said by way of preliminary work. "Resolving by knowledge" is said by way of the knowledge of direct-knowledge (abhiññā-ñāṇa). Therefore, he adverts to many (with preliminary minds); at the end of those preliminary minds, he enters (the basic jhāna); emerging from that attainment, he adverts again, "May I be many," and after the three or four preceding minds that arise after that adverting mind, he resolves with a single moment of direct-knowledge called "resolution" (adhiṭṭhāna) by way of completion. This is how the meaning in the Paṭisambhidāmagga should be understood.

The phrase "just like the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka" is said to provide a personal witness to the manifestation of many bodies. The story is as follows: Those two brothers were named Panthaka (Road) because they were born on the road while traveling. The elder was named Mahāpanthaka. He became a monk and attained Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). After becoming an Arahant, he ordained his younger brother, Cūḷapanthaka.
16:
Just as a fragrant red lotus (kokanada) might be in full bloom in the early morning with its fragrance unfaded, behold the resplendent Angīrasa, shining like the sun in the sky.

[Note 1: This refers to the states of consciousness known as preliminary (parikamma), access (upacāra), conformity (anuloma), and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). For a person of sharp wisdom, the supernormal knowledge (abhiññā) consciousness arises after three moments of access, conformity, and change-of-lineage.]

[Note 2: Connect this as 'by the supernormal knowledge named...']

He taught him this verse. However, Cūḷapanthaka was unable to master it even in four months. Then, the Elder Mahāpanthaka, saying, "You are an unfit person (abhabba) in this Dispensation," expelled him from the monastery.

At that time, the Elder Mahāpanthaka was the meal-allocator (bhattuddesaka). The physician Jīvaka approached the Elder and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept a meal at our house tomorrow for the Blessed One and five hundred monks." The Elder accepted for the other monks, excluding Cūḷapanthaka.

[Note 1: Regarding 'unfit' (abhabba)—the Commentary explains: This Dispensation has practice (paṭipatti) as its essence, and practice is rooted in learning (pariyatti). You are unable to master the learning; therefore, you are an 'unfit' person who cannot attain the Path.]

Cūḷapanthaka stood at the gateway and wept. The Blessed One, seeing him with his divine eye, approached him and asked, "Why are you weeping?" Cūḷapanthaka explained the situation. Then the Blessed One comforted him, saying, "Bhikkhu, do not grieve. No one is called 'unfit' in my Dispensation merely because they cannot recite." Taking him by the arm, the Buddha entered the monastery, miraculously created a piece of rough cloth, and gave it to him, saying, "Here, monk, rub this cloth and recite repeatedly: 'Rajoharaṇaṃ, rajoharaṇaṃ' (Removal of impurity, removal of impurity)."

[Note 1: No one is truly 'unfit' because the practice of insight (vipassanā-dhura) is the primary essential factor.]

[Note 2: He is addressed as 'Bhikkhu' (monk) using the conventional term for a renunciant (even though he was a novice). Alternatively, he is called 'Bhikkhu' in anticipation of his future monkhood, just as the Bodhisatta is sometimes referred to as 'the Buddha' when he was traveling to Rājagaha.]

As he followed these instructions, the cloth became soiled and dark. Then Cūḷapanthaka realized: "The cloth was pure; there was no fault in it. Indeed, this fault belongs only to this body." Having gained this perception, he applied knowledge to the five aggregates, developed insight, and reached the vicinity of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) knowledge. Then the Blessed One, emitting a radiance, spoke these verses:

Lust is called dust, but actual dust is not.
"Dust" is a designation for lust.
Having abandoned this dust, the wise
Dwell in the Dispensation of the One Free from Dust.
17:
Note: Having attained the perception of foulness and the perception of impermanence, and having discerned mind and matter, one applies knowledge to the five aggregates. Developing insight through the sequence beginning with the knowledge of comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana-ñāṇa), one brings insight to the vicinity of conformity (anuloma) and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) through the sequence beginning with the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa). (Sub-commentary)

[17] Hatred is a stain, but dust is not called a stain;
'Stain' is a designation for hatred.
Having abandoned this stain, the wise
Dwell in the teaching of the One free from stains.

'Dosa'—hatred or ill-will—is a stain or impurity. 'Reṇu'—fine dust—is not called a stain. This name 'stain' (raja) is a designation for hatred. The wise, having abandoned this stain of hatred, dwell in the teaching of the Buddha, who is free from the stain of defilements.

Delusion is a stain, but dust is not called a stain;
'Stain' is a designation for delusion.
Having abandoned this stain, the wise
Dwell in the teaching of the One free from stains.

'Moha'—delusion or ignorance—is a stain or impurity. Fine dust is not called a stain. This name 'stain' is a designation for delusion. The wise, having abandoned this stain of delusion, dwell in the teaching of the Buddha, who is free from the stain of defilements.

At the conclusion of these three verses, the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka attained the nine supramundane states, accompanied by the four analytical insights and the six higher powers, as if they were placed right into his hands.

On the second day, the Teacher went to the house of the physician Jīvaka together with the community of monks. Then, at the conclusion of the water-offering, when the rice gruel was being offered, he covered his bowl with his hand. Jīvaka asked, "Why, Bhante?" The Teacher replied, "There is still one monk at the monastery." Jīvaka sent a man, saying, "Go, invite that venerable one and return quickly."

After the Blessed One had departed from the monastery—
The Venerable Cūḷapanthaka, having created a thousand versions of himself, sat in the delightful mango grove until the time for the meal was announced.

Then that man went and saw the monastery grounds glowing uniformly with the color of saffron robes. He returned and said, "Bhante, the monastery is full of monks; I do not know which one is that venerable one." Then the Blessed One told him, "Go, grab the hem of the robe of the monk you see first, and say, 'The Teacher calls for you,' and bring him here." The man went and grabbed the hem of the robe of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka himself. At that very moment, all the created monks vanished. The Elder dismissed the man, saying, "You may go," and after attending to his bodily needs such as washing his face, he arrived first and sat in the seat designated for him. It is in reference to this that it was said, "Just like the Venerable Cūḷapanthaka."

In such creation, if they are created without specific distinction, the many created forms are exactly like the possessor of psychic power. Whatever the possessor of psychic power does—whether in postures like sitting or standing, or in actions like speaking or remaining silent—they do the same. However, if he wishes to make them of various appearances,
18:
Some appear to be in their youth, some in middle age, and some in the final stage of life. [18] Some appear with long hair,

Note 1: This is a fluent Burmese translation of the term 'nimmitattā'; literally, it means 'due to the state of being created.' Similar translations will follow.
Note 2: This is also a fluent Burmese translation. Literally, it means 'if one desires to perform various modes.'

some with half-shaved heads, some with fully shaved heads, some with mixed black and white hair, some with half-red robes, and some with pale yellow robes. If one wishes to make them perform activities such as clear recitation of words (padabhāṇa), preaching the Dhamma (dhammakathā), melodious chanting (sarabhañña), asking and answering questions, boiling dye, sewing robes, washing robes, and so forth, or to make them appear in various other ways—the possessor of psychic power, having emerged from the foundation jhāna (pādakajjhāna), performs the preliminary preparation (parikamma) in this manner: 'Let this many monks be of the first age,' and so on. Then, having entered the jhāna again and emerged, he should resolve (adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ). Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, the created monks appear exactly in the various ways desired. This concludes one part.

The same method applies to such feats as 'having been many, he becomes one' and so forth.

Note 1: Reciting the Pali clearly to make the meaning known through the power of words is called 'padabhāṇa.' (Commentary)
Note 2: Chanting Suttas and so on with a pleasant voice to inspire devotion is called 'sarabhañña.' (Commentary)
Note 3: (1) First, entering the foundation jhāna of supernormal knowledge; (2) emerging from that jhāna and making a preliminary preparation with sense-sphere mind for the desired creation; (3) entering the foundation jhāna of supernormal knowledge again; (4) emerging from that jhāna and resolving with the fourth jhāna supernormal knowledge mind (preceded by sense-sphere minds like adverting, preliminary, access, and change-of-lineage); (5) the completion of the desired creation simultaneously with that mind of resolution. This sequence applies to all creations by resolution.

The following is a special point: If this monk, having created many as described, then thinks, 'I will walk back and forth alone, I will recite alone, I will ask questions alone,' or if, out of fewness of wishes (appicchatā), he thinks, 'This monastery has few monks; if people come and see so many identical monks, they will wonder where they came from and realize it is the Elder's psychic power,' and thus desires to become one again before the resolved time expires—he should enter the foundation jhāna, emerge, perform the preliminary preparation saying 'May I be one,' enter the foundation jhāna again, emerge, and resolve 'May I be one.' Simultaneously with the mind of resolution, he becomes one. If he does not do this, he will naturally become one when the determined time expires.

387. In the phrase 'manifestation and disappearance' (āvibhāvaṃ tirobhāvaṃ), he makes manifestation and he makes disappearance.

Note 1: This Pali is from the Iddhividha-ñāṇa section of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, Sīlakkhandhavagga-pāḷi. The full Pali will be cited in later explanations for easy reference.

This is the intended meaning. Indeed, regarding this meaning, it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: 'Manifestation means it is not obstructed by anything, not hidden, open, and evident. Disappearance means it is obstructed by something, hidden, covered, and closed.' Among these two, if this possessor of psychic power wishes to make something manifest, he turns darkness into light, or makes the hidden open, or makes the unmanifest manifest.

Note: (a) 'When the mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it to the modes of psychic power. He enjoys various modes of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one.' (b) 'Manifestation and disappearance.' (c) 'He goes unhindered through walls, enclosures, and mountains as if through space.' (d) 'He dives in and out of the earth as if in water.' (e) 'He walks on water without sinking as if on earth.' (f) 'He travels through the air cross-legged like a winged bird.' (g) 'He touches and strokes with his hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful.' (h) 'He wields mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world.' (Sīlakkhandhavagga-pāḷi).

Paragraph (a) from the above Pali was cited and explained at the beginning of this description. The subsequent paragraphs starting from (c) will be cited and explained in order. Now, paragraph (b) is cited to be explained as follows:

How? If this possessor of psychic power wishes to make himself or another visible, even if hidden or far away, he emerges from the foundation jhāna, adverts, and performs the preliminary preparation: 'Let this dark place become full of light,' or 'Let this hidden thing be opened,' or 'Let this unmanifest thing become manifest.' Then, he resolves in the same manner as previously described.
19:
Simultaneously with the mind of resolve, it happens exactly as resolved. Even though they are far away, others see [him], and he himself sees if he wishes to see.

[19] 388. Who has previously performed this miracle?¹ The Blessed One has performed it. As for how he performed it: The Blessed One, having been invited by Cūḷasubhaddā (the daughter of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika), [traveled] from the city of Sāvatthī to the city of Sāketa, which was seven leagues (yojanas) away, using five hundred palatial mansions (flying vehicles) created by the deity Vissakamma.² At that time, he made a resolve so that the people of Sāketa could see the people of Sāvatthī, and the people of Sāvatthī could see the people of Sāketa. Having descended in the middle of Sāketa, he split the earth in two, making it visible as far as Avīci [hell]; he also parted the sky in two,¹ making it visible as far as the Brahma world.

Notes
၁- Paṭi (opposite) + hara (to carry/remove) = paṭihara -> pāṭihāriya (an act that removes opposition). This pāṭihāriya is translated into Burmese as 'pyatiha'. There are three types of such miracles: (1) Iddhi-pāṭihāriya (miracle of psychic power), (2) Ādesanā-pāṭihāriya (miracle of mind-reading), (3) Anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya (miracle of instruction). Here, since it refers to the first type, the word pāṭihāriya is translated as 'miracle of psychic power'.
၂- Vissa (all) + kamma (action/work) = Vissakamma (one who can create or perform all kinds of tasks).

Furthermore, this meaning of making things clearly visible should also be illustrated by the descent from the celestial realm. It is said that the Blessed One, after performing the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) and liberating eighty-four thousand beings from the bonds of defilements, reflected, "Where did the Buddhas of the past go after performing the Twin Miracle?" and saw that they went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Having seen this, he stepped on the surface of the earth with one foot, placed the second foot on Mount Yugandhara, then lifted the first foot and stepped on the summit of Mount Sineru. There, he entered the rains retreat (vassa) on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat¹ in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven on the summit of Mount Sineru and began teaching the Abhidhamma discourse to the deities who had gathered from ten thousand world systems, starting from the beginning.

Notes
၁- If the lower celestial mansions situated in the sky, which obstruct the higher mansions, are removed, it is said that the sky, the location of those lower mansions, is removed or parted. With this intention, it is said in the Visuddhimagga, 'parting the sky in two.' (Sub-commentary) The reason people today do not see celestial mansions is not because other mansions are hiding them, but because they are subtle forms (rūpa) that cannot be seen with human eyes. Therefore, the resolve made so that humans can see those subtle objects is described as if splitting the sky; this is how it should be understood.

At the time for the morning alms round, he created a created Buddha-image (nimmitabuddha). That created Buddha continued to teach the Abhidhamma (from where the teaching had reached). The (living) Blessed One (having descended to this earth in the Himalayan region) used the Nagalatā dragon-creeper tooth-stick, washed his face at Lake Anotatta, received alms-food in the region of Uttarakuru (the Northern Continent),² and partook of the meal near Lake Anotatta.

Notes
၁- In the present age, although the world has been repeatedly explored by airplanes and spacecraft, Mount Sineru has not been found.
