Therefore, since Mount Sineru is the abode of deities, just as deities cannot be seen with human eyes, it is appropriate to consider it as a collection of forms (rūpa) so subtle and clear that they cannot be seen by human eyes. The seven surrounding mountain ranges should be understood in the same way.
၂- Here, the first meaning is the literal grammatical meaning of the word Uttarakurūsu, which is in the plural. In words denoting provinces (janapada) like Kāsi, Kosala, including Kuru, there is a grammatical rule to use the plural in reference to the kings who own those provinces.

The Venerable Sāriputta went there and paid homage to the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave the method (naya) to the Elder, saying, "Today, I have taught this much Dhamma." In this way, he taught the Abhidhamma discourse continuously for three months. Hearing that Dhamma, eighty crores of deities and Brahmas attained the realization of the Four Noble Truths.

The assembly of people, twelve leagues in diameter, who had gathered at the site of the Twin Miracle, remained there, having set up camp, intending to leave only after seeing the Blessed One.
20:
This translation is rendered precisely so that it may be taken exactly as stated in that instruction. The second meaning, indicated by 'or' (vā), is from the Pyay Recension Nissaya. That meaning is consistent with the introductory words of the Atthasālinī, which state 'gacchati'—he goes to the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru). In this context, if it were in the singular as 'Uttarakurusmiṃ', it would be perfectly aligned with that Atthasālinī introduction. It is mentioned in the scriptures that morning time in what was formerly called Jambudīpa (now India) is evening time in the Northern Continent called Uttarakuru. Nowadays, it is very clear from radio broadcasts that when it is morning in India, it is evening in the continent of America. Therefore, there is reason to consider that the Northern Continent called Uttarakuru, where the Buddha went for alms at that time, might be the continent of America.

Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika, the younger brother of the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, supported that entire multitude of people with all necessary provisions. The gathered people, wishing to know 'Where is the Blessed One?', requested and asked the Venerable Anuruddha. The Venerable Anuruddha, having radiated light and looking with his divine eye, saw the Blessed One spending the rains retreat in that Tāvatiṃsa heaven and informed them.

Those people requested the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna to pay homage to the Blessed One on their behalf. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, in the very midst of the assembly, dove into the great earth, pierced through Mount Sineru, and [20] emerged right at the feet of the Blessed One. While bowing at the Blessed One's feet, he said, 'Venerable Sir, the inhabitants of Jambudīpa say they will only return to their homes after they have paid homage to and seen the Blessed One's feet.'

The Blessed One asked, 'Moggallāna, where is your elder brother, Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, staying now?' 'He is staying in the city of Saṅkassa, Venerable Sir,' he replied. 'Moggallāna, let those who wish to see me go to the city of Saṅkassa tomorrow. Tomorrow, on the Uposatha day of the Mahāpavāraṇā full moon at the end of the rains, I shall descend to the city of Saṅkassa,' the Buddha declared. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied, 'Very well, Venerable Sir,' paid homage to the Blessed One, and descended by the same path he had come, reaching the presence of the people. During his going and coming, he made a determination (adhiṭṭhāna) so that the people could see him. This was the first manifest miracle of psychic power performed by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in this context. (Note 1)

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having returned as described, reported the matter as told by the Blessed One and said, 'Do not think it is far; depart only after you have had your morning meal.' The Blessed One informed Sakka, the King of Devas, 'Great King, tomorrow I shall go to the world of men.' The King of Devas commanded Vissakamma, 'Dear friend, tomorrow the Blessed One wishes to go to the world of men; create three flights of stairs: one of gold, one of silver, and one of gems.' He did as commanded. On the second day, the Blessed One, standing on the summit of Mount Sineru, looked towards the eastern world-element. Thousands of world-systems opened up and appeared like a single courtyard. Just as it was clear towards the east, so too towards the west, the north, and the south—he saw everything opened up. He saw downwards as far as Avīci and upwards as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm. (Note 2)

Note 1: This is a translation for smooth Burmese; a literal translation would be: 'In this matter, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna first performed this manifest miracle of psychic power.'
Note 2: According to this view, it must be taken that there are no mansions in the Formless Realms (Arūpa-bhūmi).

On that day, it is said that the miracle known as Loka-vivaraṇa (Opening of the Worlds), which makes manifest many hundreds of thousands of world-systems and all beings, took place. Humans saw the devas, and devas saw the humans. In seeing thus, humans did not have to look up, nor did devas have to look down; all saw each other face-to-face right before them. The Blessed One descended by the central stairway made of gems. The devas of the six sense-sphere heavens descended by the golden stairway on the left. The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas and Mahābrahma (Note 3) descended by the silver stairway on the right. The King of Devas carried the bowl and robes. Mahābrahma held the three-yojana white parasol. Suyama held the yak-tail fan. Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandharvas, taking the Beluva-paṇḍu lute which was three gāvutas in size, descended making offerings to the Tathāgata. On that day, there was no being who, having seen the Blessed One, did not give rise to a longing for Buddhahood. This was the manifest miracle performed by the Blessed One in this context.

Note 3: The sub-commentary explains this as Sahampati Brahma. Sahampati Brahma was a monk named Sahaka during the time of Kassapa Buddha; having attained the first jhāna, he was reborn in the first jhāna realm with a lifespan of an entire aeon, as stated in the commentaries to the Pāsarāsi Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, etc. The Sīlakkhandhavagga Pāḷi and others state that the first Brahma to appear at the beginning of an aeon is called Mahābrahma. According to the sense of those commentaries and the Pāḷi, since Sahampati Brahma was not the Brahma who appeared at the beginning of the aeon, the mention of 'Mahābrahma' here refers to Sahampati himself.
21:
The deity king Suyama, holding a yak-tail fan, and the Gandhabba deity named Pañcasikha, holding the lute named Beluvapaṇḍu—which is about three gāvutas in size and has a pale yellow color like a ripe wood-apple—descended while making offerings to the Blessed One. On that day, there was no being who, upon seeing the Blessed One, did not develop a desire to become a Buddha. This is the manifest miracle created by the Blessed One in this instance.

[21] To show another way: Elder Dhammadinna, a resident of Talangara in the island of Tambapaṇṇi, was sitting on the courtyard of the shrine at Tissamahāvihāra. While preaching the Apaṇṇaka Sutta, which begins with, "Monks, a monk possessed of three qualities has entered upon the sure way (apaṇṇaka-paṭipadā)," he directed his fan downwards, and it became a single open space as far as Avīci. Then he directed the fan upwards, and it became a single open space as far as the Brahma world. The Elder Dhammadinna—

Note: There is a point to consider whether this refers to one or many. In the Dhammapada Commentary, regarding this instance of descending from Tāvatiṃsa, it is stated in the plural as "Mahābrahmāno" (Great Brahmas).

1. This is the meaning of "Api ca." In this method, it is not to show the possessor of psychic power, but only to show the hell realms and heavenly realms.

—preached the Dhamma by threatening with the terrors of hell and by enticing with the bliss of heaven. Some became Stream-enterers, some became Once-returners, Non-returners, or Arahants. Here ends one section.

389. If one wishes to perform disappearance (tirobhāva), one makes light into darkness, makes the unhidden hidden, or makes the manifest unmanifest. How? If this possessor of psychic power wishes to make himself or another invisible, even if they are unhidden or standing nearby, he emerges from the basic jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) and reflects, "Let this place of light become a place of darkness," or "Let this unhidden thing become hidden," or "Let this manifest thing become unmanifest." Having performed the preparatory work (parikamma), he resolves (adhiṭṭhāti) in the manner already described. Simultaneous with the mind of resolution, it becomes exactly as resolved. Others, even if standing nearby, do not see him. The possessor of psychic power, if he himself does not wish to see, does not see others either.

390. Who has performed this miracle before? The Blessed One has performed it. As for how he performed it: the Blessed One made the noble youth Yasa, who was sitting nearby, invisible so that his father could not see him.

Note: 1. According to the sequence of the Blessed One's teaching, it should be understood that after inclining the mind toward heavenly pleasures with the "Talk on Heaven" (sagga-kathā), he then teaches the faults of sensual pleasures, etc., to enable the attainment of the Paths and Fruits. It is not merely to remain attached to heavenly pleasures. (Shown based on the Ṭīkā).

Similarly, having gone to meet King Mahākappina for a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas, he established the King in the Fruit of Non-returning and his thousand ministers in the Fruit of Stream-entry. When Queen Anojā, accompanied by a thousand women, arrived following the King's path and sat nearby, the Blessed One made the King and his retinue invisible to her. When Queen Anojā asked, "Venerable Sir, have you seen the King?", he asked, "What do you think, Anojā? Is it better for you to seek the King, or to seek yourself?" She replied, "It is better to seek myself, Venerable Sir." To the Queen who was sitting respectfully, he preached the Dhamma so that she and her thousand women were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. The ministers were established in the Fruit of Non-returning, and King Mahākappina was established in the Fruit of Arahantship. Furthermore, [22] Elder Mahinda, who on the day of his arrival in the island of Tambapaṇṇi made a resolution so that King Devānampiyatissa could not see the other persons who came with him, also performed this miracle of making others invisible.
22:
Note: 1. The sentences have been split in the translation to avoid being overly long in Burmese. If not split, it would read: "...preached the Dhamma so that Queen Anojā and her thousand women were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry, the ministers in the Fruit of Non-returning, and King Mahākappina in the Fruit of Arahantship."

391. To show another way: every miracle where the possessor of psychic power is manifest is called manifestation (āvibhāva). A miracle where the possessor of psychic power is not manifest is called disappearance (tirobhāva). There, in the miracle of manifestation, both the psychic power achieved and the possessor of the power are visible. This is to be illustrated by the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya). Indeed, regarding that Twin Miracle, it is said: "Here, the Tathāgata performs the Twin Miracle, which is not shared with disciples. A mass of fire proceeds from the upper part of his body, and a stream of water proceeds from the lower part of his body." Thus, both were visible. In the miracle of disappearance, only the psychic power achieved is visible, not the possessor of the power. This is to be illustrated by the Mahaka Sutta and the Brahmanimantanika Sutta. Indeed, in those suttas, only the psychic power created by the Venerable Mahaka and the Blessed One was visible, not the possessors of the power. This statement is—

"Sitting to one side, Citta the householder said to the Venerable Mahaka: 'It would be good, Venerable Sir, if the Noble Mahaka would show me a miracle of psychic power surpassing human states.' 'In that case, householder, spread your upper robe on the porch and scatter a bundle of grass on it.' 'Yes, Venerable Sir,' Citta the householder replied to the Venerable Mahaka, spread his upper robe on the porch, and scattered a bundle of grass on it. Then the Venerable Mahaka entered the monastery and performed such a feat of psychic power that a flame came out through the keyhole and the gap between the door-leaves and burnt the grass, but did not burn the upper robe."

Note: 1. Connect this with "...is in accordance with the statement that it did not burn..." and "...is in accordance with what was preached..."

This is in accordance with that statement.

Furthermore:

"Monks, then I performed such a feat of psychic power that Baka Brahma, his retinue, and the Brahmas of his assembly would hear my voice but would not see me. Having disappeared, I spoke this verse:

[23] 'Having seen the danger in existence,
And for those seeking the end of existence,
I did not praise any existence,
Nor did I cling to delight.'

(O Marisas—you Brahmas who are seeking to see me), I, having seen the danger such as aging, sickness, and death within the round of existence, and having seen the repeated becoming of those who seek the end of existence but are not yet free from attachment—

Note: 1. This is the meaning of the word 'antaradhito' (having disappeared); connect this word with the phrase 'spoke this verse.'

—having seen this, I did not praise any existence whatsoever..."
23:
“'Having seen the danger in existence, and for those seeking non-existence, I did not praise any existence, nor did I cling to the delight [of craving].' (M. Ni. 1.504)

392. In the passage, 'He goes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, through mountains, as if through space,' the term 'tirokuṭṭaṃ' means to the other side of the wall, or the part beyond the wall. This same method applies to the other terms. 'Kuṭṭa' is a designation for the wall of a house. 'Pākāra' refers to the surrounding enclosure wall of a house, a monastery, a village, and so on. 'Pabbata' refers to either a mountain of earth or a mountain of stone. 'Asajjamāno' means without sticking, without touching, or without colliding. 'Seyyathāpi ākāse' means as if in the sky.

A person with psychic power who wishes to travel in this manner enters the meditative attainment of the space-kasina (ākāsa-kasiṇa). After emerging, they contemplate a wall, an enclosure, or any mountain among those such as Mount Sineru or the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and after performing the preliminary work (parikamma), they should resolve: 'Let there be space.' It then becomes space. For one who wishes to descend or ascend, it becomes hollow; for one who wishes to pass through, it becomes a hole. That person with psychic power then travels through that wall, enclosure, or mountain, which has become hollow or has a hole, without being hindered.

Regarding this, the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷābhaya said: 'Friends, what is the purpose of entering the space-kasina? If one wishes to create elephants, horses, and so on, does one enter an elephant-kasina or a horse-kasina? Is it not that mastery (vasībhāva) in the eight attainments, having performed the preliminary work on any kasina whatsoever, is the standard? Whatever one desires, that very thing happens.'

The monks replied: 'Venerable, in the Pali text, only the space-kasina is mentioned; therefore, this entering of the space-kasina must certainly be stated.' The following is the Pali from the Paṭisambhidāmagga regarding this matter:

'Naturally, he is one who has attained mastery of the space-kasina attainment. He contemplates beyond the wall, beyond the enclosure, beyond the mountain. Having contemplated, he resolves with knowledge: "Let there be space." It becomes space. He goes unhindered through the wall, the enclosure, and the mountain. Just as ordinary people without psychic power go unhindered through a place that is not closed or fenced in by anything, even so, that person with psychic power, who has attained mastery over the mind, goes unhindered through the wall, the enclosure, and the mountain, as if through space.' (Paṭi. Ma. 3.11)
24:
"Just like traveling in the sky"—this is the Pali from the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

[24] To explain by raising an objection: if a mountain or a tree should arise in the path of that monk while he is traveling after making a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), must he re-enter the attainment and resolve again? There is no fault in resolving again. Indeed, re-entering the attainment and resolving is similar to taking dependence (nissaya) from a preceptor (upajjhāya). However, because this monk of psychic power has already resolved, "Let there be space," it remains as open space. By the power of the previous resolution itself, it is impossible for a mountain or a tree produced by seasonal conditions (utu) to arise in his path. If, however, another person of psychic power creates something, the first creation is more powerful. Therefore, the mountain, tree, etc., of the later creator would have to go either above or below that space created first.

Notes:
1. This is the precise and complete meaning of the term 'cetovasippatta'. However, the Burmese phrasing is smoother if the words in parentheses are skipped.
2. Connect "By the power of the previous resolution itself..." with "...it is impossible for it to happen."

393. In the phrase "diving and surfacing even in the earth" (pathaviyāpi ummujjanimujjanti), 'ummujja' refers to surfacing and 'nimujja' refers to diving. A person of psychic power who wishes to perform diving and surfacing in the earth should enter the water-kasina (āpo-kasiṇa) attainment, emerge from it, define an area saying, "Let the earth in this much space be water," perform the preliminary work (parikamma), and resolve in the manner already described. Simultaneously with the resolution, the earth in the defined area becomes only water. That person of psychic power performs diving and surfacing in that water. In this regard, the following is the Pali from the Paṭisambhidāmagga as evidence:

"By nature, he is one who has mastered the attainment of the water-kasina. He contemplates the earth. Having contemplated it, he resolves with knowledge, 'Let it be water.' It becomes water. That person of psychic power performs diving and surfacing in the earth (which has become water). Just as ordinary people without psychic power perform diving and surfacing in water, even so, that person of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind performs diving and surfacing in the earth, just as if it were in water." (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.11).

Notes:
1. This cites the Pali marked (d) from the Pali shown on page 59. Its full Burmese translation is: "He also performs diving and surfacing in the earth, just as in water."
2. According to the Pali which places 'ummujja' (surfacing) before 'nimujja' (diving), it should be translated in that order. However, according to the actual process and Burmese usage, diving occurs first; therefore, it is translated as "diving and surfacing."

He does not only perform diving and surfacing; he also performs whatever action he desires, such as bathing, drinking, washing his face, or washing items like robes and bowls. It is not only water that is created; even among substances like ghee, oil, honey, and molasses, whatever he desires, he contemplates, "Let this and that substance be this much," performs the preliminary work, and resolves; it becomes exactly as resolved. For one who takes it out and places it in a vessel, the ghee remains as ghee (even inside the vessel), the oil and so forth remain as oil and so forth, and the water remains as water. In that water (created from earth), he gets wet only if he wishes to be wet; if he does not wish to be wet, he does not get wet. That earth becomes water only for that creator; for other people, it remains only earth. There, people even walk on foot, travel by vehicles, and even perform farming and so on.
25:
If this person of psychic power wishes it to be water for those other people as well, [25] it becomes so (as desired). However, when the determined time has passed, except for the water that was originally in pots, tanks, etc., the rest of the defined area of created water reverts to being earth.

394. In the phrase "even on water without breaking the surface" (udakepi abhijjamāne), water that sinks when stepped upon is called 'bhijjamāna' (breaking or sinking water). The opposite, water that does not break or sink, is called 'abhijjamāna'. A person of psychic power who wishes to travel on such water that does not break or sink should enter the earth-kasina (pathavī-kasiṇa) attainment, emerge from it, define an area saying, "Let the water in this much space be earth," perform the preliminary work, and resolve in the manner already described. Simultaneously with the resolution, the water in the defined area becomes only earth. That person of psychic power walks on that earth (created from water). In this regard, the following is the Pali as evidence:

"By nature, he is one who has mastered the attainment of the earth-kasina. He contemplates the water. Having contemplated it, he resolves with knowledge, 'Let it be earth.' It becomes earth. That person of psychic power walks on the water that does not break. Just as ordinary people without psychic power walk on the earth that does not break, even so, that person of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind walks on the water that does not break, just as if it were on earth." (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.11).

Notes:
1. This cites the Pali marked (e) from the Pali shown on page 59. Its full Burmese translation is: "He also walks on water that does not break, just as on earth."

He does not only walk; he also performs whatever posture (iriyāpatha) he desires. He does not only create earth; even among things like gems, gold, mountains, and trees, whatever he desires, he contemplates and resolves in the manner already described, and it becomes exactly as resolved. That water becomes earth only for that creator; for other people, it remains only water, and fish, turtles, water-crows, and other creatures move about as they please (in that water). If this person of psychic power wishes to make that water earth for other people as well, he can certainly do so. However, when the defined time has passed, it reverts to being only water.

395. In the phrase "he travels cross-legged" (pallaṅkena kamati), it means he travels (while sitting) in a cross-legged position. In the phrase "a winged bird" (pakkhī sakuṇo), it means a bird possessed of wings. A person of psychic power who wishes to travel in this way should enter the earth-kasina jhana, emerge from it, and if he wishes to travel while sitting, he should define an area the size of a cross-legged seat, perform the preliminary work, and resolve in the manner already described. If he wishes to travel while lying down, an area the size of a couch; if he wishes to travel on foot, an area the size of a path—thus, having defined an appropriate area, he should resolve, "Let it be earth," in the manner already described. Simultaneously with the resolution, it becomes only solid earth. In this regard, the following is the Pali as evidence:

Notes:
[26] "He travels cross-legged in the sky like a winged bird." In this regard (in detail): By nature, he is one who has mastered the attainment of the earth-kasina. He contemplates the sky. Having contemplated it, he resolves with knowledge, 'Let it be earth.' It becomes earth. That person of psychic power walks, stands, sits, and lies down in the sky above.
26:
"Just as ordinary people without psychic power walk, stand, sit, and lie down on the natural ground, so too does that possessor of psychic power, who has attained mastery over the mind, walk back and forth in the sky above... [and] lie down." This is from the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi.

A bhikkhu who wishes to travel through the sky should also possess the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). Why? Because in between, there may be mountains, trees, and so forth, produced by seasonal conditions (utu-samuṭṭhāna), or nagas, garudas, and so forth, might create them out of jealousy. It is for the purpose of seeing these obstacles. What should be done upon seeing those mountains, trees, and so forth? Having entered the foundation jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) and emerged from it, one should perform the preliminary work (parikamma) and make the determination (adhiṭṭhāna): "Let there be space (ākāsa)."

However, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said: "Friends, what is the use of re-entering the attainment? Is not the mind of that possessor of psychic power, which functions through the power of miracles, already concentrated?¹ By that mind which functions through the power of miracles, whatever place he determines to be space, that very place becomes space alone." Even though he said so, one should proceed according to the method mentioned in the miracle of passing through walls (tirokuṭṭa-pārihāriya).²

Notes:
1. Regarding the phrase "Is not the mind already concentrated?"—it means that the mind of the possessor of psychic power, while performing a miracle, is indeed well-placed and concentrated; it is not unconcentrated as at other times. This statement is merely the opinion of the Elder Cūḷābhaya. Indeed, previously, one entered the earth-kasiṇa jhāna and determined it to be earth to walk upon it; now, space is desired, therefore one must indeed enter the space-kasiṇa jhāna. For this reason, the Commentary states, "Even though he said so..." (Ṭīkā).
2. Regarding the phrase "one should proceed according to the method mentioned in the miracle of passing through walls"—it means that just as in that miracle, walls and such become space by determination, so too in this case, one should proceed by making the newly appeared mountains, trees, and so forth into space by determination. Alternatively, the method mentioned in the miracle of passing through walls refers to the statement: "If a mountain or a tree should grow in the interval while that bhikkhu is traveling by determination..." and so forth. By this statement, it is indicated that it is not possible for a mountain or a tree produced by seasonal conditions to appear in the path of that bhikkhu through the power of his previous determination.

To provide another reason: this possessor of psychic power should also be one who has attained the divine eye for the purpose of descending in a suitable place. Indeed, if this possessor of psychic power were to descend at a bathing place or a village gate, which are unsuitable places for descending, he would become conspicuous to the general public (as a bhikkhu arriving through the sky). Therefore, after looking with the divine eye and avoiding unsuitable places, he can descend in a suitable (secluded) place.

396. Regarding the statement "He touches and strokes with his hand even this moon and sun, so mighty and powerful,"¹ their great psychic power (mahiddhika) is to be understood by their movement above forty-two thousand yojanas, and their great majesty (mahānubhāva) by their providing light to three continents simultaneously.² Alternatively, they are of great psychic power due to such high and distant movement in the sky and providing light, and for that same reason, they are of great majesty.

Notes:
- It is shown that the interference that might be made by nagas and so forth cannot cause an obstacle to the travel. (Ṭīkā)
1. This is a translation of the Pāḷi passage marked (cha) from the Pāḷi shown on page 59, provided for easy understanding.
2. Regarding the manner of providing light to three continents: while staying in the center of one continent, they illuminate the eastern continent with the light of the setting sun/moon and the western continent with the light of the rising sun/moon.
27:
(Based on the Ṭīkā). Because of this manner of providing light, it is said that while three continents are lit, one continent is dark.

Because of such great psychic power, they are said to have great majesty (mahānubhāva). "Touches" (parāmasati) means he grasps, or alternatively, he touches a certain part. "Strokes" (parimajjati) means he strokes all around like the surface of a mirror. This psychic power of the possessor of power is accomplished solely by the strength of the foundation jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) of direct knowledge (abhiññā); there is no specific restriction of a particular kasiṇa attainment in this matter. Indeed, the following is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

[27] "Regarding the statement 'He touches and strokes with his hand even this moon and sun, so mighty and powerful'—the detail is: In this world, that possessor of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind adverts to the moon and sun; having adverted, he determines with knowledge: 'Let them be within arm's reach (hatthapāsa).' They become within arm's reach. That possessor of psychic power, whether sitting or lying down, touches and strokes the moon and sun with his hand. Just as ordinary people without psychic power touch and stroke any physical object within arm's reach, so too does that possessor of psychic power, whether sitting... (pe)... stroke them."

If such a possessor of psychic power wishes to go and touch them, he goes and touches them. If he wishes to touch them while sitting or lying down right here in this human world, he determines: "Let them be within arm's reach." By the power of the determination, they come and stay within arm's reach like a palm fruit fallen from its stalk, and he touches them; or he touches them by expanding and lengthening his own hand. If he expands his hand, does the "clung-to" (upādinnaka) matter of the body expand, or the "not-clung-to" (anupādinnaka) matter? The not-clung-to matter expands, depending on the clung-to matter.

On this point, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga said: "How is it, friends? Does the clung-to matter not become small or large? When a bhikkhu exits through a keyhole and such, does the clung-to matter not become small? When he creates a large body, is it not large, like that of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna?"

## Taming the Naga King Nandopananda

It is said that on one occasion, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, invited him: "Venerable Sir, please accept alms at our house tomorrow together with five hundred bhikkhus," and then departed. The Blessed One, having accepted the invitation (by remaining silent), passed the remainder of that day and the night, and at the time of dawn, surveyed the ten-thousandfold world system. Then, the Naga King named Nandopananda appeared within the range of the Blessed One's knowledge.
28:
The Blessed One reflected, "This Naga king has appeared in the range of my knowledge. Does he have the supporting condition (for faith)?" Upon reflecting, he saw, "This Naga has wrong view; he has no confidence in the Triple Gem." Then he reflected, "Who can release this Naga from his wrong view?" and he saw the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.

[28] Then, when the night had turned to dawn, after attending to his physical needs, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, inform the five hundred monks that the Tathāgata is going on a journey to the celestial realms." On that day, preparations were being made for the Naga king Nandopananda's banquet. That Naga king Nandopananda was seated on a divine jewel-throne, with a divine white parasol being held over him, surrounded by three types of dancers¹ and his Naga retinue, looking over the arrangement of food and drink served in divine jewel-vessels. Then the Blessed One, making himself visible to the Naga king, proceeded towards the Tāvatiṃsa heaven together with the five hundred monks, passing directly above the Naga king's canopy.

At that time, such an evil wrong view arose in the Naga king Nandopananda: "These shaveling ascetics enter and leave the Tāvatiṃsa heaven by passing over our realm. From now on, I will not allow these monks to go scattering the dust of their feet upon our heads." He then rose and went to the foot of Mount Sineru, abandoned his natural form, and wrapped his coils around Mount Sineru seven times. Then, spreading his hood above, he covered the Tāvatiṃsa heaven with his downward-turned hood, causing it to disappear from sight.

Note: 1. Dancers of three ages: those of marriageable age, maidens, and young girls. (Sub-commentary)

Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, previously standing in this place, I could see Mount Sineru, I could see the surroundings of Sineru, I could see Tāvatiṃsa, I could see the Vejayanta Palace, and I could see the banner flying atop the Vejayanta Palace. What, Venerable Sir, is the cause, what is the reason that I now see neither Mount Sineru... nor the banner atop the Vejayanta Palace?"¹ "Raṭṭhapāla, this Naga king named Nandopananda is angry with you all. He has wrapped his coils around Mount Sineru seven times and, covering it with his hood above, has created darkness." "Venerable Sir, I shall tame him." The Blessed One did not grant permission. Then the Venerable Bhaddiya, the Venerable Rāhula, and all the monks in succession rose up (to tame him). The Blessed One did not grant permission.

Finally, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna said, "Venerable Sir, I shall tame him." "Tame him, Moggallāna," the Blessed One permitted. The Elder abandoned his natural form, created a massive Naga form, and wrapped his coils around Nandopananda fourteen times. Placing his own hood above Nandopananda's hood, [29] he pressed him against Mount Sineru.

Note: 1. Here, only the essential meaning is translated in summary.
29:
The Naga king Nandopananda emitted smoke. The Elder Mahāmoggallāna also emitted smoke, as if to say, "Not only your body has smoke, mine has it too." The Naga king's smoke did not distress the Elder, but the Elder's smoke distressed the Naga king (causing him weariness)¹. Then the Naga king emitted flames. The Elder also emitted flames, as if to say, "Not only your body has fire, mine has it too." The Naga king's flames did not distress the Elder, but the Elder's flames distressed the Naga king (causing him weariness). The Naga king thought, "This person presses me against Mount Sineru and emits both smoke and flames." He then asked, "Friend, who are you?" "Nanda, I am Moggallāna," he replied. "Venerable Sir, please remain in your own form as a monk," the Naga said.

The Elder Mahāmoggallāna abandoned that created Naga form and entered through Nandopananda's right ear-hole and exited through the left ear-hole; he entered through the left ear-hole and exited through the right ear-hole. Likewise, he entered through the right nostril and exited through the left nostril; he entered through the left nostril and exited through the right nostril. Then the Naga king opened his mouth. The Elder entered through the mouth and walked back and forth inside the belly from east to west¹. Then the Blessed One said, "Moggallāna, pay attention; this Naga is of great psychic power." The Elder Mahāmoggallāna replied, "Venerable Sir, the four bases of power (iddhipāda) have been developed by me, practiced frequently, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well-undertaken. Let alone one Nandopananda, Venerable Sir, I could tame a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand Naga kings like Nandopananda."

Note: 1. 'Distressed' (bādhati) means it caused only weariness. (Sub-commentary) It means it was not a cruel or merciless oppression.
Note: 1. The sub-commentary explains that because the Naga was lying east to west, the walking was done in that direction.

The Naga king thought, "I did not see him when he entered. Now, when he exits, I will place him between my fangs and chew him up." He then said, "Venerable Sir, please come out. Do not distress me by walking back and forth inside my belly." The Elder Mahāmoggallāna came out and stood outside. The Naga king, seeing him and thinking, "This is that Moggallāna," released a blast of air from his nose. The Elder Mahāmoggallāna entered the fourth jhāna. Even a single hair-pore of the Elder could not be moved by that nasal wind. It is said that the other monks were capable of performing all the miracles from the beginning, but upon reaching this point of the nasal wind, they would not have been able to enter jhāna with such rapid mindfulness as the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Seeing this, the Blessed One did not permit those other monks to tame the Naga king.
30:
[30] The Naga King thought: "I cannot move even a single hair of this monk with the wind from my nose; this monk is indeed of great power." The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, discarding his monk's form, created the form of a Garuḍa and, displaying a fierce Garuḍa-wind, pursued the Naga King. The Naga King, discarding his naga form, created the form of a youth and, bowing at the feet of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, said: "Venerable Sir, I go to you for refuge."

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having subdued the Naga King and rendered him harmless, said: "Nanda the Naga King, the Teacher has arrived; come, let us go," and took him to the presence of the Blessed One. The Naga King paid homage to the Blessed One and said: "Venerable Sir, I go to you for refuge." The Blessed One said: "May you be happy, Naga King," and then, surrounded by the assembly of monks, proceeded to the house of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika.

Anāthapiṇḍika asked: "Venerable Sir, why have you arrived so late in the day?"

"Because a battle took place between Moggallāna and the Naga King Nandopananda," the Buddha replied. "Venerable Sir, who won and who was defeated?" he asked. "Moggallāna won, and Nandopananda was defeated," the Buddha replied. Anāthapiṇḍika then said: "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One accept my alms for seven consecutive days; for seven days, I shall perform a grand offering to the Venerable Moggallāna." Having said this, he performed a grand offering for seven days to the five hundred monks headed by the Buddha.

With reference to this great body created during the subduing of Nandopananda as described, it was said: "When he creates a great body, then it is great, just like that of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna." Even though this was said, the monks stated: "Depending on the internal matter (upādinnaka), only the external matter (anupādinnaka) increases." The logical conclusion in this matter of increasing the size of hands and so on is that only the external matter increases.

That person of psychic power, having acted as described, does not merely touch the moon and the sun. If he so desires, he can make them into a footstool and place his feet on them; he can make them into a bench and sit on them; he can make them into a couch and lie on them; he can make them into a backrest and lean against them. Furthermore, just as one person of psychic power can do this, so can another. Indeed, even if hundreds of thousands of monks were to do this, it would be accomplished for each and every one of them. The movement and the illumination of the moon and the sun remain

##

just as they were before. To give an analogy: just as when a thousand bowls are filled with water, the image of the moon appears in all the bowls, yet the moon's natural movement and illumination remain as they are, so too is this psychic miracle like that analogy.

397. "Even as far as the Brahma-world" (Yāva brahmalokāpi) means taking even the Brahma-world as the limit (meaning even up to the Brahma realm). "He wields power with his body" (Kāyena vasaṃ vatteti) means that in that Brahma-world, he exercises his will by means of his body (meaning he makes it follow his will, or it happens according to his will). The meaning of that sentence should be understood by following the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi. Indeed, the following is the Pāḷi that explains this matter:
31:
[31] "Regarding 'Even as far as the Brahma-world, he wields power with his body,' the detailed explanation is: If that person of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind (through the eight attainments) wishes to go to the Brahma-world, he resolves that what is far be near: 'Let it be near,' and it becomes near. He resolves that what is near be far: 'Let it be far,' and it becomes far. He resolves that the many be few: 'Let it be few,' and it becomes few. He resolves that the few be many: 'Let it be many,' and it becomes many. With the divine eye, he sees the form of that Brahmā. With the divine ear, he hears the sound of that Brahmā. With the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others, he knows the mind of that Brahmā.

Note: 1. The Pāḷi marked (ja) from the Pāḷi shown in the note on page 59 is cited here.

If that person of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind wishes to go to the Brahma-world with a visible body, he directs the mind to follow the body; he resolves the mind according to the body. Having directed the mind to follow the body and resolved the mind according to the body, he enters into the perception of ease and the perception of lightness, and goes to the Brahma-world with a visible body. If that person of psychic power who has attained mastery over the mind wishes to go to the Brahma-world with an invisible body, he directs the body to follow the mind; he resolves the body according to the mind. Having directed the body to follow the mind and resolved the body according to the mind, he enters into the perception of ease and the perception of lightness, and goes to the Brahma-world with an invisible body.

In front of that Brahmā, he creates a mind-made form (manomaya-rūpa), complete in all its limbs and parts, with no faculty lacking. If that person of psychic power walks, the created form also walks there. If that person of psychic power stands, sits, or lies down, the created form also lies down there. If that person of psychic power emits smoke, emits flames, preaches the Dhamma, asks a question, or being asked a question, answers it, the created form also, being asked a question there, answers it. If that person of psychic power stands with, speaks with, or engages in discussion with that Brahmā, the created form also stands with, speaks with, or engages in discussion with that Brahmā there. Whatever that person of psychic power does, the created form does that very thing." This is the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi.

[32] In that Pāḷi, regarding the phrase "He resolves that what is far be near," it means that after emerging from the basic jhāna, he contemplates making the distant deva world or Brahma world near. Having contemplated and performed the preliminary work (parikamma), he enters the jhāna again and resolves: "Let it be near," and it becomes near. The same method applies to the remaining terms.

In such creation, who has ever taken what is far and made it near? The Blessed One has done so. The manner in which he did so: When the Blessed One was proceeding to the deva world at the conclusion of the Twin Miracle, he made Mount Yugandhara and Mount Sineru appear near, and placing one foot from the ground onto the summit of Mount Yugandhara, he placed his second foot on the summit of Mount Sineru.

Who else besides the Blessed One has done this? The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera has done so. The manner in which he did so: The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera, after having his morning meal, departed from Sāvatthī and [traveled] twelve yojanas...
32:
1. By the words "At the end of the Twin Miracle," it refers to the accomplishment through the psychic power of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi) of the extraordinary journey to Tāvatiṃsa in three strides (tivikkama). However, in the Pāthika Commentary (the commentary on the Lakkhaṇa Sutta), it is stated as the result and benefit of the mark of well-placed feet (suppatiṭṭhitapāda-lakkhaṇa). These two statements should be understood by reconciling them without contradiction. (Sub-commentary)

He caused the assembly to reach the city of Saṅkassa safely within that very moment, having shortened the journey of thirty yojanas.

To give another example, Cūḷasamuddatthera in the island of Tambapaṇṇi also did so. It is said that during a time of famine, seven hundred monks came to the Elder early in the morning. The Elder reflected, "The community of monks is large; where will there be a village for alms?" Seeing no such place in the entire island of Tambapaṇṇi, he saw that "It will be in Pāṭaliputta on the other side of the ocean." He then had the monks take their bowls and robes and called them, "Come, venerable sirs, let us go for alms." Shortening the earth, he proceeded to Pāṭaliputta. The monks asked, "Venerable sir, what city is this?" He replied, "Venerable sirs, it is the city of Pāṭaliputta." They said, "Venerable sir, Pāṭaliputta is said to be far away." He replied, "Venerable sirs, those called elderly monks take what is far and make it near." They asked, "Venerable sir, where is the Great Ocean?" He said, "Venerable sirs, did you not come across a small blue canal in the middle of the way?" They replied, "Yes, venerable sir, we crossed it; but the ocean is indeed vast." He then said, "Venerable sirs, those called elderly monks make even what is large small."

Note 1: Translated by slightly rearranging for the flow of the Burmese language. According to the original Pali order, it would be "shortening the journey to the city of Saṅkassa which is thirty yojanas, within that very moment."

Just as Cūḷasamuddatthera did, Tissadattatthera also, having bathed in the evening and donned his upper robe, when the thought arose in his mind, "I will worship the Mahābodhi tree," made the Mahābodhi tree near.

Who has taken the near and made it far? The Blessed One did so. The Blessed One made the distance between himself and Aṅgulimāla, though near, to be far. Here ends one section.

Furthermore, who has made the many few? The Venerable Mahākassapa did so. It is said that in the city of Rājagaha, on a festival day, five hundred maidens taking moon-cakes were going for the sake of playing at the festival. Although they saw the Blessed One, they gave nothing. However, seeing the Elder who was coming behind, they said, "Our Elder is coming, let us give him cakes." All the maidens brought their cakes and approached the Venerable Mahākassapa. The Venerable Mahākassapa took his bowl out of its bag and made all the cakes just enough to fill a single bowl. The Blessed One sat in front, waiting for the Venerable Mahākassapa. The Venerable Mahākassapa brought the cakes and offered them to the Blessed One.

Note 1: Regarding the Mahābodhi tree, it refers to the Mahābodhi tree where the Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka) is situated. Immediately after the thought to worship it arose, he shortened the earth and the ocean, making the Mahābodhi near. (Sub-commentary)

Furthermore, in the story of Illīsa the Treasurer, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna made the few many. In the story of Kāka-valiya, the Blessed One also made the few many. The manner of doing so: The Venerable Mahākassapa, after spending seven days in the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), wishing to show favor to the poor, stood for alms at the door of the house of a poor man named Kāka-valiya. When Kāka-valiya's wife saw the Elder, she poured into his bowl the saltless sour gruel she had cooked for her husband. The Venerable Mahākassapa took that gruel and placed it in the hand of the Blessed One. The Blessed One made a determination (adhiṭṭhāna) to make it sufficient for the large community of monks.
33:
The rice gruel brought in a single bowl was sufficient for all the monks. Kākavaliya also attained the position of a treasurer on the seventh day. Here ends one section.

It is not only making a small amount into a large amount; even in matters such as making what is sweet not sweet, or what is not sweet sweet, everything desired by the possessor of psychic power is accomplished. To elaborate, an Elder named Mahā Anula, seeing many monks who had gone for alms and received only plain rice without curry, sitting and eating on the bank of the Ganges River, resolved, "Let the water in the Ganges become clarified butter (sappimaṇḍa)," and gave the perception of butter to the novices. Those novices brought it in small bowls and offered it to the Saṅgha of monks.

## All the monks and novices partook of the meal along with the sweet and excellent clarified butter.

Regarding the phrase "with the divine eye" (dibba-cakkhu) and so forth, the meaning is: while remaining right here in this human world, by expanding the light, one sees the form of that Brahmā. Furthermore, while remaining right here, one hears all the sounds of that Brahmā speaking, and knows his mind. In the phrase "he directs the mind by means of the body," it means he directs (transforms) the mind by the power of the physical body. Taking the mind of the basic jhāna (pādaka-jhāna), he applies it to the body. He makes it follow the body, having a slow movement. Indeed, the movement of the body is slow [Note 1]. In the phrase "he attains the perception of bliss (sukha-saññā) and the perception of lightness (lahu-saññā)" [Note 2], he attains the perception of bliss [Note 3] and the perception of lightness, enters it, touches it, and fully reaches it [Note 4].

What is called "perception of bliss" is the perception associated with equanimity (upekkhā). Indeed, equanimity is called bliss because it is peaceful. Furthermore, that same perception of bliss [Note 5] should also be known as "perception of lightness" because it is liberated from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and from opposing factors such as initial thought (vitakka) and so forth. For one who has attained that, even the physical body becomes as light as a tuft of cotton. Such a person, like a tuft of cotton lifted by the wind [34], goes to the Brahma world with an extremely light visible body as described. A possessor of psychic power who goes in this way, if he so desires, creates a path in the sky by the power of the earth-kasina jhāna and goes on foot; if he so desires, [he uses] the wind-kasina jhāna to [direct] the wind...

Notes:
1. Indeed, the movement of the body is slow—meaning it is caused by the slow great elements (mahābhūta). In this context, this is the intended meaning: a yogi who directs (transforms) the mind by the power of wanting to go with the visible body, after emerging from the basic jhāna, performs the preliminary work (parikamma), "Let this mind have a slow movement like the body." Referring to such preliminary work, it is said, "taking the mind of the basic jhāna." After performing the preliminary work, he enters [jhāna] again and, resolving with knowledge, applies that mind to the body, making it have a slow movement similar to the body. (Ṭīkā)
2. The word "attaining" (okkamma) is explained by "attains" (okkamati). Connect it with "the mind which has [the basic jhāna] as its object."
3. Perception of bliss means the perception that arises together with bliss; it is a term that highlights perception. (Ṭīkā) As for bliss—in the fourth jhāna, there is no bliss, only equanimity. That equanimity itself is called bliss here because it is peaceful. Therefore, the collection of mind and mental factors (citta-cetasika) that arise together with that peaceful equanimity and perception is called "perception of bliss." Thus, upon reaching the fourth jhāna, one simply reaches that perception of bliss. In this context, however, only the perception associated with the supernormal knowledge mind (abhiññā-citta) that performs psychic feats is called "perception of bliss."
4. Here, the words "enters, touches, fully reaches" further explain the word "attains."
5. Connect it as: "That same perception of bliss... should also be known as perception of lightness."
34:
By resolving (to blow as desired), he goes by the wind like a tuft of cotton. Indeed, in this matter, the desire to go is the only measure [1]. To illustrate, if there is a desire to go, that possessor of psychic power who has resolved his mind as described [2], being propelled by the momentum of his determination like an arrow shot by an archer, goes with a visible body.

In the phrase 'he directs the body by the power of the mind,' he takes the material body [3] and mounts it upon the (foundation jhāna) mind [4]. He makes the movement as swift as the mind. Truly, the movement—the arising—of the mind is swift. In the phrase 'he enters upon the perception of happiness and the perception of lightness,' it means he enters upon the perception of happiness and the perception of lightness that arise together with the mind of psychic creation, which has the material body as its object.

Notes:
1. In going this way with a visible body, the preliminary work and determination made by the power of the desire to go toward the intended destination are the only measures. By that much, the going is accomplished. Therefore, reaching the desired place can occur even without creating a path or resolving upon the wind. (Ṭīkā)
2. This means having resolved the mind as previously described.
3. 'Taking the material body' means taking it with the preliminary mind by way of making the material body the object. (Ṭīkā)
4. 'Mounts it upon the mind' means he mounts it upon the foundation jhāna mind, thinking, 'Let this body be like this mind.' He makes it possess the same quality as that mind. Therefore, it is said, 'He makes the movement as swift as the mind.' The 'movement of the mind' refers to the arising of the mind. (Ṭīkā)

The meaning of the remaining terms should be understood in the manner already stated. This miracle of directing or transforming the material body by the power of the mind is indeed a movement similar to the movement of the mind. When it is asked whether this possessor of psychic power, traveling with an invisible body, goes at the moment of arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhiti), or dissolution (bhaṅga) of that mind of determination, one Elder said he goes in all three moments. As to whether that possessor of psychic power goes himself or sends a created form (nimmitarūpa), he does as he pleases. However, in this Pali text, only his going in person is mentioned.

In the term 'manomaya' (mind-made), it is called 'mind-made' because it is created by the mind of direct knowledge through determination. The phrase 'with unimpaired faculties' (ahīnindriya) is spoken in terms of the shape and form of the eyes, ears, etc. However, in the created form, there is no sensitive matter (pasāda-rūpa). The statement, 'If the possessor of psychic power walks to and fro, the created form also walks to and fro there,' and so on, is all said with reference to a form created by a disciple (sāvaka). But a form created by the Buddha performs whatever action the Blessed One performs; it also performs other actions according to the Blessed One's will. Here ends one part.

I shall now explain the manner of wielding power with the body. Among the psychic powers shown according to this Pali, if that possessor of psychic power, while staying right here in this human world, sees the form of a Brahma with the divine eye, hears the sound of a Brahma with the divine ear, or knows the mind of a Brahma with the knowledge of the minds of others, he is not yet said to be 'wielding power with the body' merely by such seeing, hearing, or knowing. Furthermore, if that possessor of psychic power, while staying right here, stands with, speaks with, or engages in discussion with that Brahma, he is not yet said to be 'wielding power with the body' by that much. Furthermore, if that possessor of psychic power performs a determination such as 'resolving that what is far be near' [1], he is not yet said to be 'wielding power with the body' by that much. Furthermore, if that possessor of psychic power goes to the Brahma world with either a visible or an invisible body, he is not yet said to be 'wielding power with the body' by that much. However, when he reaches the procedure described as 'he creates a form in front of that Brahma' and so on [35],
35:
by that much, he is said to be 'wielding power with the body.' The rest of the collection of miracles is mentioned here to show the preliminary stages of wielding power with the body. This psychic power is first the power of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi) shown in the explanation of the term 'iddhividha'.

398. Furthermore, the distinction between the power of transformation (vikubbanā-iddhi) and the mind-made power (manomaya-iddhi) is as follows [2]. A possessor of psychic power wishing to perform transformation—

Notes:
1. Translated slightly for smoothness in Burmese. Literally: 'There is also that determination of the possessor of psychic power, such as resolving that what is far be near.'
2. Translated with slight modification.

'That possessor of psychic power, abandoning his natural appearance, shows the appearance of a youth, or shows the appearance of a nāga, or shows the appearance of a garuḍa, or shows the appearance of an asura, or shows the appearance of Sakka, or shows the appearance of a deva, or shows the appearance of a Brahma, or shows the appearance of the ocean, or shows the appearance of a mountain, or shows the appearance of a lion, or shows the appearance of a tiger, or shows the appearance of a leopard; he also shows an elephant, he also shows a horse, he also shows a chariot, he also shows infantry, he also shows various kinds of military arrays.'

Among these appearances of a youth and so on as taught, he should resolve upon whichever form he desires. If he resolves (upon the appearance of a youth), he should emerge from the foundation jhāna for direct knowledge which has one of the objects such as the earth-kasina, and then advert to his own appearance as a youth. Having adverted and completed the preliminary work, he should again attain (the jhāna), and upon emerging, resolve: 'Let me be a youth of such a nature.' Simultaneously with the mind of determination, he becomes a youth, just like Devadatta (who created a form when about to go to Prince Ajātasattu). This is the method in all cases.

What is special is that the words 'he also shows an elephant' and so on are spoken here in terms of showing an elephant etc. externally. In that external creation, without resolving 'Let me be an elephant,' he should resolve, 'Let there be an elephant' [1]. The same method applies to horses and so on. This is the power of transformation (vikubbanā-iddhi).

399. Furthermore, a possessor of psychic power wishing to create a mind-made material body should emerge from the foundation jhāna, first advert to his own body, and by the method already mentioned, resolve: 'Let it be hollow.' The whole body becomes hollow. Then, having adverted to another body inside that body and performed the preliminary work, he resolves by the same method: 'Let there be another body inside this body.' Then another body appears inside that body. That possessor of psychic power pulls that created body out, just as one might pull out a reed from the muñja grass, or a sword from its scabbard,

Notes:
1. The Paṭisambhidāmagga Commentary examines this explanation: In the Visuddhimagga, it is said, 'The words "he also shows an elephant" etc. are spoken here in terms of showing an elephant etc. externally... the same method applies to horses and so on.' This statement contradicts the original text 'abandoning his natural appearance' (pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā) and the nature of transformation power (vikubbanā-iddhi). Indeed, showing another appearance by the power of determination without abandoning the natural appearance as taught in the Pali sequence is called 'power of determination' (adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi). Showing oneself in another form or manner by the power of determination after abandoning the natural appearance is called 'transformation power' (vikubbanā-iddhi). (This is the analysis given in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Commentary.)

or a snake from a basket. Thus it is said: 'Here, a bhikkhu creates from this body another body, having form, mind-made, with all its limbs and parts, with unimpaired faculties. Just as if a man were to pull out a reed from the muñja grass, it would occur to him: "This is the muñja grass, this is the reed,"
36:
...just like taking a snake out of a basket, or rather, from its slough. Therefore:

"In this Dispensation, a monk creates from this physical body another body, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and parts, not lacking any faculty. To give a simile, just as if a man were to pull out a reed from its sheath, and that man would have this knowledge: 'This is the sheath, this is the reed; the sheath is one thing, the reed is another, but the reed has been pulled out from the sheath itself.'"

This and other such passages have been taught. To explain further: in this matter of mind-made potency (manomayiddhi), just as the reed and so on are similar to the sheath and so on, likewise, the mind-made body is exactly similar to the physical body of the one possessing the potency. This is Mind-made Potency.

Thus, the Twelfth Chapter called the Description of the Kinds of Potency (Iddhividha-niddesa) in the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga), composed for the gladdening of good people, is concluded.
37:
Note 1: This is the meaning of the word 'karaṇḍā'. Therein, the first meaning is in accordance with the Ṭīkā which explains it as 'peḷāya' (basket). The second meaning is in accordance with the Paṭisambhidāmagga Commentary which explains it as 'purāṇataca-kañcukato' (from the old skin-slough). This Ṭīkā also mentions that some explain it as 'nimmokāti ca' (from the slough). In this context, since the snake and the 'karaṇḍa' must be similar, only the second meaning, 'from the slough', is appropriate.

These three similes are presented for the purpose of illustration. This is Mind-made Potency.

Thus, the Twelfth Chapter called the Description of the Kinds of Potency (Iddhividha-niddesa) in the Path of Purification, composed for the gladdening of good people, is concluded.

## (The Detailed Description of the Kinds of Potency is finished.)

## 13. Description of the Direct Knowledges (Abhiññā-niddesa)

## Discussion on the Divine Ear Element (Dibba-sota-dhātu-kathā)

400. Now the turn has come to describe the Divine Ear element. In that regard, and in the three direct knowledges that follow, the meaning of the words beginning with "When his mind is thus concentrated... [up to]... attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the divine ear element" should be understood in the manner already described. I shall explain only what is specific to each.

In the passage concerning the divine ear element, in the words 'dibbāya sota-dhātuyā': it is 'divine' (dibba) because it is like that of the devas. To explain:

Note 1: The divine ear direct knowledge (dibba-sota-abhiññā) itself is called the divine ear element.
Note 2: The three direct knowledges refer to the knowledge of penetrating the minds of others (cetopariya-abhiññā), the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-abhiññā), and the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-abhiññā), as shown on page 3 of the third volume of this Burmese translation.
Note 3: 'In all' means in all these Pali passages—both the one describing the divine ear element and those describing the remaining three direct knowledges. (Ṭīkā)
†: The first two terms to be explained from the original Pali—'So dibbāya sota-dhātuyā visuddhāya atikkanta-mānusikāya ubho sadde suṇāti dibbe ca mānuse ca ye dūre santike ca'—are presented first. The Burmese translation of that entire Pali passage is as follows:

The sensitive ear-element (pasāda-sota-dhātu) of the devas arises due to wholesome kamma; it is not obstructed by bile, phlegm, blood, etc. Because it is free from defilements, it is capable of receiving and hearing objects even at a distance. This ear-element of direct knowledge, produced by the power of the monk's development of energy (vīriya-bhāvanā), is just like that of the devas. Because it is like the devas' ear, it is called 'divine'. Alternatively, it is called 'divine' because it is obtained by means of the 'divine abiding' (dibba-vihāra) and because he himself relies on the divine abiding.

Note: That practitioner monk, with the divine ear element which is purified and surpasses that of humans, hears both kinds of sounds: those of the devas and those of humans; and sounds that are far and near. (This is the Burmese translation of that Pali).
1: 'Arises due to wholesome kamma' means it arises due to wholesome kamma called 'good conduct' (sucarita) which leads to birth in the deva world, being well-practiced through the perfection of faith, pure view, seeing the benefits, etc. (Ṭīkā)
2: Because it is accomplished and perfected only through the power of energetic striving, all development of the wholesome (kusala-bhāvanā) is called 'development of energy' (vīriya-bhāvanā). Alternatively, the development of the basis of success (iddhipāda) endowed with the formations of striving is also called 'development of energy'. It arises through the power of that development of energy. (Ṭīkā)

It is called 'ear element' (sota-dhātu) because of the sense of hearing and because of its soulless nature. Alternatively, it is like an ear element because it performs the function of the ear element; therefore, it is called 'ear element'. [The meaning is] 'with that (direct knowledge) ear element which is like the devas' ear'.

'Purified' (visuddhāya) means completely pure and free from defilements. 'Surpassing the human' (atikkanta-mānusikāya) means surpassing the human range of hearing and thus surpassing and standing beyond the human fleshy ear (maṃsa-sota-dhātu). 'Hears both sounds' (ubho sadde suṇāti) means he hears two kinds of sounds. Which two? Namely, sounds in the deva world and sounds in the human world; it means the sounds of devas and the sounds of humans. By this, it should be understood that all remaining sounds are included. 'Those far and near' (ye dūre santike ca) means those sounds that exist far away, even in another world-system (cakkavāḷa), and those that are near, even the sounds of organisms residing in one's own body; it means he hears those.
38:
Regarding sounds nearby, even the sounds of insects within one's own body are included; it means one hears sounds both near and far. By this statement, it should be understood that all sounds are encompassed without exception.

How is this direct knowledge of the divine ear element (dibbasotadhātu-abhiññā) produced? That monk, having attained the fourth jhāna which is the basis for direct knowledge, and having emerged from it, should first direct his mind—with a preparatory concentration mind (parikamma-samādhi) that is well-established (i.e., a momentary concentration that serves as the preparation for the divine ear knowledge)—towards the coarse and loud sounds in the forest, such as those of lions and so on, which are within the range of the ordinary ear. He should also attend to the sound of bells in the monastery, the sound of drums, the sound of conch shells, the sound of novices and young monks reciting with all their might, the sound of people speaking normally such as 'What, venerable sir?' or 'What, friend?', the sound of birds, the sound of the wind, and the sound of footsteps. [38] He should attend to the sizzling sound of boiling water, the crackling sound of palm leaves drying in the sun, and the sounds of ants and termites. In this way, starting from the coarsest and loudest sounds, he should attend to subtle sounds in successive order.

That yogi monk should attend to the 'sound-sign' (sadda-nimitta) of sounds in the eastern direction. (Note: The 'sound-sign' refers to the sound itself as the cause for the arising of knowledge; alternatively, it refers to the coarse or subtle quality of the sounds grasped in succession.) He should attend to the sound-sign of sounds in the western, northern, southern, lower, and upper directions, and in the southeast, northwest, northeast, and southwest directions. He should attend to the sound-sign of sounds that are both coarse and subtle. To such a yogi monk who attends in this way, those sounds become clear even to his ordinary mind; however, they become exceedingly clear to his mind in preparatory concentration.

To that yogi monk who is thus attending to the sound-sign, at the moment when it can be said, 'Now the divine ear element will arise,' mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana) arises, taking one or another of those sounds as its object. When that mind has ceased, four or five javanas occur. Among these four or five, the first three or four are sense-sphere javanas called preparation (parikamma), access (upacāra), conformity (anuloma), and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). The fourth or fifth is the absorption (appanā) mind associated with the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere. Among those, the knowledge that arises together with that absorption javana mind should be understood as the 'divine ear element.' After that absorption mind has occurred, he is said to have 'fallen into' that stream of knowledge. (Note: This means the divine ear element has become internal, and the monk no longer needs to strive for its development.)

A yogi wishing to strengthen that knowledge should delimit an area of one finger-breadth and develop it, thinking, 'I will hear sounds within this range.' Then, he should develop it by delimiting areas of two finger-breadths, four finger-breadths, eight finger-breadths, a span (vidatthi), a cubit (ratana), the inside of a room, a porch, a mansion, a precinct, a monastery, a village, a district, and so on, up to the edge of the world-system (cakkavāḷa) or even beyond.

The yogi monk who has attained direct knowledge in this way can hear sounds—even those within the space touched or pervaded by the kasina-sign which was the object of the basis jhāna—through the power of direct knowledge without re-entering the basis jhāna. And when hearing in this way, even if there is a single roar of noise from conch shells, drums, and tabors up to the Brahma world, if he wishes to distinguish them individually, he is indeed able to distinguish them, thinking, 'This is the sound of a conch, this is the sound of a drum.'

## The explanation of the Divine Ear element is finished.

## Explanation of the Knowledge of Penetrating Others' Minds
[39] 401. In the explanation of the knowledge of penetrating others' minds, regarding the term 'cetopariyañāṇāya', because it delimits (pariya) the mind (ceto)...
39:
## The Explanation of the Knowledge of Discerning the Minds of Others

1. The words in parentheses are for the particle 'pi'; they are shown in parentheses because they do not seem beneficial for this context.

2. "With the mind thus concentrated... [etc.] ... attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind to the knowledge of discerning the minds of others." This is called *ceto-pariya* (discerning the mind). It is called *ceto-pariya-ñāṇa* because it delimits (*pariya*) the mind and knows (*ñāṇa*) it; the meaning is "for the sake of that knowledge."

*Para-sattānaṃ* means of other beings, excluding oneself. *Para-puggalānaṃ* (of other persons) has the same meaning as *para-sattānaṃ*. The difference in phrasing is made for the sake of the listeners (*veneyya*) and the elegance of the teaching (*desanā-vilāsa*). *Cetasa ceto* means [knowing] their mind with one's own mind. *Paricca pajānāti* means that having delimited, one knows in various ways and aspects, such as with lust, etc.

How is this knowledge produced? This knowledge is accomplished through the power of the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu*), which serves as the preliminary work (*parikamma*) for this knowledge. Therefore, that meditating bhikkhu should expand the light and, with the divine eye, look at the color of the blood that exists depending on the heart-matter (*hadaya-rūpa*) of another, and thus seek out the mind.

**Note:**
This is cited to explain the term *ceto-pariya-ñāṇāya* (for the sake of the knowledge of discerning the minds of others) from the Pali text which states: "He discerns with his own mind the mind of other persons; he knows a mind with lust as a mind with lust, a mind without lust as a mind without lust," and so on. Later, terms such as *para-sattānaṃ* are also extracted and explained.
1. Here, it is translated concisely for easy understanding.
2. This is the meaning of the word *paricca*; it should be connected as "knows by delimiting."

[The bhikkhu] should expand [the light] and, with the divine eye, observe the color of the blood depending on the heart-matter of another and seek the mind. The way to know by seeking is: when a joyful mind (*somanassa*) occurs, the blood is red like a ripe banyan fruit. When a mind of grief (*domanassa*) occurs, it is dark like a ripe jambu fruit. When an equanimous mind (*upekkhā*) occurs, it is clear like sesame oil. Therefore, that meditating bhikkhu, by observing the color of another's heart-blood and seeking the mind, should make the knowledge of discerning the minds of others reach strength, thinking: "This [red] heart-blood matter arises from the faculty of joy; this [dark] heart-blood matter arises from the faculty of grief; this [clear] heart-blood matter arises from the faculty of equanimity."

**Note:**
1. *Hadaya-rūpa* is not the heart-base (*hadaya-vatthu*) itself, but rather the physical heart-matter; (it is translated as heart-matter in accordance with that explanation). This heart-matter is said to be like a lotus bud on the outside and like the inside of a bitter loofah on the inside. The blood to be described now exists depending on this heart-matter. The heart-base (*hadaya-vatthu*) exists depending on this blood. (Ṭīkā)
2. From here, it shows how the mind can be known by seeing the color of the heart-blood with the divine eye.
3. This should be connected as: "that meditating bhikkhu should observe, seek, and make it reach strength."

When that knowledge has reached strength in this way, he can gradually know all sense-sphere minds, fine-material sphere minds, and immaterial-sphere minds, moving from mind to mind even without seeing the heart-matter. Indeed, the following was said in the ancient Commentary:

"If it is asked, 'In the immaterial realm, whose heart-matter does one [with psychic power] who wishes to know another's mind see? Whose alteration of the faculties does he observe?' The answer is: he sees none. This is the domain of one with psychic power, who, by directing attention to a mind anywhere, knows the sixteen types of mind. However, this explanation [of looking at the heart-blood] is for the sake of a beginner who has not yet achieved proficiency [in this knowledge]."

In the passage *sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ*, etc., the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed should be understood as 'mind with lust' (*sarāga-citta*). The remaining wholesome and indeterminate consciousness of the four planes should be understood as 'mind without lust' (*vītarāga-citta*).

**Note:**
1. The grammatical case meaning has been changed in translation for easier understanding.
2. The specific details of these eight minds can be found in the later section on the Description of Aggregates (*Khandha-niddesa*). The details of subsequent minds can also be found in that same section.
3. Consciousness belonging to the four planes—sense-sphere, fine-material, immaterial, and supramundane—is translated as "belonging to the four planes."

The four minds consisting of the two hate-rooted minds and the two minds of doubt and restlessness are not included in this dyad (of mind with lust and mind without lust). However, some elders include them [as minds without lust]. The two minds associated with grief (*domanassa*) are called 'mind with hate' (*sadosa-citta*). All wholesome and indeterminate consciousness of the four planes is called 'mind without hate' (*vītadosa-citta*). The remaining ten unwholesome minds are not included in this dyad. However, some elders include them [as minds without hate].
40:
[40] Regarding these two terms, samohaṃ and vītamohaṃ: in the specific sense, excluding those mixed with greed and hatred, only the two types of (delusion-rooted) consciousness associated with doubt (vicikicchā) and restlessness (uddhacca) are called samoha (consciousness with delusion). However, since delusion (moha) occurs in all unwholesome consciousness, all twelve types of unwholesome consciousness (akusala citta) should be understood as samoha consciousness. The remaining (wholesome and indeterminate) consciousness is called vītamoha (consciousness without delusion).

Consciousness that occurs following sloth and torpor (thina-middha) (lazy and sluggish) is called saṅkhitta (shrunken consciousness)—contracted or withdrawn consciousness. Consciousness that occurs following restlessness (uddhacca) is called vikkhitta (scattered consciousness)—distracted consciousness. Fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) and immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) consciousness are called mahaggata (exalted consciousness). The rest¹ are called amahaggata (non-exalted consciousness).

Note:
(The) adjective is reduced by one for the sake of smooth Burmese phrasing.
1. Although these four types of consciousness are not associated with lust, they are not the opposite of lust, so they are not called vītarāga.

All consciousness belonging to the three planes—sensuous (kāma), fine-material (rūpa), and immaterial (arūpa)—is called sa-uttara (surpassable consciousness), meaning there is a consciousness superior to it. Supramundane consciousness (lokuttara) is called anuttara (unsurpassable consciousness), meaning there is no consciousness superior to it. Consciousness that has reached access concentration (upacāra) or absorption concentration (appanā) is called samāhita (concentrated consciousness). Consciousness that has reached neither access nor absorption is called asamāhita (unconcentrated consciousness).

Consciousness that has attained liberation through substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), through suppression (vikkham-bhana), through eradication (samuccheda), through tranquilization (paṭipassaddhi), or through escape (nissaraṇa) is called vimutta (liberated consciousness). Consciousness that has not attained these five types of liberation should be understood as avimutta (unliberated consciousness).

In this way, a bhikkhu who has attained the direct knowledge of penetrating the minds of others (cetopariya-abhiññā) understands all these types, such as this consciousness with lust as 'consciousness with lust,' ... [and so on] ... and understands unliberated consciousness as 'unliberated consciousness.'² This concludes one section.

## The Explanation of the Knowledge of Penetrating the Minds of Others is finished.

Note:
1. Consciousness remaining from the exalted (mahaggata) refers to the 54 sense-sphere consciousnesses and 8 supramundane consciousnesses.
2. The types of consciousness to be known by this knowledge are presented in 16 categories: (1) with lust and without lust, (2) with hatred and without hatred, (3) with delusion and without delusion, (4) shrunken and scattered, (5) exalted and non-exalted, (6) surpassable and unsurpassable, (7) concentrated and unconcentrated, (8) liberated and unliberated.
