When knowing these consciousnesses with the knowledge of penetrating the minds of others, one does not only know them generally as 'consciousness with lust,' etc., but can also know the entirety of how one thinks and intends.

## Explanation of the Knowledge of Recollecting Past Lives

402. In the explanation of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇāya¹ means: for the sake of that knowledge which occurs in recollecting the aggregates lived in the past. The aggregates lived (existed) in past lives are called pubbenivāsa. Nivuttha (lived) refers to those states² that were possessed (as one's own), experienced, and which arose and ceased within one's own continuity.

Alternatively,³ states that were lived in are called nivuttha (nivāsa). States that were known and delimited by one's own consciousness through the 'dwelling' of the sense object (the act of taking an object) are (nivuttha). Furthermore, in the recollection of Buddhas and Arahants whose round of rebirth has ended, states known by the consciousness of others are also (nivuttha). Only the Buddhas can attain and recollect those states known by the consciousness of others. The mindfulness (sati) by which one recollects or remembers the sequence of aggregates lived in the past is called pubbenivāsānussati. The knowledge associated with that mindfulness is called pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa. 'For the sake of the knowledge of recollecting past lives' means for the purpose of attaining that knowledge—this is the meaning of the term pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇāya.¹

Anekavihitaṃ means of many kinds,² or alternatively, taught or explained in many ways.² Pubbenivāsaṃ refers to the continuity of existence lived in various past lives, starting from the life immediately preceding.

Note:
1. This is cited to explain a new term not yet clarified from the Pali text: "So evaṃ samāhite citte ... āneñjappatte pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇāya cittaṃ abhinīharati abhininnāmeti, so anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati."
2. Here, nivāsa-nivuttha (lived) refers to states that were possessed as one's own, taken as objects, experienced, and states that arose in one's own continuity at that time.
3. This alternative explanation shows how states are called nivāsa because they were known by consciousness in the past. It also shows that there are two kinds: states known by one's own consciousness and states known by the consciousness of others. Among these, it is shown that only the Buddhas can recollect the states known by the consciousness of Buddhas and Arahants who have attained Parinibbāna.
41:
1. In these sentences, the translation is rendered smoothly in Burmese without strictly following the Pali word order.
2. Through these two explanations, the term 'anekavihitaṃ' is shown to mean 'of many kinds' or 'taught and expanded in many ways.'

[It refers to] the sequence of aggregates. Regarding 'anussarati' (recollects), one recollects and contemplates by following the sequence of aggregates or by way of death and rebirth. To expand on the manner of recollection, these six types of individuals can recollect this Pubbenivāsa (past lives): (1) Titthiyas (ascetics of other sects), (2) Pakatisāvakas (ordinary disciples), (3) Mahāsāvakas (great disciples), (4) Aggasāvakas (chief disciples), (5) Paccekabuddhas, and (6) Sammāsambuddhas.

Among them, the Titthiyas can only recollect forty aeons (kappas), not beyond that. Why? Because of weak wisdom. Indeed, their wisdom is weak because they lack the knowledge that discerns mind and matter (nāmarūpa-pariccheda). Ordinary disciples, because of strong wisdom, can recollect even a hundred or a thousand aeons. The eighty Great Disciples can recollect up to a hundred thousand aeons. The two Chief Disciples can recollect up to one incalculable (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons. Paccekabuddhas can recollect up to two incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. This is because the period during which these Great Disciples and others made their aspirations and fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) is only this much in extent. For the Sammāsambuddhas, however, there is no limit to the aeons [they can recollect]; they can recollect as much as they wish.

Note 1: This explanation shows that the practice of insight (vipassanā) is a special cause for the knowledge of recollecting past lives (Pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). (Ṭīkā)

Furthermore, Titthiyas can only recollect by following the sequence of aggregates; they are unable to recollect by skipping the sequence and going by way of death and rebirth. To illustrate with a simile, just as the blind cannot go to a desired place [independently], Titthiyas cannot skip over to a desired point; just as the blind walk without letting go of their staff, so do these Titthiyas recollect without letting go of the sequence of aggregates. Ordinary disciples can recollect by the sequence of aggregates and can also transition by way of death and rebirth. The eighty Great Disciples are the same. For the two Chief Disciples, there is no need for the sequence of aggregates; having seen the death (cuti) of one existence, they see the rebirth (paṭisandhi); then seeing the death of another existence, they see the rebirth—thus they proceed by transitioning only by way of death and rebirth. Paccekabuddhas are the same.

For the Sammāsambuddhas, however, there is no need for the sequence of aggregates, nor is there a need to transition by way of death and rebirth. Indeed, for those Buddhas, whatever point they desire, whether below or above, across many billions of aeons, becomes clear. Therefore, even across many billions of aeons, they condense them like an elided (peyyāla) Pali text and arrive at whatever point they desire, proceeding by way of a 'lion's leap' (sīhokkanta).

Note 1: Recollecting the rebirth of an existence immediately after recollecting the death of that same existence, without contemplating the middle part of that life, is called recollecting by way of death and rebirth. (Based on Ṭīkā)

The knowledge of the Buddhas proceeding in this way is like an arrow shot by an archer who has practiced the art of hitting a hair-tip—similar to the Bodhisatta Sarabhaṅga—which falls exactly on the target without snagging on trees or creepers in between; it does not snag, it does not miss. Likewise, it does not snag or miss in the intervening births; without snagging or missing, it grasps exactly the desired point (recollecting and knowing it).

Furthermore, among these beings who recollect past lives, the vision of past lives of the Titthiyas appears like the light of a firefly. For Ordinary Disciples, it appears like the light of a lamp. For Great Disciples, like the light of a torch. For Chief Disciples, like the light of the morning star (Osadhī-tāraka). For Paccekabuddhas, like the light of the moon. For the Buddhas, the vision of past lives appears like the orb of the autumn sun adorned with a thousand rays.
42:
Notes:
1. The wisdom... likewise, connect with 'not clinging in intervening lives,' etc.
2. Connect with 'of the trained... archer.'

[42] Furthermore, the sectarians' recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa) is like the walking of the blind by feeling with the tip of a staff. The recollection of ordinary disciples (pakatisāvaka) is like crossing a small stream on a single-log bridge. The recollection of great disciples (mahāsāvaka) is like crossing on a plank bridge wide enough for four or five people. The recollection of chief disciples (aggasāvaka) is like crossing on a cart-road bridge. The recollection of Paccekabuddhas is like traveling on a main highway used by many merchants. The recollection of the Buddhas, the Exalted Ones, is like traveling on a great highway wide enough for twenty or thirty carts to pass simultaneously.1

In this context, however, the disciples' knowledge of the recollection of past lives is intended. Therefore, it was explained: "'He recollects' means he remembers by following and following according to the sequence of the aggregates or according to the sequence of death (cuti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi)."

403. Therefore, a beginner monk who wishes to recollect in this way should, after his meal, having returned from his alms-round, go to a secluded place, and withdrawing from external objects, being well-composed [in meditation], enter the four jhānas in succession. Having emerged from the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā), he should first reflect on his most recent sitting. Then he should reflect on the spreading of the seat, the entering of the dwelling, the putting away of the bowl and robes, the time of eating, the time of returning from the alms-village, the time of wandering for alms in the village, the time of entering the village for alms, the time of leaving the monastery, the time of worshipping at the terrace of the stupa and the terrace of the Bodhi tree, the time of rinsing and washing the bowl, the activities from the time of taking the bowl until washing the face, the activities at dawn, the activities in the middle watch, and the activities in the first watch. In this way, in reverse order, he should reflect on the activities performed throughout the entire night and day. This much is clear even to an ordinary mind, but it is extremely clear to a mind in preparatory concentration (parikamma-samādhi).

If, however, any of these activities is not clear, he should again enter the basic jhāna (pādaka-jhāna), emerge, and reflect. By doing this, it becomes as clear as when a lamp is lit in the dark. In this same reverse order, he should reflect on the activities performed on the second day, the third, fourth, and fifth days, the tenth day, half a month ago, a month ago, and up to a year ago. By this same method, for ten years, twenty years, and so on, until the time of his rebirth-linking in this life, he should reflect. Then he should reflect on the name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that occurred at the moment of death in the previous life. A wise monk is indeed able to uncover rebirth-linking and take the name-and-form at the moment of death as an object even at the first attempt.

However, because the name-and-form in the previous life has ceased without remainder and another [set of name-and-form] has arisen due to new kamma, that point of death in the previous life is like a place thickly veiled and concealed, like blind darkness, and is difficult to see for one of weak wisdom. Even so, such a person [43] should not give up or admit defeat, saying, 'I am unable to uncover rebirth-linking and take the name-and-form that occurred at the moment of death as an object.' He should repeatedly enter that same basic jhāna, emerge, and reflect on that point of death.

Note:
1. The phrase 'wide enough for twenty or thirty carts' is an explanation from the sub-commentary (ṭīkā). Even if such a vast highway might not be seen in the present day, it should be understood as an illustration to highlight the quality of the Buddha's knowledge.
43:
The benefit is that such a person [Note 1], for example, like a strong man cutting a great tree for the pinnacle of a gabled house, who, though unable to cut the whole trunk because his axe-edge is blunted merely by cutting the branches, twigs, and leaves, does not give up his task. Instead, he goes to a smithy, has the axe sharpened, and returns to cut again. If it becomes blunt again, he has it repaired in the same way and continues cutting. As he cuts in this manner, because there is no need to re-cut what is already cut, and because he continually cuts what is not yet cut, he will before long bring the great tree down. In the same way, a monk who has emerged from the basic jhāna (pādakajjhāna), no longer reflecting on what was previously reflected upon, reflects only on the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Thus, before long, he will be able to open up the rebirth-linking and take as his object the mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) that occurred at the moment of death (cuti). This meaning should also be illustrated by the examples of a wood-cutter and a hair-cutter (barber).

In that context, the knowledge that occurs by taking the object from the last sitting up to the rebirth-linking is not yet the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa); rather, it is called the knowledge of preparatory concentration (parikamma-samādhi-ñāṇa). Some teachers (eke) call it the knowledge of the past (atītaṃsa-ñāṇa). However, their statement is not appropriate if it refers to fine-material sphere knowledge (rūpāvacara-ñāṇa). When [Note 2] that yogi monk transcends the rebirth-linking and the mind-door advertence (manodvārāvajjana) arises taking as its object the mind-and-matter that occurred at the moment of death, and when that advertence has ceased, four or five impulsions (javanas) occur taking that same object. Among these four or five, the preceding ones are of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), named 'preparatory' (parikamma) and so on, according to the method previously mentioned. The last impulsion (the fourth or fifth) is the absorption mind (appanā-citta) belonging to the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere. At that time, the knowledge that arises in that monk together with that absorption mind is called the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsanussati-ñāṇa). 

With the mindfulness associated with that knowledge, he can follow and recollect his past manifold previous existences [Note 3]. [What is that sequence of aggregates? It is as follows: He recollects one birth [Note 4], two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of world-contraction and expansion. (He recollects:) 'In such a place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a life-span. Passing away from there, I reappeared in such a place. There too I had such a name... (etc.)... and such a life-span.' Thus, with their aspects and particulars, he can follow and recollect his manifold previous existences.]

[Note 1: Such a person... in the same way... rising... no longer reflecting on what was already reflected—connect these phrases accordingly.]

[Note 2: When... the mind-door advertence arises; when that has ceased... impulsions occur; at that time—connect these phrases accordingly.]

[Note 3: The text in these brackets is the translation of the Pali: 'Seyyathidaṃ, ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo... pe... iti sākāraṃ sa-uddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati' as cited in the Visuddhimagga.]

[Note 4: 'Ekampi jātiṃ'—this phrase is translated by reversing the order to make the Myanmar phrasing smooth while maintaining the collective numbering and grammatical function.]

404. In that passage, 'one birth' (ekampi jātiṃ) means one continuity of aggregates included within a single existence, starting from rebirth-linking and ending in death. The same method applies to 'two births' and so on. In the phrase 'many aeons of world-contraction' (aneke pi saṃvaṭṭakappe) and so on, it should be understood that the aeon that is decreasing and being destroyed is the aeon of contraction (saṃvaṭṭakappa), and the aeon that is increasing and evolving is the aeon of expansion (vivaṭṭakappa).
44:
In that context, by the term 'aeon of contraction' (saṃvaṭṭa), the 'aeon of the duration of contraction' (saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī) is also included, because it has that contraction as its root. Similarly, by 'aeon of expansion' (vivaṭṭa), the 'aeon of the duration of expansion' (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī) is also included. When taken in this way, the incalculable aeons (asaṅkhyeyya-kappa) mentioned as: "Monks, there are these four incalculable aeons. Which four? The contraction, the duration of contraction, the expansion, and the duration of expansion" are fully encompassed.

Among those four aeons, the aeons of destruction called contraction (saṃvaṭṭa) are of three kinds: (1) contraction by fire (tejo-saṃvaṭṭa), (2) contraction by water (āpo-saṃvaṭṭa), and (3) contraction by air (vāyo-saṃvaṭṭa). The three limits of contraction (saṃvaṭṭa-sīmā) are the Ābhassara realm, the Subhakiṇha realm, and the Vehapphala realm.

When the world is destroyed by fire, it burns and is destroyed from the Ābhassara realm downwards (the Ābhassara realm itself is not destroyed). When it is destroyed by water, it is dissolved and destroyed from the Subhakiṇha realm downwards (the Subhakiṇha realm itself is not destroyed). When it is destroyed by air, it is dispersed and destroyed from the Vehapphala realm downwards (the Vehapphala realm itself is not destroyed). In terms of the broad surrounding area, every time there is destruction, the entire Buddha-field (Buddha-khetta)—which consists of a hundred billion world-systems—is destroyed.

There are three kinds of Buddha-fields: (1) the birth-field (jātikkhetta), (2) the authority-field (āṇākkhetta), and (3) the range-field (visayakkhetta). Among these, the birth-field extends to ten thousand world-systems; this birth-field trembles at the time of the Bodhisatta's final rebirth-linking and so forth. The authority-field extends to a hundred billion world-systems; in this authority-field, the power of the protective chants (parittas) such as the Ratana Sutta, Khandha Paritta, Dhajagga Paritta, Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, and Mora Paritta prevails. The range-field is infinite and immeasurable; regarding this range-field, it is said: "As far as he wishes, he can make his voice known." In this range-field, the Buddha knows whatever he wishes to know. Among these three Buddha-fields, one authority-field is destroyed. When that authority-field is destroyed, the birth-field included within it is also destroyed. When they are destroyed, they are destroyed together; when they are established, they are established together. The destruction and establishment of that aeon should be understood as follows.

## The Destruction of the World by Fire

405. At the time when the aeon is destroyed by fire, at the very beginning, a great world-destroying cloud arises and rains a single great rain throughout a hundred billion world-systems. People, being delighted, bring out all kinds of seeds and sow them. When the crops have grown just enough for a cow to graze, a sound like the braying of a donkey is heard, and not even a single drop of rain falls anymore. From that time on, the rain is completely cut off. Referring to this very event, the Blessed One said:

"Monks, there comes a time when for many years, for many [45] hundreds of years, for many thousands of years, for many hundreds of thousands of years, it does not rain."
45:
Beings who live depending on rain die and are reborn in the Brahma world; the deities who live depending on flowers and fruits also (pass away and are reborn in the Brahma world). When a long period of time has passed in this manner, the water in various places reaches exhaustion. Then, gradually [1], even the fish and turtles die and are reborn in the Brahma world; the beings in hell also (are reborn in the Brahma world). Among those beings, some teachers (eke) say that the beings in hell perish when the seventh sun appears.

There is no such thing as being reborn in the Brahma world without attaining jhāna. Among the aforementioned humans and others, some beings are oppressed by the danger of famine.

Note
1. Gradually—by this word, it is shown that it does not happen all at once, but occurs bit by bit, with some earlier and some later. This should be understood similarly in subsequent instances.

Some beings are not worthy of attaining jhāna; how then are they reborn in the Brahma world? They are reborn through the power of jhāna attained in the deva world. The way it happens is that at that time, the Kāmāvacara devas known as Loka-byūha, with loosened topknots, disheveled hair, weeping faces, wiping away tears with their hands, wearing red garments, and assuming a very distorted and terrifying appearance, wander through the paths of humans and proclaim: "Friends, one hundred thousand years from now, the destruction of the world (kappa-vuṭṭhāna) will occur. This entire world will perish. Even the great ocean will dry up. This great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will be burnt up and destroyed. The destruction of the world will reach as far as the Brahma world. Friends, develop loving-kindness (mettā); friends, develop compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā). Support your mother, support your father, and be respectful to the elders in the family."

Hearing the words of those Loka-byūha devas, most humans and earth-bound deities (bhummā devatā) are moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Having gentle hearts toward one another, they perform meritorious deeds such as mettā and are reborn in the deva world. In that deva world, they eat divine food (sudhā-bhojana), perform preliminary work (parikamma) on the air-kasina (vāyo-kasiṇa), and attain jhāna. Other beings (other than humans and earth-bound deities), however, are reborn in the deva world through kamma to be experienced in a future life (aparāpariya-vedanīya kamma). Indeed, there is no being wandering in saṃsāra who is devoid of aparāpariya-vedanīya kamma. Those beings also attain jhāna in that deva world in the same way. Thus, through the power of jhāna attained in the deva world, all beings are reborn in the Brahma world. Here ends one section.

To continue the description of the world's destruction: After a long period of time following the cessation of the world-destroying rain, a second sun appears. Indeed, there is this statement taught by the Blessed One:

"Monks, there comes a time..." Thus, the Sattasūriya Sutta should be understood in detail.

When that second sun appears, [46] the distinction between night and day is no longer perceived.
46:
When one sun sets, another sun appears [1]. In the world, there is only continuous heat from the sun. Just as there is a sun-deity (Suriya-devaputta) in the normal sun, there is no such deity in the world-destroying sun. Between these two, while the normal sun is shining, clouds and streaks of smoke move in the sky. When the world-destroying sun is shining, the sky is free from smoke and clouds, and is as pure as the surface of a mirror. Except for the five great rivers [2], the water in other small rivers and such dries up.

Note
1. The order of rising and setting has been reversed from the original to flow better with the preceding and following sentences.
2. According to the suttas taught in Middle India, only the five great rivers famous in Middle India—Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Mahī, and Sarabhū—are shown. Other similar great rivers should be understood in the same way.

After a long period of time following that, a third sun appears. Due to the appearance of this third sun, even the great rivers dry up.

After a long period of time following that, a fourth sun appears. Due to the appearance of this fourth sun, the seven great lakes in the Himālaya, which are the sources of the (five) great rivers—namely, Sīhapapāta, Haṃsapātana, Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Anotatta, Chaddanta, and Kuṇāla—dry up.

After a long period of time following that, a fifth sun appears. Due to the appearance of this fifth sun, the water in the ocean gradually dries up until not even enough remains to wet a finger-joint.

After a long period of time following that, a sixth sun appears. Due to the appearance of this sixth sun, the entire world-system (cakkavāla) becomes filled with a single mass of smoke. Because of the smoke, all moisture is exhausted. Just like this world-system, one hundred thousand million other world-systems also become the same.

After a long period of time following that, a seventh sun appears. Due to the appearance of this seventh sun, this entire world-system, along with one hundred thousand million world-systems, becomes a single sheet of blazing flame. The peaks of Mount Sineru, which are a hundred yojanas or more in extent, crumble and vanish even in the sky. That flame rises and burns the realms of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika). Having burnt the golden mansions, jewel mansions, and ruby mansions in that deva realm, it catches fire in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. In this manner, it catches fire up to the First Jhāna Brahma realm. Having burnt the mansions of the three types of Brahmas in that First Jhāna realm, it reaches and stays at the Ābhassara realm (which is on the same level as Parittābhā and Appamāṇābhā). That flame does not go out as long as there is even an atom of conditioned formation (saṅkhāra) remaining.
47:
When all physical formations are exhausted, it extinguishes without leaving even ashes, like a flame burning ghee or oil. The lower sky and the upper sky become one, in total darkness.

## The Evolution of the World

406. Then, after a long period of time, a great cloud arises and first rains down very finely. Gradually, it rains with torrents the size of lotus stalks, pestles, and palm trunks, filling all the burnt places in the hundred thousand crores of world systems, and then it ceases and disappears. Below and all around that water, a great mass of wind arises and makes the water a single mass, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. How does it make such a vast mass of water a single mass? By providing openings. Indeed, that wind provides openings to that mass of water in various places. Thus, being compressed and solidified by the wind, the water gradually recedes and descends. As the water recedes further and further, the Brahma realms appear in the place of the Brahma worlds, and the Deva realms appear in the place of the four higher sense-sphere heavens up to Yāma.

When it reaches the place where the previous earth stood, powerful winds arise. These powerful winds block the water, making it breathless like water held in a water-filter (dhammakaraṇa) with its top opening closed. As the sweet water is exhausted and recedes, the earth-essence (rasa-pathavī) arises on the surface. It is endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, like the film on the surface of thick milk-rice without water.

Note: 1. According to the sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) which explains 'taṃ udakaṃ' and 'assa vātassa', it should be translated as 'that mass of water to that wind'.

At that time, beings who were first reborn in the Ābhassara Brahma realm, having passed away from there due to the exhaustion of their lifespan or merit, are reborn here. These beings are self-luminous and travel through the air. Following the method described in the Aggañña Sutta, they taste that earth-essence, and being overcome by craving, they begin to eat it greedily. Then their self-luminance disappears, and darkness falls. Seeing the darkness, they are afraid.

Then, to dispel their fear and generate courage, the sun's orb (suriya-maṇḍala), fifty yojanas in diameter, appears. Seeing the sun, they are joyful and glad, thinking, 'We have obtained light.' They name it 'Suriya' because it arose to dispel their fear and generate courage (sūra-bhāva).

Note: 1. Scientists say the sun is about 864,393 miles in diameter. It is worth considering whether such a large sun appeared suddenly at that moment or had existed before. It is reasonable to assume that it existed before, but because the beings were self-luminous, they did not notice it. Only when their own light disappeared and they longed for light did the sun's orb appear to them.
48:
They thought, 'It has arisen to dispel our fear and generate courage, so let it be named Suriya.' Thus they gave it the name Suriya.

Then, after the sun had provided light for the day and set, they thought, 'The light we obtained has also disappeared,' and they were afraid again. They thought, 'It would be good if we could obtain another light.' As if knowing their thought, the moon's orb (canda-maṇḍala), forty-nine yojanas in diameter, appeared. Seeing it, they were even more joyful and glad, thinking, 'It has arisen as if knowing our desire (chanda), so let it be named Canda.' Thus they gave it the name Canda. When the moon and sun had thus appeared, the constellations and stars appeared.

Note: 1. Scientists state that stars are suns from other world systems. In that sense, it is reasonable to assume that the constellations and stars existed before, but were not noticed while beings relied on their own light. They only became apparent when their own light disappeared.

From that time on, night and day were known, and gradually fortnights, months, seasons, and years. On the very day the moon and sun appeared, Mount Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, and the Himavanta mountains also appeared. They appeared simultaneously on the full moon day of Phagguna. How? Just as when millet rice is being cooked, bubbles rise all at once; some places rise high, some are low and indented, and some are level. In the same way, mountains formed in the high places, oceans in the low places, and islands in the level places.

Then, as those beings continued to eat the earth-essence, gradually some became beautiful and some became ugly. Those who were beautiful looked down upon those who were ugly. Because of their excessive pride and contempt, that earth-essence disappeared. Then the earth-crust (bhūmi-pappaṭaka) appeared. Then, by the same process of pride, that also disappeared. Then the 'padālatā' creeper appeared. By the same process, that also disappeared. Then self-ripening rice (sāli) appeared, without husk or powder, pure and fragrant.

Then vessels appeared for them. They placed the rice in the vessels and set them on stone slabs; a flame arose spontaneously and cooked it. That rice was beautiful and white like jasmine buds; there was no need for soup or curry. Whatever flavor they desired to eat, that very flavor arose. However, from the time they began to consume that coarse food, excrement and urine were produced. Then, for the purpose of discharging it, the orifices of the body broke open; the male sex appeared in the male, and the female sex appeared in the female.
49:
At that time, for the purpose of discharging excrement and urine, apertures appeared in those people. In the male, male characteristics appeared, and in the female, female characteristics appeared.

[49] When these appeared, the woman gazed intently at the man for a long time, and the man gazed intently at the woman for a long time. Because of this long and intent gazing, the burning of sensual lust arose in them. Due to that arising, they engaged in sexual intercourse. Because of their indulgence in this unwholesome practice (asaddhamma), which is not the way of the virtuous, the wise censured them. (They were harassed by being pelted with dust, ashes, and cow dung.) Therefore, to conceal that unwholesome practice, they built houses. While living in houses, in due course, they followed the example of a certain lazy being and began to hoard and store up food.

Note:
1. While others went to the rice fields to take only enough for one day, a lazy person took enough for two days. Following this example, they began taking enough for two days, three days, and so on.

From that time onwards, both fine and coarse husks enveloped the rice grains, and the rice no longer regrew in the places where it had been harvested.

Those people gathered together and lamented: "Alas, wicked things have appeared among beings! Formerly, we were mind-made (having spontaneous births), and we fed on joy (pīti)." This should be understood in detail according to the method taught in the Aggañña Sutta. After that, they established boundaries for the rice fields. Then, a certain being stole the portion of rice belonging to another. They rebuked him twice, and on the third time he stole, they struck him with hands, clods of earth, and sticks. When such things as theft, censure, lying, and the taking up of sticks occurred, those people gathered and deliberated: "Friends, what if we were to elect one being (as a leader)? He would rightly censure those who should be censured, blame those who should be blamed, and banish those who should be banished. We, in turn, shall provide him with a portion (a tenth) of our rice."

Among those beings who had thus deliberated and reached a decision, the Blessed One himself, who was then a Bodhisatta in this very eon, was the most handsome, the most pleasant to behold, the most majestic, endowed with wisdom, and capable of exercising restraint and encouragement. They approached that Bodhisatta, made their request, and elected him. He was known by three names: "Mahāsammata" because he was elected by the great multitude; "Khattiya" because he was the lord of the fields; and "Rājā" (King) because he delighted others in accordance with the law. Indeed, whatever wonderful station exists in the world, the Bodhisatta is the very first person in that station. Thus, with the Bodhisatta as the first person, the circle of the Khattiya (warrior-noble) caste was established, and subsequently, the castes of Brāhmaṇas and others were formed and established.
50:
In the process of the world's destruction and re-establishment, the period from the falling of the great cloud of world-destruction until the cessation of the flames is called the one incalculable eon of "Saṃvaṭṭa" (Dissolution).

[50] The period from the cessation of the flames that destroy the world until the falling of the great world-forming rain that fills and completes a hundred thousand crores of world-systems is called the second incalculable eon of "Saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī" (Duration of Dissolution).

The period from the falling of the great world-forming rain until the appearance of the moon and sun is called the third incalculable eon of "Vivaṭṭa" (Evolution).

The period from the appearance of the moon and sun until the falling of the great cloud of world-destruction again is called the fourth incalculable eon of "Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī" (Duration of Evolution). These four incalculable eons constitute one Great Eon (Mahākappa). Thus, the destruction by fire and the re-establishment of the world should be understood.

## Destruction of the World by Water

407. Furthermore, at the time when the world is destroyed by water, it should be understood in detail according to the method previously mentioned, starting from the arising of the great cloud of world-destruction. However, the following is the distinction: just as the second sun appeared in the destruction by fire, so in this destruction by water, a great rain of corrosive water (khārudaka) falls. Initially, it falls as a very fine drizzle, and then,

Note:
1. In this Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī eon, there are 64 intermediate eons (antarakappa). When the human lifespan decreases from an incalculable age to ten years, many people perish through one of the three calamities: the eon of disease (rogantara), the eon of weapons (satthantara), or the eon of famine (dubbhikkhantara). The few remaining people then cultivate wholesome qualities, and the lifespan increases from ten years back to an incalculable age. One such cycle of decrease and increase is called one intermediate eon. There are 64 such eons. According to some teachers (keci-vāda), there are 20 such intermediate eons. It should be understood that the other three incalculable eons are equal in duration to this Vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī incalculable eon.

gradually increasing, it falls in great torrents, filling a hundred thousand crores of world-systems. Wherever the extremely corrosive rainwater touches, the earth, mountains, and so on, crumble and perish. The water is held in place from all sides by the winds. The corrosive water reaches from the earth up to the second jhāna Brahma realms. In those Brahma realms, it dissolves the three Brahma worlds—Parittābha, Appamāṇābha, and Ābhassara—and stops upon reaching the Subhakiṇhā realm (becoming level with the Parittasubha and Appamāṇasubha realms). As long as even a minute amount of conditioned formations (saṅkhāra) remains, that corrosive water does not subside or disappear. But after it has overwhelmed and destroyed all conditioned formations touched by the water of world-destruction, it suddenly and quickly subsides and vanishes. The lower space and the upper space become one, enveloped in total darkness. All other details are the same as previously described. The only difference here is that when the world re-emerges after destruction by water, the world appears starting from the Ābhassara Brahma realm. Furthermore, beings pass away from the Subhakiṇhā realm and are reborn in places such as the Ābhassara realm.
51:
In the event of such world-destruction, from the time the great cloud of world-destruction rains until the cessation of the salty rain of world-destruction, this one incalculable aeon (asaṅkhyeyya-kappa) should be known as the aeon of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭa-kappa). From the cessation of the salty rain until the great cloud of world-recreation rains, this second incalculable aeon should be known as the aeon of remaining dissolved (saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī-kappa). From the raining of the great cloud of world-recreation until the appearance of the moon and sun, this third incalculable aeon should be known as the aeon of evolution (vivaṭṭa-kappa).

From the appearance of the moon and sun until the great cloud of world-destruction rains again, this fourth incalculable aeon should be known as the aeon of remaining evolved (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī-kappa). These four incalculable aeons constitute one great aeon (mahākappa). As previously explained, the destruction and re-establishment of the world by water should be understood.

## Destruction of the World by Wind

[51] 408. Furthermore, at the time when the world is destroyed by wind, from the very beginning, the great cloud of world-destruction arises; this should be understood in detail according to the method previously mentioned. However, this is the distinction: just as the second sun appeared in the destruction by fire, so here, wind arises for the purpose of destroying the world. First, it raises coarse dust, then fine dust, fine sand, coarse sand, pebbles, stones, and so on, up to rocks as large as gabled houses, and great trees standing on uneven ground. Having risen from the earth into the sky, these rocks and trees do not fall back but are pulverized into powder right there in the sky and vanish.

Then, in due course, wind arises beneath the great earth, turns the earth upside down, and tosses it into the sky. Regions of earth measuring a hundred yojanas, or two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred yojanas, break apart and, being tossed by the force of the wind, are pulverized in the sky and vanish. The wind lifts the Cakkavāḷa mountains and Mount Sineru and tosses them into the sky. These Cakkavāḷa and Sineru mountains strike against one another, are pulverized, and perish. In this same manner, destroying the mansions on the ground and the mansions in the sky, it destroys the six deva worlds of the sense sphere and a hundred thousand million (koṭi-sata-sahassa) world systems. In those hundred thousand million world systems, Cakkavāḷa mountains strike Cakkavāḷa mountains, Himavanta mountains strike Himavanta mountains, and Sineru mountains strike Sineru mountains, becoming pulverized and perishing. The wind carries and blows from the earth up to the third jhāna plane. There, it destroys the three Brahma worlds and stops upon reaching the Vehapphala plane. Having thus destroyed all conditioned things (saṅkhāra), the wind itself vanishes. The lower sky and the upper sky become one, in total darkness. All this is similar to what has been said. The distinction here is that the world manifests starting from the Subhakiṇha Brahma world. Furthermore, passing away from the Vehapphala plane, beings are reborn in the Subhakiṇha plane and so on.

In the event of the world's destruction, from the time the great cloud of world-destruction rains until the cessation of the wind of world-destruction, this one incalculable aeon should be known as the aeon of dissolution (saṃvaṭṭa-kappa). From the cessation of the wind of world-destruction until the great cloud of world-recreation rains, this second incalculable aeon should be known as the aeon of remaining dissolved (saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī-kappa). From the raining of the great cloud of world-recreation until the appearance of the moon and sun, this third incalculable aeon should be known as the aeon of evolution (vivaṭṭa-kappa).
52:
From the appearance of the moon and sun until the great cloud of world-destruction rains again, this fourth incalculable aeon should be known as the aeon of remaining evolved (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī-kappa). These four incalculable aeons constitute one great aeon (mahākappa). As previously explained, the destruction and re-establishment of the world by wind should be understood.

## Causes of World Destruction, etc.

[52] 409. For what reason does the world perish in this way? It perishes because of the unwholesome roots (akusala-mūla). To elaborate, when the three unwholesome roots are abundant, the world perishes in this manner. Among them, when greed (rāga) is more excessive, it perishes by fire. When hatred (dosa) is more excessive, it perishes by water. Some, however, say that when hatred is more excessive, it perishes by fire, and when greed is more excessive, it perishes by water. When delusion (moha) is more excessive, it perishes by wind. Even in perishing thus, it perishes by fire for seven consecutive times, and on the eighth time, it perishes by water. Again, it perishes by fire for seven times, and on the eighth time, by water. In this way, perishing by water every eighth time, after it has perished by water seven times, it again perishes by fire for seven times. By this point, sixty-three aeons have passed. Then, when the turn to perish by water arrives, the wind finds its opportunity and destroys the world, including the Subhakiṇha planes where the lifespan is a full sixty-four aeons.

410. To continue with the commentary: a bhikkhu who, recollecting his former dwellings, follows the sequence of the aggregates (khandha) and remembers, also recollects many aeons of dissolution, many aeons of evolution, and many aeons of dissolution and evolution among these aforementioned aeons. How? In the manner beginning with "There I was..." (amutrāsiṃ).

In that context of recollection, "There I was" means: "In such-and-such an aeon of dissolution (Note 1), I was in such-and-such a birth, or womb, or destination (gati), or station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), or abode of beings (sattāvāsa), or community of beings." "Such was my name" means he was named Tissa or Phussa. "Such was my clan" means he was of the Kaccāna clan or the Kassapa clan. These two phrases (Note 2) are taught in terms of the bhikkhu's recollection of his own name and clan in a past life. Furthermore, if he wishes to recollect his perfection of appearance, his coarse or fine livelihood, his abundance of pleasure or pain, or his short or long lifespan in that past life, he can indeed recollect all of that. Therefore, it is said: "Such was my appearance... such was the end of my lifespan."

Notes:
1. In the aeon of dissolution, beings exist only in the Brahma worlds; therefore, this statement should be taken as a mere example for recollection in other aeons as well.
2. Connect this with "taught in terms of... recollection."

In that context, "Such was my appearance" means he had a fair complexion or a dark/golden-brown complexion, and so on. "Such was my food" means his food was rice and meat, or his food was naturally occurring fruits, and so on. "Such was my experience of pleasure and pain" means he experienced various kinds of bodily and mental pleasure and pain, categorized as being connected with or detached from sensual desires, and so on.
53:
‘Such was the life-span’ means a life-span of a hundred years or a life-span of eighty-four thousand aeons (and so forth). ‘Passing away from that life, I was reborn in such a place’ means that I [53] passed away from that existence, from that womb, from that destination, from that station of consciousness, from that abode of beings, or from that group of beings, and was reborn again in such an existence, womb, destination, station of consciousness, abode of beings, or group of beings. ‘There too I was’ means that in that existence too, in that womb, destination, station of consciousness, or abode of beings, and in that group of beings, I was reborn again. ‘Such was my name’ and so forth is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

Alternatively, to explain: ‘I was in such a place’ (amutrāsiṃ)—this kind of recollection is the recollection that follows back through previous times in succession as far as one desires. ‘Passing away from there’ (so tato cuto)—this kind of reflection is the reviewing as one returns. Therefore, by the words ‘reborn here’ (idhūpapanno), it should be understood that the phrase ‘I was reborn in such a place’ (amutra udapādiṃ) is spoken with reference to the place of rebirth immediately preceding this life. The phrase ‘There too I was’ (tatrāpāsiṃ) and so forth is stated to show the monk's recollection of the name, clan, etc., in the existence immediately preceding this final existence. ‘Passing away from there, I was reborn here’ (so tato cuto idhūpapanno) means ‘Passing away from that immediately preceding place of rebirth, I was born in this present life in such a khattiya family or such a brāhmaṇa family.’ ‘Thus’ (iti) means in the manner described. ‘With their aspects and particulars’ (sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ) means with particulars in terms of name and clan, and with aspects in terms of appearance and so forth. Indeed, by name and clan, a being is designated as ‘Tissa’ or ‘Kassapa’ and so on. By appearance and so forth, they are known through distinctions such as being dark-skinned, fair-skinned, or yellow-skinned. Therefore, name and clan are called ‘particulars’ (uddesa). The others, such as appearance and so forth, are called ‘aspects’ (ākāra). The concluding statement ‘He recollects his manifold past lives’ (anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati) has a clear and obvious meaning. This section ends here.

## The Exposition on the Knowledge of Recollecting Past Lives is Finished.

Note: 1. Connect this with the phrase 'stated to show...'

## Exposition on the Knowledge of the Passing Away and Rebirth of Beings, known as the Divine Eye

411. In the passage explaining the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, ‘for the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth’ (cutūpapātañāṇāya) means for the passing away and for the rebirth. The knowledge by which the passing away and rebirth of beings is known is meant by the term ‘knowledge of the divine eye’.

Note: 1. This refers to the opening of the term 'cutūpapātañāṇāya' from the Buddha's words: 'With the mind thus concentrated... he directs and inclines his mind to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; he understands how beings pass according to their actions: "These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct by body, speech, and mind, revilers of noble ones, holders of wrong view, undertaking actions based on wrong view; with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a state of ruin, even in hell. But these worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of good conduct by body, speech, and mind, not revilers of noble ones, holders of right view, undertaking actions based on right view; with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, even in a heavenly world." Thus with the divine eye, purified... he understands beings.' This term 'cutūpapātañāṇāya' has not yet been explained from the Pali. Later, terms not yet explained from the Pali will also be extracted and explained. To make it easy for those who do not know Pali to understand, I will first provide a summary translation of that Pali.

That monk, having attained the fourth jhāna, when the mind is thus concentrated... and has reached imperturbability, directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
54:
That monk, thus inclining [his mind], with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu)—which is exceptionally purified and surpasses the human eye (or, with the eye of knowledge which is like the divine eye)—sees beings. (What kind of beings does he see?) He sees beings passing away (cuti), beings being reborn (upapatti), the lowly and the noble, the beautiful and the ugly, those who have gone to a happy destination (sugati) and those who have gone to a miserable destination (duggati). He understands beings passing according to their kamma (yathākammūpage): 'Friends, these beings were endowed with misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views. At the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of deprivation, an unhappy destination, the abyss, or hell. But these beings, friends, were endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind; they were not revilers of the noble ones, held right views, and undertook actions based on right views. At the breaking up of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a happy destination, in the heavenly world.' Thus, with the purified divine eye... he understands beings. (This is the translation of the Pali for the knowledge of the divine eye.)

Because it is produced by the merit of good conduct (sucarita-kamma), it is not disturbed by bile, phlegm, blood, etc., and is thus free from impurities. Therefore, it is capable of receiving and seeing objects even at a distance. This eye of knowledge [called the divine eye] is also like that divine eye because it is produced by the power of the development of energy [54]. Because it is thus like the divine eye, it is called the 'divine eye' (dibba-cakkhu). Alternatively, it is called 'divine' (dibba) because it is obtained by the power of the jhāna called 'divine abiding' (dibba-vihāra), and because he himself relies on that divine abiding. It is also called 'divine' because it has great radiance through the grasping of the light-kasiṇa (āloka-kasiṇa). It is also called 'divine' because it has a marvelous range of movement, seeing forms situated behind walls and so forth. All these [derivations of the word 'divine'] should be understood according to the science of grammar.

It is called an 'eye' (cakkhu) because of the sense of seeing. Alternatively, it is called an 'eye' because it is like an eye by performing the function of seeing. It is 'purified' (visuddha) because it is the cause for the purification of view by seeing the passing away (cuti) and the reappearing (upapatti). Indeed, one who sees only the passing away and not the reappearing holds the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi), thinking that one is cut off after death. One who sees only the reappearing and not the passing away from a previous life holds the view that a new being has appeared. But one who sees both transcends both of those wrong views. Therefore, that monk's knowledge of seeing passing away and rebirth is the cause for the purification of view. The sons of the Buddha (monks) see both of these; therefore, I have explained: 'It is purified because it is the cause for the purification of view by seeing the passing away and the reappearing.'

It is said to 'surpass the human' (atikkantamānusaka) because it can see forms beyond the range of ordinary humans and the coarse forms they see, such as distant forms, hidden forms, and subtle divine forms. Alternatively, it is called 'surpassing the human' because it surpasses the natural human eye (maṃsa-cakkhu). (This means: 'with that divine eye which is purified and surpasses the human eye'). 'He sees beings' means he observes beings just as one would with the natural human eye.

[Note 1: Shown as derived from the root divu in the sense of radiance (juti); in this sense, dibbeṇa should be translated as 'radiant'.]

[Note 2: Shown as derived from the root divu in the sense of movement (gati); in this sense, dibbeṇa should be translated as 'able to go through or see through walls, mountains, etc.']

'Lowly' (hīna) means despised, looked down upon, or ignored due to birth, family, or wealth that is inferior because it is the result of delusion (moha). 'Noble' (paṇīta) is the opposite, being the result of non-delusion. 'Beautiful' (suvaṇṇa) means having a desirable, lovely, and pleasing complexion because it is the result of non-hatred (adosa). 'Ugly' (dubbaṇṇa) means having an undesirable, unlovely, and unpleasing complexion because it is the result of hatred (dosa); it also means 'deformed'. 'Well-faring' (sugata) means gone to a happy destination (sugati); or it means wealthy and of great riches because it is the result of non-greed (alobha). 'Ill-faring' (duggata) means gone to an unhappy destination (duggati); or it means poor with little food and drink because it is the result of greed (lobha).

'Passing according to their kamma' (yathākammūpage) means approaching [a destination] according to whatever kamma has been accumulated. Here, the function of the divine eye was stated by the previous words 'passing away', etc. But by this phrase [yathākammūpage], the function of the 'knowledge of passing according to kamma' is stated. And this is the order of the arising of that knowledge: here, the monk...
55:
Having explained the meanings of the terms *visuddha* (purified) and *atikkantamānusaka* (surpassing that of humans), this is an inflectional explanation (*vibhatyanta*) that returns to the original case endings. While it is of great benefit in the Pali language, it is not so in the Burmese translation; however, to ensure the completeness of the *Visuddhimagga*, that explanation is also demarcated and shown within parentheses.

In these two terms, 'passing away' (*cavamāna*) and 'being reborn' (*upapajjamāna*), it is not possible to see with the divine eye at the exact moment of death with the death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*), nor at the exact moment of rebirth with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-citta*). However, those who are nearing death and will pass away shortly are called 'passing away' (*cavamāna*). Those who have taken rebirth and have just been born are called 'being reborn' (*upapajjamāna*). Thus, it is shown that one sees those beings who are passing away and being reborn.

'Inferior' (*hīna*) means those who are despised and looked down upon by way of birth, class, wealth, etc., because they are associated with the consequences of delusion (*moha*). 'Superior' (*paṇīta*) means the opposite of inferior because they are associated with the consequences of non-delusion (*amoha*). 'Beautiful' (*suvaṇṇa*) means endowed with a desirable, pleasing, and lovely appearance because they are associated with the consequences of non-hatred (*adosa*). 'Ugly' (*dubbaṇṇa*) means endowed with an undesirable, unpleasing, and hateful appearance because they are associated with the consequences of hatred (*dosa*). 'Faring well' (*sugata*) means those who have reached a happy destination (*sugati*); alternatively, it means those who are wealthy and have great possessions because they are associated with the consequences of non-greed (*alobha*). 'Faring ill' (*duggata*) means those who have reached a miserable destination (*duggati*); alternatively, it means those who are poor, destitute, and lack food because they are associated with the consequences of greed (*lobha*).

'Faring according to kamma' (*yathākammūpaga*) means approaching (a new existence) by means of whatever kamma they have performed and accumulated.

Among these, the function of the divine eye (*dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa*) is stated by the preceding qualifying terms such as 'passing away' (*cavamāne*), etc. However, by this term ['faring according to kamma' (*yathākammūpaga*)], the function of the knowledge of faring according to kamma (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*) is stated. The following is the sequence of how that knowledge arises: In this Dispensation, a monk extends light downwards [55] towards the hell realms and sees the beings in hell experiencing great suffering. Such seeing is solely the function of the divine eye. That monk then reflects: 'By performing what kind of kamma do these beings experience such suffering?' Then, the knowledge having that kamma as its object arises in that monk, thinking: 'By performing such and such kamma.' Similarly, he extends light upwards towards the celestial realms and sees beings in the Nandana Grove, Missaka Grove, Phārusaka Grove, etc., experiencing great prosperity. Such seeing is also solely the function of the divine eye. That monk then reflects: 'By performing what kind of kamma do these beings experience such prosperity?' Then, the knowledge having that kamma as its object arises in that monk, thinking: 'By performing such and such kamma.' This knowledge is called 'knowledge of faring according to kamma' (*yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa*). For this knowledge, there is no separate preliminary work (*parikamma*). Just as in the case of this knowledge, there is also no separate preliminary work for the 'knowledge of the future' (*anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa*). These two knowledges have the divine eye as their basis and are accomplished only along with the divine eye.

In 'bodily misconduct' (*kāya-duccarita*), etc., an action practiced badly or wickedly is called misconduct (*duccarita*). Alternatively, a practice that is corrupt due to the putridity of defilements is called misconduct. Misconduct (committed) by way of the body is bodily misconduct. Alternatively, misconduct arising from the bodily door is bodily misconduct. The same method applies to verbal misconduct (*vacī-duccarita*), etc. 'Are endowed with' (*samannāgatā*) means they are possessed of. 'Revilers of Noble Ones' (*ariyānaṃ upavādaka*) means those who, desiring harm, revile, abuse, or disparage Noble Ones—the Buddha, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha, down to even lay stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*)—either by way of a 'final matter' (an offense involving loss of monkhood) or by disparaging their qualities such as jhāna, etc. In this context, one who says, 'These people have no recluse-dharma; they are not recluses,' is said to revile by way of a 'final matter'. One who says, 'They have no jhāna, liberation, path, or fruit,' is to be understood as reviling by way of disparaging their qualities. Whether he reviles knowingly or unknowingly, in both cases, it is a reviling of Noble Ones (*ariyūpavāda*). It is a heavy kamma, similar to the immediate kamma (*ānantariya*), and is an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the Path; however, it is remediable. To clarify this, the following story should be understood.

It is said that in a certain village, an elder and a young monk were wandering for alms. At the very first house, they received a ladleful of hot gruel. The elder was suffering from wind-pains in his stomach. He thought: 'This gruel is suitable for me; I will drink it before it gets cold.' He sat on a piece of wood brought by people for a doorsill and drank it. The other monk, feeling disgusted, said: 'This old man is overcome by excessive hunger; he has done something shameful for us.'
56:
It is beneficial only in Pāḷi. It is shown just for the sake of completeness.

3. Connect it as: "They revile even a lay Stream-enterer (*Sotāpanna*)." If one reviles in such a way, it should be known that it constitutes the kamma of reviling a Noble One (*ariyūpavāda-kamma*).

One who says things like "These people have no meditative absorption (*jhāna*), no liberation (*vimokkha*), no path (*magga*), or no fruition (*phala*)," with the intent to disparage their virtues, is said to revile by way of destroying reputation. Whether that person reviles knowingly or unknowingly, in both ways, they incur the kamma of reviling a Noble One. It is a heavy kamma, similar to the *ānantariya* kammas; it obstructs the way to heaven and obstructs the Path. However, it can still be remedied. To clearly understand this *ariyūpavāda-kamma*, the following story should be known:

In a certain village, an elder monk (*thera*) and a young monk were wandering for alms. At the very first house, they received a ladleful of hot gruel. The elder monk was suffering from wind ailment in his stomach. Therefore, thinking, "This gruel is suitable for me; I will drink it before it gets cold," the elder monk sat on a log brought by lay devotees to be used as a doorsill and drank it. The young monk, feeling disgusted by this, said, "This elder is very greedy; he makes us feel ashamed."

After finishing the alms-round in the village and returning to the monastery, the elder monk said to the young monk, "Friend, do you have any footing in this Sāsanā?" "Yes, Bhante, I am a Stream-enterer (*Sotāpanna*)," he replied. "Friend, if so, do not strive for the higher paths anymore; you have reviled an Arahant," the elder said. The young monk then paid homage and asked for forgiveness. Thus, that reviling kamma of the young monk became as it was before, without fault.

Therefore, if any other person reviles a Noble One, that person should go to where the reviled Noble One is. If the reviler is senior, he should sit in a squatting position and ask for forgiveness, saying, "I said such and such to the Venerable; please forgive me for that fault." If the reviler is junior, he should pay homage (with the five-point prostration), sit in a squatting position with palms joined, and ask for forgiveness, saying, "Bhante, I said such and such to you; please forgive me for that fault." If that Noble One has departed to another place, one should go personally or send a resident pupil or someone else to ask for forgiveness.

If it is not possible to go personally or send someone else, one should go to the monks residing in that Noble One's monastery. If they are junior to oneself, one should sit in a squatting position; if they are senior, one should act with respect according to the method mentioned for the elder, and ask for forgiveness, saying, "Bhantes, I said such and such to the Venerable named so-and-so; may that Venerable forgive me." Even if the person does not forgive in one's presence, this same method of asking for forgiveness in their absence should be performed.

If the reviled person is a monk who wanders alone, and his dwelling place or destination is unknown, one should go to a wise monk and say, "Bhante, I said such and such to the Venerable named so-and-so. Remembering those words, I feel remorse; what should I do?" That wise monk will say, "Do not worry; the elder forgives you. Calm your mind." Then, the monk who spoke excessively should face the direction where the Noble One went, join his palms, and say, "Please forgive me." If that Noble One has attained Parinibbāna, one should go to the place where the deathbed was situated, or even to the cemetery where the cremation took place, and ask for forgiveness. When this is done, there is no longer an obstacle to heaven or an obstacle to the Path; it becomes pure as before. Here ends one section.

*Micchādiṭṭhikā* means having perverted and wrong views. *Micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā* means having various types of kamma undertaken and performed by the power of wrong views; those who also incite others to bodily kamma etc., which have wrong view as their root...
57:
1. The use of the plural 'you' instead of the singular 'you' may be intended to encourage one who is depressed, or it may be because there were others who joined in the accusation along with that monk.

2. By this word, the period before cremation is intended; by the subsequent word 'after' (paraṃ), the period during or after cremation is intended.

In such matters, they also urge others (and those who so urge are also called 'those who undertake wrong view and action'). To explain further: by mentioning verbal misconduct, the kamma of insulting Noble Ones (ariyūpavāda) is already included. By mentioning mental misconduct, wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) is already included. Even though they are included, stating these two kammas separately should be understood as serving the purpose of showing their great blame (mahāsāvajjabhāva). Indeed, insulting a Noble One carries great blame because it is similar to the immediate kammas (ānantariya). There is also this statement spoken by the Blessed One:

'Sāriputta, just as a monk possessed of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the path of Arahantship would realize the fruit of Arahantship in this very life, Sāriputta, I say this kamma of insulting Noble Ones is just like that. If one does not abandon that speech, does not abandon that thought, and does not relinquish that view, one is cast into hell just as a burden is laid down.'

(Note: The comparison 'just like that' means that just as the fruit of Arahantship follows the path immediately and certainly, the kamma of insulting a Noble One certainly leads to hell if no apology is made.)

There is no other unwholesome kamma more blameworthy than wrong view. In accordance with this, it was said:

'Monks, I do not see even a single other thing that is so blameworthy as this, namely, monks, wrong view. Monks, wrong views are the most blameworthy of all faults.'

'Kāyassa bhedā' (with the breaking up of the body) means the relinquishing of the grasped aggregates (upādiṇṇakhandha) which are identified as 'my body'. 'Paraṃ maraṇā' (after death) means at the moment of taking up the newly arisen aggregates immediately after relinquishing that body. Alternatively, 'kāyassa bhedā' means the cutting off of the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). 'Paraṃ maraṇā' means after the death-consciousness (cuticitta). The entire sequence of words starting with 'apāya' are all synonyms for hell (niraya).

Indeed, it is called 'apāya' because it is devoid of 'aya'—the merit regarded as the cause for reaching heaven and liberation—or because of the absence of 'aya' as the arrival of happiness. It is called 'duggati' (bad destination) because it is the resort of suffering; or, because of the abundance of faults, unwholesome kamma is called 'duṭṭha' (corrupt), and the destination (gati) produced by that corrupt kamma is 'duggati'. It is called 'vinipāta' (perdition) because those who do evil fall into it involuntarily. (Note: It means a realm where one falls without wishing to fall.)

Alternatively, it is called 'vinipāta' because those who are perishing fall there with their limbs and parts being broken up. It is called 'niraya' (hell) because there is no 'aya' known as enjoyment there.

Alternatively, by the term 'apāya', the animal realm (tiracchānayoni) is indicated. Indeed, the animal realm is an 'apāya' because it is removed from the happy destinations (sugati), but it is not a 'duggati' because of the existence of powerful beings like naga kings. By the term 'duggati', the ghost realm (pettivisaya) is indicated. Indeed, that ghost world is both an 'apāya' and a 'duggati', as it is removed from happy destinations and is a destination of suffering. However, it is not a 'vinipāta' because it is not a downfall like that of the asuras. By the term 'vinipāta', the host of asuras (asurakāya) is indicated. Indeed, according to the stated meaning, it is both an 'apāya' and a 'duggati', and it is called 'vinipāta' because it is a downfall from all types of prosperity. By the term 'niraya', only hell such as Avīci, which has many varieties, is indicated. Here ends one section.

'Upapannā' means they have approached, meaning they are reborn there. The 'white side' (good conduct) such as bodily good conduct should be understood as the opposite of the 'black side' already described.
58:
[58] Only the following point.

Note 1: The section related to wholesome merit is called sukka-pakkha—the bright side; the section related to unwholesome demerit is called kaṇha-pakkha—the dark side.

This is the distinction. In that bright side, by the name sugati (happy destination), the human destination (manussa-gati) is also taken. By the name sagga (heaven), only the celestial destination (deva-gati) is taken. In this context, it is called sugati because it is a good destination. It is called sagga because it is an excellent place due to sense objects such as forms. All these, both sugati and sagga, are called loka (world) because they are subject to disintegration. This is the explanation of the meaning of the terms.

The entire passage beginning with 'Thus with the divine eye' is the concluding statement. 'Thus with the divine eye... he sees'—this is the summary of the meaning here.

412. A clansman who is a beginner and wishes to see in this way should make the basis jhana (pādaka-jhāna), which has a kasina as its object, capable of being directed in every way. He should bring close any one of these three kasinas: the fire kasina (tejo-kasiṇa), the white kasina (odāta-kasiṇa), or the light kasina (āloka-kasiṇa). He should develop it by making it the object of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna). The intention is that he should not yet produce absorption (appanā) in those kasinas. For if he produces absorption, it becomes the basis for the basis jhana, not for the preliminary work (parikamma). Among these three kasinas, the light kasina is the most excellent. Therefore, he should produce either that light kasina or one of the other two according to the method mentioned in the 'Description of Kasinas' and develop it while remaining only on the stage of access concentration. The method of expanding the sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) should also be understood according to the method mentioned in that 'Description of Kasinas'.

He should see forms only within the area he has expanded. While he is looking at forms, the turn for his preliminary work passes. Then the light disappears. When the light disappears, the forms are no longer seen. Then this yogi should repeatedly enter the basis jhana, and after emerging from it, he should diffuse the light. By doing so, the light gradually gains strength. Thus, to whatever extent he delimits the area, saying 'Let there be light here,' the light remains in that very place. Even if he sits and watches all day, the seeing of forms continues. Here, the man traveling with a grass torch at night is the simile.

A certain man was traveling at night with a grass torch. His torch went out. Then the even and uneven places were not clear to him. He rubbed that torch on the ground and made it burn again. That torch, having ignited, produced a light greater than the previous one. In this way, for one who repeatedly ignites the extinguished torch, the sun eventually rises. When the sun has risen, there is no more work for the torch; so, discarding it, he travels even all day. In this simile, the light of the kasina during the preliminary work should be understood as the light of the torch. [59] The inability to see even and uneven places when the torch is extinguished is like the inability to see forms when the light disappears because the turn for preliminary work has passed while one is looking at forms.
59:
Rubbing the torch is like repeatedly entering access concentration. Producing a light greater than the previous one is like the diffusion of a stronger light by the yogi who performs the preliminary work again. The rising of the sun is like the light that has gained strength remaining according to the delimited area. Discarding the grass torch and traveling even all day is like discarding the limited light and seeing forms even all day with the light that has gained strength.

In that seeing, when a form that is not within the range of the fleshly eye (maṃsa-cakkhu) of that monk—such as a form inside the belly based on the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu), or based on the surface under the earth, or a form beyond a wall, a mountain, or a rampart, or a form in another world system—comes into the range of the eye of knowledge (ñāṇa-cakkhu) and becomes as if seen with the fleshly eye, then it should be understood that the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) has arisen. To explain further: among these seeing consciousnesses, only that divine eye knowledge is capable of seeing the form; the preceding consciousnesses of advertence and preliminary work are not capable of seeing the form.

That divine eye can be a danger to a worldling (puthujjana). Why? Because wherever he resolves 'Let there be light,' the light becomes continuous even by penetrating the earth, oceans, and mountains. When that happens, fear arises in that worldling as he sees terrifying forms such as yakkhas and rakkhasas in those lit places. Because of such fear, he reaches a state of mental distraction and his jhana falls away. Therefore, one should be heedful when seeing forms with the divine eye.

In that statement, this is the sequence of the arising of the divine eye knowledge. Having made that form of the aforementioned kind the object, after the mind-door advertence (manodvārāvajjana) has arisen and ceased, four or five javanas arise making that same form the object—all this should be understood in the same way as previously mentioned. Here too, the advertence and the three or four preceding consciousnesses are sense-sphere consciousnesses (kāmāvacara) accompanied by initial and sustained application. The consciousness that accomplishes the task of seeing at the fourth or fifth final stage is a fine-material sphere consciousness (rūpāvacara) associated with the fourth jhana. The knowledge associated with that consciousness is called 'knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings' and also 'divine eye knowledge.' Here ends one section.

## The explanation of the Divine Eye Knowledge called the Knowledge of Passing Away and Rebirth is finished.

## Miscellaneous Explanation

413. Thus the Lord, the Knower of the five aggregates, the true Refuge, has taught those five superknowledges (abhiññā) as mentioned;
60:
After knowing these supernormal knowledges (abhiññā), one should also know the miscellaneous explanation that will now be presented.

[60] To elaborate—among these five supernormal knowledges, there is the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), also known as the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cutūpapāta-ñāṇa). There are also two peripheral knowledges of that divine eye: the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of [beings] passing away according to their kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa). With these two knowledges and the five knowledges such as the modes of supernormal power (iddhividha), there are seven types of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā-ñāṇa) in this context. Now, in order to avoid confusion in the classification of their objects:

One should demonstrate the occurrence of the seven supernormal knowledges within the four triads of objects (ārammaṇa-ttika) taught by the Great Sage (in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī).

In this regard, this is the demonstration. The Great Sage taught four triads of objects. Which four? (1) The triad of limited objects (parittārammaṇa-ttika), (2) the triad of path objects (maggārammaṇa-ttika), (3) the triad of past objects (atītārammaṇa-ttika), and (4) the triad of internal objects (ajjhattārammaṇa-ttika).

414. Among those seven knowledges, the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (iddhividha-ñāṇa) occurs with seven types of objects: limited (sensual) objects, sublime (mahaggata) objects, past objects, future objects, present objects, internal objects, and external objects. How? When that iddhividha-ñāṇa [Note 1] desires to travel with an invisible body by making the physical body dependent on the mind, it inclines the physical body by the power of the mind, and unifies or imposes it upon the sublime mind. At that time, the body, which is referred to as the object of action [Note 2], becomes the object. Thus, because the physical body is the object, it has a limited object (it takes a sensual-sphere phenomenon as its object). When it desires to travel with a visible body by making the mind dependent on the physical body, it inclines the mind by the power of the physical body, and unifies or imposes the basis-jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) mind upon the physical body. At that time, the jhāna mind, which is referred to as the object of action, becomes the object. Thus, because the sublime mind is the object, it has a sublime object (it takes a sublime phenomenon as its object).

Furthermore, that same iddhividha-ñāṇa takes that very basis-jhāna mind, which has ceased in the past, as its object; therefore, it has a past object. For those who make a resolution for the future, such as the Elder Mahākassapa and others at the time of the great enshrinement of the relics, their knowledge has a future object. It is said that when the Elder Mahākassapa was performing the great enshrinement of the relics, he resolved: "In the future, for two hundred and eighteen years, may these perfumes not dry up, may these flowers not wither, and may these lamps not be extinguished." Everything happened exactly according to that resolution. The Elder Assagutta, at the Vattaniya (Viñjhāto) monastery,

Note 1: Connect as "That iddhividha-ñāṇa has sensual phenomena as its object," etc.

Note 2: "Upayogaladdhaṃ"—If translated strictly as "the body which has obtained the accusative case," it would be difficult for those unfamiliar with Pali grammar to understand; therefore, it is translated as above. It means that by saying "it inclines the physical body" as an object, it is the object of the mind that causes the inclination.
61:
seeing the Saṅgha of monks eating dry food without curry, resolved: "Day by day, let the water-tank have the taste of buttermilk in the morning." When [water] is taken in the morning, it is buttermilk; when taken in the evening, it is just ordinary water. Furthermore, [61] when traveling with an invisible body by making the physical body dependent on the mind, [the iddhividha-ñāṇa] has a present object.

At the time of inclining the mind by the power of the body, or the body by the power of the mind, and at the time of creating [an appearance] such as the form of a child for oneself, it has an internal object because it takes one's own body and mind as objects. At the time of creating and showing external forms such as elephants and horses, it has an external object. Thus, the occurrence of the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (iddhividha-ñāṇa) with seven types of objects should be understood.

415. The knowledge of the divine ear (dibba-sota-ñāṇa) occurs with four types of objects: limited (sensual), present, internal, and external. How? Because that knowledge takes sound as its object, and since sound is a limited (sensual) phenomenon, it has a limited object. Furthermore, because it occurs by taking only a currently existing sound as its object, it has a present object. When that knowledge hears the sound from within one's own stomach, it has an internal object. When it hears the sounds of others, it has an external object. Thus, the occurrence of the knowledge of the divine ear with four types of objects should be understood.

416. The knowledge of penetration of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) occurs with eight types of objects: limited (sensual), sublime (mahaggata), immeasurable (appamāṇa/magga), past, future, present, and external.
