How? When that knowledge knows the sensual-sphere (kāmāvacara) minds of others, it has a limited object. When it knows fine-material-sphere or immaterial-sphere minds, it has a sublime object. When it knows the path and fruition, it has an immeasurable object. To explain further: in this context, a worldling (puthujjana) cannot know the mind [Note 1] of a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). A stream-enterer cannot know the mind of a once-returner (sakadāgāmī). A once-returner cannot know the mind of a non-returner (anāgāmī). A non-returner cannot know the mind of an arahant. An arahant, however, can know the minds of all. Also, another person who is higher can know the mind of a lower person; this distinction should also be understood. When it knows a path-mind, it has the path as its object.

However, when it knows the minds of others within seven days in the past or within seven days in the future, then it has a past object or a future object respectively.

How does it have a present mind as its object? What is called "present" is of three kinds: (1) the momentary present (khaṇa-paccuppanna), (2) the continuity present (santati-paccuppanna), and (3) the duration present (addhā-paccuppanna). Among these, a phenomenon that has reached the stages of arising, presence, or dissolution is called the momentary present. A phenomenon included within one or two cycles of physical continuity (rūpa-santati-vāra) is called the continuity present. In that regard, for a person who has been sitting in the dark and goes to a place with light, the object is not clear until it becomes clear; [62] within this interval, one or two cycles of physical continuity should be understood. For a person who has been in the light and enters a room, until the color becomes clear, within this interval, one or two cycles of physical continuity should be understood.

Note 1: This refers only to the path and fruition minds of the stream-enterer; it should be understood that their mundane minds can be known. The same applies to not knowing the minds of those in higher stages.
62:
Furthermore, even when standing at a distance and seeing the hand gestures of washermen or the movements of striking bells and drums, the sound is not yet heard. From that moment of seeing until that sound is heard, within this interval, one or two material continuity-cycles (rūpa-santati-vāra) should be understood. Thus say the Reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya (Majjhima-bhāṇaka) first.

The Reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya (Saṃyutta-bhāṇaka), however (Note 1), having spoken of two kinds of continuity—material continuity and immaterial continuity—say: the period before the water-line made by someone treading in water at the shore becomes clear; the period before the heat in the body of someone who has come from a long journey subsides; the period before the darkness disappears for someone who has entered a room from the sunlight; the period before the flickering of the eyes subsides for someone who, having meditated in a room, opens a window during the day and looks out—this is called material continuity (rūpa-santati). Two or three impulsion-cycles (javana-vāra) are called immaterial continuity (arūpa-santati). They say both of these are 'continuity present' (santati-paccuppanna).

Note
1. Connect 'The Reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya...' with '...say'.

Furthermore, the collection of mind and matter delimited by a single life (from rebirth to death) is called 'duration present' (addhā-paccuppanna). With reference to this duration present, it is stated in the Bhaddekaratta Sutta:
'Friends, whatever mind and whatever phenomena (are manifest at the moment of cognizing), both are the present. If, in that present, consciousness is bound by desire and lust, because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, one delights in that. Delighting in that, one is pulled along (by craving and views) among present phenomena.' To explain further: among these presents, the continuity present appears in the Commentaries. The duration present appears in the Sutta texts.

Among these three types of present, some teachers (keci) say: 'The momentary present mind is the object of the knowledge of penetration of others' minds (ceto-pariya-ñāṇa).' For what reason? Because the mind of the psychic person and the mind of the other arise at the same moment. This is their analogy: just as when a handful of flowers is thrown into the sky, one flower's stalk will certainly pierce another flower's stalk, so too, when one adverts to the minds of a multitude with the intent 'I shall know the minds of others,' one's mind will certainly pierce another's mind at the moment of arising (uppāda-khaṇa), the moment of presence (ṭhiti-khaṇa), or the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-khaṇa).

However, regarding the statement of those teachers (Note 1): whether one adverts for a hundred years or a thousand years, the adverting mind with which one adverts and the superknowledge-impulsion mind (abhiññā-javana) with which one knows—because these two minds do not exist together, and because of the fault of the adverting and impulsion minds having different objects in undesired cases (except for the Path and Fruit processes) (Note 2), this view is rejected in the Commentaries as improper.
63:
Note
1. Connect 'Regarding the statement of those teachers...' with '...is rejected in the Commentaries'.
2. In the Path process, the adverting, preliminary, access, and conformity minds take mundane mind and matter as objects, while the change-of-lineage, Path, and Fruit take Nibbāna as the object. In the Fruit process, the adverting and preliminary impulsions take mundane mind and matter as objects, while the Fruit takes Nibbāna as the object. Only in these Path and Fruit processes is there a tradition of the adverting/base impulsions and the Path/Fruit impulsions having different objects; in other processes, there is no such tradition. The meaning is that it is improper because the objects differ without such a tradition.

The following statement is a clear explanation regarding the knowledge of that present mind. A person with the power of the knowledge of penetration of others' minds, wishing to know another's mind, adverts. The adverting mind (āvajjana), taking the momentary present mind as its object, ceases along with that mind. Then four or five impulsions (javana) arise. Among these, the last impulsion is the supernormal mind (iddhi-citta) that knows the other's mind (the ceto-pariya-abhiññā mind). The remaining three or four impulsions are sense-sphere impulsions (kāmāvacara-javana). That very mind which ceased along with the adverting mind is the object of all those four or five impulsions. These adverting and impulsion minds do not have different objects because they have the present as an object in terms of duration (addhā). Even though they share the same object, only the superknowledge mind knows the other's mind, not the others. For example, in the eye-door process, only eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) sees the form, not the other minds. Thus, this superknowledge mind has the present mind as its object by way of continuity present (santati-paccuppanna) and duration present (addhā-paccuppanna). Alternatively, since continuity present also falls within duration present, it should be understood that this superknowledge mind takes the present mind as its object solely by way of duration present.

Because it takes another's mind as its object, it has an external object (bahiddhā-rammaṇa). Thus should the occurrence of the knowledge of penetration of others' minds among the eight types of objects be understood.

417. The knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) occurs among eight types of objects by way of: sense-sphere (kāma), sublime (mahaggata), immeasurable (appamāṇa), path (magga), past (atīta), internal (ajjhatta), external (bahiddhā), and not-to-be-declared (navattabba). How? When recollecting sense-sphere aggregates (kāmāvacara-khandha), it has sense-sphere phenomena as its object. When recollecting fine-material or immaterial sphere aggregates, it has sublime phenomena as its object. When recollecting a Path developed or a Fruit realized by oneself or others in the past, it has immeasurable phenomena as its object. When recollecting only a developed Path, it has the Path as its object. Invariably, however, this knowledge of recollection of past lives takes only the past as its object.

Among those knowledges (Note 1), even if the knowledge of penetration of others' minds and the knowledge of [beings] passing away according to their kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa) also take the past as an object, nevertheless, among those two knowledges, the knowledge of penetration of others' minds can only take as its object a mind that occurred in the past within seven days. Indeed, that knowledge of penetration of others' minds cannot know aggregates other than the mind, or phenomena connected with the aggregates. Furthermore, it is said to have the Path as its object only figuratively (pariyāya), because it takes a mind associated with the Path as its object. Moreover, the object of the knowledge of passing away according to kamma is merely past volition (cetanā).

Note
1. From here until the phrase 'this is the method of the Commentaries' in this paragraph, the distinction between the knowledge of penetration of others' minds, the knowledge of passing away according to kamma, and the knowledge of recollection of past lives is shown according to the ancient Commentaries.
64:
Thereafter, the view of the author himself, Venerable Buddhaghosa, is presented.

There is no such thing as past aggregates or anything connected with those aggregates not being an object of the knowledge of recollection of past lives. [64] Indeed, it should be understood that this knowledge of recollection of past lives has a range similar to that of the range of Omniscient Knowledge regarding past aggregates and things connected with them. This is the method of the Commentaries in this matter. However, since it is stated in the Paṭṭhāna: "Wholesome aggregates are a condition by way of object-condition for the knowledge of various powers (iddhividha-ñāṇa), the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa), the knowledge of [beings] passing away according to kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa), and the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa)" (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.404), the four aggregates also become objects of the knowledge of penetration of minds and the knowledge of [beings] passing away according to kamma. Among these, the objects of the knowledge of [beings] passing away according to kamma are only wholesome and unwholesome aggregates.

Furthermore, this knowledge of recollection of past lives has an internal object at the time of recollecting one's own aggregates, and an external object at the time of recollecting the aggregates of others. At the time of recollecting names, lineages, and the signs of the earth-kasiṇa, etc., in such a way as: "In the past, there was the Blessed One named Vipassī; his mother was named Bandhumatī, and his father was named Bandhumā" (Dīgha Nikāya 2.12), it has an object that is undeclared (navattabba). In this context, "name and lineage" should be understood as the meaning of the sound established by convention and connected with the aggregates, and not the sound itself. For the sound itself, being included in the base of sounds (saddāyatana), is limited (paritta). As it is said: "The analysis of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā) has a limited object" (Vibhaṅga 749). This view is our preferred choice in this matter. Thus, the occurrence of the knowledge of recollection of past lives with respect to eight kinds of objects should be understood.

418. The knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa) occurs with respect to four kinds of objects by way of limited, present, internal, and external objects. How? Since that knowledge of the divine eye makes visible form its object, and that form is limited (sense-sphere), it has a limited object. Because it occurs only when the form is actually present, it has a present object. When seeing the forms within one's own belly, etc., it has an internal object. When seeing the forms of others, it has an external object. Thus, the occurrence of the knowledge of the divine eye with respect to four kinds of objects should be understood.

419. The knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) occurs with respect to eight kinds of objects by way of limited, sublime, immeasurable, path, future, internal, external, and undeclared objects. How? When that knowledge of the future knows, "This person will be reborn in the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) in the future," it has a limited object. When it knows, "He will be reborn in the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) or the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara)," it has a sublime object. When it knows, "He will develop the path or realize the fruit," it has an immeasurable object. When it knows specifically, "He will develop the path," it has the path as its object. By necessity, however, that knowledge of the future has only the future as its object.
65:
[65] Among those knowledges, although the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) also has the future as its object, it can only take as its object the mind within seven days of the future. It does not know other aggregates or things connected with the aggregates. As for the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa), according to the method stated under the knowledge of recollection of past lives, there is no object in the future that it cannot know. When it knows, "I shall be reborn in such and such a life," it has an internal object. When it knows, "Such and such a person will be reborn in such and such a life," it has an external object. When it knows names and lineages in such a way as: "In the future, the Blessed One named Metteyya will arise; a brahmin named Subrahmā will be his father, and a brahmin woman named Brahmavatī will be his mother" (Dīgha Nikāya 3.107), it has an undeclared object, just as stated in the section on the knowledge of recollection of past lives. Thus, the occurrence of the knowledge of the future with respect to eight kinds of objects should be understood.

420. The knowledge of [beings] passing away according to kamma (yathākammūpaga-ñāṇa) occurs with respect to five kinds of objects by way of limited, sublime, past, internal, and external objects. How? When that knowledge of [beings] passing away according to kamma knows sense-sphere kamma, it has a limited object. When it knows fine-material sphere or immaterial sphere kamma, it has a sublime object. Because it knows only the past, it has a past object. When it knows one's own kamma, it has an internal object. When it knows the kamma of others, it has an external object. Thus, the occurrence of the knowledge of [beings] passing away according to kamma with respect to five kinds of objects should be understood. To explain further, regarding the statement in the ancient commentary that it takes both internal and external as objects in the triad of internal objects, that statement was made considering that it also has both internal and external as objects when it knows internal at one time and external at another time. This concludes one part.

In the Path of Purification, composed for the purpose of gladdening virtuous people, this is the
Thirteenth Chapter
called the Description of Direct Knowledges.

## (End of the Description of Direct Knowledges)

## 14. Khandha-niddesa - Description of the Aggregates
## Paññā-kathā - Discussion on Wisdom

[66] 421.
66:
## 14. Description of the Aggregates (Khandhaniddesa)

Discussion on Wisdom (Paññākathā)

421. Now [1], a monk who is possessed of a concentration-development that is firmer because it has the benefits [2] acquired through the powers of direct knowledge (abhiññā) as previously described, has already fully developed the concentration which was indicated by the term 'mind' (citta) in the following teaching: 'A man wise, established in virtue, developing mind and wisdom.' [3]

Immediately after that (concentration), however, wisdom should be developed. And because that wisdom has been taught in extreme brevity, it is not even easy to understand, let alone to develop. For those [three] reasons [4], this set of questions is presented in order to show the details of that wisdom and the method of its development:

(a) What is wisdom?
(b) In what sense is it wisdom?

Notes:
1. 'Now' connects to 'this set of questions is presented.'
2. This means having already acquired the benefits known as the direct knowledges (abhiññā).
3. The monk... has already developed... wisdom should be developed.
4. This refers to these three reasons: that concentration has been developed, that wisdom must be developed, and that it is not easy to develop.

(c) What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?
(d) How many kinds of wisdom are there?
(e) How is it to be developed?
(f) What is the benefit of developing wisdom?

422. The answer to those questions is as follows:

(a) Regarding the question 'What is wisdom?', wisdom is of many kinds and various types. If one were to attempt to show all those varieties, the explanation would not achieve the desired purpose and would further lead to distraction. Therefore, we shall speak only of what is intended here: Wisdom is insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) associated with wholesome consciousness (kusala-citta).

423. (b) Regarding the question 'In what sense is it wisdom?', it is wisdom in the sense of the act of understanding (pajānana). What is this 'act of understanding'? It is the act of knowing in various ways, which is distinct from the modes of perceiving (sañjānana) and cognizing (vijānana). To explain: although the state of knowing an object is common to perception (saññā), consciousness (viññāṇa), and wisdom (paññā), perception is merely the act of perceiving the object as 'blue' or 'yellow,' etc. It is not able to reach the penetration of the characteristics as 'impermanent, suffering, and non-self.' Consciousness knows the object as 'blue' or 'yellow,' etc., and it also reaches the penetration of the characteristics; however, it is not able, by striving further, to reach the manifestation of the Path (magga). Wisdom knows the object in the manner stated, reaches the penetration of the characteristics, and, by striving further, also reaches the manifestation of the Path.

To illustrate this with an analogy: suppose a heap of coins (kahāpaṇa) is placed on a money-changer's [1] table. Three people—an inexperienced child, a villager, and a money-changer—see it. [67] Among them, the inexperienced child knows only the variety of the coins, such as their being decorated, long, square, or round;
67:
Note:
1. In the Visuddhimagga Nissaya by Pyay Sayadaw, the word 'heraññika' is translated as 'pwe-min' (money-changer). It should be understood as a royal appraiser of gold and silver. Western scholars translate it as 'money-changer' or 'banker'. In the Abhayarama Abhidhana Nissaya, it is translated as 'treasury minister' or 'treasury keeper'. In U Cakkapala's Abhidhana Nissaya, it is 'minister of the gold treasury'. Some teachers translate 'heraññika' as 'goldsmith', but this is inappropriate because there is a separate word for goldsmith, 'suvaṇṇakāra'.

He (the child) does not know, 'This is a treasure designated as an internal or external utility for humans.' The villager knows the various colors and shapes, and he also knows, 'This is a treasure designated as an internal or external utility for humans.' However, he does not know the distinction: 'This coin is genuine, this coin is counterfeit, this coin is half-alloy.' The money-changer, however, knows all those varieties. In knowing thus, he knows by looking at the coin, by hearing the sound when it is struck, by smelling it, by tasting it, and by weighing it in his hand. He even knows, 'It was made in such-and-such a village, town, city, mountain, or riverbank,' and 'It was made by such-and-such a master.' (This is the analogy).

This (the way perception, consciousness, and wisdom know) should be understood as being like this analogy. To compare the analogy with the subject: Perception is like the inexperienced child seeing the coins, because it only grasps the mode of appearance of the object as blue, etc. Consciousness is like the villager seeing the coins, because it grasps the mode of the object as blue, etc., and further reaches the penetration of the three characteristics. Wisdom is like the money-changer seeing the coins, because after grasping the mode of the object as blue, etc., and reaching the penetration of the three characteristics, it further reaches the manifestation of the Noble Path. Therefore, this knowing in various ways, distinct from the modes of perceiving and cognizing, should be understood as 'knowing in a particular way' (pajānana). It is with reference to this kind of knowing that I said: 'It is wisdom in the sense of knowing in a particular way.'

Furthermore, that wisdom is not necessarily present in every state of consciousness where perception and consciousness exist. However, when it is present (in a state of consciousness associated with wisdom), it cannot be separated from those states (perception and consciousness). It is subtle and difficult to see because of the impossibility of obtaining a distinction such as 'This is perception, this is consciousness, this is wisdom.' Therefore, the Venerable Nāgasena said:

'Great King, the Blessed One has performed a difficult task.'
'Venerable Nāgasena, what difficult task has the Blessed One performed?'
'Great King, the Blessed One has performed a difficult task in declaring the distinction of the immaterial mental states (mind and mental factors) that arise on a single object, saying: "This is contact, this is feeling, this is perception, this is volition, this is consciousness."'
68:
[68] 424. (c) Regarding the question, "What are the characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause of that wisdom?": Wisdom has the characteristic of penetrating the true nature of phenomena (dhammas). It has the function of destroying the darkness of delusion (moha) which covers the true nature of phenomena. It has non-confusion as its manifestation (the way it appears in knowledge). Because it was said, "One who is concentrated knows and sees things as they really are," concentration (samādhi) is its proximate cause.

## Classification of Wisdom

425. (d) Regarding the question, "How many kinds of wisdom are there?": Firstly, wisdom is of one kind by way of its characteristic of penetrating the true nature of phenomena.

It is of two kinds by way of mundane wisdom and supramundane wisdom. Likewise, it is of two kinds by way of: being with taints (sāsava) and without taints (anāsava); the definition of mentality (nāma) and materiality (rūpa); being accompanied by joy (somanassa) and equanimity (upekkhā); and the stage of seeing (dassana) and the stage of development (bhāvanā).

It is of three kinds by way of: being based on reflection (cintāmayā), learning (sutamayā), and development (bhāvanāmayā). Likewise, it is of three kinds by way of: limited (paritta), exalted (mahaggata), and immeasurable (appamāṇa) objects; skill in progress (āya), skill in decline (apāya), and skill in means (upāya); and internal application (ajjhattābhinivesa), etc.

It is of four kinds by way of: knowledge regarding the Four Truths; and by way of the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).

426. Among these, the onefold category has an obvious meaning. In the twofold category, wisdom associated with the mundane path is called mundane wisdom. Wisdom associated with the supramundane path is called supramundane wisdom. Thus, it is of two kinds by way of mundane and supramundane.

In the second dyad, wisdom that is an object of the taints (āsavas) is called sāsava (with taints). Wisdom that is not an object of those taints is called anāsava (without taints). In terms of ultimate reality, these two are simply mundane and supramundane wisdom. The same method applies to dyads such as "wisdom that is not associated with taints but is with taints, and wisdom that is neither associated with taints nor with taints." Thus, it is of two kinds by way of sāsava and anāsava, etc.

In the third dyad, for one who wishes to begin insight (vipassanā), the wisdom in defining the four immaterial aggregates is called the wisdom of defining mentality (nāma-vavatthāpana-paññā). The wisdom in defining the material aggregate is called the wisdom of defining materiality (rūpa-vavatthāpana-paññā). Thus, it is of two kinds by way of defining mentality and materiality.

In the fourth dyad, wisdom in the two wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses (accompanied by joy) and in the sixteen path consciousnesses associated with the four jhānas according to the fivefold method is called wisdom accompanied by joy. Wisdom in the two wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses (accompanied by equanimity) and in the four path consciousnesses associated with the fifth jhāna is called wisdom accompanied by equanimity. Thus, it is of two kinds by way of being accompanied by joy and equanimity.

[69] In the fifth dyad, wisdom in the first path is called wisdom of the stage of seeing (dassana-bhūmi).
69:
Wisdom in the remaining three paths is called wisdom of the stage of development (bhāvanā-bhūmi). Thus, it is of two kinds by way of the stage of seeing and the stage of development.

427. Among the triads, in the first triad, wisdom obtained without hearing from another, being produced by the power of one's own reflection, is called wisdom based on reflection (cintāmayā-paññā). Wisdom obtained by hearing from another, being produced by the power of what has been heard, is called wisdom based on learning (sutamayā-paññā). Wisdom produced by the power of development in any manner, which has reached absorption (appanā), is called wisdom based on development (bhāvanāmayā-paññā). For it was said:

"Therein, what is wisdom based on reflection? In the spheres of work (kammāyatana) managed by wisdom, or in the spheres of arts (sippāyatana) managed by wisdom, or in the spheres of science (vijjāṭṭhāna) managed by wisdom, or the knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kammassakata-ñāṇa), or the knowledge in conformity with the truths (saccānulomika-ñāṇa) such as 'materiality is impermanent,' 'feeling is... perception is... mental formations are... consciousness is impermanent'—whatever such conformable acceptance (khanti), view (diṭṭhi), preference (ruci), opinion (muti), reflection (pekkha), or acceptance of reflection on phenomena (dhamma-nijjhāna-khanti) one obtains without hearing it from another, this is called wisdom based on reflection. ... If one obtains it by hearing from another, this is called wisdom based on learning. All wisdom of one who has attained meditative attainment (samāpanna) is wisdom based on development."

Thus, it is of three kinds by way of reflection, learning, and development.

In the second triad, wisdom occurring with sense-sphere phenomena as its object is called wisdom with a limited object (parittārammaṇā). Wisdom occurring with fine-material or immaterial sphere phenomena as its object is called wisdom with an exalted object (mahaggatārammaṇā); that is mundane insight. Wisdom occurring with Nibbāna as its object is called wisdom with an immeasurable object (appamāṇārammaṇā); that is supramundane insight. Thus, it is of three kinds by way of limited, exalted, and immeasurable objects.

In the third triad, 'āya' means progress or increase. That progress is of two kinds: by way of the decrease of harm and the arising of benefit. Skill therein is skill in progress (āyakosalla). As it was said:

"Therein, what is skill in progress? 'When I attend to these phenomena, unarisen unwholesome states do not arise, and arisen unwholesome states are abandoned; or, when I attend to these phenomena, unarisen wholesome states arise, and arisen wholesome states lead to further existence, to expansion, to development, and to fulfillment.' Whatever wisdom, understanding, ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, or right view there is in that (non-arising of unwholesome states, etc.), this is called skill in progress (āyakosalla)."
70:
[70] Furthermore, apāya means lack of progress or ruin. This ruin is of two kinds: the loss of benefit and the arising of harm. Skill in these two is called apāya-kosalla (skill in decline). How is it taught?

"Among those (three skills), what is apāya-kosalla? When I attend to these things, unarisen wholesome states do not arise"—and so on.

In all matters, the immediate and situational skill and wisdom regarding the means (upāya) or causes of the arising of various (beneficial) states is called upāya-kosalla (skill in means). How is it taught?

"All wisdom regarding the means in those various matters is upāya-kosalla."

Thus, there are three kinds: āya-kosalla, apāya-kosalla, and upāya-kosalla.

In the fourth triad, insight wisdom that begins by taking (contemplating) one's own aggregates is called ajjhattābhinivesa-paññā. Insight wisdom that begins by taking the aggregates of others or external inanimate matter (not connected with the faculties) is called bahiddhābhinivesa-paññā. Insight wisdom that begins by taking both internal and external is called ajjhattabahiddhābhinivesa-paññā. Thus, there are three kinds: ajjhattābhinivesa-paññā, etc.

428. Among the tetrads, in the first tetrad, knowledge that arises concerning the truth of suffering is knowledge of suffering (dukkhe ñāṇa). Knowledge that arises concerning the truth of the origin of suffering is knowledge of the origin of suffering (dukkhasamudaye ñāṇa). Knowledge that arises concerning the truth of the cessation of suffering is knowledge of the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodhe ñāṇa). Knowledge that arises concerning the truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of suffering (dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇa). Thus, there are four kinds based on knowledge of the four truths.

In the second tetrad, the four paṭisambhidā (analytical knowledges) are the four knowledges that have reached distinction regarding meanings and so forth. For it is said:

"Knowledge of meanings is attha-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of dhammas (causes) is dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of the expression of those dhammas in language is nirutti-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of the knowledges is paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā."

Therein, "meaning" (attha) is, in brief, a term for the result of a cause. For a result is called attha because it is reached, attained, or arrived at in accordance with the cause. In detail, these five things should be understood as attha:

(1) any result produced by conditions,
(2) Nibbāna,
(3) the meaning of what is spoken,
(4) resultant (vipāka),
(5) functional (kiriya).

For one who reviews that meaning, the distinct knowledge regarding that meaning is attha-paṭisambhidā. 

"Dhamma" is also, in brief, a term for a cause. For a cause is called dhamma because it bears, maintains, or allows for the arrival of various results. [71] In detail, these five things should be understood as dhamma:

(1) any cause that produces a result,
(2) the Noble Path,
71:
(3) the spoken language (Pali),
(4) wholesome (kusala),
(5) unwholesome (akusala).

These five causal things should be understood as dhamma. For one who reviews that dhamma (cause), the distinct knowledge regarding that cause is dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Indeed, this same sense is shown in the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga by way of analysis:

"Knowledge of suffering is attha-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of the origin of suffering is dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of the cause is dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of the result of the cause is attha-paṭisambhidā. Those things that are born, become, arisen, produced, manifested—knowledge of these (resultant) things is attha-paṭisambhidā. Those things from which those (resultant) things are born, become, arisen, produced, manifested—knowledge of those (causal) things is dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of old age and death is attha-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of the origin of old age and death is dhamma-paṭisambhidā... [p]... Knowledge of the cessation of formations is attha-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of formations is dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Here, a monk knows the Dhamma: the Sutta, Geyya... [p]... Vedalla. This is called dhamma-paṭisambhidā. He knows the meaning of that which is spoken: 'This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement.' This is called attha-paṭisambhidā. Which things are wholesome? At a time when a wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen... [p]... these things are wholesome. Knowledge of these wholesome things is dhamma-paṭisambhidā. Knowledge of their result (vipāka) is attha-paṭisambhidā."

"Knowledge of the expression of those dhammas in language" means the natural expression (sabhāva-nirutti), the unerring usage regarding those meanings and causes. In the utterance or vocalization of that expression, having heard the sound of what is uttered or spoken, the distinct knowledge regarding that natural expression—known as dhamma-nirutti, which is the Māgadhi language, the root language of all beings—whereby one knows "This is natural expression; this is not natural expression," is called nirutti-paṭisambhidā. For one who has attained nirutti-paṭisambhidā, upon hearing an utterance such as "phasso, vedanā," knows "This is natural expression." But upon hearing an utterance such as "phassā, vedano," he knows "This is not natural expression."

[72] "Knowledge of the knowledges" means for one who reviews by taking as object the knowledge that occurs in all (meanings, causes, and language)...
72:
Similarly, it is correct only if it is feminine ending in '-ā' as 'vedanā'; if it is masculine ending in '-o' as 'vedano', it is wrong.

It is the knowledge that has knowledge as its object. Alternatively, it is the knowledge that understands in detail those aforementioned knowledges by way of their respective objects, functions, and so on; this is the meaning of paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā. This is the essential meaning.

429. These four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) reach distinction in two stages: the stage of the trainee (sekkhabhūmi) and the stage of the non-trainee (asekkhabhūmi). Among them, for the Chief Disciples and Great Disciples, they reach distinction in the stage of the non-trainee (as Arahants). For individuals such as the Elder Ānanda, Citta the householder, Dhammika the lay follower, Upāli the householder, and Khujjuttarā the lay follower, they reach distinction in the stage of the trainee.

These analytical knowledges, which reach distinction in these two stages as mentioned, become clear and sharp through these five factors: (1) adhigama—attainment of the supramundane; (2) pariyatti—learning; (3) savana—hearing; (4) paripucchā—inquiry; and (5) pubbayoga—former application. Among these, adhigama means the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship. Pariyatti means the learning of the Buddha’s words. Savana means respectfully listening to the Sublime Dhamma, taking it to heart as one's own welfare. Paripucchā means the discussion and determination of the meaning of difficult words (ganthipada) and difficult meanings in the Pali texts, Commentaries, and so forth. Pubbayoga means the practice of insight (vipassanā) up to conformity knowledge (anuloma) near change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), by way of the 'going and returning' (gatapaccāgata) duty (practicing meditation while going for and returning from alms) in the dispensations of former Buddhas.

Other teachers, however, say as follows:
(1) pubbayoga—former application; (2) bāhusacca—erudition; (3) desabhāsā—knowledge of local languages; (4) āgama—mastery of the Buddha’s words; (5) paripucchā—inquiry; (6) adhigama—attainment; (7) garusannissaya—reliance on a teacher; and (8) mittasampatti—excellence in friendship. These eight are the causes for attaining the analytical knowledges.

Among these, pubbayoga is as already explained. Bāhusacca means proficiency in various treatises and various arts. Desabhāsā means proficiency in the 101 languages and dialects. Specifically, it is proficiency in the Magadhi language. Āgama means the learning of the Buddha’s words by heart, at the very least even as much as the Opammavagga.¹ Paripucchā means inquiring into the determination of the meaning of even a single verse.

Note:
1. The teachers state that the Yamaka-vagga of the Dhammapada is called the Opammavagga; other teachers (apare) state in the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) that the Yamaka-vagga of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa is called the Opammavagga.

Adhigama means the attainment of the state of a Stream-enterer... or... the state of an Arahant. Garusannissaya means living in the presence of teachers who are of great learning and analytical wit. Mittasampatti means the acquisition of noble friends who possess such qualities.

Among these, the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas reach the analytical knowledges by relying on pubbayoga and adhigama. The disciples reach them by relying on all these aforementioned causes. However, for the purpose of reaching the analytical knowledges, [73] there is no such thing as practicing a separate meditation (kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā).
73:
In truth, for trainees (sekhas), the attainment of the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) is completed at the very end of the liberation (vimokkha) that is the fruition of training (sekha-phala). For non-trainees (asekha/arahants), it is completed at the very end of the liberation that is the fruition of non-training (asekha-phala). Indeed, just as the ten powers (dasabala) of the Buddhas are completed [through the fruition of Arahantship], the analytical knowledges of the Noble Ones (ariyas) are completed through the Noble Fruition (ariya-phala) itself. Therefore, with reference to these analytical knowledges, I have said: "It is of four kinds by way of the four analytical knowledges."

## (The explanation of the divisions of wisdom is finished).

Note: 1—The phrase "those who are of such nature" means those who possess much learning and ready wit (paṭibhāna).

## Definition of the Soil, Root, and Body of Wisdom

430. (e) To the question "How should wisdom be developed?": Here, the states (dhammas) classified as aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), faculties (indriya), truths (sacca), and dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), etc., are the soil (bhūmi) of this (insight) wisdom.

Note: 1—The word "etc." should be understood to include nutriment (āhāra) and so on. If it is asked: "Why are these many states taken and described as the soil or object of insight? Does not any one of them, such as the aggregates, suffice to complete the task?" The answer is: No, it does not. To benefit three types of beings, the collection of the three—aggregates, bases, and elements—should be taken. If they were not so taken and described, it would not provide a comprehensive benefit to all. Indeed, beings are of three types: those who are confused about matter (rūpa), those who are confused about mind (nāma), and those who are confused about both. Among them, for those confused about mind, the aggregates are shown by dividing mental states into four. For those confused about matter, the bases are shown by dividing material states into eleven. For those confused about both, the elements are shown by dividing both [mind and matter]. Similarly, beings are of three types by way of faculties: those with sharp faculties, those with medium faculties, and those with dull faculties; and also as those who prefer a brief, medium, or detailed explanation. For these three types of beings, the aggregates and so on are shown respectively. Furthermore, the description of the faculties is for the benefit of easily grasping the characteristic of non-self (anatta), as follows: "Although these faculties exercise governance over their co-nascent states, that governance is merely a functional accomplishment according to the nature of things. Not even a single person has any governance over these faculties according to their own will. These faculties are empty of a self (atta) that is an owner; they do not occur according to one's will."

(The object) is the soil. The two purifications, namely, purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi) and purification of mind (citta-visuddhi), are the roots (mūla) of this (insight wisdom). The five purifications, namely, purification of view (diṭṭhi-visuddhi), purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi), purification by knowledge and vision of what is and what is not the path (maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi), purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi), and purification by knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi), are the body (sarīra). Therefore, one should develop (this insight wisdom) by first establishing familiarity with knowledge through learning and inquiry regarding those states (aggregates, etc.) which are the soil, then by fulfilling the two purifications which are the roots, and finally by fulfilling the five purifications which are the body. This is the summary here.

431. The following is the detailed explanation. Regarding the statement: "The states classified as aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, truths, and dependent origination, etc., are the soil (object) of this (insight) wisdom":

Note: The collection of these four types of states—aggregates, bases, elements, and faculties—brings benefit and occurs only when seen by way of their occurrence (pavatti), their cessation (nivatti), and the causes of both (tadubhaya-hetu). Otherwise, they do not bring benefit. Therefore, the truths and dependent origination are also shown. (Commentary)

In that statement, "aggregates" means the five aggregates: the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha), the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), and the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha).

## Explanation of the Aggregate of Matter

432. Among those (five aggregates), all states that have the characteristic of being molested (ruppana) by cold, heat, etc., should be understood collectively as the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha).

Note: 1—Connect "Among those (five aggregates)..." with "...should be understood as the aggregate of matter."
2—Matter that is normally hot or balanced changes and is molested when it meets with the opposite, cold. Matter that is normally cold or balanced changes and is molested when it meets with heat. Matter that is balanced by being full of food changes and is molested when hungry. The matter of one who is not thirsty changes and is molested when thirsty. It is molested by swelling, etc., due to the bite of mosquitoes and so on. Because it is molested (ruppati) when meeting with such opposing conditions, it is called matter (rūpa). It should not be taken that every single piece of matter is being molested [visibly] at every moment, nor should the dissolution at the sub-moment of passing away (bhaṅga-khaṇa) be taken as the characteristic of being molested (ruppana). In the continuity of Brahmas, there is no molestation (ruppana) through meeting with opposites like cold and heat; however, if they were to meet such opposites, they would certainly be molested, thus they do not transcend the nature of being molested (ruppana). Therefore, the matter of Brahmas is also called rūpa. Alternatively, the Commentary states it is called rūpa because there is change and molestation even while being good, by the power of supportive conditions (anuggāhaka-paccaya). In such cases of "good molestation," it should be understood to include matter that is cheerful due to joy and happiness, matter of laughter, matter of clapping hands, and matter that moves, bends, or stretches due to the mind's desire to bend, stretch, or move.

Although this matter, called the aggregate of matter, is of only one kind by way of the characteristic of being molested, it is of two kinds by way of the division into primary elements (bhūta-rūpa) and derived matter (upādā-rūpa).

Among them, primary matter is of four kinds: the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), the water element (āpo-dhātu), the fire element (tejo-dhātu), and the air element (vāyo-dhātu). Their characteristics, functions, and manifestations have been described in the section on the meditation of the definition of the four elements. By way of proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna), however, all four of these elements have the other three remaining elements as their proximate cause.

Note: 1—Connect "Derived matter..." with "...is of twenty-four kinds."
2—Itthindriya: Itthi (female) + indriya (faculty/governance). It means the matter that governs the female continuity (for the occurrence of female-related matter and mental states). Therefore, it is translated as "the matter that governs the state of being female" for easy understanding. It is also called itthibhāva-rūpa. The same applies to purisindriya.
3—Jīvitindriya: Jīvita (life) + indriya (governance). The matter that governs life. Without this matter, one cannot live.

Derived matter is of twenty-four kinds: (1) eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), (2) ear-sensitivity (sota-pasāda), (3) nose-sensitivity (ghāna-pasāda), (4) tongue-sensitivity (jivhā-pasāda), (5) body-sensitivity (kāya-pasāda), (6) visible form (rūpārammaṇa), (7) sound (saddārammaṇa), (8) odor (gandhārammaṇa), (9) flavor (rasārammaṇa), (10) femininity faculty (itthindriya), (11) masculinity faculty (purisindriya), (12) life faculty (jīvitindriya), (13) heart-base (hadaya-vatthu), (14) bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti), (15) vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti), (16) space element (ākāsa-dhātu), (17) lightness of matter (lahutā),
74: Therefore, this matter is called the life-faculty (jīvitindriya); it is also called life-matter (jīvita-rūpa). ## 4. Hadaya-vatthu (Heart-base): The physical base of the heart. The Commentaries state that the 79 types of consciousness, known as the mind-element (mano-dhātu) and mind-consciousness-element (mano-viññāṇa-dhātu), arise depending on this matter. This will be encountered later. ## 5. In the Pali, the term 'rūpassa' is paired with 'rūpassa lahutā' ... 'rūpassa aniccatā'. Here, for ease of reading, it is translated without the term 'rūpassa'. These are merely the modes of the ultimate realities called produced matter (nipphanna-rūpa), such as lightness. This will become clear later. [74] There are 24 varieties: (18) mudutā (malleability), (19) kammaññatā (wieldiness), (20) upacaya (accumulation), (21) santati (continuity), (22) jaratā (decay), (23) aniccatā (impermanence), and (24) kabaḷīkāra-āhāra (nutriment). ## 433. Among these 24 types of derived matter (upādā-rūpa), eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) has the characteristic of clarity of the great elements (bhūta-rūpa) that are capable of being struck by visible forms. Note: 1. The meaning to be shown here is already included in Note 5 of page 201. 2. The nutritive essence (ojā) contained in morsels of food, etc., which are made into balls and eaten, is called kabaḷīkāra-āhāra. The nutritive essence contained in other groups of matter is also called kabaḷīkāra-āhāra. 3. Connect it as: 'Eye-sensitivity has the characteristic of clarity.' The characteristic of clarity, the nature of clarity itself, is eye-sensitivity. Since one might ask 'What kind of clarity?', it says 'capable of being struck by visible forms,' meaning a nature of clarity sufficient for forms to appear. This qualifier is a simplified translation of the term 'rūpābhighātāraha'. Literally translated, it means 'worthy of the direct impact of forms.' Whether a visible form actually appears or not, it refers to the nature of clarity sufficient for it to appear. If asked 'Clarity of what?', it is the clarity of the great elements. This translation, 'clarity of the great elements,' is consistent with the statement 'the derived matter called eye-sensitivity arises depending on the great elements.' In the Abhidhammatthasarūpadīpaka by the Myo-pyin-gyi Sayadaw, page 527, it is also stated: Alternatively, it has the characteristic of clarity of the great elements produced by karma rooted in the desire to see. It has the function (rasa) of drawing in visible objects. It has the manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) of serving as the basis for eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa). It has the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the great elements produced by karma rooted in the desire to see. Note: The Pali says 'pasādo upādāya catunnam mahābhūtānam' (sensitivity depending on the four great elements), and the Commentary says 'pasādo pavattapasādo upādiyitvā cattāri mahābhūtāni' (sensitivity proceeding having depended on the four great elements). Thus, it is called 'sensitivity' (pasāda) because it is the clarity depending on the four great elements, or the clarity of the four great elements themselves. In the Pyay version of the Visuddhimagga Nissaya, etc., the Pali 'bhūtānam pasādo' is translated as 'making the great elements clear,' and 'bhūtapasādalakkhaṇam' as 'having the characteristic of making the great elements clear.' In that interpretation, saying 'sensitivity-matter makes the great elements clear' is as if sensitivity-matter assists the great elements to become clear, making it seem as though the clarity of the great elements depends on sensitivity-matter. Therefore, having doubt in that meaning, the phrase 'bhūtapasāda' is translated as 'the clarity of the great elements.' The same should be understood for the following sections. 1. The term 'daṭṭhukāmatā' is translated briefly as 'the craving that desires to see' for clarity. Literally, it means 'the state of desiring to see (which is craving).' Karma rooted in that craving refers to karma performed with such a wish, or karma occurring in one who is not yet free from such craving. Thus, the Sub-commentary explains: 'Kāma-taṇhā or rūpa-taṇhā, which is the root of karma producing an existence (attabhāva) with complete or incomplete sense-bases (eye, etc.), deserves the designation "desire to see," etc., because it is a longing for an existence with those sense-bases. Therefore, the second method is stated for all sensitivity-matters.' Furthermore, it explains: 'In this context of karma rooted in the desire to see, if the desire to see and the remaining desires to hear, etc., existed prior to the moment of undertaking the karma that produces that particular existence, there is no need for further explanation. If they did not exist prior, then the fact that they have not yet been eradicated by the Noble Path is the reason (for saying the desire to see, etc., exists).' This informs us that the nature of clarity of the great elements produced by that karma is called eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda). 'Clarity' and 'lucidity' are synonymous. 1. Rasa has two aspects: function (kicca) and achievement (sampatti). Here, it refers to function-rasa. Therefore, 'function' is explicitly mentioned. In subsequent sections, it will not be shown. Depending on the clear eye, visible forms are seen and known. In that seeing and knowing, because the eye acts as if it draws in the forms, it is said to have the function of drawing in (āviñchana-rasa). Here, 'drawing in' means assisting or bringing the person or the mind to see the form. Thus, it is translated as 'the function of drawing in.' The same applies hereafter. 2. Manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) has two aspects: the mode of appearing (upaṭṭhānākāra) and the fruit (phala). Here, it is the mode of appearing to the yogi's meditative knowledge. Therefore, it is translated as above. In subsequent sections, the terms 'to meditative knowledge' and 'manifestation' will not be shown. It has the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of the great elements produced by karma rooted in the desire to see. Ear-sensitivity (sota-pasāda) has the characteristic of clarity of the great elements capable of being struck by sound. Alternatively, it has the characteristic of clarity of the great elements produced by karma rooted in the desire to hear. It has the function of drawing in sound objects. It has the manifestation of serving as the basis for ear-consciousness (sota-viññāṇa). It has the proximate cause of the great elements produced by karma rooted in the desire to hear. Nose-sensitivity (ghāna-pasāda) has the characteristic of clarity of the great elements capable of being struck by smells. Alternatively, it has the characteristic of clarity of the great elements produced by karma rooted in the desire to smell. It has the function of drawing in smell objects. It has the manifestation of serving as the basis for nose-consciousness (ghāna-viññāṇa). It has the proximate cause of the great elements produced by karma rooted in the desire to smell. Note: 1. Since 'pada' means cause and 'ṭhāna' also means cause, these two causal terms are used together to mean the 'proximate cause' (near cause). Although eye-sensitivity has other causes like karma (since it is karma-born matter), it arises depending on the great elements; thus, the great elements are the proximate cause of eye-sensitivity. Tongue-sensitivity (jivhā-pasāda) has the characteristic of clarity of the great elements capable of being struck by tastes. Alternatively, it has the characteristic of clarity of the great elements produced by karma rooted in the desire to experience taste. It has the function of drawing in taste objects. It has the manifestation of serving as the basis for tongue-consciousness (jivhā-viññāṇa). It has the proximate cause of the great elements produced by karma rooted in the desire to experience taste. Body-sensitivity (kāya-pasāda) has the characteristic of clarity of the great elements capable of being struck by tangible objects (phoṭṭhabba). Alternatively, it has the characteristic of clarity of the great elements produced by karma rooted in the desire to touch. It has the function of drawing in tangible objects. It has the manifestation of serving as the basis for body-consciousness (kāya-viññāṇa). It has the proximate cause of the great elements produced by karma rooted in the desire to touch. ## 434. Some teachers (Keci) say: 'Eye-sensitivity is the clarity of the great elements in which the fire-element (tejo-dhātu) is predominant. Note: 1. The term 'sāyitukāmatā' could be translated as 'the state of desiring to lick' or 'the craving to lick.' However, since that might imply only licking with the tongue, it is translated as above for clarity. 2. 'Some teachers' refers to certain teachers among the Mahāsaṅghika sect. Indeed, among them, Vasudharma said: 'In the eye, fire is predominant; in the ear, air; in the nose, earth; in the tongue, water. In the body-sensitivity, all four elements are equal.' To show that the predominance of fire, etc., in the eye, etc., is due to the predominance of fire in their supporting elements, it is said: 'Eye-sensitivity is the clarity of the great elements in which the fire-element is predominant,' and so on. (Sub-commentary) Ear, nose, and tongue sensitivities are the clarity of the great elements in which the air, earth, and water elements are predominant. Body-sensitivity is the clarity of all the great elements (in equality).' Other teachers (Apare) say: 'Eye-sensitivity is the clarity of the great elements in which the fire-element is predominant. Note: 1. What is the distinction in saying body-sensitivity is of all great elements? Is it not true that the clarity of elements where fire, etc., are predominant is also the clarity of all great elements? That is true. However, the phrase 'of all great elements' here indicates the meaning 'of the great elements in equality.' This is because the statement is made by excluding the predominance of any single part. To elaborate: just as in the cases where fire, etc., are individually predominant, body-sensitivity does not arise where two or three elements are predominant and others are weak. Therefore, body-sensitivity arises through the equality of all four great elements. Thus, the word 'sabba' (all) in this context should be understood to indicate equality. (Sub-commentary) Ear, nose, tongue, and body sensitivities are the clarity of the great elements in which the space (ākāsa), air, water, and earth elements are predominant.' Those teachers (Keci and Apare) should be asked: 'Bring forth a Sutta as evidence.' (If so asked), they will certainly not find any Sutta. However, some among them provide the reason: 'Because the qualities of fire, etc., such as light and color, support and assist (in seeing, etc.).' Note: 1. In 'the qualities of fire, etc.,' this refers to the light and color of fire (such as a lamp), the sound of air, the smell of earth, and the taste of water (such as saliva). This should be applied appropriately in the views of the Keci and Apare teachers, meaning that the qualities of those respective elements support and assist in the grasping and knowing of color, etc. This is the intended meaning.
75:
Only when they occur together with co-nascent conditions such as light and so on can the eye-sensitivity and others clarify [perceive] visible forms and so on. The view of other teachers (apare) is that the status of space (ākāsa) as a decisive support (upanissaya) for ear-consciousness is a quality. However, just as fire and others are called primary elements (bhūta-rūpa), space does not exist as a primary element; therefore, it was said "according to what is appropriate." (Note: Although space, called vivara, is not referred to as a primary element in Buddhist literature, it is still called a primary element in Indian [non-Buddhist] literature; the other teachers seem to speak by adopting that terminology. Therefore, the explanation continues with "Alternatively..."). Alternatively, according to the non-Buddhist meaning that the void called space is a quality of the primary elements, just like light and color, one should apply as appropriate: the light and color of fire, the sound of the void, the smell of air, the taste of saliva, and the touch of the earth element (due to their support and benefit). (Ṭīkā)

One should ask those who provide such reasons: "Who says that light and so on are qualities of fire and so on?" Indeed, among the primary elements that are inseparable and unified, it is impossible to say, "This is the quality of this element, that is the quality of that element." Here is an explanation. If they should say: "Just as you [the Commentators] desire the functions of well-supporting and so on of the earth element and others due to the predominance of those primary elements in various structures (material groups), so too, because we see the predominance of color and so on in structures where fire and so on are predominant, this meaning—that light, color, etc., are qualities of fire, etc.—should be accepted and desired by you."

(Note: Regarding the statement "because we see the predominance of color and so on," it means that because we see these specific colors and so on, such as the bright color in fire, the sound heard according to its nature in the wind, the fragrant smell in the earth, and the sweet taste in water, the first proponents (keci) say that "color and so on are the qualities of fire and so on." By this same method, the second proponents are also refuted. Ṭīkā)

If they should say so, the rebuttal is: If the smell in cotton (where earth is predominant) were more intense than the smell in liquor (where water is predominant), and if the color of cold water were inferior to the color of hot water (where fire is predominant), then we might accept and be pleased with your assertion. However, neither of these two cases exists. Therefore, abandoning this speculation of differentiation based on the supporting elements, you [the other teachers] should accept this meaning: "Just as in a single material group (kalāpa), even though there is no differentiation of the primary elements, color, taste, and so on are distinct from one another, so too, the eye-sensitivity and others are distinct from one another even though there is no other specific cause [in the elements]."

What then is the cause of their mutual distinction? Kamma alone is the cause of their differentiation. Therefore, their distinction is due to the difference in Kamma, not due to the difference in primary elements. Indeed, if there were a difference [imbalance] in the primary elements, sensitivity (pasāda) itself would not arise. For the Ancients (Porāṇā) say: "Sensitivity is of the balanced [elements], not of the unbalanced."

(Note: Alternatively, it should be noted that this is said to refute the doctrine of the teacher Kaṇāda, who stated that the elements of fire, space, earth, water, and air, which possess special qualities like color, produce the eye and so on. Ṭīkā. These explanations of the views of the keci and apare are very profound and are the domain of the great wise ones.)

435. Among these five sensitivities which are distinct due to the difference in Kamma as stated, the eye and the ear perceive objects that have not reached [them] (asampatta-visaya-gāhaka). This is because they are the cause of consciousness regarding an object that is not attached to their own physical support.

(Note: Nowadays, because voices spoken over the telephone or wireless, and broadcasts from stations are heard instantly, and visible forms broadcast by television are seen instantly, there may be doubt regarding the statement that one sees and hears colors and sounds that have not arrived. In this matter, they do arrive at a distance where they can be seen or heard; however, they do not come to strike the eye-sensitivity or ear-sensitivity. If they did, they could not be seen or heard, just as one cannot see the color inside the eye. In the Ṭīkās, regarding the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), it is taught that mind-produced sound is an object of ear-consciousness; if it were said that it must reach the ear to be heard, then since there may be no mind-produced sound externally, such sound could not be heard. Therefore, they explain that the sound is heard at its original location. Because the reflection of color is seen in the eye, it is difficult to accept the statement that color does not reach the eye. Similarly, because very harsh sounds are felt striking unpleasantly in the ear, it is difficult to accept the statement that sound does not reach the ear. Therefore, in the Atthasālinī Commentary (351) on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, it is mentioned that the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā says "reaching the objective field (āpātagatattā) is called 'having reached' (sampatta)." According to that view, the eye and ear are also called sampatta-gocara—having objects that have reached them. Thus, if one cannot intellectually accept the view that "the eye and ear perceive objects that have not reached them," one can adopt the view of the ancient Commentary that they are "sampatta-gocara.")

The nose, tongue, and body sensitivities perceive objects that have reached [them] (sampatta-visaya-gāhaka). This is because they are the cause of consciousness regarding an object (smell, taste, touch) that is attached to their own physical support, both by way of the support and by themselves.

(Note: Connect the two instances of "and" with the word "attached." The first indicates that the objects of smell and taste are attached through their supporting elements; the second indicates that the objects of touch—earth, fire, and air—are attached by themselves.)

436. Among these five sensitivities, the eye-sensitivity is [as follows]: In the world, that mass of flesh which is resembling a blue lotus petal, variegated with black and white circles and surrounded by dark eyelashes, is called the "eye." In the center of the black circle of that physical eye (sasambhāra-cakkhu), which is surrounded by the white circle—at the place where the bodily form of those standing in front appears—pervading the seven layers of the eye like oil poured into seven layers of cotton, [the eye-sensitivity] stands, being benefited, supported, protected, and surrounded by the four elements which perform the functions of supporting, binding, maturing, and moving, just like a prince is tended by four nurses who perform the functions of carrying, bathing, dressing, and fanning, and being sustained by temperature, mind, and nutriment, and by life...
76:
The language is more refined.
5- Connect with: "at the prominent place... the seven layers of the eye."
6- Connect with: "being spread... having received assistance," etc.

Being assisted by the four elements which perform their respective functions, supported by temperature (utu), mind (citta), and nutriment (āhāra), protected by the life-faculty (jīvita-rūpa), and surrounded by the [co-nascent] qualities of color (vaṇṇa), odor (gandha), taste (rasa), and so on; it stands as the size of a louse's head¹, fulfilling the role of base (vatthu) and door (dvāra) for eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) and its associated states as appropriate². Indeed, this was said by the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera:

"By which eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) a person sees forms;
This is small and subtle, comparable to a louse's head."

Ear-sensitivity (sota-pasāda) is located inside the ear-hole of the physical ear (sasambhāra-sota), in a place shaped like a finger-stall (or ring) covered with fine red hairs. Assisted by the aforementioned four elements, supported by temperature, mind, and nutriment, protected by life, and surrounded by color and so on, it stands fulfilling the role of base and door for ear-consciousness (sota-viññāṇa) and its associated states as appropriate.

Note:
1- By the phrase "spread through the seven layers of the eye," it is shown that the eye-sensitivity exists in many groups (kalāpas). The phrase "the size of a louse's head" is said because it occurs in an area of that size. (Ṭīkā)
2- This means it fulfills the role of the physical base for eye-consciousness, and the role of the door for other consciousnesses belonging to the eye-door process, such as adverting (āvajjana) and receiving (sampaṭicchana).

Nose-sensitivity (ghāna-pasāda) is located inside the nose-hole of the physical nose (sasambhāra-ghāna), in a place shaped like a goat's hoof. With the aforementioned types of assistance, support, protection, and surroundings, it stands fulfilling the role of base and door for nose-consciousness (ghāna-viññāṇa) and its associated states as appropriate.

Tongue-sensitivity (jivhā-pasāda) is located on the upper surface of the middle of the physical tongue (sasambhāra-jivhā), in a place shaped like the tip of a lotus petal. With the aforementioned types of assistance, support, protection, and surroundings, it stands fulfilling the role of base and door for tongue-consciousness (jivhā-viññāṇa) and its associated states as appropriate.

Furthermore, wherever there is kamma-born matter (upādinnarūpa) in this body, the body-sensitivity (kāya-pasāda) stands, spread like oil soaked in a layer of cotton. With the aforementioned types of assistance, support, protection, and surroundings, it stands fulfilling the role of base and door for body-consciousness (kāya-viññāṇa) and its associated states as appropriate.

Just as the snake, crocodile, bird, dog, and jackal incline towards their respective habitats—namely, an anthill, deep water, the sky, and the village (or charnel ground where corpses are discarded)—so too should these sensitivities of the eye and so on be understood as inclining towards their respective objective fields such as visible forms and so on.

437. Among the subsequent objects such as visible forms: Visible form (rūpa) has the characteristic of impinging on the eye. Its function is to be the objective field of eye-consciousness. It is manifested as the resort (gocara) of that same eye-consciousness. Its proximate cause is the four great elements. Just as it is with this visible form, so it is with all other derived matter (upādā-rūpa); they all have the four great elements as their proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). However, where there is a distinction, we shall explain it.
77:
That visible object is of many kinds by way of blue, yellow, and so on.

[77] The object of sound (sadda) has the characteristic of impinging on the ear-sensitivity. Its function is to be the object of ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa). It is manifested as the resort of that same ear-consciousness. It is of many kinds, such as the sound of a drum, the sound of a tabor, and so on.

The object of smell (gandha) has the characteristic of impinging on the nose-sensitivity. Its function is to be the object of nose-consciousness (ghānaviññāṇa). It is manifested as the resort of that same nose-consciousness. It is of many kinds, such as the smell of roots, the smell of heartwood, and so on.

The object of taste (rasa) has the characteristic of impinging on the tongue-sensitivity. Its function is to be the object of tongue-consciousness (jivhāviññāṇa). It is manifested as the resort of that same tongue-consciousness. It is of many kinds, such as the taste of roots, the taste of stems, and so on.

438. The female faculty (itthindriya) has the characteristic of the state of being female.1 Its function is to show "this is a woman."2 It is manifested as the cause of the female sex (itthilinga), female signs (itthinimitta), female behavior (itthikutta), and female deportment (itthi-ākappa).3

Notes:
1. Here, "cause of being female" refers to the cause of the name "female" and the cause of recognizing as "female." However, because the female form and mental states arise depending on this matter, the name "cause of being female" or "cause of being an female" is also appropriate.
2. It is as if it shows the continuity of matter associated with the female faculty as "female" or "a female"; therefore, it is stated as above. (Based on the Ṭīkā).
3. Having rounded shoulders, and having hands and feet that are not clean or grand, is called itthilinga—the female form. The lack of cleanliness of the breasts, the absence of beard and mustache, the way of dressing the hair, and the way of wearing the sarong (htamein) are the causes for recognizing as female, and thus called itthinimitta—female signs. In childhood, playing with imitation trays and pestles, or playing at spinning with soft clay balls, etc., is called itthikutta—female behavior. The manner of standing and walking that is not clean or grand is called itthi-ākappa—female deportment. Another method from the Aṭṭhakathā is: the female organ for excreting urine is called itthilinga (this sign is an easy way to distinguish male and female in newborns); the voice and desires are called itthinimitta; the manner of standing, walking, sitting, chewing, and eating that is not clean or grand is called itthikutta; the female form is called itthi-ākappa. (Ṭīkā)

The male faculty (purisindriya) has the characteristic of the state of being male. Its function is to show "this is a man." It is manifested as the cause of the male sex (purisalinga), male signs (purisanimitta), male behavior (purisakutta), and male deportment (purisa-ākappa). Both the female faculty and the male faculty pervade the entire body, just like the body-sensitivity (kāyapasāda). However, it should not be said that they are located where the body-sensitivity is located, or that they are located where it is not. Like visible form and taste, etc., there is no confusion (mixing) between them.

439. The life faculty (jīvitindriya) has the characteristic of maintaining co-nascent kamma-born matter.1 Its function is to make them proceed (continue) or to make them subsist.1 It is manifested as the establishing of those same co-nascent kamma-born matters. Its proximate cause is the primary elements (bhūta) that are to be maintained.2 To explain further: although it has the function of maintaining and so on, the life faculty maintains the co-nascent kamma-born matter only during the moment of its existence, just as water maintains lotuses and so on.

Notes:
1. Kamma-born matter exists only for its own moment. However, the life faculty maintains the co-nascent kamma-born matter as the cause of its continuous proceeding (pavattithetubhāvena). Therefore, it is said to have the characteristic of maintaining co-nascent kamma-born matter. Indeed, just as nutriment is the cause for the subsistence of nutriment-born matter, kamma alone cannot be the cause for the subsistence of kamma-born matter. Why? Because kamma does not exist at that moment. (Ṭīkā)

1. The term "them" refers to the co-nascent (kamma-born) matters. Pavattanaṃ—making them occur continuously or making them proceed as they usually do—is yāpanaṃ—making them go on or making them subsist. (Ṭīkā). Yāpana is translated as "making subsist" (မျှစေခြင်း) in Burmese, which is difficult to understand. The literal meaning is "making go." In this context, making them go as they usually go, making them occur as they usually occur, making them stay as they usually stay, and making them live as they usually live should be taken as yāpana—making go. If taken this way, it agrees with the Aṭṭhakathā's statement pavattana—making occur continuously. The life faculty, within its own moment of arising, presence, and dissolution, makes the co-nascent kamma-born matters full of strength and alive, and also makes the newly arising kamma-born matters within that moment strong. In this way, although it can only provide full strength within a single moment, it should be understood as making the successive newly arising kamma-born matters proceed continuously.
2. The word yāpayitabba is explained as pavattetabba in the Ṭīkā. Therefore, the phrase yāpayitabbabhūta is translated as "the primary elements that are to be made to go or made to subsist"—it should be understood as the primary elements that are to be made to go, occur, or live as they usually do.

Although they are produced by their respective causes (kamma), the life faculty maintains those phenomena, just as a nurse maintains a child (who is the child of another). It proceeds only in connection with the material phenomena that it causes to proceed, just as a pilot proceeds along with the boat. It does not proceed after the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga), because both itself and the matters it causes to proceed no longer exist. It does not establish them at the moment of dissolution, because it is itself dissolving. For example, a wick and oil that are being consumed cannot maintain the flame. However, it is not devoid of the power of maintaining, causing to proceed, and establishing, because it accomplishes those respective tasks at the aforementioned moments.

440. The heart-base (hadayavatthu) has the characteristic of being the support for the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu). Its function is to uphold those same two elements. It is manifested as the carrying of them.
78: Inside the heart [78] (Note: Connect 'Inside the heart' with 'blood'), as described in the discourse on mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati), the blood exists, being supported by the primary elements which perform functions such as maintaining and carrying, being sustained by temperature (utu), mind (citta), and nutriment (āhāra), being protected by the life-faculty (āyu), and serving as the physical base (vatthu) for the mind-element (manodhātu), the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu), and their associated mental factors. ## 441. The specific mode (ākāravikāra) which assists in the stiffening, upholding, and moving of the body (the group of co-nascent material phenomena) produced by the mind-born air element (cittaja-vāyodhātu) (Note: Connect 'mind-born air element' with 'specific mode') that brings about such actions as moving forward, is called bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti). It has the function of manifesting the intention (of the person). It is manifested as the cause of bodily movement. Its proximate cause is the mind-born air element. To explain further: this bodily intimation is called 'kāyaviññatti' because it is the cause for making one's intention known through bodily movement, and because it is itself known through that body, which is characterized by bodily movement (Note: Kāya-bodily movement + viññatti-making intention known = kāyaviññatti; or Kāya-bodily movement + viññatti-being known = kāyaviññatti). Furthermore, it should be understood that actions such as moving forward occur because of the movement of temperature-born matter (utujarūpa), etc., which are connected to the mind-born matter moved by that bodily intimation. The specific mode which assists in the striking of the kamma-born earth element by the mind-born earth element (cittaja-pathavīdhātu) (Note: Connect 'mind-born earth element' with 'specific mode'. Due to the intention to speak, air elements arise in the throat, etc. The hardness within those air elements is the mind-born earth element, which strikes the kamma-born earth element in the throat, producing sound like a flute or two sticks striking) that brings about the breaking of speech, is called vocal intimation (vacīviññatti). It has the function of manifesting the intention (of the speaker). It is manifested as the cause of the vocal sound. Its proximate cause is the mind-born earth element. To explain further: this vocal intimation is called 'vacīviññatti' because it is the cause for making one's intention known through the vocal sound of speech, and because it is itself known through that speech, which is characterized by the vocal sound (Note: Vacī-vocal sound + viññatti-making intention known = vacīviññatti; or Vacī-vocal sound + viññatti-being known = vacīviññatti). For example, just as in a forest, seeing a sign indicating water, such as an ox skull set up and tied, one knows 'there is water here,' so too, by perceiving bodily movement and vocal sound, bodily and vocal intimations are known. ## 442. The space element (ākāsadhātu) has the characteristic of delimiting matter (Note: The gap between material groups (kalāpa) is called space. Within a kalāpa, matter is inseparable and intermingled). It has the function of showing the limits of material groups. It is manifested as the boundaries of material groups. Alternatively, it is manifested as the state of non-contact (Note: Space is not tangible, so it does not touch the matter it is adjacent to) or as holes and apertures. Its proximate cause is the delimited material groups. By this space element, among the delimited material groups, it becomes clear that 'this material group is above that one,' 'this is below that,' or 'this is across, to the front, back, left, or right of that' (Note: This indicates that relative positions apply only between kalāpas, not within a single kalāpa). ## 443. Lightness of matter (rūpassa lahutā) has the characteristic of non-sluggishness (Note: Being light and quick). It has the function of dispelling the heaviness of material phenomena. It is manifested as quick transformation. Its proximate cause is light material phenomena. Malleability of matter (rūpassa mudutā) has the characteristic of non-rigidity (or being soft). It has the function of dispelling the rigidity of material phenomena. It is manifested as non-opposition in all bodily and vocal activities. Its proximate cause is malleable material phenomena.
