Their function is to crush the distress of the body and consciousness. They are manifested as the peaceful and non-agitated state of the body and consciousness. They have the (tranquil) body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be understood as the opposites of defilements such as restlessness (uddhacca), which cause the non-tranquillity of the body and consciousness.

Note 1: Daratha means sārambha—excessive exertion, or distress/fever. This name daratha is a name for defilements dominated by restlessness (uddhacca) which have suffering (dukkha) and displeasure (domanassa) as their cause, or which arise because of suffering and displeasure. Alternatively, it is a name for the four mental aggregates that occur in such a distracted and distressed manner. The state of being cool and free from agitation by crushing distress is called the state of being cool and free from agitation. (Commentary).

Lightness of the body (of mental factors) is called kāyalahutā. Lightness of consciousness is called cittalahutā. These two kinds of lightness have the characteristic of quieting the heaviness of the body and consciousness. Their function is to crush the heaviness of the body and consciousness. They are manifested as the non-sluggishness of the body and consciousness. They have the (light) body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be understood as the opposites of defilements such as stiffness and torpor (thīna-middha), which cause the heaviness of the body and consciousness.

Malleability of the body (of mental factors) is called kāyamudutā. Malleability of consciousness is called cittamudutā. These two kinds of malleability have the characteristic of quieting the rigidity of the body and consciousness.

Note 1: Defilements dominated by restlessness are called defilements such as restlessness. Alternatively, starting from restlessness, all defilements are included. The same applies to the remaining (subsequent) statements. (Commentary).

Note 2: Garubhāva—the name "heaviness" refers to the four mental aggregates dominated by stiffness and torpor (thīna-middha), or occurring in such a manner. (Commentary).

Note 3: The state of being rigid (unable to be respectful or humble) is called thambha—rigidity. This name refers to the four mental aggregates dominated by wrong view (diṭṭhi) and conceit (māna), or occurring in such a manner. (Commentary).

Their function is to crush the rigidity of the body and consciousness. They are manifested as non-resistance (towards an object), or they cause the non-resistance of associated states towards an object. They have the (malleable) body and consciousness as their proximate cause. They should be understood as the opposites of defilements such as wrong view (diṭṭhi) and conceit (māna), which cause the rigidity of the body and consciousness.

Wieldiness of the body (of mental factors) is called kāyakammaññatā. Wieldiness of consciousness is called cittakammaññatā. These two kinds of wieldiness have the characteristic of quieting the unwieldiness of the body and consciousness. Their function is to crush the unwieldiness of the body and consciousness. They are manifested as the success and perfection of the body and consciousness in taking an object. They have the (wieldy) body and consciousness as their proximate cause. Of the body and consciousness...

Note 1: Kammaññatā means being good for work, or being fit for work. Akammaññabhāva means the state of being unfit for work, or unwieldiness; it is the unfitness for performing wholesome deeds such as giving (dāna) and virtue (sīla). In terms of ultimate reality, these are the defiling states such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda), or the four unwholesome aggregates dominated by sensual desire. (Commentary).
96:
They should be understood as being the opposites of the remaining unwholesome states such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) which cause unfitness in work, as bringing about faith in objects of devotion, and as bringing about endurance and suitability for engagement in beneficial deeds, just like pure gold.

[96] Proficiency and healthiness of the body is called kāyapāguññatā. Proficiency and healthiness of the mind is called cittapāguññatā. These two kinds of proficiency have the characteristic of healthiness (agelaññabhāva) of the body and mind. They have the function of crushing the unhealthiness (gelaññanimaddana) of the body and mind. They manifest as the absence of defects (nirādīnavapaccupaṭṭhāna). They have the healthy body and mind as their proximate cause. They should be understood as the opposites of unwholesome states such as lack of faith (asaddhiya) which cause unhealthiness of the body and mind.

Straightness of the body is called kāyujukatā. Straightness of the mind is called cittujukatā. These two kinds of rectitude have the characteristic of uprightness (ajjava) of the body and mind. They have the function of crushing crookedness (kuṭilabhāvanimaddana) of the body and mind. They manifest as non-crookedness (ajimhatā). They have the straight body and mind as their proximate cause.

Note
1. Unwholesome states such as lack of faith (asaddhiya) and their associated unwholesome states are called the unhealthiness of the body and mind. (Commentary)

They should be understood as the opposites of deceit (māyā), treachery (sāṭheyya), etc., which cause crookedness of the body and mind.

Note
1. Deceit (māyā) has the characteristic of hiding one's own existing faults. Treachery (sāṭheyya) has the characteristic of displaying virtues one does not possess. These unwholesome aggregates occurring through such deceitful and treacherous ways, along with their associated defilements, are called māyā, sāṭheyya, etc. (Commentary)
2. In this context, through cittapassaddhi etc., only the mind becomes tranquil, light, malleable, wieldy, proficient, and straight. However, through kāyapassaddhi etc., not only the group of mental factors (nāmakāya) but also the group of material form (rūpakāya) becomes tranquil, light, malleable, wieldy, proficient, and straight. Therefore, the Blessed One taught the duality of these states in the case of passaddhi etc., but not in all cases. (Commentary) Although these factors—passaddhi, lahutā, mudutā, kammaññatā, pāguññatā, and ujukatā—are present in every wholesome consciousness, they are difficult to realize through personal experience. They become clearly discernable when one practices meditation and reaches access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), or when reaching knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa). Therefore, if one wishes to know them through personal experience, one should practice meditation effectively.
3. Here, chanda (desire to act/wish) is merely the wish to obtain an object. It is not the kind of wishing found in craving (taṇhā) which involves attachment and delight. The desire to perform wholesome deeds, to give, to listen to the Dhamma, to practice meditation, and to attain the true Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna—these are only this wholesome chanda, not greed (lobha) or craving (taṇhā).

471. Chanda is a term for the desire to act (kattukāmatā). Therefore, chanda has the characteristic of the desire to act; it has the function of searching for an object (ārammaṇapariyesana). It manifests as the need for an object (atthikatā). That very desired object is its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). In taking an object of the mind, this chanda should be understood as being like the stretching out of a hand.

472. Adhimokkha means the decision regarding an object. It has the characteristic of conviction or decision (sanniṭṭhāna). It has the function of not wavering (asaṃsappana). It manifests as determination (nicchaya). It has the thing to be decided as its proximate cause. It should be understood as being like a boundary pillar (indakhīla) because of its steadiness in the object.

473. Making is called kāra. Making (the object) in the mind (manasi) is manasikāra. It is also called manasikāra because it makes the mind different from the preceding mind. This manasikāra is of three types: (1) object-directing (ārammaṇapaṭipādaka), (2) process-directing (vīthipaṭipādaka), and (3) impulsion-directing (javanapaṭipādaka).

Note
1. "From the preceding mind" means from the preceding life-continuum (bhavaṅga). "Makes the mind different" means it brings about the cognitive process (vīthi) and impulsion (javana) which are distinct from the life-continuum. By the definition "making the mind different from the preceding mind," it refers to the process-directing manasikāra, which is the five-door adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana) that causes cognitive processes to arise, and the impulsion-directing manasikāra, which is the mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana) that causes impulsion (javana) to arise. (Commentary)

Among these, object-directing manasikāra is the making, placing, or attending (kāra) in the mind (manasi). It has the characteristic of conducting (sāraṇa) [associated states to the object]. It has the function of yoking (saṃyojana) associated states to the object. It manifests as facing the object (ārammaṇābhimukhabhāva). It has the object as its proximate cause. It is included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). It should be understood as being like a charioteer (sārathi) of the associated states because of its directing them to the object. Furthermore, the name "process-directing manasikāra" is a term for five-door adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana). The name "impulsion-directing manasikāra" is a term for mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana). These two are not intended here.

474. Neutrality (majjhattatā) in those [associated] states (tatra) is called tatramajjhattatā. It has the characteristic of balancing (samavāhita) the associated mind and mental factors. It has the function of preventing deficiency or excess (ūnādhikatanivāraṇa); or it has the function of cutting off partiality (pakkhapātupacchedana). It manifests as neutrality (majjhattabhāva). It should be understood as being like a charioteer looking on with indifference at thoroughbred horses (ājānīya) that are moving evenly, because of its state of looking on with indifference at the mind and mental factors that are proceeding evenly.

Note
1. Although this mental factor of tatramajjhattatā is present in every wholesome consciousness, to know its characteristic, function, and manifestation, and how it is like a charioteer indifferent to thoroughbred horses through personal experience...
97:
[97] Compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā) should be understood in the same manner as described in the Description of the Divine Abodes (Brahmavihāra-niddesa). Indeed, the compassion and appreciative joy described there are fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) states that have reached absorption (appanā); however, those presented here are sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) states. This is the only distinction.

Some teachers (keci) desire to include loving-kindness (mettā) and equanimity (upekkhā) among the inconstant factors (aniyata); this view should not be accepted. This is because, in terms of ultimate reality, loving-kindness is simply the mental factor of non-hatred (adosa), and equanimity is simply the mental factor of neutrality of mind (tatramajjhattatā).

475. Abstinence from bodily misconduct is called abstinence from bodily misconduct (kāya-duccarita-virati). The same method applies to the remaining two abstinences. In terms of characteristics and so forth, all three of these abstinences have the characteristic of non-transgression of the objects of bodily misconduct and so forth, and the characteristic of non-violation.

Note: This is extremely difficult. A meditator who has reached the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) understands these characteristics and the similarity to a charioteer through personal experience. Therefore, if one wishes to know this through experience, one should practice the development of insight through the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna-vipassanā) until reaching the knowledge of rise and fall.
1. The objects of bodily misconduct and so forth refer to the lives of others, the property of others, the wives of others, etc. (Commentary)

They have the function (rasa) of shrinking away from the objects of bodily misconduct and so forth. They manifest (paccupaṭṭhāna) as the state of non-action regarding such misconduct. They have faith (saddhā), shame (hiri), fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), fewness of wishes (appicchatā), and other such virtues as their proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). They should be understood as the state of the mind turning away from the performance of evil.

476. Thus, it should be understood that these thirty-six mental formations (saṅkhāra) associate with the first sense-sphere wholesome consciousness (kāmāvacara-kusala-citta). As with the first, so too with the second; the only distinction here is the state of being prompted (sasaṅkhārika).

With the third wholesome consciousness, it should be understood that the remaining thirty-five formations associate, excluding non-delusion (amoha). The same applies to the fourth; the only distinction here is the state of being prompted.

Furthermore, among the formations mentioned for the first consciousness, the remaining thirty-five associate with the fifth consciousness, excluding rapture (pīti). As with the fifth, so too with the sixth; the only distinction here is the state of being prompted.

Note: 
1. By indicating the act of shrinking away from the objects of bodily misconduct, it should be understood that it refers to shrinking away from the misconduct itself. Indeed, it is not appropriate to say that the abstinences have the non-performance of the objects of misconduct as their manifestation; rather, it is only appropriate to say they have the non-performance of misconduct as their manifestation. (Commentary)
2. Because they do not associate with wisdom called non-delusion (amoha), these second and third [types of] consciousness are called dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta).

As with the sixth, so too with the seventh; the only distinction here is the state of being prompted. With the seventh consciousness, it should be understood that the remaining thirty-four formations associate, excluding non-delusion (amoha). The same applies to the eighth; the only distinction here is the state of being prompted.

Among the formations mentioned for the first sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, the remaining thirty-three formations associate with the first fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) absorption consciousness, excluding the three abstinences (virati). Among those thirty-three, the thirty-two formations excluding initial application (vitakka) associate with the second absorption consciousness. Among those thirty-two, the thirty-one excluding sustained application (vicāra) associate with the third absorption consciousness. Among those thirty-one, the thirty excluding rapture (pīti) associate with the fourth absorption consciousness.

Note:
1. These fifth and sixth types of consciousness are accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā-sahagata) and therefore do not associate with rapture (pīti); the same applies to the seventh and eighth. Those two types of consciousness are dissociated from knowledge and thus do not associate with non-delusion (amoha).
2. Although thirty-three are mentioned for this absorption consciousness, it should be noted that in the absorption of compassion, appreciative joy is not included (making 32); in the absorption of appreciative joy, compassion is not included (making 32); and in the absorptions of kasinas etc., neither compassion nor appreciative joy are included (making 31). Furthermore, in sense-sphere wholesome consciousness, compassion associates only when feeling pity; appreciative joy associates only when rejoicing in another's prosperity; right action (sammā-kammanta) associates only when abstaining from bodily misconduct; right speech (sammā-vācā) associates only when abstaining from verbal misconduct; and right livelihood (sammā-ājīva) associates only when abstaining from wrong livelihood. Apart from these, when ordinary wholesome consciousness arises during acts of giving, showing respect, etc., compassion, appreciative joy, and the three abstinences do not associate. This distinction should also be noted.

Among those thirty, the twenty-eight formations excluding the inconstant (aniyata) factors of compassion and appreciative joy associate with the fifth absorption consciousness. Those same twenty-eight associate with the four immaterial-sphere (arūpāvacara) wholesome consciousnesses. The only distinction in these immaterial-sphere absorption consciousnesses is the state of being immaterial-sphere.

Among the supramundane (lokuttara) wholesome consciousnesses, for the path-consciousness (magga-viññāṇa) associated with the first absorption, the formations should be understood according to the method stated for the first fine-material sphere consciousness (excluding compassion and appreciative joy and including the three abstinences). For the path-consciousnesses differentiated by the second absorption and so forth, the formations should be understood according to the method stated for the second fine-material sphere consciousness and so forth (excluding compassion and appreciative joy and including the three abstinences). The distinction is that in these supramundane consciousnesses, compassion and appreciative joy are absent, [98] the three abstinences are always present, and they are supramundane. Thus, the formations that are primarily wholesome should be understood as just described.

Note:
98:
1. Although the three abstinences (viratī) will be shown later to replace compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā), they are shown here in parentheses for the ease of those with little scriptural knowledge. In the first jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), subtracting the 2 factors of compassion and appreciative joy from 33 leaves 31; adding the three abstinences to that makes 34 factors.

2. It should be understood that in the second jhāna, there are 33 factors after subtracting initial application (vitakka) from the 34; in the third jhāna, there are 32 after subtracting sustained application (vicāra); and in the fourth and fifth jhānas, there are 31 after subtracting rapture (pīti).

477. Among unwholesome consciousnesses, the fixed formations (niyata-saṅkhāra) associated with the first unwholesome consciousness rooted in greed (lobhamūla) consist of 13 formations explicitly mentioned (sarūpena āgatā) and 4 "or-whatever" (yevāpanaka) formations, totaling 17. Among them, the 13 formations explicitly mentioned are: contact (phassa), volition (cetanā), initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), energy (vīriya), life (jīvita), concentration (samādhi), shamelessness (ahirika), fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa), greed (lobha), delusion (moha), and wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). The 4 "or-whatever" formations are: desire (chanda), decision (adhimokkha), restlessness (uddhacca), and attention (manasikāra).

478. Therein, one who is not ashamed is "shameless" (ahirika). The state of being shameless is "shamelessness" (ahirikaṃ). The state of not fearing [wrongdoing] is "fearlessness of wrongdoing" (anottappaṃ). Of these two, shamelessness has the characteristic of not loathing bodily misconduct, etc., or the characteristic of lack of shame. Fearlessness of wrongdoing has the characteristic of not fearing those same misconducts, or the characteristic of lack of dread. This is the brief explanation. The detailed explanation should be understood by way of the opposite of what was said regarding shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa).

Note:
1. Connect as: "The fixed formations are 17." This has been translated with slight modifications for ease of understanding.
2. In this Burmese translation, the term remains "ahirika," but in Pali, it is distinguished by gender: the person who is shameless is "ahiriko" (masculine), and the state of being shameless is "ahirikaṃ" (neuter). "Ahiriko" is a common noun, while "ahirikaṃ" is an abstract noun (bhāvataddhita); they are distinguished in this way.

479. The state by which one covets, or which itself covets, or just the act of coveting is "greed" (lobha). The state by which one is deluded, or which itself is deluded, or just the act of being deluded is "delusion" (moha). Among these, greed has the characteristic of grasping an object like "monkey-glue" (a trap). Its function is sticking to the object like a piece of meat thrown onto a hot pan. It is manifested as not letting go, like the staining of oil. Its proximate cause is seeing enjoyment in things that lead to fetters (saṃyojaniya-dhamma). It should be seen that as it increases in the form of the river of craving (taṇhā), it carries one away to the woeful states (apāya), just as a swift-flowing river carries things to the great ocean.

480. Delusion has the characteristic of blindness of the mind, or the characteristic of lack of knowledge. Its function is non-penetration, or the function of concealing the true nature of the object. It is manifested as wrong practice, or as darkness. Its proximate cause is unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra). It should be seen as the root of all unwholesome states.

Note:
1. Here, "delusion" (moha) refers only to the lack of knowing things as they truly are; it does not mean being in a faint or unconscious state. Not knowing the true nature of things such as impermanence (anicca), and instead knowing them wrongly as permanent (nicca), etc., or knowing them in the ordinary way one is accustomed to, is the power of delusion.

481. The state by which one sees wrongly, or which itself sees wrongly, or just the act of seeing wrongly is "wrong view" (micchādiṭṭhi). It has the characteristic of unwise conviction. Its function is misinterpretation (pāramāsa). It is manifested as a wrong obsession. Its proximate cause is the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones (ariya), etc. It should be seen as the greatest fault.

[99] 482. The state of being excited without being able to focus on the object is "restlessness" (uddhacca). It has the characteristic of disquiet, like water ruffled by the wind. Its function is instability.
99:
[Restlessness] is like a banner or a flag fluttering in the wind; it manifests [to knowledge] as whirling; it is like ashes flying up when struck by a stone.

Note:
1. Delusion (moha) perceives impermanence, suffering, and non-self as permanence, happiness, and self as it normally does. Wrong view (diṭṭhi) wrongly perceives and clings to the mental and physical phenomena, which are not self, as a self; or that this self is eternal and unchanging; or that it is completely annihilated at death; or that there is no kamma and its results, and so on. Thus, they differ in the way they misperceive.
2. Here, "and so on" includes things like being unwilling to listen to the Dhamma of the virtuous.

It has improper attention that causes mental unrest as its proximate cause. It should be understood as the state of mental distraction or the cause of mental wandering. The remaining factors such as contact (phassa) and so on should be understood in the same way as mentioned in the section on wholesome mental formations (kusala saṅkhāra). Indeed, it is only the state of being unwholesome and the state of being base because of being unwholesome that distinguishes these unwholesome contact and other factors from the wholesome ones.

483. As just described, it should be understood that these 17 mental formations are associated with the first unwholesome consciousness. The same should be understood for the second unwholesome consciousness as well; however, the distinction here in the second unwholesome consciousness is its prompted nature (sasaṅkhārika) and the occasional presence of sloth and torpor (thīna-middha).

Among them, shrinking and laziness is called sloth (thīna); being dazed and heavy (in the sense of being incapable and weary) is called torpor (middha).

Note:
1. This is the meaning of the term cetaso avūpasame. According to the Ṭīkā, which explains that "the locative case is used in the sense of a result to be accomplished," this is translated to show the purpose and to make the Burmese translation smooth.
2. This means that sloth and torpor also occasionally associate with that prompted consciousness.
3. According to the traditional translation of thīna as "dullness" and middha as "drowsiness," it is translated here as "being dazed." This state is also commonly described as being "foggy" or "droopy," so "drooping" is also shown.

Shrinking without making an effort is the meaning of sloth (thīna); being weary while lacking capability is the meaning of torpor (middha). Sloth and torpor combined are called thīna-middha. Among them, sloth has the characteristic of lack of effort, the function of removing energy, and manifests [to knowledge] as shrinking. Torpor has the characteristic of unwieldiness, the function of closing [the doors of consciousness], and manifests as shrinking; or it causes nodding and sleepiness. Both of these have improper attention toward boredom, laziness, and so on as their proximate cause.

In the third unwholesome consciousness, the remaining formations should be understood as those mentioned in the first, excluding wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). However, conceit (māna) is occasional here. This is the distinction. That conceit has the characteristic of haughtiness, the function of self-exaltation, and manifests as the desire for prominence like a banner. It has greed dissociated from views as its proximate cause and should be regarded as being like madness.

In the fourth unwholesome consciousness, the remaining formations should be understood as those mentioned in the second, excluding wrong view. Here too, conceit is among the occasional ones.

Furthermore, the remaining formations mentioned in the first, excluding rapture (pīti), are associated with the fifth unwholesome consciousness. The same applies to the sixth consciousness; the only distinction here is its prompted nature and the occasional association of sloth and torpor.

In the seventh unwholesome consciousness, the remaining formations mentioned in the fifth, excluding wrong view, should be understood to associate.

Note:
1. This means that conceit also occasionally associates with this consciousness dissociated from views. Therefore, this consciousness dissociated from views should be understood in two ways: as associated with conceit and as dissociated from conceit.
2. When conceit associates with this consciousness, there are 19 formations; among them, sloth, torpor, and conceit are occasional and should be understood to associate only sometimes.
3. From the 17 formations in the first consciousness, subtracting rapture leaves 16 that associate with the fifth consciousness; in the sixth consciousness, adding sloth and torpor makes 18.

The distinction is that in this seventh consciousness, conceit is occasional. In the eighth unwholesome consciousness, the remaining formations mentioned in the sixth, excluding wrong view, should be understood to associate. Here too, conceit is among the occasional ones. This concludes one part.

484. Furthermore, among the two types of consciousness rooted in hatred (dosamūla), the fixed formations (niyata saṅkhāra) associated with the first consciousness are 11 that appear in their own form, 4 "or-whatever" (yevāpanaka) formations, and 3 occasional ones...
100:
There are 4 yevāpanaka formations (making a total of 15), and 3 aniyata (occasional) formations. Thus, there are 18 formations associated with the first aversion-rooted (dosamūla) consciousness. Among these, the 11 formations that appear explicitly (sarūpa) are: phassa (contact), cetanā (volition), vitakka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), vīriya (energy), jīvita (life faculty), samādhi (concentration), ahirika (shamelessness), anottappa (fearlessness of wrongdoing), dosa (aversion), and moha (delusion). The 4 yevāpanaka formations are: chanda (desire), adhimokkha (decision), uddhacca (restlessness), and manasikāra (attention). The 3 aniyata formations are: issā (envy), macchariya (stinginess), and kukkucca (remorse).

485. Therein, dosa (aversion) is so called because it corrupts, or it corrupts by itself, or it is merely the act of corrupting.

Note:
1. From the 16 formations of the fifth consciousness, diṭṭhi (wrong view) is excluded, leaving 15. It should be known that when māna (conceit) is added to these 15, 16 formations are sometimes associated.
2. In the sixth consciousness, diṭṭhi is excluded from the 18 formations, leaving 17 associated with the eighth consciousness. It should be known that when māna is added to these 17, 18 formations are sometimes associated.

Mere resentment or anger is called dosa. It has the characteristic of ferocity or harshness, like a struck poisonous snake. Its function is to spread or manifest in a distorted manner through its own occurrence or by causing undesirable objects; or its function is to cause the body to tremble; or it has the function of fulfillment through the trembling of the body, like the falling of poison. Alternatively, its function is to burn its own physical support, like a forest fire. It manifests (to knowledge) as destroying oneself and others, like an enemy who has found an opportunity. Its proximate cause is the grounds for resentment (āghātavatthu). It should be regarded as putrid urine mixed with poison.

486. The act of envying is issā. It has the characteristic of envying (jealousy) the success of others. Its function is to be dissatisfied with that very success of others. It manifests as turning away from it. Its proximate cause is the success of others. It should be regarded as a fetter (saṃyojana).

487. The state of being stingy is macchariya. It has the characteristic of concealing one's own success, whether already attained or yet to be attained. Its function is the inability to endure the sharing of those very successes with others. It manifests as shrinking (due to dislike of sharing one's own success with others); or it manifests as a state of bitterness. Its proximate cause is one's own success. It should be regarded as a deformity or distortion of the mind.

488. Ku (contemptible) + kata (done) = kukata (a contemptible deed). The state of that kukata is kukkucca (remorse). It has the characteristic of subsequent regret. Its function is grieving while recollecting evil deeds done or good deeds not done. It manifests as remorse. Its proximate cause is deeds done or not done. It should be regarded as a state of slavery. The remaining formations such as phassa, etc., have the same explanations as previously mentioned. This concludes one section.

Note:
1. Although it is said to be the cause of kukata, it is actually the cause of the mind that regrets and worries, thinking 'a contemptible deed has been done.' Therefore, the Commentary (Ṭīkā) explains: 'In the word kukata (a contemptible deed), a good deed that should have been done but was not done is also called kukata. Indeed, people say, "I did not do that good deed; that non-doing is a kukata (contemptible deed)." For this reason, it will be said that its function is grieving while recollecting evil deeds done or good deeds not done. Thus, a bad deed done or a good deed not done is called kukata. The mind that arises with the intention of remorse based on that kukata is also called kukata because it arises together with it (or because it takes that kukata as its object). Thus it is said that the state of that kukata is kukkucca.' Therefore, the cause of kukata should be understood as the cause of the mind that regrets and worries, thinking 'alas, a contemptible deed has been done.'

Thus, it should be known that these 18 formations are associated with the first aversion-rooted consciousness. The same applies to the second consciousness; however, the distinction is that the second consciousness is prompted (sasaṅkhārika) and there is the possibility of thina-middha (sloth and torpor) among the aniyata formations.

489. Between the two delusion-rooted (mohamūla) consciousnesses, first, in the one associated with doubt (vicikicchā-sampayutta), there are 11 formations that appear explicitly: phassa, cetanā, vitakka, vicāra, vīriya, jīvita, cittatthiti, ahirika, anottappa, moha, and vicikicchā.
101:
There are 2 yevāpanaka formations, namely uddhacca (restlessness) and manasikāra (attention); thus, there are 13 formations in total.

490. Therein, cittatthiti (stability of mind) is a weak concentration (samādhi) which is merely the staying of the mind in the process of occurrence. Vi (devoid of) + cikicchā (remedy) = vicikicchā; it is a state devoid of remedy, or a state difficult to cure. It has the characteristic of doubting (regarding the Buddha, etc., who should be believed). Its function is wavering. It manifests as indecision or a state of being in two minds; or it manifests as taking various aspects of an object that are not certain. Its proximate cause is unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) which leads to doubt. It should be regarded as a factor that creates an obstacle to practice (paṭipatti). The remaining formations such as phassa, etc., have the same explanations as previously mentioned.

In the consciousness associated with restlessness (uddhacca-sampayutta), excluding vicikicchā from the formations mentioned for the doubt-associated consciousness, the remaining 12 formations are present. Furthermore, because vicikicchā is absent in this restlessness-associated consciousness, adhimokkha (decision) also arises. Together with that adhimokkha, there are 13 formations.

Specifically, because of the presence of adhimokkha, concentration (samādhi) is stronger (than in the doubt-rooted mind). Furthermore, in this consciousness, uddhacca (restlessness) appears explicitly (sarūpa). Adhimokkha and manasikāra appear by way of yevāpanaka. Thus should the unwholesome (akusala) formations be understood.

491. Among the indeterminate (abyākata) formations, first, the resultant indeterminates (vipāka-abyākata) are of two kinds: rootless (ahetuka) and rooted (sahetuka). Among them, the formations associated with rootless resultant consciousness are called rootless. Among those rootless resultant formations, first, those associated with wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) are 4 formations that appear explicitly: phassa, cetanā, jīvita, and cittatthiti; and 1 yevāpanaka formation, manasikāra. Thus, there are five. The formations associated with ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness are also these same five.

The formations associated with the two kinds of mind-element (mano-dhātu, i.e., receiving) – wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant – are these five plus vitakka, vicāra, and adhimokkha, making eight. The same eight are associated with the three kinds of rootless mind-consciousness element (ahetuka-manoviññāṇa-dhātu, i.e., investigating). Specifically, it should be known that among these three, pīti (rapture) is also associated with the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata).

Note:
1. It should be known that 9 formations are associated with the investigating consciousness accompanied by joy, including pīti.

Furthermore, the formations associated with rooted resultant consciousness are called rooted (sahetuka). Among them, first, the formations associated with the eight sense-sphere resultant (kāmāvacara-vipāka) consciousnesses are similar to the formations associated with the eight sense-sphere wholesome (kāmāvacara-kusala) consciousnesses. However, specifically, among the occasional (aniyata) formations, karuṇā (compassion) and muditā (appreciative joy) are not present in resultants because they have the concept of beings as their object. Indeed, sense-sphere resultants have only limited (paritta/kāma) phenomena as their objects. Not only are karuṇā and muditā absent, but the three abstinences (virati) are also not present in resultants. For there is the saying: 'The five precepts are purely wholesome (kusala).'
102:
Furthermore, the mental formations (saṅkhāra) associated with the resultant consciousness (vipākacitta) of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara), and the supramundane (lokuttara) are identical to the mental formations associated with the wholesome consciousness (kusalacitta) of those three types.

492. Functional indeterminate (kiriyā-abyākata) mental formations are also of two kinds: rootless (ahetuka) and with roots (sahetuka). Among them, those associated with rootless functional consciousness are called rootless. These rootless functional mental formations are similar to the mental formations associated with the wholesome-resultant mind-element (manodhātu [i.e., receiving consciousness]) and the two wholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness elements (manoviññāṇadhātu [i.e., investigating consciousness]). The distinction, however, is that in the two rootless functional mind-consciousness elements (mind-door adverting and the smile-producing consciousness), energy (viriya) is present. Due to the presence of energy, concentration (samādhi) becomes powerful. This is the distinction in these mind-door adverting and smile-producing consciousnesses.

Furthermore, the mental formations associated with functional consciousness with roots are called "with roots" (sahetuka). Among those functional mental formations with roots, first, those associated with the eight functional consciousnesses of the sense sphere with roots are similar to the mental formations associated with the eight wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere, excluding the three abstinences (virati). Furthermore, the mental formations associated with the functional consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere and the immaterial sphere are in every way identical to the mental formations associated with the wholesome consciousnesses of those same spheres. Thus, the indeterminate (abyākata) mental formations should be understood. Here ends one section.

This preceding explanation is a detailed exposition of the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).

This analysis of the five aggregates is a detailed exposition of the aggregates according to the method of the Word-Analysis (padabhājanīya) in the Abhidhamma.

## Analysis of the Past, etc.

493. The Blessed One said:
"Whatever matter (rūpa) there is, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—collecting it all together and summarizing it, this is called the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). Whatever feeling (vedanā) there is... whatever perception (saññā) there is... whatever mental formations (saṅkhāra) there are... whatever consciousness (viññāṇa) there is, whether past, future, or present... [as before] ...summarizing it, this is called the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha)."
Thus, the aggregates were explained in detail.

In those words of the Buddha, the term "whatever" (yaṃ kiñci) is a term that includes everything without exception. The term "matter" (rūpaṃ) is a term that defines and restricts the meaning from being too broad or over-extended. Thus, by the combination of these two words ("whatever matter")...

[Notes]
1. The meaning to be shown here is already included in page 308, note 1.
2. From the 36 mental formations associated with wholesome sense-sphere consciousness, subtracting the three abstinences, it should be understood that 33 mental formations are associated with functional sense-sphere consciousness with roots. Among them, non-delusion (amoha) is associated only with the four consciousnesses associated with knowledge; joy (pīti) is associated only with the four consciousnesses accompanied by pleasure, just as in the wholesome consciousnesses. Furthermore, compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā) should be understood to be associated only when feeling pity or rejoicing in another's success.

[Additional Note]
By the word "whatever" (yaṃ kiñci), according to the Pali method, neuter terms like mind-consciousness, sense-bases, etc., could be taken; if so, unnecessary meanings would also be included.
103:
Therefore, to avoid such unnecessary meanings, He makes a complete inclusion of matter (rūpa). After that, He endeavors to analyze that matter through terms such as 'past' and so on. Indeed, some of that matter is past (gone by), some is future (yet to come), and so forth. The same method applies to feeling (vedanā) and the others.

494. In that regard, matter is called 'past' in four ways: by way of period (addhā), continuity (santati), occasion (samaya), and moment (khaṇa). Likewise for 'future' and 'present'.

By way of period (addhā), for an individual in a single life, what is before rebirth (paṭisandhi) is past; what is after death (cuti) is future; and what is in between rebirth and death—or between the past and future—is present.

Note: To prevent taking [other things], He limits it by saying 'rūpaṃ - matter'. By this word, it means all that is matter only, excluding other things like consciousness (viññāṇa), etc.
1. In the Pali, it says 'Whatever matter, past, future, or present...' Following that Pali order, the translation says 'After that...' etc. In the Burmese translation, it is not possible to follow the Pali order exactly, so it is translated starting from 'being past, future, present' etc.
2. A long duration is called addhā (period). The uninterrupted sequence of matter and mind is called santati (continuity). In this context, as will be shown later, the sequence of the same kind of matter is called santati.

By way of continuity (santati), matter produced by the same kind of temperature (utu) or the same kind of nutriment (āhāra), though occurring earlier or later, is called present. Matter produced by a different kind of temperature or nutriment before that is past, and after that is future. Mind-produced matter (cittaja-rūpa) produced within a single five-door cognitive process (pañcadvāravīthi), a single sequence of mind-door impulsion (manodvārajavana), or a single meditative attainment (samāpatti) is called present. Before that is past, and after that is future. For kamma-produced matter (kammaja-rūpa), there is no division into past etc. by way of its own separate continuity; however, its status as past etc. should be understood by way of the support it receives from matter produced by temperature, nutriment, and mind.

By way of occasion (samaya), matter occurring continuously within occasions such as a single muhutta, morning, evening, night, or day is called present in relation to that specific occasion. Before that is past, and after that is future.

By way of moment (khaṇa), matter included within the three moments such as arising (uppāda) is present. Before that (before reaching the three moments) is future, and after that (having passed the three moments) is past.

Note: 1. The time of ten finger-snaps is 1 khaṇa. 10 khaṇa is 1 laya. 10 laya is 1 khaṇalaya. 10 khaṇalaya is 1 muhutta. (Abhidhāna verses 66-7).
2. Here, khaṇa is not the time of ten finger-snaps, but only the moments of arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhiti), and dissolution (bhaṅga) of a single unit of matter. These three moments are the existing moments of matter and constitute its lifespan. The lifespan of arising, presence, and dissolution of mind and mental factors is only one-seventeenth of the lifespan of matter.

Alternatively, matter whose causal and conditional functions (hetu-paccaya-kicca) have passed is past. Matter whose causal function is finished but conditional function is not yet finished is present. Matter that has not reached either function is future. Or, it is present at the moment it performs its own function; before that moment (before performing its function) it is future; after that function is performed (having ceased) it is past. In this classification of past etc., only the explanation by moment (khaṇa) and function (kicca) is literal (nippariyāya); the rest are figurative (pariyāya).

495. The division into internal (ajjhatta) and external (bahiddha) is as previously stated. However, here it should be understood that all matter occurring within the continuity of individual beings, called personal internal (niyakajjhatta), is internal; matter occurring in the continuity of others (such as the sensitive eye, etc.) is external. The division into gross (oḷārika) and subtle (sukhuma) is also as previously stated.

Note: 1. Refers to the division of internal and external shown on page 231. However, since that explanation is not yet complete for this context, it is further divided here. 2. Refers to what was shown on page 231.

496. The division into inferior (hīna) and superior (paṇီta) is of two kinds: figurative (pariyāya) and literal (nippariyāya). Therein, compared to the matter of Akaniṭṭha Brahmās, the matter of Sudassī Brahmās is inferior. That same matter is superior compared to the matter of Sudassa Brahmās. In this way, the state of being inferior or superior should be understood figuratively down to the matter of beings in hell. Literally, however, the matter upon which unwholesome resultant consciousness (akusala-vipāka) arises taking it as an object is inferior. The matter upon which wholesome resultant consciousness (kusala-vipāka) arises taking it as an object is superior.
104:
[104] These two types of matter, distant matter and near matter, are also to be understood in the manner already described. However, in this context, the state of being distant or near should also be understood by way of relative location.

497. 'Having gathered and condensed all that matter into one' means: all that matter, which has been explained in detail individually by terms such as 'past' and so on, is brought together by wisdom into a single category characterized by the nature of being affected (ruppana-lakkhaṇa), and is called the 'aggregate of matter' (rūpakkhandha). This is the meaning here. By this, it is shown that all matter, by coming into the state of a group based on the characteristic of being affected, is called the rūpakkhandha. Indeed, there is no such thing as a rūpakkhandha apart from matter.

498. Just as with matter, feeling (vedanā) and the others are also called the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) and so forth, by coming into the state of a group based on the characteristic of being felt (vedayita-lakkhaṇa) and so on. Indeed, there are no such things as the aggregate of feeling and so forth apart from feeling and the others.

To show the distinction: in the classification of past and so on, among these feelings etc., the past, future, and present nature of feeling should be understood by way of continuity (santati) and by way of moments (khana) and so on. Therein, by way of continuity, feeling included within a single process of the five doors (pañcadvāravīthi), a single sequence of mind-door impulsions (manodvārajavana), or a single attainment (samāpatti), as well as feeling occurring in well-associated connection with a single object such as the Buddha or the Dhamma, is called 'present'. What is prior to that is 'past', and what is subsequent is 'future'. By way of moments and so on, the feeling that is included within the triad of moments, situated in the middle of the preceding and succeeding parts, and is currently performing its own function, is called 'present'. Prior to that (before reaching the triad of moments), it is 'future'; subsequent to that (after reaching the triad of moments and having performed its own function), it is 'past'. The distinction between internal and external feeling should be understood by way of one's own internal states (niyakajjhatta).

499. The distinction between gross (oḷārika) feeling and subtle (sukhuma) feeling should be understood by way of kind (jāti), nature (sabhāva), person (puggala), mundane (lokiya), and supramundane (lokuttara), as taught in the Vibhaṅga in the manner beginning: 'Unwholesome feeling is gross; wholesome and indeterminate feelings are subtle.'

First, by way of kind (jāti): unwholesome feeling is of an unpeaceful nature because it is the cause of performing blameworthy actions and because of the heat of the defilements; therefore, it is grosser than wholesome feeling. It is grosser than resultant indeterminate (vipākābyākata) feeling because it involves concern (byāpāra), effort (ussāha), produces results (savipāka), has the heat of defilements, and is blameworthy. It is grosser than functional indeterminate (kiriyābyākata) feeling because it produces results, has the heat of defilements, has the suffering of defilements, and is blameworthy. Wholesome and indeterminate feelings, however, are subtle compared to unwholesome feeling by way of the reverse of what was stated. Both wholesome and unwholesome feelings are grosser than the two types of indeterminate feelings, as appropriate, because they involve concern, effort, and produce results. [105] Conversely, the two types of indeterminate feelings are subtle compared to those wholesome and unwholesome feelings. In this way, the state of being gross or subtle should first be understood by way of kind (jāti).

500. By way of nature (sabhāva): painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) is gross because it lacks any pleasantness and because it is turbulent and agitated.
105:
It means according to each cause and each feeling. Wholesome and unwholesome feelings are grosser than resultant indeterminate feelings because of all three reasons; they are grosser than functional indeterminate feelings because they produce results and because they involve the activity and effort associated with producing results.

(Sub-commentary) Activities and efforts not related to producing results also exist in functional indeterminate feelings; therefore, in terms of such activity and effort, it should not be said that wholesome feeling is grosser than functional feeling—this is understood from that sub-commentary explanation.

2. "With vibration" (savipphāra) means "with movement all around" (sapariphanda). "Not peaceful" (anupasanta)—this is the meaning (Sub-commentary). This is a translation made clear in accordance with that explanation.

Because it causes agitation, is terrifying, and is overwhelming and oppressive, it is grosser than the other two feelings. The other two feelings, however, are subtler than painful feeling as appropriate, because they are enjoyable, peaceful, sublime, delightful (or: endearing), and neutral. Both pleasant and painful feelings are grosser than neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling because they are vibrating, expanding, and agitated, and because they are manifest. That neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is subtler than those two feelings of pleasure and pain by the reverse of what was said. Thus, grossness and subtleness should be understood by way of essence (sabhāva).

501. By way of person (puggala), the feeling of one not in attainment is grosser than the feeling of one in attainment because it is scattered among various objects; conversely, the other is subtle. Thus, grossness and subtleness should be understood by way of person.

By way of mundane and supramundane, feeling that can be an object of taints is called "with taints" (sāsava) and is mundane.

Note: 1. This is a translation based on the existing text "majjhattato". If it were "majjhaṭṭhato", it would be translated as "because it stands in the middle of pain and pleasure", which would be clearer.

Because it is a cause for the arising of taints, an object of floods (ogha), an object of bonds (yoga), an object of ties (gantha), an object of hindrances (nīvaraṇa), an object of clinging (upādāna), an object of defilements that cause burning (saṃkilesa), and because it is common to worldlings (puthujjana), it is grosser than the "taintless" (anāsava) feeling. The taintless feeling is subtler than the feeling with taints by the reverse of what was said. Thus, grossness and subtleness should be understood by way of mundane and supramundane.

502. In the aforementioned classification of gross and subtle, confusion regarding nature (jāti) and so on should be avoided. The way to avoid it is: although a feeling associated with unwholesome resultant body-consciousness is subtle (sukhuma) because it is indeterminate (abyākata) by way of nature, it is gross (oḷārika) by way of essence and so on. Indeed, it has been said: "Indeterminate feeling is subtle. Painful feeling is gross. The feeling of one in attainment is subtle. The feeling of one not in attainment is gross. Feeling with taints is gross. Taintless feeling is subtle."

Note: 1. This refers to the ability to be an object of the floods, not necessarily that it is currently being taken as an object. The same applies to the subsequent terms.
2. Connect this as: "it is gross because it is common to worldlings."
3. Here also, it is translated as "than" (htet) according to common usage (instead of "below").

Just like painful feeling, pleasant feeling and others are gross by way of nature but subtle by way of essence and so on. Therefore, the grossness and subtleness of feelings should be understood so that there is no confusion by way of nature and so on. To understand: indeterminate feeling is subtler than wholesome and unwholesome feelings by way of nature.
106:
In that regard, what is indeterminate feeling? Is it painful feeling or pleasant feeling? Is it the feeling of one in attainment or one not in attainment? Is it feeling with taints or taintless feeling? Such distinctions of essence and so on should not be misapplied. This method applies everywhere.

Furthermore, because it is said, "Feeling should be seen as gross or subtle by comparing this or that feeling," even among unwholesome feelings, hate-rooted feeling is grosser than greed-rooted feeling because it burns its own support like fire; greed-rooted feeling is subtle. Even hate-rooted feeling is gross if it is fixed (niyata), and subtle if it is not fixed. Even fixed feeling is gross if it is "aeon-lasting" (kappaṭṭhitika), otherwise it is subtle.

Note: Among those aeon-lasting fixed feelings, if it is unprompted (asaṅkhārika), it is gross; if it is prompted (sasaṅkhārika), it is subtle. Greed-rooted feeling is gross if associated with wrong view, and subtle if not. That feeling is also gross if it is fixed, aeon-lasting, and unprompted; otherwise, it is subtle. In general, unwholesome feeling is gross if it has many results, and subtle if it has few results. Wholesome feeling is gross if it has few results, and subtle if it has many results.

Another way of considering: Sense-sphere wholesome feeling is gross; fine-material sphere feeling is subtle. Beyond that, immaterial-sphere feeling is subtle; beyond that, supramundane wholesome feeling is subtle. Among sense-sphere wholesome feelings, feeling consisting in giving (dānamaya) is gross; feeling consisting in virtue (sīlamaya) is subtle; beyond that, feeling consisting in meditation (bhāvanāmaya) is subtle. Among feelings consisting in meditation, that with two roots (duhetuka) is gross; that with three roots (tihetuka) is subtle. Among three-rooted feelings, the prompted is gross; the unprompted is subtle. Among fine-material sphere feelings, the first jhāna feeling is gross... and so on... the fifth jhāna feeling is subtle. Among immaterial-sphere feelings, the feeling associated with the sphere of infinite space is gross... and so on...

Note: 1. Here, the name "asaṅkhārika" is as it exists in the Visuddhimagga.
2. Here also, the names "sasaṅkhārika" and "asaṅkhārika" are as they exist in the Visuddhimagga.

the feeling associated with the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is indeed subtle. Among supramundane feelings, the feeling associated with the path of stream-entry is gross... and so on... the feeling associated with the path of arahantship is indeed subtle. This method should be understood for resultant and functional feelings of various planes, and for feelings described by way of pain, etc., non-attainment, etc., and with taints, etc.

By way of location (okāsa), pain in hell is gross; pain in the animal realm is subtle... and so on... pain in the realm of devas who wield power over others' creations (paranimmitavasavatti) is indeed subtle. Likewise, pleasure should also be applied appropriately in all locations. By way of the object (vatthu) upon which it arises, any feeling that has an inferior object is gross; a feeling that has a superior object is subtle.

In the distinction between inferior and superior, the gross feeling should be seen as inferior, and the subtle feeling as superior.

503. The term "distant" (dūra) means "unwholesome feeling is distant from wholesome and indeterminate feelings." The term "near" (santike) means "unwholesome feeling is [near] to unwholesome feeling..."

Note: 1. "Having an inferior object" means the feeling that arises by taking the inferior object of one eating coarse rice is gross because of the nature of having an inferior object.
107:
The feeling of one eating rice mixed with meat is subtle because of the excellence of its basis. (Commentary)

It is analyzed in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi in such a way as: "Near to unwholesome feeling," and so forth. Therefore, unwholesome feeling is far from wholesome and indeterminate (avyākata) feelings because of its different nature, its lack of association, and its dissimilarity. Likewise, wholesome and indeterminate feelings are far from unwholesome feeling. This is the method in all sections. Furthermore, unwholesome feeling is near to unwholesome feeling because of its similar nature and its similarity—this is how it should be understood. This preceding statement is an introductory explanation in the detailed analysis of the aggregate of feeling as past and so forth.

Furthermore, the coarseness and subtleness of perception (saññā), formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa) associated with those respective feelings should be understood in the same way as this feeling.

## Discussion on the Determination of Order and So Forth

504. Having understood thus, again in those very aggregates—

For the sake of the development of knowledge in the aggregates, by way of order, distinction,
Neither less nor more, simile, and likewise
By way of being seen in two ways, for the success of the benefit of one seeing thus,
The method of determination should be well understood by the wise.

In that verse, regarding "by way of order," there are many kinds of order: order of arising (uppatti-kkama), order of abandoning (pahāna-kkama), order of practice (paṭipatti-kkama), order of planes (bhūmi-kkama), and order of teaching (desanā-kkama).

Among those many orders, the order stated as: "First there is the kalala (embryo), from the kalala comes the abbuda (fetal foam)," and so forth, is the order of arising. The order stated as: "States to be abandoned by vision (sotāpatti-magga), states to be abandoned by development (the three higher maggas)," and so forth, is the order of abandoning. The order stated as: "Purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi), purification of mind (citta-visuddhi)," and so forth, is the order of practice. The order stated as: "Sense-sphere states (kāmāvacara), fine-material-sphere states (rūpāvacara)," and so forth, is the order of planes. The order stated as: "The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts," or "Talk on giving, talk on virtue," and so forth, is the order of teaching. Among these, the order of arising is not suitable here because the aggregates do not arise in a sequential order like the kalala and so forth. The order of abandoning is also not suitable because wholesome and indeterminate aggregates are not to be abandoned. The order of practice is also not suitable because unwholesome aggregates are not to be practiced. The order of planes is also not suitable because feeling and so forth are included within all four planes. Only the order of teaching is suitable.

To explain its suitability in detail: The Blessed One, desiring to free the assembly of veneyya beings (those to be guided) who have fallen into the flood of views of self-clinging by taking the five aggregates as a whole, by showing the differentiation of the compact mass (samūhaghana)—

Note: Desiring to free them from the clinging to self by showing the individual differentiation of the group of mentality and materiality (samūhaghana) which appears as a single unit or a single person, the Blessed One, who seeks the welfare of beings, first taught the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) which is coarse and distinct, being the object of the eye and so forth, for the sake of easy grasping by those respective beings.
108:
Next, He taught the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) which experiences pleasant and unpleasant objects. Then, He taught the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) which grasps the aspect of the object of feeling in the manner of: "Whatever one feels, that one perceives." Then, He taught the formations (saṅkhāra) which perform actions by the power of perception. Finally, He taught the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) which is the support and the chief of those, feeling and so forth. Thus should the method of determination by way of order be understood.

505. "By way of distinction" means by way of the distinction between the aggregates (khandha) and the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha). What is the distinction between them? The aggregates are taught in a general sense. The aggregates of clinging are taught specifically by way of being associated with taints (sāsava) and being objects of clinging (upādāniya). As it is said:

"Bhikkhus, I will teach you the five aggregates and the five aggregates of clinging; listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates? Whatever matter, bhikkhus, is past, future, or present... or near, this is called the aggregate of matter. Whatever feeling... whatever consciousness... or near, this is called the aggregate of consciousness. These, bhikkhus, are called the five aggregates. And what, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates of clinging? Whatever matter, bhikkhus, is past, future, or present... or near, that is associated with taints and is an object of clinging, this is called the aggregate of matter-clinging. Whatever feeling... whatever consciousness... or near, that is associated with taints and is an object of clinging, this is called the aggregate of consciousness-clinging. These, bhikkhus, are called the five aggregates of clinging."

In this Pāḷi text, while there are feelings and so forth that are taintless (anāsava), there is no such thing as matter that is taintless. However, since its status as an aggregate is suitable in the sense of a "mass" (rāsaṭṭhena), it is taught among the aggregates. Furthermore, since its status as an aggregate of clinging is suitable both in the sense of a "mass" and in the sense of being "associated with taints," it is taught among the aggregates of clinging. As for feeling and so forth, only those that are not objects of taints are taught among the aggregates. Those feelings and so forth that are objects of taints are taught among the aggregates of clinging. In this context, "aggregates of clinging" (upādānakkhandha) should be understood to mean the aggregates which are the objects of clinging. In this section of the Visuddhimagga, however, all those states, whether associated with taints or taintless, are intended to be grouped together as "aggregates."

506. Regarding "by way of being neither less nor more": Why did the Blessed One teach exactly five aggregates, neither less nor more? It is because of the inclusion of all conditioned states (sankhata) by way of similar nature, because the basis for the grasp of self (atta) and what belongs to self (attaniya) is limited to these five, and because other aggregates such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) are included within these five.
109:
To explain in detail, when the many conditioned things (saṅkhata dhamma) are grouped according to their similar nature, matter (rūpa) is one aggregate by way of being grouped together through the similar nature of matter (deformation). Feeling (vedanā) is one aggregate by way of being grouped together through the similar nature of feeling (experiencing). The same method applies to perception (saññā) and so on. Therefore, because all conditioned things are grouped together by their similar nature, only five aggregates are taught.

Furthermore, these five things, matter and so on, are the extent of the basis for the grasping of 'self' (attā) and 'what belongs to self' (attaniya). Indeed, the Blessed One said:

'Bhikkhus, when there is matter, by clinging to matter, by being engrossed in matter, such a wrong view arises: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self." When there is feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness, by clinging to consciousness, by being engrossed in consciousness, such a wrong view arises: "This is mine, this I am, this is my self."' 

Because the basis for the grasping of self and what belongs to self is limited to these five things, matter and so on, only five aggregates are taught. Moreover, although other groups of five dhammas such as the aggregate of virtue (sīla-kkhandha) and so on are taught, they are included within the aggregate of volitional formations (saṅkhāra-kkhandha) and thus fall within these five aggregates. Because other aggregates like the aggregate of virtue are included within them, only five are taught. In this way, the method of determination by way of being neither less nor more should be understood.

507. In the section 'By way of similes', the detailed explanation is: The aggregate of clinging to matter (rūpūpādānakkhandha) is like a sickroom or a hospital, because it is the dwelling place for the aggregate of clinging to consciousness (viññāṇūpādānakkhandha), which is like a sick person, by way of the bases (vatthu), doors (dvāra), and objects (ārammaṇa). The aggregate of clinging to feeling (vedanūpādānakkhandha) is like a sickness, because it oppresses. The aggregate of clinging to perception (saññūpādānakkhandha) is like the cause of the sickness, because feelings associated with lust and so on arise through the power of perceptions of sensuality and so on. The aggregate of clinging to volitional formations (saṅkhārūpādānakkhandha) is like resorting to unsuitable food or climate, because it is the root cause of the sickness of feeling. Indeed, it is said: 'They construct feeling for the sake of feeling.' Furthermore, it is said: 'Due to the performance and accumulation of unwholesome kamma, resultant body-consciousness arises, accompanied by pain.' The aggregate of clinging to consciousness (viññāṇūpādānakkhandha) is like a sick person, because it is not free from the sickness of feeling. Alternatively, these aggregates of clinging, matter and so on, are respectively like a prison, thirty-two types of torture, a crime, an executioner, and a criminal. They are also like a dish, food, seasoning, a server, and an eater. In this way, the method of determination by way of similes should be understood.

508. In the section 'By way of how they should be viewed in two ways', the method of determination should be understood by viewing them in two ways: briefly and in detail. Briefly, the five aggregates of clinging should be viewed as an enemy with a raised sword, according to the method taught in the Āsīvisūpama Sutta; as a heavy burden, according to the Bhāra Sutta; as a devourer, according to the Khajjanīya Sutta; and as impermanent, suffering, non-self, conditioned, and a murderer, according to the Yamaka Sutta. In detail, among these five aggregates, matter should be viewed as a lump of foam because it cannot withstand pressure; feeling should be viewed as a water bubble because it is enjoyable for only a moment; perception should be viewed as a mirage because it causes one to speak erroneously.
110:
Formations should be seen as a banana trunk because they are coreless. Consciousness should be seen as a magic trick because it is deceptive. Especially, even if it is very excellent, the internal form should be seen as foul (asubha). Feeling should be seen as suffering (dukkha) because it is not free from the three types of suffering (actual suffering, suffering due to change, and suffering due to formations). Perception and formations should be seen as non-self (anatta) because they are uncontrollable. Consciousness should be seen as impermanent (anicca) because it has the nature of arising and passing away.

509. "To one who sees thus, there is the achievement of the purpose" means that for one who sees in these two ways, briefly and in detail as just described, there is the achievement of the purpose; the method of conclusion should be understood through that achievement of the purpose. To explain:

Briefly, one who sees the five aggregates of clinging as an enemy with a raised sword, etc., is not troubled by the aggregates. In detail, one who sees form, etc., as being like a lump of foam, etc., no longer perceives a core in the coreless aggregates.

Furthermore, especially, one who sees the internal form as foul (asubha) fully understands the nutriment consisting of edible food; he abandons the perversion (vipallāsa) of seeing beauty in the foul; he crosses the flood of sensuality (kāmogha); he is detached from the bond of sensuality (kāmayoga); he becomes taintless regarding the taint of sensuality (kāmāsava); he breaks the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhākāyagantha); and he does not cling to the clinging to sensuality (kāmupādāna).

One who sees feeling as suffering (dukkha) fully understands the nutriment consisting of contact (phassāhāra); he abandons the perversion of seeing pleasure in suffering; he crosses the flood of existence (bhavogha); he is detached from the bond of existence (bhavayoga); he becomes taintless regarding the taint of existence (bhavāsava); he breaks the bodily tie of ill-will (byāpādakāyagantha); and he does not cling to the clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna).

One who sees perception and formations as non-self (anatta) fully understands the nutriment consisting of mental volition (manosañcetanāhāra); he abandons the perversion of seeing self in what is non-self; he crosses the flood of views (diṭṭhogha); he is detached from the bond of views (diṭṭhiyoga); he becomes taintless regarding the taint of views (diṭṭhāsava); he breaks the bodily tie of the insistence that 'This is the truth' (idamsaccābhinivesakāyagantha); and he does not cling to the clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna).

One who sees consciousness as impermanent (anicca) fully understands the nutriment consisting of consciousness (viññāṇāhāra); he abandons the perversion of seeing permanence in the impermanent; he crosses the flood of ignorance (avijjogha); he is detached from the bond of ignorance (avijjāyoga); he becomes taintless regarding the taint of ignorance (avijjāsava); he breaks the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances (sīlabbataparāmāsakāyagantha); and he does not cling to the clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna).

[111] Seeing in the way of a murderer, etc., as mentioned, has great benefits. Therefore, a wise person should see the aggregates in the way of a murderer, etc. This is the exhortation.

This is the fourteenth chapter called the Description of the Aggregates (Khandha-niddesa) in the section on the Development of Understanding in the Path of Purification, composed for the gladdening of good people.

## (The Description of the Aggregates is finished)
