558. To explain in another way, it should not be said that 'Nibbāna does not exist.' Why? Because it would lead to the futility (barrenness) of the practice for reaching Nibbāna. To elaborate: if Nibbāna did not exist, the Right Practice (sammā-paṭipatti)—which is preceded by Right View and comprised of the three groups [of the Path] such as Virtue (sīla)—would become futile or barren. But this Right Practice is not futile. (Why?) Because it leads to the attainment of Nibbāna. This is one point.

Notes
1. The Ṭīkā states that this entire paragraph is a later addition to the text.

If it is argued: 'The futility of the practice does not occur. (Why?) Because it leads to non-existence (abhāva),'1 (this statement, which claims Nibbāna is merely the non-existence of the aggregates by saying it leads to non-existence), is not appropriate. (Why?) Because even though past and future aggregates do not exist, the attainment of Nibbāna is not accomplished [merely by their absence]. If it is argued: 'The non-existence of the currently arising present (vattamāna) aggregates is Nibbāna,' that is also not appropriate. (Why?) Because the non-existence of those currently arising present aggregates is impossible; and if they did not exist, they would reach the state of not being present; and because there would be the fault of the non-existence of the attainment of the Nibbāna-element with residue (saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) at the moment of the Path which depends on the currently arising aggregates. If it is argued: 'There is no fault because at that moment of the Path, the defilements are not present,'

Notes
1. Here, according to the nature of things, if one takes it as the 'cessation by non-arising' (anuppāda-nirodha) of defilements and aggregates that should be produced by the Noble Path, it is acceptable. Although it is called 'non-existence' (abhāva), it is not a total nothingness. The peace of the defilements and aggregates is clearly present. This peace of defilements and aggregates is the very goal of those who wish to be liberated from saṃsāra.

that statement is also not appropriate. (Why?) Because it would lead to the uselessness of the Noble Path (ariya-magga). Indeed, if it were as the opponent says, even before the moment of the Noble Path (at the moments of anuloma, gotrabhū, etc.), the defilements would not be present. Therefore, the uselessness of the Noble Path (in its function of abandoning defilements) would result. Therefore, (because Nibbāna is not unknowable, because practice is not futile, and because Nibbāna is not mere non-existence, etc.1), all these reasons (given by the opponent who claims Nibbāna is unknowable, etc.) are not sound or valid reasons.

559. If it is argued: 'Nibbāna is destruction (khaya),' because of the teaching: 'Friend Jambukhādaka, that which is the destruction of lust (rāgakkhaya), the destruction of hatred (dosakkhaya), and the destruction of delusion (mohakkhaya)—this is called Nibbāna,' etc., that is not appropriate. (Why?) Because the fruition of Arahatship (arahatta-phala) would also then be reduced to mere destruction. Indeed, that fruition of Arahatship is also [140] pointed out in the same way: 'Friend, that which is the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion—this is called the fruition of Arahatship,' and so forth.
140:
There is still a little more to be said: [If Nibbāna were merely the destruction of lust, etc.], it would be incorrect because of the flaw of Nibbāna having a brief duration, and so forth. To explain further—according to the opponent's view:

Note 1: This alternative meaning is a summary taken from the explanation in the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā).

If Nibbāna were merely destruction, Nibbāna would come to have a brief duration, possess the characteristics of the conditioned (saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa), and be attainable without Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma). Furthermore, because of having conditioned characteristics, it would be included within conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma). Being included within conditioned phenomena, it would be consumed by the fires of lust and so forth. Because it is consumed, it would also be called suffering (dukkha). Thus, these flaws would arise.

If it is argued that there is no flaw as stated by the Commentary because Nibbāna is that absolute destruction from which there is no further occurrence in the future—this is not correct. This is because such absolute destruction does not exist [as a separate entity], and even if it did, it could not overcome the aforementioned flaws of such destruction, and because the Noble Path (ariya-magga) would [wrongly] become Nibbāna. Indeed, the Noble Path causes the destruction of flaws like lust; therefore, it is called destruction (khaya). From that destruction onwards, there is no further occurrence of flaws like lust.

Note 1: For those who are currently experiencing the arousal of lust, etc., the calming of that lust through the enjoyment of suitable objects is mentioned here as a point of criticism. If the opponent meant this, the criticism would be valid. However, the opponent likely does not mean such temporary calming of lust. They likely mean the cessation where defilements can no longer arise due to the power of the Noble Path, because Nibbāna is an extremely subtle and noble state. Therefore, these criticisms should be carefully considered.
2: Since there is indeed the absolute destruction of lust, etc., due to the power of the Noble Path, and since this destruction alone might be what is meant, this argument also requires careful consideration.

In reality, because Nibbāna is the support (upanissaya) by way of metaphor for that destruction (khaya) called cessation (nirodha)—which is non-arising—Nibbāna (the object of the Path) is the support for that destruction which is the non-arising of defilements. It is called "destruction" (khaya) by way of metonymy (phalūpacāra), as it is proximate to that destruction. Why is it not taught in its own nature? Because it is extremely subtle.

Note 1: The non-arising of the aggregates of defilements due to the power of the Noble Path is called cessation (nirodha) or destruction (khaya). Just as that destruction is accomplished by the power of the Path, it is also accomplished because of Nibbāna, which is the object of the Path. Therefore, Nibbāna is called the support (upanissaya) of that destruction. However, it is not a literal upanissaya-paccaya. Thus, it says "called upanissaya by way of metaphor." Connect this with "it is taught as destruction (khaya)." The meaning here is that because Nibbāna is the support for the destruction of lust, etc., Nibbāna is figuratively taught as "the destruction of lust" (rāgakkhaya), etc., using the name of the effect for the cause (phalūpacāra). Therefore, one should not take Nibbāna as merely the destruction of lust, etc., but as the object of the Path which is the cause of that destruction. In this context, phalūpacāra means designating the cause by the name of the effect, just as ghee is called "life" (āyu) or molasses is called "phlegm."

Its extreme subtlety is established by the fact that it brought about the Buddha's state of being unconcerned [about teaching] and that it is to be seen with the Noble Eye.

560. This Nibbāna, as explained, is an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) state because it is attainable only by a Noble Person (ariya) endowed with the Noble Path. It has no beginning (appabhava) because there is no prior limit [to its existence]. If it is argued that it is not without a beginning because it exists when the Path exists, that should not be said, because it is not produced by the Path. Indeed, this Nibbāna is only to be attained by the Path, not produced by it. Therefore, it is indeed without a beginning. Because it has no beginning, it is without aging and death. Because of the absence of beginning, aging, and death, it is permanent (nicca).

If it is argued that "just as Nibbāna is permanent, so too are atoms (aṇu), primordial nature (pakati), the self (purisa), time (kāla), etc., permanent,"

Note 1: In the view of the Buddha's time, it was said that when the Buddha reflected on the depth and subtlety of the Dhamma after his enlightenment, he became unconcerned about teaching. This is mentioned according to that account.
2: In the doctrine of the sage Kaṇāda, the combination of two or three atoms perishes, but the smallest atom (paramāṇu) is said to be permanent. In the doctrine of the sage Kapila, when combined with the self (purisa), the primordial nature (pakati) produces things that perish, but the pakati itself—the state of equilibrium of the three qualities (sattva, rajas, tamas)—is said to be permanent. Similarly, the self (purisa) is said to be permanent. Those who believe in time (kāla) say time is permanent. These views were not based on Nibbāna in the Buddha's Dispensation but were held according to their own theories. However, in later times, they might have argued in comparison with Nibbāna. These arguments are being addressed here.

this is incorrect because of the absence of a proving cause (sādhana-hetu). If it is argued that "those atoms, etc., are permanent because Nibbāna is permanent," this is incorrect because the characteristic of the reason (hetu-lakkhaṇa) is inappropriate and incomplete (or: because the reason 'because Nibbāna is permanent' does not reach the status of a proving cause). If it is argued that "those atoms, etc., are permanent like Nibbāna because they lack arising, etc.," this is incorrect because atoms, etc., are not established [as real entities].

Note 1: This is the meaning of the text 'hetulakkhaṇassa anupapattito.' For a detailed explanation of this according to the rules of logic (nyāya), see the footnotes on pages 488-490 of the third volume of our Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā Nissaya.
2: The eightfold kalāpas (groups of matter) included in atoms and sub-atomic particles are evident. However, the solid, indivisible atoms and sub-atomic particles as conceived by opponents do not exist. Furthermore, the primordial nature (pakati) and the self (purisa) do not exist at all. The non-existence of time as a real entity is also clear.

561. In truth, because of the existence of the aforementioned reasoning, only this Nibbāna is permanent. It is called formless (arūpa) because it transcends the nature of form. It is the single goal (niṭṭhā) because there is no distinction between the finality of the Buddhas and others. It is called Nibbāna with a remainder of fuel (saupādisesa-nibbāna) because it is designated based on the subsiding of defilements of one who has reached Nibbāna through meditation, while there is still a remainder of the result-resultant aggregates called upādi. Furthermore, for an Arahant who has abandoned the result of future kamma by completely abandoning the origin (samudaya), there is the non-arising of the process-aggregates after the final (death) consciousness, and the disappearance of the aggregates that had arisen. [141] Thus, the absence of the remainder of aggregates called upādi is established. It is called Nibbāna without a remainder of fuel (anupādisesa) because it is designated based on the absence of that remainder of upādisesa aggregates.

Note 1: The etymological definition (vacanattha) 'saha upādisesena paññāpīyati' is omitted here as it might seem redundant to the reader. Upādi (clung-to aggregates) + sesa (remainder) + saha/sa (with) = Nibbāna as the cessation of defilements along with the remainder of upādi aggregates. Since an Arahant has a remainder of resultant aggregates before Parinibbāna, their state of cessation of defilements is called saupādisesa-nibbāna.
2: The mental and physical aggregates that arise continuously due to kamma are called process-aggregates (pavatti-khandha).
3: Here too, the etymological definition is omitted. Na/An (none) + upādisesa (remaining aggregates) = Nibbāna without a remainder of aggregates. This is the Nibbāna accomplished after the final death-consciousness of an Arahant.

Regarding the discussion of Nibbāna in this Visuddhimagga, I have presented my own view on Nibbāna, based on the statements of the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries, starting from page 502 of the third volume of the Mahāṭīkā Nissaya. I shall present those words here for the further knowledge of those reading the Myanmar translation.

In this matter, based on the detailed analysis of the Commentary and Sub-commentary, and based on the Sub-commentary's explanation of the word 'appavatti' in the Commentary's phrase 'ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ' as 'appavatti-nimittaṃ' (the sign of non-occurrence), many consider that the actual Nibbāna, the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca), which is the object of the Path and Fruition, is not merely the nature of the cessation of defilements, aggregates, and formations (saṅkhāra). In considering this deeply: there should only be these two—the continuous occurrence of the round of suffering (defilements, kamma, and resultant aggregates) and the cessation where that round of suffering cannot arise. There should be no separate reality apart from these two. (In this statement, the Path and Fruition, which are not the round of suffering, are also aggregates and are included in the summary). If such a separate reality existed, where and how would it exist? Does it exist in the continuity of each individual? Does it exist in a separate place? Or is it pervasive? It is difficult to answer. According to the teaching 'unestablished' (appatiṭṭhaṃ), one might answer that it has no location. However, it is difficult to be satisfied with the answer that it has no location while being a reality that is not merely cessation. In the formless realm (arūpa-bhūma), although mental phenomena have no physical base (vatthu-rūpa), they have a realm as their location. Therefore, mental phenomena in the formless realm are understandable.

Furthermore, that Nibbāna, which is said to be not merely the nature of cessation, is only something to be known by the Path, Fruition, and Reviewing knowledge. It is not that one reaches that Nibbāna upon attaining Parinibbāna, nor does one experience its taste. Therefore, it seems like something invented merely to be an object for the Path and Fruition, like the concepts of pakati and purisa.

What is truly necessary is only the cessation of defilements, kamma, and resultant aggregates that occur continuously in a cause-and-effect relationship. Only for that cessation is the holy life (brahmacariya) practiced in the Buddha's Dispensation. Therefore, to the question 'For what purpose is the holy life practiced under the Buddha?', great elders like Venerable Puṇṇa answered, 'It is practiced for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā-parinibbānatthaṃ).'

This being so, one should consider: according to the Buddha's word 'a single goal' (ekā niṭṭhā), should that single goal be the nature of the cessation (santi-lakkhaṇa) of defilements, kamma, and resultant aggregates? Or should it be a separate reality that is not the nature of cessation? In our view, we wish to take the nature of the cessation of defilements, kamma, and resultant aggregates as the 'single goal.' The reason is that it should be identical in meaning to 'This alone is the end of suffering' (esevanto dukkhassa) in the teaching: 'Neither here, nor beyond, nor between the two; this alone is the end of suffering.' In that text, when translating 'This alone is the end (anta) of the suffering of defilements and the round of existence,' in accordance with the Sub-commentary which explains 'eseva' as 'abhāvo' (non-existence), it only yields the meaning of 'non-existence, voidness, and cessation.' This meaning alone is consistent with the preceding sentence: 'Neither here... nor beyond... nor in both.' In that teaching, meanings such as 'the cause of non-existence,' 'the place of non-existence,' 'the cause of cessation,' or 'the place of cessation' cannot be obtained. There is no such traditional translation, nor is there such an explanation here. Therefore, the meaning of 'anta' in this teaching and 'niṭṭhā' in the teaching 'a single goal' should be taken as 'the non-existence, voidness, and cessation of suffering.' This itself should be called the 'nature of peace' (santi-lakkhaṇa).

Similarly, in the term 'cessation of suffering' (dukkha-nirodha), we believe the Buddha intended only the cessation of suffering. We do not think it means 'the cause of cessation.' In the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries, there is no explanation of 'the sign of the cessation of suffering' (dukkha-nirodha-nimittaṃ) in this context. If it were explained as 'the sign of the cessation of suffering' like 'the sign of non-occurrence' (appavatti-nimittaṃ), and if it were taken as the state that causes the cessation of suffering, then only the Noble Path should be taken as the referent. Why? Because just as the cause of suffering is the Truth of Origin (samudaya-sacca), the cause of the cessation of suffering should only be the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). If the word 'nirodha' is treated as a locative (adhikaraṇa-sādhana) meaning 'the place where suffering ceases,' it should be taken as a metaphorical designation (upacāra-pariyāya), similar to how the Itivuttaka (p. 221) refers to anupādisesa-nibbāna—which is merely the nature of the cessation of the aggregates of existence—as the place of cessation (yamhi nirujjhanti bhavāni sabbaso).
141:
Furthermore, in the context of reverse Dependent Origination (paṭiloma paṭiccasamuppāda), the commentaries state that Nibbāna is taught through passages such as: 'With the cessation of this, that ceases; with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases...'

Note: In this passage, 'nirodhā' means 'due to cessation', 'nirujjhati' means 'it ceases', and 'nirodho' means 'cessation'. It should not be translated as 'because of the nature of the cause of cessation, the cause of cessation occurs'; there is no such explanation. Therefore, in this reverse Dependent Origination text, it is clear that only the nature of cessation is shown as the true Nibbāna. In this context, when it is said 'ignorance ceases', one should not raise the objection: 'Does only ignorance cease?' This is also clear. Therefore, one should also consider the statements regarding the multiplicity of Nibbāna, such as 'rāgakkhayo' (the destruction of lust) being one Nibbāna, and 'dosakkhayo' (the destruction of hatred) being another Nibbāna. Just as the simultaneous cessation of all defilements like ignorance and all cycles of karma and result (kammavaṭṭa and vipākavaṭṭa) due to the power of the Noble Path is taught in parts as 'with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease', if one fairly understands that the simultaneous destruction and peace of all defilements like lust, hatred, and delusion is taught in parts as 'destruction of lust', 'destruction of hatred', etc., then there is no reason why the view that the destruction of lust itself is Nibbāna should be inappropriate. One should be mindful of the proverb: 'Even the wise may lapse in mindfulness.'

Furthermore, just as in 'with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease', Nibbāna is taught directly through 'destruction of lust', etc. As for the Path and Fruition (magga-phala), if one takes them to be taught figuratively (upacāra-pariyāya) because they take Nibbāna (called 'destruction') as their object or because they are the cause of the destruction of lust, etc., there is also no reason for this to be inappropriate. This point should also be noted.

Therefore, to ensure consistency across all Pali texts and to directly achieve the desired benefit according to the phrase 'for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging' (anupādā parinibbānatthaṃ), Nibbāna should be understood as follows:

(1) Nibbāna as the nature of cessation, which is the object of the Path and Fruition, is the general Nibbāna (sāmaṇya-nibbāna) characterized by the cessation and emptiness of all defilements, karma, and conditioned phenomena of mind and matter. For this reason, it is also taught as 'the supreme emptiness' (parama-suññaṃ).

(2) Nibbāna with residue (saupādisesa-nibbāna), which is the cessation of defilements, and Nibbāna without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna), which is the cessation of the aggregates and conditioned phenomena, are specific Nibbānas (visesa-nibbāna) that are parts of that general Nibbāna which is the object of the Path and Fruition. These specific Nibbānas are included within the general Nibbāna. Thus, in the Itivuttaka Pali (p. 221), it is shown that the Arahants, having known these two Nibbāna elements (through the Path of Arahantship) as 'this unconditioned state, the end of the craving for existence', are liberated through the Fruition of Arahantship with the destruction of the bonds of existence. If Saupādisesa and Anupādisesa Nibbāna were merely the results of the Nibbāna that is the object of the Path and were not themselves the object, the Buddha would not have said 'having known this' (etadaññāya). This point should be deeply noted.

However, when the Path and Fruition take Nibbāna as an object, they do not do so by making specific distinctions such as 'lust is ceased' or 'hatred is ceased'. Nor do they make distinctions such as 'matter is ceased' or 'mind is ceased'. In reality, they take as their object and directly realize only the nature of the cessation and absence of all defilements, karma, matter, mind, aggregates, and formations.

In this matter, some might look down upon the nature of the cessation of defilements, karma, matter, mind, and aggregates, thinking of it as a mere concept of non-existence (abhāva-paññatti) where nothing exists. They might think it is not profound. One should not think so. It is because it is so profound that those without perfections (pāramī) are unable to bring about the cessation of defilements and aggregates. Because the cessation of these defilements and aggregates is so precious and noble, the Path and Fruition that can bring about this cessation are also noble and precious.

Consider this: mundane supernormal powers (lokiya-abhiññā), such as the ability to create through psychic power, see, hear, or know anything at will, are very precious and noble from a worldly perspective. However, because they cannot bring about the peace of defilements and aggregates, they are not as precious or noble as the knowledge of the Path and Fruition. Considering this, one will understand the cessation of defilements and aggregates as the most excellent. Therefore, the Arahant Elder Puṇṇa, after declining by saying, 'I do not practice for the sake of the benefit of the Path knowledge called the Purification of Knowledge and Vision,' answered, 'I practice for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging (anupādā parinibbānatthaṃ)—the cessation of the aggregates of mind and matter without any cause of clinging.'

If one wishes to know about Nibbāna more extensively than this, please examine and reflect on Chapter 6, pages 320 to 348, of the second volume of the 'Manual of Vipassanā Meditation' compiled by us.

Nibbāna is not non-existent in the ultimate sense (paramattha) because it is known through a special knowledge achieved through firm and progressive effort without slackening, and because it was taught by the All-Knowing Buddha. Indeed, the following was taught: 'Atthi, bhikkhave, ajātaṃ abhūtaṃ akataṃ asaṅkhataṃ'—'Monks, there is the unconditioned, which is not born (due to a meeting of causes like feelings, etc.), not become (spontaneously without cause), and not made (by any cause).'

This preceding statement is the concluding decision in the explanation of the cessation of suffering (dukkha-nirodha-niddesa).

## Detailed Explanation of the Path

562. Furthermore, the eight factors taught in the section on the practice leading to the cessation of suffering (dukkha-nirodha-gāminī-paṭipadā) have already been explained in terms of meaning in the section on the aggregates. However, in this context of the Truth of the Path, we shall explain them further to clarify the distinctions of these path factors occurring in a single moment.

In brief (Note 1: It is said 'in brief' because it will be explained in detail later in the section on the Purification of Knowledge and Vision), for a yogi practicing to realize the Four Noble Truths, the eye of wisdom that completely uproots the latent tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya) while taking Nibbāna as its object is called Right View (Sammā-diṭṭhi). It has the characteristic of seeing rightly, the function of manifesting the elements (or manifesting the Four Noble Truths), and it appears to knowledge as the destruction of the darkness of ignorance. For the person endowed with Right View, the nature that directs the mind toward the object of Nibbāna and completely destroys wrong intention (micchā-saṅkappa) associated with that Right View is Right Intention (Sammā-saṅkappa). It has the characteristic of rightly directing the mind toward the object, the function of reaching or entering (the object of Nibbāna), and it appears to knowledge as the abandoning of wrong intention.

For the person who thus sees with Right View and intends with Right Intention, the nature of abstaining from wrong speech (micchā-vācā) that completely uproots wrong verbal conduct associated with that very intention is called Right Speech (Sammā-vācā). It has the characteristic of embracing (the listeners and associated states) (Note 2: This is translated according to the Mūla-ṭīkā on the Sacca-vibhaṅga. In the Mahā-ṭīkā, there is no mention of embracing listeners; however, since it is a clear meaning, it should definitely be there, and the word 'janānaṃ' might have been lost in later transcriptions), the function of abstaining from wrong speech, and it appears to knowledge as the abandoning of wrong speech. For the person who abstains in this manner, the nature of abstaining from killing, etc., which completely uproots wrong action (micchā-kammanta) associated with that very abstinence, is called Right Action (Sammā-kammanta). It has the characteristic of originating (blameless actions), the function of abstaining from wrong action, and it appears to knowledge as the abandoning of wrong action. Furthermore, for that person endowed with Right Speech and Right Action, the nature of abstaining from wrong livelihood (micchā-ājīva) which completely cuts off pretension (kuhana), etc., and which is the purification of that Right Speech and Right Action, is called Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva). It has the characteristic of purifying body and speech, the function of carrying out a proper livelihood, and it appears to knowledge as the abandoning of wrong livelihood.

At that time, for that person standing firmly on the ground of virtue (sīla) called Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood, whatever exertion and effort there is that is appropriate to those factors, associated with them, and completely cuts off laziness, is called Right Effort (Sammā-vāyāma). It has the characteristic of supporting and encouraging, the function of preventing unarisen unwholesome states from arising, etc., and it appears to knowledge as the abandoning of wrong effort. For that person who exerts in this way, the nature of the mind's non-forgetfulness that shakes off and removes wrong mindfulness (micchā-sati) associated with that Right Effort [142] is called Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati). It has the characteristic of standing near the object, or the characteristic of the object being present, the function of not forgetting the object, and it appears to knowledge as the abandoning of wrong mindfulness. For the person whose mind is well-guarded by such supreme and unsurpassed mindfulness, the one-pointedness of mind called Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi), which destroys wrong concentration (micchā-samādhi) associated with that mindfulness...

## The Eightfold Path in Detail

In this section, I shall also show how to develop the Truth of the Path by citing the Pali and Commentaries related to the eight path factors.

'Katamā ca bhikkhave sammādiṭṭhi, yaṃ kho bhikkhave dukkhe ñāṇaṃ, dukkhasamudaye ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhe ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati bhikkhave sammādiṭṭhi.' (Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, etc.)

'Monks, what is Right View? Monks, that which is knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin of suffering, knowledge of the cessation of suffering, and knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—this, monks, is called Right View.'

Through 'knowledge of suffering', etc., the meditation on the Four Truths is shown. Among these four truths, the first two are the truths of the cycle (vaṭṭa-sacca), and the last two are the truths of the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa-sacca). Among them, the meditation is focused on the truths of the cycle; there is no such focus on the truths of the cessation of the cycle. To explain: after learning the first two truths from a teacher, either in brief or in detail, the yogi makes an effort by repeatedly reciting them. As for the latter two truths, he performs his task merely by hearing that 'the Truth of Cessation is desirable, pleasant, and noble' (Note: This shows the inclination of the mind toward those two truths; through such inclination, the task regarding those two truths is completed—Commentary). The yogi who acts in this way penetrates the four truths at once (at the moment of the Noble Path) through a single penetration and realizes them through a single realization. He penetrates the Truth of Suffering through the penetration of full understanding (pariññā-paṭivedha), the Truth of Origin through the penetration of abandoning (pahāna-paṭivedha), the Truth of Cessation through the penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha), and the Truth of the Path through the penetration of development (bhāvanā-paṭivedha). He realizes the Truth of Suffering through the realization of full understanding (pariññā-abhisamaya)... up to... he realizes the Truth of the Path through the realization of development (bhāvanā-abhisamaya). As stated, for that yogi (before reaching the Noble Path), in the preliminary stage, penetration (paṭivedha) occurs in the two truths of Suffering and Origin through learning (uggaha), questioning (paripucchā), hearing (savana), memorizing (dhāraṇa), and reflecting (sammasana). In the two truths of Cessation and the Path, penetration occurs only through hearing (savana). (This shows that there is no need for special reflection on Cessation and the Path; the task is completed merely by hearing). In the subsequent stage while reaching the Noble Path, penetration occurs through the completion of the task in the three truths of Suffering, Origin, and the Path. In the Truth of Cessation, penetration occurs by taking it as an object. (This shows that 'through the Noble Path knowledge, one realizes Nibbāna as an object, and through such realization, the tasks of full understanding, abandoning, and development in the other three truths are completed')... Thus, regarding the four truths which are deep and difficult to see, the Buddha taught 'knowledge of suffering', etc., referring to the arising of knowledge in the preliminary stage through the power of learning, etc. (Commentary on Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, etc.)

Note: In the above commentary, it is said that one must learn the Truth of Suffering, which is the five aggregates of clinging, and the Truth of Origin, which is craving, either in brief or in detail. Among them, the Truth of Origin is easy to know. The Truth of Suffering has already been shown to be the five aggregates of clinging. These are the physical and mental phenomena that clearly arise whenever one sees, hears, smells, eats, touches, or thinks in one's own continuity. If one does not observe them as they arise and does not know them as they truly are—that they are mere mind and matter, that they are arising and passing away incessantly, and that they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self—then one clings to them as 'I', 'a being', or 'a self'. One clings to them with pleasure and delight as 'mine'. One clings to them as 'permanent', 'pleasant', and 'beautiful'. Because they can be clung to in this way, the Buddha taught the phenomena that are apparent during seeing, etc., as the 'aggregates of clinging' (upādānakkhandha)—the aggregates that are the objects of clinging.

In the Khandhavagga Saṃyutta, the Buddha taught the method of observing through insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) by analyzing: 'One knows matter as impermanent; one knows feeling, perception, and formations as impermanent; one knows consciousness as impermanent,' etc.

In the Saḷāyatanavagga Saṃyutta also, the Buddha taught the method of observing the five groups of phenomena at the six doors—eye, object, consciousness, contact, and feeling—saying 'one knows the eye as impermanent,' etc. According to those teachings, if one constantly observes whatever clearly appears during seeing, hearing, etc., one knows the aggregates of clinging called the Truth of Suffering as they truly are in terms of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. This knowledge is the penetration of reflection (sammasana-paṭivedha-ñāṇa). Every time one observes and knows them as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, the craving (taṇhā) that would have arisen by clinging to those known aggregates as permanent, pleasant, and self with delight and attachment finds no opportunity to arise and ceases through the nature of non-arising. Therefore, the task of penetration by abandoning (pahāna-paṭivedha), which is knowing by abandoning the origin, is also completed. The karma that would have followed from that craving and the results of that karma also find no opportunity to arise and are ceased. Such cessation of karma, its results, and the aggregates of a new existence in a momentary fashion is the momentary cessation (tadaṅga-nirodha) achieved through insight. Therefore, the task of penetration by realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha), which is the realization of momentary cessation, is also completed. Every time one observes, the insight Right View (vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi) that knows the truths of suffering as they truly are, along with the path factors like Right Intention, is the mundane Truth of the Path. Therefore, the task of penetration by development (bhāvanā-paṭivedha), which is the development of the mundane Truth of the Path, is also completed. Knowing in this way, which completes the task of knowing the four truths appropriately, is called 'penetration of reflection' (sammasana-paṭivedha) in the commentaries; in the Buddha's Pali, it is taught as 'knowledge of suffering', etc. With this much, one should be able to understand briefly how insight Right View and Path Right View occur.

In the Pali, Right Intention (Sammā-saṅkappa) is taught as three: intention of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa), intention of non-ill will (abyāpāda-saṅkappa), and intention of non-harming (avihiṃsā-saṅkappa). The commentary explains that these three are distinct in the preliminary stage, but at the moment of the Noble Path, a single Right Intention occurs, completing the three tasks. During insight meditation also, because there is no opportunity for intentions of sensual desire, etc., to arise in relation to the objects known as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, it should be said that these three tasks are completed by a single insight intention.

Regarding Right Speech, etc., when one abstains from wrong speech, Right Speech occurs; when one abstains from wrong action, Right Action occurs; when one abstains from wrong livelihood, Right Livelihood occurs. The commentary states that these occur individually in the preliminary stage, but all three occur at the moment of the Path. During insight meditation also, because wrong speech, etc., find no opportunity to arise in relation to the objects known as impermanent, etc., even though the actual abstinence factors (virati) might not be present, it should be taken that Right Speech, etc., are included by way of completing the task of momentary abstinence from wrong speech, etc. Only by taking it this way can one understand the meaning of the commentary's statement about depending on momentary seclusion (tadaṅga-viveka) in the Pali on the development of path factors (Kosala Saṃyutta, etc.) which says 'he develops Right Speech... based on seclusion'.

Regarding Right Effort (Sammā-vāyāma), the commentary states that because the efforts to prevent unarisen unwholesome states, etc., are distinct, they are distinct in the preliminary stage, but at the moment of the Path, a single Right Effort path factor completes all four tasks. During insight meditation also, it should be said that a single insight Right Effort can complete all four tasks.

As for Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati), the commentary states that during insight meditation, the contemplations of the body, etc., are distinct, but at the moment of the Noble Path, a single Right Mindfulness completes all four tasks of the foundations of mindfulness. There is nothing to add here.

As for Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi), it is distinct as the first jhāna, second jhāna, etc., when mundane jhānas occur in the preliminary stage; it is similarly distinct at the moment of the Noble Path. This distinction has already been shown in the Visuddhimagga, paragraph 798, in the section on the knowledge of equanimity toward formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa).

In the Pali texts like the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, when analyzing Right Concentration, it is analyzed only through the four jhānas. Based on that Pali, some say: 'Mundane Right Concentration occurs only when one attains jhāna concentration; only with such concentration can one practice insight meditation well.' Because they do not realize that access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and the momentary concentration of insight (vipassanā-khaṇika-samādhi) equivalent to it are included as subordinate or lesser forms when jhāna concentration is shown as the primary or excellent method, they speak in that way. Access concentration and momentary concentration are similar to the first jhāna in terms of being free from hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and being associated with the five jhāna factors: initial application, sustained application, zest, happiness, and one-pointedness. When free from hindrances, there is purification of mind (citta-visuddhi).
142:
If the purification of mind (cittavisuddhi) is complete, it is sufficient for the attainment of the purification of wisdom (paññāvisuddhi), such as the purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi).

Therefore, in the commentaries on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the sections on postures (iriyāpathapabba), clear comprehension (sampajaññapabba), and attention to the elements (dhātumanasikārapabba), etc., are described as access meditation subjects (upacāra-kammaṭṭhāna) that can lead to access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), as well as meditation subjects that can lead to the attainment of the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna.

Furthermore, in the Okāsādhigama Sutta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Chakkanipāta, taught by the Venerable Mahākaccāna, it is stated that by attaining access concentration through the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), etc., and practicing insight (vipassanā), one can realize Nibbāna. Relying on this Okāsādhigama method, in the second paragraph of section 362 of this Visuddhimagga, it is shown that access concentration can also bring about the benefits of insight. Additionally, at the end of section 166 in the description of the six recollections (cha-anussati-niddesa), it is mentioned that the Elder Phussadeva, having developed joy (pīti) by focusing on the qualities of the Buddha and practicing insight on that joy, became an Arahant.

During the time of the Blessed One, among the vast audiences of hundreds and thousands who listened to the Dhamma, when their minds were prepared (kallacitta), malleable (muducitta), free from hindrances (vinīvaraṇacitta), uplifted (udaggacitta), and confident (pasannacitta), the Blessed One taught the exalted teaching (sāmukkaṃsika-desanā) of the Four Noble Truths. While listening to that Dhamma, they attained the extraordinary states of the Path and Fruit through the sequence of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa).

Note: Among those thousands of audience members, it is not mentioned that they attained Jhana; it is evident that they attained the extraordinary Path and Fruit by practicing insight with access concentration free from hindrances.

In this very Visuddhimagga, in the description of the purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi-niddesa), page 222, section 662, it is stated that access concentration along with the eight attainments (samāpatti) is called purification of mind. In section 798, regarding the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa), it is also stated that the Path arising in a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) who lacks Jhanic concentration is associated with the first Jhana.

Furthermore, in the Pali texts such as 'He develops the enlightenment factor of concentration based on seclusion' (samādhisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ), the commentaries state that insight concentration (vipassanā-samādhi) depends on momentary seclusion (tadaṅga-viveka). This enlightenment factor of concentration is indeed the factor of Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi) in the context of the Path factors.

Therefore, access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and momentary concentration of insight (vipassanā-khaṇika-samādhi) should be understood as being included in the teaching of the first Jhana by way of the subordinate or lesser method (omaka-naya).

These eight path factors, from Right View to Right Concentration, as shown in the Visuddhimagga and in this footnote, are mundane (lokiya) at the moment of practicing insight. When that insight matures and becomes the Noble Path (ariya-magga), they become supramundane path factors (lokuttara-magganga). In this context of the description of the Truth of the Path (maggasacca-niddesa), only the supramundane path factors should be taken; however, since they cannot be separated from insight, the insight path factors must also be taken as the foundation. Therefore, it is stated in the Sammohavinodanī Commentary as follows:

'Esa lokuttaro ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, yo sahalokiyena maggena dukkha-nirodha-gāminī paṭipadāti saṅkhaṃ gato.'

'Esa'—these aforementioned eight path factors; 'lokuttaro'—are supramundane; 'aṭṭhaṅgiko ariyo maggo'—is the Noble Eightfold Path.

The state of mental stability is called Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi). It has the characteristic of non-distraction of the mind, or it has the characteristic of not being distracted itself. Its function is to place the mind well upon the object. It is manifested to knowledge as the abandonment of wrong concentration (micchā-samādhi). This is the method of understanding in the description of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. In this way, the decision regarding birth (jāti), etc., in these Truths should be understood.

563. By way of the function of knowledge: The decision should also be understood by way of the function of the knowledge of the Truths. To explain in detail: The knowledge of the Truths is of two kinds—knowledge of conformity (anubodha-ñāṇa) and knowledge of penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa). Among them, the knowledge of conformity is mundane; it occurs regarding the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path by way of hearing (anussava), etc. The knowledge of penetration is supramundane; it penetrates the four Truths by making Nibbāna the object and by completing the functions (such as abandoning, etc.).

Note: 'Yo'—that Noble Path; 'saha lokiyena maggena'—together with the mundane insight path; 'dukkha-nirodha-gāminī paṭipadāti saṅkhaṃ gato'—reaches the designation of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

1. Unlike the knowledge of penetration which occurs only once, it is called 'anubodha' because it tends to arise repeatedly (anu-anu = repeatedly + bodha = knowing). Alternatively, knowing that follows after hearing, reflecting on the manner, or contemplating and accepting what has been seen is called 'anubodha'; that very 'anubodha' is the knowledge itself, hence it is called 'anubodha-ñāṇa'. Indeed, that knowledge of conformity does not know by direct experience; it knows by being preceded by reflection through the power of hearing, etc. (Sub-commentary). By these last two sentences, it seems it does not refer to insight knowledge known by direct perception; that direct insight knowledge should be included in 'penetration' (paṭivedha).

As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, he who sees suffering, also sees the origin of suffering, also sees the cessation of suffering, and also sees the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' This entire passage should be cited.

The function of that knowledge of penetration will become clear in the purification by knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).

Furthermore, regarding the four mundane knowledges of the Truths, among those four, the knowledge of suffering, arising and prevailing, causes the personality view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) to recede or stop.

Note: 1. By realizing Nibbāna through direct vision, one can also fully comprehend suffering; the origin is also abandoned as much as it should be—and completely abandoned by the Path of Arahantship; the Path, having arisen in one's own continuity, has completed the function of development. This completion of functions like full comprehension, abandoning, and development is what is meant by 'knowing'.

2. For one who has studied and well-understood the truths of materiality and mentality as suffering, the personality view that perceives those material and mental states as a person or being does not arise prominently or firmly; this is what is meant by 'causing to recede'. However, by this much, the attachment to personality view is not yet entirely removed; it will still arise occasionally. The manner in which view is removed by insight knowledge will be shown in the section on purification of view.

The knowledge of the origin causes the annihilation view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) to recede. The knowledge of cessation causes the eternalism view (sassata-diṭṭhi) to recede. The knowledge of the path causes the non-action view (akiriya-diṭṭhi) to recede. Alternatively, the knowledge of suffering causes the recession of the perversion of perception in the fruit, known as the perception of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self in the aggregates which are devoid of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. The knowledge of the origin causes the recession of the perversion of the cause, which is the presumption of a cause in what is not a cause, such as the belief that the world proceeds due to a Creator (Issara), Primal Matter (Padhāna), Time (Kāla), or Nature (Sabhāva), etc.

Note: 1. The non-action view is the wrong view that even if one performs wholesome deeds, no merit is produced, etc. It means that for one who hears and accepts the arising of the path factors called the Truth of the Path through insight, such wrong views are removed.

2. Those who believe in a Creator (Issara) say that God creates, governs, destroys, and withdraws the world. Those who believe in Primal Matter (Padhāna) say that the world manifests from an unmanifested nature (Prakṛti) and (when it is time to perish) disappears while remaining latent in that nature. (They call the state where the three qualities of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas are balanced and unmanifested 'Prakṛti'; when combined with the 'Purisa' or self, this Prakṛti transforms into 'Mahat', etc., and becomes 'Vikṛti'. Because this Prakṛti is unmanifested, it is called 'Avyatta'; because it measures and limits, it is called 'Māyā'; because it causes the unordained 'Mahat', etc., to arise, it is called 'Padhāna'. For more details, see Visuddhimagga Burmese Translation Vol. 4, p. 8, and Mahāṭīkā Nissaya Vol. 4, p. 211). The followers of Time say, 'Time creates beings, Time destroys beings, Time awakens those who sleep; Time is hard to overcome.' The followers of Nature say, 'Just as the tip of a thorn is sharp, just as fruits are round, just as the diversity of beasts, birds, snakes, and scorpions exists, the world arises and perishes by its own inherent nature.' The term 'etc.' (ādi) includes the Atomists who say 'the world arises from atoms,' and the Pubbekatahetu-vādins who say 'everything is due to past karma alone.' The Fatalists (Niyati-vādins) say, 'The world is permanent, like a jewel threaded on an unbreakable string; there is no human action in this world.' The Accidentalists (Yadicchā-vādins) say, 'Things arise by chance, they perish by chance; happiness and suffering occur by chance. Therefore, all beings are subject to chance.' These are also called Adhiccasamuppatti-vādins. All such improper doctrines of causality are to be understood as included by the term 'etc.' (Sub-commentary).

The knowledge of cessation causes the recession of the perversion of cessation, which is the grasping of the formless realms, the peak of the world (the realm of non-percipient beings or the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception), etc., as the state of deliverance (apavagga) or Nibbāna. 

Note: 1. Connect the words 'arising' and 'being' with 'perversion of practice'.

2. Grasping the formless realms (like Rāma, Udaka, and Āḷāra) or the peak of the world (like the Nigaṇṭhas), such as the realm of non-percipient beings or the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as the state of deliverance (apavagga) or Nibbāna is called 'apavagga-gāha'. The term 'etc.' includes 'the non-arising of Primal Matter, the self which is not associated with qualities (not joined with Prakṛti) remaining only in its own self, the state of having a world similar to the Creator Brahma, the state of being near him, or merging with him (doctrines of liberation),' and 'the doctrines of Nibbāna in the present life' (the latter is found in the Brahmajāla Sutta of the Sīlakkhandha Pali). These should be understood as included. To explain further: the non-arising of Primal Matter means not transforming or changing into the states of Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, etc., or not manifesting. The followers of the Kapila school say that by knowing the difference between the self (Purisa) and Nature (Prakṛti), and by causing the merging of the self with happiness, suffering, and delusion (Sattva, Rajas, Tamas) to cease, then Primal Matter no longer becomes Mahat, etc.; this non-becoming of Primal Matter into Mahat is called 'vimokkha' (liberation). 'Not associated with qualities' refers to the self not being associated with the nine qualities of the self according to the Kanāda view: Buddhi (intellect), happiness, suffering, desire, aversion, effort, merit (dhamma), demerit (adhamma), and mental formations (saṅkhāra). 'Salokatā' means having a world similar to Brahma. 'Being near' means being born in the vicinity of that Brahma. 'Merging' means becoming one with that Brahma-self. This shows the doctrine that individual small selves are parts of the great Brahma-self, and when they re-enter and merge into that great Brahma-self, they are free from suffering. (Sub-commentary).

The knowledge of the path causes the recession of the perversion of the means, which is the grasping of what is not the path to Nibbāna—such as the various forms of devotion to sensual pleasures or devotion to self-mortification—as the path to Nibbāna. Therefore, the following verse is stated:

Note: 1. 'Devotion to sensual pleasures' (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) is the belief that there is no deliverance from suffering (apavagga) apart from satisfying the senses like the eyes, seeing the face of a son, etc., and acting accordingly. 'Devotion to self-mortification' (attakilamathānuyoga) is the belief that liberation comes through practicing austerities (tapa) that cause pain and exhaustion, such as fasting, pulling out hair with palm seeds, living naked, or following the practices of cattle or dogs, and acting accordingly. (Sub-commentary). The 'kāmasukhallikānuyoga' shown in this sub-commentary refers only to the practice regarding the path to Nibbāna; it should not be taken as the only form of sensual indulgence. In fact, all forms of enjoying sensual pleasures are included in kāmasukhallikānuyoga. That is why in the Araṇavibhaṅga Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pali, it is taught as a low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and useless extreme that should be avoided: 'One should not follow devotion to sensual pleasures, which is low, vulgar...' Furthermore, in the Pāsādika Sutta of the Pāthika-vagga, Dīgha Nikāya, p. 108, it is stated that Buddhist monks are free from these four types of devotion to pleasure: (3 types) making oneself happy through killing, stealing, and lying; (1 type) enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure. Therefore, when using the four requisites, etc., one should use them with reflection, such as 'Wisely reflecting, he uses the robe...' to be free from devotion to sensual pleasures, or by attending to them with either serenity (samatha) or insight (vipassanā).

'Loke lokappabhave, lokatthagame sive ca tadupāye.
Sammuyhati tāva naro, na vijānāti yāva saccāni.'

'As long as a person does not know the Truths, so long does he remain deeply confused and perverted regarding the world (the Truth of Suffering), the origin of the world (the Truth of Origin), the cessation of the world (Nibbāna), and the means to reach that Nibbāna.'

In this way, the decision regarding these Truths should also be understood by way of the function of knowledge.

564. By way of the classification of things included: (In detail) All remaining states, excluding craving and supramundane states, are included in the Truth of Suffering. The 36 types of craving-thought-processes are included in the Truth of Origin. The Truth of Cessation is unmixed and stands alone. By way of the heading of Right View, the road to power of investigation (vīmaṃsiddhipāda), the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), the power of wisdom (paññābala), and the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga) are included in the Truth of the Path. By the designation of Right Thought, [143] the three types of thought such as the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka) are included; by the designation of Right Speech, the four types of verbal good conduct are included;
143:
By indicating Right Action, the three types of bodily good conduct are included.

Note 1: Through the power of the three types of craving—sensual craving, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—occurring in the twelve bases, thirty-six types of craving-behavior should be known.

Note 2: This is the direct meaning of the term 'sammādiṭṭhimukhena' (by way of Right View); meanings such as 'by way of the leadership or primacy of Right View' are also possible. However, since it is identical in essence to the base of power of investigation (vīmaṃsiddhipāda), etc., it should not be said to be a follower or non-primary. Therefore, the meaning that other unnamed states of the same essence are included by being expressed as the 'head' or 'way' is not inappropriate.

By way of Right Livelihood, fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and contentment (santuṭṭhitā) are included. Alternatively, because all these—Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood—are virtue dear to the Noble Ones (ariyakanta-sīla), and because such virtue is to be received with the hand of faith (saddhā), and because they exist when those exist, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), the power of faith (saddhābala), and the desire-to-act as a base of power (chandiddhipāda) are included. By indicating Right Effort, the four right efforts, the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya), the power of energy (vīriyabala), and the factor of enlightenment of energy (vīriyasambojjhaṅga) are included. By indicating Right Mindfulness, the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness are included. By indicating Right Concentration, the three concentrations starting with that with initial and sustained thought, and the concentration of mind (citta-samādhi) pertaining to the base of power of mind, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and the factors of enlightenment of rapture (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā) are included. Thus, the decision should be understood here by way of the classification of included states.

565. In the section 'By way of Similes', the detail is as follows: The Truth of Suffering should be regarded as a burden (bhāra); the Truth of the Origin as the taking up of the burden (bhārādāna); the Truth of Cessation as the laying down of the burden (bhāranikkhepana); and the Truth of the Path as the means for laying down the burden (bhāranikkhepanupāya). Alternatively, the Truth of Suffering should be regarded as a disease, the Truth of the Origin as the cause of the disease, the Truth of Cessation as the cure of the disease, and the Truth of the Path as the medicine.

Note 1: This is the meaning of the term 'citta-samādhi'. The Commentary explains that this term refers to the base of power of mind (cittiddhipāda). Just as in the Pali 'cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayaṃ', 'citta' indicates concentration, the same Commentary states that concentration is also indicated by the base of power of mind.

Alternatively, the Truth of Suffering should be regarded as a famine, the Truth of the Origin as a drought, the Truth of Cessation as abundance, and the Truth of the Path as good rain. Furthermore, these Four Noble Truths should be understood by way of similes by comparing them with: an enemy, the root of enmity, the extirpation of enmity, and the means for extirpation; a poison tree, its root, the cutting of the root, and the means for cutting it; fear, the cause of fear, fearlessness, and the means for attaining it; and the hither shore, the great flood, the further shore, and the effort to reach that further shore. Thus, the decision should be understood here by way of similes.

566. In the section 'By way of the Tetrad', the detail is as follows: Among these four truths, there is that which is suffering but not the Noble Truth; there is that which is the Noble Truth but not suffering; there is that which is both suffering and the Noble Truth; and there is that which is neither suffering nor the Noble Truth. This method also applies to the Truth of Origin, etc. Therein, the states associated with the Path and the fruits of asceticism (sāmaññaphala) are 'suffering' because of the statement 'Whatever is impermanent is suffering' and because of being the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā), but they are not the Noble Truth [of Suffering].

Note 1: Samana (the Noble monk whose defilements are stilled) + nya (the state of being) = sāmañña (the state of being one whose defilements are stilled, i.e., the four Paths). Because they are the fruits of these four Paths, they are called sāmaññaphala (fruits of asceticism).

Cessation is the Noble Truth but not suffering. The other two Noble Truths, namely Origin and Path, might be suffering due to impermanence, but they are not suffering in the sense of the truth to be fully understood (pariññeyya) for which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. However, in every way, the five aggregates of clinging, excluding craving, are both suffering and the Noble Truth. The states associated with the Path and the fruits of asceticism are neither suffering nor the Noble Truth in the sense of the truth to be fully understood for which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. In this way, by applying it appropriately to the Origin, etc., the decision should be understood here by way of the tetrad.

Note 1: Since craving is included within the five aggregates of clinging and since that craving is the Truth of Origin, it is shown that the aggregates are taken while excluding craving.

Note 2: [The application to Origin, etc.]: Defilements other than craving, etc., are called 'Origin' (samudaya) in the sense of being the primary cause (according to the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga). Taking this Visuddhimagga as a commentary on the Suttas, they are not the 'Noble Truth' (according to the Sutta teaching). Cessation is the Noble Truth but not the Origin. The other two Noble Truths might be called 'Origin' in the sense of being a condition for their own fruit, but they are not the 'Origin' in the sense of that which is to be abandoned (pahātabba) for which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. In every way, craving is both the Origin and the Noble Truth. The states associated with the Path and the fruits of asceticism are neither the Origin nor the Noble Truth in the sense of that which is to be abandoned for which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. The cessation of formations and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are called 'Cessation' but not the Noble Truth. The Origin is the Noble Truth but not Cessation. The other two Noble Truths might be called 'Cessation' because they possess momentary cessation (bhaṅga), but they are not 'Cessation' in the sense of that which is to be realized (sacchikātabba) for which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. In every way, the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) is both Cessation and the Noble Truth. The remaining explanation (regarding states associated with the Path, etc.) follows the same method. Factors of the path other than the Noble Path are called 'Path' (magga) but not the Noble Truth. Cessation is the Noble Truth but not the Path. The other two Noble Truths might be called 'Path' because they are practices leading to existence, but they are not the 'Path' in the sense of that which is to be developed (bhāvetabba) for which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. In every way, the practice leading to cessation is the Path.

[144] 567. In the section 'By way of Emptiness', the detail is as follows: All truths are empty of a feeler, a doer, one who is extinguished, or one who goes, in the ultimate sense.
144:
It is also called the Noble Truth. The rest of the words are as previously explained. (Sub-commentary)

1- In the Visuddhimagga, the compound words are extracted and analyzed; since they were already analyzed in this Myanmar translation, only the essential points are presented here.

Because of their absence, they should be understood as void of a feeler and so on. Therefore, this verse is said:

'For suffering alone exists, but no sufferer is found;
The doer is not, but only the deed is there.
Nirvana is, but not the man who enters it;
The path is, but no traveler on it is seen.'

'Dukkham-eva hi—only suffering exists; na koci dukkhito—not any sufferer exists. Kārako na—there is no doer; kiriyāva vijjati—only the deed exists. Atthi nibbuti—there is peace (extinction); na nibbuto pumā—there is no person who is extinguished. Maggam-atthi (maggo atthi)—there is only the practice-path to reach Nibbāna; gamako na vijjati—there is no traveler.'

'Suffering exists without a sufferer,
The deed exists without a doer.
Cessation exists without one who is extinguished,
The Path exists without a traveler.'
(It is also translated in this way)

Note 1: The phrase 'only the deed is there' refers to the Truth of the Origin (Samudaya). Alternatively, because the Truths of Suffering and Origin are counted as the round of result (vipāka-vaṭṭa) and the round of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa), it refers to the state of the doer as the Truth of Suffering. Indeed, although the action (kiriya) is the work to be done, it is distinct from a doer; when that action arises solely due to its own causes, it is merely a conventional term to say 'an action is performed' within the continuity of mental and physical phenomena called suffering. The same applies to the one who is extinguished and the traveler. (Sub-commentary)

Alternatively—
'Void of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self; the first two are void of self, as is the Deathless state. The Path is devoid of permanence, happiness, and self; thus is voidness in them.'

Purimadvayaṃ—the first two truths, Suffering and Origin, are void of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self. Amatapadaṃ—the Deathless Nibbāna is void of self. Maggo—the Noble Path is void of permanence, happiness, and self. Iti—thus, tesu—in those four truths, suññatā—the state of voidness (veditabbā—should be understood).

Alternatively, the three truths are void of Cessation (Nirodha), and Cessation is void of the other three. Among these four truths, the two causal truths are void of the fruit. (Why?) Because of the absence of Suffering in the Origin, and because of the absence of Cessation in the Path.

Note 1: 'Because of the absence of Suffering in the Origin' means that in craving (taṇhā) which produces a new existence (at the moment of its occurrence), the new existence does not yet exist. Alternatively, just as the transformations (vikāra) of the Proponents of Prakṛti (such as Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, etc.) remain hidden and exist only as Prakṛti (the equilibrium of the three qualities: Sattva, Rajas, Tamas) before they transform (i.e., before they become manifest as Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, etc.); similarly, suffering associated with the Origin does not exist in the form of the Origin. (Sub-commentary)

(Indeed), the cause does not contain the fruit as a 'seed' or 'embryo' like the Prakṛti of the Proponents of Prakṛti. The fruit truth is also void of the cause. (Why?) Because Suffering and Origin, and Cessation and Path, do not occur together simultaneously. (Indeed) The fruit of a cause does not exist together with the cause, unlike the 'double-atom' (dvi-aṇuka) etc., of those who hold the theory of Inherence (Samavāyavādī). Therefore, this verse is said:

'Here, three are void of Cessation, and by those three, Cessation is also void. The cause is void of the fruit, and the fruit is void of its cause.'

Note: The Proponents of Prakṛti believe that when Prakṛti combines with Puruṣa, Mahat and others become manifest; before such transformation, Mahat and others are said to be hidden within Prakṛti. This means that suffering is not hidden within the Origin like those Mahat etc., hidden in Prakṛti.

1- The Proponents of Prakṛti say that when Prakṛti is joined with Puruṣa, it exists together with Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, the five Tanmātras, the eleven faculties, and the five elements that are to be transformed, as if carrying the 'embryo' of those transformations. This means there is no such 'embryo' of suffering in the Origin, nor an 'embryo' of Cessation in the Path.

2- This is the meaning of 'hetu-phalaṃ', translated as 'the fruit of the cause'; the essence is simply 'the fruit'.

'The group of three is void of Cessation, and Nibbāna is void of those three. The causal truth is void of the fruit, and the fruit is void of that cause.'

Thus, the decision by way of voidness should be understood.

568. Regarding the phrase 'by way of one-fold etc.': In detail, among these four truths, the Truth of Suffering is entirely one-fold by way of its nature of occurrence (pavaṭṭi). It is two-fold as mind and matter. It is three-fold by way of the divisions of rebirth (upapatti-bhava) in the sense-sphere, fine-material sphere, and immaterial sphere. It is four-fold by way of the four nutriments. It is five-fold by way of the five aggregates of clinging.

The Truth of the Origin is also one-fold by way of its nature as the producer (pavaṭṭaka). It is two-fold as associated with or dissociated from wrong view. It is three-fold by way of craving for sense-pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. It is four-fold by way of being abandoned by the four paths. It is five-fold by way of delight in forms and so on. It is six-fold by way of the six classes of craving.

[145] The Truth of Cessation is also one-fold by way of being the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu). Figuratively, it is two-fold as Cessation with residue (sa-upādisesa) and without residue (anupādisesa).

Note 1: This is the Nissaya meaning of 'pavaṭṭi-bhāvato'. The continuous flow of resultant mind and matter is called 'pavaṭṭi'. Therefore, it would be clearer to translate it as 'by way of being the continuous flow of mind and matter'.

Note 2: This is the Nissaya meaning of 'pavaṭṭaka-bhāvato'. It would be clearer to translate it as 'by way of being that which causes the continuous flow'.

It is three-fold by way of the cessation of the three planes of existence. It is four-fold by way of being attained or realized by the four paths.
145:
It is fivefold by way of the cessation of the five kinds of delight, such as delight in forms, etc.; and it is sixfold by way of the destruction of the six groups of craving (taṇhā-kāya).

The Path (Magga-sacca) is also single by way of being something to be developed (bhāvetabba). It is twofold by way of calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), or by way of the path of seeing (dassana-magga) and the path of development (bhāvana-magga). It is threefold by way of the three aggregates, such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha), etc. Indeed, this Path, being partial (sappadesa), is included in the three complete (nippadesa) aggregates—virtue and so on—just as a city is included in a country. In accordance with this, it is said:

"Friend Visākha, the three aggregates are not included in the Noble Eightfold Path, but, friend Visākha, the Noble Eightfold Path is included in the three aggregates. Friend Visākha, whatever is Right Speech, whatever is Right Action, and whatever is Right Livelihood—these states are included in the aggregate of virtue. Whatever is Right Effort, whatever is Right Mindfulness, and whatever is Right Concentration—these states are included in the aggregate of concentration. Whatever is Right View and whatever is Right Intention—these states are included in the aggregate of wisdom."

Note 1: Regarding the division into calm and insight, teachers say that Right View and Right Intention are insight, while the remaining five are calm. Indeed, since virtue also supports calm, it is included in calm; this is the view of those teachers. Alternatively, it should be understood that this division is stated according to the origin, where a path attained through the vehicle of calm is called calm, and a path attained through the vehicle of pure insight is called insight. (Ṭīkā)

To explain further: among these eight path factors, the three—Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood—are virtue itself. Therefore, they are included in the aggregate of virtue by way of their common nature (sajātito). (Although the Pali text uses the locative case 'sīlakkhandhe'—in the aggregate of virtue—it should be understood with the instrumental sense 'by the aggregate of virtue' in accordance with the commentary.) Among the three path factors beginning with Right Effort, concentration (samādhi) by its own nature is not able to fix upon an object in the state of one-pointedness. It is only able to do so when it receives the benefit and support of effort (vīriya) performing the task of uplifting and mindfulness (sati) performing the task of non-drifting (not forgetting).

In this regard, there is this simile: Suppose three friends enter a garden to enjoy a festival. One of them sees a Champaka tree in full bloom but cannot reach the flowers even by raising his hand. Then the second friend bends down and offers his back. Even standing on his back, the first friend is shaky and unable to pick them. Then the third friend offers his shoulder for support. Standing on the back of one and leaning on the shoulder of the other, the first friend picks the flowers as he pleases, wears them, and enjoys the festival. This is how the occurrence of concentration should be understood.

[146] To illustrate by connecting the simile with the subject: The three states such as Right Effort should be understood as the three friends who entered the garden together. The object should be understood as the Champaka tree in full bloom. Concentration, which is unable by itself to fix upon the object in one-pointedness, should be understood as the friend who could not reach the flowers even by raising his hand. Right Effort should be understood as the friend who offered his back. Right Mindfulness should be understood as the friend who offered his shoulder for support. Just as the first friend, standing on the back of one and leaning on the shoulder of the other, could pick the flowers as he pleased, so too, when effort performs the task of uplifting and mindfulness performs the task of non-drifting, concentration receives their benefit and support and is able to fix upon the object in one-pointedness. Therefore, among these three, only concentration is included in the aggregate of concentration by way of its common nature, while Right Effort and Right Mindfulness are included in the aggregate of concentration by way of their function (of supporting concentration).

Between Right View and Right Intention, wisdom (paññā) is not able by itself to judge the object as impermanent, suffering, and non-self; it is only able to do so when thought (vitakka) strikes at it, so to speak.

How? Just as an assayer (money-changer), having placed a coin in his hand and wishing to look at all its parts, is unable to see it from all sides merely with his eyes; he is only able to see it here and there by turning it over with his knuckles and fingers. In the same way, wisdom is not able by itself to judge the object by way of impermanence, etc. It is only able to judge the object that is taken up and presented by thought (vitakka), which has the characteristic of directing the mind towards the object and the function of striking and turning it over. Therefore, in this aggregate of wisdom, only Right View is included in the aggregate of wisdom by way of its common nature, while Right Intention is included in the aggregate of wisdom by way of its function (which is similar to the function of wisdom).
146:
1. 'As if striking from the beginning' means striking all around with a function similar to that of wisdom, such as 'impermanent, impermanent' and so forth. (The prefix 'ā-' here is interpreted in the sense of 'all around' (parito), although in the explanation of Vitakka in paragraph 71, it was interpreted as 'from the beginning' (ādito). Based on that explanation, it was translated above.) Wisdom penetrates and knows only what is given by taking and considering (ādāya ūhitvā), as if turning it over, such as 'impermanent in the sense of exhaustion (khayaṭṭhena), suffering in the sense of fear (bhayaṭṭhena)' and so forth. (In the Visuddhimagga, it is 'ādāyādāya', and it is translated accordingly.) Although Right View (Sammā-diṭṭhi) and Right Thought (Sammā-saṅkappa) arise together, Right Thought is shown as preceding in terms of providing assistance. (Sub-commentary)

2. 'By way of common origin' (sajātito) means by way of the same nature of wisdom as in 'knowledge of suffering' and so forth. In the phrase 'by way of action' (kiriyato), it refers to an action similar to the function of wisdom.

Note: 'Action' (kiriyā) refers to this. In the previous section on concentration, the action that assists and is appropriate for concentration was called 'action'. This is the distinction between these two types of action. (Sub-commentary)

In this way, the Path is included within these three aggregates. Therefore, I have said, 'It is threefold by way of the three aggregates.' It is fourfold only by way of the Path of Stream-entry and so forth.

Alternatively, all Truths are onefold because they are unfailing (avitatha) or because they are to be known by higher knowledge (abhiññeyya). They are twofold by way of mundane and supramundane, or conditioned and unconditioned. They are threefold by way of being abandoned by vision (dassana), abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā), and not to be abandoned. They are fourfold by way of full understanding (pariññeyya) and so forth. Thus, the decision regarding these Truths should be understood by way of the onefold and so forth.

[147] 569. Regarding 'by way of similarity and difference', in detail, all Truths are similar in being unfailing, being empty of self, and being difficult to penetrate. In accordance with this, it was said:

'Ānanda, what do you think of this? Suppose a man standing at a distance were to shoot an arrow through a very narrow keyhole without missing, shot after shot. And suppose another man were to pierce a hair split into a hundred pieces—or many pieces—with the tip of another hair. Which of these two tasks is more difficult to do, more difficult to achieve?' 'Venerable Sir, the task of the man who pierces a hair split into a hundred or many pieces with the tip of another hair is more difficult to do and more difficult to achieve.' 'Ānanda, those who penetrate according to reality that "This is suffering"... [p.] ... "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering," penetrate something much more difficult to penetrate than hitting the tips of those hairs.'

Note:
1. This is the meaning of the word 'sata'. Just as in 'satapadī' (centipede), 'satatejo' (the sun with many rays of power), 'sahassaraṃsī' (the sun with many thousands of rays), the word 'sata' should be taken to mean 'many' or 'innumerable'.
2. 'Koṭiyā' means with the tip of the arrow or the tip of the hair. 'Koṭiṃ' means the tip of the hair itself. (Sub-commentary) According to this view, one should take it as attaching a piece of hair to the tip of an arrow and hitting the tip of another piece of hair with it. It also seems appropriate to take it as the difficulty of aligning the tips of many hair strands that have been cut in the middle.

The Truths are different by way of defining them by their own characteristics (such as oppression (bādhana), etc.). The first two Truths are similar because they are deep and difficult to penetrate in their profound meaning, because they are mundane, and because they are with taints (sāsava). They are different by way of cause and effect, and by way of what is to be fully known (pariññeyya) and what is to be abandoned (pahātabba). The latter two Truths are also similar because they are deep and difficult to penetrate in their profound meaning, because they are supramundane, and because they are without taints (anāsava). They are different by way of the object and the state that takes the object, and by way of what is to be realized (sacchikātabba) and what is to be cultivated (bhāvetabba). The first and third Truths are similar in being pointed out as results. They are different by way of being conditioned and unconditioned. The second and fourth Truths are similar in being pointed out as causes. However, they are different by way of being unwholesome and wholesome. The first and fourth Truths are similar in being conditioned.

Note:
1. Because suffering and its origin are manifest in the continuity of beings, they are clear in a general sense. However, to know them according to reality as suffering and the cause of suffering is difficult. Therefore, they are said to be deep.
2. The Truths of Cessation and the Path are deep by their very nature. Therefore, they are said to be difficult to penetrate and difficult to know.
