3. Since Nibbāna is also attained through the Path, it is pointed out as the result of that Path. Therefore, it is said 'in being pointed out as results'. This is in accordance with 'Knowledge of the cessation of suffering is the discrimination of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā)'. (Sub-commentary)

They are different by way of mundane and supramundane. The second and third Truths are similar in being neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee (nevasekkhanāsekkhā)—being neither the property of trainees (sekkha) nor the property of non-trainees (asekkha/arahants).
147:
They are dissimilar in terms of being states that have an object and states that do not have an object.

In this way, through these various methods and modes, the wise should understand the similarity and dissimilarity of the Noble Truths. Here ends the detailed explanation of the Truths.

This is the sixteenth chapter, titled the "Description of the Faculties and Truths" (Indriya-sacca-niddesa), in the section on the Development of Wisdom within the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga), composed for the gladdening of good people.

## (The detailed explanation of the Faculties and Truths is finished)

## Conclusion

In the Visuddhimagga, there are 23 chapters (niddesa). The Burmese translation of the final part, from Chapter 17 to the conclusion, was published as the fourth volume in 1333 (Burmese Era). (The reason for publishing that volume first is stated in its preface.) The translation of Chapters 1 to 6 was published as the first volume in 1334. The translation of Chapters 7 to 11 was published as the second volume in 1336 and is currently in distribution. The third volume, containing Chapters 12 to 16, was completed as a final manuscript on the New Moon day of the first month of Vāso in 1336. It will soon appear as a printed book. Since the new Burmese translation of the Visuddhimagga is now entirely complete from beginning to end, the following concluding words are written here.

The renowned teacher known as Mahasi,
Who proclaims the true path of Satipaṭṭhāna,
Has performed missionary work by composing many treatises.
During the Sixth Council, he bore the responsibility of the final review.1

## Note.
1. This means he bore the responsibility of the final proofreading, known as Othāna-sodheyya-patta, during the Sixth Buddhist Council.

Questioning the Pali, scrutinizing the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries,1
The Venerable Sobhana Paṇḍita, Agga Mahā Thera,
Wrote this golden Burmese translation of the Visuddhimagga smoothly.
In 1336, on the New Moon day of the first Vāso,2
This treatise was successfully completed, free from dangers.
Likewise, may all beings be free from danger and harm.
May all their pure intentions be fulfilled and successful.
May they be happy, developing loving-kindness, compassion, and appreciative joy.
May those of distinction read and understand this treatise.
Having understood it, may they practice and reach the true path.
May they quickly realize the true bliss of the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna.
Thus, may the Exalted Sasana shine like the sun.

## Here ends the new Burmese translation of the Visuddhimagga.3

Note
1. This means he performed the duty of the Questioner (Pucchaka) during the Council for the Pali, and the duty of scrutiny for the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries.
2. "Pa-vā-kway-ti-thi" refers to the New Moon day of the first month of Vāso.
3. These concluding words are to be printed at the end of the fourth volume of the Burmese Visuddhimagga when it is reprinted.

Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa.

## 17. Paññābhūmi-niddesa - Description of the Soil of Wisdom

## Showing Dependent Origination

[148] 570. Now,1 among the states that are the soil (objects) of this (insight) wisdom2—which were previously mentioned as "the aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, truths, dependent origination, etc."—the state of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) and the states produced by dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppanna-dhamma) included by the word "etc."2 remain (to be explained). Therefore, the time has now come to explain3 those (two remaining)2 states.

Note
† The number in square brackets indicates the page number in the second volume of the Visuddhimagga.
† The number without brackets indicates the paragraph number in the Visuddhimagga.
1. Connect "Now... remain... the time has now come."
2. Words in parentheses are additions, explanations, meanings of elided words, or alternative translations.
3. Although the literal meaning of "vaṇṇanākkamo" is "the order of explanation," it is translated as "the time to explain" for the sake of smooth Burmese.

Among those (two) states, the causes such as ignorance (avijjā) should first be understood as Dependent Origination. Indeed, the Blessed One said:

"And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination? With ignorance as condition, bhikkhus, volitional formations come to be; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, mentality-materiality; with mentality-materiality as condition, the sixfold base; with the sixfold base as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is called dependent origination."2

"Bhikkhus, what is dependent origination? Bhikkhus, because of the cause of not-knowing—ignorance, volitional formations—saṅkhāra occur;"
148:
## 17. Description of the Soil of Understanding: Discussion on Dependent Origination

570. With volitional formations as condition, rebirth-consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, mentality-materiality arises; with mentality-materiality as condition, the sixfold sense base arises; with the sixfold sense base as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition,

Note 1: This is the meaning of the word 'veditabbā', which is expressed in the plural in Pali to agree with the object 'dhammā' (phenomena). In Myanmar, it is smoother to say 'should be known' without the plural marker. Therefore, the plural marker 'kun' is placed in parentheses for those who wish to omit it according to Myanmar usage. The same applies hereafter.

Note 2: This Pali text of the teaching on Dependent Origination is presented here in its original form so that it can be easily compared with the later explanations of terms like 'sambhāvanti' and 'evaṃ'.

craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, becoming as cause (kamma-bhava) arises; with becoming as condition, birth arises; with birth as condition, aging and death arise; and sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. In this way, there is the arising of this entire mass of suffering which is unmixed with happiness. Monks, this (nature of causes such as ignorance) is called Dependent Origination—thus He has spoken.

Aging, death, and other effects should be known as dependently arisen phenomena. Indeed, the Blessed One said:

Note 1: Showing only 'kamma-bhava' (karmic becoming) here instead of 'upapatti-bhava' (resultant becoming) is for the sake of ease in understanding. However, when 'kamma-bhava' is shown, its result, 'upapatti-bhava', should also be understood as included.

Note 2: Connect as 'arising... in this way'. It means the arising of successive effects like volitional formations due to successive causes like ignorance, as previously shown.

Note 3: According to this sentence, it seems that only the arising of the mass of suffering, which are the effects like volitional formations due to causes like ignorance, is meant by 'Dependent Origination'.

Note 4: The words in parentheses are provided to clarify the meaning in accordance with the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).

Note 5: In Pali, 'vuttaṃ' is used as a passive verb because it is expressed with the third-case unexpressed agent 'bhagavatā' and because the focus is on the object. However, in Myanmar, the subject 'the Buddha' can also be the expressed subject. Furthermore, the meaning is clearer if 'vuttaṃ' is translated as 'should be spoken'. Therefore, the passive marker 'ap' is placed in parentheses to be omitted if desired. The same applies hereafter. Occasionally, both the passive and plural markers are shown as '(at kun)'. In such cases, they can be omitted according to Myanmar idiom.

'Monks, what are dependently arisen phenomena? Monks, aging and death are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Monks, birth is... becoming is... clinging is... craving is... feeling is... contact is... the sixfold sense base is... mentality-materiality is... consciousness is... volitional formations are... Monks, ignorance is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Monks, these (effects such as aging and death) are called dependently arisen phenomena'—thus He has spoken.

Note 1: The teaching that 'aging and death are impermanent' is intended to make known the impermanence of things subject to aging and death; it is not taught to imply that aging and death themselves should be permanent, nor to suggest that it would be good if they were permanent.

571. The following is the summary of the meaning of these scriptural passages. The causal factors such as ignorance should be known as 'Dependent Origination' (Paṭiccasamuppāda). The effects produced by those various causal factors should be known as 'Dependently Arisen Phenomena' (Paṭiccasamuppanna-dhamma). Why is this [149] known? It is known by the words of the Blessed One.
149:
Indeed, the Blessed One, in the Sutta teaching on dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena, stated:

''And what, monks, is dependent origination? With birth as condition, monks, aging and death come to be. Whether Tathāgatas arise or not, that element stands, that stability of the Dhamma, that fixed course of the Dhamma, that specific conditionality (idappaccayatā). The Tathāgata fully awakens to this and realizes it. Having fully awakened to it and realized it, he declares it, teaches it, makes it known, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it, makes it plain, and says: 'See! Monks, with birth as condition, aging and death come to be.' Monks, with becoming as condition, birth comes to be... Monks, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be... Whether Tathāgatas arise or not... he makes it plain and says: 'See! Monks, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be.' Thus, monks, that which therein is the actuality (tathatā), the unfalsity (avitathatā), the not-otherwiseness (anaññathatā), this specific conditionality—this, monks, is called dependent origination.''

572. Thus, the Blessed One, in teaching dependent origination through synonyms such as 'actuality' (tathatā), stated that the causal factors themselves are dependent origination. Therefore, dependent origination should be understood as having the characteristic of being the cause for phenomena such as aging and death; it has the function of connecting suffering; and it manifests to knowledge as a wrong path.

Furthermore, this dependent origination is called 'actuality' (tathatā) because those specific phenomena arise from those specific conditions which are neither deficient nor excessive. It is called 'unfalsity' (avitathatā) because when the conditions have reached harmony, there is no non-occurrence of the phenomena produced from them even for a moment. It is called 'not-otherwiseness' (anaññathatā) because one phenomenon does not arise from the conditions of another phenomenon. It is called 'specific conditionality' (idappaccayatā) because it is the condition, or the collection of conditions, for these aforementioned phenomena such as aging and death.

573. In this context, the etymology (vacanattha) is as follows: the conditions for these [phenomena] are 'idappaccaya'. The state of being these conditions is 'idappaccayatā'. Or, the collection of these conditions is 'idappaccayatā'. The grammatical rule for the formation of this word should be sought from the books of grammar.

## The View of Some (Keci-vāda)

574. Some teachers, however, [conceiving the etymology as] 'arising dependently and rightly, independent of causes such as Prakṛti or Puruṣa imagined by other sects,' assert that dependent origination is merely the [act of] arising. That statement is not appropriate.
150:
By the word 'rightly' (sammā), the meaning of 'sam' in 'samuppāda' is shown. By the particle 'ca' (and), it is shown that it is not merely 'depending on' but also 'rightly arising' in combination. By the word 'arising', the meaning of 'uppāda' is shown. Therefore, Paṭicca + Sam + Uppāda = Paṭiccasamuppāda, which yields the direct grammatical meaning: 'rightly arising depending on causes'. Some teachers (Keci) accept this very grammatical meaning. If one investigates whether these 'Keci' teachers belong to the Mahāvihāravāsī, Abhayagirivāsī, or Jetavanavāsī sects, or if they were elders residing in Jambudīpa, no definitive answer can be given because there is no explanation in the Ṭīkā or other commentaries. If that view were the doctrine of the elders of Jambudīpa, it could also be a doctrine descended from the Elder Mahāmoggaliputtatissa, and thus that view should be considered seriously.

2. The hermit Kapila, who founded the Pakati-vāda (Sāṅkhya), stated that when Pakati (Primal Nature) unites with the Atta called Purisa, 'Mahā' arises from that Pakati; from Mahā comes Ahaṃkāra (ego), from that the five Tanmātras, and the eleven Indriyas. From the Tanmātras, the five gross elements (Bhūta-rūpa) arise. In this sequence, the entire world of sentient and insentient beings arises. The hermit Kaṇāda, who founded the Aṇu-vāda (Vaiseṣika), stated that the entire world arises from the combination of minute atoms (Paramāṇu). Some hermits outside the Dispensation say it arises through the creation of a God called Issara.

Why [is the view of 'mere arising' rejected]? Because there is no Sutta in the Pāḷi Canon to be relied upon, because it contradicts the Suttas, because the profundity and the methods are not possible, and because it violates grammatical rules (sadda-bheda).

To elaborate, there is no Sutta passage that states, "Mere arising is called Paṭiccasamuppāda." Furthermore, for one who asserts that mere arising is Paṭiccasamuppāda, there is the fault of contradicting the Padesavihāra Sutta. How is it contradictory? Because of the statement: "Then, the Blessed One, during the first watch of the night, reflected on Paṭiccasamuppāda in forward and reverse order..." and so on. Thus, the reflection on Paṭiccasamuppāda is the Buddha's Paṭhamābhisambuddhavihāra (the initial dwelling after enlightenment), and the Padesavihāra is a dwelling in a portion of that. As it is said: "Monks, that dwelling by which I dwelt when first enlightened, in a portion of that dwelling I have now dwelt."

Note: The theists say it arises by the creation of a God called Issara. As they say, if it were to arise because of Pakati-Purisa, Aṇu, or Issara, it would not be 'rightly arising'. To show that it is not connected to such causes imagined by those outside the Dispensation, but arises solely due to true causes such as ignorance (avijjā), the term 'Sam' (rightly) is used. This 'rightly' means without regard to the causes like Pakati-Purisa imagined by the heretics, and this passage explains that it is solely due to true causes like ignorance. Therefore, note that the phrase 'without regard to the causes like Pakati-Purisa imagined by the heretics' is the explanation of the word 'rightly'. If one wishes to know the Pakati-vāda etc. in detail, see the Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā Nissaya, Volume 4, page 211 onwards.

1. From the perspective of the Keci-vādīs, they might cite the Suttas on Paṭiccasamuppāda presented here as evidence. This is because in the statement: "Thus is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. This, monks, is called Paṭiccasamuppāda," it appears as if the Buddha intends for the arising of the mass of suffering through successive causes and effects to be known as Paṭiccasamuppāda.

...reflected [in forward and reverse order]. Reflection on Paṭiccasamuppāda is called the Buddha's Paṭhamābhisambuddhavihāra. Dwelling in a portion of that Paṭhamābhisambuddhavihāra is called Padesavihāra. The Buddha's teaching is as follows:
"Monks, I have known the Four Noble Truths (become a Buddha), and by whichever dwelling (reflecting on Paṭiccasamuppāda) I dwelt at first, in a portion of that dwelling I have now dwelt (during this past fortnight)."

To clarify further, in that Padesavihāra Sutta, it should be understood that the Buddha dwelt by seeing Paṭiccasamuppāda, not by seeing mere arising. The Buddha's teaching is as follows:
"I, dwelling thus in the Padesavihāra, know this: 'Feeling arises due to the cause of wrong view; feeling arises due to the cause of right view; feeling arises due to the cause of wrong intention...'" and so on; it should be understood in full detail.

Thus, as shown, for one who says mere arising is Paṭiccasamuppāda, there is the fault of contradicting the Padesavihāra Sutta. Similarly, there is the fault of contradicting the Kaccāna Sutta.

Note: 1. Reflecting on the process such as "with ignorance as cause, volitional formations arise" is called reflecting in forward order (anuloma). Reflecting on the process in reverse, such as "with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease," is called reflecting in reverse order (paṭiloma).
2. Connect with "...is called the initial dwelling."

To elaborate further, in the Kaccāna Sutta also, by the words: "Kaccāna, for one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with right wisdom, the notion of non-existence in the world, or the view that there is nothing after death, does not occur," the Buddha showed the forward Paṭiccasamuppāda, which shows the sequential causes, as 'Loka-samudaya' (the origin of the world) for the purpose of completely uprooting the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi). He did not show mere arising. Indeed, by showing mere arising, the complete uprooting of annihilationism does not occur. It only occurs by showing the non-interruption of causes. This is because when there is no interruption of causes, there is no interruption of effects. Thus, as shown, for one who says mere arising is Paṭiccasamuppāda, there is also the fault of contradicting the Kaccāna Sutta.

Regarding the statement 'because the profundity and the methods are not possible': The Blessed One taught this: "Ānanda, this Paṭiccasamuppāda is deep and it appears deep." Profundity is of four kinds; I shall explain those four kinds of profundity later. That profundity does not exist in mere arising. Teachers explain this Paṭiccasamuppāda as being adorned with fourfold methods; that group of four methods also does not exist in mere arising. Thus, as stated, because the profundity and the methods are not possible, mere arising is not called Paṭiccasamuppāda.

## Violation of Grammatical Rules
575. Regarding the statement 'because of the violation of grammatical rules': This word 'paṭicca' also achieves its grammatical purpose when it is used in connection with the same agent and denotes a preceding action or time. How? As in the passage: 'Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ' (Depending on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises).

Note: 1. It means that they explain Paṭiccasamuppāda by adorning it with the four methods.
2. Connect as: "This word 'paṭicca' also... being used in connection with a preceding action... achieves its purpose." Here, by the particle 'also', it is shown that not only other words ending in the 'tvā' suffix, but this word 'paṭicca' also achieves its purpose only when used in connection with a preceding action.
3. In saying 'nhātvā bhuñjati' (having bathed, he eats), the agent who performs the action of bathing and the action of eating is one and the same.
151:
In the expression 'having eaten, he sleeps' (bhutvā sayati), the agent who performs the act of eating and the act of sleeping is one and the same. Similarly, in this case of 'having depended, it arises', there should be a single agent for the act of depending and the act of arising. Where there are two such verbs with the same agent, the suffix -tvā is attached to the preceding verb; only then is the intended meaning accomplished.

As it is in the Pali texts. (Note 1) In the view of some teachers (keci), because it is joined with the word uppāda (arising) as a bhāvasādhana (abstract noun), there is no common agent, and thus it results in a grammatical flaw (saddabheda); it does not accomplish any purpose. (Note 2) Thus, due to this grammatical flaw, mere arising is not called 'Dependent Origination' (paṭiccasamuppāda).

In that context, if someone were to counter, 'We shall join it with the word hoti (is), as in paṭiccasamuppādo hoti (Dependent Origination occurs),' that is not tenable. Why? Because of the lack of connection and because of the fault of 'the arising of arising' (uppādappatti). To elaborate: in these passages—'Bhikkhus, I will teach you Dependent Origination. And what, bhikkhus, is Dependent Origination? ... This, bhikkhus, is called Dependent Origination' (SN 12.1)—the word hoti does not form a connection with even a single one of these terms. Furthermore, 'arising' does not 'arise'. If it did, one would arrive at the [further] arising of arising. This concludes one point.

Note 1: In the phrase 'Eye and forms having depended, eye-consciousness arises' (cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ), both the act of depending and the act of arising have the single agent 'eye-consciousness.' Thus the word paṭicca can accomplish the purpose of understanding the meaning of the sentence. Similarly, here too, both the act of depending and the act of arising should have a single agent. For a detailed explanation of the formation of the word with the -tvā suffix in the preceding time, see Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā-nissaya, Vol. 3, p. 547 ff., 565 ff.

Note 2: In the view of some teachers (keci), the word samuppāda is not an agent (kattā) but a bhāvasādhana (abstract noun) expressing the mere state of arising, and thus has no agent. Therefore, the word paṭicca cannot be grammatically formed with the -tvā suffix in the preceding verb. This means the grammatical rule that the -tvā suffix must be applied to the preceding verb among two verbs having the same agent is violated. However, from the perspective of the keci teachers, as in the expressions 'having gone, staying in a safe place' (Vism. II, 302, line 20), 'having fled, staying in a safe region' (Vism. II, 303, line 15), and 'having climbed, sitting' (Vism. II, 304, line 8), the meaning 'having depended, arising rightly' could be argued as grammatically sound and appropriate. The fact that this type of word meaning does not violate grammatical rules is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā, Vol. 2, p. 237, line 28 ff.

576. Also, for those who think: 'The state of these specific conditions is idappaccayatā (specific conditionality); and "state" (bhāva) (Note 1) means the mode (ākāra) which is the cause for the manifestation of formations etc. from ignorance etc.; and the term "Dependent Origination" applies to that particular modification of formations'—their view is not tenable. Why? Because [the Buddha] spoke of ignorance etc. as the causes. To elaborate: the Blessed One said, 'Therefore, Ānanda, this itself is the cause, this is the source, this is the origin, this is the condition for aging and death, namely, birth... [for formations, namely, ignorance]' (DN 15). By this, he stated that ignorance etc. themselves are the causes, not their particular modes.

Note 1: Bhāva (state), being, and cause are similar in meaning; they refer to the 'basis for the application of the term' (sadda-pavattinimitta). This is a matter for Pali scholars.

Therefore, what I said—'Dependent Origination should be understood as the causal states (paccaya-dhammā)'—should be known as correctly stated.

## Etymologies of the term Paṭiccasamuppāda

577. Furthermore, the notion that 'this Dependent Origination refers only to arising' based on the shadow of the word 'Dependent Origination' should be dispelled by taking the following meaning of this term. Indeed, the Blessed One [said]:

Since this word [Dependent Origination] is applied in two ways
To the collection of states produced from that [concurrence],
Therefore this [cause] is called so
By a metaphorical use of the effect (phalūpacāra).

To elaborate: teachers desire this word 'Dependent Origination' in two ways regarding the collection of effects produced from a collection of causes. How? Because that collection of effects, when realized, leads to welfare and happiness, the wise ought to realize (paccetum) it; because it is worthy of being realized, it is paṭicca. (Note 1) Furthermore, when it arises, it arises together (saha) and rightly (sammā), not singly nor without cause; therefore it is samuppāda. Thus, that collection of effects is paṭicca because it is worthy of being realized, and samuppāda because it arises together and rightly; hence it is called paṭiccasamuppāda.

Note 1: Paṭi (manifest/towards) + icca (to be known/realized) = Paṭicca (an effect worthy of being realized). In this sense, this word paṭicca is not a -tvā suffix form but a -tya suffix form, being a word with three genders: paṭicco, paṭiccā, paṭiccaṃ. This three-gendered paṭicca word is not commonly found in the Pali Piṭaka. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, p. 50, where 'avijjā paṭicca' etc. occurs, its commentary states it can be both a -tya suffix and a -tvā suffix form.

Alternatively, it is samuppāda because it arises together. However, it arises only by depending on (paṭicca) the concurrence of causes without letting go; thus also it is called paṭiccasamuppāda. Furthermore...
152:
This collection of causes, beginning with ignorance (avijjā), is the cause of that collection of effects (such as volitional formations, etc., which are called Paṭiccasamuppāda). Because it is the cause of that collection of effects (called Paṭiccasamuppāda), this collection of causes beginning with ignorance is also spoken of as 'Paṭiccasamuppāda' by way of metaphorical designation of the effect (phalūpacāra).

Just as in the world, molasses, which is the cause of phlegm, is spoken of as 'molasses is phlegm'; and just as in the Dispensation, the arising of the Buddhas, which is the cause of happiness, is spoken of as 'the arising of the Buddhas is happiness'; so too, it should be understood that this [collection of causes] is spoken of as 'Paṭiccasamuppāda' by way of metaphorical designation of the effect.

578. Alternatively, the etymological definition is:
This collection of causes is called 'paṭicca' because it is 'gone towards' (approached) mutually. And it is called 'samuppāda' because it produces effects together (in combination).

To explain further: This collection of causes, which is pointed out in the teaching of Dependent Origination with individual causes like ignorance at the head for the manifestation of volitional formations and so on, is called 'paṭicca' because the constituent factors of the harmony of conditions have 'gone towards' (approached) each other in the sense of producing their respective effects and in the sense of being non-deficient. This cause, so called 'paṭicca', is also called 'samuppāda' because it produces effects that occur together and are inseparable from one another. In this way, since that collection of causes is both 'paṭicca' and 'samuppāda', it is called 'Paṭiccasamuppāda'.

579. Another method of etymological definition:
This collection of causes (beginning with ignorance) produces states mutually, dependently, equally, and together. Therefore, the Sage (the Buddha) has spoken of it thus in this Dispensation.

To explain further: Among the conditions pointed out with ignorance at the head, those conditions which produce states such as volitional formations are not able to produce them without depending on one another or when there is a deficiency of one another. Therefore, this collection of causes beginning with ignorance produces states by depending [on one another], not just partially but equally (harmoniously), and not in a sequence of before and after but together (simultaneously). Thus, the Sage, who is skilled in terminology that follows the true meaning (paramattha), has spoken of it in this Dispensation as 'Paṭiccasamuppāda'.

580. The benefit of the Buddha speaking thus is:
By the first term (paṭicca), the non-existence of Eternalism (Sassata-vāda) and so on is shown. By the subsequent term (samuppāda), the destruction of Annihilationism (Uccheda-vāda) and so on is shown. By the combination of both terms, the method [of the Middle Way] is fully illustrated.

Regarding the phrase 'by the first term', it should be understood as follows:
153:
By the word *paṭicca*, which illustrates the concurrence of causes, the non-existence of Eternalism (*sassata-vāda*), the theory of no-cause (*ahetu-vāda*), the theory of an uneven cause (*visama-hetu-vāda*), and the theory of the Supreme Ruler (*vasavatti-vāda*) is illustrated. This is because the phenomena of the three rounds (*vaṭṭa*), which occur continuously, are dependent on the concurrence of causes.

Note:
1. *Paṭicca* (dependent on each other) + *samuppāda* (causing effects to arise concurrently and simultaneously) = *Paṭiccasamuppāda* (the doctrine where effects arise concurrently in dependence on one another). This explains the intended meaning of the term *Paṭiccasamuppāda*.
2. Eternalism (*sassata-vāda*) is the view that the self (*atta*), which is called a person or being, does not perish; even when the body perishes, the self remains eternal in some place.
3. The theory of no-cause (*ahetu-vāda*) is the view that happiness and suffering have no cause and arise spontaneously by chance.
4. The theory of an uneven cause (*visama-hetu-vāda*) is the view that the world exists by the power of nature (*pakati*), atoms (*aṇu*), time (*kāla*), etc. It is the belief in an incorrect or uneven cause.
5. The theory of the Supreme Ruler (*vasavatti-vāda*) is the view that the world is created by a God called Issara, Purisa, or Pajāpati. It is the belief that everything happens according to God's will.

Indeed, what benefit would the concurrence of causes be to those who hold Eternalism or those who hold the theory of no-cause? Thus it should be understood. Regarding the latter word, by the word *samuppāda*, which illustrates the arising of phenomena (such as formations, etc.), the theories of Annihilationism (*uccheda-vāda*), Nihilism (*natthika-vāda*), and the theory of Non-action (*akiriya-vāda*) are demolished and abandoned because phenomena arise from the concurrence of causes. Therefore, the demolition of Annihilationism and other views is illustrated. Indeed, while phenomena are arising repeatedly by the power of preceding causes, how can there be annihilation, or how can Nihilism and the theory of Non-action occur? Thus it should be understood.

Regarding the combination of the two words, by the entire term *paṭiccasamuppāda*, because those various phenomena arise without breaking the continuity of the sequence of cause and effect when there is a concurrence of those respective causes, the following are illustrated: (1) the Middle Way (*majjhimā paṭipadā*), (2) the abandonment of the theories "he who acts is he who experiences" or "one acts and another experiences," (3) not clinging firmly to local parlance such as "man" or "woman," and (4) not overstepping (not rejecting) worldly designations. This is the meaning of the mere word *paṭiccasamuppāda*.

Note:
1. Annihilationism (*uccheda-vāda*) is the view that a being is completely cut off and ceases to exist at death.
2. Nihilism (*natthika-vāda*) is the view that there are no results of wholesome or unwholesome deeds.
3. The theory of Non-action (*akiriya-vāda*) is the view that even if one kills or steals, no demerit is incurred, and even if one gives or abstains from killing, no merit is gained.
4. "Because those various phenomena arise..." should be connected to "the correct path is illustrated."
5. The Middle Way here refers to the arising of appropriate effects due to relevant causes without falling into the two extremes of Eternalism and Annihilationism.

(1) Because the round of kamma and the round of result are different in nature and time, one who understands Dependent Origination is free from the view that "the doer himself experiences." Because the effect arises within the same continuity of mind and matter where the kamma occurred, one is also free from the view that "the doer is one, and the experiencer is another." This is because, according to the principle of continuity, the mind and matter at the time of doing and the mind and matter at the time of experiencing occur in a single continuity and are thus called the same person.
(2) One who understands Dependent Origination realizes it is merely a continuity of cause, effect, mind, and matter; thus, they are free from clinging firmly to designations like "real woman" or "real man" as ordinary people do.
(3) Not overstepping worldly designations means using terms like "being," "man," "woman," "pot," or "cup" according to conventional usage without analyzing whether a being refers to matter or feeling, etc.
(4) Here, a special grammatical explanation from the Sub-commentary (*Ṭīkā*) is presented: *Paṭicca* (depending on the appropriate cause) + *sam* (connected effect) + *uppāda* (arising) = *Paṭiccasamuppāda* (the arising of a connected effect in dependence on the appropriate cause). In short, it means the arising of an effect through dependence. This is easier to remember than the Commentarial etymologies. However, it also points to taking the cause along with its productive power, not just the arising of the effect. This should be taken as a figure of speech (*phalūpacāra*) as shown in the Commentary.

## The Difficulty of Explaining the Meaning of Dependent Origination

581. Furthermore, the Blessed One, when teaching Dependent Origination, set forth the text in the manner beginning with "With ignorance as condition, formations come to be." A teacher wishing to explain the meaning of this text of Dependent Origination must enter the assembly of the Proponents of Analysis (*Vibhajjavādins*), and while not misrepresenting the teachers, not overstepping his own doctrine (the doctrine of the Mahāvihāra residents), not being preoccupied with criticizing the doctrines of others (such as the Abhayagiri residents), not contradicting the Suttas, conforming to the Vinaya, looking to the four Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*), illustrating the Dhamma, grasping the meaning, and explaining that same meaning again through other methods, the explanation of the meaning should be made. Not only that, but the explanation of the meaning of Dependent Origination is inherently difficult. As the ancients said:

"Truth, a being, rebirth-linking,
And the mode of conditions;
These four things are hard to see,
And extremely difficult to teach."

Note:
If one says, "I understand that the same consciousness from previous lives has migrated to this life," it contradicts the Suttas which teach that eye-consciousness is impermanent, etc.
154:
2. If one says that the Buddha taught that practicing deeds that cause obstacles, such as sexual misconduct, does not actually cause obstacles for a monk, or if one says that an offense is incurred due to a transgression in a dream, such statements are said to be inconsistent with or contrary to the Vinaya.

3. For the four Great Authorities (Mahāpadesa), see the Mahāvagga Pāḷi of the Dīgha Nikāya, page 102, and its Commentary, page 155, etc.

4. Regarding 'being' (satta): Teachers explain it as the state of being void of a 'being'. Even though they say so, in truth, both the term 'being' and the fulfillment of a being's necessary functions in the formations (saṅkhāra) which are void of a being (are difficult to understand and explain). (Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā). The term 'satta' is the name given to what is called a 'being'. It should be said that this is difficult to see. The designation 'being' occurs based on the collection of mental and physical phenomena (nāma-rūpa) that arise continuously in a sequence. Without clinging to the part that this designation of 'being' is absolutely not different from those physical and mental bases, or the part that it is absolutely different from them—

Because of that (the fact that the explanation of the meaning of Dependent Origination is done in such a way, and that it is difficult to do), it is not easy for anyone other than those who have reached the scriptures (Āgama) known as the Pāḷi Canon and the attainment (Adhigama) of the Path and Fruit to explain the meaning of Dependent Origination. Having weighed this—

## Pledge and Exhortation

[154] Desiring to explain the Dependent Origination now, I find no footing, like one who has plunged into the deep ocean.

However, this Dispensation (Sāsana), adorned with various methods of teaching, and the path of the former teachers (the commentarial tradition) continue uninterrupted.

Therefore, relying on both, I shall begin the explanation of the meaning of this Dependent Origination. Listen to it with a concentrated mind.

It is indeed worthy of encouragement; the former teachers said:
'If anyone listens to this Dependent Origination with respect, making it as if it were ingrained in their very bones,

Note:
It is difficult for one who is not proficient in Dependent Origination to correctly grasp (the nature of a being) and to explain it so that others understand. (Anuṭīkā). For a more detailed explanation, see the notes in the Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā Nissaya, Volume 3, pages 575-6.
1. 'Finding no footing' refers to the inability to find it through one's own individual wisdom. (Ṭīkā)

That person will gain a distinction in the later period compared to the earlier period. Having gained that distinction between the earlier and later periods, they shall reach Nibbāna, the place where the King of Death cannot see.'

582. (The word 'iti' seems redundant here). As I have pledged to explain, I shall now elaborate. In 'with ignorance as condition, formations [arise]' (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā) and so on, from the very beginning,

the decision should be known by: diversity of teaching, meaning and characteristics, singlefoldness etc., and the determination of factors.

## Diversity of Teaching

In that verse, regarding 'diversity of teaching': In detail, the Blessed One's teaching of Dependent Origination is fourfold, like the gathering of creepers by four men: teaching from the beginning to the end, or from the middle to the end; and teaching from the end to the beginning, or from the middle to the beginning.

To elaborate: Among the four men gathering creepers, one first sees only the root of the creeper. He cuts the creeper at the root, pulls the whole thing, takes it, and uses it for his work. In the same way, the Blessed One teaches Dependent Origination from the beginning to the end, thus: 'So it is, bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, formations [arise]... [p] ...with the condition of becoming, birth [arises]; with birth as condition, aging and death [arise].'

Note:
1. 'Distinction in the later period' means that from the moment one begins the effort (to listen), one gains a distinction of knowledge and a distinction of the exhaustion of defilements (which have never occurred before) moment by moment. This is the intended meaning. (Ṭīkā)
2. Connect 'from the very beginning' with 'should be known'.
3. 'In the same way' refers only to the relevant points of comparison; it does not mean it is identical to the creeper gatherer's act of seeing only the root, etc.

Furthermore, among those men, one first sees the middle part of the creeper. He cuts it in the middle, pulls only the upper part (the tip), takes it, and uses it for his work. In the same way, the Blessed One teaches [155]: 'For one who delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it, delight arises.'
155:
“That delight which is in feelings is clinging (upādāna). With clinging as condition, becoming (bhava) occurs; with becoming as condition, birth (jāti) occurs.” In this manner, He teaches from the middle until the end.

Furthermore, just as among those (aforementioned) men, one sees the tip of a creeper first, and having grasped it at the tip, he follows it along the tip, takes the whole thing down to the root, and applies it to his work; similarly, the Blessed One teaches Dependent Origination from the end back to the beginning, saying: “It has been said: ‘With birth as condition, aging and death occur.’ Monks, do aging and death occur with birth as condition, or not? How does it appear to you in this matter?” “Venerable Sir, aging and death occur with birth as condition. Thus it appears to us in this matter: with birth as condition, aging and death occur.” “With becoming as condition, birth occurs... p... with ignorance as condition, volitional formations (saṅkhāra) occur. Thus it has been said. Monks, do volitional formations occur with ignorance as condition, or not? How does it appear to you in this matter?”

Furthermore, just as among those men, one sees only the middle of the creeper first, and having cut it in the middle, he descends downwards, takes it down to the root, and applies it to his work; similarly, the Blessed One teaches from the middle back to the beginning, saying: “Monks, what is the cause, what is the origin, what is the birth, what is the source of these four nutriments (āhāra)? These four nutriments have craving (taṇhā) as their cause, craving as their origin, craving as their birth, and craving as their source. What is the cause of craving? Feeling (vedanā)... contact (phassa)... the six sense bases (saḷāyatana)... name-and-form (nāmarūpa)... consciousness (viññāṇa)... what is the cause of volitional formations? ...p... volitional formations have ignorance as their cause... p... ignorance as their source.”

583. If it is asked: “Why does He teach in these four ways?” (The answer is:) Because Dependent Origination is auspicious in every way (samantabhaddaka), and because He Himself has attained grace in teaching (desanā-vilāsa). To elaborate, Dependent Origination is auspicious in every way; (because it is so auspicious,) it leads to the penetration of the Noble Path, or the penetration of the nature of Dependent Origination, from whichever of those four teachings (one follows). Furthermore, the Blessed One has attained grace in teaching through His possession of the four kinds of fearlessness (vesārajja) and the four kinds of analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā), and by having reached the fourfold depth.1 Because He has attained grace in teaching, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma through various methods.

Specifically, His teaching in forward order (anuloma) starting from the beginning should be understood as being for the purpose of showing the continuous occurrence (of the round of existence) through their respective causes and for showing the order of arising (uppatti-kkama) to those beings who are confused about the analysis of the causes of the round of existence. The teaching in backward order (paṭiloma) starting from the end (is for the purpose of showing): “Alas, this world of beings has fallen into suffering; [156] rebirth also...”

Note
1. Regarding “having reached the fourfold depth”: it should be understood as the state of being firmly established by finding a footing in the deep subjects of Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, and Paṭivedha (the Doctrine, the Meaning, the Teaching, and the Penetration) (Sub-commentary).
156:
It should be understood that [this] is the teaching that was preached. 

In this context, although it should be said 'the teaching which is the cause of preaching' by deriving the word-definition as *desīyati etāya*, it is stated as 'the teaching that was preached' for the sake of smoothness in the Burmese language. If the term *desanā* is translated as 'the act of preaching,' it fits well in the first and second sentences of the teaching, but it does not fit in the third and fourth. In the final sentence beginning with *tāsu yā*, that meaning of 'the act of preaching' is entirely inappropriate. Therefore, the term is translated simply as 'the teaching that was preached.' Furthermore, the word *pavattā* is translated in conjunction with the subject and its attributes, similar to the word *hoti*, also for the sake of linguistic smoothness in this sentence.

'The world is fallen into trouble; it is born, it ages, it dies, it passes away, and it is reborn'—observing the world of beings who have reached such suffering in this manner (DN 2.57, SN 2.4), and following the penetrative insight (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) attained in the period prior to Buddhahood, [this teaching was preached] for the purpose of showing the causes (such as the arising of a new existence) of those respective sufferings such as aging and death, which He Himself had realized.

The teaching that proceeds from the middle to the beginning [is preached] for the purpose of showing the sequence of cause and effect starting from the past, having carried [the discourse] back to the past ages (namely *avijjā* and *saṅkhāra*) by following the determination of the causes of nutriment. The teaching that proceeds from the middle to the end [is preached] for the purpose of showing the future, starting from the arising of the causes of the future (existence) in the present age. Among those four types of teaching, the *anuloma-desanā* (teaching in forward order) is preached from the beginning for the purpose of showing the continuous occurrence [of the factors of existence] and the order of their arising through their respective causes, such as ignorance, for the sake of those beings to be led (*veneyya*) who are greatly confused about the causes of the round of suffering. It should be understood that this *anuloma-desanā* is laid down here (in this *Paññābhūminiddesa*) as the primary basis for exposition.

## The Reason for Teaching with Ignorance at the Beginning

584. Let us explain further by raising a question: In this teaching of *Paṭiccasamuppāda*, why is ignorance (*avijjā*) taught at the very beginning?

Is ignorance causeless, a root cause of the world, like the 'Prakṛti' (Primordial Matter) of the *Pakativādins*? This is the question. It is not causeless. Indeed, the Blessed One stated the cause of ignorance: 'With the arising of taints (*āsava*), there is the arising of ignorance' (MN 1.103). However, there is a figurative method (*pariyāya*) by which it may be a root cause. What is that method? It is its status as the 'head' (chief) of the discourse on the round of rebirth (*vaṭṭakathā*).

Indeed, when the Blessed One teaches the *vaṭṭakathā*, He does so by making two factors the head. He may make ignorance the head, as He said: 'Bhikkhus, a prior limit of ignorance is not evident, such that one could say, "Before this, ignorance did not exist, then it came to be." But, bhikkhus, it is said thus: "Ignorance is seen to have this as its condition (idappaccaya)"' (AN 10.61). Or He may make craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) the head, as He said: 'Bhikkhus, a prior limit of craving for existence is not evident, such that one could say, "Before this, craving for existence did not exist, then it came to be." But, bhikkhus, it is said thus: "Craving for existence is seen to have this as its condition"' (AN 10.62).

585. Why does the Blessed One, when teaching the *vaṭṭakathā*, make these two factors the head? It is because they are the special causes of kamma that leads to happy and miserable destinations (*sugati* and *duggati*). To elaborate, ignorance is the special cause of kamma leading to miserable destinations. Why? Because a worldling (*puthujjana*) overwhelmed and oppressed by ignorance is like a cow to be slaughtered (*vajjhagāvī*) who is oppressed by the distress of being scorched by fire and beaten by clubs. Because of being afflicted by that distress, even though it is not pleasant and brings her harm, [157] she strives to drink hot water. Similarly, because of the heat of defilements, even though it is not pleasant and brings harm to oneself by leading to a miserable destination, the worldling performs various kammas that lead to miserable destinations, such as taking life. Furthermore, craving for existence is the [special cause] of kamma leading to happy destinations...
157:
4. Drinking hot water is neither enjoyable for that cow nor does it bring her benefit; nevertheless, it is said that the cow drinks the hot water.

5. Due to the burning of defilements... [one] undertakes various [unwholesome] kammas—connect this.

[Craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā)] is the special cause [for kamma leading to happy destinations]. Why? Just as that aforementioned cow, oppressed by thirst for cold water, drinks cold water—which is enjoyable and relieves her fatigue—so too the ordinary person (puthujjana), oppressed by craving for existence, undertakes various kammas leading to happy destinations, such as abstaining from taking life. These are enjoyable because of the absence of the heat of defilements and they relieve the fatigue of suffering in unhappy destinations by leading to a happy destination.

Notes:
1. Connect: The ordinary person... undertakes various kammas.
2. Connect: Just as [the cow], being thirsty for cold water... undertakes the drinking of cold water.
3. Connect: Due to the absence of the heat of defilements... [one] undertakes various kammas.
4. It is said that the Savara (wild tribes), when they are about to kill a cow, repeatedly apply heat with fire and beat it so that the meat does not stick to the bone; then they make it drink hot water to purge its bowels. After purging, they kill the cow, which is swollen and whose meat has separated from the bone. Therefore, the commentator provides the analogy of being roasted by fire. In that analogy, just as the cow to be slaughtered undertakes the drinking of hot water because she is oppressed by ignorance (not knowing), so too the ordinary person undertakes kamma that leads to unhappy destinations. Furthermore, just as that cow, seeing the fault in drinking hot water, undertakes the drinking of cold water through the power of craving, so too the ordinary person, because ignorance is very strong, sees the fault in kamma leading to unhappy destinations and undertakes kamma leading to happy destinations through the power of craving. Indeed, in the case of suffering, craving follows after ignorance; in the case of happiness, ignorance follows after craving. (Sub-commentary explanation): In this context, although 'gāvī' (cow) is mentioned, it should not be taken as only a female cow, but as cattle in general, because the Savara kill bulls as well, and the word 'gāvī' can denote cattle in general.

586. Furthermore, among those two states [ignorance and craving] which are the heads of the discourse on the round (vaṭṭakathā), in some suttas the Blessed One teaches a discourse rooted in a single state. For example: "So, bhikkhus, with ignorance as proximate cause, volitional formations; with volitional formations as proximate cause, consciousness," and so on. Also: "Bhikkhus, in one who dwells contemplating gratification in things that can be clung to, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging," and so on. In some suttas, He teaches a discourse rooted in both. For example: "Bhikkhus, for the fool who is hindered by ignorance and joined with craving, this body has thus been produced. So there is this body and external name-and-form; thus this dyad. Dependent on the dyad, there is contact and the six bases, touched by which the fool experiences pleasure and pain," and so on. Among these discourses, this one—"With ignorance as condition, volitional formations"—should be understood here as a discourse rooted in a single state by way of ignorance. Thus first, the decision should be understood by way of the variety of teaching.
