Three aggregates are a condition for one aggregate; two aggregates are a condition for two aggregates and rebirth kamma-produced matter by way of resultant condition. The aggregates are a condition for the heart-base (vatthu) by way of resultant condition.”

Notes:
1. Summary of Kamma-paccayo:
(1) Wholesome and unwholesome kamma-volition (cetanā) is called asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika kamma-paccayo); the resultant consciousness, mental factors, and kamma-produced matter which are the effects of that kamma are called the asynchronous kamma-condition-produced states (nānākkhaṇika kamma-paccayuppanna).
(2) The 89 volitions (cetanā) are called co-nascent kamma condition (sahajāta kamma-paccayo); the 89 associated consciousnesses, 51 mental factors, mind-produced matter, and rebirth kamma-produced matter are called the co-nascent kamma-condition-produced states (sahajāta kamma-paccayuppanna).
2. These qualifiers, according to the Ṭīkā (Niruṣṣāho santabhāvo), are not qualifiers of 'peace' (santa), but of 'state/nature' (bhāva). Therefore, it means 'peace that is devoid of effort (byāpāra)'.
3. Connect as: 'assists by way of being peaceful'.

Notes on Resultant Condition:
1. Summary: The 36 resultant consciousnesses and 38 mental factors are called the resultant condition (vipāka-paccayo); the associated mental states and mind-produced matter and rebirth kamma-produced matter are called the resultant-condition-produced states (vipāka-paccayuppanna).

## (15) Āhāra-paccayo (Nutriment Condition)

608. The four nutriments that assist by way of supporting materiality and mentality—or, by their nature of supporting—are called the nutriment condition. As the Blessed One taught:

“Edible food (kabaḷīkāro āhāro)—which, though not originally a morsel, is made into a morsel (the nutriment called nutritive essence (ojā) produced by the four causes: kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment)—is a condition for this physical body (the group of matter produced by four causes and three causes) by way of nutriment condition.

Notes:
2. Although it causes the arising of nutriment-produced matter etc., the act of supporting is the primary function of nutriments. Therefore, it is said 'by way of supporting materiality and mentality'. (Ṭīkā)
3. Food is not yet a 'morsel' before being eaten; it is made into a morsel when eaten. Therefore, according to Pali grammar, the term 'kabaḷīkāra' is formed to mean a change from its original state. It is translated as 'made into a morsel', meaning 'that which is eaten'.
4. Here, 'tijakāya' (body produced by three causes) refers to the group of matter existing at the first moment of support by nutriment and during the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

Mental nutriments (contact, volition, and consciousness) are conditions for associated mental states and for the matter produced by those mental nutriments by way of nutriment condition.”

In the Pañhāvāra, it is also stated:
“At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate nutriments (contact, volition, and consciousness) are conditions for associated mental aggregates and rebirth kamma-produced matter by way of nutriment condition.”

Notes:
1. Summary of Nutriment Condition:
(1) Nutritive essence (ojā) produced by the four causes is the nutriment condition; the group of matter produced by the four causes (excluding the nutritive essence of the same group) is the nutriment-condition-produced state.
(2) The three mental nutriments (contact, volition, consciousness) are the nutriment condition; the associated consciousness, mental factors, mind-produced matter, and rebirth kamma-produced matter are the nutriment-condition-produced states.

## (16) Indriya-paccayo (Faculty Condition)

609. The twenty faculties, excluding the femininity faculty and masculinity faculty, which assist by way of predominance (control), are called the faculty condition. Among those twenty faculties, the eye-faculty and others—namely, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties, as well as the faculties of pleasure and pain—assist only the mental states (the five-fold sense consciousness); the remaining thirteen faculties assist both materiality and mentality. As the Blessed One taught:

“The eye-faculty is a condition for the eye-consciousness element... etc. The ear-faculty... the nose-faculty... the tongue-faculty... the body-faculty is a condition for the body-consciousness element and its associated mental states by way of faculty condition. Physical life-faculty is a condition for kamma-produced matter of the same group by way of faculty condition. Mental faculties (8 by essence, 15 by classification) are conditions for associated mental states and for the matter produced by those faculties by way of faculty condition.”

In the Pañhāvāra, it is also stated:
“At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate faculties are conditions for associated mental aggregates and rebirth kamma-produced matter by way of faculty condition.”

Notes:
1. The 8 mental faculties by essence are: life, consciousness, feeling, faith, energy, mindfulness, one-pointedness, and wisdom. Among these, feeling is divided into five (pleasure, pain, joy, grief, equanimity), and wisdom is divided into four (faculty of wisdom, the faculty 'I shall know the unknown', the faculty of highest knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known), thus making 15 faculties by classification.
2. Summary of Faculty Condition:
(1) The five sensitive material faculties (pasāda-rūpa) that arose with the preceding life-continuum (atīta-bhavaṅga) and serve as the base for the five-fold sense consciousness are called the pre-nascent faculty condition (purejātindriya-paccayo); the five-fold sense consciousness and 7 associated mental factors are the pre-nascent faculty-condition-produced states.
(2) Physical life-faculty is called the physical life-faculty condition (rūpa-jīvitindriya-paccayo); the other kamma-produced matter in the same group is the physical life-faculty-condition-produced state.
(3) Mental faculties (life, consciousness, feeling, faith, energy, mindfulness, one-pointedness, wisdom) are called the co-nascent faculty condition (sahajātindriya-paccayo); the associated consciousness, mental factors, mind-produced matter, and rebirth kamma-produced matter are the co-nascent faculty-condition-produced states.

## (17) Jhāna-paccayo (Jhāna Condition)

610. The seven jhāna factors (constituents of jhāna)—classified as wholesome etc. (according to initial application, sustained application, rapture, joy, grief, equanimity, and one-pointedness)—which assist by way of close contemplation (fixed scrutiny), excluding the two feelings of pleasure and pain in the two sets of five-fold sense consciousness, are called the jhāna condition. As the Blessed One taught:

“Jhāna factors are conditions for mental states associated with jhāna and for the matter produced by those jhāna factors [171] by way of jhāna condition.”

In the Pañhāvāra, it is also stated:
“At the moment of rebirth-linking, resultant indeterminate jhāna factors are conditions for associated mental aggregates and rebirth kamma-produced matter by way of jhāna condition.”

Notes:
1. Connect as: 'The jhāna factors (...) which assist...'.
171:
2. Among the five types of feelings, pleasure (sukha) and pain (dukkha) are strictly not Jhana factors, and thus it is said they should be excluded as mentioned above. By saying this, it should also be understood that equanimity (upekkhā) and one-pointedness (ekaggatā) associated with the five-fold sense-consciousness (pañca-viññāṇa) are also not Jhana factors. However, since these two (equanimity and one-pointedness) do become Jhana factors when associated with other types of consciousness, it is not said here that they should be excluded. This will be shown at the end of the Path Condition (magga-paccaya).

3. Here, the word 'all' refers only to all varieties such as wholesome (kusala) and so on; it does not refer to all states within every mental arising (cittuppāda).

4. A brief summary to be noted regarding this Jhana Condition: The Jhana factors—initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), feeling (vedanā), and one-pointedness (ekaggatā)—excluding those in the ten-fold sense-consciousness (dve-pañca-viññāṇa), are called the Jhana Condition (jhāna-paccaya). The 79 associated consciousnesses, 52 mental factors, mind-produced matter (cittaja-rūpa), and rebirth-linking kamma-produced matter (paṭisandhi-kammaja-rūpa) are called the Jhana-conditioned states (jhāna-paccayuppanna).

## (18) Magga-paccaya (Path Condition)

611. The twelve path factors (magganga), such as the wholesome and so on, which assist by way of being a means of exit (attainment) [1] in an indefinite manner, or by way of right or wrong [2], are called the Path Condition (magga-paccaya). The manner in which (the Buddha) taught is:
'The path factors are a condition for the states associated with the path and for the matter produced by them by way of Path Condition.'
In the Panhavara (Question Section), it is also taught:
'At the moment of rebirth-linking, the path factors which are resultant indeterminate (vipāka-abyākata) are a condition for the associated mental aggregates and for the rebirth-linking kamma-produced matter by way of Path Condition.'

Notes:
1-2. Right path factors such as Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) are a means of exit by way of truth. Wrong path factors such as Wrong View (micchā-diṭṭhi) are a means of exit by way of falsehood. Here, 'exit' (niyyāna) refers to the successful completion of its respective function. It does not mean exit from the cycle of birth (vaṭṭa); this point should be specifically noted.
3. The twelve path factors are the eight right path factors: Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi), Right Thought (sammā-saṅkappa), Right Speech (sammā-vācā), Right Action (sammā-kammanta), Right Livelihood (sammā-ājīva), Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma), Right Mindfulness (sammā-sati), and Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi); and the four wrong path factors: Wrong View (micchā-diṭṭhi), Wrong Thought (micchā-saṅkappa), Wrong Effort (micchā-vāyāma), and Wrong Concentration (micchā-samādhi). Wrong Speech, Wrong Action, Wrong Livelihood, and Wrong Mindfulness do not have separate ultimate realities (dhammas); they are merely unwholesome volition (akusala-cetanā) and unwholesome mental arisings occurring in those modes. Therefore, these four wrong path factors are not shown in the Dhammuddasavāra of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī or in this Path Condition section.

Special Note: It should be understood that these two conditions, Jhana Condition and Path Condition, are not obtained in the ten-fold sense-consciousness and the rootless consciousnesses (ahetuka-citta) respectively [1].

## (19) Sampayutta-paccaya (Association Condition)

612. The mental states (consciousness and mental factors) which assist by way of being associated (sampayutta)—meaning having the same base, the same object, the same arising, and the same cessation [2]—are called the Association Condition (sampayutta-paccaya). The manner in which (the Buddha) taught is:
'The four immaterial aggregates are a condition for one another by way of Association Condition' [3].

## (20) Vippayutta-paccaya (Dissociation Condition)

613. Material states that assist mental states (consciousness and mental factors), and mental states that assist material states, by way of not reaching the state of having the same base etc., or by way of not having the same location etc. [4], are called the Dissociation Condition (vippayutta-paccaya). This Dissociation Condition is of three kinds: co-nascent dissociation (sahajāta-vippayutta), post-nascent dissociation (pacchājāta-vippayutta), and pre-nascent dissociation (purejāta-vippayutta). Indeed, (the Buddha) taught this:
'Co-nascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for mind-produced matter by way of Dissociation Condition. Post-nascent wholesome aggregates are a condition for this pre-arisen body by way of Dissociation Condition.'

Furthermore, in the Sahajata-vibhaṅga of the indeterminate (abyākata) section:
'At the moment of rebirth-linking, the resultant indeterminate aggregates are a condition for kamma-produced matter by way of Dissociation Condition. The aggregates are a condition for the physical base (vatthu). The physical base is a condition for the aggregates by way of Dissociation Condition.'

Pre-nascent dissociation should be understood only by way of the physical bases such as the eye-faculty. The manner in which (the Buddha) taught is:
'The pre-nascent eye-base (cakkhāyatana) is a condition for eye-consciousness... the body-base (kāyāyatana) is a condition for body-consciousness by way of Dissociation Condition. The physical base is a condition for resultant indeterminate and functional indeterminate (kiriya-abyākata) aggregates... the physical base is a condition for wholesome aggregates... the physical base is a condition for unwholesome aggregates by way of Dissociation Condition' [1].

Notes:
1. A brief summary to be noted regarding this Path Condition: The nine path factors—wisdom (paññā), initial application (vitakka), Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, effort (vīriya), mindfulness (sati), concentration (samādhi), and Wrong View (micchā-diṭṭhi)—are called the Path Condition. The 71 rooted consciousnesses, 52 mental factors, rooted mind-produced matter, and rooted rebirth-linking kamma-produced matter associated with those path factors are called the Path-conditioned states (magga-paccayuppanna).
2. 'Being associated' (sampayutta) is the reason for saying or knowing that they are conjoined. Therefore, the four factors such as having the same base are called the factors of association (sampayutta-aṅga).
3. A brief summary to be noted regarding this Association Condition: The 89 consciousnesses and 52 mental factors (the collection of mental states in both life-continuum and rebirth) are called both the Association Condition and the conditioned states.
4. Connect with: 'assist by way of not having the same location etc.' This means assisting by being devoid of the characteristics of association such as having the same location, or by not being mixed together as one. It means assisting without being mixed or joined.
1. In this Dissociation Condition, there are three types: co-nascent, post-nascent, and pre-nascent. The brief summary for co-nascent dissociation is the same as the co-nascent summary...

## (21) Atthi-paccaya (Presence Condition)

614. A state which assists by way of being present (atthi-bhāva)—which is the characteristic of the present (arising and existing based on a cause) [1]—to a state that is also similarly present, or by way of supporting it, is called the Presence Condition (atthi-paccaya). (The Buddha) laid down the matrix (mātikā) of this Presence Condition in seven ways [172] by way of mental aggregates, great essentials (mahābhūta), mentality-materiality (nāma-rūpa), consciousness and mental factors, great essentials, bases (āyatana), and physical base (vatthu-rūpa). The manner in which (the Buddha) taught is:
172:
The matrix is laid down. As it was said: “(1) The four immaterial aggregates are related to one another by way of presence condition (atthi-paccaya). (2) The four great essentials (mahābhūta) are related to one another... (3) At the moment of conception, mind (nāma) and matter (rūpa) [the heart-base] are related to one another... (4) Consciousness and mental factors are related to mind-produced matter... (5) The great essentials are related to derived matter (upādā-rūpa)... (6) The eye-base is related to the eye-consciousness element... etc... the body-base... etc... the visible-object base... etc... the tangible-object base is related to the body-consciousness element and its associated states by way of presence condition. The visible-object base... etc... the tangible-object base is related to the mind-element and its associated states... (7) The matter depending on which the mind-element and mind-consciousness element arise, that matter is related to the mind-element, the mind-consciousness element, and their associated states by way of presence condition.” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.21)

Note: Similar to the points to be noted in paragraphs (3) and (4). In the case of post-nascent dissociated (pacchājāta-vippayutta), the summary of points to be noted is similar to the points for post-nascent. In the case of pre-nascent dissociated (purejāta-vippayutta), the summary of points is similar to the brief points (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) of pre-nascent dependence (purejāta-nissaya).
1. Connect as: “supporting by way of being currently present.”

In the Investigation Chapter (Pañhāvāra), however, after setting out the headings as (1) co-nascence presence, (2) pre-nascence presence, (3) post-nascence presence, (4) nutriment presence, and (5) faculty presence, the detailed explanation is first given for (1) co-nascence presence as: “One aggregate is related to the other three aggregates and to mind-produced matter by way of presence condition,” and so forth (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.435). (2) In pre-nascence presence, the explanation is given by way of the pre-nascent eye-base, etc.; or by way of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible object, sound, smell, taste, tangible object, heart-base, visible-object base... eye-base... body-base, and heart-base. (3) In post-nascence presence, the explanation is given by way of the relation of the post-nascent consciousness and mental factors to this pre-nascent body. (4-5) In nutriment presence and faculty presence, the explanation is given as: “Nutriment (nutritive essence), which is not literally a morsel but acts like one, is related to this body by way of presence condition. The physical life-faculty is related to kamma-produced matter by way of presence condition.” (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.435).

Note: 1. Here, the 11 items from the eye to the heart-base are the object pre-nascence presence condition that supports insight (vipassanā). Then, visible object and sound are the conditions that support the divine eye and divine ear higher powers (abhiññā). Then, the five bases such as the visible-object base are the object pre-nascence presence condition that supports eye-consciousness, etc. Then, the six base-matters such as the eye-base are the base pre-nascence presence condition that supports eye-consciousness, etc.
2. The summary of points to be noted for this presence condition: (1) Co-nascence presence is similar to co-nascence; (2) Pre-nascence presence is similar to pre-nascence; (3) Post-nascence presence is similar to post-nascence; (4) Nutriment presence is similar to the nutriment condition of edible food; (5) Faculty presence is similar to the physical life-faculty.

## (22) Natthi-paccaya (Absence Condition)
615. Immaterial states (mental states) that have just ceased and support the immaterial states arising immediately after them by providing the opportunity for their occurrence are called the absence condition. As the Buddha taught: “Consciousness and mental factors that have just ceased are related to the consciousness and mental factors that have arisen following them, or the present ones, by way of absence condition.”

## (23) Vigata-paccaya (Disappearance Condition)
Those very states of the absence condition are called the disappearance condition because they support by way of their disappearance. As the Buddha taught: “Consciousness and mental factors that have just disappeared are related to the consciousness and mental factors that have arisen following them, or the present ones, by way of disappearance condition.”

Note: 1. Here, the first meaning is the traditional interpretation given by Burmese teachers: “paṭi” (imitating/following) + “uppannānaṃ” (arisen) = “paṭuppannānaṃ” (arisen following the previous). The second meaning is the translation according to the Paṭṭhāna Commentary and Mahāṭīkā, which explain “paṭuppannānaṃ” as “paccuppannānaṃ” (present). 2. Absence condition is similar to proximity condition (anantara-paccaya). 3. Disappearance condition is also similar to proximity condition.

## (24) Avigata-paccaya (Non-disappearance Condition)
Furthermore, those very states of the presence condition should be understood as the non-disappearance condition because they support by way of their non-disappearance. Although the absence and presence conditions are understood as the disappearance and non-disappearance conditions respectively, this dyad (duka) was taught by the power of the Buddha’s omniscience, which adorns the teaching to make it beautiful, or according to the needs of those to be guided. This is just as the “dissociated from root” dyad (hetu-vippayutta-duka) was taught even though the “rootless” dyad (ahetuka-duka) had already been taught. Here ends the section explaining the Paṭṭhāna conditions.

## Detailed Explanation of the Phrase “Avijjāpaccayā Saṅkhārā”
[173] 616. As stated, among these 24 conditions, this ignorance (avijjā) supports meritorious volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) in two ways; however, it supports other (demeritorious) volitional formations in many ways.
173:
It should be understood that for the final [imperturbable] volitional formations, that ignorance assists in a single way.

Notes:
1. The non-disappearance condition (avigata-paccaya) is the same as the presence condition (atthi-paccaya).
2. Because it is a translation of the word 'puññānaṃ', the additional term 'abhisankhāra' is shown in brackets for those who wish to take the precise meaning with the Pali. However, in the meanings of 'paresam' and 'pacchimānam', it would be inappropriate if the primary meaning 'abhisankhāra' were not included; therefore, in those places, the meaning is stated without brackets.

In that verse, 'for the meritorious in two ways' means it assists [meritorious volitional formations] in two ways: by way of object condition and by way of decisive support condition. To explain: when one contemplates ignorance as being subject to destruction and fall—or, when one contemplates that it has been destroyed or has fallen—it assists sense-sphere meritorious volitional formations by way of object condition. When one knows a mind associated with delusion (of oneself or another) by means of a mind associated with direct knowledge (known as the knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and knowledge of the future), it assists fine-material sphere [meritorious volitional formations] (by way of object condition). Furthermore, for one who, [seeing the fault of ignorance and] desiring Nibbāna which is free from the round, fulfills and accumulates sense-sphere meritorious bases such as giving, and for one who produces fine-material sphere jhānas, it assists both those [sense-sphere and fine-material sphere] meritorious volitional formations by way of decisive support condition. Similarly, for one who, being intensely deluded by ignorance (which conceals the faults of existence), desires the prosperity of sense-sphere existence or fine-material sphere existence and performs those very two types of meritorious volitional formations, it assists by way of decisive support condition.

For other volitional formations, 'in many ways' means it assists demeritorious volitional formations in many ways. How? When greed and so on arise taking this ignorance as an object, it assists by way of object condition.

Notes:
1. If one wishes to speak in full, include the 'efficacy' (satti) as before, such as 'by way of the efficacy of object condition'. Note the same for subsequent instances.
2. Connect the subject 'ignorance' with the verbs 'assists'.
3. Among the three types of decisive support condition, this refers to natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya). Note that when 'decisive support' is mentioned generally hereafter, it refers to natural decisive support.
4. Connect this subject with the verb 'assists'.

When one enjoys it by giving it weight, it assists by way of object-predominance and object-decisive support. For one who, being intensely deluded by ignorance and not seeing the danger, commits life-taking and so on, it assists by way of decisive support condition. For the second impulsive moment (javana) and so on, it assists by way of proximity, contiguity, proximity-decisive support, repetition, absence, and disappearance conditions. For one who performs any kind of unwholesome act, it assists by way of root, conascence, mutuality, support, association, presence, and non-disappearance conditions. Thus, it assists in many ways.

It should be understood that for the final volitional formations, that ignorance assists in a single way means it assists imperturbable volitional formations only by way of decisive support condition. This nature of ignorance as a decisive support should be understood in the same way as stated for meritorious volitional formations.

## Can it occur from a single cause?

In this matter, (stopping, the objector) says: Does this ignorance (alone, without relying on other aids) assist volitional formations? Or are there other (aiding) causes as well? What should be said in this matter? (Your objection is not yet complete; state the remaining objection). If it assists as a single [cause], then the doctrine of a single cause arises. Or if there are other causes, then is it not inappropriate to state a single cause as 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]'? It is not inappropriate; (it is indeed appropriate). Why?

In this world, there is no single result from a single cause, nor many results. There is no single result from many causes. However, there is a purpose in showing a single cause and a single result. Therefore, (it is appropriate).

[174] To explain: In this world, there is no such thing as a single result from a single cause, nor many results. Nor is there a single result from many causes. In fact, only many results arise from many causes.

This is true: from many causes such as climate, soil, seed, and water, one sees only many results such as color, smell, and taste, which are called the sprout. Nevertheless, 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise. With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises'—thus, the showing of a single cause and result is done (in various places). In such showing, there is a benefit; there is a purpose intended.

To explain: In some discourses, the Blessed One shows a single cause or result according to the prominence (of the factor), in some discourses according to clarity, and in some discourses according to uniqueness (unshared nature), in accordance with His knowledge that beautifies the teaching and the (inclinations of) those to be taught.
174:
The manner of showing this is as follows: In the teaching, "With contact as condition, feeling arises," the Buddha speaks of a single cause and a single effect because of its predominance. Indeed, contact is the predominant cause of feeling because feeling is determined according to contact. And feeling is the predominant effect of contact because contact is determined according to feeling.

Note:
1. In the phrase "With ignorance as condition, formations arise," a single cause is shown. In the phrase "With formations as condition, consciousness arises," a single effect is shown. In this manner, a single cause and a single effect are shown in various places. (Sub-commentary)
2. The subsequent sentence explains the preceding one. The meaning is that 'attha' (benefit/purpose) here does not refer to the result arising from a cause, nor to wealth, etc., but only to the intended benefit known as 'payojana' (purpose), which is to be understood through such a presentation.
3. Connect this with the verb "He showed these causal terms."
4. Regarding the phrase "because feeling is determined according to contact":
By such passages as, "Bhikkhus, dependent on a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises," and "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three—eye, forms, and eye-consciousness—is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises," (connect with 'determined'). It means that pleasant feeling, etc., and feeling born of eye-contact, etc., are determined according to the contact that causes pleasant feeling, etc., and according to eye-contact, etc. To clarify: although the eye and forms, etc., are the same, there is no change in the pleasantness, etc., without the power of contact. Although forms and attention, etc., are the same, there is no change in the feeling born of eye-contact, etc., without the power of impact (contact). Even when other conditions are the same, there is no confusion between pleasant feeling, etc., and feeling born of eye-contact, etc., in terms of being gross or subtle, etc., except by the power of contact. This is the intended meaning of the phrase "because feeling is determined according to contact." The fact that contact is the unerring cause of pleasant feeling, etc., as just stated, is itself called "determining contact according to feeling." Alternatively, it is the determination of a specific effect by a specific cause; therefore, in both instances (determining feeling and determining contact), it is called "determination." (Sub-commentary)

In the teaching, "Illnesses arising from phlegm," he mentions a single cause because of its manifestation. Indeed, in the occurrence of such illness, phlegm is manifest, while causes such as kamma are not—or rather, kamma, nutriment, temperature, mind, improper food, bile, wind, and external effort are not manifest. (The reason is that the disease is cured by treating the phlegm).

In the teaching, "Bhikkhus, whatever unwholesome states there are, all of them have unwise attention as their root," he mentions a single cause because of its specificity.

Note:
Unwise attention is the specific cause of unwholesome states (not shared with wholesome or indeterminate states). Physical bases, objects, etc., are common causes (shared with others). Because it is such a specific cause, he mentions only one cause.

For that reason, in this teaching of Dependent Origination, although other causes of formations such as the physical base, object, and conascent states exist, this ignorance is shown as the cause of formations because of its predominance, since it is the cause of other causes like craving, etc., as stated: "In one who dwells contemplating gratification (in things that can be fettered), craving increases; (with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, becoming—the kamma that causes birth—which is formations, arises)" and "With the arising of taints, there is the arising of ignorance." It should also be understood as being shown as the cause of formations because of its manifestation, as stated: "Bhikkhus, an ignorant person, having arrived at ignorance, performs even a meritorious formation," (since meritorious formations do not occur in an Arahant who is free from ignorance, it is also a specific cause). Thus, it is shown as the cause of formations because it is manifest and specific. Not only this, but by the very explanation given for showing a single cause and effect, the intended benefit (payojana)—which is to make the Dhamma known according to the inclination of those to be taught (veneyya)—should be understood in all instances where a single cause and effect are shown (such as "With contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises"). This concludes one section.

## How Ignorance Can Be a Condition for Merit

618. Here, an objector raises a challenge: Even if this is so, how is it fitting for ignorance—which is blameworthy and has exclusively undesirable results—to be a condition for meritorious formations and imperturbable formations? For sugarcane does not grow from a neem seed.
175:
(The answer is:) Why should it not be appropriate? (It is indeed appropriate). For in the world:
[175] A condition that is opposing to the produced phenomena is established, as is a condition that is non-opposing; likewise, a condition that is similar is established, as is one that is dissimilar. However, those produced phenomena are not exclusively "resultants" (vipāka) [ripened from the condition]. (Therefore, it is appropriate).
To elaborate: A condition that is opposing or non-opposing in terms of presence, nature, function, etc., of the produced phenomena is established in the world. To explain further, a preceding mind is an opposing condition for a subsequent mind in terms of presence. The learning and training of arts and sciences in a previous time is also an opposing condition (in terms of presence) for the performance of those arts and sciences in a later time. Kamma is an opposing condition for kamma-born matter in terms of nature. Milk and so forth are opposing conditions for curd and so forth (in terms of nature). Light is an opposing condition for eye-consciousness in terms of function, and molasses and so forth for liquor and so forth (in terms of function). However, the eye, visual objects, and so forth are non-opposing conditions for eye-consciousness and so forth in terms of presence. Preceding impulsions (javana) and so forth are non-opposing conditions for subsequent impulsions and so forth, both in terms of nature and function.
Regarding the next section: Just as opposing and non-opposing conditions are established, so too are similar and dissimilar ones. To elaborate, similar matter, known as temperature (utu) and nutriment (āhāra), is a condition for matter (temperature-born and nutriment-born matter); and rice seeds and so forth are conditions for rice fruit and so forth. Dissimilar matter is also a condition for mentality (arūpa), and mentality is a condition for matter. Cow hair, sheep wool, horns, curd, and sesame powder and so forth are conditions for nejā grass, arrow grass, and fragrant grass (sarabhū), etc. However, those produced phenomena for which these opposing, non-opposing, similar, and dissimilar factors are conditions, are not necessarily the "resultants" (vipāka) of those factors.
Thus, because of this arising of cause and effect, although this ignorance (avijjā) has an absolutely undesirable fruit by way of its result, and is faulty by way of its own nature, it should be understood as a condition for all these volitional formations such as the formation of merit (puññābhisaṅkhāra), etc., according to the circumstances, by way of being an opposing or non-opposing condition in terms of presence, function, and nature, and by way of being a similar or dissimilar condition. This conditionality of ignorance has already been stated (in paragraph 593) in this manner: "To elaborate, for one in whom the ignorance regarding suffering and so forth is not yet abandoned, through that ignorance regarding suffering and the past, etc., he grasps the suffering of the round of rebirths as happiness, and initiates the three types of formations which are the causes of that very suffering."

## On Delusion Regarding Death, Rebirth, etc., as the Cause of the Three Formations
619. Furthermore, this other method (exposition) should also be known:
"In the round of rebirths, regarding death and reappearance,
And the characteristics of formations,
He who is deluded concerning dependently arisen phenomena,
He performs these three types of formations;
Therefore, ignorance is the condition for these three."
[176] If it is asked, "How does one who is deluded regarding death, rebirth, and so forth perform these three types of formations?" Firstly, one deluded about death does not grasp it correctly as "the dissolution of the aggregates (mental and material) at the end of a life-existence, in any state of becoming, mode of birth, or destiny." Instead, he wrongly conceives that "a being dies" or "the soul of a being moves to another body," and so forth.

Notes:
1. In the Pyay Nissaya, it is translated this way. Since the manner of support was explained in detail previously, and hereafter only the manner of being a condition will be shown without showing the manner of support, it is appropriate only to question the conditionality of formations; it is not appropriate to question the support, nor to explain it later.
2. Connect with "The condition of the phenomena...". According to the Pyay Nissaya, it should be translated as: "A condition, or a phenomenon that renders support, which is either opposing or non-opposing, similar or dissimilar to the phenomena, is evident or established." Here, for the sake of clarity, the word 'paccayo' (condition) is translated with all four terms like 'opposing condition,' etc.
1 (p. 176). Connect with "Condition for the subsequent mind...". In Pyay Nissaya: "The preceding mind, for the subsequent mind, being opposing by way of presence, is the condition." The verb 'is established/evident' cannot simultaneously connect with both the first subject 'preceding mind' and the second subject 'condition.' Therefore, it should be considered whether it was intended to mean 'being a condition, it is established.' However, that meaning also does not clearly show the conditionality. Understand the differences in the following sections similarly.
2 (p. 176). The preceding mind is not currently existing but has ceased; the subsequent mind is currently existing. Thus, it means 'opposing' by way of existence and non-existence.
5 (p. 176). Kamma is opposing to matter in terms of the nature of 'bending' (mentality) vs 'deforming/changing' (matter), and 'perceiving an object' vs 'not perceiving an object,' etc. (Ṭīkā).
6 (p. 176). Milk has a sweet taste, curd has a sour taste; thus they are opposing in nature. (Ṭīkā).
1 (p. 177 context). Light has no function of knowing, eye-consciousness has the function of knowing; thus they are opposing. (Ṭīkā).
2. Molasses has no function of intoxicating, liquor has the function of intoxicating; thus they are opposing. (Ṭīkā).
3. Both cause and effect are currently existing, so they are said to be non-opposing. (Ṭīkā).
4. Cow hair and sheep wool are conditions for nejā grass; it is said that nejā grass grows where these hairs accumulate. The word 'avi' means sheep, so 'aviloma' is translated as sheep wool. However, since the Anuṭīkā explains it as 'red goats,' it could be taken as goat. But since the word 'eḷakā' does not mean goat but sheep, it is not appropriate to translate it as goat. Furthermore, horns are the condition for arrow grass; curd and sesame powder are conditions for fragrant grass, etc. In terms of essence, moss is the condition for spinach; a donkey and a mare are the conditions for a mule, and so forth. (Ṭīkā).
176:
One who is confused about rebirth (upapāta)—which is the occurrence of a new existence—does not correctly grasp rebirth as it is: "The manifestation of the aggregates (khandhā) [the initial mind and matter] in all states of existence, origins, and destinations is called rebirth or the beginning of a new life." Instead, such a person wrongly conceives, "A being is reborn [as a whole entity]," or "It is the manifestation of a new body for the self-entity called a being."1

Note
1. The manifestation of a new body means: when the old body in this human life is discarded through death, a new body belonging to the afterlife appears. How so? It is just as stated [in verses such as the Bhagavad Gita].

One who is confused about saṃsāra1 does not correctly grasp the process of mind and matter—saṃsāra—as it is described: "The uninterrupted succession of aggregates, bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) is called saṃsāra." Instead, they wrongly conceive, "This self-entity called a being moves from this present world (human life) to another world, and comes from another world to this world."2

Note
"Just as a man discards worn-out clothes and takes on other new ones, so the self, seeking happiness, discards the worn-out body in this world and takes on a new one."
(Bhagavad Gita 2.22) Based on this commentary (Ṭīkā) statement, some speak as if Buddhist scriptures accept the above verse. In truth, it is not accepted; it is merely cited as an example of how wrong views (micchā-diṭṭhi) arise due to ignorance (avijjā) when one does not know rebirth as it truly is.
1. Connect with: "One who is confused... wrongly conceives."
2. In this context, although one should say "comes" and "goes," it is stated here in accordance with the sequence of death (cuti) and rebirth (paṭisandhi) mentioned earlier.

One who is confused about the characteristics of formations (saṅkhāra) does not grasp—or does not know—the individual characteristics (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa)1 or the general characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa)2 of formations. Consequently, they wrongly conceive of the formations of mind and matter as a self-entity, as the property of a self-entity,3 as permanent, as beautiful, or as pleasant and good.

One who is confused about dependently arisen phenomena (paṭiccasamuppanna-dhamma) does not correctly grasp the occurrence of formations and so on due to ignorance and other causes.

Note
1. Here, "formations" (saṅkhāra) refers to conditioned formations (saṅkhata-saṅkhāra) produced by a combination of causes.
2. Individual characteristic (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa) refers to the inherent nature of each phenomenon: such as the characteristic of being deformed (ruppana) for matter, the characteristic of inclining toward an object (namana) for the mind, the characteristic of hardness or roughness (kakkhalatta) for the earth element (pathavī), and the characteristic of touching an object (phusana) for contact (phassa). Since the characteristic of matter does not pertain to the mind, and the characteristic of the mind does not pertain to matter; since the characteristic of earth does not pertain to water (āpo), etc.; and since the characteristic of contact does not pertain to feeling (vedanā), etc., these individual characteristics are also called specific characteristics (visesa-lakkhaṇa).
3. General characteristic (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa) refers to characteristics common to all mental and physical phenomena: the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa), the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa), and the characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa). These three pertain to all formations of mind and matter that arise and pass away; therefore, these three are called general characteristics.
4. If one clings to any one of the five aggregates—or two, three, or four—as the self, then the remaining aggregates are clung to as "belonging to the self" (attaniya), as parts of the self (Ṭīkā). It should also be understood that clinging to the whole body as the self and then clinging to "my hand," "my foot," etc., is also clinging to them as "belonging to the self."

Instead, they wrongly conceive: "The self either knows or it does not know";1 "That same self [which will experience the results of happiness and pain in the next life] both acts [merit or demerit] itself and causes others to act";2

Note
1. These are translations of the text "attā jānāti vā na jānāti vā." The first meaning is a direct translation; the second adds "iti" to mean "conceives that the self knows." This is because proponents of the self-theory do not cling to both (that it knows and does not know) simultaneously, but rather cling specifically to either "the self knows" or "the self does not know."
2. The Sāṅkhya school (followers of Kapila) wrongly conceives that the self knows. The followers of Kaṇāda (Aṇu-vāda) and the Ājīvakas (Jains) wrongly conceive that the self does not know. Indeed, the teacher Kaṇāda holds that the self does not know by its own nature or alone, but only knows when combined with the quality of intellect called 'Mahat' (Ṭīkā). For a broader study of these Kapila doctrines, see the Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā Nissaya, Volume 4, page 210, etc.
3. This statement shows the clinging to the idea that the doer of the deed and the experiencer of the result are the same person. It may seem similar to Buddhist teaching, but it is not. The one who clings to the self believes, "This same self, this same person, performed the deed, and this same self, this same person, experiences the result; the self from the old life reaches the new life to experience it—it is one and the same." In Buddhist teaching, "There is no self-entity when the deed is performed; there is only a succession of mental phenomena like intention (cetanā) and physical phenomena that perform the act. These mental and physical phenomena are constantly changing, new and old, like a flowing river. Within that same succession of mind and matter, when conditions are right, new mind and matter arise as the result of that deed."

"That self [which performed or caused the deed] enters into rebirth at the moment of conception. Atoms (paramāṇu) and the creator god (Issara) and others, by means of the embryonic stages like the kalala-drop, establish the body [by producing double-atoms, etc., or by the power of divine will] and complete the sense bases such as the eye. Being endowed with sense bases, that self touches [the object], feels, craves, clings, and exerts effort.3 That same self that exerts effort then exists in another life." Or they wrongly conceive, "All beings, as self-entities, are transformed and matured into the states of humans, devas, birds, etc., through fixed necessity and coincidence; or they reach various different states such as humans, devas, and birds through fixed necessity, coincidence, and inherent nature."

That person, being blinded by ignorance so that their vision of wisdom is lost, conceives wrongly in this way.5 Just as a blind person wandering on the ground might tread upon the right path or the wrong path, on level ground or uneven ground, so too does he perform meritorious formations, demeritorious formations, and imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra).

Note
5. [This note refers to the analogy of the blind man performing the three types of formations.]
177:
“The arising of a new result is conventionally described as ‘a person experiencing the result,’ but in truth, there is no experiencing person, being, or self; there is only the continuity of mind and matter. Therefore, it is not in accordance with the Buddha's teaching.

1- Connect as: ‘Having established the body well... they fulfill.’
2- By this word, the arising of the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) is shown.
3- By this word, it is shown that kamma-process becoming (kammabhava) occurs.
4- Connect as: ‘Or... one wrongly conceives.’
5- Connect as: ‘While thinking... likewise, one strives and acts.’

It should be understood that one strives and performs meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), and imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra), just as one might arrive at a good and right path, or a wrong path that is not the way, or an upland, or a pit, or level ground, or uneven ground.

Therefore¹—

‘Just as a man born blind, without a guide,
Sometimes walks on the right path, and sometimes on the wrong path;
So too the fool, wandering in saṃsāra without a guide,
Sometimes performs merit, and sometimes performs demerit.
But when he understands the Dhamma and realizes the Four Truths—
or, when he understands Nibbāna (through the path-knowledge) and realizes the (remaining) Truths (through the completion of his task)—
then, with the cessation of ignorance, he will live in peace (having stilled all suffering of defilements).’

This is the detailed explanation of the phrase ‘avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā’ (with ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]).

## Detailed Explanation of the Phrase ‘Saṅkhārapaccayā Viññāṇaṃ’

620. In the phrase ‘saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ,’ consciousness (viññāṇa) refers to the sixfold consciousness beginning with eye-consciousness. Among these, eye-consciousness is of two types: wholesome resultant (kusalavipāka) and unwholesome resultant (akusalavipāka).

Note:
1- Connect as: ‘Therefore... this word is spoken.’

Ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness are likewise of two types each. Mind-consciousness¹ is of twenty-two types: two mind-elements (manodhātu) which are wholesome and unwholesome resultants (known as the two receiving consciousnesses); three rootless mind-consciousness elements (ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu, known as the three investigating consciousnesses); eight sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses with roots (sahetuka-kāmāvacara-vipākacitta); five fine-material-sphere resultant consciousnesses (rūpāvacara-vipāka); and four immaterial-sphere resultant consciousnesses (arūpāvacara-vipāka). Thus, these twenty-two types exist². In this way, these six types of consciousness encompass all thirty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses (lokiya-vipāka-viññāṇa). Supramundane resultants are not included here as they are not applicable to the discourse on the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).

In that regard, the question may arise: ‘How is it to be known that this aforementioned consciousness of thirty-two types arises with volitional formations as condition?’ (The answer is:) Because of the absence of result (vipāka) when there is no accumulated kamma. Indeed, these thirty-two types of consciousness are results, and a resultant consciousness does not arise in the absence of accumulated kamma. If it could arise (without kamma), then all results would arise for all beings. But they do not. Therefore, it should be known that ‘this consciousness arises with volitional formations as condition.’

If it is asked, ‘Which consciousness arises from which volitional formation?’ Firstly, from the condition of sense-sphere meritorious volitional formations (kāmāvacara-puññābhisaṅkhāra)³, sixteen consciousnesses arise: the five wholesome resultant consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness; within mind-consciousness, one mind-element (manodhātu, known as receiving consciousness); two mind-consciousness elements (manoviññāṇadhātu, known as investigating consciousness); and eight sense-sphere great resultant consciousnesses (kāmāvacara-mahāvipāka). As the Blessed One taught:

‘Due to the performance and accumulation of sense-sphere wholesome kamma, resultant eye-consciousness arises (1), ...ear-consciousness arises (2), ...nose-consciousness arises (3), ...tongue-consciousness arises (4), [178] ...body-consciousness arises (5), ...resultant mind-element arises (6), ...mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata) arises (7).’

Note:
1- Connect as: ‘Mind-consciousness... is of twenty-two types.’
2- In this sentence, the specific terms are translated into clear and concise Burmese prose rather than the word-for-word Nissaya method for easier understanding; similar passages hereafter will be translated in this same manner.
3- Connect as: ‘Due to the condition... sixteen consciousnesses arise.’
178:
...mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity (a feeling that is neither glad nor sad) arises (8). ...mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta) arises (1, 9). ...mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge arises with prompting (sasaṅkhārika, due to a combination of causes involving inducement) (2, 10). ...mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy and dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta) arises (3, 11). ...mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy and dissociated from knowledge arises with prompting (4, 12). ...mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge arises (5, 13). ...mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge arises with prompting (6, 14). ...mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge arises (7, 15).

Note:
1. By this statement, unprompted (asaṅkhārika) consciousness is shown. The same applies hereafter.
2. By this statement, prompted (sasaṅkhārika) consciousness is shown. The same applies hereafter.

...mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge arises with prompting (8, 16)."

Furthermore, due to the condition of meritorious formations of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-puññābhisaṅkhāra), five fine-material sphere resultant consciousnesses arise. As the Blessed One said:
"Due to the performance and accumulation of that same fine-material sphere wholesome kamma, as a resultant, quite secluded from objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and secluded from subjective sensuality (kilesakāma), one enters and dwells in the first jhāna (1)... the second jhāna (2)... the third jhāna (3)... the fourth jhāna (4)... one enters and dwells in the fifth jhāna (5)."

In this way, due to the condition of meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), twenty-one kinds of consciousness arise.

Furthermore, due to the condition of demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), seven kinds of consciousness arise: the five consciousnesses beginning with eye-consciousness, one mind element, and one mind-consciousness element, which are unwholesome resultants. As the Blessed One said:
"Due to the performance and accumulation of unwholesome kamma, eye-consciousness arises as a resultant (1)... ear- (2)... nose- (3)... tongue- (4)... body-consciousness arises (5)... mind element arises as a resultant (1, 6)... mind-consciousness element arises as a resultant (1, 7)."

Furthermore, due to the condition of imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra), four immaterial sphere resultant consciousnesses arise. As the Blessed One said:
"Due to the performance and accumulation of that same immaterial sphere wholesome kamma, as a resultant, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement... one enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite space (1)... accompanied by the perception of the base of infinite consciousness (2)... accompanied by the perception of the base of nothingness (3)... with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, one enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (4)."

[179] 621. Having understood the consciousness that arises due to the condition of formations in this way, one should now understand the following mode of its occurrence. As for the mode of occurrence: all this (32-fold) consciousness is of two kinds by way of the course of existence (pavatti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
179:
Among them, these 13 kinds of consciousness—the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness (10), the two mind elements, and the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy (1)—arise only during the course of existence in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhava).

Notes:
1. Dhammasaṅgaṇī p. 136, etc.
2. Connect these adjectives with 'to the fourth jhāna'.
3. Dhammasaṅgaṇī p. 117.
4. Pañca (five) + vokāra (constituent/aggregate) = the 26 realms (11 kama realms and 15 rupa realms) having five aggregates are called pañcavokāra-bhava.

The remaining 19 kinds of consciousness arise appropriately in the three realms of existence, both during the course of existence and at rebirth-linking.

How? First, the five kinds of consciousness such as eye-consciousness, which are wholesome resultants, arise for one who has been reborn through either wholesome or unwholesome resultants. When the faculties (indriya) such as the eye have reached maturity in due order, these consciousnesses arise based on the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), etc., taking as their object a desirable (iṭṭha) or neutral-desirable (iṭṭha-majjhatta) object such as a visible form that has come into range. They perform the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. Similarly, the five kinds of consciousness such as eye-consciousness which are unwholesome resultants also arise. The difference is that the objects of those unwholesome resultant consciousnesses are exclusively undesirable (aniṭṭha) or neutral-undesirable (aniṭṭha-majjhatta). This is the only difference. Furthermore, these ten kinds of consciousness have fixed doors, objects, bases, and locations, and they also have fixed functions.

Immediately after the wholesome resultant eye-consciousness, etc., the wholesome resultant mind element (receiving) arises, taking the same object as those eye-consciousnesses, etc., based on the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu), performing the function of receiving (sampaṭicchana). Similarly, the unwholesome resultant mind element arises immediately after the unwholesome resultant consciousnesses. Furthermore, these two mind elements have unfixed doors and objects, but fixed bases, locations, and functions.

Moreover, the rootless mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy arises immediately after the wholesome resultant mind element, taking the same object as that mind element, based on the heart-base, performing the function of investigation (santīraṇa). In the six doors, when there is a strong object, for beings of the sense sphere, it usually occurs at the end of the impulsion (javana) associated with greed, cutting off the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) process, and it occurs once or twice by way of registration (tadārammaṇa) of the object grasped by the impulsion—so it is stated in the Middle Commentary (Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā). However, in the Abhidhamma Commentary, two thought-moments are mentioned for registration. This consciousness receives two names: 'registration' (tadārammaṇa) and 'after-life-continuum' (piṭṭhi-bhavaṅga). It has unfixed doors and objects, a fixed base, and unfixed locations and functions. Thus, these 13 should be understood as occurring only during the course of existence in the five-constituent realm.
180:
This tadārammaṇa (registration) usually occurs at the end of lobha-javana (greed-rooted impulsion); however, it is stated in the Majjhima Commentary that javana occurs once or twice by way of tadārammaṇa regarding an object already taken. In the Abhidhamma Commentary, two moments of consciousness occur in the stage of tadārammaṇa. This consciousness receives two names: tadārammaṇa and piṭṭhibhavaṅga. It has variable doors and objects, a fixed physical base, and variable places and functions. As stated, it should be understood that first, thirteen types of consciousness arise only during the course of existence (pavatti-kāla) in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhūmi).

[180] Among the remaining nineteen (resultant) consciousnesses, there is none that does not occur by way of its appropriate rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). During the course of existence, first, the two rootless mind-consciousness elements (ahetuka-manoviññāṇadhātu)—namely, the wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant (upekkhā-sahagata santīraṇa)—perform the function of investigation (santīraṇa-kicca) immediately after the wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant mind-elements (manodhātu) in the five doors. They perform the function of registration (tadārammaṇa-kicca) in the six doors by the method previously mentioned. When there is no occurrence of cognitive-process consciousness (vīthi-citta) that cuts the life-continuum after the rebirth-linking taken by itself, they perform the function of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-kicca). Finally, they perform the function of death (cuti-kicca). Thus, performing four functions, they arise having a fixed physical base and variable doors, objects, places, and functions.

Note:
It seems to mean that it can also occur at the end of other impulsions such as dosa-javana, moha-javana, kāmāvacara-kusala-javana, and kiriya-javana. However, in the Mūla-ṭīkā, it is explained: "In noting tadārammaṇa by way of javana, since somanassa-tadārammaṇa is mentioned immediately after somanassa-javana, it should be understood as referring only to somanassa-sahagata (lobha-javana). The reason for saying 'usually' is that sometimes ahetuka-tadārammaṇa can occur at the end of tihetuka-javana." For a more extensive explanation, see the Visuddhimagga Mahā-ṭīkā Nissaya, Volume 4, pages 75-76.
1. Connect with: "The rootless mind-consciousness elements... arise while performing four functions."
2. Connect with: "Afterwards... the function of the life-continuum."

The eight sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses with roots (sahetuka-kāmāvacara-vipāka) perform three functions: the function of registration in the six doors by the aforementioned method; the function of the life-continuum when there is no occurrence of cognitive-process consciousness that cuts the life-continuum after the rebirth-linking taken by itself; and finally, the function of death. Thus, performing three functions, they arise having a fixed physical base and variable doors, objects, places, and functions.

The five fine-material sphere resultant consciousnesses (rūpāvacara-vipāka) and the four immaterial sphere resultant consciousnesses (arūpāvacara-vipāka) perform two functions: the function of the life-continuum when there is no occurrence of cognitive-process consciousness that cuts the life-continuum after the rebirth-linking taken by itself; and finally, the function of death. Among those fine-material and immaterial resultants, the fine-material sphere resultant consciousnesses have a fixed physical base and object, but variable places and functions. The immaterial sphere resultant consciousnesses, however, always lack a physical base, have a fixed object, and variable places and functions. Thus, as stated, the thirty-two types of resultant consciousness arise during the course of existence due to the condition of volitional formations (saṅkhāra). In this occurrence, those various volitional formations (such as puññābhisaṅkhāra, etc.) assist those thirty-two resultant consciousnesses by way of kamma-condition (kamma-paccaya) and strong dependence-condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya).

622. Regarding the occurrence at the time of rebirth-linking: The statement "Among the remaining nineteen resultant consciousnesses, there is none that does not occur by way of its appropriate rebirth-linking" is difficult to understand because it is too brief. Therefore, to show the detailed method of that statement, the following questions are raised:

Note:
1. In this context, it directly means: "They arise while performing four functions, having a fixed physical base and variable doors, objects, places, and functions."

"How many rebirth-linkings are there? How many rebirth-linking consciousnesses are there? By which consciousness and in which existence does rebirth-linking occur? What is the object of rebirth-linking?"

(The answer is:) Including the non-percipient (asaññasatta) (material) rebirth-linking, there are twenty rebirth-linkings. The rebirth-linking consciousnesses are the same nineteen types previously mentioned. Among those nineteen, rebirth-linking occurs in the four woeful planes (apāya) by the unwholesome-resultant rootless mind-consciousness element. Rebirth-linking occurs in the human world for those born blind, born deaf, born insane, born mute, or as eunuchs, etc., by the wholesome-resultant (rootless mind-consciousness element). Rebirth-linking occurs for meritorious persons in the six sense-sphere celestial realms and among humans by the eight sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses with roots. Rebirth-linking occurs in the fine-material Brahma world by the five fine-material sphere resultant consciousnesses. Rebirth-linking occurs in the immaterial world by the four immaterial sphere resultant consciousnesses. Furthermore, by whichever consciousness rebirth-linking occurs in whichever realm, that rebirth-linking in that realm is called the rebirth-linking appropriate to that consciousness.
181:
Furthermore, the objects of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) are briefly of three kinds: past, present, and non-describable (navattabba). It should be understood that rebirth-linking in the non-percipient realm (asaññasatta) has no object.

Notes:
1. Just as a person born blind (jaccandha) is called 'blind from the womb' and a person born insane (jāti-ummattaka) is called 'insane from the womb,' here, jāti-badhira is translated as 'deaf from the womb' and jāti-eḷamūga as 'mute from the womb.'
2. Here, the phrase 'and so forth' includes those who are mammana (stammerers/stutterers) and others. (Commentary)

Among those rebirth-linkings, or among those three kinds of objects: The object of Viññāṇañcāyatana rebirth-linking and Nevasaññānāsaññāyatana rebirth-linking is only past. The object of the ten sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) rebirth-linkings is either past or present. The object of the remaining seven rebirth-linkings [1] is only non-describable (navattabba), which cannot be said to be either past or present.

## Explanation of the Arising of Rebirth-linking Consciousness
As stated, rebirth-linking occurring with one of the three objects arises only immediately after the death-consciousness (cuti-citta), which has either a past or a non-describable object. There is no such thing as a death-consciousness with a present object. Therefore, it should be understood how rebirth-linking, having one of the three objects (past, present, or non-describable), occurs by way of happy or unhappy destinations immediately after a death-consciousness that has one of the two objects (past or non-describable).

623. The detailed manner of occurrence is as follows: First, for an individual with evil kamma staying in a happy sense-sphere realm [2], because the Buddha taught: "Those (previously committed) evil kammas appear to that person at the time of death (like shadows of a mountain falling in the evening)," while lying on the deathbed [2], either the evil kamma accumulated or the kamma-sign (kamma-nimitta) [the object perceived when that kamma was performed] appears at the mind-door (mano-dvāra).

Notes:
1. This refers to the five fine-material resultants (rūpa-vipāka), Ākāsānañcāyatana resultant, and Ākiñcaññāyatana resultant.
2. Connect 'for an individual with evil kamma... while lying on the deathbed' with 'appears at the mind-door.' It means it becomes manifest.

Taking that appearing kamma or kamma-sign as its object, immediately after the impulsion-process (javana-vīthi) ending with registration (tadārammaṇa), the death-consciousness arises taking the object of the life-continuum (bhavanga). When that death-consciousness ceases, the rebirth-linking consciousness pertaining to a woeful state arises, being particularly inclined [1] by the power of unabandoned defilements (kilesa), taking as its object [2] that very kamma or kamma-sign that had appeared. This is rebirth-linking with a past object occurring immediately after a death-consciousness with a past object.

For another person, by the power of the aforementioned evil kamma at the time of death, a sign of destiny (gati-nimitta) such as the appearance of flames in hell appears at the mind-door. For that person, or within that person's mental continuum [3], after the life-continuum has arisen and ceased twice, three types of process-consciousnesses arise taking that sign of destiny as the object: one adverting (āvajjana), five near-death impulsions (maraṇāsanna-javana) which are slow in momentum due to the proximity of death [4], and two registrations (tadārammaṇa). Thereafter, one death-consciousness arises taking the object of the life-continuum.

Notes:
1. This is an attribute of the rebirth-linking consciousness; it is a causal attribute (hetumanta-visesana) because it contains a causal meaning. It means the rebirth-linking consciousness arises continuously because it is specially inclined by the power of defilements like ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā) which have not yet been abandoned by the Noble Path.
2. Connect 'taking as its object... the rebirth-linking consciousness arises.'
3. Connect 'for that person, or within that person's mental continuum... three types of process-consciousnesses arise.'
4. Connect this cause only with 'slow in momentum.' Because death is near, the impulsions are not powerful; they have a weak and slow momentum. Therefore, they cannot occur seven times as in normal times, but only five times.

By this point, eleven thought-moments [1] have passed. Then, while that very sign of destiny object still has a remaining lifespan of five thought-moments [2], the rebirth-linking consciousness arises taking that same object. This is rebirth-linking with a present object occurring immediately after a death-consciousness with a past object.

[182] For another person, at the time of death, a disagreeable (aniṭṭha) object, which is the cause for greed and so forth, appears at one of the five doors (such as the eye-door). For that person...
182: 1. The eleven mental moments (cittakkhana) are: bhavanga-calana (vibration of the life-continuum), bhavangupaccheda (arrest of the life-continuum), manodvārāvajjana (mind-door adverting), five moments of maraṇāsanna-javana (near-death impulsion), two moments of tadārammaṇa (registration), and one moment of cuti-citta (death consciousness). These are the eleven moments. 2. If we add the remaining five mental moments to the previous eleven from the past life, there are only sixteen mental moments. Does this not contradict the statement that the lifespan of matter is seventeen mental moments? To this, the commentators (Ṭīkā teachers) say: These sixteen moments are counted from the time the material object becomes distinct. There is approximately one mental moment called atīta-bhavanga (past life-continuum) before it becomes distinct. If that atīta-bhavanga moment is included, it becomes seventeen mental moments; thus, there is no contradiction. 3. This object is the object of the unwholesome resultant (akusala-vipāka) of the new life's rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death consciousness. The object of an unwholesome resultant is only an undesirable object (aniṭṭhārammaṇa). If one dies based on a desirable kamma-sign (iṭṭhārammaṇa kamma-nimitta) near death, would the unwholesome resultant of rebirth-linking, etc., not be taking a desirable object? To address this potential objection, the phrase 'hīnaṃ ārammaṇaṃ' (an inferior object) is used. It means that even if it is naturally a desirable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa), it is called an inferior, undesirable object. Why? Because it is the object of inferior defilements such as lust (rāga) which cause the unwholesome resultant to arise. Note: For example, even if it is noble food, if it is in a dog's mouth, it is merely an inferior and undesirable object. Alternatively, it is called an undesirable object because it is the object of rebirth-linking in the woeful states (apāya). After the cognitive process ending in votthabbana (determining) has occurred in sequence, due to the proximity of death, the javanas have weak momentum; thus, five javanas and two registration moments arise. Following that, one death consciousness arises, taking the object of the life-continuum. By this point, fifteen mental moments have passed: two bhavangas, adverting, seeing (eye-consciousness), receiving, investigating, determining, five javanas, two registrations, and one death consciousness. At that time, while there is still one mental moment of life remaining for that person, the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) arises taking that very same kamma-sign object. This is also a rebirth-linking with a present object immediately following a death consciousness that had a past object. This described process is the manner of the arising of a rebirth-linking in a woeful state (duggati-paṭisandhi) with a past or present object, immediately following a death in a happy state (sugati-cuti) which had a past object. 624. Furthermore, for one situated in a woeful state (duggati) who has accumulated faultless wholesome kamma (anavajja-kamma), that wholesome kamma or its sign (kamma-nimitta) appears at the mind-door in the manner already described. By substituting the dark side (kaṇhapakkha) with the bright side (sukkapakkha), everything should be understood as in the previous method. This is the process of rebirth-linking in a happy state (sugati-paṭisandhi) with an object that is past or present, immediately following death in a woeful state (duggati-cuti) which had a past object. 625. Furthermore, for one situated in a happy state (sugati) who has accumulated faultless wholesome kamma, because of the Buddha's teaching: 'Those [wholesome deeds] hang over [or appear to] him at that time,' while lying on the deathbed, the accumulated wholesome kamma or its sign (kamma-nimitta) appears at the mind-door. This indefinite statement (kamma or kamma-nimitta) should be understood as applying only to those with accumulated sense-sphere wholesome kamma (kāmāvacara-kusala-kamma). For those with accumulated sublime kamma (mahaggata-kamma), only the kamma-sign (kamma-nimitta) appears. Immediately following the javana-vīthi—which may either end in registration (tadārammaṇa) or be a pure javana process without registration—that arises taking that appearing kamma or kamma-sign as its object, the death consciousness arises taking the object of the life-continuum. When that death consciousness ceases, the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) pertaining to a happy state (sugati) arises, inclined by the power of unabandoned defilements, taking that very same kamma or kamma-sign that had appeared as its object. This is a rebirth-linking that has either a past object or an inexpressible object (navattabba, such as a concept/paññatti) immediately following a death consciousness that had a past object. Note: A pure javana process without registration refers to the javana process taking a sublime (mahaggata) kamma-sign as its object; this javana process should be understood as a proximity (upacāra) to the sublime resultant. For another person, at the time of death, by the power of sense-sphere wholesome kamma, a sign of a happy destiny (sugati-nimitta)—such as the red color of a mother's womb in the human world, or the appearance of gardens, celestial mansions, and wish-fulfilling trees in the deva world—appears at the mind-door.
183:
For that person, following the sequence already described regarding the signs of an unhappy destination (duggati-nimitta), the rebirth-consciousness arises immediately after the death-consciousness. This is a rebirth with a present object occurring immediately after a death-consciousness with a past object.

For another person, at the time of death, relatives [Note 2] say, "Dear, this offering to the Buddha is being made for your benefit; gladden your mind." Having spoken thus, they present objects to the five sense-doors: a visual object (rūpārammaṇa) by way of flower garlands, banners, and streamers; an auditory object (saddārammaṇa) by way of listening to the Dhamma or offerings of music; an olfactory object (gandhārammaṇa) by way of incense, perfumes, and scents; a gustatory object (rasārammaṇa) by way of honey, molasses, and such, saying, "Dear, taste this; it is a gift to be given for your benefit"; or a tactile object (phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa) by way of Chinese silk, Somāra cloth, and such, saying, "Dear, touch and feel this; it is a gift to be given for your benefit."

When those objects such as sights come into range [Note 1] for that person, at the end of the determining consciousness (votthappana) that arises in sequence—or, when the determining consciousness has arisen and ceased [Note 3]—because the momentum is weakened by the proximity of death, five impulsion-moments (javana) and two registration-moments (tadārammaṇa) arise. Then, taking the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), one death-consciousness arises. At the end of that death-consciousness, rebirth-consciousness arises with that same object which lasted for a single thought-moment. This too is a rebirth with a present object immediately after a death-consciousness with a past object.

[Note 1: Connect with "comes into range at the time of death."]
[Note 2: Connect with "relatives... having spoken... present at the five doors."]
[Note 3: Here, the first meaning is the translation of the existing text 'uppannavotthabbanāvasāne'. The second meaning is a translation based on the expected reading 'uppanne votthabbanāvasāne'.]

626. Furthermore, for another person who has attained sublime states (mahaggata) through earth-kasina jhāna and so forth, and resides in a happy destination (sugati), at the time of death, one of the following comes into range at the mind-door: a sense-sphere wholesome kamma, a sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta), or a sign of destination (gati-nimitta) [Note 1]; or a kamma-nimitta such as the earth-kasina [Note 2]; or a sublime consciousness of the first or third immaterial sphere [Note 3]. Alternatively, a sublime object that causes the arising of wholesome states comes into range at either the eye-door or the ear-door [Note 3]. For that person, at the end of the determining consciousness that arises in sequence, because the momentum is weakened by the proximity of death, five impulsion-moments (javana) arise. For those in sublime destinations (rūpa and arūpa), there is no registration (tadārammaṇa); therefore, immediately after the impulsion, one death-consciousness arises taking the object of the life-continuum. At the end of that death-consciousness, a rebirth-consciousness arises, pertaining to [Note 4] either a sense-sphere happy destination or a sublime happy destination, taking one of the objects as they appeared. This is a rebirth taking one of the past, present, or "not-to-be-described" (navattabba) objects, immediately after a happy-destination death-consciousness with a "not-to-be-described" object.

[Note 1: This object appears to one who will be reborn in a sense-sphere happy destination.]
[Note 2: This object appears to one who will be reborn in the fine-material sphere or the first or third immaterial spheres.]
[Note 3: This object appears to one who will be reborn in the second or fourth immaterial spheres.]
[Note 4: Connect with "the rebirth-consciousness... pertaining to... arises."]

Following this same method, rebirth immediately after an immaterial-sphere (arūpa) death should also be understood [Note 1]. This mode of occurrence is a happy-destination rebirth with a past, "not-to-be-described," or present object, immediately after a happy-destination death-consciousness with a past or "not-to-be-described" object.

[Note 1: The reason for specifically explaining the rebirth after immaterial-sphere death (arūpa-cuti) is that there is no fine-material-sphere rebirth (rūpāvacara-paṭisandhi) immediately after an immaterial-sphere death. Furthermore, there is no lower immaterial-sphere rebirth immediately after a higher immaterial-sphere death. Therefore, after the death-consciousness of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññā-cuti), there is no rebirth taking a "not-to-be-described" (navattabba) object. If rebirth occurs in that same plane, it takes a past object; if in the sense-sphere, it takes either a past or present object. For the three lower immaterial-sphere deaths, one should appropriately associate them with immaterial rebirth taking either a past or "not-to-be-described" object, or sense-sphere rebirth taking either a past or present object. This is specifically stated to clarify these distinctions. (Summary of the Ṭīkā).]
184:
