Among the death-consciousness (cuti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) shown from paragraph 625 onwards, the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) that takes a past object consists of these 11: the 9 fortunate sense-sphere death-consciousnesses (kāmasugati-cuti) and the 2 death-consciousnesses of the second and fourth immaterial (arūpa) realms. The death-consciousness that takes an 'indescribable' (navattabba) object consists of these 7: the 5 fine-material death-consciousnesses (rūpa-cuti) and the 2 death-consciousnesses of the first and third immaterial realms. Therefore, it is stated in the Mūlaṭīkā: 'There are eleven kinds with past objects and seven kinds with indescribable objects' (atītārammaṇā ekādasavidhā navattabbārammaṇā sattavidhā). The second and fourth immaterial rebirth-linkings (arūpa-paṭisandhi) take only the past object of the first and third immaterial wholesome consciousness. The remaining sublime rebirth-linkings (mahaggata-paṭisandhi) take the 'indescribable' object of concepts (paññatti) such as kasiṇa. Sense-sphere rebirth-linkings (kāma-paṭisandhi) take past objects; when they obtain a sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta) or a sign of destiny (gati-nimitta) that has not yet ceased, they also take present objects.

Either the sign of kamma or the sign of destiny appears at the mind-door, or an object that is the cause for the arising of unwholesome states (the five sense objects) appears at the five doors. When such an object appears, at the end of the sequence of death-consciousness (cuti) for that person, a rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) arises, taking one of those appearing objects that are included in the woeful states (duggati). This is the manner of occurrence of a (duggati) rebirth-linking with past or present objects immediately following a woeful death-consciousness (duggati-cuti) with a past object. By this sequence of words, the occurrence of the nineteen-fold consciousness by way of rebirth-linking has been explained.

628. All this resultant consciousness (vipāka-viññāṇa), in the manner described:

'When occurring at rebirth-linking, it proceeds in two ways through kamma;
And by divisions such as mixed, etc., its division is two-fold, etc.'

The elaboration of this summary verse is: This nineteen-fold resultant consciousness, when occurring at the moment of rebirth-linking, proceeds in two ways through kamma. Indeed, one's own productive kamma (janaka-kamma) serves as a condition for this resultant consciousness by way of asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) and natural strong dependence condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya). To provide the evidence:

Notes:
1. Connect 'At the end of the death-consciousness... the rebirth-linking consciousness arises.'
2. Connect 'The rebirth-linking consciousness... included in the woeful states.'
3. Sandhimhi: This is the meaning translated in accordance with the text paṭisandhimhi. In the Pyay version of the nissaya, it is translated as 'by way of rebirth-linking,' stating that the locative case (sattamī) is used in the sense of the instrumental case (tatiyā).
4. Since the evidence for asynchronous kamma condition was already shown in the description of resultant consciousness starting with 'due to the performance of wholesome kamma,' etc., only the evidence for natural strong dependence condition, which has not been shown, is cited here. (Ṭīkā)

'Wholesome and unwholesome kamma is a condition for the resultant by way of strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya)'—this was taught by the Blessed One. Furthermore, the divisions of this consciousness occurring (through kamma) in this way, such as mixed (rebirth-linking mixed with matter), etc., should be understood as two-fold, etc.

What are those divisions? Although this resultant consciousness is single by way of rebirth-linking, it is two-fold by way of being mixed or unmixed with matter (missa-amissa). It is three-fold by way of the planes of existence: sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava), fine-material existence (rūpa-bhava), and immaterial existence (arūpa-bhava). It is four-fold by way of the modes of birth (yoni): egg-born (aṇḍaja), womb-born (jalābuja), moisture-born (saṃsedaja), and spontaneous birth (opapātika). It is five-fold by way of the destinies (gati): (hell, hungry ghost, animal, deva, human). It is seven-fold by way of the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). It is eight-fold by way of the abodes of beings (sattāvāsa).

629. Among those two, the mixed and unmixed rebirth-linking consciousness:

'The mixed is two-fold by the division of sex;
And the one with sex is there two-fold;
Two or three decads,
At the minimum, together with the first.'

To explain: 'The mixed is two-fold by the division of sex' means that among the mixed (with matter) and unmixed (without matter) rebirth-linking consciousness mentioned, the mixed rebirth-linking consciousness occurs in planes other than the immaterial plane (arūpa-bhava).

Note:
1. The immaterial plane is the place of occurrence for unmixed rebirth-linking, which has no further divisions.

That mixed rebirth-linking consciousness is two-fold: with sex (sa-bhāva) and without sex (a-bhāva). This is because in the fine-material plane (rūpa-bhava), it arises without the sex-materiality (bhāva-rūpa) known as the femininity faculty (itthindriya) and masculinity faculty (purisindriya); whereas in the sense plane (kāma-bhava), except for the rebirth-linking of a congenital eunuch (jāti-paṇḍaka), it arises only with sex-materiality.
185:
[185] Among those two, the statement 'the sabhāva consciousness also has two divisions' means: among those two, the sabhāva rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhivijñāṇa) is indeed of two kinds because it arises together with either the female sex-materiality (itthibhāva-rūpa) or the male sex-materiality (pumbhāva-rūpa).

Regarding the phrase 'at the minimum, two or three decads (dasaka-kalāpas) together with the beginning': in the dyad of 'mixed' and 'unmixed', there is the initial rūpamissa rebirth-linking consciousness (mixed with materiality). Together with that rebirth-linking consciousness, at the minimum, either two decads arise by way of the base-decad (vatthu-dasaka) and body-decad (kāya-dasaka), or three decads arise by way of the base-decad, body-decad, and sex-decad (bhāva-dasaka). There is no reduction of materiality below these two or three decads. Furthermore, when this minimum quantity of material groups arises in the two modes of birth called egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja), it arises with the name 'kalala' (embryonic drop), having the size of a drop of clarified butter picked up by a single fiber of wool (jāti-uṇṇā). In that preceding statement, the distinction of possibility and impossibility according to the destinations (gati) of the modes of birth should be understood.

Notes:
1. One who lacks sex-materiality from the time of rebirth-linking is called a jāti-paṇḍaka. One who lacks sex-materiality after birth or after the sex-materiality has formed, due to castration etc., is called an opakkami-paṇḍaka. This is said to clarify the status of the opakkami-paṇḍaka.
2. For those lacking sex-materiality, two decads arise; for those not lacking it, three arise. This refers to womb-born beings (gabbhaseyyaka). In other types of rebirth, many kalāpas arise simultaneously. In the body of a Brahma, which is many gāvutas in size, many kalāpas arise simultaneously.
3. Regarding the size of the kalala-drop: some say jāti-uṇṇā is the hair of a newborn lamb; others say it is the hair of a pure-bred lamb from the Himālayas; others say it is the hair of a lamb extracted by cutting the mother's womb (Visuddhimagga-ṭīkā). Among these three views, the second is found in Mūla-ṭīkā II, 17.
4. To state this sentence directly: 'This collection of 2 or 3 material decads arises in egg-born and womb-born modes of birth; it has the size of a drop of clarified butter picked up by a fiber of wool, and is called kalala.' This size is also shown in Sammohavinodanī, p. 20. Western doctors say rebirth occurs from the union of the mother's ovum and the father's sperm, and this combined substance is too small to be seen with the naked eye. If one wishes to reconcile this with their view, one should consider that the 2 or 3 decads arise due to kamma within that union of ovum and sperm. This would be consistent with the Sīlakkhandha Pali (72) which states, 'This material body of mine is composed of the four great elements and is born from mother and father,' and it is also suitable when considering the resemblance to the parents' appearance and complexion.

630. In hell (niraya-gati) and among the devas, excluding the earth-dwelling ones (bhamma), the first three modes of birth do not exist. In the [other] three destinations, all four modes of birth exist.

In that summary verse, by the word 'and' in 'and among the devas,' it should be understood that just as in hell and among devas (excluding earth-dwelling ones), the first three modes of birth do not exist in the nijjhāmatanhika hungry ghosts (petas) as well. Indeed, they are only of spontaneous birth (opapātika). But in the remaining three destinations—namely animals, hungry ghosts, and humans—and among the previously excluded earth-dwelling devas, all four modes of birth exist. Among those modes of birth:

Thirty and nine [materialities arise] in the fine-material beings; seventy at the maximum; or otherwise, thirty at the minimum in the moisture-born and spontaneously born.

First, among the fine-material Brahmas who are of spontaneous birth, thirty-nine materialities arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness by way of four groups: the eye-decad, ear-decad, base-decad, and the life-nonad (jīvita-navaka). Excluding the fine-material Brahmas, among other beings of moisture-born and spontaneous birth, at the maximum, seventy materialities arise by way of the eye-decad, ear-decad, nose-decad, tongue-decad, body-decad, base-decad, and sex-decad. These seventy materialities are constant among the [sense-sphere] devas.
186:
In the preceding passage (starting with the eye-decad), this group of materiality consisting of ten types—namely, color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, the four great elements, eye-sensitivity, and life-faculty—is called the eye-decad (cakkhu-dasaka). The remaining decads (dasaka) and nonads (navaka) should be understood in the same way. [186] At the minimum, for a neuter person who is born blind, born deaf, and lacks the nose-sensitivity at rebirth, thirty types of materiality arise by way of the tongue-decad (jivhā-dasaka), body-decad (kāya-dasaka), and heart-base-decad (vatthu-dasaka). Furthermore, the appropriate variations between the maximum and minimum should also be understood.

631. Having understood this, again:

The distinction of similarity and difference between death-consciousness (cuti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) should be understood by way of aggregates (khandha), objects (ārammaṇa), destinations (gati), roots (hetu), feelings (vedanā), zest (pīti), initial application (vitakka), and sustained application (vicāra).

To elaborate: The distinction of similarity and difference by way of these aggregates, etc., should be known between the two types of rebirth-linking—mixed and unmixed—and the death-consciousness that immediately preceded it in the past. This is the meaning of that verse.

How is it to be understood? Sometimes, immediately after a formless-sphere death-consciousness (arūpa-cuti) consisting of four aggregates, there occurs a rebirth-linking that is also of four aggregates and is not different even in terms of its object. Sometimes, after a death-consciousness with a non-sublime external object, there occurs a rebirth-linking with a sublime internal object. This is the method regarding the formless spheres alone.

Furthermore, sometimes, immediately after a formless-sphere death-consciousness of four aggregates, there is a sense-sphere rebirth-linking (kāmāvacara-paṭisandhi) of five aggregates. Sometimes, immediately after a sense-sphere death-consciousness or a fine-material-sphere death-consciousness of five aggregates, there is a formless-sphere rebirth-linking of four aggregates. Similarly, after a death-consciousness with a past object, there is a rebirth-linking with a present object. After some happy-destination (sugati) death-consciousness, there is an unhappy-destination (duggati) rebirth-linking. After a rootless (ahetuka) death-consciousness, there is a rooted (sahetuka) rebirth-linking. After a double-rooted (duhetuka) death-consciousness, there is a triple-rooted (tihetuka) rebirth-linking. After a death-consciousness accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā), there is a rebirth-linking accompanied by joy (somanassa). After a death-consciousness without zest (pīti), there is a rebirth-linking with zest. After a death-consciousness without initial application (vitakka), there is a rebirth-linking with initial application. After a death-consciousness without sustained application (vicāra), there is a rebirth-linking with sustained application. After a death-consciousness without both initial and sustained application, there is a rebirth-linking with both initial and sustained application.

In this manner, and by the reversal of each of the aforementioned distinctions, the application should be made as appropriate.

## No Transmigration from a Past Life

632. As stated: Having obtained its conditions (such as ignorance, etc.), this consciousness, being a mere phenomenon (dhamma-matta), is said to reach another existence (bhavantara). There is no transmigration (saṅkanti) of it from that past life, nor does it occur without a cause from that past life.

To elaborate: As stated, when this consciousness, having obtained its conditions (namely, volitional formations together with ignorance, etc.), arises as a mere phenomenon of materiality and mentality (rūpārūpa-dhamma-matta), it is said to reach another existence. No 'being' (satta) is produced; no 'soul' (jīva) is produced. Moreover, there is no transmigration of that consciousness from the past life to this present life.
187:
There is no manifestation in this present life that is independent of the causes from that past life, or rather, in that past life. I shall explain the [arising of] that consciousness through the evident sequence of the falling away (cuti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) of a human being.

[187] In the past life, whether by one's own nature, or by the effort of oneself or another to cause death,

Note: This is a translation centered on consciousness (viññāṇa), in accordance with the Pyay edition Nissaya, which explains it as 'due to the absence—merely the phenomena of mind and matter (rūpārūpa-dhamma-mattaṃ)'. This translation is appropriate as this section explains rebirth-linking consciousness. However, since 'etaṃ viññāṇaṃ' and 'dhamma-mattaṃ' should refer to the same thing, yet are explained as 'rūpārūpa-dhamma-mattaṃ', it is difficult to say they are identical or different. Here, it could be said that the commentator refers to all mind and matter of rebirth-linking. Therefore, it is more suitable to translate 'etaṃ' and 'dhamma-mattaṃ' together as follows:

'Having obtained the causes as stated, this mere phenomenon (which has newly arisen) is said to have "arrived in another existence".'

1. In this sentence also, it is more suitable to translate as follows: To explain further, having obtained the causes (such as formations along with ignorance, etc.) as stated, this mere phenomenon of mind and matter which has newly arisen is said to have 'arrived in another existence'.

In this context, the explanation 'uppajjamānaṃ' (arising) is intended to make it clear that it is not an old thing moving from a previous life, but something new; therefore, the word 'newly' is included in the translation to convey that meaning.

When death is imminent, or for one who is near death,1 being unable to endure the onset of the 'swords' of death-proximate feelings which are so intense2 that they cut the bonds of all limbs and joints—while the body is gradually drying up like a green or moist palm leaf cast in the sun, and the faculties such as the eye-faculty are ceasing, or as if they are ceasing,4 and while the body-faculty, mind-faculty, and life-faculty remain only in the location of the heart-base, the consciousness5 depending on the heart-base remaining at that moment, occurs by taking as its object either the kamma—described as formations which have obtained the remaining causes such as ignorance—which is one of the following: weighty kamma (garuka), habitual kamma (āciṇṇaka), death-proximate kamma (āsanna), or kamma-performed-in-the-past (kaṭattā); or the sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta) or sign of destiny (gati-nimitta) manifested by that kamma. In this manner,

Note:
1. Connect 'for one who is near death' with 'unable to endure'.
2. Connect 'intense' with 'swords of feelings'.
3. Since the preceding sentence mentioned 'death and rebirth-linking of a human being', 'asahantassa' is translated here as 'of a human being who is unable to endure'. Connect 'of a human being' with 'in the body'.
4. Here, the first meaning is a literal translation according to the text 'niruddhesu'. In the human world, at the time of death, the eye and so on usually cease first; if taken as describing this general cessation, the literal translation is suitable. However, to avoid contradiction with statements showing cuti occurring after the five-door process, the sub-commentaries (Ṭīkā) explain it as 'referring to reaching a state of extreme weakness'. To align with this, the second meaning 'as if they are ceasing' is added.
5. Connect 'consciousness' with 'occurs by taking as its object'.
6. Connect 'one of the' with 'kamma'.

Because ignorance and craving have not yet been abandoned in that consciousness which is thus occurring,1 craving inclines [the mind] toward that object (the kamma, kamma-nimitta, or gati-nimitta) whose faults are concealed by ignorance, and the formations3 occurring together with the death-proximate impulsion (javana) consciousness push [that consciousness toward that object]. Being inclined by craving and pushed by formations through the power of the mental continuity4 (consisting of death-proximate impulsion, falling away, and rebirth-linking), that consciousness abandons its former support in the previous life and, like a man jumping across a ditch by clinging to a rope tied to a tree on the near bank, it proceeds solely by means of conditions such as the object and so on, whether it reaches5 or does not reach6 another support (in the next life) produced by kamma.

Note:
1. Connect 'consciousness' with 'inclines' and 'push'.
2. Connect this reason with 'concealed by ignorance' and 'inclined by craving'.
3. 'Co-nascent formations' (sahajāta-saṅkhāra) refer to the volitions (cetanā) occurring with the death-proximate impulsion consciousness; alternatively, they refer to all mental factors such as contact (phassa) and so on (Ṭīkā). According to this Ṭīkā, the volitions or mental factors like contact occurring with the death-proximate impulsion are called formations. It should be understood that these formations push the consciousness into the object such as kamma, which is the basis for rebirth-linking.
4. 'Inclined by craving, pushed by formations' does not refer to a single moment of mind, but to this mental continuity of death-proximate impulsion, falling away, and rebirth-linking.
5-6. Whether it reaches or obtains the support called the heart-base in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), or does not reach or obtain it in the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava), it proceeds continuously only due to the conditions of the object, associated states, and kamma. In this context, 'assādayamānaṃ' means 'pāpuṇantaṃ' (reaching) or 'paṭilabhamānaṃ' (obtaining) (Ṭīkā).

To clarify further, among these two—the falling away (cuti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) consciousness—the former is called the 'falling away' (cuti) mind because it shifts or passes away from the manifest existence. The latter is called the 'rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhi) mind because it is the very first connection to another existence, or because it links another existence, another womb, another destiny, and so on. It should be understood that this consciousness in the new existence neither comes from the previous life to this present life, nor does it manifest without causes such as kamma, formations, the inclination [by craving], and objects like kamma from that previous life.

## Analogies of the Echo, etc.

633. In this matter (of the rebirth-linking consciousness not coming from the previous life, yet not being without causes from the previous life), the echo and so on are the analogies. Furthermore, because of the continuity of the series, there is neither identity (being the same person) nor absolute difference.

To explain further: In this matter of the rebirth-linking consciousness not coming from the previous life to this life, and its arising due to causes included in the past life, phenomena such as an echo, a lamp flame, a seal impression, and a reflection are the analogies. To clarify, the echo, lamp flame, seal impression, and reflection arise having the original sound and so on as their cause.1 They arise without moving to another location where the cause is, or without moving from the location of the cause to another location, and this rebirth-linking consciousness is just the same.

Note:
1. By this analogy, it is made known by comparison that the rebirth-linking mind arises not without causes from the previous life.

Furthermore, in this process, because of the continuity of the series, there is neither identity nor difference. If there were absolute identity when there is continuity of the series, curd would not be produced from milk. If there were absolute difference, the curd would not be dependent on the milk. This is the method in all things that are causes and things produced from causes.

Note:
1. By this analogy, it is made known by comparison that phenomena do not move from the previous life. However, this is difficult to understand. Therefore, the explanation from the sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) will be shown. 'Honti aññatra agantvā' means they have the sound and so on as their cause without going to or reaching the location of the cause such as the original sound, because they did not exist prior to their arising. Similarly, this rebirth-linking consciousness arises due to causes such as ignorance without going to or reaching the location of the cause, because it did not exist prior to its arising. Therefore, this rebirth-linking consciousness does not come to this life from the previous life, which is the location of the cause; just as an echo and so on do not come from the location of the original sound. Nor does it arise without the causes from that previous life; just as an echo and so on do not occur without the original sound. This is the meaning. Alternatively, 'honti aññatra agantvā' means they do not exist in the location of the cause prior to arising and then move to another location to arise from that cause, because they did not exist prior to arising. Nor is it that they do not arise because of the original sound and so on; this rebirth-linking consciousness is just the same. It should be applied in the manner stated (Ṭīkā).
188:
Furthermore, I shall point out the fault: if both extremes were to be fallen into as mentioned, there would be the destruction of all worldly conventions (such as "the seed of red rice, the fruit of red rice", etc.). Such destruction of worldly conventions is not desired. Therefore, regarding these consciousnesses (which are cause and effect connected by a continuity), one should not assume absolute identity nor absolute difference.

## Important Objection and Clarification

634. Here, an objector raises an objection: "If there is the manifestation of a new consciousness in a new life without any transmigration from the old life, then, because the old aggregates (khandhas) in this human existence have ceased, and because the kamma which is the cause of the result (consciousness) does not go or reach there (the new life where the result arises), that result would belong to another (person other than the one who performed the kamma), and it would arise from another cause (other than the kamma performed). Furthermore, if there is no enjoyer (of the result), since it has been stated that only phenomena reach another life, to whom would that result belong? Therefore, this arrangement—this statement (that only phenomena arise without transmigration of a being or soul)—is not good." To this objection, the following answer is given:

The result that arises in a single continuity
Is not of another, nor from another;
The cultivation of seeds
Is the proof of this matter.

Note 1: Stated in paragraph 632.

To explain further: when a result arises in a single continuity, since absolute identity and absolute difference are excluded in that (continuity of phenomena where kamma occurred), it is not said to belong to another continuity or another person, nor to arise from another cause. The logical reason is that the cultivation of seeds proves this point. To elaborate: when the cultivation of mango seeds and the like is performed, if the necessary conditions are obtained in the continuity of that seed, a specific fruit arises at a later time. That specific fruit does not belong to other seeds, nor does it arise due to the cultivation of other seeds. However, those seeds and that cultivation do not reach the place where the fruit stands. In the same way, the accomplishment of this meaning should be understood. Furthermore, this meaning should be understood through the examples of learning, arts, and medicine, which are applied to a child's body and yield results in the adult's body at a later time.

Note 2: The special cultivation of seeds such as mango and citron (mātuluṅga) involves treating them with the four sweets (catumadhura) and lac-dye. In this analogy, the being who possesses kamma is like the specially cultivated seed; kamma is like the special cultivation; the continuity of the being's rebirth-consciousness and so on is like the continuity of the seed's sprout and so on. The arising of a sweet mango or a citron with red pulp in that continuity of the sprout is just like the arising from that specific mango or citron seed and from that special cultivation. Similarly, the arising of the result such as consciousness should be understood as belonging only to the being who performed the kamma and as arising only because of that kamma. (Sub-commentary)

Note 1: The learning of knowledge (vijjā), the study of arts (sippa), and the application of medicine performed on a child's body do not reach the adult's body. Nevertheless, due to those causes—learning, studying, and application—the sharpness of wisdom, the mastery of arts, and the freedom from disease occur and are accomplished in the adult's body. Those qualities like sharpness of wisdom do not belong to another. Why? Because they arise in the adult's body which is part of the same continuity of mind and matter (nāma-rūpa) as that child.

Regarding the statement, "If there is no enjoyer, to whom would that result belong?":

By the very arising of the result,
The convention of "enjoyer" is established;
Just as by the production of fruit,
The convention "the tree bears fruit" is established.

To explain further: just as by the arising of a fruit, which is a part of the physical phenomena called a "tree", it is said that "the tree bears fruit" or "it is fruiting", so too, by the production of the result of pleasure and pain, which is called "enjoyment" and is a part of the aggregates called "deva" or "human", it is said that "the deva or human enjoys" or "is happy" or "is suffering". Therefore, there is no need for any other "enjoyer" here.
189:
The sharpness of that wisdom and so forth do not arise from another cause, independent of the training in wisdom and so forth undertaken in youth. Why? Because if there were no training in wisdom in youth, there would be no result such as sharpness of wisdom in adulthood. Similarly, in this context, the result such as rebirth-linking consciousness arising in the mental continuum (at the moment of the near-death javana, death, and rebirth-linking) is not the result of another person (other than the doer of kamma), nor does it arise from another cause. To further clarify the point of objection: by this illustration, it only shows that without formations, there is no result; it does not show the rejection of other causes. (Ṭīkā)

Through the very arising of the result called pleasure and pain—which is termed 'enjoyment' [Note 1] and is a part of the five or four aggregates—a person or a deva is said to 'enjoy' or is called 'happy' or 'suffering'. Therefore, in this matter, it is said that there is no purpose for a 'doer' (atta-kattā) called an 'enjoyer' who is distinct from the aggregates.

[189] 635. Although the manifestation in a new existence without shifting from the old existence, and the resolution of the objection therein, are appropriate and complete, [one might ask]: Do these formations (saṅkhāras) serve as conditions for the result while they are present, or while they are not present? If they serve as conditions while present, their resultant effect (vipāka) should arise at the very moment of their occurrence. If they serve as conditions while not present, they would always be bringing about or producing results both before and after they have occurred. To such a person, this should be said:

Because of having been performed, these are conditions,
Yet they do not always bring forth results;
In this matter, a guarantee and such
Should be understood as the illustration.

To explain: Formations serve as conditions for their own results only because they have been performed (katattā), not because they are present or because they are not present. As it was said: "Because of having performed and accumulated wholesome kamma of the sense sphere, the resultant eye-consciousness arises," and so forth (Dhs. 431). However, having served as conditions for their appropriate results, they do not bring forth results again, because the resultant effect has already been matured and produced. To clarify this meaning, the following illustration of a guarantee and so forth should be understood: In the world, when a person stands as a guarantor for the delivery of some property, or buys goods [Note 2], or takes a loan [Note 3], the mere performance of that act of guaranteeing, buying, or borrowing serves as the condition for the delivery of that property and so forth. It is not the presence or absence of the act [at the time of delivery] that is the condition. Furthermore, after the delivery of that property and so forth, he no longer carries the responsibility or remains liable. Why? Because the delivery and so forth have already been performed. In the same way, formations serve as conditions for their own results only because they have been performed; they do not continue to bring forth or produce results after they have given the appropriate result. By this sequence of words, the occurrence of rebirth-linking consciousness, which exists in two ways—as mixed and unmixed—by way of the condition of formations, has been shown.

## Summary of the Arising of All 32 Types of Resultant Consciousness

636. Now, for the purpose of dispelling confusion that may arise regarding all those thirty-two resultant consciousnesses:

By way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence,
In the realms and so forth, these formations
Should be understood as to which [resultants]
And in what manner they are conditions.

In that verse, 'realms and so forth' refers to the three realms of existence (bhava), the four modes of birth (yoni), the five destinations (gati), the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). In these realms and so forth, at the time of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence, these aforementioned formations serve as conditions for certain resultant consciousnesses. (Those resultant consciousnesses should be understood); and the manner in which they serve as conditions, such as through kamma-condition and so forth, (in that manner also, those formations should be understood).

Notes:
1. Connect these adjectives with the substantive 'result'.
2-3. By these two phrases, the meaning of 'and so forth' in the expression 'guarantee and so forth' is shown.
190: They also perform service by way of the kamma condition and so on; in that manner, they (those formations) should be known. This is the meaning of the verse. ## [190] Among those formations and consciousnesses to be known, first, regarding meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra): the meritorious formation consisting of the eight types of sense-sphere wholesome volitions (kāmāvacara-kusala-cetanā) conditions nine types of resultant consciousnesses [1] in the happy course of the sense-sphere (kāmabhava sugati) at the time of rebirth (paṭisandhi) in two ways: by way of asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) and by way of natural decisive support condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya). The meritorious formation consisting of the five types of fine-material sphere wholesome volitions (rūpāvacara-kusala-cetanā) conditions five types of resultant consciousnesses in the fine-material sphere (rūpabhava) only at the time of rebirth [2]. (Note 1: The 9 resultant consciousnesses are the eight great resultants and the wholesome resultant equanimity-accompanied investigating consciousness. Note 2: According to the text 'paṭisandhiyaṃ eva,' this is a literal translation; since conditioning rebirth also implies conditioning the life-continuum and death, it is appropriate to include them under rebirth here. However, in the case of formless wholesome states mentioned later, life-continuum and death are specifically mentioned as the course of life.) Furthermore, the aforementioned sense-sphere meritorious formation conditions seven types of sense-sphere (rootless wholesome) resultant consciousnesses—excluding the equanimity-accompanied rootless functional mind-consciousness element (or rather, excluding the equanimity-accompanied investigating consciousness)—in the happy course of the sense-sphere during the course of life (pavatti) in the two ways mentioned, but not at the time of rebirth. That same sense-sphere meritorious formation conditions five types of resultant consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, receiving, and two types of investigating consciousness) in the fine-material sphere in the same way during the course of life, but not at rebirth. Moreover, in the woeful course of the sense-sphere, it conditions eight types of sense-sphere (rootless wholesome) resultant consciousnesses in the same way during the course of life, but not at rebirth. Among those woeful courses, in hell, this meritorious formation conditions the experience of pleasant objects during events such as the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’s visits to hell; furthermore, pleasant objects are indeed obtainable among animals and powerful ghosts (peta). That same sense-sphere meritorious formation conditions all sixteen types of wholesome resultant consciousnesses in the happy course of the sense-sphere in the same way, both during the course of life and at rebirth. Generally, however, meritorious formations (both sense-sphere and fine-material) condition ten types of resultant consciousnesses [1] in the fine-material sphere in the same way, both during the course of life and at rebirth. (Note 1: This refers to the five rootless wholesome resultants and five fine-material resultants obtainable in the fine-material realm.) Demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), consisting of the twelve types of unwholesome volitions, condition one type of consciousness (equanimity-accompanied investigating) in the woeful course of the sense-sphere in the same way at the time of rebirth, but not during the course of life. It conditions six types of unwholesome resultant consciousnesses (excluding equanimity-accompanied investigating) during the course of life, but not at rebirth. It conditions all seven types of unwholesome resultant consciousnesses both during the course of life and at rebirth. Furthermore, in the happy course of the sense-sphere, it conditions those same seven consciousnesses in the same way during the course of life, but not at rebirth. In the fine-material sphere, it conditions four types of resultant consciousnesses (unwholesome resultant eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, receiving, and investigating) in the same way during the course of life, but not at rebirth. Such conditioning occurs through the seeing of undesirable sights and hearing of undesirable sounds in the sense-sphere; however, in the Brahma world, there are no such things as undesirable sights and so on. Likewise, in the sense-sphere celestial realms (the higher heavens), [undesirable sights and so on do not exist] [1]. (Note 1: This statement is made according to the majority; indeed, for those sense-sphere deities, pleasant sights and so on appear frequently, and undesirable objects appear only occasionally. The occasional appearance occurs for some deities at times such as when the 'prior signs' appear before death, involving undesirable objects like the withering of worn flowers. (Ṭīkā)) Imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) condition four types of resultant consciousnesses in the formless sphere (arūpabhava) in the same way, both during the course of life and at rebirth [2]. (Note 2: Here, life-continuum and death are specifically mentioned as being conditioned during the course of life.)
191: [191] As stated, first of all, it should be understood how these formations are conditions for which resultant consciousnesses by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and the course of existence (pavatti) in the various states of existence, and in what manner they are conditions, such as by way of kamma-condition and so on. In this same way, they should be understood in the modes of birth (yoni) and so on. 637. Herein, this is a brief indication starting from the beginning—among these formations, first, meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra), having given rebirth-linking in the two states of existence (sense-sphere and fine-material), produce all their own results. Likewise, they produce all their own results after giving rebirth-linking in the four modes of birth such as the egg-born and so on; in the two destinations (gati) known as devas and humans (Note 1: This is said by way of the majority. Indeed, for those sense-sphere devas, pleasant objects such as visible forms are mostly manifest; only occasionally do unpleasant objects appear. The occasion of appearing is only for some devas at times such as when the prior signs (pubbanimitta) appear before death, encountering unpleasant objects like the wilting of worn flowers. (Ṭīkā)); and in the four stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) known as: (1) those with different bodies and different perceptions (nānattakāya-nānattasaññī) (Note 1: Sense-sphere devas, humans, and vinipātika-asuras are called different bodies, different perceptions), (2) those with different bodies and the same perception (nānattakāya-ekattasaññī) (Note 2: Brahmas in the three planes of the first jhāna and beings in the four woeful states are called different bodies, same perception. Among them, the bodies of Brahmapurohita are larger than those of Brahmapārisajja, and the bodies of Mahābrahma are larger than those of Brahmapurohita), (3) those with the same body and different perceptions (ekattakāya-nānattasaññī) (Note 3: Brahmas of the second jhāna are called same body, different perceptions. Among them, they have one of the two rebirth-linking perceptions: the jhāna-perception of vitakka-less jhāna or the jhāna-perception of vitakka-and-vicāra-less jhāna), and (4) those with the same body and the same perception (ekattakāya-ekattasaññī) (Note 4: Brahmas in the third jhāna plane and the fourth jhāna plane, other than non-percipient beings, are called same body, same perception). In the abode of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), since this meritorious formation conditions only materiality, it gives rebirth-linking and produces its results accordingly in the four abodes of beings (sattāvāsa) (which are equivalent to the four stations of consciousness). Therefore, this meritorious formation is a condition, as appropriate, for the twenty-one resultant consciousnesses (Note 5: Refers to the 16 sense-sphere resultants and 5 fine-material resultants) in the rebirth-linking and the course of existence (Note 2: In this context, it specifically refers to the conditioning during the course of existence with respect to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and death (cuti)) in these two states of existence, four modes of birth, two destinations, four stations of consciousness, and four abodes of beings, in the manner already described. Demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra), however, ripen and give results by way of rebirth-linking only in the single sense-sphere existence, in the four modes of birth, in the three remaining destinations (other than devas and humans), in the single station of consciousness known as those with different bodies and the same perception, and in the single abode of beings of that same nature. Therefore, these demeritorious formations are conditions for the seven resultant consciousnesses in the rebirth-linking and the course of existence in that one state of existence, four modes of birth, three destinations, one station of consciousness, and one abode of beings, in the manner already described. Imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra), however, ripen and give results by way of rebirth-linking only in the single immaterial existence, in the single opapātika (spontaneously born) mode of birth, in the single deva destination, in the three stations of consciousness starting with the base of infinite space, and in the four abodes of beings starting with the base of infinite space. Therefore, these imperturbable formations are conditions for the four immaterial resultant consciousnesses in the rebirth-linking and the course of existence in that one state of existence, one mode of birth, one destination, three stations of consciousness, and four abodes of beings, in the manner already described. Thus, [192] As stated, these formations are conditions for which resultant consciousnesses by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence in the states of existence and so on.

## Detailed Explanation of the Phrase "With Consciousness as Condition, Mentality-Materiality"

638. In the phrase "With consciousness as condition, mentality-materiality"...

The decision should be known by way of the classification of mentality and materiality, by way of their occurrence in existence and so forth, by way of inclusion, and by way of the method of condition.

To explain in detail: In the phrase "by way of the classification of mentality and materiality"—mentality (nāma) refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling (vedanā), because they bend (namana) towards the object. Materiality (rūpa) refers to the four great elements (mahābhūta) and the derived materiality (upādāyarūpa) dependent on the four great elements. The classification of this mentality and materiality (as pleasant feeling, etc., or as the earth element, etc.) has already been stated in the "Description of the Aggregates" (Khandha-niddesa). Thus, in this phrase "With consciousness as condition, mentality-materiality," the decision should first be known by way of the classification of mentality and materiality.

In the phrase "by way of their occurrence in existence and so forth"—mentality occurs in all existences (bhava), modes of birth (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and abodes of beings (sattāvāsa), except for one abode of beings (the non-percipient beings). Materiality occurs in two existences (Sense-sphere and Fine-material sphere), four modes of birth, five destinations, the first four stations of consciousness [Note 1], and five abodes of beings (including the non-percipient beings).

Among these mentality-materiality factors thus occurring, for those womb-born [Note 2] and egg-born beings who lack sex-materiality (bhāva-rūpa), at the moment of rebirth-linking, two primary groups of materiality (santatisīsa) [Note 1]—namely the base-decad (vatthu-dasaka) and the body-decad (kāya-dasaka)—and the three mental aggregates (nāma-khandha) appear. 

Notes:
1. Refers to "beings different in body and different in perception," etc., shown in the first paragraph of section 637.
2. The name gabbhaseyyaka refers to the womb-born (jalābuja).

Therefore, for those womb-born and egg-born beings lacking sex-materiality, in detail [Note 3], twenty factors from the side of materiality [Note 4] and the three mental aggregates [Note 5]—these twenty-three factors—should be known as "mentality-materiality conditioned by consciousness." However, by the method of taking only what has not been taken (i.e., avoiding duplicates), by removing 9 material factors from one primary group (santatisīsa), 14 factors (should be known). For those womb-born and egg-born beings who possess sex-materiality, by adding the sex-decad (bhāva-dasaka), 33 factors (should be known). For them also, by the method of not repeating what has been taken, by removing 18 material factors from two primary groups (santatisīsa), 15 factors (should be known as mentality-materiality conditioned by consciousness).

Furthermore, among spontaneously born (opapātika) beings, for those such as the Brahmas of the first jhāna, at the moment of rebirth-linking, four primary groups (santatisīsa)—by way of the eye-decad, ear-decad, base-decad, and the life-nonad (jīvitindriya-navaka)—and the three mental aggregates appear. Therefore, for those Brahmas, in detail, thirty-nine factors from the side of materiality and the three mental aggregates—[193] these forty-two factors—should be known as "mentality-materiality conditioned by consciousness."

Notes:
1. Santatisīsa refers to the original groups (kalāpa) at the root of the continuity of groups. (Sub-commentary)
2. Connect with: "for those egg-born... these 23 factors... should be known as mentality-materiality."
3. Connect with: "In detail... twenty... twenty-three." Here, "in detail" means taking material factors of the same type without reduction.
4. Although there is no materiality of change (vikāra-rūpa) at the moment of rebirth-linking, there is materiality of characteristics (lakkhaṇa-rūpa) and the space-element (ākāsa-rūpa). Therefore, wishing to exclude those lakkhaṇa-rūpa and ākāsa-rūpa which are not produced in the ultimate sense, it is called "the side of materiality" (rūpa-rūpa). (Sub-commentary). Materiality (rūpa-rūpa) refers to concrete materiality (nipphanna-rūpa) which is produced in the ultimate sense.

During the course of existence (pavattikāla), in all planes where materiality arises, among the kamma-born materiality that arises with the rebirth-linking consciousness, the pure octad (suddhaṭṭhaka)—which is temperature-originated, i.e., caused by the fire element called temperature²—appears at the static phase (ṭhitikkhana) of the rebirth-linking consciousness.³ However, the rebirth-linking consciousness does not cause materiality to arise. The reason is: just as a man who is about to fall or is falling from a precipice is unable to support another person who is also about to fall or is falling, similarly, that rebirth-linking consciousness is unable to cause materiality to arise because its supporting base-materiality (vatthu-rūpa) is weak. In the period following the rebirth-linking consciousness, starting from the first life-continuum (paṭhama-bhavaṅga), the pure octad caused by consciousness arises. After the moment of rebirth-linking, due to the fire element called temperature and due to consciousness, the sound-nonad decad (sadda-navaka-kalāpa)⁴ arises at the time sound is produced. For womb-born beings (gabbhaseyyaka) who live depending on nutriment swallowed (kabaḷīkārāhāra)⁵—

"Whatever food the mother eats,
Rice or drink,
By that the person in the mother's womb

2. Temperature-originated means materiality caused by temperature, i.e., temperature-born materiality (utujarūpa).
3. The group of eight—earth, water, fire, air, color, smell, taste, and nutritive essence—is called the pure octad (suddhaṭṭhaka-kalāpa).
4. The eight phenomena in the pure octad plus sound-materiality—these 9 together—are called the sound-nonad decad.

As it is said, the pure octad caused by nutriment arises in the body pervaded by the nutriment swallowed by the mother. For spontaneous beings, the pure octad caused by nutriment arises when they first swallow the saliva in their own mouths. Thus, by way of the nutriment-born pure octad and the two sound-nonads (which can possibly occur) that are temperature-born and consciousness-born, there are these 26 types of materiality¹, and together with the 70 varieties of kamma-born materiality mentioned earlier—referring to those that occur three times² in each mind-moment—there are 96 varieties of materiality³ and 3 mental aggregates. Therefore, in brief⁴, these 99 phenomena should be understood as "mentality-materiality conditioned by consciousness." Alternatively, since sound-materiality appears only occasionally, it is not constant (aniyata). Therefore, by excluding both the temperature-born and consciousness-born sound-materiality, these 97 phenomena should be understood as "mentality-materiality conditioned by consciousness" for all beings as appropriate. Indeed, for all those beings, whether they are sleeping, heedless, eating, or drinking, by day or by night, these (97) phenomena constantly arise due to the condition of consciousness⁵.

Indeed, at the moment that fivefold sense-consciousness arises, only mentality (mental factors) arises because of that consciousness. Thus it should be known as 'mentality-materiality conditioned by consciousness'.

If it is argued that it is inappropriate (to say only materiality arises from consciousness) because there is no consciousness in non-percipient beings, this statement is not inappropriate (it is indeed appropriate).

Consciousness which is the cause of mentality-materiality should be understood in two ways: as resultant consciousness (vipāka-viññāṇa) and non-resultant consciousness (avipāka-viññāṇa). Because of this—

In this way, the decision regarding the term 'viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ' should be understood by way of synthesis.

## Detailed Explanation of the Term 'With Name-and-Form as Condition, the Sixfold Base'

641. In the term 'With name-and-form as condition, the sixfold base' (nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatanaṃ):

The group of the three mental aggregates should be understood as 'name' (nāma); the primary elements, the physical bases, etc., should be understood as 'form' (rūpa). That name-and-form, which is formed as a 'one-remains' (ekasesa) compound, assists that sixfold base (saḷāyatana), which is likewise formed as a 'one-remains' compound.

To explain further: among the name and form which are the causal conditions for the sixfold base itself, 'name' refers to the group of three aggregates beginning with feeling (vedanā); 'form' refers to the four primary elements, the six physical bases, and the life-faculty, which are included within one's own continuity and occur by rule; such primary elements and physical bases should be understood as 'form'. Furthermore, it should be understood that name-and-form—formed as a 'one-remains' compound where 'name' and 'form' and 'name-and-form' are called 'name-and-form'—assists the sixfold base, which is formed as a 'one-remains' compound where the 'sixth base' (chaṭṭhāyatana) and the 'sixfold base' (saḷāyatana) are called 'the sixfold base'. Why? Because in the formless realm (arūpa), only name is the condition, and that name is the condition only for the sixth base, not for any other. Indeed, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: 'With name as condition, the sixth base' (nāmapaccayā chaṭṭhāyatanaṃ). Therefore, it should be so understood.

In that regard, it might be asked: 'How is it to be known that name-and-form is the condition for the sixfold base?' (The answer is:) Because of its existence when name-and-form exists. To explain: when such and such name and form exist, such and such base comes to be; it does not occur otherwise. The fact of its existence being dependent on the existence of the other will become clear in the 'Method of Conditions' (paccayanaya) itself. Therefore:

'Whether at rebirth or during the course of existence, whatever [name-and-form] is a condition for whatever [base], and in whatever manner it is a condition, all that should be understood by the wise.'

In that verse, the following is the explanation of the meaning:

In the formless realm, at rebirth and during the course of existence, name alone is the condition in seven ways or six ways at minimum.
197:
To show the manner: In the formless realm, at rebirth and during the course of existence, name alone assists that base in seven ways or six ways at minimum.

How? Firstly, at the moment of rebirth, name assists the sixth base (chaṭṭhāyatana) in seven ways at minimum through the conditions of: Conascence (sahajāta), Mutuality (aññamañña), Dependence (nissaya), Association (sampayutta), Resultant (vipāka), Presence (atthi), and Non-disappearance (avigata). In an augmented sense, however, among these names, some assist by way of Root condition (hetu-paccaya), and some assist by way of Nutriment condition (āhāra-paccaya). In this way, it assists by other ways as well; by the power of those conditions such as Root, the maximum and minimum (augmentation and diminution) should be understood.

During the course of existence (pavattikāla) also, resultant name (vipāka-nāma) assists in the very same manner already stated. Name other than resultant, however, assists at minimum by the six conditions already mentioned, excluding the Resultant condition. In an augmented sense, among these non-resultant names, some assist by way of Root condition and some by way of Nutriment condition. In this way, it assists by other ways as well; by the power of those conditions such as Root, the maximum and minimum should be understood.

In other realms (other than the formless), at the moment of rebirth, that name assists the sixth base in the same way in seven ways; to the bases other than the sixth, that name assists in six ways.

To explain further: in the realm of five aggregates (pañcavokāra) other than the formless realm, that resultant name, being a companion to the heart-base (hadayavatthu), assists the sixth base, the mind-base (manāyatana), in seven ways at minimum, just as stated for the formless realm. To the other five bases such as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), however, that resultant name, being a companion to the four great elements, assists in six ways by the power of the conditions of: Conascence, Dependence, Resultant, Dissociation (vippayutta), Presence, and Non-disappearance. In an augmented sense, among these resultant names, some assist by way of Root condition and some by way of Nutriment condition. In this way, it assists by other ways as well. By the power of those conditions such as Root, the maximum and minimum should be understood.

During the course of existence also, it occurs in that way: resultant [name] is the condition for resultant [base]; non-resultant [name] is the condition for non-resultant [base]; [each] is a condition for the sixth [base] in six ways.

To explain further: in the course of existence in the realm of five aggregates, just as at the moment of rebirth, resultant name assists the resultant sixth base in seven ways at minimum. Non-resultant name, however, assists the non-resultant sixth base at minimum in six ways, by removing the Resultant condition from those seven. In this verse, or rather, in this manner of assistance during the course of existence, the maximum and minimum should be understood by the very same method already stated.

In that same [course of existence], resultant [name] would be the condition for the remaining five [bases] in four ways; non-resultant [name] is also declared in this very same way.

To explain further: in that very same course of existence, to the remaining five bases such as the eye-base, which have the eye-sensitivity etc. as their physical base, the other resultant name assists in four ways through the conditions of: Post-conascence (pacchājāta), Dissociation, Presence, and Non-disappearance. Just as it is for the resultant, the non-resultant is also declared in this very same way. Therefore, it should be understood that even with the distinction of wholesome (kusala) etc., they assist in four ways.
198:
In that same course of existence (pavatti) of the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhava), the resultant mentality (vipāka-nāma) which has its base in the eye-sensitivity and so on, other than at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), assists the five bases such as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) excluding the mind-base (manāyatana) in four ways by way of post-nascence (pacchājāta), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions. Just as with resultant mentality, non-resultant mentality should also be shown in the same way. Therefore, it should be understood that mentality, categorized as wholesome and so on, assists those eye-bases and so on in four ways. [198] As stated thus, first, mentality alone assists such and such a base at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence; and in such a manner it assists, so should those respective bases be understood.

As for how matter (rūpa) assists: among these two, name and matter, matter does not assist even a single base in the formless realm (arūpa-bhava). However, in the five-constituent realm (pañcavokāra-bhava), at the moment of rebirth-linking, the heart-base (vatthu-rūpa) among matter assists the sixth base (manāyatana) in six ways. The great essentials (bhūta-rūpa) assist the five bases in four ways generally (without distinguishing between rebirth-linking and the course of existence).

To explain further: at the moment of rebirth-linking (in the five-constituent realm), the heart-base among matter assists the sixth, the mind-base (manāyatana), in six ways by way of conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions. The four great essentials, however, generally assist all five bases such as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, according to whichever base arises, in four ways by way of conascence, support, presence, and non-disappearance conditions.

The life-faculty matter (jīvita-rūpa) assists these five bases (eye-base, etc.) in three ways. Nutriment matter (āhāra-rūpa) also assists (these five bases in three ways) during the course of existence. These same five matter-bases (eye-base, etc.) assist the sixth, the mind-base, in six ways. The heart-base assists that same mind-base in five ways.

To explain further: at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence, the life-faculty matter assists these five bases such as the eye in three ways by way of presence, non-disappearance, and faculty (indriya) conditions. Nutriment matter also assists in three ways by way of presence, non-disappearance, and nutriment (āhāra) conditions; and that assistance of nutriment matter occurs only during the course of existence in the body followed by nutriment for those beings who live on nutriment, not at rebirth-linking. Those five bases such as the eye-base assist the sixth mind-base, known as eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, in six ways by way of support, pre-nascence (purejāta), faculty, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions during the course of existence, not at rebirth-linking. Excluding the five consciousnesses, the heart-base assists that remaining mind-base in five ways by way of support, pre-nascence, dissociation, presence, and non-disappearance conditions only during the course of existence, not at rebirth-linking. As stated thus, matter alone assists such and such a base at rebirth-linking and in the course of existence; and in such a manner it assists, so should those respective bases be understood.

As for how both name and matter assist: whichever name and matter together assist whichever base...
199:
...and in such a manner they assist, that name-and-matter and that base should be understood by the wise in that manner throughout rebirth-linking and the course of existence.

[199] What is this that should be understood? First: at the moment of rebirth-linking in the five-constituent realm, name-and-matter, consisting of the group of three aggregates (mentality) and the heart-base (matter), assists the sixth base (manāyatana) by way of conascence, mutuality, support, resultant (vipāka), association (sampayutta), dissociation (vippayutta), presence, non-disappearance conditions, and so on. This is just a brief indication here. However, by following the method stated, one is able to apply it to all; therefore, the detail is not shown here. This concludes one part.

This is the detailed explanation of the phrase 'With Name-and-Form as condition, the Six Sense Bases' (nāmarūpa-paccayā saḷāyatanaṃ).

## Detailed Explanation of the Phrase 'With the Six Sense Bases as condition, Contact'
642. In the phrase 'With the Six Sense Bases as condition, Contact' (saḷāyatana-paccayā phasso):
In brief, there are only six kinds of contact, such as eye-contact and so on. In detail, those contacts are thirty-two, like the consciousness (conditioned by formations).

To explain further: in the statement that contact arises because of the six bases as condition, in brief, there are only these six kinds of contact: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact. In detail, however, eye-contact and so on—that is, eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact—are ten, being five wholesome resultants and five unwholesome resultants. The remaining mind-contacts are twenty-two, being associated with the twenty-two mundane resultant consciousnesses. In this way, all these contacts are thirty-two, like the consciousness stated to be conditioned by formations.

Furthermore, among those six bases called 'saḷāyatana' which are the conditioning causes of this thirty-two-fold contact...
Some wise men desire the 'six bases' (saḷāyatana) to be the eye-base and so on occurring in the internal (ajjhatta) continuity together with the sixth, the mind-base. Some wise men also desire it to be the six bases together with the six external (bāhira) bases.

In that phrase, first, those teachers who, considering that 'this is a discourse on the karmically acquired (upādiṇṇaka) result of mundane kamma', show the condition and the conditionally arisen only as pertaining to one's own continuity. Following the Vibhaṅga Pali text which says 'With the mind-base (chaṭṭhāyatana) as condition, contact', they consider that 'in the formless realm, the mind-base assists contact, and elsewhere, by way of total inclusion, the six bases assist contact'. Having made a 'single-term-remaining' (ekasesa) of similar forms, they desire the eye and so on, which are internal together with the mind-base, to be the 'six bases'. Indeed, both that mind-base and those six bases come to be designated simply as 'the six bases' (saḷāyatana).

Other teachers, however, show only the conditionally arisen effect as pertaining to one's own continuity, but show the conditioning cause as also pertaining to a different continuity. Those teachers, wishing to show all those bases that assist contact [200], also include the external bases...
200:
Having grasped [the external bases], even those six internal bases such as the eye-base, together with the external bases such as the form-base, are desired to be known as the 'sixfold sense base' (saḷāyatana). Indeed, in the dvanda compound sentence 'the sixth base, and the sixfold sense base, and the sixfold sense base,' when the elision of all but one (ekasesa) is performed on these three terms, it is referred to simply as 'saḷāyatana.'

In this matter, [an objector] raises a challenge: 'A single contact does not arise from all bases, nor do all contacts arise from a single base. However, this contact is stated as one, saying "with the sixfold sense base as condition, contact arises." Why is it stated thus?' The following is the answer to that challenge: It is true that a single contact does not arise from all bases, nor do all contacts arise from a single base. However, a single contact does arise from many bases. For example, eye-contact arises due to the eye-base, the form-base, the mind-base known as eye-consciousness, and the mental-object base (dhammāyatana) which consists of the remaining associated states. In the same way, this should be applied appropriately to all cases such as ear-contact, etc. Therefore:

'The Buddha, the Steadfast One (Tādi), who is endowed with the quality of Tādi,¹ has shown here that this contact, though it is one, arises from many bases by using the singular designation.'

Note:
1. A Buddha or an Arahant who can look upon desirable and undesirable objects with equanimity is called 'Tādi.' The ability to remain unshaken and view both types of good and bad objects equally is called the 'quality of Tādi' (tādiguṇa).

'By using the singular designation' means that by this singular designation, 'with the sixfold sense base as condition, contact arises,' the Buddha, endowed with the quality of Tādi, showed that a single contact arises from many bases; this is the meaning. Regarding the bases:

'One should clearly demonstrate the five bases (eye, etc.) as conditioning [this contact] in six ways; the one mind-base that follows those five should be shown as conditioning it in nine ways; and the six external bases should be shown as conditioning it in accordance with their occurrence.'

In that verse, the following is the detailed explanation: First, the five bases such as the eye-base condition the fivefold contact such as eye-contact in six ways by way of support (nissaya), pre-nascence (purejāta), faculty (indriya), dissociation (vippayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions. The one resultant mind-base (vipāka-manāyatana) that follows those five bases conditions the resultant mind-contact (vipāka-manosamphassa), which has many varieties,¹ in nine ways by way of conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), resultant (vipāka), nutriment (āhāra), faculty (indriya), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions. Among the external bases, the form-base conditions eye-contact in four ways by way of object (ārammaṇa), pre-nascence (purejāta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions. Similarly, the sound-base, etc., condition ear-contact, etc., in four ways. Specifically,

Note:
1. 'Many varieties' refers to contacts other than those of the two sets of fivefold consciousness (dve-pañcavijñāṇa), such as those associated with wholesome resultants (kusalavipāka) occurring at the five doors, etc.
201:
(Sub-commentary)
To mind-contact (manosamphassa), those five bases such as form, etc., and the mental-object base (dhammāyatana) condition it similarly in four ways, or merely by way of the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). In this manner, one should clearly demonstrate the six external bases as conditioning this contact in accordance with their occurrence. This concludes one section.

This aforementioned explanation is the detailed discourse on the phrase 'with the sixfold sense base as condition, contact arises' (saḷāyatanapaccayā phasso).

## Detailed Explanation of the Phrase 'With Contact as Condition, Feeling Arises'
643. In the phrase 'with contact as condition, feeling arises' (phassapaccayā vedanā):

The feelings, which are only six by way of the doors such as those born of eye-contact,¹ were taught [by the Buddha]; those feelings should be understood as eighty-nine by way of their classification.

In the Vibhaṅga, the commentary on this phrase, it is also stated: 'Feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact... nose... tongue... body... feeling born of mind-contact' (Vibh. 231). Thus, the feelings were taught as being only six by way of the doors. However, by way of classification, they are understood as eighty-nine because they are associated with the eighty-nine types of consciousness.

Nevertheless, among these eighty-nine types of feeling, it is said [by the wise] that only the thirty-two types of feeling associated with resultant consciousness (vipāka-citta) are intended in this phrase 'with contact as condition, feeling arises.'

Note:
1. Connect with 'feelings such as...'

Among those thirty-two feelings, to the five feelings associated with the fivefold consciousness at the five doors, contact such as eye-contact conditions them in eight ways; to the remaining feelings (receiving, investigating, and registering), it conditions them in one way. In the mind-door also, to the [registering feelings], that conascent mind-contact conditions them similarly in eight ways.

To explain in detail: among those thirty-two feelings, to the five feelings that have the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), etc., as their physical basis at the five doors, contact such as eye-contact conditions them in eight ways by way of conascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), support (nissaya), resultant (vipāka), nutriment (āhāra), association (sampayutta), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata) conditions. To the sense-sphere resultant feelings (kāmāvacara-vipāka-vedanā) occurring by way of receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigating (santīraṇa), and registering (tadārammaṇa) at each of the remaining doors, that contact such as eye-contact conditions them in only one way by way of natural decisive support condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya).

Regarding the statement 'In the mind-door also, it is the same,' the detail is: in the mind-door also, to the sense-sphere resultant feelings occurring by way of registering (tadārammaṇa), that contact known as conascent mind-contact (sahajāta-manosamphassa) conditions them in the same way in eight ways. To the resultant feelings of the three planes of existence occurring by way of rebirth (paṭisandhi), life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti), [it also conditions them in eight ways].
202:
Specifically, in the mind-door [202], for the sense-sphere feelings (kāmāvacara-vedanā) that occur by way of registration (tadārammaṇa), the mind-contact associated with mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjanasampayutta-manosamphassa) assists in only one way, by the power of the natural decisive support condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya).1 This concludes one section.

This preceding explanation is the detailed exposition on the phrase "With contact as condition, feeling [arises]" (phassapaccayā vedanā).

Note:
1. Regarding the causal condition, some teachers also desire it even when it is not a kamma-result (vipāka). Therefore, the phrase "Specifically, in the mind-door" and so on, states the conditionality of contact associated with mind-door adverting. This statement should be understood as a brief indication. By this method, the fact that all contact, whether immediate or not, assists its respective resultant feeling by way of decisive support (upanissaya) should be applied. (Ṭīkā)

## Detailed Exposition on the Phrase "With Feeling as Condition, Craving [Arises]"

644. Regarding the phrase "With feeling as condition, craving [arises]" (vedanāpaccayā taṇhā):

In this world, the Blessed One has shown six kinds of craving by way of the division of craving for forms (rūpa-taṇhā) and so on. Among these six, each should be understood as being of three types according to the mode of occurrence.

To elaborate: in this phrase "With feeling as condition, craving [arises]," just as a son is designated or called by a name derived from his father, such as "the merchant's son" or "the brahmin's son," so too in the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga, six kinds of craving are shown by names derived from their objects: craving for forms (rūpa-taṇhā), craving for sounds (sadda-taṇhā), craving for odors (gandha-taṇhā), craving for tastes (rasa-taṇhā), craving for tangibles (phoṭṭhabba-taṇhā), and craving for mental objects (dhamma-taṇhā).

Among those six kinds of craving, each craving is to be understood as being of three types according to the mode of occurrence: craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā), craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). To elaborate: when craving for forms (rūpa-taṇhā) itself occurs enjoying a visible object that has come into the range of the eye by way of enjoying sensual pleasure, it is then called craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā). When it occurs together with the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) that clings to that same visible object as "stable and permanent," it is then called craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā). Indeed, lust (rāga) accompanied by the eternalist view is called craving for existence. But when it occurs together with the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) that clings to that same visible object as "it will be cut off, it will perish," it is then called craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā). Indeed, lust accompanied by the annihilationist view is called craving for non-existence. This same method applies to craving for sounds and so on. Therefore, these six kinds of craving become eighteen.

Those eighteen kinds of craving become thirty-six when applied to internal visible objects, etc. (18) and external visible objects, etc. (18). Thus, there are thirty-six past cravings, thirty-six future cravings, and thirty-six present cravings, making a total of one hundred and eight kinds of craving. When these one hundred and eight are summarized again, they should be understood as being only six kinds of craving by way of objects such as forms, etc., or only three kinds of craving by way of craving for sensual pleasures, etc.

As for how craving arises because of feeling: just as these beings, enjoying their son and out of affection for him, provide for and honor the wet-nurse, so too, enjoying the feeling [203] that arises by way of objects such as forms, etc., and out of affection for that feeling, they provide great honor and gifts to the painter, the harpist, the perfumer, the cook, the weaver, and the physician who prepares rejuvenating medicines2—those who provide the objects such as forms and so on.

Note:
1. For a detailed study of the manner of clinging with this annihilationist view and the occurrence of craving for non-existence, see Volume II, page 65 of our Paṭiccasamuppāda Dhamma and page 135 of the Bhārasutta Dhamma.
2. In this simile, feeling should be understood as the son. The objects such as forms, which are the cause of feeling, should be understood as the milk. The six providers, such as the painter, who provide the six objects such as forms, should be understood as the wet-nurse who provides the milk. Among those six, it should be understood that the weaver provides the tangible object (soft cloth), and the physician provides the mental object (dhamma-ārammaṇa) by way of the nutritional essence (ojā) contained in the rejuvenating medicine and by way of the life-faculty supported by that essence. (Ṭīkā)
203:
Therefore, this craving in its entirety should be understood as being conditioned by feeling.

Furthermore, in this phrase [Feeling conditions Craving], only resultant pleasant feeling is intended; thus, this feeling serves as a condition for craving in one way only.

'In one way' means it serves as a condition by way of decisive support condition (pakatūpanissaya-paccaya). Alternatively...

One who is in pain longs for pleasure; one who is in pleasure desires even more; and equanimity, because of its peaceful nature, is also spoken of as pleasure.

Therefore, all three types of feeling serve as conditions for craving; thus it was taught by the Great Sage: "Feeling conditions craving."

Note 1: By the words "Alternatively...", it is shown that it is not only resultant pleasant feeling [that is the condition]; rather, all three resultant feelings are specifically the decisive support conditions for craving. Generally, even non-resultant feeling [is a decisive support condition]. Equanimity is spoken of as pleasure because of its peaceful nature; because it is so called, that equanimity also becomes a decisive support condition for craving by way of desiring more. However, equanimity that is the result of unwholesome kamma is included under pain because it is undesirable (aniṭṭha). Other equanimity, which is the result of wholesome kamma, is included under pleasure because it is desirable (iṭṭha). Therefore, that equanimity can be said to be a decisive support condition just like pain. (Sub-commentary)

Furthermore, although craving arises because of the condition of feeling, it cannot occur without underlying tendencies (anusaya). Therefore, for the Arahant—who has lived the holy life (magga-brahmacariya) and has abandoned evil—that craving no longer arises. Here ends one section.

This is the detailed explanation of the phrase "Feeling conditions craving" (vedanāpaccayā taṇhā).

## Detailed Explanation of the Phrase "Craving conditions Clinging" (taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ)

645. In the phrase "Craving conditions clinging"—

There are four types of clinging. These should be clarified by way of analysis of meaning, by way of brevity and expansion, and by way of order.

In this verse, the following is the clarification: Clinging to sense-pleasures (kāmupādāna), clinging to views (diṭṭhupādāna), clinging to rules and observances (sīlabbatupādāna), and clinging to the doctrine of self (attavādupādāna)—these are the four types of clinging in this context. The following is the analysis of their meanings: It is called "clinging to sense-pleasures" because it firmly clings to the objects of sense-desire known as "kāma". (Alternatively) It is called "kāma" because it delights and desires, and it is called "upādāna" because it clings firmly; for these two reasons, it is called "kāmupādāna". "Upādāna" means firm grasping or clinging. Indeed, the prefix "upa" in this term has the sense of "firmness", as in such words as "upāyāsa" (intense despair) and "upakkuṭṭha" (greatly censured). Furthermore, it is called "diṭṭhi" because it sees wrongly, and that "diṭṭhi" is also "upādāna"; for these two reasons, it is called "clinging to views" (diṭṭhupādāna). Alternatively, it is called "diṭṭhupādāna" because it clings to wrong views. Indeed, in such instances as "The self and the world are eternal," a later wrong view firmly clings to an earlier wrong view. Furthermore, it is called "clinging to rules and observances" (sīlabbatupādāna) because it firmly clings to habits and practices. (Alternatively) That nature is both "sīlabbata" and "upādāna"; for these two reasons, it is called "sīlabbatupādāna". Indeed, such things as the cow-habit and cow-vow are themselves "clinging" because of the conviction that "purification comes through such practice."
