There, 'having sought' is the literal meaning of the word 'pariyeseyya', while 'should place it nearby' is the meaning required in that rule. Therefore, to include both meanings, the ancient teachers translated it as 'having sought, if he should place it nearby.' Here also, it should be noted that it is translated in the same way.
1. The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is left aside [1] because it is extremely subtle, and disciples cannot discern it at the beginning of their practice.
2. Jhānaṅga—Jhana factor—means the constituent parts of the jhana [2].
3. By the word 'etc.' [3], manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) and proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) are to be taken. In this method of discerning, it is shown that one must discern the mental states of the jhana that have just occurred in one's own continuity, and in doing so, one must discern them by way of characteristic, etc. Therefore, when discerning mentality, one must discern the consciousness and mental factors that have just occurred in one's own continuity in this same way. When discerning materiality, one must discern the materiality that is currently manifest at the six doors (dvāra). In doing so, one must not discern them by name, shape, or number, but only by characteristic, etc. Special care should be taken to ensure this conforms to the Visuddhimagga.
4. 'All these also' [4] is a translation of the Pali 'sabbampi'. It means 'one should define all these states, and one should define a portion of these states.' If this type of term is encountered later, it should be understood in this same way.
5. Thereafter... closely observing that mentality... while searching... he sees the heart-base—this is how it should be connected [5].

...should leave aside the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and, having emerged from any of the remaining fine-material-sphere jhanas (4) or immaterial-sphere jhanas (3), should discern the jhana factors such as initial application (vitakka), etc., and the (mental) states (such as contact, etc.) associated with those jhana factors by way of their characteristics, functions, etc. Having discerned them, all these states should be defined as 'mentality' (nāma) in the sense of bending, because they bend towards the object.

Thereafter, just as a man, having seen a snake inside his house and following it, sees its lair; even so, this practitioner (yogāvacara), closely observing that mentality and searching, 'On what does this mentality depend for its occurrence?', sees the heart-base (hadayarūpa) which is the physical basis of that mentality. Then he discerns the great elements which are the support for the heart-base, and the remaining derived materiality (upādāyarūpa) which depends on the great elements. Thus he discerns materiality. He defines all this as 'materiality' (rūpa) because it is molested (deformed). Then he briefly defines mentality and materiality: 'Mentality has the characteristic of bending towards the object; materiality has the characteristic of being molested' (The state that has the characteristic of bending towards the object is mentality; the state that has the characteristic of being molested is materiality).

## (2) Method of Discerning Starting with the Four Elements

664. As for the method of discerning starting with materiality: whether it be a suddhavipassanāyānika (one who has pure insight as a vehicle) [1] or this aforementioned samathayānika, he discerns the four elements briefly or in detail by way of any of the various methods for discerning the elements mentioned in the 'Definition of the Four Elements' meditation subject. When the elements have become manifest to him by way of their true nature, function, and characteristic...

Note:
1. A person who develops only insight from the beginning without developing access concentration or absorption concentration is called a suddhavipassanāyānika because they have a vehicle for reaching Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna that is pure insight. Suddha (pure/only) + vipassanāyāna (insight vehicle) + ika (one who has) = suddhavipassanāyānika. It means one who practices pure insight without a basis of serenity.
223:
2. Connect with the phrase 'In those various methods'—

When the elements appear to that meditator by way of their own true characteristics [223], 'In the hair produced by kamma (kamma-samuṭṭhāna), there are 10 types of matter by way of the body-decad (kāya-dasaka-kalāpa), namely: the four elements, color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, life-faculty, and body-sensitivity. In that same hair, because of the presence of sex-materiality, there are 10 types of matter by way of the sex-decad (bhāva-dasaka-kalāpa). In that same hair, there are also another 24 types of matter: the octad with nutritive essence as the eighth (ojaṭṭhamaka) produced by nutriment (āhāra-samuṭṭhāna), that produced by temperature (utu-samuṭṭhāna), and that produced by consciousness (citta-samuṭṭhāna).'

Notes:
1. 'By way of their own true characteristics'—this meaning is translated precisely in accordance with the explanation given in the Mahāṭīkā, Vol. 2, p. 257. This commentary explanation was already cited in Note 1 on page 47 (of this book); please refer back to it.
2. 'When they appear... 44 types of matter become manifest'—connect these.
3. Hair produced by kamma refers to the root of the hair located within the flesh of the head.
4. Earth, water, fire, air—these are the four elements. Vaṇṇa—color; gandha—odor; rasa—flavor; ojā—nutritive essence; jīvita—life-faculty; kāyaprasāda—body-sensitivity which is clear enough to receive touch.
5. In a woman's continuity, there is feminine sex-materiality (itthibhāva-rūpa); in a man's, masculine (pumbhāva-rūpa).
6. The group of eight—earth, water, fire, air, color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence—is called the ojaṭṭhamaka (octad with nutritive essence as the eighth). It is also called aṭṭhaka-kalāpa or aṭṭha-kalāpa. These eight types of matter usually arise together and cannot be separated; therefore, they are also called inseparable matter (avinibbhoga-rūpa).

'...In this way, 44 types of matter become manifest. Similarly, in the 24 parts produced by the four causes, 44 types of matter each become manifest. In the four parts—sweat, tears, saliva, and snot—which are produced by temperature and consciousness, 16 types of matter each become manifest by way of two ojaṭṭhamaka-kalāpas. In the four parts—undigested food, feces, pus, and urine—which are produced by temperature only, 8 types of matter each become manifest by way of the ojaṭṭhamaka-kalāpa.'

Notes:
1. Regarding '44 types of matter become manifest', it does not mean they all appear simultaneously, nor does it mean they appear one after another in sequence. It is also not intended to instruct one to contemplate all 44. In truth, if one contemplates the earth element (tangible matter) in the hair and that single earth element becomes manifest, then all 44 types of matter within that hair are considered manifest. The task of contemplating all 44 is thus accomplished. How is it accomplished? If one truly knows a single earth element, there is no opportunity for defilements to arise by clinging to those 44 types of matter as a 'person' or 'being'. Because defilements have no chance to arise and are stilled, the task of contemplation is complete. Therefore, it is said, 'When the elements appear... 44 types of matter become manifest.' This should be understood similarly in subsequent passages describing manifestation.
2. The 24 parts refer to the 32 parts minus the eight parts: sweat, tears, saliva, snot, undigested food, feces, pus, and urine.

'This is the method for knowing the manifestation of matter in the 32 parts. When these 32 parts (groups of matter) become manifest, another 10 parts also become manifest. Among them, in the fire-part produced by kamma (kammaja-pācaka) that digests eaten food, etc., 9 types of matter become manifest: the ojaṭṭhamaka group and the life-faculty. Similarly, in the mind-born (cittaja) in-breath and out-breath part, 9 types of matter become manifest: the ojaṭṭhamaka group and sound (sadda). In the remaining eight parts produced by the four causes, 33 types of matter each become manifest by way of the group of nine with life as the ninth (jīvita-navaka-kalāpa) and three ojaṭṭhamaka-kalāpas.'

Notes:
1. In the 24 parts: (24 x 5) = 120 kalāpas; (24 x 44) = 1056 types of matter. In the 4 parts produced by two causes: (4 x 2) = 8 kalāpas; (4 x 16) = 64 types of matter. In the 4 parts produced by temperature: 4 kalāpas; (4 x 8) = 32 types of matter. Total for the 32 parts: 132 kalāpas, 1152 types of matter.
2. The eight parts are: three fire-parts—santappana (feverish heat), jīraṇa (aging heat), paridāha (burning heat); and five air-parts—uddhaṅgama (upward-going wind), adhogama (downward-going wind), kucchisaya (wind in the stomach), koṭṭhāsaya (wind in the intestines), and aṅgamaṅgānusārī (wind pervading the limbs).
3. In the digestive fire: 1 jīvita-navaka-kalāpa, 9 types of matter. In the in-breath/out-breath: 1 sadda-navaka-kalāpa, 9 types of matter. In the remaining eight parts: (8 x 4) = 32 kalāpas; (8 x 33) = 264 types of matter. Total for the 10 parts: 34 kalāpas, 282 types of matter.

When these primary and derived types of matter become manifest to that meditator by way of the 42 parts in detail as described, another 60 types of matter also become manifest by way of the bases and doors: five decad-groups (dasaka-kalāpa) such as the eye-decad, and the heart-base decad. The meditator, having grouped all those types of matter (totaling 1494) together by the characteristic of being molested (ruppana-lakkhaṇa), sees: 'This is materiality.'

Note:
1. Because the 5 bases and doors like the eye are manifest, 5 groups like the eye-decad (50 types of matter) appear; because the heart-base matter is manifest, the heart-base decad (10 types of matter) appears.
224:
2. In the 6 doors, there are 6 kalāpas, totaling 60 rūpas.
3. In the 32 parts (koṭṭhāsa), there are 132 kalāpas, totaling 1152 rūpas.
In the 10 parts, there are 34 kalāpas, totaling 282 rūpas.
In the 6 doors, there are 6 kalāpas, totaling 60 rūpas.
In the whole body, there are a total of 172 kalāpas and 1494 rūpas.

In the Mahāṭīkā, Volume I, page 466, and the Saccasaṅkhepa, however, in the 6 doors where 6 kalāpas and 60 rūpas are found, the kāyadasaka is excluded, counting only 5 kalāpas and 50 rūpas; in respiration, the saddarūpa is also excluded, counting only the octad-kalāpa (aṭṭhakalāpa) of 8 rūpas. Therefore, the count is reduced by 1 kalāpa and 11 rūpas from the above figures. However, by adding 2 utuja and cittaja saddanavaka-kalāpas (18 rūpas), according to those texts, there are 173 kalāpas and 1501 rūpas.

For the yogi who has thus discerned matter (rūpa), mental phenomena (nāma) become evident through the doors. The way they become evident is: the 81 mundane consciousnesses—namely, the 10-fold sense-consciousness (dvepañcavijñāṇa), the 3-fold mind-element (manodhātu), and the 68-fold mind-consciousness element (manovijñāṇadhātu)—as well as the 7 mental factors (cetasika) that generally arise with those (81) consciousnesses—namely, contact (phassa), feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), volition (cetanā), life-faculty (jīvita), one-pointedness (ekaggatā), and attention (manasikāra)—become evident [Note 1]. Supramundane (lokuttara) consciousnesses, however, do not come under discernment (contemplation) for either the pure-insight practitioner (suddhavipassanāyānika) or the tranquility practitioner (samathayānika), because they are states that have not been known or attained [Note 2]. The yogi groups all those (mental phenomena) together by the characteristic of inclining towards an object and contemplates, "This is Nāma." In this way, one type of yogi defines Nāma and Rūpa in detail, prioritizing the analysis of the four elements.

## (3) Method of Contemplation by way of the 18 Elements (Dhātu)

[224] 665. Another yogi (defines Nāma and Rūpa) by way of the 18 elements. How? In this Dispensation, a monk [Note 3], after reflecting on the elements [Note 4] thus: "In this person (this body), there is the eye-element... p... the mind-consciousness element," the world [Note 5] recognizes as "eye" that lump of flesh tied with the small string of a nerve in the eye-socket, which is variegated with white and black circles and is long and wide. Disregarding that lump of flesh, he defines the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) of the kind mentioned in the section on derived matter (upādā-rūpa) in the Description of the Aggregates (Khandha-niddesa) as the "eye-element" (cakkhudhātu).

Notes:
1. At the moment of seeing, based on the eye-door, the group of consciousnesses and mental factors starting from adverting (āvajjana) and ending with registration (tadārammaṇa) that occur in that door become evident. Similarly, in the case of hearing, etc., based on the ear-door, etc., the group of consciousnesses and mental factors occurring in those doors become evident.
2. This means they cannot be contemplated, and they should not/ought not be contemplated.
3-4. Connect: "The monk... after reflecting... without taking... defines as the eye-element."
5. Connect: "The world (the people)... recognizes."

As for the 4 elements which are its support, the 4 surrounding rūpas—color (vaṇṇa), odor (gandha), flavor (rasa), and nutritive essence (ojā)—and the 1 life-faculty (jīvitindriya) which is the protector, these are the 9 conascent rūpas. In that same place (the anatomical eye [Note 1]), there are 20 kamma-born rūpas (kammaja-rūpa) by way of the body-decad (kāyadasaka) and sex-decad (bhāvadasaka) kalāpas, and 24 non-kamma-born (anupādinna) rūpas by way of the three octad-kalāpas (ojāṭṭhamaka) such as those born of nutriment (āhāra-samuṭṭhāna). Thus, there are 53 other rūpas (remaining from the eye-sensitivity), and he does not define those 53 rūpas as the "eye-element." This same method applies to the ear-element and so on. However, in the case of the body-element (kāyadhātu), the remaining rūpas are 43. Some teachers, however, count the temperature-born and mind-born rūpas as 9 each including sound, and say there are 45 (remaining rūpas).

Thus, as explained, these 5 sensitivities (pasāda-rūpa) and the 5 objective rūpas—visible form (rūpa), sound (sadda), odor (gandha), flavor (rasa), and tangible (phoṭṭhabba)—which are their objects, these 10 rūpas are the 10 elements (dhātu). The remaining rūpas are only the mind-object element (dhamma-dhātu). Furthermore, the consciousness that arises depending on the eye-sensitivity and having visible form as its object is called the eye-consciousness element (cakkhuvijñāṇadhātu). In this way, the five pairs of sense-consciousness (dvepañcavijñāṇa) are the five consciousness elements (vijñāṇadhātu).

Notes:
1. Sa (together with) + sambhāra (constituents/structure) + cakkhu (eye) = sasambhāra-cakkhu: the physical eye together with the structure of 54 rūpas.
2. Connect: "The 20 kamma-born rūpas... the 24 non-kamma-born rūpas... that are situated."

The three mind-element consciousnesses are the single mind-element (manodhātu). The 68 mind-consciousness element consciousnesses are the (single) mind-consciousness element (manovijñāṇadhātu). Therefore, the 81 mundane consciousnesses are the 7 consciousness elements. The mental factors such as contact (phassa) associated with those consciousness elements are the mind-object element (dhamma-dhātu). In this manner, among these 18 elements, ten and a half elements are Rūpa, and seven and a half elements are Nāma. Thus, one type of yogi defines Nāma and Rūpa by way of the 18 elements.

## (4) Method of Contemplation by way of the 12 Bases (Āyatana)

666. Another yogi (defines Nāma and Rūpa) by way of the 12 bases. How? By the same method mentioned for the eye-element, excluding the 53 rūpas, he defines only the eye-sensitivity as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana). By the same method mentioned for the eye-element, he defines the ear-element, nose-element, tongue-element, and body-element as the ear-base (sotāyatana), nose-base (ghānāyatana), tongue-base (jivhāyatana), and body-base (kāyāyatana). He defines the five phenomena that are their objects as the visible-form base (rūpāyatana), sound-base (saddāyatana), odor-base (gandhāyatana), flavor-base (rasāyatana), and tangible-base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana). He defines the 7 mundane consciousness elements as the mind-base (manāyatana). He defines the mental factors such as contact (phassa) associated with that mind-base, as well as the remaining group of rūpas (remaining from the eye-base, etc.), as the mind-object base (dhammāyatana).
225:
In this way, among these twelve bases (āyatana), ten and a half bases are form (rūpa), and one and a half bases are name (nāma). Thus, one yogi defines name and form by way of the twelve bases.

## (5) Method of Discerning by Way of Aggregates

667. Another yogi defines [name and form] more concisely than that by way of the aggregates (khandha). How?

In this dispensation, a monk defines in this body the four elements (dhātu) originating from four causes, the four types of matter dependent on them—namely, color (vaṇṇa), odor (gandha), flavor (rasa), and nutritive essence (ojā)—the five sensitive materialities (pasāda-rūpa) such as the eye-sensitivity, the heart-base materiality (hadaya-vatthu), the sex-materiality (bhāva-rūpa), the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), and sound (sadda) which originates from two causes (consciousness and temperature). These seventeen types of matter are called 'suitable for comprehension' (sammasanūpaga), 'produced' (nipphanna) matter, and 'real matter' (rūparūpa).

However, these ten types of matter—namely, bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti), vocal intimation (vacīviññatti), the space element (ākāsadhātu), lightness of matter (rūpassa lahutā), malleability of matter (rūpassa mudutā), wieldiness of matter (rūpassa kammaññatā), integration (upacaya), continuity (santati), decay (jaratā), and impermanence (aniccatā)—are not 'suitable for comprehension.' They are merely the modes, alterations, and boundaries between real matters; they are not produced matter (nipphanna-rūpa) and not real matter (rūparūpa). Nevertheless, because they are the modes, alterations, and boundaries of real matter, they are reckoned as 'matter' (rūpa).

Notes:
1. 'A monk defines' should be connected to the context of discernment.
2. Bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti): A specific bodily movement that makes one's intention known to others. Vocal intimation (vacīviññatti): A specific vocal movement that makes one's intention known to others. Space element (ākāsadhātu): The boundaries surrounding groups of matter (rūpa-kalāpa). Lightness of matter: The buoyancy of the group of produced matter. Malleability: The softness of the group of produced matter. Wieldiness: The ability of the group of produced matter to perform actions such as bending, stretching, or moving. These three (lightness, malleability, and wieldiness) are particularly evident when one can easily bend, stretch, move, or speak as desired. Integration (upacaya): The initial arising of produced matter. Continuity (santati): The subsequent continuous arising of produced matter. Both integration and continuity are the 'arising' (uppāda) moment of produced matter. Decay (jaratā): The aging of produced matter, which is its 'static' (ṭhiti) moment. Impermanence (aniccatā): The non-permanence or destruction of produced matter, which is its 'dissolution' (bhaṅga) moment.
3. The 'modes of real matter' refers to bodily intimation, vocal intimation, integration, continuity, decay, and impermanence.
4. The 'special alterations of real matter' refers to lightness, malleability, and wieldiness.

They are merely the boundaries between real matters. They are not produced matter, nor are they real matter. However, as they are modes, alterations, and boundaries of real matter, they are included in the count of 'matter.' In this manner, all these twenty-seven types of matter constitute the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). The feeling (vedanā) that arises together with the eighty-one types of mundane consciousness is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). The perception (saññā) associated with that feeling is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha). The formations (saṅkhāra) are the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). The consciousness (viññāṇa) is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). Thus he defines: the aggregate of matter is 'form' (rūpa), and the four immaterial aggregates are 'name' (nāma). In this way, one yogi defines name and form by way of the five aggregates.

Notes:
1. The 'boundaries between real matters' refers to the space element (ākāsadhātu).
2. The word 'also' in 'all these types of matter also' indicates that even a part of these matters constitutes the aggregate of matter.
3. Supramundane (lokuttara) consciousness and mental factors are not the objects of insight (vipassanā), hence the specification 'with the eighty-one mundane consciousnesses.'
4. The qualifier 'associated with that (feeling)' is used here to place perception, formations, and consciousness on equal footing without having to separately specify 'consciousness called the eighty-one mundane consciousnesses' for each.

## (6) Method of Discerning by Way of Name and Form

668. Another yogi defines name and form concisely: 'Whatever matter there is, all matter consists of the four great elements and matter derived (upādā-rūpa) from the four great elements.' Having thus grasped form in this self-identity (the body) briefly, and having grasped the mind-base (manāyatana) and a portion of the mental-object base (dhammāyatana) as 'name,' he defines name and form concisely: 'This is name and this is form; these two are called name-and-form.'

## Method of Discerning to Make the Immaterial Clear

669. If, while defining form through various methods (such as discerning the four elements) and then attempting to grasp the immaterial (nāma), the immaterial does not appear to the yogi because of its subtlety, he should not give up his task. Instead, he should repeatedly contemplate, attend to, grasp, and define form again and again. For as form becomes thoroughly clarified, disentangled, and purified for him, the immaterial states that have that form as their object become clear of their own accord.

To illustrate with a simile: just as when a man with vision looks at the reflection of his face in an unclean mirror, the reflection does not appear clearly, and he does not [give up] saying 'the reflection does not appear.'

Notes:
1. For a beginner, matters that are not yet clearly apparent are called 'unclean.' They are called 'tangled' because similar and different types of matter are joined and interconnected. When the knowledge matures and they appear clearly and distinctly, they are called 'purified.'
226:
They are called 'disentangled' because they are not mixed with each other or with different types of materiality. This is a metaphorical expression. In reality, it refers to the purity and lack of entanglement of knowledge.

Just as a man, though his reflection does not appear at first, does not discard the mirror [226] in disappointment, but rather rubs it again and again; when the mirror is clean, his reflection appears naturally.

Or just as one desiring oil, having put sesame powder (sesame flour) into a mortar and sprinkled it with water, does not discard the sesame powder even if oil does not come out after grinding once or twice; rather, he sprinkles it with hot water again and again, kneads it, and grinds it. As he does so, clear sesame oil comes out.

Or just as one desiring to clear water, having taken a clearing nut (kataka) and placed his hand inside the water pot, does not discard the clearing nut even if the water does not clear after rubbing it once or twice; rather, he rubs it again and again. As he does so, the mud and silt settle, and the water becomes pure and clear.

In the same way, that yogi monk, without laying down his burden (giving up), should repeatedly contemplate, attend to, grasp, and define materiality alone.

Note 1: Tila (sesame) + piṭṭha (powder/flour) = tilapiṭṭha (sesame powder). The sub-commentary explains it as 'sesame powder'. Thus, it is translated here according to the root meaning as 'sesame powder', with the sub-commentary's meaning 'sesame flour' in parentheses. Usually, one puts whole sesame seeds in a mortar, not powder; however, it is called so because it will become powder when ground.

Indeed, as materiality is well-washed and purified (through contemplation) by that yogi, becoming disentangled and perfectly clear, in that same way, the defilements opposed to that knowledge settle down like sediment. The mind becomes clear like water above mud. The mental states (immaterial states) that take that materiality as their object appear naturally.

Just like these aforementioned metaphors, this meaning can also be illustrated by other metaphors such as sugarcane (squeezing juice), a thief (interrogation), an ox (training to the yoke), curds (extracting the essence of butter), fish (cooking), and so on.

## Explanation of the Manner in which Mental States Appear

670. For that yogi whose grasping of materiality is thus well-purified, mental states appear in three ways: by way of contact (phassa), by way of feeling (vedanā), or by way of consciousness (viññāṇa). How? For one yogi, while grasping the elements in this way: "The earth element has the characteristic of hardness (the nature of hardness is the earth element)," contact (phassa) is the first impact (upon the object). The feeling associated with it is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha); perception is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha); volition together with contact is the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha); and the mind is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). Thus they appear.

Note 1: If translated strictly according to the Pali terms—ucchucoragoṇadadhimacchādīhi—it would be "sugarcane, thief, ox, curds, fish, etc." This might be difficult to understand, so meanings are added in parentheses for clarity.

Note 2: "By way of contact" means that when contact appears, all associated mental aggregates appear as well. This implies that the task of contemplating all of them is accomplished. The same applies to appearing by way of feeling and consciousness.

Similarly, while grasping "The earth element in the hair has the characteristic of hardness... [etc.] ...The earth element in the in-breath and out-breath has the characteristic of hardness," contact is the first impact. The feeling associated with it is the aggregate of feeling... [etc.] ...the mind is the aggregate of consciousness. Thus they appear. In this way, mental states appear by way of contact.

For another yogi, while grasping the elements in this way: "The earth element has the characteristic of hardness," the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), which is the feeling that experiences the flavor of that object, appears.
227:
(If feeling is apparent), the perception associated with that feeling is the aggregate of perception (saññā-khandha).

Notes:
1. By the phrase "and so forth," it indicates the three methods of contemplation for the remaining three elements: "The water element has the characteristic of flowing; the fire element has the characteristic of heat; the air element has the characteristic of supporting."
2. This means that other groups of mental aggregates also become manifest in this way. However, it does not mean to indicate that one should contemplate those other mental aggregates by reflecting on them. Therefore, instead of saying "manasikaroti—attends to" or "upaparikkhati—contemplates," it only says "upaṭṭhāti—becomes manifest (appears)."
3. In this elision (peyyāla), 40 remaining parts of the 42 body parts, such as body hair (lomā), are omitted.

The contact (phassa) and volition (cetanā) associated with that feeling are the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhāra-khandha). The consciousness associated with that feeling is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇa-khandha). Thus it becomes manifest. Similarly, when one grasps (contemplates) the hair as, "The earth element has the characteristic of hardness... etc... in the in-breath and out-breath, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness," the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-khandha), which is the feeling of the taste of that object (the earth element, etc.), becomes manifest... etc... the consciousness associated with that feeling is the aggregate of consciousness. Thus it becomes manifest. In this way, mental phenomena become manifest by way of feeling.

For another yogi, when grasping (contemplating) the elements as, "The earth element has the characteristic of hardness," and so forth, the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇa-khandha), which is the consciousness that cognizes the object (the earth element, etc.), becomes manifest. (When consciousness is apparent), the feeling associated with that consciousness is the aggregate of feeling; the perception is the aggregate of perception; the contact and volition are the aggregate of mental formations. Thus it becomes manifest. Similarly, when one grasps (contemplates) the hair as, "The earth element has the characteristic of hardness... etc... in the in-breath and out-breath, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness," the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇa-khandha), which is the consciousness that cognizes the object, becomes manifest. (When consciousness is apparent), the feeling associated with that consciousness is the aggregate of feeling; the perception is the aggregate of perception; the contact and volition are the aggregate of mental formations. Thus it becomes manifest. In this way, mental phenomena become manifest by way of consciousness.

By this same method (upāya)¹, in the 42 parts of the elements, starting with "In the hair produced by kamma, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness," one should apply the full range of methods by way of the four elements in each part, and also in the remaining bases for grasping materiality such as the eye element (cakkhu-dhātu) and so forth, which are the primary objects (mukha)¹.

Note:
1. Upāya: A method or means by which a certain purpose or benefit is achieved. Here, it refers to the method of completing the grasping of the remaining mental phenomena by making contact (phassa), etc., the primary focus.

671. I shall further instruct: Since mental phenomena become clearly manifest in three ways only to the yogi whose grasping of materiality is well-purified, only such a yogi should make an effort to grasp mental phenomena, and not any other. The fault is this: if² one gives up materiality and begins to grasp mental phenomena when only one or two material phenomena have become manifest, one will fall away from the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), just like the mountain cow³ described in the development of the earth kasiṇa. However, for the yogi who makes an effort to grasp mental phenomena after the grasping of materiality is well-purified, the meditation subject reaches growth, increase, and abundance.

Notes:
1. By grasping the eye element as the primary object, the 53 types of materiality associated with it are grasped. Therefore, the eye element is the primary (mukha) means for grasping those 53 types of materiality. The same should be understood for the ear element (sota-dhātu), etc.
2. Connect "If..." with "...makes an effort."
3. This refers to a cow that, before her front legs are firm, lifts her hind legs and slips from the mountain and dies; she does not reach the new place and cannot return to her old place, thus losing both. This is the intended meaning.

That yogi defines the four immaterial aggregates that become manifest by way of contact, etc., as "Nāma" (mentality). He defines the four great elements which are the objects of those mental aggregates, and the derived materiality (upādā-rūpa) dependent on those four great elements, as "Rūpa" (materiality). In this way, he [opens up] all phenomena of the three planes (tebhūmaka)—namely the 18 elements, 12 bases, and 5 aggregates—as if opening a box (samugga)¹ with a sword (khagga).

Note:
1. The names "box" or "casket" are translations of the word *samugga*. A box or casket that is tightly closed with its lid appears as a single object. When it is pried open with a sword, the lid and the base are separated; this is an analogy for how mentality and materiality are distinguished. In old Nissaya and Burmese translations, *samugga* was translated as "pan-kat." Nowadays, very few people would know the shape of a "pan-kat." According to the Kavi-myet-hman spelling book, a "pan-kat" was an item used by ancient kings and ministers to hold betel and flowers; it was also called a betel tray, flower tray, or betel container. The Mahāṭīkā of the Visuddhimagga explains *samugga* as "samuggaṃ mañjūsāsadisaṃ mahāsamuggaṃ," meaning a large *samugga* similar to a chest or box. This explanation only makes clear that it is large and like a box, but since boxes come in many shapes, the exact shape of a *samugga* is difficult to determine. In dictionary Nissayas, the word *samugga* is translated as a wicker basket or a round box.
228:
They translate it as a flower basket, a flower tray, or a casket. In the commentary to the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, it is illustrated with an example: inside a large box called a peḷā, five small caskets called samugga are placed; inside one of those samugga caskets, four small boxes called karaṇḍa are placed; and inside each karaṇḍa box, various types of clothing and ornaments are stored. In the commentary to the Samugga Jātaka of the Navanipāta, the word samugga is defined as a karaṇḍa casket; it explains that a Dānava ogre put his human wife into a casket called a samugga, swallowed it, and carried her with him wherever he went. Therefore, the word samugga [can be understood as] a flower basket, a flower tray, a casket, or a small box.

Just as one might split a twin palm shoot or palm root—which appears as one before being split but becomes two halves when split—one distinguishes [reality] into two parts: Name and Form. One reaches the conclusion that beyond mere Name and Form, there is no other being, person, deva, or Brahma.

## Comparison with Many Suttas

672. That yogi, having distinguished Name and Form according to their true nature as described, further distinguishes and decides the meaning—'This is only Name (which inclines towards an object) and Form (which is deformed and does not know the object); there is no such thing as a being, no such thing as a person'—by means of many Suttas, for the purpose of better abandoning this worldly designation 'being, person,' for the purpose of transcending the delusion of a being, and for the purpose of establishing the mind on the level of non-delusion. Indeed, it was said:

Note: All the translated meanings such as [flower basket, etc.] should be considered appropriate. However, because the object called 'flower basket' is difficult to recognize nowadays, and because the 'casket' and 'small box' appear as one before opening but clearly become two when opened, making it an easily understood metaphor, they are translated here as 'casket' and 'small box'.

1. Tāla (palm tree) + kanda (bulb/tuber) = tālakanda (palm bulb/root). Large palm trees do not have bulbs or tubers; only the young palm root that people today roast or boil and eat is the bulb or tuber of the palm tree. It also appears as one before being split, but becomes two halves when split. Therefore, the word tālakanda is translated here as 'palm shoot' or 'palm root'. In current Nissayas and translations, it appears as 'palm bud/sprout'. It seems it was originally written as 'palm bulb-sprout' by taking the word kanda to mean bulb or sprout. The word kanda cannot mean 'bud'.

'Just as with the assembly of parts, the word "chariot" is used, so when the aggregates exist, there is the convention "a being".'

This statement was spoken by the bhikkhunī named Vajirā.

Furthermore:

'Just as, friends, space enclosed by timber, vines, clay, and grass is reckoned as a "house," even so, space enclosed by bones, sinews, flesh, and skin is reckoned as a "form-body".'

This statement was spoken by the Venerable Sāriputta.

Furthermore:

'Only suffering arises, suffering stays and passes away. Nothing but suffering arises, nothing but suffering ceases.'

This statement was also spoken by the bhikkhunī named Vajirā.

## Clarification of Name and Form through Similes

673. In this way, through hundreds of Suttas, only Name and Form are illustrated, not a being or a person. Therefore, just as when parts such as the axle, wheels, frame, and pole are arranged in a certain way, there is the mere designation 'chariot,' but in the ultimate sense, when each part is examined, there is no such thing as a 'chariot';

And just as when the building materials of a house, such as timber and so on, stand enclosing a space in a certain way, there is the mere designation 'house,' but in the ultimate sense, (when each part is examined), there is no such thing as a 'house';

And just as when the fingers, thumb, and so on, are positioned in a certain way, there is the mere designation 'fist'; when the lute-bowl, strings, and so on, (are positioned in a certain way), there is the mere designation 'lute'; when the elephant corps, cavalry, and so on, (are positioned in a certain way), there is the mere designation 'army'.
229:
[229] When city walls, ramparts, houses, and gates are arranged in a certain way, there is the mere conventional designation "city." When the trunk, branches, twigs, and leaves are arranged in a certain way, there is the mere conventional designation "tree." However, in the ultimate sense, when each part is examined individually, there is no such thing as a "tree." In the same way, when the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha) are present, there is the mere conventional designation "being" (satta) or "person" (puggala). But in the ultimate sense, when each phenomenon is examined, there is no "being" that is the basis for the grasping of "I am" (asmi) or "I" (ahaṃ).

Note: The word "asmi" (I am) indicates the clinging of conceit (māna). By the word "I am," it includes all verbal actions of pride such as "I am capable," "I know," "I am noble," or "I am accomplished." The word "ahaṃ" (I) should be understood as indicating the clinging of wrong view (diṭṭhi) and craving (taṇhā).

In the ultimate sense, one sees that there is only mind and matter (nāma-rūpa). The vision of a practitioner who sees in this way is called the vision of knowledge according to reality (yathābhūta-dassana).

674. But whoever rejects this vision of seeing things as they truly are and holds the view that "a being truly exists," must accept either its destruction or its non-destruction. If he accepts its non-destruction, he falls into the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). If he accepts its destruction, he falls into the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). Why? Because, unlike curd which remains as a successor to milk (when the milk changes), there is no other substance that remains as a successor to that self (atta) when it is destroyed.

Note: One must accept one or the other; it is impossible to reject both while holding that a being exists. If one holds that the self, called a being, does not perish but moves from life to life, he falls into the eternalist view. If one holds that a being is completely destroyed at death, he falls into the annihilationist view, because he believes nothing of the self remains. In the right view (sammā-diṭṭhi), while the current process of mind and matter perishes at death and there is no self, if craving is not yet abandoned, a new process of mind and matter arises due to the power of kamma, continuing into a new life. Thus, it does not fall into annihilationism because it doesn't say everything ends, nor into eternalism because it doesn't say the same self moves to the next life. In the present life, there is only a process of mind and matter; no person or self exists in the ultimate sense. For a Buddha or an Arahant who is free from craving, when they attain Parinibbāna, no new mind and matter arise because the cause is absent; the process simply ceases. This is not the destruction of a self, but the cessation of the process. Thus, one stands in the Middle Way of Right View.

If one holds that "a being exists eternally," it is called lagging behind (olīyanti). If one holds that "it is annihilated," it is called overreaching (atidhāvanti). Therefore, the Blessed One said:

"Bhikkhus, overwhelmed and obsessed by two views, some devas and humans lag behind, some overreach, and only those with vision see."

"And how, bhikkhus, do some lag behind? Bhikkhus, devas and humans delight in being, rejoice in being, and are satisfied with being. When the Dhamma is taught to them for the cessation of being, their minds do not leap forward, do not gain confidence, do not settle, and do not resolve. Thus, bhikkhus, some lag behind."

"And how, bhikkhus, do some overreach? Some, being troubled, ashamed, and disgusted by being, delight in non-being (vibhava), thinking: 'Sirs, since this self is annihilated and destroyed upon the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, this is peaceful, this is sublime, this is reality.' Thus, bhikkhus, some overreach."

"And how, bhikkhus, do those with vision see? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees what has come to be as having come to be (bhūtaṃ bhūtato passati). Having seen what has come to be as having come to be, he practices for the sake of disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what has come to be. Thus, bhikkhus, those with vision see." (Itivuttaka 49).

Note: If one is free from defilements, kamma cannot produce results, so new mind and matter do not arise, and only the suffering of the process of mind and matter ceases. While one should hold this view, overreaching occurs when one holds that existence ceases simply by death even when defilements are not yet abandoned.

"Sirs, when this self is annihilated and destroyed upon the breakup of the body..."
230:
...it perishes; it no longer exists after death. This cessation, this destruction, this non-existence is peaceful; this cessation, this destruction, this non-existence is sublime; this cessation, this destruction, this non-existence is true and unerring"—thus they delight and desire. Monks, in this way, some pass beyond.

Monks, how do those with the eye (of wisdom) see? Monks, in this teaching, a bhikkhu sees an arisen phenomenon (the five aggregates) as an arisen phenomenon. Having seen an arisen phenomenon as an arisen phenomenon, he practices for disenchantment, for dispassion, and for the cessation (of that phenomenon). Monks, in this way, those with the eye (of wisdom) see.

[238] 675. Therefore, for example: a wooden machine (mechanical puppet) is empty of a self, soulless, and without effort or activity. However, by the power of the combination of wood and strings, it moves and it stands; it appears as if it has effort and as if it has activity. In the same way, this mind and matter (nāmarūpa) are also empty of a self, soulless, and without effort or activity. However, by the power of the mutual combination of mind and matter, they move and they stand; they appear as if they have effort and as if they have activity. Thus should it be understood. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"Nāma and rūpa truly exist here,
But no being or man is found herein;
It is empty, like a constructed machine,
A mere mass of suffering, similar to grass and wood."

This (mind and matter) is not only illustrated by the analogy of the wooden machine; it should also be illustrated by other analogies such as the bundle of reeds. Just as when two bundles of reeds are set up leaning against each other, one serves as a support for the other, and when one falls, the other also falls; even so, in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhava), mind and matter proceed by depending on each other; one is the support for the other. When one falls by way of death, the other also falls. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"Nāma and rūpa are a pair,
Both are mutually dependent;
When one is broken, both are broken,
Because they are conditions (for each other)."

Note 1: The phrase "because they are conditions" is a translation of the word paccayā. In current sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) texts, it appears as paccayā hontāpi. According to that version, it would be translated as "even though they are conditions for each other, when one breaks, both break." The meaning is not clear. The meaning is only clear as: when one thing that is mutually a cause and dependent on the other breaks, the other also breaks because it lacks its supporting cause. Therefore, the word paccayā is taken as a qualitative attribute (hetumanta-visesana) and translated as "because they are conditions for each other." In the sub-commentary, it should also simply be paccayā hontā without the word pi.

676. Alternatively, another analogy: Just as when a sound arises depending on a drum struck with a drumstick, the drum is one thing and the sound is another; the drum and the sound are unmixed. The drum is empty of the sound, and the sound is empty of the drum. In the same way, when mind arises depending on matter (rūpa) known as the "base, door, and object," the matter is one thing and the mind is another; mind and matter are unmixed. Mind is empty of matter, and matter is empty of mind. Nevertheless, just as the sound arises depending on the drum, the mind arises depending on matter. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"The mental states with contact as the fifth do not arise from the eye,
Nor from the object, nor from between the two;
Conditioned things arise depending on causes,
Just as the sound of a drum that is struck."

[231] The mental states with contact as the fifth related to hearing do not arise from the ear...
231:
1. The mental states with contact as the fifth—namely, contact, feeling, perception, intention, and consciousness—do not arise from the sound, nor from the ear, nor from between the two... [Pe]... 

The mental states related to smelling, with contact as the fifth, do not arise from the nose, nor from the odor, nor from between the two... [Pe]... 

The mental states related to tasting, with contact as the fifth, do not arise from the tongue, nor from the flavor, nor from between the two... [Pe]... 

The mental states related to touching, with contact as the fifth, do not arise from the body, nor from the tangible, nor from between the two... [Pe]... 

Conditioned states (related to thinking) do not arise from the heart-base, nor do they emerge from the mental-object base (dhammāyatana). Conditioned states arise depending on causes (such as the heart-base, mental objects, and attention). For example, it is like the way the sound of a drum arises when it is struck.

677. Furthermore, in this context, mentality (nāma) is powerless; it is unable to occur by its own power. It does not eat, drink, speak, or maintain postures such as walking. Materiality (rūpa) is also powerless; it is unable to occur by its own power. For it has no desire to eat, drink, speak, or maintain postures. Rather, materiality occurs depending on mentality, and mentality occurs depending on materiality. When there is mentality's desire to eat, drink, speak, or maintain postures, materiality eats, drinks, speaks, and maintains postures.

To clarify this meaning, they cite this analogy: Suppose a blind man and a cripple both wish to travel to a certain place. The blind man says to the cripple, "Friend, I can perform the task of walking with my legs, but I have no eyes with which to see the even and uneven ground." The cripple says to the blind man, "Friend, I can perform the task of seeing with my eyes, but I have no legs with which to go forward or backward." Then the blind man, being glad, lifts the cripple onto his shoulders. The cripple, sitting on the blind man's shoulders, says, "Leave the left, take the right; leave the right, take the left." There, the blind man [232] is powerless and weak; he cannot go by his own power and strength. The cripple is also powerless and weak; he cannot go by his own power and strength. Yet, it is not that their traveling does not occur; it does occur by depending on each other. In the same way, mentality is powerless; it cannot arise by its own power, nor can it occur in those various activities such as going. Materiality is also powerless; it cannot arise by its own power, nor can it occur in those various activities such as seeing. Yet, it is not that the arising or occurrence of this pair, mentality and materiality, does not happen; it does happen by depending on each other. Therefore, the following verses are said:

Conditioned states do not arise by their own power, nor do they stand by their own power. Being weak in themselves, they arise following the will of other causes.

These conditioned states arise due to the support of other states;
232:
They arise because of being supported by and taking other states as objects. These conditioned states are produced by object-conditions and other states.

Just as people travel on the ocean depending on a boat, so the body of mentality (nāma-kāya) occurs depending on materiality (rūpa).

Just as a boat travels on the ocean depending on people, so the body of materiality (rūpa-kāya) occurs depending on mentality (nāma).

Just as both people and the boat travel on the ocean depending on each other, so both mentality and materiality are mutually dependent.

The correct seeing of mentality and materiality—which stands on the ground of non-delusion (asammoha-bhūmi) after overcoming the perception of a being (satta-saññā) by the meditator who defines mentality and materiality in these various ways—should be understood as "Purification of View" (diṭṭhivisuddhi). The terms "definition of mentality-materiality" (nāmarūpa-vavatthāna) and "delimitation of formations" (saṅkhāra-pariccheda) are also synonyms for this same Purification of View.

In the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga) composed for the purpose of gladdening good people, in the section on the development of wisdom, this is the Eighteenth Chapter, titled "Description of the Purification of View."

## The Description of the Purification of View is concluded.

## 19. Description of the Purification by Overcoming Doubt

## Discussion on the Discerning of Conditions (Paccaya-pariggaha-kathā)

[233] 678. As for the occurrence of the Purification by Overcoming Doubt: The knowledge that stands having overcome doubt regarding the three periods of time by discerning the conditions of this very mentality and materiality (already discerned) is called "Purification by Overcoming Doubt" (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi).

A meditating monk who wishes to fulfill that (Purification by Overcoming Doubt), like a skilled physician who, having seen a disease, seeks its origin and cause, or like a compassionate man who, seeing a young infant lying on its back on the road, considers, "Whose son is this?" and looks for the child's parents—so he sets about seeking the root-causes and supporting causes of that mentality and materiality.

At the very beginning, that meditator considers thus: "Mentality and materiality are not without cause. (They must certainly have a cause; for if they were without cause), they would be the same in all places..."
233:
...because it would lead to the same state [of arising] for all persons [2] at all times [1].

It is not caused by a 'Lord' (Issara)—the Owner or Creator—and the like [3], because there is no such thing as a Lord or Creator who exists apart from name-and-form [4]. Even in the view of those teachers who say, 'The Lord and the like are just name-and-form,' the name-and-form designated as 'Lord' and so on would then be without a cause.

Notes:
1. In the time before the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) etc. arises, and in the time after it has ceased, there is no cause or basis for eye-consciousness etc. However, if it could arise without a cause, then eye-consciousness etc. would arise at all those times without a cause. Thus, it is meant that it would lead to the same state by eye-consciousness etc. arising at all times without a cause.
2. For those who are blind, for the formless Brahmas, and for the non-percipient (asaññasatta) Brahmas, there is no cause or basis for eye-consciousness etc. However, if it could arise without a cause, then eye-consciousness etc. would arise for such persons as well without a cause. Thus, it is meant that it would lead to the same state by eye-consciousness etc. arising for all persons without a cause. Here, the mention of eye-consciousness etc. is merely an illustration; in truth, if things could arise without a cause, then every distinction in the world would arise for everyone in every place and at all times.
3. By the word 'and the like,' one should include Nature (Pakati), the Soul (Purisa), the Progenitor (Pajāpati), Time (Kāla), and so on.
4. If a Lord or Creator truly existed, they would also have to be just name-and-form; there are no Lords etc. who are independent of name-and-form. If they are considered independent of name-and-form, they would be a mere name or designation for something that does not exist; in reality, they do not exist. Therefore, it means that such non-existent Lords etc. are useless and do not enter into the truth.

Because it would result in being without a cause, the meditator reflects that there must be root causes and supporting conditions for this name-and-form. 'What then are those causes?'

## 1. The First Method of Discerning Conditions

679. After reflecting on the root causes and supporting conditions of name-and-form as stated, that meditator discerns the root causes and supporting conditions of this physical body (rūpakāya) thus: When this body is born, it is not born inside blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, or water-lilies [1], etc., nor is it born inside jewels, pearls, or necklaces, etc. On the contrary, it is born between the stomach (āmasaya) and the bowels (pakkāsaya), with the belly-lining behind and the backbone in front, surrounded by the entrails and mesentery. Being itself foul-smelling, loathsome, and disgusting, it is born in the extremely cramped space of the womb, which is foul-smelling and loathsome, like a worm born in rotting fish, rotting bread, a cesspool, or a sewer [2].

Notes:
1. Based on the term 'blue lotus' (nīluppala), the 'Uppala' lotus should be understood as a lotus of the same species as the blue lotus. Regarding the 'Paduma' and 'Puṇḍarīka' lotuses, the Commentaries decide: 'A lotus with fewer than a hundred petals, or a red lotus, is called Puṇḍarīka; a lotus with a hundred petals, or a white lotus, is called Paduma.' In the Dictionary (Abhidhāna), however, it says: 'A common lotus is called Paduma; a white lotus is called Puṇḍarīka; and a small lotus, a water-lily, or a white lotus that blooms in the evening is called Saugandhika.'
2. A 'cesspool' (tamsī-twin) is a place where washing-water, impurities from childbirth, etc., are discarded. A 'sewer' (tamsī-myaung) is the place where that washing-water, impurities from childbirth, etc., flow along with mud. This should be noted in accordance with the Mūlapaṇṇāsa Commentary (1.83).

For this physical body which is born in such a manner, these four factors—ignorance (avijjā), craving (taṇhā), clinging (upādāna), and kamma—are the root causes (hetu) because they produce it. Nutriment (āhāra) is the supporting condition (paccaya) because it sustains it. Thus, these five factors are the root causes and supporting conditions.

Among these five, the three factors starting with ignorance are the dependence (upanissaya) for this body, just as a mother is the support for a young child. Kamma produces it, just as a father begets a son.
234:
Just as a nurse supports a child (by feeding and caring for it), so nutriment supports (this material body by feeding and caring for it); thus he discerns the supporting condition.

Having thus discerned the conditions for the material body (rūpakāya), he again discerns the conditions for the mental body (nāmakāya) in this way: "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises," and so on.

When that yogi sees the occurrence of mentality-materiality due to conditions in this way, he contemplates: "Just as this mentality-materiality occurs due to conditions in the present time, so it occurred due to conditions in the past, and so it will occur due to conditions in the future."

Notes:
1. Connect as: "is the root cause of this material body... is the supporting cause... are the root and supporting causes."
2. This root cause is also called the "generative cause" (janaka-paccaya).
3. Connect as: "Having discerned... he discerns."

## Overcoming the Sixteen Types of Doubt

680. For that yogi who contemplates in this way, the five types of doubt concerning the past (the previous sequence of aggregates) are abandoned: "Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past?"

Notes:
1. Connect the word "yogi" with the final verb "abandons" at the end of the section.
2. These two doubts arise based on the views of Eternalism (sassata) and Fortuitous Origination (adhiccasamuppatti).
3. The Commentaries and Sub-commentaries explain that this doubt refers to whether one was a king, a brahmin, a layman, or a deity. It could also refer to whether the self possessed form, feeling, etc., in the past.
4. This refers to doubt regarding physical appearance—whether one was tall, short, fair, or dark. The Sub-commentary also mentions doubt regarding the mode of occurrence, such as whether one was created or arose without a cause.
5. This is similar to the third type of doubt, but specifically concerns the sequence of successive existences.

The five types of doubt concerning the future (the future sequence of aggregates) are also abandoned: "Shall I be in the future? Shall I not be in the future? What shall I be in the future? How shall I be in the future? Having been what, what shall I become in the future?"

Regarding the present time, he also has doubts concerning his own aggregates: "Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where did this being come from? Where will it go?"

Notes:
1. Doubt as to whether the "self" (attā) one perceives actually exists or not.
2. The Commentaries explain this as doubting whether one is truly a king, etc. However, since such doubt does not contradict the practice of Insight (vipassanā) and is not overcome simply by knowing mentality-materiality, it should be reflected upon. It is more appropriate to take it as doubting whether the self possesses form, feeling, etc.
3. The Sub-commentary explains this as doubt regarding the shape or size of the internal soul (jīva-attā). This includes doubting whether it possesses form, etc.

All these sixteen types of doubt are abandoned.

Note 1: "Abandons" (pahīyati) here means the disappearance or removal through the abandonment by suppression (vikkham-bhana-pahāna). Thus, it means doubt ceases within the yogi's continuity, just as in the Dhajagga Sutta where "will be abandoned" means "will disappear."

## The Second Method of Discerning Conditions

681. Another yogi sees the causes of mentality in two ways, as common and uncommon, and the causes of materiality in four ways, such as kamma, etc. To explain: The causes of mentality are of two kinds: common and uncommon. Among them, the six doors such as the eye and the six objects such as forms are the common (sādhāraṇa) causes of mentality, because all types of mentality, categorized as wholesome and so on, arise because of those doors and objects.

Attention (manasikāra) and so on are the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) causes. For wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), hearing the True Dhamma, and so on, are causes only for wholesome mentality; the opposite (unwise attention, etc.) is for unwholesome; kamma, etc., for resultant (vipāka) mentality; and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), etc., for functional (kiriya) mentality.

Notes:
2. Connect as: "sees the causes... which are of two kinds / four kinds."
3. This refers to the divisions of wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional, as well as specific divisions like joy-associated (somanassa-sahagata). In short, it refers to the 81 mundane consciousnesses and 52 mental factors.
235:
The cause such as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is associated only with functional mentality (kiriya-nāma). This is the reason for it being called 'uncommon' (asādhāraṇa).

As for the causes of matter (rūpa), they are these four causes: kamma, consciousness (citta), temperature (utu), and nutriment (āhāra). Among these, kamma, which is only of the past, assists kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa). Consciousness while arising assists mind-born matter (cittaja-rūpa). Temperature and nutriment assist temperature-born matter (utuja-rūpa) and nutriment-born matter (āhāraja-rūpa) at the moment of presence (ṭhitikkhaṇa). In this manner, one meditator performs the discernment of the causes of mentality-materiality.

Having seen the occurrence of mentality-materiality due to causes in the present in this way, that meditator contemplates: "Just as this mentality-materiality has occurred due to causes in the present life-period, so too it occurred due to causes in the past life-period, and so too it will occur due to causes in the future life-period." For the meditator contemplating thus, the sixteen kinds of doubt regarding the three periods of time are abandoned in the manner already stated (in paragraph 680).

Notes:
1. It means it is only the cause of wholesome mentality.
2. It means it is only the cause of unwholesome mentality.
3. It means it is only the cause of resultant mentality.
4. It means it is only the cause of functional mentality.
5. It means it causes kamma-born matter to arise.

## 3. The Third Method of Discerning Causes

682. Another meditator, having seen the arrival at aging of those very formations (saṅkhāra) known as mentality-materiality and the dissolution of those that have aged, [discerns:] "This so-called aging and death of formations exists when there is birth (jāti); birth exists when there is becoming (bhava); becoming exists when there is clinging (upādāna); clinging exists when there is craving (taṇhā); craving exists when there is feeling (vedanā); feeling exists when there is contact (phassa); contact exists when there are the six bases (saḷāyatana); the six bases exist when there is mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa); mentality-materiality exists when there is consciousness (viññāṇa); consciousness exists when there are formations (saṅkhāra); and formations exist when there is ignorance (avijjā)." In this way, he performs the discernment of the causes of mentality-materiality by way of reverse dependent origination (paṭiloma-paṭiccasamuppāda). Then, for that meditator, the sixteen kinds of doubt are abandoned in the manner already stated.

## 4. The Fourth Method of Discerning Causes

683. Another meditator performs the discernment of the causes of mentality-materiality by way of the forward dependent origination (anuloma-paṭiccasamuppāda) as previously shown in detail: "Thus, with ignorance as condition, formations come to be," and so on. Then, for that meditator, doubt is abandoned in the manner already stated.

## 5. The Fifth Method of Discerning Causes

684. Another meditator [discerns:] "In the previous kamma-process becoming (kamma-bhava), the nature of delusion (not knowing suffering, etc.) is ignorance (avijjā); the efforts are formations (saṅkhāra); the longing and desire is craving (taṇhā); the approaching and clinging is clinging (upādāna); and the volition is becoming (bhava). Thus, these five things that were completed while performing the kamma-process becoming in the previous life are the causes for rebirth-linking in this present life. In this present life, the rebirth-linking consciousness associated with the previous life is consciousness (viññāṇa); the descending (the group of descending states) is mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa); the clarity is the base (āyatana); the touching is contact (phassa); and the experiencing is feeling (vedanā). Thus, these five things are the results that have arisen in this present life-process (upapatti-bhava) due to the kamma performed in the past. In this present life, because of the maturity of the bases (when the eye, ear, etc., bases mature), delusion is ignorance (avijjā)... (pe)... volition is becoming (bhava). Thus, these five things that are completed while performing the kamma-process becoming in this present life are the causes for rebirth-linking in the future life." In this way, by way of this method of teaching, he performs the discernment of the causes of mentality-materiality by way of the cycle of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa) and the cycle of result (vipāka-vaṭṭa).

Notes:
1-2. Connect as: "The meditator... having seen... abandons doubt." Here too, it means doubt is removed by being distant through the abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna) in that meditator's continuity. Note the same for what follows.
3. Connect as: "The meditator... performs the discernment of the causes of mentality-materiality."

## Explanation of the Different Kinds of Kamma

685. In that statement "by way of the cycle of kamma and the cycle of result," kamma is fourfold:
(1) Kamma to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya-kamma),
(2) Kamma to be experienced in the next life (upapajjavedanīya-kamma),

Notes:
1. Diṭṭhadhamma = present life + vedanīya = kamma whose result is to be experienced.
236:
(2) Upapajja-vedanīya-kamma: Kamma to be experienced in the life immediately following this one.
(3) Aparāpariya-vedanīya-kamma: Kamma to be experienced in the third life and onwards. [Note 1]
(4) Ahosi-kamma: Lapsed kamma, which has occurred but cannot produce a result.
Among these four types of kamma, within a single javana-vīthi (impulsion process) consisting of seven javanas:
Wholesome or unwholesome, the volition of the first javana is called diṭṭhadhamma-vedanīya-kamma. This kamma gives its result in this very life (existence). If it is unable to give its result, it becomes ahosi-kamma (lapsed kamma) by virtue of the triad teaching: "There was kamma, but there was no kamma-result; there will be no kamma-result; there is no kamma-result."
The volition of the seventh javana, which completes the wholesome act such as giving (dāna) or the unwholesome act such as killing (pāṇātipāta), is called upapajja-vedanīya-kamma. This kamma gives its result in the immediately following existence (the second life). If it is unable to give its result, it becomes ahosi-kamma in the same manner as mentioned before.
The volitions of the five middle javanas between the first and the seventh are called aparāpariya-vedanīya-kamma. This kamma gives its result in the future, such as the third life onwards, whenever it gains an opportunity. As long as the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra), the continuity of mind and matter (nāma-rūpa khandhā), persists, this kamma never becomes ahosi-kamma.

686. Furthermore, there are four other types of kamma:
(1) Garuka-kamma: Weighty kamma, which is either very grave unwholesome kamma or very powerful wholesome kamma.
[Note 1: Aparā - other than the present and the next life + pariyāya - in the turn of existence - in the third life etc. + vedanīya - kamma with results to be experienced.]
(2) Bahula-kamma: Habitual kamma, which is performed many times and well-cultivated. [Note 1]
(3) Āsanna-kamma: Death-proximate kamma, which is performed or remembered at the time of death.
(4) Kaṭattā-kamma: Reserve kamma, which is merely performed (deeds done).
Among these four, whether wholesome or unwholesome, between weighty (garuka) and light (lahuka) kamma, if there is a weighty unwholesome kamma such as matricide (mātughātaka-kamma) [Note 2] or a weighty wholesome kamma of the sublime state (mahaggata), that weighty kamma alone ripens first and produces its result.
Similarly, between habitual kamma (bahula) and non-habitual kamma (abahula), if there is habitual kamma performed and cultivated many times, such as the state of being virtuous (susīlya) or the state of being immoral (dussīlya), that habitual kamma alone ripens first and produces its result.
Āsanna-kamma is the kamma remembered at the time of death. Indeed, a person is reborn in a new existence by means of whatever kamma they are able to remember when death is near.
Kamma that is free from these three aforementioned types and has gained repeated cultivation [Note 3] is called kaṭattā-kamma. In the absence of those three types of kamma, this kaṭattā-kamma pulls (produces) the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).

[Note 1: This kamma is called āciṇṇa-kamma (frequently practiced kamma) in the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.]
[Note 2: By the words "such as," one should include parricide (pitughātaka), killing an Arahant (arahantaghātaka), wounding a Buddha (lohituppāda), causing a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda), and fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) which firmly holds that there is no kamma or its result.]
[Note 3: If the text in the Visuddhimagga reads aladdhāsevanaṃ, it should be translated as "not having gained cultivation"; only then will it be distinct from bahula-kamma.]

687. There are another four types of kamma:
(1) Janaka-kamma: Productive kamma, which produces the resultants and kamma-born matter.
(2) Upatthambhaka-kamma: Supportive kamma.
(3) Upapīḷaka-kamma: Obstructive kamma, which approaches and oppresses.
(4) Upaghātaka-kamma: Destructive kamma, which approaches and cuts off or kills.
Among these four, janaka-kamma can be either wholesome or unwholesome. This janaka-kamma produces the kamma-born matter and the resultant mental aggregates (vipāka-nāma-khandhā) both at the moment of rebirth-linking and during the course of existence (pavatti).
Upatthambhaka-kamma cannot produce its own result; it supports the pleasure or pain that is currently arising in the resultant state produced by another kamma's rebirth-linking, causing it to persist for a long time.
Upapīḷaka-kamma oppresses and hinders the pleasure or pain that is currently arising in the resultant state produced by another kamma's rebirth-linking, and does not allow it to continue for a long time.
Upaghātaka-kamma, being itself either wholesome or unwholesome, kills another weak kamma, prevents its result, and creates an opportunity for its own result. When an opportunity is thus created by kamma, that resultant is said to have arisen.
237:
[237] In this way, the distinction of these twelve types of kamma (in terms of being powerful or weak) and the distinction of their results (in terms of being low or sublime, etc.) are fully evident in their true nature only to the Buddhas' Knowledge of the Result of Kamma (kammavipākañāṇa); it is not shared by the disciples. However, a meditator (vipassaka) should know the distinction of kamma and the distinction of result in part. Therefore, this distinction of kamma is shown here merely as an indication.

688. Thus, by placing these twelve types of kamma (which are merely parts that cause the present sequence of results) into the [collective] cycle of kamma (kammavaṭṭa), a meditator performs the discernment of the conditions for mentality-materiality by way of the cycle of kamma and the cycle of result.

## Seeing Only Kamma and Result

That meditator, having seen the occurrence of mentality-materiality due to causes through the cycle of kamma and the cycle of result as described, sees: 'Just as this mentality-materiality arises due to causes in the present life (through the cycle of kamma and the cycle of result), so too it arose due to causes in the past through the cycle of kamma and the cycle of result, and so too it will arise due to causes in the future through the cycle of kamma and the cycle of result.'

In this way, there is only kamma and the result of kamma, only the cycle of kamma and the cycle of result, only the flow of kamma and the flow of result, only the continuity of kamma and the continuity of result, only the action and the fruit of the action.

Kamma and results proceed; results have kamma as their origin (or: results are the origin of kamma). From kamma, there is again a new existence; in this way, the world (the continuity of mentality-materiality) proceeds.

Note:
1. This means due to the causes of the cycle of kamma and the cycle of result.
2. In the present life, the results such as 'consciousness, mentality-materiality, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling' lead to the arising of craving, clinging, and the process of becoming (kammabhava). Only when interpreted this way can it be understood that kamma causes result, and that very result causes kamma again, and that kamma causes result again, thus revolving continuously.

The meditator who sees in this way abandons all sixteen types of doubt that are spoken of starting with 'Was I in the past?' and so on, concerning the past and other times. In all three planes of existence, four modes of birth, five destinations, seven stations of consciousness, and nine abodes of beings, only mentality-materiality proceeding by way of the connection between cause and effect is apparent. That meditator sees no 'doer' over and above the cause, nor an 'experiencer' over and above the occurrence of the result. When there is a cause, the wise use the conventional term 'doer'; when there is the occurrence of a result, they use the conventional term 'experiencer'—this is well seen by him with right insight-wisdom.

689. Therefore, the ancients said:
'There is no doer of kamma, nor an experiencer of the result;
Only pure phenomena proceed—this is the right view.
While kamma and result thus proceed with their causes,
Like the seed and the tree, their first beginning is not known,
Nor is their non-occurrence seen in the future saṃsāra.'

Note:
- The three planes of existence (bhava) are: the sense plane, the fine-material plane, and the immaterial plane.
- The four modes of birth (yoni) are: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneous birth.
- The five destinations (gati) are: hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts (petas), the human realm, and the deva realm.
- The seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) are: (1) Beings with different bodies and different perceptions, such as humans and some devas; (2) Beings with different bodies and the same perception, such as the Brahmas of the first jhāna and beings in the lower realms; (3) Beings with the same body and different perceptions, such as the Brahmas of the second jhāna; (4) Beings with the same body and the same perception, such as the Brahmas of the third jhāna and the Vehapphala Brahmas (the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas are also included here); (5) Beings in the base of infinite space; (6) Beings in the base of infinite consciousness; (7) Beings in the base of nothingness.
238:
These are the seven.
The nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa) are these nine: the aforementioned seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) plus the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). They are called the nine abodes of beings because they are the dwelling places of beings.
Just as the beginning is not known and cannot be known, the beginning of kamma and its resultant (vipāka) is not known and cannot be known. In the future, as long as the round of rebirths (saṃsāra)—the continuous process of the aggregates of mentality and materiality—exists, the non-arising or cessation of kamma and its resultant is not seen and cannot be seen.

[238] Because they do not know this meaning (that there is no person who performs kamma, etc.), the sectarians, lacking the personal desire for right vision, cling to the perception of a 'being'. Holding views of eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) and annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi), they conflict with one another and adopt the sixty-two types of wrong views.
Bound by the bond of views, they are swept away by the stream of craving (taṇhā). Being swept away by the stream of craving, they are not liberated from suffering.
A monk, a disciple of the Buddha, having known this meaning in the manner described (that there is no person who performs kamma, etc.), penetrates the profound and subtle condition that is empty (of a being and of a result).
Kamma does not exist within the resultant (Note 1); the resultant does not exist within the kamma (Note 2). Both are empty of each other, yet there is no fruit without kamma.
Note 1: Just as the threads, which are the cause, do not remain unchanged within the cloth, which is the result, kamma does not remain within the resultant; it is not that kamma itself becomes the resultant without perishing.
Note 2: Just as the ear of grain does not exist as a whole within the stalk, which is the cause, the resultant does not lie latent within the kamma at the time of its occurrence; it arises anew only at the moment of its manifestation.
They are empty of each other; however, the result cannot occur without the cause, kamma.
For example, fire is not in the sun, nor in the sun-gem (magnifying glass), nor in the dried cow-dung. Nor does that fire exist outside of them. Yet, fire arises because of the combination of factors such as sunlight.
Similarly, the resultant is not found within the kamma, nor does it exist outside of the kamma. Kamma also does not exist within that resultant.
Kamma is empty of the result; the result does not exist in the kamma. In reality, however, the result arises from that kamma, depending solely on kamma.
Indeed, in this world, there is no Deva or Brahma who is the creator of the round of rebirths—the process of the aggregates. Only pure phenomena (dhamma) proceed, conditioned by the collection of causes.

## Full Understanding of All Phenomena
690. In this way, having grasped the conditions of mentality-materiality by way of the round of kamma and the round of resultants, and having abandoned doubt regarding the three periods of time, all past, future, and present phenomena become clearly known to that yogi by way of death (cuti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) (Note 1).
Note 1: If one understands and accepts the nature of the passing away and arising of death and rebirth-linking, which are the end and beginning of a life, then all phenomena included within that life are considered known; it means they are understood, or it amounts to knowing them.
This wisdom of knowing mentality-materiality along with its causes is called 'Full Understanding of the Known' (ñātapariññā), the wisdom that analytically understands what should be known.
That yogi knows thus: The aggregates that arose due to kamma in the past life ceased right there in that past life. In this present life, however, other aggregates have arisen due to the cause of past kamma. There is not even a single phenomenon that has come from the past life to this present life.
In this present life as well, the aggregates produced by kamma will cease (within this life). In the next new life, other aggregates will arise. Not even a single phenomenon will go from this life to the next new life.

## Example of the Connection Between Two Lives
