In truth, the sound of recitation from the teacher's mouth does not enter the student's mouth, yet it is not that the recitation in the student's mouth does not occur due to the teacher's recitation; it does indeed occur. [239] Similarly, the medicated water drunk by a messenger does not enter the stomach of the sick person, yet it is not that the illness of the sick person is not cured due to the messenger drinking the medicated water; it is indeed cured. The decorations applied to the face do not go into the reflection of the face in a mirror...
239:
It is not meant that one knows all these things as precisely and clearly as if knowing with omniscient knowledge or direct insight knowledge.

Just as the decoration applied to the face appears in the reflection of the face in a mirror or the like due to the cause of that decoration, yet the decoration itself does not pass into the reflection; and just as the flame of one lamp does not pass over to another wick, yet the flame in the other wick arises due to the cause of the flame from the original wick; similarly, not even a single state (dhamma) passes over from the past life to this life, nor from this life to a future life. Yet, it is not that the aggregates, bases, and elements (khandha-āyatana-dhātu) do not arise in this life due to the cause of the aggregates, bases, and elements in the past life; they do indeed arise. And it is not that the aggregates, bases, and elements will not arise in the future life due to the cause of the aggregates, bases, and elements in this present life; they will indeed arise.

Just as eye-consciousness, which occurs immediately after the mind-element (mano-dhātu), does not come from that mind-element, yet it is not that it does not arise immediately after that mind-element; it does indeed arise. (Note 1)

Notes:
1. When a visible object appears at the eye-door, the five-door adverting consciousness (pañcadvārāvajjana) which adverts to that object arises. After that, the eye-consciousness which sees that object arises. Then, the receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana), the investigating consciousness (santīraṇa), and the determining consciousness (votthapana) arise once each. Then, seven moments of impulsion (javana) and two moments of registration (tadārammaṇa) occur, after which life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurs as if in sleep. This completes one eye-door cognitive series (vīthi) that sees a visible object. In this series, the first adverting consciousness, the five-door adverting, is called 'mind-element' (mano-dhātu) here. Immediately after that consciousness ceases, eye-consciousness arises. In this process, the mind-element called five-door adverting does not itself transform into eye-consciousness; that mind-element, having arisen, ceases completely. However, due to the proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya) of that mind-element, eye-consciousness arises anew immediately after it; it is meant that it does not fail to arise.

Similarly, the mental continuum occurs at the time of rebirth-linking. The preceding death-consciousness (cuti-citta) ceases, and subsequently, the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) arises.

There is no state that performs the function of intervening between that death-consciousness and rebirth-linking consciousness; there is no interval between them. Nothing at all passes over from this death-consciousness, yet the rebirth-linking consciousness arises.

691. For the yogi who has thus understood all phenomena by way of death and rebirth-linking, the knowledge of discerning the causes of mind and matter (nāmarūpa-paccaya-pariggaha-ñāṇa) becomes fully strengthened in every way. The sixteen kinds of doubt are more thoroughly abandoned. (Note 1)

Not only those sixteen, but also the eight kinds of doubt, such as 'doubting the Teacher,' etc. (Note 2), are also abandoned. The sixty-two kinds of wrong views are suppressed.

Notes:
1. Here also, it means that in the mental continuum of that yogi, the sixteen kinds of doubt are further distanced and removed by way of abandonment by suppression (vikkhamphana-pahāna).
2. By the word 'etc.', it refers to these seven: 'doubts the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training (sikkhā), the past, the future, both the past and future, and dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).'

## Designation as Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma, etc.

The knowledge that stands having overcome doubt regarding the three periods of time by discerning the causes of mind and matter through these various methods should be understood as 'Purification by Overcoming Doubt' (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi). 'Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma' (Dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa), 'Knowledge of things as they really are' (Yathābhūta-ñāṇa), and 'Right Vision' (Sammā-dassana) are all synonyms for this Purification by Overcoming Doubt. Indeed, it has been said:

'Ignorance is the cause, formations are the results produced by the cause. Both these states are results produced by causes—such wisdom in discerning the cause is called Knowledge of the Stability of Dhamma.'

'When one contemplates as impermanent, what states does one know and see as they really are? How does Right Vision occur? How, by following that [vision], are all formations well seen as impermanent? Where is doubt abandoned? ... When one contemplates as suffering ... When one contemplates as non-self, what states does one know and see as they really are? ... Where is doubt abandoned?' If such a question is asked:

[240] 'One who contemplates as impermanent knows and sees the sign of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta) as it really is; therefore, it is called the knowledge of Right Vision. Seeing thus, by following that [vision], all formations are well seen as impermanent. In this collection of states well seen, doubt is abandoned. One who contemplates as suffering knows and sees the continuous occurrence of mind and matter (upādinnaka-pavatta) as it really is. ... One who contemplates as non-self knows and sees both the sign of formations and the continuous occurrence of mind and matter as they really are; therefore, it is called the knowledge of Right Vision. Seeing thus, by following that [vision], all formations are well seen as non-self. In these states well seen, doubt is abandoned.' Thus it should be answered.
240:
If it is asked: "Are these states—knowledge of things as they really are (yathābhūta-ñāṇa), right vision (sammādassana), and knowledge of overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-ñāṇa)—different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they the same in meaning and different only in phrasing?" The answer is: "These states—knowledge of things as they really are, right vision, and knowledge of overcoming doubt—are the same in meaning and differ only in phrasing." This is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

## On Being Called a Lesser Stream-enterer
The benefit is as follows: A vipassanā yogi endowed with this knowledge of overcoming doubt, also known as knowledge of things as they really are, finds relief¹ and a firm footing¹ in the Buddha's Dispensation and is of certain destiny², thus being called a "Lesser Stream-enterer" (Cūḷasotāpanna).

Note 1: In the ultimate sense (paramattha), "relief" in the Dispensation refers to the Noble Fruit (ariya-phala), and "footing" refers to the Noble Path (ariya-magga). Although this yogi has not yet attained that Noble Path and Fruit, because they stand in the practice that is the cause for attaining them, they are as if they have found relief and a footing. Therefore, it is said, "having found relief and having found a footing." (From the Sub-commentary).

Therefore, a monk, desiring the knowledge of overcoming doubt, should always be mindful and comprehend the causes of mind and matter in every way. Here it ends.

This is the nineteenth chapter, titled the Exposition of the Purification by Overcoming Doubt (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi-niddesa), in the section on the Development of Wisdom in the Visuddhimagga, composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.

## End of the Detailed Exposition of the Purification by Overcoming Doubt.

Note 2: A vipassanā yogi with non-declining Purification by Overcoming Doubt is endowed with mundane perfection and purity of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Therefore, even if they have not yet known or attained anything higher than this Purification by Overcoming Doubt, they are destined for a happy rebirth (sugati). For this reason, they are called a Lesser Stream-enterer. (Also from the Sub-commentary). In this Sub-commentary, special attention should be paid to the qualifying phrase "with non-declining Purification by Overcoming Doubt" and the causal phrase "because of being endowed with the perfection and purity of virtue, etc." By the method of inversion, these phrases show that such a yogi's destiny is certain only if the Purification by Overcoming Doubt does not decline; if it declines, it is not certain. Similarly, the destiny is certain only if virtue, etc., remain perfect; if virtue, etc., are ruined, it is not certain.

## 20. Detailed Exposition of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and What Is Not the Path
## Sammasanakathā—Explanation of the Knowledge of Comprehension

[241] 692. The knowledge that stands having discerned the right path and the wrong path in this way—"This (the wisdom of insight that proceeds correctly) is the right path; this (the aura, light, etc.) is not the right path"—is called the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and What Is Not the Path (Maggāmaggañāṇadassana-visuddhi)¹.

A yogi wishing to fulfill that Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and What Is Not the Path should practice methodical insight (naya-vipassanā) called comprehension by groups (kalāpa-sammasana)².

Note 1: Magga (right path) + amagga (not the path/wrong path) + ñāṇa (knowledge) + dassana (vision) + visuddhi (purification). This is the meaning of each term.
Note 2: "He contemplates those states" (te dhamme samanupassati)—insight that contemplates states individually in their respective order in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception occurs only to Buddhas, not to disciples. Therefore, desiring to show group insight (kalāpa-vipassanā) which contemplates by groups in this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this was taught. (Burmese translation of the Commentary on the Anupada Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa).
In that Sutta, the way Venerable Sāriputta practiced insight is shown. It details how he contemplated the mental factors of the jhānas, such as initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), happiness (sukha), one-pointedness (ekaggatā), and contact (phassa), in the four fine-material jhānas and the lower three immaterial jhānas.
242:
(General characteristics) are not apprehended in the same way as the individual characteristics of materiality and mentality, which are established and manifest by their own nature as fixed entities. Rather, those general characteristics (impermanence, etc.) are apprehended and known like qualities superimposed upon the individual characteristics, because they can only be apprehended and known by making the aspects of destruction, oppression by rise and fall, and the absence of following one's will the primary focus. Therefore, the Commentator said, "applying the three general characteristics." (2-387)

The specific characteristics such as hardness, contact, etc., which belong only to a particular materiality or mentality, are called individual characteristics (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa) or specific characteristics (visesa-lakkhaṇa). The characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, which apply equally to all material and mental phenomena, are called general characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa).

1. "Having characteristic as object" means taking the characteristic as the object of focus.

Knowing the individual characteristics of mental and material phenomena is indeed predominant (1).

From the knowledge of comprehension by groups (kalāpa-sammasana-ñāṇa) up to the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) is the domain—the field—of the full understanding by investigating (tīraṇa-pariññā). Indeed, during this period, knowing the general characteristics is predominant.

From the knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅga-ñāṇa) upwards is the domain—the field—of the full understanding by abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). Indeed, from that knowledge of dissolution onwards, the seven contemplations (2), which accomplish the abandoning of the perception of permanence and so on, are predominant. As it is taught: "Contemplating as impermanent, one abandons the perception of permanence; contemplating as suffering, one abandons the perception of pleasure; contemplating as non-self, one abandons the perception of self; becoming revulsed, one abandons delight; becoming dispassionate, one abandons lust; causing cessation (contemplating cessation), one abandons origination; relinquishing, one abandons grasping."

In these three types of full understanding mentioned in this manner, because only the knowledge of the delimitation of mental and material phenomena (nāmarūpa-pariccheda-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of discerning causes (paccaya-pariggaha-ñāṇa) have been accomplished, this yogi has attained only the full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā). The others, namely the full understanding by investigating and the full understanding by abandoning, are yet to be attained (should be strived for). Therefore, when the full understanding by investigating occurs, the knowledge of what is path and what is not-path (maggāmagga-ñāṇa) arises. That full understanding by investigating occurs immediately after the full understanding of the known. Therefore, I have said: "A yogi who wishes to fulfill that purification by knowledge and vision of what is path and not-path should first apply effort in the knowledge of comprehension by groups (kalāpa-sammasana-ñāṇa)."

Notes:
1. "Knowing the individual characteristics is predominant" means it is the most noble. Alternatively, it means that knowledge alone governs, or it is the domain of that knowledge.
2. These seven contemplations are explained in detail in the section on the knowledge of dissolution.

694. In that (knowledge of comprehension by groups), this is the text from the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

"What is the wisdom in defining past, future, and present phenomena by summarizing them, which is the knowledge of comprehension (1)? Whatever materiality there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—one defines all materiality as impermanent: this is one comprehension. One defines it as suffering: this is one comprehension. One defines it as non-self: this is one comprehension. Whatever feeling... whatever consciousness... one defines it as non-self: this is one comprehension.

Notes:
1. In the word 'vavatthāne', if the locative case is taken, it should be translated as "in defining." However, since it refers to the wisdom involved in defining, and should also be a word ending in the nominative case, it is translated here as "defining" to make the meaning smooth.
2. If the word 'sammasane' ends in the locative, it should be translated as "in comprehending." Here, as in Note 1, it is translated according to the smoothness of the meaning.

(Whatever feeling... far or near) (1) one defines all that feeling (as impermanent: this is one comprehension... whatever perception... whatever mental formations... as impermanent... whatever consciousness...) (2) one defines all that consciousness as impermanent... as non-self: this is one comprehension.

One defines the eye, past, future, or present... aging-and-death as impermanent: this is one comprehension. One defines it as suffering... as non-self: this is one comprehension.

Materiality—past, future, or present—is impermanent in the sense of exhaustion, suffering in the sense of fear, and non-self in the sense of corelessness. Wisdom in defining it by summarizing it thus is the knowledge of comprehension. Feeling... perception... mental formations (3)... consciousness (3)... eye... aging-and-death... is the knowledge of comprehension.

Materiality—past, future, or present—is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to fall, subject to dispassion, subject to cessation. Wisdom in defining it by summarizing it thus is the knowledge of comprehension. Feeling... consciousness... eye... aging-and-death, past, future, or present, is impermanent, conditioned... subject to cessation. Wisdom in defining it by summarizing it thus is the knowledge of comprehension."
243:
It is called the Knowledge of Comprehension (Sammasana-ñāṇa).

Wisdom that summarizes and determines that "Materiality—whether past, future, or present—is impermanent, a conditioned thing (saṅkhata) formed by a combination of causes, dependent on causes, subject to exhaustion, subject to decay, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation" is called the Knowledge of Comprehension. Feeling...

Notes:
1-2. The paragraphs within parentheses are words slightly expanded from the Pali ellipses (peyyāla) to make it easier for those with less scriptural knowledge to understand.
3. If such large punctuation marks are found before a sentence is complete, they should also be noted as ellipses (peyyāla).

(Perception is... Mental formations are...) Consciousness is... The eye is... [etc.] ...Aging and death are impermanent, conditioned things formed by a combination of causes... [etc.] ...subject to cessation. Wisdom that summarizes and determines in this way is called the Knowledge of Comprehension.

[243] Wisdom that summarizes and determines that "Because of birth (jāti), there is aging and death (jarāmaraṇa); without birth, there is no aging and death" is called the Knowledge of Comprehension. This applies to the past duration of time and the future duration of time as well: "Because of birth, there is aging and death; without birth, there is no aging and death." Wisdom that summarizes and determines in this way is called the Knowledge of Comprehension. "Because of existence (bhava), there is birth... [etc.] ...Because of ignorance (avijjā), there are mental formations (saṅkhāra); without ignorance, there are no mental formations." Wisdom that summarizes and determines in this way is called the Knowledge of Comprehension. This applies to the past duration of time and the future duration of time as well: "Because of ignorance, there are mental formations; without ignorance, there are no mental formations." Wisdom that determines in this way is called the Knowledge of Comprehension.

That reflective consideration is called 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing; it is called 'wisdom' (paññā) in the sense of understanding in various ways. Therefore, it is said: "Wisdom that summarizes and determines past, future, and present phenomena is the Knowledge of Comprehension through reflective consideration." Here ends the Pali passage.

In this Pali, through the ellipsis (peyyāla) indicated by "the eye... [etc.] ...aging and death," it should be understood that the following groups of phenomena are summarized: the phenomena occurring at the doors along with the six doors and six objects, the five aggregates, the six doors, the six objects, the six consciousnesses, the six contacts, the six feelings, the six perceptions, the six volitions, the six cravings, the six thoughts, the six examinations, the six elements, the ten kasinas, the thirty-two parts of the body, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twenty-two faculties, the three elements (of existence), the nine types of existence, the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, the four attainments, and the twelve factors of dependent origination.

Note 1: Peyyāla (ellipsis) means 'capable of being protected/preserved.' It refers to a summarized phrase that the wise are capable of expanding and preserving so that it is not lost.

Indeed, it was said in the Abhiññeyyaniddesa (Description of things to be known by direct knowledge):

"Monks, all should be known with direct knowledge (abhiññeyya). And what, monks, is the 'all' that should be known with direct knowledge? The eye, monks, should be known with direct knowledge. Forms... eye-consciousness... eye-contact... and whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too should be known with direct knowledge. The ear... [etc.] ...and whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too should be known with direct knowledge.

Forms... [etc.] ...consciousness... the eye... [etc.] ...the mind... forms... [etc.] ...mental objects... eye-consciousness... [etc.] ...mind-consciousness... eye-contact... [etc.] ...mind-contact..."
244:
...volition regarding mental objects (dhamma-sañcetanā). Craving for forms (rūpa-taṇhā)... [etc.] ...craving for mental objects (dhamma-taṇhā). Thought regarding forms (rūpa-vitakka)... [etc.] ...thought regarding mental objects (dhamma-vitakka).

Examination regarding forms (rūpa-vicāra)... [etc.] ...examination regarding mental objects (dhamma-vicāra) (should be known with direct knowledge).

The earth element... [etc.] (1) ...the consciousness element. The earth kasina (jhāna)... [etc.] (2) ...the consciousness kasina (jhāna). Hair... [etc.] ...urine, the brain (should be known with direct knowledge).

The eye base... [etc.] (3) ...the mental-object base. The eye element... [etc.] (4) ...the mind element, the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element. The eye faculty... [etc.] (5) ...the faculty of one who has known (should be known with direct knowledge).

The sense-sphere element, the fine-material element, the immaterial element. Sense-sphere existence, fine-material existence, immaterial existence, percipient existence, non-percipient existence, neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient existence, one-constituent existence, four-constituent existence, five-constituent existence (should be known with direct knowledge).

The first jhāna... [etc.] ...the fourth jhāna. The liberation of mind through loving-kindness... [etc.] ...the liberation of mind through equanimity. The attainment of the base of infinite space... [etc.] ...the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Ignorance should be known with direct knowledge... [etc.] ...aging and death should be known with direct knowledge."

Notes:
1. Here, the ellipsis (pe) hides the four elements: water, fire, air, and space.
2. Here, the ellipsis (pe) hides the eight kasinas: water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, white, and space.
3. Here, the ellipsis (pe) hides: forms, ear, sounds, nose, odors, tongue, tastes, body, tangibles, and the mind base.
4. Here, the ellipsis (pe) hides: forms, eye-consciousness, ear, sounds, ear-consciousness, nose, odors, nose-consciousness, tongue, tastes, tongue-consciousness, body, tangibles, and body-consciousness elements.
5. Here, the ellipsis (pe) hides: the faculties of ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, life, femininity, masculinity, pleasure, pain, joy, grief, equanimity, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, the 'I shall know the unknown' faculty, and the faculty of final knowledge.

Because all these (groups of things to be known with direct knowledge) were taught in detail in the Abhiññeyyaniddesa as mentioned, they are summarized here with ellipses (peyyāla). Specifically, the supramundane (lokuttara) states mentioned in this summarized list should not be taken in this context of insight (vipassanā) because they are not to be comprehended (as impermanent/suffering/non-self). To guide further: there are those (material and mental) phenomena that are suitable for comprehension; among those, a person should begin the practice of comprehension on whichever phenomena are clear to them and can be easily grasped and observed.

695. Among those phenomena suitable for comprehension, the following is the application of the method of beginning by way of the aggregates (khandha):

"Whether past... [etc.] ...whatever materiality exists, one determines all that materiality as impermanent; this is one comprehension. One determines it as suffering and as non-self; this is another comprehension." By this procedure, this monk determines all materiality—even that which is indicated indefinitely as "whatever materiality"—by dividing it into eleven categories, such as the past triad and the four dyads beginning with internal, etc. He determines all materiality as impermanent; he comprehends it as impermanent.

How? By the very method taught hereafter. Indeed,
245:
"Form that is past, future, or present is impermanent in the sense of exhaustion (khayaṭṭhena)"—this statement is taught [later].

Therefore, this yogi monk [contemplates]: "Whatever form existed in the past, that form was exhausted in the past itself; it does not reach this present existence; thus it is impermanent in the sense of exhaustion."

"Whatever form is future and will arise in the next existence, that too will be exhausted in that future existence itself; it will not go to a further existence; thus it is impermanent in the sense of exhaustion."

"Whatever form is present, that too is exhausted right here; it does not go from here [to the next]; thus it is impermanent in the sense of exhaustion."

"Whatever form is internal, that too is exhausted internally; it does not become external; thus it is impermanent in the sense of exhaustion."

"Whatever form is external... gross... subtle... inferior... superior... far... near, that too is exhausted right there; it does not become far; thus it is impermanent in the sense of exhaustion."

All these contemplations constitute one comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa) by way of "impermanent in the sense of exhaustion." However, by way of division, there are eleven kinds.

Furthermore, all that form, past etc., is suffering in the sense of fear (bhayaṭṭhena). "In the sense of fear" means because of being fearful. Indeed, what is impermanent is a source of fear, as in the case of the devas in the Sīhopama Sutta. Thus, this contemplation of suffering is also one comprehension by way of "suffering in the sense of fear." By way of division, there are eleven kinds.

Just as it is suffering, so too all that form is non-self in the sense of corelessness (asārakaṭṭhena). "In the sense of corelessness" means because of the absence of a core of self as imagined [by outsiders] such as: "The self is the owner (sāmī), the resident (nivāsī—who remains while the body perishes), the doer (kāraka—of all actions like going and seeing), the feeler (vedaka—of good and bad), and the self-willed (sayaṃvasī—who can control things as desired)." Indeed, that which is impermanent and suffering cannot even prevent its own impermanence or the oppression by rise and fall; how then could it have the nature of a doer, etc.? Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, if this form were self, this form would not lead to oppression," and so forth. Thus, this [contemplation] as non-self...

Note 1: The word 'ābādhāya' is translated as 'for oppression'. [Translators] usually translate it as 'for pain/sickness'. Form cannot feel pain, nor can perception, formations, or consciousness. The root 'bādh' does not mean pain; it only means oppression. The five aggregates are oppressed by aging, sickness, etc. Therefore, it is translated here as 'for oppression'.
246:
...this contemplation is also one comprehension by way of "non-self in the sense of corelessness." By way of division, there are eleven kinds. This same method applies to feeling and so on.

696. The reason for teaching again is: an impermanent thing is definitely of the nature of being conditioned (saṅkhata), etc. Therefore, for the purpose of showing synonyms (pariyāya) of the word 'impermanent', and for the purpose of showing the occurrence of attention (manasikāra) in various modes, the Pali text is stated again: "Form that is past, future, or present is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation." This same method applies to feeling and so on.

## Contemplation by Way of the Forty Modes

697. For the purpose of making that same comprehension of impermanence, suffering, and non-self in the five aggregates firm and stable, the Blessed One—in the analysis (Vibhaṅga) of the question: "By which forty modes does one acquire conformable patience (anulomika-khanti)? By which forty modes does one enter the path of rightness (sammattaniyāma)?"—taught as follows:

"Seeing the five aggregates as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as a plague, as a disaster, as a terror, as a menace, as fickle, as perishable, as unenduring, as no protection, as no shelter, as no refuge, as empty, as vain, as void, as non-self, as a danger, as subject to change, as coreless, as the root of calamity, as a murderer, as non-existence, as subject to taints, as conditioned, as Mara's bait, as subject to birth, as subject to aging, as subject to illness, as subject to death, as subject to sorrow, as subject to lamentation, as subject to despair, as subject to defilement"—

by these forty modes, "Seeing the five aggregates as impermanent, one acquires conformable patience. Seeing that the cessation of the five aggregates is permanent Nibbāna, one enters the path of rightness," and so on.

In this way, while analyzing conformable knowledge (anulomana-ñāṇa), the comprehension of impermanence etc. was stated in detail. By way of that [method] also, he comprehends these five aggregates.

Note 1: See previous note 5 on page 290.

698. How? That yogi contemplates each aggregate as impermanent (1) because it does not go beyond the end which is destruction, and because it has a beginning and an end. He contemplates it as suffering (2) because it is constantly oppressed by arising and vanishing, and because it is the basis for suffering. He contemplates it as a disease (3) because it must be sustained by requisites like food and clothing, and because it is the root of illnesses.
247:
One contemplates it as a boil (gaṇḍato) because it is associated with the three kinds of suffering, because it oozes the pus and impurities of defilements, and because it is swollen, ripened, and bursts through birth, aging, and breaking (4).

One contemplates it as a dart (sallato) because it produces pain, because it pricks within, and because it is difficult to extract (5).

One contemplates it as a calamity (aghato) because it is blameworthy, because it brings ruin and destruction, and because it is the basis for evil (6).

One contemplates it as an affliction (ābādhato) because it causes a lack of independence and because it is the proximate cause of illness (7).

One contemplates it as a stranger (parato) because it does not occur according to one's will and because it is uncontrollable (8).

Notes:
1-2. Connect as: "That yogi contemplates each aggregate..."
3. The three kinds of suffering (dukkha) are: (1) Dukkha-dukkha: physical and mental pain; (2) Vipariṇāma-dukkha: physical and mental pleasure [which changes]; (3) Saṅkhāra-dukkha: the suffering inherent in the collection of conditioned formations.
4. A sick person must depend on others for help, such as being lifted, and cannot act according to their own will. Similarly, those with aggregates must depend on others and other conditions, thus they do not occur according to one's will. This means it causes one to depend on others and other conditions instead of one's own will.

One contemplates it as disintegrating (palokato) because it is greatly destroyed by illness, aging, and death (9).

One contemplates it as a plague (ītito) because it brings many disasters (vyasana) (10).

One contemplates it as a menace (upaddavato) because it brings great unforeseen harms and because it is the basis for all troubles (11).

One contemplates it as a terror (bhayato) because it is the source of all fears and because it is the opposite of the supreme relief known as the cessation of suffering (12).

One contemplates it as an adversity (upasaggato) because it is followed by many harms, because it is beset by faults such as greed, and because it is intolerable like a malignant possession (13).

One contemplates it as fickle (calato) because it is shaken by illness, aging, and death, as well as by worldly conditions (lokadhamma) such as gain and loss (14).

One contemplates it as perishable (pabhaṅguto) because it tends to reach destruction through effort or by its own nature (15).

One contemplates it as unenduring (addhuvato) because it falls and perishes at every moment and because it lacks any state of firmness (16).

One contemplates it as no protection (atāṇato) because it does not guard and because safety cannot be obtained from it (17).

One contemplates it as no shelter (aleṇato) because it is not fit to be relied upon and because it does not perform the function of a shelter even for those who rely on it (18).

Notes:
1. Upaddava refers to royal punishment and so on.
2. The term "and so on" indicates fame (yasa), obscurity (ayasa), blame (nindā), praise (pasaṃsā), pleasure (sukha), and pain (dukkha).

One contemplates it as no refuge (asaraṇato) because it lacks the state of removing fear for those who take refuge in it (19).

One contemplates it as empty (rittato) because it is devoid of the states of permanence, beauty, happiness, and self as imagined by worldlings (20).

One contemplates it as vain (tucchato) because of being empty, or because it is insignificant. Indeed, in the world, what is insignificant is called vain (21).

One contemplates it as void (suññato) because it is devoid of [a self conceived as] a master (sāmī) of the house of aggregates, an inhabitant (nivāsī), a doer (kāraka), a feeler (vedaka), or a director (adhiṭṭhāyaka) (22).

One contemplates it as non-self (anattato) because it itself lacks ownership and so on (23).

One contemplates it as a danger (ādīnavato) because the process is suffering and because that suffering is a fault. Alternatively, it is called ādīnava because it proceeds or goes very miserably; this is a name for a wretched person. The aggregates are also wretched, and because they are like a wretched person, one contemplates them as miserable (24).
250:
In that nutritive-essence-as-the-eighth octad (ojāṭṭhamaka), when the nutritive essence (ojā) reaches its static phase (ṭhī), it produces another nutritive-essence-as-the-eighth octad. In this manner, it connects four or five successions of occurrences. What is called temperature-origination with kamma as condition (kammapaccaya utusamuṭṭhāna) is when the fire element born of kamma (kammaja-tejo-dhātu) reaches its static phase and produces a temperature-born nutritive-essence-as-the-eighth octad. In that octad as well, the temperature produces another nutritive-essence-as-the-eighth octad. In this manner, it connects four or five successions of occurrences. Thus, the arising of kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) should be understood.

Note 1: The 7 groups of material decads—eye-decad, ear-decad, nose-decad, tongue-decad, body-decad, sex-decad, and heart-base-decad—amount to 70 types of matter in essence.
Note 2: The term should be understood as 'consciousness supported by kamma' and 'the phenomena produced by that consciousness'; the same applies to subsequent terms.

702. Among mind-born (cittaja) phenomena, this classification should be understood: (1) Consciousness (citta), (2) Mind-produced (citta-samuṭṭhāna), (3) Mind-conditioned (citta-paccaya), (4) Mind-conditioned nutriment-produced (citta-paccaya āhāra-samuṭṭhāna), and (5) Mind-conditioned temperature-produced (citta-paccaya utu-samuṭṭhāna). Therein, consciousness refers to the 89 types of consciousness.

Note 1: Although already shown in the section on the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), the 89 types of consciousness will be briefly enumerated here for easy reference and understanding:
12 unwholesome consciousness, 18 rootless consciousness, 24 sense-sphere beautiful consciousness, 15 fine-material-sphere consciousness, 12 immaterial-sphere consciousness, and 8 supramundane consciousness; totaling 89 types of consciousness.

Among them, the 12 unwholesome consciousness (akusala-citta) are: 8 consciousness rooted in greed (lobhamūla-citta)—namely, one unprompted (asaṅkhārika) consciousness accompanied by joy (somanassa) and associated with wrong view (diṭṭhigata-sampayutta), one prompted (sasaṅkhārika) consciousness, one unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy and dissociated from wrong view (diṭṭhigata-vippayutta), one prompted consciousness (totaling 4 accompanied by joy); and similarly, 4 consciousness accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā).
2 consciousness rooted in hatred (dosamūla-citta)—namely, one unprompted and one prompted consciousness accompanied by displeasure (domanassa).
2 consciousness rooted in delusion (mohamūla-citta)—namely, one consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt (vicikicchā-sampayutta), and one consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness (uddhacca-sampayutta).

Note: The 18 rootless consciousness (ahetuka-citta) are: 7 unwholesome-resultants (akusala-vipāka)—namely, eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, and likewise ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness; body-consciousness accompanied by pain (dukkha); receiving consciousness accompanied by equanimity, and investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
8 wholesome-resultant consciousness (kusala-vipāka)—namely, eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity, and likewise ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness; body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure (sukha); receiving consciousness accompanied by equanimity, investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity, and investigating consciousness accompanied by joy.
3 functional consciousness (kiriya-citta)—namely, five-door adverting consciousness accompanied by equanimity, mind-door adverting consciousness accompanied by equanimity, and smile-producing consciousness (hasituppāda) accompanied by joy.

The 24 sense-sphere beautiful consciousness (kāmāvacara-sobhana-citta) are: 8 great wholesome consciousness (mahākusala-citta)—namely, one unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta), one prompted consciousness, one unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy and dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta), one prompted consciousness (totaling 4 accompanied by joy); and similarly, 4 consciousness accompanied by equanimity. Likewise, there are 8 great resultant consciousness (mahāvipāka) and 8 great functional consciousness (mahākiriya).

The 15 fine-material-sphere consciousness (rūpāvacara-citta) are: 5 fine-material-sphere wholesome consciousness—namely, first jhāna, second jhāna, third jhāna, fourth jhāna, and fifth jhāna consciousness. Likewise, there are 5 resultant consciousness and 5 functional consciousness.

The 12 immaterial-sphere consciousness (arūpāvacara-citta) are: 4 wholesome consciousness—namely, consciousness of the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Likewise, there are 4 resultant consciousness and 4 functional consciousness.

The 8 supramundane consciousness (lokuttara-citta) are: 4 wholesome consciousness—namely, the path consciousness of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahatship; and 4 resultant consciousness—namely, the fruition consciousness of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arahatship.

Among these, it should be understood that 32 types of consciousness produce matter, posture, and intimation. 26 types of consciousness produce only matter and posture. 19 types of consciousness produce only matter. 16 types of consciousness do not produce matter, posture, or intimation.

To explain in detail: Among the 54 sense-sphere consciousness, the 32 types of consciousness that produce matter, posture, and intimation are: 8 wholesome consciousness, 12 unwholesome consciousness, 10 functional consciousness other than the mind-element, and 2 direct-knowledge (abhijñā) consciousness (wholesome and functional).

The 26 types of (absorption-impulsion) consciousness that produce matter and posture, but not intimation, are: 10 fine-material-sphere (wholesome and functional) consciousness excluding resultants (and direct-knowledge), 8 immaterial-sphere (wholesome and functional) consciousness, and 8 supramundane consciousness.

Note 1: To make it clear for readers, the meaning of the verse is translated in an easy-to-understand way. A strictly grammatical translation would be: 'Among those, the 32 types, 26 types, 19 types, and 16 types of consciousness should be known as those that produce or do not produce matter, posture, and intimation.'
Note 2: This means 'other than the five-door adverting consciousness'.
Note 3: 'Excluding resultants' means setting aside resultant consciousness. Regarding direct-knowledge consciousness, the sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) gives two views: (1) it should be included in the exclusion because it is part of the fine-material wholesome/functional fifth jhāna and was already included in the previous group of 32; (2) it need not be explicitly mentioned as 'remaining' implies what is left after those already mentioned.

The 19 types of consciousness that produce only matter, but not posture or intimation, are: 10 sense-sphere life-continuum (bhavaṅga) consciousness, 5 fine-material-sphere life-continuum consciousness, 3 mind-elements, and 1 rootless resultant mind-consciousness element accompanied by joy.

The 16 types of consciousness that do not produce matter, posture, or intimation are: the twice five-fold consciousness (10), the rebirth-linking consciousness of all beings, the death-consciousness of Arahants, and the 4 immaterial resultant consciousness.

Among these, the consciousness that produce matter do not do so at the static phase (ṭhī) or the dissolution phase (bhaṅga). This is because at those moments, the consciousness is weak. However, at the arising phase (uppāda), the consciousness is strong; therefore, at that arising phase, it produces matter depending on the heart-base (hadayavatthu) which has arisen previously.

What is called mind-produced (citta-samuṭṭhāna) refers to the three mental aggregates and the 17-fold variety of matter: 'the sound-nonad (sadda-navaka), bodily intimation, vocal intimation, space element, lightness, malleability, wieldiness, integration, and continuity.'
251:
Mind-conditioned (cittapaccaya) refers to the matter produced by the four causes, as taught in the statement: "Later-arising consciousness and mental factors are a condition for this pre-arising body (by way of post-nascence condition)." Nutriment-origination conditioned by mind (cittapaccaya-āhārasamuṭṭhāna) means that the nutritive essence (ojā) within mind-born matter, upon reaching its static phase (ṭhī), produces another octad with nutritive essence as the eighth (ojaṭṭhamaka).

Notes:
1. The five-door adverting consciousness and the two types of receiving consciousness are called the mind element (manodhātu).
2. The 76 types of consciousness, excluding the ten-fold sense-consciousness and the three mind elements, are called the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu). Among them, the joy-accompanied investigating consciousness, being a rootless resultant, is called the 'rootless resultant joy-accompanied mind-consciousness element'.
3. This refers to the three aggregates associated with consciousness: the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), and the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).

In this manner, it connects successions of two or three stages. Temperature-origination conditioned by mind (cittapaccaya-utusamuṭṭhāna) means that the temperature (utu) produced by consciousness, upon reaching its static phase, produces another octad with nutritive essence as the eighth. In this manner, it connects successions of two or three stages. Thus, the arising of mind-born matter should be understood.

703. Regarding things born of nutriment (āhāraja), the following classification should be understood: (1) nutriment (āhāra), (2) nutriment-origination (āhārasamuṭṭhāna—matter produced by nutriment), (3) nutriment-conditioned (āhārapaccaya—matter supported by nutriment), (4) nutriment-origination conditioned by nutriment (āhārapaccaya-āhārasamuṭṭhāna—nutriment-produced matter supported by nutriment), and (5) temperature-origination conditioned by nutriment (āhārapaccaya-utusamuṭṭhāna—temperature-produced matter supported by nutriment). Among these, nutriment (āhāra) refers to edible food (kabaḷīkāra āhāra). Nutriment-origination (āhārasamuṭṭhāna) refers to the 14 types of nutriment-born matter: the octad with nutritive essence as the eighth, the space element (ākāsadhātu), lightness (lahutā), malleability (mudutā), wieldiness (kammaññatā), integration (upacaya), and continuity (santati), which are produced by the nutritive essence (ojā) that has reached its static phase, having obtained the support of and being established in the clung-to (upādinna) kamma-born (kammaja) primary elements. Nutriment-conditioned (āhārapaccaya) refers to the matter (produced by the four causes) as taught in the statement: "Edible food is a condition for this body by way of nutriment condition." Nutriment-origination conditioned by nutriment (āhārapaccaya-āhārasamuṭṭhāna) means that the nutritive essence within nutriment-born matter, upon reaching its static phase, produces another octad with nutritive essence as the eighth. In that octad as well, the nutritive essence produces another

Notes:
1. Upādinna: The mundane kamma that can be reached by craving and views + ādinna: taken as a result = upādinna: the result of mundane kamma. The Commentary (Ṭīkā) states that matter such as mind-origination conditioned by kamma can also be called kamma-born because kamma is its root cause; therefore, the term upādinna is used here for further specification.

octad with nutritive essence as the eighth; in this manner, it connects the process for ten or twelve successions. Nutriment consumed on one day (at one time) can provide support for up to seven days. Divine nutritive essence, however, can provide support for one or even two months. Nutriment consumed by a mother also spreads through the child's body and produces matter. Nutriment smeared on the body also produces nutriment-born matter. Kamma-born nutriment is called clung-to (upādinna) nutriment. That kamma-born nutriment also produces nutriment-born matter upon reaching its static phase. Within those nutriment-born matters (produced by kamma-born nutriment), the nutritive essence also produces another nutriment-born matter—in this manner, it connects successions of four or five stages. Temperature-origination conditioned by nutriment (āhārapaccaya-utusamuṭṭhāna) means that the fire element (tejodhātu) produced by nutriment, upon reaching its static phase, produces the octad with nutritive essence as the eighth, which is called temperature-origination (utusamuṭṭhāna) or temperature-born (utuja). In these instances of nutriment-origination and nutriment-conditioned matter, this nutriment-matter serves as a condition by way of producing (janaka) the nutriment-born matters. For the remaining types of matter (kamma-born, mind-born, and temperature-born), it serves as a condition by way of support (nissaya), nutriment (āhāra), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). Thus, the arising of nutriment-born matter should be understood.

704. Regarding things born of temperature (utuja), the following classification should be understood: (1) temperature (utu), (2) temperature-origination (utusamuṭṭhāna—matter produced by temperature), (3) temperature-conditioned (utupaccaya—matter supported by temperature), (4) temperature-origination conditioned by temperature (utupaccaya-utusamuṭṭhāna—temperature-produced matter supported by temperature), and (5) nutriment-origination conditioned by temperature (utupaccaya-āhārasamuṭṭhāna—nutriment-produced matter supported by temperature). Among these, temperature (utu) refers to the fire element (tejodhātu) produced by the four causes. This temperature is of two kinds: hot temperature and cold temperature. Temperature-origination (utusamuṭṭhāna) means that the temperature produced by the four causes, having obtained the support of clung-to (upādinna) matter, produces temperature-born matter in the body upon reaching its static phase.
252:
That temperature-produced matter (utuja-rūpa) is of fifteen kinds: the group of nine with sound as the ninth (saddanavaka-kalāpa), [252] the space element (ākāsadhātu), lightness (lahutā), softness (mudutā), wieldiness (kammaññatā), integration (upacaya), and continuity (santati). What is called 'temperature as a condition' (utupaccaya) means that temperature is the supporting condition for the continuous arising and ceasing of matter produced by the four causes. What is called 'temperature-originated by temperature-condition' (utupaccaya-utusamuṭṭhāna) means that the fire element (tejo-dhātu) originated from temperature, upon reaching its static phase (ṭhī), produces another group of eight with nutritive essence as the eighth (ojaṭṭhamaka); in that too, temperature produces another, and in this way, even in the non-clung-to (anupādinna) external world, temperature-originated matter continues to arise for a long time. What is called 'nutriment-originated by temperature-condition' (utupaccaya-āhārasamuṭṭhāna) means that the nutritive essence (ojā) originated from temperature, upon reaching its static phase, produces another group of eight with nutritive essence as the eighth; in that too, the nutritive essence produces another, and in this way, it connects the process for ten or twelve times. Among those temperature-originated and temperature-conditioned factors, this temperature is the condition that acts as the generator (janaka) for temperature-produced matter; for the remaining types of matter (kamma-produced, mind-produced, and nutriment-produced), it is a condition by way of the power of support (nissaya), presence (atthi), and non-disappearance (avigata). Thus, the arising of temperature-produced matter should be seen. When one sees the arising of matter in this way, it is called 'contemplating matter' at that time.

## The Manner of Contemplating the Arising of the Immaterial

705. Just as one who contemplates matter should see the arising of matter, so too, one who contemplates the immaterial (arūpa) should see the arising of the immaterial. This arising of the immaterial should be seen only by way of the eighty-one types of mundane consciousness (lokiya-cittuppāda).

The manner of the arising of the immaterial is as follows: This immaterial, by the power of kamma accumulated in the previous life, arises at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) as nineteen types of consciousness.1 The manner of its arising should be understood in the same way as explained in the Exposition of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda-niddesa). That same immaterial, consisting of nineteen types of consciousness, occurs by way of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) starting from the consciousness immediately following the rebirth-linking consciousness,2 and by way of the death consciousness (cuti) at the end of life.3 Among those nineteen types of consciousness, those belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) occur by way of registration (tadārammaṇa) when there is a strong object at the six doors.4

During the course of existence (pavatti-kāla),5 due to the non-destruction of the eye-sensitivity, the appearance of visible forms, the presence of light, and having attention (manasikāra) as the cause,6 eye-consciousness arises together with its associated states. To explain further: at the static phase (ṭhī-khaṇa) of the eye-sensitivity,1 a visible form that has also reached its static phase2 strikes the eye-sensitivity.

Notes:
1. This refers to the 19 types of rebirth-linking consciousness: 2 rootless (investigating accompanied by equanimity), 4 with two roots (great resultant dissociated from knowledge), 4 with three roots (great resultant associated with knowledge), 5 fine-material resultants, and 4 immaterial resultants. The life-continuum and death consciousness are also these same 19.
2. This means it occurs as the life-continuum (bhava + aṅga = bhavaṅga), which is a constituent of the entire life.
3. This means it occurs as the death consciousness.
4. This refers to the 8 great resultants and 2 investigating consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity as sense-sphere consciousness; more fully, 11 types of consciousness including investigating accompanied by joy are understood as registration consciousness.
5. The period from the first life-continuum after rebirth-linking until death is called the course of existence (pavatti-kāla).
6. This phrase shows that eye-consciousness can arise only when all four conditions are met: non-destruction of eye-sensitivity, appearance of visible form, presence of light, and attention.

Similarly, ear-consciousness arises when four conditions are met: non-destruction of ear-sensitivity, appearance of sound, presence of space (ākāsa), and attention. Here, 'presence of space' means an unobstructed opening from the source of sound to the ear-hole.
Nose-consciousness arises when four conditions are met: non-destruction of nose-sensitivity, appearance of smell, dependence on the air element, and attention. Here, 'dependence on the air element' means the entry of air carrying the smell into the nose.
Tongue-consciousness arises when four conditions are met: non-destruction of tongue-sensitivity, appearance of taste, dependence on the water element (moisture), and attention. Here, 'dependence on the water element' means obtaining the water element or moisture that wets the tongue.
Body-consciousness arises when four conditions are met: non-destruction of body-sensitivity, appearance of tangible object, dependence on the earth element, and attention. Here, 'dependence on the earth element' means obtaining the earth element which is the support of the body-sensitivity.
Mind-consciousness arises when four conditions are met: non-destruction of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), appearance of mental object (dhammārammaṇa), dependence on the heart-base (vatthu-rūpa), and attention. The life-continuum is said to be 'destroyed' if it cannot cause the adverting consciousness to arise immediately after it, and 'not destroyed' if it can. 'Dependence on the heart-base' means depending on the matter called the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) located within the heart.
1. 'Strikes at the static phase': visible form cannot appear in the eye-sensitivity that is just arising; it appears only when it reaches the static phase (ṭhī).
2. A visible form that is just arising also cannot appear at the eye-door; it can only appear when it reaches the static phase. Therefore, it is specifically stated as 'having reached the static phase'.

...strikes the eye-sensitivity.1 When that visible form strikes and appears, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) arises and ceases twice. Then, the functional mind-element called five-door adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana) arises, performing the function of adverting to that same object. Immediately following that, either a wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness or an unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness arises while seeing that same visible form.2 Then, the resultant mind-element called receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchanna) arises, receiving that same visible form.3 Then, the rootless resultant mind-consciousness element called investigating consciousness (santīraṇa) arises, investigating that same visible form.4 Then, [253] the rootless functional mind-consciousness element accompanied by equanimity, called determining (votthapana), which is the mind-door adverting consciousness, arises, determining that same visible form. Then, among the sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, and functional consciousnesses, one consciousness arises, occurring for five or seven impulsion (javana) moments.5

Notes:
1. 'Strikes' means appearing.
2. If it is an undesirable object (aniṭṭhārammaṇa), an unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness arises; if it is a desirable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa), a wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness arises. Thus, one of them arises according to the quality of the object.
3. Here too, either an unwholesome-resultant or wholesome-resultant receiving consciousness arises according to the object. Alternatively, unwholesome-resultant receiving follows unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness, and wholesome-resultant follows wholesome-resultant. The same applies to investigating consciousness.
4. For an ordinary desirable object, wholesome-resultant investigating accompanied by equanimity arises; for an extremely desirable object (ati-iṭṭhārammaṇa) like the Buddha, investigating accompanied by joy arises.
5. The 8 sense-sphere wholesome, 12 unwholesome, and 9 functional consciousnesses (including the smile-producing and great functional) are called the 29 sense-sphere impulsions (kāma-javana). At the time of death or during fainting, only five impulsion moments occur; at other times, seven occur.

Or else, a rootless consciousness accompanied by equanimity arises.1 Then, for sense-sphere beings, among the eleven types of registration consciousness,2 one registration consciousness arises according to the impulsion and the object.3

Notes:
1. This refers to the mind-door adverting consciousness performing the function of determining (votthapana). When the object is not clear enough to trigger impulsion, that determining consciousness itself arises two or three times and then the life-continuum follows. This process is called the second 'void' process (mogha-vāra).
2. These are the same 11 registration consciousnesses mentioned in Note 4 on page 208.
3. 'According to the impulsion and the object' means: if there is a triple-rooted impulsion, a triple-rooted or double-rooted registration arises, and so on, according to the impulsion; if there is a desirable object, a registration accompanied by joy arises, and so on, according to the object (from Mahāṭīkā).
253:
In this commentary's explanation, it is clear that in the case of a desirable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa), there are 5 somanassa-tadārammaṇas; in a moderately desirable object (iṭṭhamajjhattārammaṇa), there are 5 kusalavipāka upekkhā-tadārammaṇas; and in an undesirable object (aniṭṭhārammaṇa), there is an akusalavipāka upekkhā-santīraṇa tadārammaṇa. The manner in which tadārammaṇa occurs according to the javana is not yet clear. In this very commentary, in the explanation of the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) in the description of aggregates (khandhaniddesa), it is stated as follows:

Regarding the occurrence of tadārammaṇa, the following is a fixed rule: Immediately following any one of the kāmakusala-javanas, lobhamūla-javanas, mohamūla-javanas, or somanassa-sahagata-kiriya-javanas, in the case of a very great object (atimahantārammaṇa), any one of the 5 somanassa-tadārammaṇas occurs. Similarly, immediately following any one of the kāmakusala-javanas, akusala-javanas, or upekkhā-sahagata-kiriya-javanas, any one of the 6 upekkhā-tadārammaṇas occurs. (Mahāṭīkā).

According to the above commentary, it is to be noted as a fixed rule that after a somanassa-kiriya-javana, only a somanassa-tadārammaṇa occurs, and [after an upekkhā-kiriya-javana], only an upekkhā-tadārammaṇa occurs. However, after kāmakusala-javanas, lobhamūla-javanas, and mohamūla-javanas, there are limitations.

The same method applies to the remaining doors as well. [Note 1: In the ear-door, substitute ear-consciousness for eye-consciousness; in the nose-door, nose-consciousness; in the tongue-door, tongue-consciousness; in the body-door, body-consciousness. This is the only difference. Thus it is said, "The same method applies to the remaining doors." However, in the mind-door, the mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana) consciousness arises first, contemplating the six types of objects that have appeared, and immediately after that, the javana consciousnesses arise. This sequence of consciousness is also distinct.]

Since there is no specific note, it is known only that any one of the 11 tadārammaṇas may occur without distinction. This is also stated in the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.

In the great Abhidhamma commentary named Atthasālinī, which is the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pāḷi, the occurrence of tadārammaṇa is defined by the javana as follows: In a desirable object, after a first mahākusala consciousness javana, a similar first mahāvipāka consciousness tadārammaṇa occurs. Similarly, after the second, third, and fourth mahākusala consciousness javanas, the second, third, and fourth mahāvipāka consciousness tadārammaṇas occur respectively. In a moderately desirable object, after the 4 mahākusala upekkhā-javanas, the 4 mahāvipāka upekkhā-tadārammaṇas occur respectively. For an ahetuka person, in a desirable object, after the 2 ñāṇavippayutta somanassa-javanas, a somanassa-santīraṇa tadārammaṇa occurs; in a moderately desirable object, after the 2 ñāṇavippayutta upekkhā-javanas, a kusalavipāka upekkhā-santīraṇa tadārammaṇa occurs. In a desirable object, after the 4 lobhamūla somanassa-javanas, a somanassa-santīraṇa tadārammaṇa occurs; in a moderately desirable object, after the 4 lobhamūla upekkhā-javanas and 2 dosamūla-javanas, a kusalavipāka upekkhā-santīraṇa tadārammaṇa occurs. If a dosa-javana occurs in a desirable object, tadārammaṇa does not arise. After the 2 mohamūla-javanas, in a desirable object, a somanassa-santīraṇa tadārammaṇa occurs; in a moderately desirable object, a kusalavipāka upekkhā-santīraṇa tadārammaṇa occurs. Furthermore, it is stated that just as after kusala-javanas, tadārammaṇa should also occur after kiriya-javanas. If an akusala-javana vīthi occurs between kusala-javana vīthis, a tihetuka tadārammaṇa can still occur immediately after that akusala-javana. In this context, the phrase "according to the javana" seems to refer to the explanation in the Atthasālinī. However, in the Mūlaṭīkā, it is stated that tadārammaṇa should not occur after a kiriya-javana.

In the mind-door, mahaggata (sublime) consciousnesses also arise. [Note 1: "Mahaggata consciousnesses also arise" refers to these 18 mahaggata javana consciousnesses: 10 rūpāvacara kusala and kiriya javanas, and 8 arūpāvacara kusala and kiriya javanas. In this mind-door, the 8 lokuttara (supramundane) javanas also arise. However, since they are not states to be contemplated by vipassanā (insight), they are likely omitted.]

In this way, the arising of the immaterial (nāma) should be observed in the six doors. When the arising of the immaterial is observed in this manner, it is called "contemplating the immaterial at times."

By contemplating materiality (rūpa) at times and immateriality (nāma) at times as mentioned, and by applying the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) and practicing in sequence (such as the knowledge of rise and fall, etc.), a yogi fulfills the development of wisdom (paññā-bhāvanā).

## Rūpasattakasammasanakathā: Explanation of the Seven Ways of Contemplating Materiality

706. Another yogi contemplates formations (saṅkhāra) by applying the three characteristics through the seven ways of contemplating materiality and the seven ways of contemplating immateriality. Therein, when one applies the characteristics through these seven modes: (1) ādānanikkhepana—by way of taking up and laying down; (2) vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgama—by way of the disappearance of aging; (3) āhāramaya—by way of materiality produced by nutriment; (4) utumaya—by way of materiality produced by temperature; (5) kammaja—by way of materiality born of kamma; (6) cittasamuṭṭhāna—by way of materiality originated by consciousness; and (7) dhammatārūpa—by way of natural materiality; it is called contemplating by way of the sevenfold materiality (rūpasattaka).

Therefore, the ancient teachers said:
"By way of taking up and laying down, by way of the disappearance of aging,
By way of nutriment, temperature, kamma, and consciousness,
And by way of natural materiality, one contemplates in detail through these seven modes."

Among those seven, ādāna (taking up) is rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). Nikkhepana (laying down) is death (cuti). Thus, the yogi delimits a hundred years by these two—taking up and laying down—and applies the three characteristics to formations. How? All formations within this interval are impermanent. Why? Because they are constantly occurring by way of arising and passing away, because they are subject to change, because they are temporary, and because they exclude permanence. [Note 1: The absence of a permanent nature is itself the exclusion of permanence. Indeed, impermanent things, by their very impermanent nature, are said to exclude permanence for those who know (Translation from the Ṭīkā).]

Furthermore, formations that have arisen reach the moment of presence (ṭhīkhana); in the moment of presence, they are oppressed by aging; having reached aging, they inevitably break up. Therefore, they are suffering (dukkha) because they are constantly oppressed by arising and passing away, because they are unbearable, because they are the basis for suffering, and because they exclude happiness.

Furthermore, regarding these three stages: "May formations that have arisen not reach the moment of presence," "May formations that have reached the moment of presence not age," and "May formations that have aged not break up"— [254] there is no such thing as occurring according to one's will for anyone. They are void of that state of occurring according to one's will. Therefore, [they are non-self (anatta), being void of an abiding entity (nivāsī), a doer (kāraka), an experiencer (vedaka), or a director (adhiṭṭhāyaka)...]
254:
For those who see the nature of impermanence, it is as if those impermanent things are confessing and denying their permanence, saying: "Though many think we are permanent, we are indeed impermanent, just as you see."

Because it is void [of a self that seems to be a controller], because it has no owner, because it does not occur according to one's will, and because it denies the state of a self, one applies the three characteristics: "Anattā—they are not self, there is no self."

707. Having applied the three characteristics to materiality delimited by a hundred years through the method of "taking up and laying down" as mentioned, he then applies them through the "vanishing of the stages of life" (vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgama). In that context, "vanishing of the stages of life" means the cessation of materiality that has grown old through the stages of life. He applies the three characteristics by way of the cessation of that materiality which has aged through the stages—this is the meaning.

How? That yogi divides those same hundred years into three stages: the first stage of life, the middle stage of life, and the last stage of life. Among these three stages, the first 33 years are called the first stage. The next 34 years are called the middle stage. The next 33 years are called the last stage. Thus, having divided them into these three stages, he applies the three characteristics: "The materiality occurring in the first stage ceases right there without reaching the middle stage; therefore, it is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is non-self." "The materiality occurring in the middle stage also ceases right there without reaching the last stage; therefore, it too is impermanent, suffering, and non-self." "The materiality occurring for 33 years in the last stage has no ability to go on after death; therefore, it too is impermanent, suffering, and non-self."

708. Having thus applied the three characteristics through the vanishing of the stages of life by way of the first stage and so on, he applies them again through the vanishing of the stages of life by way of these ten decades (dasaka):
(1) Manda-dasaka—the decade of tenderness,
(2) Khiḍḍā-dasaka—the decade of play,
(3) Vaṇṇa-dasaka—the decade of beauty,
(4) Bala-dasaka—the decade of strength,
(5) Paññā-dasaka—the decade of wisdom,
(6) Hāni-dasaka—the decade of decline,
(7) Pabbhāra-dasaka—the decade of stooping,
(8) Vaṅka-dasaka—the decade of being bent,
(9) Momūha-dasaka—the decade of doting,
(10) Sayana-dasaka—the decade of lying down.

Among these ten decades, for a person living a hundred years, the first ten years are called the Manda-dasaka; at that time, he is tender, fickle, and just a child. The next ten years are called the Khiḍḍā-dasaka; at that time, he is full of delight in playing. The next ten years are called the Vaṇṇa-dasaka; at that time, his appearance reaches its fullness. The next ten years are called the Bala-dasaka; at that time, his strength and power reach their fullness. The next ten years are called the Paññā-dasaka; at that time, his wisdom is well-established. It is said that even for one who is naturally [255] void of wisdom, at least a little wisdom arises during this decade of wisdom.
255:
The next ten years are called the Hāni-dasaka; at that time, his delight in play, appearance, strength, and wisdom decline.

Note 1: The word "kira" is translated as "it is said" or "so they say," which is equivalent to "it is reported." Therefore, "kira" is translated here as "it is said."

The next ten years are called the Pabbhāra-dasaka; at that time, his body stoops forward. The next ten years are called the Vaṅka-dasaka; at that time, his body is bent like the handle of a plough. The next ten years are called the Momūha-dasaka; at that time, he is very deluded and forgets whatever he does. The next ten years are called the Sayana-dasaka; a person of a hundred years mostly spends his time lying down.

Regarding that (materiality of a hundred years), this yogi, in order to apply the three characteristics through the vanishing of the stages of life by way of these (ten) decades, contemplates thus: "The materiality occurring continuously in the first decade ceases right there in that first decade without reaching the second decade; therefore, that materiality of the first decade is impermanent, suffering, and non-self" (thus he applies the three characteristics). "In the second decade... [up to] ...the materiality occurring continuously in the ninth decade ceases right there in the ninth decade without reaching the tenth decade. The materiality occurring continuously in the tenth decade ceases right here in this life without reaching a new existence; therefore, that materiality of the tenth decade is also impermanent, suffering, and non-self"—thus he applies the three characteristics.

709. Having thus applied the three characteristics through the vanishing of the stages of life by way of the (ten) decades, he again divides those same hundred years into twenty parts of five years each and applies the three characteristics through the vanishing of the stages of life. How? That yogi contemplates thus: "The materiality occurring continuously in the first five-year part ceases right there in that first five-year part without reaching the second five-year part; therefore, that materiality of the first five-year part is impermanent, suffering, and non-self" (thus he applies the three characteristics). "The materiality occurring continuously in the second five-year part... [up to] ...the materiality occurring continuously in the nineteenth five-year part ceases right there in the nineteenth five-year part without reaching the twentieth five-year part. The materiality occurring continuously in the twentieth five-year part has no ability to go on after death; therefore, that materiality of the twentieth five-year part is also impermanent, suffering, and non-self" (thus he applies the three characteristics).

Having thus applied the three characteristics through the vanishing of the stages of life by way of the twenty parts, he again divides them into twenty-five parts and applies the three characteristics by way of four years each. Then, dividing them into thirty-three parts by way of three years each; dividing them into fifty parts by way of two years each; and dividing them into a hundred parts by way of one year each (he applies the three characteristics).

Then, dividing one year [256] into three parts, he applies the three characteristics to that materiality vanishing through the stages of life by way of each of the three seasons: the rainy season, the winter season, and the summer season.
256:
How? The materiality that occurs continuously within the four months of the rainy season does not reach the winter season, but ceases right there in the rainy season. The materiality that occurs continuously in the winter season does not reach the summer season, but ceases right there in the winter season. The materiality that occurs continuously in the summer season does not reach the rainy season again, but ceases right there in the summer season. Therefore, the materiality occurring in those three seasons is impermanent, suffering, and non-self (thus one applies the Three Characteristics).

Having applied them in this way (by the power of the three seasons), one again divides a year into six parts. The materiality that occurs continuously within the two months of the Vassāna season (up to the full moon of Poṭṭhapāda/Tawthalin)¹ does not reach the Sarada season, but ceases right there in the Vassāna season. The materiality that occurs continuously in the Sarada season (within the two months up to the full moon of Kattika/Tazaungmon) does not reach the Hemanta season. ... [and so on] ... The materiality that occurs continuously in the Hemanta season (within the two months up to the full moon of Phussa/Pyatho) does not reach the Sisira season. The materiality that occurs continuously in the Sisira season (within the two months up to the full moon of Phagguna/Tabaung) does not reach the Vasanta season. The materiality that occurs continuously in the Vasanta season (within the two months up to the full moon of Visākha/Kason) does not reach the Gimha season. The materiality that occurs continuously in the Gimha season (within the two months up to the full moon of Āsāḷha/Waso) does not reach the Vassāna season again, but ceases right there in the Gimha season. Therefore, (the materiality occurring in those six seasons) is impermanent, suffering, and non-self; in this way, one applies the Three Characteristics to that materiality which ages and ceases.

Note
1. Since it says "within the two months (up to the full moon of Poṭṭhapāda)", this Vassāna season is counted from the first day of the waning moon of Āsāḷha. The same applies to the remaining seasons.

Having applied them as mentioned above, one then applies them by the power of the dark and bright fortnights. The materiality that occurs continuously in the dark fortnight does not reach the bright fortnight, but ceases right there in the dark fortnight. The materiality that occurs continuously in the bright fortnight does not reach the dark fortnight, but ceases right there in the bright fortnight. Therefore, one applies the Three Characteristics: impermanent, suffering, and non-self.

Then, by the power of night and day: "The materiality that occurs continuously in the night does not reach the day, but ceases right there in the night. The materiality that occurs continuously in the day also does not reach the night, but ceases right there in the day. Therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self"—thus one applies the Three Characteristics. Then, dividing that same night and day into six parts by the power of morning and so on: "The materiality that occurs continuously in the morning does not reach the noon, but ceases right there in the morning. The materiality that occurs continuously in the noon does not reach the evening. The materiality that occurs continuously in the evening does not reach the first watch of the night. The materiality that occurs continuously in the first watch does not reach the middle watch. The materiality that occurs continuously in the middle watch does not reach the last watch, but ceases right there in the middle watch. The materiality that occurs continuously in the last watch does not reach the morning again, but ceases right there in the last watch. Therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self"—thus one applies the Three Characteristics.

710. Having applied them as mentioned above, one again applies the Three Characteristics to that same materiality by the power of going forward, returning, looking straight, looking aside, bending, and stretching: "The materiality occurring during the act of going forward does not reach the act of returning, but ceases right there during the act of going forward. The materiality occurring during the act of returning does not reach the act of looking straight. The materiality occurring during the act of looking straight does not reach the act of looking aside. The materiality occurring during the act of looking aside does not reach the act of bending. The materiality occurring during the act of bending does not reach the act of stretching, but ceases right there during the act of bending¹. Therefore, it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self"—thus one applies the Three Characteristics.

Then, one divides a single step into six parts by the power of lifting, carrying, shifting, dropping, placing, and pressing. [257] Therein, 'lifting' (uddharaṇa) means raising the foot from the ground. 'Carrying' (atiharaṇa) means moving it forward. 'Shifting' (vītiharaṇa) means moving the foot this way or that upon seeing things like a stump, a thorn, or a snake².
257:
Vossajjana—releasing momentum means the lowering of the foot. Sannikkhepana—placing means the setting down of the foot on the ground. Sannirumbhana—pressing down means the pressing (treading) of the first foot against the ground at the time of lifting the other foot again. Among these six, during the lifting, the two elements of Earth (pathavī-dhātu) and Water (āpo-dhātu) are deficient and weak, while the other two elements of Fire (tejo-dhātu) and Air (vāyo-dhātu) are predominant and strong. It is the same in carrying (atiharaṇa) and carrying across (vītiharaṇa).

Note:
1. Here, the sequence of walking, returning, looking straight, etc., is merely the sequence of teaching. In the time of practicing Vipassanā, one should contemplate exactly as it occurs. For details on the method of contemplation, see the Manual of Vipassanā, Volume II (6th edition) page 118, (7th edition) page 126.
2. In this context, the Mūla-ṭīkā further distinguishes: "Bringing the foot towards the other foot that is standing is called atiharaṇa—carrying; stepping forward beyond the other foot is called vītiharaṇa—carrying across." According to that explanation, since vītiharaṇa (stepping beyond) can be found in every step, that interpretation seems more appropriate.

During the releasing of momentum, the two elements of Fire and Air are deficient and weak, while the other two elements of Earth and Water are predominant and strong. It is the same in placing and pressing down.
