Thus, having divided it into six parts, one applies the Three Characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) to that materiality which ages and ceases (vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgamarūpa) by way of those six parts.

How? That yogi contemplates thus: The elements occurring in the lifting, and the derived materiality (upādā-rūpa) dependent on those elements—all these phenomena cease right there without reaching the carrying; therefore, they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Likewise, the phenomena occurring in the carrying do not reach the carrying across. The phenomena occurring in the carrying across do not reach the releasing of momentum. The phenomena occurring in the releasing of momentum do not reach the placing. The phenomena occurring in the placing do not reach the pressing down, but cease right there in the placing. As stated, the conditioned formations (saṅkhāra) occurring in each respective part do not reach the other parts, but break apart right in their original place of occurrence, part by part, joint by joint, and segment by segment, "just like sesame seeds thrown into a hot pan, making a 'tata-tata' sound and popping." Therefore, they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self (thus one applies the Three Characteristics). For the yogi who contemplates the formations occurring in segments in this manner, the comprehension of materiality (rūpa-sammasana) becomes subtle.

711. Regarding the subtlety of this comprehension of materiality, the following is a simile: It is said that a villager from the borderlands, who was accustomed only to wooden torches or grass torches and had never seen a lamp before, came to the city. Seeing a lamp burning in the market, he asked a man, "Friend, what is this delightful thing called?" That man said to the villager, "What is there to be delighted about here? This thing called a lamp will disappear without even its path being known when the oil and the wick are exhausted." Another person said to him, "This explanation is coarse. As this lamp-wick burns down sequentially, at every third part, the flame ceases without reaching the other parts." Another person said to him, "This too is still coarse. In this lamp-wick, at every inch,
258:
at every half-inch, at every thread, and at every fiber, the flame ceases right there without reaching the next fiber." Without the fiber, the flame cannot be pointed out. This is the simile.

In that simile, the knowledge of the first man who said, "The lamp will disappear without even its path being known when the oil and the wick are exhausted," is like the yogi's application of the Three Characteristics to materiality defined by a hundred years, through birth (ādāna) and death (nikkhepana). The knowledge of the second man who said, "At every third part of the wick, the flame ceases without reaching the other parts," is like the yogi's application of the Three Characteristics to the materiality that ages and ceases, defined by a third of a hundred years (33 years).

Note:
1. In this simile, it means dividing the wick into three parts and not reaching from one part to another.
2. In this sentence, it briefly shows how four people rejected the previous person's simile and spoke more subtle similes respectively.

The knowledge of the third man who said, "At every inch, the flame ceases without reaching the other parts," is like the yogi's application of the Three Characteristics to materiality defined by 10 years, 5 years, 4 years, 3 years, 2 years, and 1 year. The knowledge of the fourth man who said, "At every half-inch, the flame ceases without reaching the other parts," is like the yogi's application of the Three Characteristics to materiality defined by four months or two months, by dividing one year into three or six parts according to each season (utu). The knowledge of the fifth man who said, "At every thread, the flame ceases without reaching the next thread," is like the yogi's application of the Three Characteristics to materiality defined by the waning and waxing fortnights, by day and night, or by dividing one day and night into six parts such as the morning and so on. The knowledge of the sixth man who said, "At every fiber, the flame ceases without reaching the next fiber," is like the yogi's application of the Three Characteristics to materiality defined by the power of moving forward and so on, or by the power of each individual part such as lifting the foot and so on. This is the correlation between the simile and its meaning.

712. That yogi, having applied the Three Characteristics to the materiality that ages and ceases in various ways as mentioned, again analyzes that same materiality, dividing it into four parts by way of nutriment-born materiality (āhāramaya-rūpa) and so on, and applies the Three Characteristics to each part. Among those four types of materiality, nutriment-born materiality becomes evident to that yogi by way of hunger and satiety. The manner of its appearance is as follows:

Materiality arising at the time of hunger is withered, exhausted, and has an ugly color and poor shape, like a burnt stump or like a crow sitting in a charcoal basket. Materiality arising at the time of satiety is full, refreshed, soft, smooth, and has a good touch.
259:
That meditator, having discerned that materiality (occurring during the time of hunger and the time of being full), contemplates: "The materiality that arises during the time of hunger does not reach the time of being full and ceases right there in that time of hunger. The materiality that arises during the time of being full also does not reach the time of hunger and ceases right there in that time of being full." Thus, he applies the three marks—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—to that nutriment-born materiality. (3)

713. *Utumaya*—Materiality produced by temperature becomes evident through the power of cold and heat. To illustrate: materiality arising in a time of heat is withered, exhausted, and of poor color. Materiality arising due to the cold season is full, refreshed, (soft, having good touch), and smooth. That meditator, having discerned that materiality (occurring in the times of heat and cold), contemplates: "The materiality that arises in the time of heat does not reach the time of cold and ceases right there in that time of heat. The materiality that arises in the time of cold also does not reach the time of heat and ceases right there in that time of cold." Thus, he applies the three marks to that temperature-born materiality. (4)

714. *Kammaja*—Materiality born of kamma becomes evident through the power of the doors (*dvāra*) which are the causes of contact. To illustrate: at the eye-door, there are 30 kamma-born materiality units by way of the eye-decad, body-decad, and sex-decad; and there are 24 supporting materiality units produced by temperature, consciousness, and nutriment—making 54 types of materiality in total that become evident. (Note: This means that when seeing occurs, the eye-door etc. become evident, and thus the group of kamma-born materiality contained in those doors becomes evident.) Similarly, 54 types of materiality become evident at each of the ear-door, nose-door, and tongue-door. At the body-door, 44 types of materiality become evident by way of the body-decad and sex-decad, as well as the temperature-born octad, etc. At the mind-door, 54 types of materiality become evident by way of the heart-base-decad, body-decad, and sex-decad, as well as the temperature-born octad, etc.

That meditator, having discerned all that materiality evident in the six doors, contemplates: "The materiality occurring at the eye-door does not reach the ear-door and ceases right there at the eye-door. (Note: 'Materiality at the eye-door' means 'materiality at the moment of seeing'; 'does not reach the ear-door' means 'does not reach the moment of hearing'.) The materiality occurring at the ear-door does not reach the nose-door. The materiality occurring at the nose-door does not reach the tongue-door. The materiality occurring at the tongue-door does not reach the body-door. The materiality occurring at the body-door does not reach the mind-door and ceases right there at the body-door." Thus, he applies the three marks to that kamma-born materiality, seeing it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. (5)

715. *Cittasamuṭṭhāna*—Materiality produced by consciousness becomes evident through the power of joy (*somanassa*) and grief (*domanassa*). To illustrate: materiality arising at a time of joy is smooth, soft, refreshed, and has a good touch. Materiality arising at a time of grief is withered, exhausted, and of poor color. That meditator, having discerned that materiality (occurring in times of joy and grief), contemplates: "The materiality occurring at the time of joy does not reach the time of grief and ceases right there at the time of joy. The materiality occurring at the time of grief does not reach the time of joy and ceases right there at the time of grief." Thus, he applies the three marks to that mind-born materiality, seeing it as impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
260:
As he discerns mind-born materiality in this way and applies the three marks to it, the following meaning becomes clear to him:

Life, the physical body (Note: The collection of materiality and mentality excluding life, pleasure, pain, and consciousness is called 'attabhāva'), and pleasure and pain are entirely distinct phenomena; they are associated only with a single moment of consciousness. The moment of their occurrence is extremely brief and swift.

Even those Brahmas of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception who live for eighty-four thousand aeons (*kappa*) do not remain the same even for two consecutive moments of consciousness.

Those aggregates (*khandhā*) of a dying person that have ceased, and those aggregates of a person living here that are currently ceasing—all these two kinds of aggregates are identical in their nature of cessation; they have vanished without any reconnection.

There is no difference in the characteristic of cessation between the aggregates that broke up in the immediate past, those that will break up in the immediate future, and those currently ceasing in between them. (Note: The translation here is simplified for flow; grammatically it refers to the aggregates that have perished and those that will perish.)

A being does not live by a future mind that has not yet arisen; one lives only by the present mind. When the mind ceases, the world is said to be dead. The conventional designation of a continuity (such as 'Tissa is alive') is based on the ultimate reality of the present mind.

Aggregates that have ceased are not stored anywhere; there is no accumulation of aggregates to be born in the future. Even those that have arisen and are present stand like a mustard seed on the point of an awl (about to fall and perish).

Those phenomena that have arisen (Note: Those that have reached the stage of presence, *ṭhitikhana*) are headed toward destruction. These present phenomena exist without mixing with the old past phenomena.

Formations (*saṅkhāra*) come from the unseen (the non-existent), and having broken up, they go to the unseen. Like a flash of lightning in the sky, they arise and they vanish. (Mahāniddesa 10)

716. Having applied the three marks to nutriment-born materiality and so on as described, he again applies the three marks to natural materiality (*dhammatārūpa*). Natural materiality refers to external materiality not connected with the sense-faculties, such as iron, copper, tin, lead, gold, silver, pearls, gems, cat's-eyes, shells, crystal, coral, rubies, emeralds, soil, stones, mountains, grass, trees, and creepers, which have been arising since the beginning of the world-cycle. This natural materiality becomes evident to the meditator through the example of an Ashoka sprout (*asokaṅkura*).

To illustrate: the Ashoka sprout is initially a tender red color; then, after two or three days, it becomes a deep, thick red; again, after two or three days, it becomes a pale red; then it takes on the color of a young leaf.
261:
[261] After that, it takes on the color of a mature sprout; then the color of a green leaf; then the color of a dark green leaf. Starting from the time it has the color of a dark green leaf, maintaining the continuity of similar materiality, in about a year it becomes a yellow withered leaf, detaches from the stalk, and falls.

Having grasped that materiality of the Asoka sprout, that yogi applies the three characteristics: "The materiality occurring during the time of light redness ceases without reaching the time of deep redness. The materiality occurring during the time of deep redness [ceases without reaching] the time of pale redness.

The materiality occurring during the time of pale redness [ceases without reaching] the time of the color of a young sprout. The materiality occurring during the time of the color of a young sprout [ceases without reaching] the time of the color of a mature sprout. The materiality occurring during the time of the color of a mature sprout [ceases without reaching] the time of the color of a green leaf. The materiality occurring during the time of the color of a green leaf [ceases without reaching] the time of the color of a dark green leaf. The materiality occurring during the time of the color of a dark green leaf [ceases without reaching] the time of a yellow withered leaf. The materiality occurring during the time of a yellow withered leaf ceases without even reaching the time of detaching from the stalk and falling. Therefore, that materiality of the Asoka sprout is impermanent, suffering, and non-self." Having thus applied the three characteristics to that materiality of the Asoka sprout, he contemplates all natural materiality in this manner. (7)

In this way, he contemplates formations by applying the three characteristics through the sevenfold contemplation of materiality (rūpasattaka).

## Explanation of the Seven Ways of Contemplating Non-materiality

717. In the statement "by way of the sevenfold contemplation of non-materiality (arūpasattaka)," the following is the table of contents (mātikā): (1) by way of group (kalāpa), (2) by way of pairs (yamaka), (3) by way of the momentary (khaṇika), (4) by way of succession (paṭipāṭi), (5) by way of the uprooting of views (diṭṭhi-ugghāṭana), (6) by way of the uprooting of conceit (māna-samugghāṭana), and (7) by way of the exhaustion of attachment (nikanti-pariyādāna). This is the table of contents.

Among these seven, "by way of group" refers to the states with contact as the fifth (phassapañcamaka). How does one contemplate by way of group? Here, a bhikkhu reflects thus: "Those states with contact as the fifth that arose in the contemplation, 'Hairs are impermanent, suffering, and non-self,' and those states with contact as the fifth that arose in the contemplation, 'Body hairs... etc... the brain is impermanent, suffering, and non-self'—all those non-material states of contemplation (phassapañcamaka) do not reach from one stage to another; being fragmented and delimited, they perish like sesame seeds making a 'crackling' sound when thrown into a hot pan. Therefore, they are impermanent, suffering, and non-self." This is the method presented in the Visuddhikathā.

In the Ariyavaṃsakathā, however, it is said: "When one contemplates with a subsequent mind as 'impermanent, suffering, and non-self' the mind that occurred while contemplating 'materiality is impermanent, suffering, and non-self' in the seven instances of the sevenfold contemplation of materiality, [262] it is called contemplating by way of group (kalāpa)."
262:
That statement is more appropriate. Therefore, we shall explain the remaining ways of contemplation according to the method of the Ariyavaṃsakathā. (1)

718. "By way of pairs (yamaka)" means: here, a bhikkhu contemplates materiality delimited by birth and death (ādāna-nikkhepa) as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," and then contemplates that very contemplating mind with another subsequent mind as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self." He contemplates materiality that disappears through the increase of age (vayovuḍḍhatthaṅgama), materiality consisting of nutriment (āhāramaya), materiality consisting of temperature (utumaya), karma-born materiality (kammaja), mind-produced materiality (cittasamuṭṭhāna), and natural materiality (dhammatārūpa) as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," and then contemplates that very contemplating mind with another

Note:
1. The non-material states contemplating the hair do not reach the time of contemplating the body hair; the non-material states contemplating the body hair do not reach the time of contemplating the nails—in this way, it means they do not reach from one part to another.

subsequent mind as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self." When contemplating in this way, it is called contemplating by way of pairs. (Note 1) (2)

719. "By way of the momentary (khaṇika)" means: here, a bhikkhu contemplates materiality delimited by birth and death as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," and then contemplates that first contemplating mind with a second mind, the second with a third, the third with a fourth, and the fourth with a fifth as "this mind is also impermanent, suffering, and non-self." He contemplates materiality that disappears through the increase of age, materiality consisting of nutriment, materiality consisting of temperature, karma-born materiality, mind-produced materiality, and natural materiality as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," and then contemplates that first contemplating mind with a second mind, the second with a third, the third with a fourth, and the fourth with a fifth as "this mind is also impermanent, suffering, and non-self." When one contemplates four minds starting from the mind that grasps materiality, it is called contemplating by way of the momentary. (3)

720. "By way of succession (paṭipāṭi)" means: having contemplated materiality delimited by birth and death as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," one contemplates that first contemplating mind with a second mind, the second with a third, the third with a fourth... etc... the tenth mind with

Note:
1. Contemplation by way of group (kalāpa) and contemplation by way of pairs (yamaka) seem similar. Contemplating the group of states with contact as the fifth as a whole, without clearly observing any single state such as contact or feeling, is called contemplating by way of group. Clearly knowing any single state such as contact or feeling and contemplating it as primary is called contemplating by way of pairs. This is how they should be distinguished. That is why, in explaining contemplation by way of pairs, it is stated, "he contemplates that contemplating mind with another subsequent mind," making the mind primary.

an eleventh mind as "this mind is also impermanent, suffering, and non-self." He contemplates materiality that disappears through the increase of age, materiality consisting of nutriment, materiality consisting of temperature, karma-born materiality, mind-produced materiality, and natural materiality as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," and then contemplates that first contemplating mind with a second mind, the second with a third, the third with a fourth... etc... the tenth mind with an eleventh mind as "this mind is also impermanent, suffering, and non-self." In this way, through successive insight, one could contemplate even for the whole day. However, by contemplating up to the tenth mind, both the meditation subject of materiality and the meditation subject of non-materiality become proficient. Therefore, it is said (in the Ariyavaṃsakathā) that the contemplation should be stopped at the tenth mind only. When contemplating in this way, it is called contemplating by way of succession. (4)

721. In these three headings—"by way of the uprooting of views," "by way of the uprooting of conceit," and "by way of the exhaustion of attachment"—there is no separate method of contemplation. [263] Whatever materiality was grasped in the lower sevenfold contemplation of materiality...
263:
In this heptad of mentality (nāma-sattaka) as well, the yogi has apprehended mentality. Seeing these two, materiality and mentality, the yogi no longer sees any other thing called a "being" beyond materiality and mentality. From the moment a being is not seen, the perception of a being (satta-saññā) is discarded. For the yogi who apprehends formations (saṅkhāra) with a mind that has discarded the perception of a being, wrong view (diṭṭhi) (which takes them as a being) does not arise. When wrong view does not arise, it is said that wrong view has been discarded. For the yogi who apprehends formations with a mind that has discarded wrong view, conceit (māna) does not arise. When conceit does not arise, it is said that conceit has been utterly uprooted. For the yogi who apprehends formations with a mind that has utterly uprooted conceit, craving (taṇhā) does not arise. When craving does not arise, it is said that the attachment (nikanti) of craving has been exhausted—this is stated in the Visuddhimagga.

In the Ariyavaṃsa Commentary, however, after setting out the headings: "By the discarding of wrong view, by the uprooting of conceit, by the exhaustion of attachment," the following method is shown:

For the yogi who takes it as "I meditate, my meditation," there is no discarding of wrong view. But for the yogi who takes it as "Formations alone contemplate formations, investigate them, determine them, apprehend them, and delimit them," there is the discarding of wrong view.

For the yogi who takes it as "I meditate well, I meditate delightfully," there is no uprooting of conceit. But for the yogi who takes it as "Formations alone contemplate formations, investigate them, determine them, apprehend them, and delimit them," there is the uprooting of conceit.

For the yogi who enjoys the meditation, thinking "I am able to meditate," there is no exhaustion of attachment. But for the yogi who takes it as "Formations alone contemplate formations, investigate them, determine them, apprehend them, and delimit them," there is the exhaustion of attachment.

If formations were a self (atta), it would be proper to take them as a self. But they are taken as a self when they are not a self. Therefore, for the yogi who sees them as non-self in the sense of being uncontrollable, as impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be, and as suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, there is the discarding of wrong view.

If formations were permanent, it would be proper to take them as permanent. But they are taken as permanent when they are impermanent. Therefore, for the yogi who sees them as impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be, as suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, and as non-self in the sense of being uncontrollable, there is the uprooting of conceit.

[264] If formations were pleasant, it would be proper to take them as pleasant. But they are taken as pleasant when they are actually suffering.
264:
Therefore, for the yogi who sees them as suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, as impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be, and as non-self in the sense of being uncontrollable, there is the exhaustion of attachment.

As stated, for the yogi who sees formations as non-self, there is the discarding of wrong view. For the yogi who sees them as impermanent, there is the uprooting of conceit. For the yogi who sees them as suffering, there is the exhaustion of attachment (nikanti). Thus, this insight stands in its respective place—so it is stated (in the Ariyavaṃsa Commentary). (5-6-7)

In this way, by means of the seven ways of contemplating mentality, one applies the three characteristics and investigates formations. Through this much investigation, the yogi's meditation on materiality and meditation on mentality both become proficient.

## Explanation of Attaining a Portion of the Great Insights

722. The yogi who has thus mastered the meditation on materiality and mentality, while penetrating even here in this "investigation-knowledge" (tīraṇa-pariññā), attains a portion of the eighteen great insights (mahā-vipassanā) which are to be reached in every aspect through "abandoning-knowledge" (pahāna-pariññā) starting from the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā) above. Thus, he abandons the states opposed to those insights.

The eighteen great insights are the wisdoms beginning with the contemplation of impermanence. Among these:

(1) While developing the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), one abandons the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā).
(2) While developing the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), one abandons the perception of pleasure (sukha-saññā).
(3) While developing the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā), one abandons the perception of self (atta-saññā).
(4) While developing the contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā), one abandons delight (nandi).
(5) While developing the contemplation of dispassion (virāgānupassanā), one abandons lust (rāga).
(6) While developing the contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā), one abandons origination (samudaya).
(7) While developing the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā), one abandons grasping (ādāna).
(8) While developing the contemplation of destruction (khayānupassanā), one abandons the perception of compactness (ghana-saññā).
(9) While developing the contemplation of fall (vayānupassanā), one abandons accumulation (āyūhana).

Note: 1. For a detailed explanation of the 18 Great Insights, see Chapter 7 of the Manual of Insight Meditation.

(10) While developing the contemplation of change (vipariṇāmānupassanā), one abandons the perception of stability (dhuva-saññā).
(11) While developing the contemplation of the signless (animittānupassanā), one abandons the sign (nimitta).
(12) While developing the contemplation of the desireless (appaṇihitānupassanā), one abandons desire (paṇidhi).
(13) While developing the contemplation of voidness (suññatānupassanā), one abandons the misinterpretation of a self (abhinivesa).
(14) While developing the insight into states based on higher wisdom (adhipaññā-dhamma-vipassanā), one abandons the misinterpretation of taking things to have essence (sārādāna-abhinivesa).
(15) While developing the knowledge and vision of things as they really are (yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana), one abandons the misinterpretation due to confusion (sammoha-abhinivesa).
265:
(16) When developing the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā), one abandons the inclination to take [formations] as a refuge or hiding place.
(17) When developing the contemplation of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā), one abandons the opposite of reflection (non-reflection).
(18) When developing the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭānupassanā), while withdrawing from formations, one abandons the inclination to be involved with or cling to formations.

[265] Among these eighteen principal insights (mahāvipassanā), this meditator has seen formations by way of the three characteristics, such as impermanence. Therefore, the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), and the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā) have been realized and attained. Furthermore, because it is stated (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga): "The contemplation of impermanence and the signless contemplation (animittānupassanā) are one in meaning, differing only in name"; "The contemplation of suffering and the desireless contemplation (appaṇihitānupassanā) are one in meaning, differing only in name"; and "The contemplation of non-self and the emptiness contemplation (suññatānupassanā) are one in meaning, differing only in name," these three insights of identical meaning have also been realized and attained.

Moreover, insight into states of higher wisdom (adhipaññā-dhamma-vipassanā) is all (and also)¹ insight. Knowledge and vision according to reality (yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana) is counted and included within the purification by overcoming doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi). Thus, these two knowledges have also been realized and attained. Among the remaining insight knowledges, some have been realized and attained, while some have not. We shall clarify the classification of these principal insights later.

To explain the validity of the previous statement, referring only to the knowledge that this meditator has realized and attained: "A meditator who is thus proficient in the meditation subjects of materiality and mentality, starting from the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā) upwards, among the eighteen principal insights to be reached in every aspect by way of full understanding as abandoning (pahānapariññā), penetrates a portion of them right here in this full understanding as investigation (tīraṇapariññā) and abandons those states that are opposed to them." This is what I have said.

## Explanation of the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away (Udayabbaya-ñāṇa)

723. Thus, that meditator¹—whose knowledge is purified by abandoning the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā) and so on, which are the opposites of the contemplation of impermanence and so forth—reaches the end of the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa)¹ and, immediately after the knowledge of comprehension,² begins the effort to attain the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), which is described² thus: "Wisdom in contemplating the change of states that have arisen in the present is the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away." In making this effort, he begins briefly at first. In that regard, the following is the text from the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

"How is wisdom in contemplating the change of states that have arisen in the present the knowledge of contemplation of arising and passing away?
Materiality (rūpa) that has been born is present; its characteristic of generation is 'arising' (udaya), its characteristic of change is 'passing away' (vaya), and the contemplation is 'knowledge.' Feeling (vedanā) that has been born... perception (saññā)... formations (saṅkhāra)... consciousness (viññāṇa)... the eye (cakkhu) that has been born... [etc.]³... becoming (bhava) that has been born is present; its characteristic of generation is 'arising,' its characteristic of change is 'passing away,' and the contemplation is 'knowledge.'"

Note:
1. In the Pali, based on the word 'sabbāpi', it is translated precisely as 'all (and also)'. There, by the word 'pi', it is shown that 'adhipaññā-dhamma-vipassanā' is not only the entire collection of insight but also a part of insight. In the Myanmar language, there is no such usage; by simply saying 'all', it conveys the meaning of 'both the whole and the part'. Therefore, for those who do not wish to follow the Pali method or cannot follow it, the words within the parentheses can be skipped, and one can read it simply as 'all', as the precise translation according to the Pali method is separated by parentheses.

1. Connect: "That meditator... reaches the end... and begins the effort."
2. Connect: "Immediately after... is described."
266:
3. Here, the elision (peyyāla) should be expanded according to the method shown on page 284. Since this is the domain of the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa), it is shown only up to 'becoming' (bhava), without including 'birth' (jāti) and 'aging-and-death' (jarāmaraṇa), as their specific rise and fall cannot be separately obtained. This is the only distinction.

'Udaya' means arising; the characteristic of change is 'vaya', meaning passing away. The seeing (of rise and fall) is called 'knowledge' (ñāṇa). This is the Pali.

[266] By this Pali method, the meditator sees the characteristic of generation, the arising, the new state of the mind-and-matter that is being produced, as 'rise' (udaya). He sees the characteristic of change, the exhaustion, the breaking up, as 'fall' (vaya). He understands thus: 'Before its arising, there was no heap or store of this unarisen mind-and-matter. Even when it is arising, it does not come from any heap or store. When it is ceasing, it does not go to any direction or intermediate direction. When it has ceased, it does not remain as a heap, a store, or a hoard in any place. Just as when a lute (vīṇā) is being played, the sound that arises did not exist as a store before its arising; nor does the sound, when arising, come from a store; nor does the sound of the lute, when ceasing, go to any direction or intermediate direction; nor does the sound that has ceased remain stored anywhere. On the contrary, depending on the lute, the plectrum (upavīṇā), and the appropriate effort of the person, it comes into being without having been, and having been, it vanishes. In the same way, all material and immaterial states (rūpārūpino dhammā) come into being without having been, and having been, they vanish.'

724. Having thus practiced the attention on rise and fall in brief, again, in the detailed analysis of this same knowledge of rise and fall:

'He sees the rise of the aggregate of materiality (rūpakkhandha) in the sense of the arising of conditions, thinking: "With the arising of ignorance (avijjā), there is the arising of materiality." He sees the rise of the aggregate of materiality in the sense of the arising of conditions, thinking: "With the arising of craving (taṇhā)... with the arising of kamma... with the arising of nutriment (āhāra), there is the arising of materiality." He also sees the rise of the aggregate of materiality while seeing the characteristic of generation (nibbattilakkhaṇa). While seeing the rise of the aggregate of materiality, he sees these five characteristics.

He sees the fall of the aggregate of materiality in the sense of the cessation of conditions, thinking: "With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of materiality." He sees the fall of the aggregate of materiality in the sense of the cessation of conditions, thinking: "With the cessation of craving... with the cessation of kamma... with the cessation of nutriment, there is the cessation of materiality." He also sees the fall of the aggregate of materiality while seeing the characteristic of change (vipariṇāmalakkhaṇa). While seeing the fall of the aggregate of materiality, he sees these five characteristics.'

Likewise: 'He sees the rise of the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) in the sense of the arising of conditions, thinking: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling." He sees the rise of the aggregate of feeling in the sense of the arising of conditions, thinking: "With the arising of craving... with the arising of kamma... with the arising of contact (phassa), there is the arising of feeling." Even while seeing the characteristic of generation...'
267:
With the arising (existence) of contact, there is the arising of feeling; thus, one sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) through the arising (existence) of its condition. By seeing the characteristic of arising, one also sees the arising of the aggregate of feeling. When seeing the arising of the aggregate of feeling, one sees these five characteristics.

With the cessation of ignorance, with the cessation of craving, with the cessation of karma, and with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling; thus, one sees the fall of the aggregate of feeling through the cessation of its conditions. By seeing the characteristic of change (vipariṇāma), one also sees the fall of the aggregate of feeling. When seeing the fall of the aggregate of feeling, one sees these five characteristics.

As with the aggregate of feeling, one also sees the rise and fall of the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), and the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha). There is only this distinction: in the case of the aggregate of consciousness, in place of contact, one says, "with the arising of mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa), with the cessation of mind-and-matter."

Thus, in seeing the rise and fall of each aggregate, ten characteristics are applied to each, and fifty characteristics are taught. By means of these fifty characteristics, one attends in detail to the rise and fall by way of condition (paccaya) and by way of the moment (khana), thinking: "In this way the arising of materiality occurs; in this way the fall of materiality occurs; in this way materiality arises; in this way materiality passes away."

725. For the meditator who attends in this way, the knowledge that "these states, having not been, come into being; having come into being, they disappear" becomes especially clear and sharp. For the meditator who thus sees the rise and fall in two ways—by condition and by moment—the distinctions of the Truths (sacca), Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), methods (naya), and characteristics (lakkhaṇa) become manifest.

726. When he sees the arising of the aggregates through the arising of ignorance, etc., and the cessation of the aggregates through the cessation of ignorance, etc., this is his seeing of rise and fall by way of condition. Furthermore, when he sees the rise and fall of the aggregates by seeing the characteristic of birth (nibbattilakkhaṇa) and the characteristic of change (vipariṇāmalakkhaṇa), this is his seeing of rise and fall by way of the moment. Indeed, the characteristic of birth exists only at the moment of arising (uppādakkhaṇa), and the characteristic of change exists only at the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa).

727. Thus, for the meditator who sees the rise and fall in two ways—by condition and by moment—the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca) becomes manifest through seeing the arising by way of condition, because of the penetration of the generating cause (janaka). The Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca) becomes manifest through seeing the arising by way of the moment, because of the penetration of the suffering of birth (jātidukkha). The Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca) becomes manifest through seeing the fall by way of condition, because of the penetration of the non-arising of conditioned things when the conditions do not arise. The Truth of Suffering itself becomes manifest through seeing the fall by way of the moment, because of the penetration of the suffering of death (maraṇadukkha). [268] Furthermore, the knowledge with which he sees rise and fall is the mundane path; thus, the Truth of the Path (maggasacca) becomes manifest, because of the abandonment of the delusion of "not knowing through personal experience" within that mundane path.
268:
By such seeing, it means that the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca) becomes clear. Later, where it says "by way of the moment," the meaning should be understood by connecting it in the same manner.

4. Understanding a meaning that was not known before through one's own wisdom is called "penetrative knowledge."

5. According to the original Pali, 'paccayavataṃ' refers to the effects that are connected with causes (arising because of causes).

728. Furthermore, by seeing the rise by way of condition, the forward Dependent Origination (anuloma paṭiccasamuppāda)¹ becomes clear to that yogi. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge that "when this cause exists, this effect comes to be." By seeing the fall by way of condition, the reverse Dependent Origination (paṭiloma paṭiccasamuppāda)² becomes clear. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge that "with the cessation of this cause, this effect ceases." By seeing the rise and fall by way of the moment, the phenomena produced by conditions (paṭiccasamuppanna) become clear. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge of the characteristics of the conditioned (saṅkhata-lakkhaṇa). Indeed, those things that have rise and fall are conditioned, and those conditioned things are also produced by conditions.

729. Furthermore, by seeing the rise by way of condition, the Method of Unity (ekatta-naya)³, which is to be taken as one and the same, becomes clear to that yogi. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge of the non-interruption of the continuity of the mental-material process through the connection of cause and effect.

Note:
1. The sequence of cause and effect taught in its natural order, such as "with ignorance as condition, formations come to be; with formations as condition, consciousness comes to be," etc., is called forward Dependent Origination (anuloma paṭiccasamuppāda).
2. The sequence of the cessation of cause and effect taught as "with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases," etc., is called reverse Dependent Origination (paṭiloma paṭiccasamuppāda).
3. The mental-material continuity arises in the next life due to the causal kamma of the previous life. In this process, because the previous life and the next life are a single continuity of mental-material process connected by cause and effect, the one who performed the causal kamma in the previous life and the one who experiences the result of that kamma in the next life are taken as the same person. The method that leads to such a conclusion is called the Method of Unity (ekatta-naya).

At that time, he abandons the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi) even better¹. By seeing the rise by way of the moment, the Method of Diversity (nānatta-naya)²—taking things as distinct—becomes clear. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge of the arising of ever-new mental and material phenomena. At that time, he abandons the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) even better. Moreover, by seeing the rise and fall by way of condition, the Method of Effortlessness (abyāpāra-naya)³—taking things as having no agency—becomes clear. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge of the fact that phenomena cannot be made to happen according to one's will. At that time, he abandons the view of self (atta-diṭṭhi), the belief in a soul or entity, even better. Furthermore, by seeing the rise by way of condition, the Method of Natural Order (evaṃdhammatā-naya)⁴—taking things as occurring according to their nature—becomes clear. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge of the arising of the effect in accordance with the cause.

Note:
1. Although wrong views were already abandoned in a gross sense during the stage of Purification of View (diṭṭhi-visuddhi), because subtler views are abandoned again at this level of insight, it is said that he "abandons even better."
2. The mental and material phenomena of the old life ceased entirely in that old life. The mental-material continuity in the new life is a continuity that arises anew only in that new life. Therefore, the mental-material continuity of the old life and the mental-material continuity of the new life must be taken as distinct. The method that leads to such a distinction is called the Method of Diversity (nānatta-naya).
3. Ignorance has no effort or agency such as "I will make formations arise." Causal formations (kamma-saṅkhāra) have no effort such as "We will make rebirth-consciousness arise." The method of knowing and taking that there is no effort or agency in the causes to produce the effects is called the Method of Effortlessness (abyāpāra-naya).
4. Only specific effects such as formations arise because of their respective causes such as ignorance. Effects do not arise from unrelated causes. The method of knowing and taking this is called the Method of Natural Order (evaṃdhammatā-naya).

Because of such knowledge, he abandons the view of non-action (akiriya-diṭṭhi)—the belief that good and bad deeds cannot or need not be done—even better.

730. Furthermore, by seeing the rise by way of condition, the characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa) becomes clear to that yogi. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge of the lack of striving in mental-material phenomena and their existence being dependent on conditions. By seeing the rise and fall by way of the moment, the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) becomes clear. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge of non-existence after having come to be, and because of the penetrative knowledge of the absence of an entity in the preceding and succeeding parts. The characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) also becomes clear. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge of the continuous oppression by rise and fall. The characteristic of individual essence (sabhāva-lakkhaṇa) also becomes clear. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge of the nature delimited by rise and fall. Within the individual essence, the temporary nature of the conditioned characteristic¹ also becomes clear. (Why?) Because of the penetrative knowledge of the absence of fall at the moment of rise, and the absence of rise at the moment of fall.

731. To that yogi, for whom the distinctions of the truths, the methods of dependent origination, and the characteristics have become clear in this way², the formations appear as ever-new, thinking: "Indeed, these phenomena, which have never arisen before, arise in this manner; and having arisen, they cease in this manner."
269:
Formations appear not merely as constantly new; in truth, they appear as lasting for a very short and brief duration, like a dewdrop at sunrise, like a water bubble, like a line drawn on water with a stick, like a mustard seed placed on the point of an awl, and like a flash of lightning. They also appear as void and devoid of essence, like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a fire-wheel seen in the dark, a city of Gandharvas, a mass of foam, or a plantain trunk.

Notes:
1. The three characteristics of the conditioned—arising (uppāda), momentary presence (ṭhiti), and dissolution (bhaṅga)—are called the characteristics of the conditioned because they are the marks by which conditioned things are known.
2. Connect this with "appear to that yogi."

By this much (of the practice of meditation), this yogi, penetrating the fifty characteristics in the manner that "only things of a nature to decay are born, and having been born, they reach decay and disappearance," attains the tender insight knowledge called the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā-ñāṇa). By attaining this tender insight knowledge, he is reckoned as one who has begun insight (āraddhavipassaka).

## Explanation of the Imperfections of Insight (Vipassanūpakkilesa)

732. At that time, for this yogi who has begun insight with this tender insight, the ten imperfections of insight (vipassanūpakkilesa) arise. Indeed, the imperfections of insight do not arise in a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) who has attained penetration (of the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna), nor in a person who practices wrongly, nor in a person who has given up the meditation subject, nor in a lazy person. However, they do arise in a son of good family who practices rightly, who is devoted to the practice, and who has begun insight (until the knowledge of rise and fall arises).

What are these ten imperfections? They are: (1) light (obhāsa), (2) knowledge (ñāṇa), (3) rapture (pīti), (4) tranquillity (passaddhi), (5) happiness (sukha), (6) resolution (adhimokkha), (7) exertion (paggaha), (8) establishment [of mindfulness] (upaṭṭhāna), (9) equanimity (upekkhā), and (10) attachment (nikanti). Thus it is said:

"How does the mind become distracted by agitation concerning the Dhamma? When one is contemplating as impermanent, light arises. He reflects on the light, thinking, 'Light is the Dhamma (a special attainment).' From that, distraction and agitation (uddhacca) arise. With a mind distracted by that agitation, he does not truly understand the establishment [of mindfulness] as impermanent. He does not truly understand the establishment as suffering... as non-self."

Likewise, "When one is contemplating as impermanent, knowledge arises... [p.] rapture... tranquillity... happiness... resolution... exertion... establishment... equanimity... attachment arises. He reflects on the attachment, thinking, 'Attachment is the Dhamma.' From that, distraction and agitation arise. With a mind distracted by that agitation, he does not truly understand the establishment as impermanent. He does not truly understand the establishment as suffering... as non-self."

Notes:
1. Regarding "By this much (of the practice of meditation)," the practice of meditation refers to the procedure of practicing until one penetrates the rise and fall, following the Pali method such as "the matter that is currently arising is called the present," or following the Pali method such as "whatever matter there is, whether past, future, or present."
1. "They certainly arise" means it is not that they do not arise; there is no case where they do not occur.
270:
Why is this? Because if the imperfections such as light do not arise, there is no opportunity for this yogi to attain the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and What Is Not the Path (maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi). (Sub-commentary explanation)

Exertion arises. Establishment arises. Equanimity arises. Attachment arises. He reflects on the attachment, thinking, "Attachment is the Dhamma." From that, distraction and agitation arise. With a mind distracted by that agitation, he does not truly understand the establishment as impermanent. He does not truly understand the establishment as suffering... as non-self."

This statement is taught (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali).

733. Among these ten imperfections such as light, "light" (obhāsa) refers to the light of insight (produced by the mind of insight). When that light arises, the yogi thinks, "Indeed, such a light has never arisen in me before; surely I have reached the Path, I have reached the Fruit." Thus, he takes what is not the Path to be the Path, and what is not the Fruit to be the Fruit. When he takes what is not the Path to be the Path and what is not the Fruit to be the Fruit, his course of insight is said to have turned aside. That yogi, abandoning his original meditation subject, sits enjoying the light itself.

Furthermore, this light arises for some monks illuminating only the area of their cross-legged seat. For some, it illuminates the inside of the room. For some, even the outside of the room. For some, the entire monastery, a quarter-league (gāvuta), half a league, one league, two leagues, three leagues... [p.] for some, it arises making a single light from the surface of the earth up to the Akanittha Brahma world. For the Blessed One, however, it arose illuminating the ten-thousandfold world system.

Regarding the different extents of this light, here is an illustrative story:

It is said that in Cittalapabbata, two elders were sitting inside a double-walled room. That day was the Uposatha of the dark fortnight, the directions were covered with clouds, and at night, the four-fold darkness prevailed. Then one elder said, "Venerable sir, now five-colored flowers are appearing to me on the lion-throne (sīhāsana) at the stupa terrace." The other said to him, "Friend, you speak of what is not wonderful; to me, now, fish and turtles in the great ocean at a distance of one league are appearing."

Notes:
1. "Double-walled room" means that inside the outer wall, there is an inner wall enclosing the central room, creating a corridor between the two walls where one can walk around. Thus, the two elders sitting in the central room had no natural light, which is why "double-walled" is specifically mentioned.
2. Regarding the "four-fold darkness," the four factors are: (1) being the 14th day Uposatha of the dark fortnight, (2) being midnight, (3) being in the middle of a thick forest, and (4) the sky being covered with clouds—as stated in the Pārājika-kaṇḍa Commentary and others. In the Mahāniddesa Pali, instead of midnight, it simply says "when the sun has set," indicating general night time.
3. "Sīhāsana" (noble seat) refers to the pedestal or throne where flowers offered at the stupa terrace are placed.
271:
At the base of that throne, the shape of hands and feet along with the claws of a lion are fashioned.

These imperfections of insight (vipassanupakkilesa) usually occur to those who have attained both tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Such a practitioner, because the defilements suppressed by meditative attainment (samāpatti) do not arise, develops the thought, 'I am an Arahant.' (How so?) It is just like the Elder Mahānāga who resided in Uccavālika, the Elder Mahādatta who resided in Haṅkana, and the Elder Cūḷasumana who resided in the Nikapennaka meditation monastery on Cittalapabbata Mountain. In this regard, the following is an account of a story:

An eminent Arahant elder named Dhammadinna, who resided in Talangara and was endowed with the analytical powers (paṭisambhidā), was a teacher who gave instructions to many monks. One day, while sitting in his place of day-rest, Dhammadinna Thera reflected: 'Has our teacher, the Great Elder Mahānāga who resides in Uccavālika, reached the goal of the monk's task (Arahantship), or not?' Upon reflecting, he saw only the state of a worldling (puthujjana) in that elder. Realizing, 'If I do not go, he will die as a worldling,' he ascended into the air by psychic power and descended near the Elder Mahānāga, who was sitting in his place of day-rest. After paying homage and performing the duties of respect, he sat to one side. When asked, 'Friend Dhammadinna, why have you come at an unusual time?' he replied, 'I have come to ask a question, Bhante.' Then, when told, 'Ask, friend; if I know, I shall answer,' he asked a thousand questions.

The Elder Mahānāga answered every question asked without any hesitation or delay. Then, [Dhammadinna] said, 'Bhante, your knowledge is very sharp. When did you attain this Dhamma?'

'Sixty years ago, friend,' he replied. When asked, 'Bhante, do you still make use of concentration (samādhi)?' he said, 'Friend, using this concentration is not a burden.' 'If so, Bhante, please create an elephant,' he requested. The Elder Mahānāga created an entirely white elephant (through supernormal power). 'Bhante, now make this elephant come towards you with its ears cocked, its tail extended, its trunk in its mouth, and making a terrifying trumpeting sound,' he requested. The Elder Mahānāga did as requested. Seeing the terrifying appearance of the elephant charging at great speed, he stood up and prepared to flee. The Arahant Dhammadinna stretched out his hand, caught the hem of the elder's robe, and said, 'Bhante, is there such a thing as fear for an Arahant?'

At that moment, the Elder Mahānāga realized his state as a worldling and said, 'Friend Dhammadinna, be my refuge,' and sat crouching at his feet. 'Bhante, I have come with the intention of being your refuge; do not worry,' he said, and taught him a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). The Elder Mahānāga took the meditation subject, and while walking on the meditation path, reached the highest fruit, Arahantship, at the third step. It is said that the Elder Mahānāga was of a hateful temperament (dosacarita). Monks of such nature tremble because of the aura of light (obhāsa). (1)

734. Ñāṇa (Knowledge) means insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). To that practitioner who is weighing and investigating material and mental phenomena, there arises a sharp, courageous, and extremely clear knowledge that has an unimpeded momentum, like the released thunderbolt of the King of Devas. (2)
272:
[272] Pīti (Rapture) means rapture associated with insight knowledge. 

To that practitioner at that time, this fivefold rapture arises, filling the entire body: minor rapture (khuddakā pīti), momentary rapture (khaṇikā pīti), showering rapture (okkantikā pīti), uplifting rapture (ubbegā pīti), and pervading rapture (pharaṇā pīti). 1 (3)

Passaddhi (Tranquility) means the tranquility of body and mind associated with insight knowledge. At that time, for that practitioner sitting (and practicing) in a place of night-rest or day-rest, there is no distress of body and mind, no heaviness, no coarseness, no unreadiness (incapacity), no sickness, and no crookedness. On the contrary, the body and mind are tranquil, light, soft, ready for work, very clear, and straight. That practitioner, with body and mind supported by this tranquility and so on, experiences at that time a non-human 2 delight. Regarding such delight, it is said:

Note:
1. For a detailed explanation of the five types of rapture, see the Manual of Vipassanā Meditation, Volume 2, pages 167 (6th ed.) - 174 (7th ed.). Also, see the same manual for detailed meanings of other imperfections (upakkilesa).
2. 'Non-human' means that ordinary humans cannot reach or obtain such delight in meditation; it is only obtainable by practitioners endowed with the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa).

'For the monk who has entered an empty hut, who has a peaceful mind, and who sees the Dhamma rightly, there arises a non-human delight.

Whenever he contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates, he gains rapture and joy. To those who discern the rise and fall, that rapture and joy are the Deathless (Nibbāna).'

Thus the Buddha taught. As stated, for that practitioner, while fulfilling this non-human delight, tranquility associated with lightness (lahutā) and so on arises. (4)

Sukha (Happiness) means the happiness associated with insight knowledge. To that practitioner at that time, an exceedingly sublime happiness arises, saturating the entire body. (5)

Adhimokkha (Decision) means faith, which is confidence and clarity. To that practitioner, a powerful faith arises, which is the supreme clarity of the mind and mental factors associated only with insight. (6)

Paggaha (Exertion) means effort or energy. To that practitioner, a well-exerted energy arises, which is neither too slack nor too tense, associated only with insight. (7)

Upaṭṭhāna (Establishment) means mindfulness (sati).
273: For that yogi, mindfulness (sati) arises, which is associated only with insight, well-manifested, well-established, immovable like a pillar deeply embedded in the ground, and like a great mountain. Whatever object that yogi reflects upon, considers, attends to, or penetrates and observes, that very object appears in that yogi's mindfulness, entering and rushing in, just as another world appears to one who has attained the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). (8) [273] Equanimity (upekkhā) refers to insight-equanimity (vipassanūpekkhā) and adverting-equanimity (āvajjanūpekkhā). At that time, for that yogi, insight-equanimity, which is neutral towards all formations (saṅkhāra), arises strongly. Adverting-equanimity in the mind-door also arises strongly. Indeed, for that yogi reflecting on various objects, that adverting-equanimity proceeds with courage and sharpness, like the released thunderbolt (vajira) of Sakka, the king of gods, or like a sharp arrow shot into a leaf-container. (9) Nikanti—attachment—means attachment to insight. For that yogi, as described, attachment (nikanti) arises, characterized by a subtle and peaceful nature, making one fond of insight adorned with light and so on. It is often impossible even to perceive such attachment as a defilement (kilesa). (10) Just as when light arises, so too when any of these—knowledge and so on—arise, the yogi thinks: 'Truly, such knowledge has never arisen in me before; such joy, tranquility, happiness, faith and clarity (adhimokkha), effort (paggaha), mindfulness (upaṭṭhāna), equanimity (upekkhā), and attachment (nikanti) have never arisen before. Surely I have reached the Path, I have reached the Fruit.' Thus, he takes what is not the Path to be the Path, and what is not the Fruit to be the Fruit. When he takes what is not the Path to be the Path and what is not the Fruit to be the Fruit, his course of insight is said to have deviated. Abandoning his original meditation subject, he remains enjoying only that attachment (nikanti). 735. Among these ten, the nine starting with light (obhāsa) are called imperfections (upakkilesa) because they are the objects of imperfections, not because they are unwholesome (akusala). However, attachment (nikanti) is both an imperfection and an object of imperfection. These are ten according to their objects. But according to the modes of grasping (gāha), they become thirty. How? For one who grasps, 'Light has arisen in me,' there is the grasping of views (diṭṭhi-gāha). For one who grasps, 'How wonderful is the light that has arisen,' there is the grasping of pride (māna-gāha). For one who enjoys the light, there is the grasping of craving (taṇhā-gāha). Thus, there are three types of grasping in light according to views, pride, and craving. It is the same for the remaining objects of imperfection. Thus, there are thirty imperfections according to the modes of grasping. An unskilled and inexperienced yogi wavers and is distracted by these thirty imperfections. As for the manner of wavering: he regards any of these, such as light, as 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' Therefore, the ancients said: 'He wavers because of light, knowledge, and joy; because of tranquility and happiness, by which the mind trembles.'
274:
[274] "One wavers because of resolution (adhimokkha), because of exertion (paggāha), because of established mindfulness (upaṭṭhāna), because of equanimity in advertence (āvajjanā-upekkhā), because of equanimity in insight (vipassanā-upekkhā), and because of attachment (nikanti)"—so they say.

## Exposition on the Determination of the Path and the Non-Path

736. But a skilled, wise, and intelligent yogi, endowed with understanding¹, when effulgence (obhāsa) and so on arise, determines with wisdom: "This effulgence has arisen in me; but this effulgence is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to fall, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation." Or else, such a reflection occurs to that yogi: "If this effulgence were the self, it would be proper to take it as 'self'. But although it is not the self, this effulgence is taken as 'self'. Therefore, it is non-self in the sense of being uncontrollable; it is impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come to be; it is suffering in the sense of being constantly oppressed by rise and fall." In this way, everything should be understood in detail according to the method mentioned in the sevenfold contemplation of materiality (rūpa-sattaka) [Note: The Burmese text says 'nāma-sattaka' but refers to the method]. As with effulgence, so also with the remaining objects of imperfection (upakkilesa).

Note
1. Skilled (kusalo)—skilled in the meditation subject; wise (paṇḍito)—possessing mature wisdom; intelligent (byatto)—learned in the scriptures; endowed with understanding (buddhisampanno)—endowed with the knowledge that knows the faults and benefits in the imperfections and the cleansing of those imperfections. Although stated in this order in the Visuddhimagga, it is translated concisely as "a skilled, wise, and intelligent yogi, endowed with understanding" for the sake of smooth Burmese phrasing.

That yogi, having reflected in this way, regards the effulgence as: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self." He regards knowledge (ñāṇa) ... [and so on] ... attachment (nikanti) as: "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self." The yogi who regards them in this way does not waver or tremble because of effulgence and so on. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"The yogi who has the wisdom that comprehends these ten states is skilled in the agitation caused by the Dhamma (dhammuddha-cca) and does not fall into distraction."

That yogi, not falling into distraction in this way, unravels that tangle of thirty kinds of imperfections and determines the path and the non-path thus: "States such as effulgence are not the path. But the insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that is free from imperfections and has entered upon the correct course is the path." The knowledge that stands having thus known the path and the non-path as "This is the path, this is not the path" should be understood as the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and What Is Not the Path (maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).

By this much (of the practice of meditation), that yogi has completed the determination of the three truths. How? In the Purification of View (diṭṭhi-visuddhi), the determination of the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) was made by the determination of mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa). In the Purification by Overcoming Doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-visuddhi), the determination of the Truth of Origin (samudaya-sacca) was made by the grasping of conditions. In this Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and What Is Not the Path, the determination of the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) is made by the ascertainment of the right path.
275: How is this so? In the stage of Purification of View (Diṭṭhivisuddhi), the definition of the Truth of Suffering (Dukkhasacca) was accomplished by the discernment of mentality and materiality. In the stage of Purification by Overcoming Doubt (Kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi), the definition of the Truth of the Origin (Samudayasacca) was accomplished by the comprehension of causes. In this stage of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and What Is Not the Path (Maggāmaggañāṇadassanavisuddhi), the definition of the Truth of the Path (Maggasacca) is accomplished by the delimitation of the correct path.
276:
In this way, the definition of the three truths has been accomplished by mundane insight knowledge alone.

This is the twentieth chapter called the Description of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and What Is Not the Path, in the section on the Development of Wisdom in the Path of Purification, composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.

## The Description of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and What Is Not the Path is finished.

## 21. Description of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way

## Discussion on the Knowledge of Rise and Fall Free from Imperfections

[276] 737. Insight that has reached its peak through the power of eight kinds of knowledge, together with the ninth, the Knowledge of Conformity to Truth—this collection of insight knowledges is called Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way (the pure knowledge and vision that is the practice for reaching the Noble Path). Among the eight, the following eight knowledges should be understood: (1) Knowledge of Rise and Fall (Udayabbayañāṇa), which is free from imperfections and is called 'insight proceeding on its course', (2) Knowledge of Dissolution (Bhaṅgānupassanāñāṇa), (3) Knowledge of Appearance as Terror (Bhayatupaṭṭhānañāṇa), (4) Knowledge of Contemplation of Danger (Ādīnavānupassanāñāṇa), (5) Knowledge of Contemplation of Disenchantment (Nibbidānupassanāñāṇa), (6) Knowledge of Desire for Deliverance (Muñcitukamyatāñāṇa), (7) Knowledge of Contemplation of Reflection (Paṭisaṅkhānupassanāñāṇa), and (8) Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations (Saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa). The ninth, 'Knowledge of Conformity to Truth', is a name for Conformity Knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa). Therefore, a meditator who wishes to perfect this Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way should begin with the Knowledge of Rise and Fall free from imperfections and apply himself to these knowledges.

738. What is the purpose of further application to the Knowledge of Rise and Fall? It is for the purpose of clearly discerning the general characteristics (lakkhaṇa). Indeed, previously, the Knowledge of Rise and Fall was defiled by the ten imperfections and was unable to clearly discern the three general characteristics according to their true nature. However, the Knowledge of Rise and Fall free from imperfections is able to do so. Therefore, further application should be made here for the purpose of clearly discerning the general characteristics.

739. By not attending to what, and by being concealed by what, do the general characteristics not appear? First, the characteristic of impermanence (aniccalakkhaṇa) does not appear because of non-attention to rise and fall, being concealed by continuity (santati). The characteristic of suffering (dukkhalakkhaṇa) does not appear because of non-attention to continuous oppression, being concealed by the postures (iriyāpatha). The characteristic of non-self (anattalakkhaṇa) does not appear because of non-attention to the resolution of the various elements, being concealed by compactness (ghana). But when rise and fall are grasped and continuity is disrupted, the characteristic of impermanence appears according to its true nature. When continuous oppression is attended to and the postures are exposed, the characteristic of suffering appears according to its true nature. When the various elements are resolved and the compactness is analyzed, the characteristic of non-self appears according to its true nature.

740. In this context, the distinction between 'impermanent' (anicca) and 'characteristic of impermanence' (aniccalakkhaṇa), 'suffering' (dukkha) and 'characteristic of suffering' (dukkhalakkhaṇa), 'non-self' (anatta) and 'characteristic of non-self' (anattalakkhaṇa) should be understood. Therein, 'impermanent' refers to the five aggregates. Why? [277] Because they have the nature of rise and fall and other changes (aging), or because after having been, they are not (they vanish).
277:
Arising, passing away, and—

Note: 
1. This means having the nature of arising, the nature of passing away, and the nature of change. "Nature of change" (aññathatta) refers to the middle stage of aging (thī) between the beginning (arising) and the end (passing away). In Pali, it is called aññathatta; accordingly, it is translated here as "other nature" (change). In short, it means "impermanent because of the three moments: arising, presence, and dissolution."

This other nature (aging) is called the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) because it is the mark by which one notes impermanence. Alternatively, the specific mode of non-existence after having arisen—disappearance—is called the characteristic of impermanence.

Because of the saying, "Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering" (Saṃ. Ni. 3.15), those very five aggregates are called dukkha (suffering). Why? Because of the continuous oppression by arising and passing away. The mode of continuous oppression is called the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa), the mark by which one notes suffering.

Because of the saying, "Whatever is suffering, that is non-self" (Saṃ. Ni. 3.15), those very five aggregates are called anatta (non-self). Why? Because they are not subject to one's will. The mode of not being subject to one's will is called the characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa), the mark by which one notes non-self.

This meditator, by means of the Knowledge of Contemplation of Arising and Passing Away (udayabbayanupassanā-ñāṇa)—which is called "insight that has entered the path" and is free from the imperfections of insight (upakkilesa)—thoroughly notes all these (impermanence, the characteristic of impermanence, etc.) according to their true nature.

## Explanation of the Knowledge of Contemplation of Dissolution (Bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa)

741. Having noted thus, as that meditator repeatedly weighs and examines mental and physical phenomena as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," his knowledge of weighing and examining becomes keen and proceeds swiftly. Formations (saṅkhāra) appear quickly. When the knowledge proceeds keenly and formations appear quickly, he no longer reaches the arising, the presence, the occurrence, or the sign (outward form) of formations. Mindfulness remains established only in the cessation, which is the exhaustion, fall, and breaking up.

To that meditator who sees, "The whole mass of mental and physical formations, having arisen in this way, ceases in this very way," there arises at that stage the insight knowledge called the Knowledge of Contemplation of Dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa). With reference to this knowledge, it is said:

"How is wisdom in contemplating dissolution after reflecting on the object knowledge of insight? The mind having materiality as its object arises and dissolves. Having reflected on that object (materiality), he contemplates the dissolution of that mind. How does he contemplate? He contemplates it as impermanent, not permanent; as suffering, not happiness; as non-self, not self. He becomes disenchanted, not delighted; he becomes dispassionate, not lustful; he causes it to cease, not to arise; he relinquishes, does not grasp.

Contemplating it as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence. Contemplating it as suffering, he abandons the perception of happiness. Contemplating it as non-self, he abandons the perception of self. [278] Becoming disenchanted, he abandons delight. Becoming dispassionate, he abandons lust. Causing it to cease, he abandons arising. Relinquishing, he abandons grasping.

With feeling as the object... [etc.] ...with perception as the object... with formations as the object... with consciousness as the object."

Note:
1. This passage—showing how the knowledge proceeds keenly, how formations appear quickly, and how the knowledge remains only in the dissolution (exhaustion and disappearance) without reaching arising or presence—describes the transition from the Knowledge of Arising and Passing Away to the Knowledge of Dissolution.
278:
Becoming disenchanted, he abandons delight; becoming dispassionate, he abandons lust; causing it to cease, he abandons arising; relinquishing, he abandons grasping.

(For a detailed explanation, see the Manual of Insight, Volume 2, 6th ed. p. 181, 7th ed. p. 196.)

With the eye as the object... [etc.]1 ...with aging and death as the object, the mind arises and dissolves... [etc.] ...relinquishing, he abandons grasping.

"The shifting of the basis (from the object's dissolution to the mind's dissolution), the turning away of wisdom (from arising to dissolution), and the power of adverting—(wisdom endowed with these three factors) is called Insight of Reflection (paṭisaṅkhā-vipassanā), which, having contemplated the dissolution of the object, contemplates again the dissolution of the observing mind.

"The defining of both objects (the seen and the unseen) as having the same nature by following the sequence of the object, and the inclination of the mind towards cessation—(wisdom endowed with these two factors) is called Insight into the Characteristic of Passing Away (vaya-lakkhaṇa-vipassanā).

"Having reflected on the object (as dissolving), he contemplates the dissolution (of the observing mind) as well, and it appears as void of self—(wisdom endowed with these three factors) is called Insight of Higher Wisdom (adhipaññā-vipassanā) because it is an excellent insight wisdom.

"One who is skilled in the three contemplations (anicca, dukkha, anatta), because of his skill in the four insights and the three appearances (upaṭṭhāna), is no longer shaken by various wrong views."

"That is called 'knowledge' in the sense of being known, and 'wisdom' in the sense of act of knowing. Therefore it is said: 'Wisdom in contemplating dissolution after reflecting on the object is knowledge of insight'" (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.51-52).

741. In that Paṭisambhidāmagga text, "after reflecting on the object" means having reflected on and known any object, having seen it as exhausted and fallen. "Wisdom in contemplating dissolution" refers to the wisdom present in contemplating the dissolution of that very knowledge which arose while knowing the object as exhausted and fallen; this is called "knowledge of insight." "How does it occur?"—this is the meaning of the question asked with the desire to explain (kathetukamyatā-pucchā). Then, to show the manner in which that knowledge occurs, it is said: "The mind having materiality as its object..." and so forth.

In that passage, "The mind having materiality as its object arises and dissolves" means the mind that takes materiality as its object arises and dissolves. Alternatively, it means the mind arises and dissolves in the state of having materiality as its object. "Having reflected on that object" means having reflected on and known that material object, having seen it as exhausted and fallen. "He contemplates the dissolution of that mind" means that with a subsequent mind, he contemplates the dissolution of the previous mind by which that material object was seen as exhausted and fallen. Therefore, the ancient teachers said: "He contemplates both the known and the knowledge."

Note:
1. The ellipsis (peyyāla) here should be expanded according to the method shown in the fourth paragraph of page 284.
279:
Therefore, in the Burmese translation of the Pali, based only on the first explanation, it is translated as "having materiality as an object."

They say: "One contemplates both the known object and the insight knowledge that knows it."

[279] In this Pali passage (regarding the contemplation of the dissolution of that knowing mind), "anupassati" (contemplates) means contemplating repeatedly, contemplating again and again in many ways. This is the meaning. Therefore, it is said: "In the phrase 'he contemplates,' how does he contemplate? He contemplates as impermanent," and so forth.

In that context, what is called dissolution (bhaṅga) is the ultimate limit of impermanence (aniccatā). Therefore, that practitioner (yogī) who contemplates dissolution contemplates all formations (saṅkhāra) as impermanent, not as permanent. Then, because the impermanent is suffering, and the suffering is non-self, he contemplates that very same impermanent thing as suffering, not as happiness; and as non-self, not as self.

Furthermore, that which is impermanent, suffering, and non-self should not be delighted in. That which should not be delighted in should not be lusted after. Therefore, following the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā), when formations are seen as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self," he becomes weary (nibbindati) of them and does not delight in them; he becomes dispassionate (virajjati) and does not lust after them.

Being thus dispassionate, he first causes lust (rāga) to cease by means of mundane knowledge (lokiya ñāṇa) and does not let it arise; the meaning is that he does not produce its arising.

Alternatively, being thus weary, just as he sees the present formations, he also causes the unseen (past and future) formations to cease by the power of inductive knowledge (anwaya-ñāṇa), and does not let them arise. He attends only to their cessation. The meaning is that he sees only their cessation, not their arising.

Practicing in this way, he relinquishes (paṭinissajjati) and does not grasp (nā diyati). What is meant by this? This insight (vipassanā) which contemplates as impermanent and so forth is called "relinquishment as giving up" (pariccāga-paṭinissagga) because it abandons the defilements (kilesa) along with the formations of the aggregates (khandhā-bhisaṅkhāra) by the power of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna). It is also called "relinquishment as entering into" (pakkhandana-paṭinissagga) because, by seeing the fault in the conditioned (saṅkhata), it inclines and enters into Nibbāna, which is the opposite.
