Therefore, the bhikkhu endowed with that insight contemplates and abandons defilements in the manner stated and enters into Nibbāna. He does not grasp defilements by way of their arising, nor does he grasp the conditioned object by way of not seeing its faults. Thus it is said, "He relinquishes and does not grasp."

743. Now, to show the abandonment of those states by means of those knowledges, it is said: "Contemplating as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā)," and so forth. In that context, "delight" (nandi) refers to craving (taṇhā) accompanied by joy (pīti). The rest is as previously explained.

[280] 744. In the verses, "shifting of the basis" (vatthu-saṅkamanā) means, after seeing the dissolution of materiality, shifting from the previous basis (the dissolution of materiality) to another basis (the dissolution of the mind) by way of seeing the dissolution of the mind that saw the dissolution of materiality.
280:
Notes:
1. Connect "This insight also... is called relinquishment as giving up... is called relinquishment as entering into." It can also be connected with the verb "is called" by translating "this insight" as the object.
2. For a detailed explanation of the meaning here, see the Manual of Insight (Vipassanā-shunee-kyan), Volume II (6th ed.), p. 424; (7th ed.), p. 452, etc.

(Continuing from the previous page): ...he sees; and by way of contemplating the dissolution of that mind again, it is the shifting from the former basis (the dissolution of materiality) to another basis (the dissolution of the mind). "Turning away of wisdom" (paññāya vivaṭṭanā) means abandoning arising and standing in dissolution. "Power of adverting" (āvajjanā-bala) is the ability to advert immediately to contemplate the dissolution of the insight mind that had dissolution as its object, after seeing the dissolution of materiality. "Insight of reflection" (paṭisaṅkhā-vipassanā) means this (wisdom endowed with three factors) is called the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā) which, after knowing the dissolution of the object, contemplates the dissolution of the insight mind.

745. "Defining both as one by following the object" (ārammaṇa-anwayena ubho ekavavatthāna) means, by following the present object seen through direct experience, one defines and decides that both (the seen and the unseen objects) have the same single nature (of dissolution), thinking: "Just like this (present formation), so too in the past the mass of formations has dissolved, and in the future it will dissolve." This is the meaning. Indeed, the ancient teachers said:

"The practitioner with pure vision in the present (formations),
Carries that inference to the past and future;
All formations are perishable,
Like dewdrops when the sun has risen."

"Intentness on cessation" (nirodhe adhimuttatā) means, after defining both types of objects (seen and unseen) as one by way of dissolution as stated, being intent on that very cessation called dissolution; it means making that cessation the priority, inclining, leaning, and tending towards it. This is the meaning. "Insight into the characteristic of passing away" (vaya-lakkhaṇa-vipassanā) means this (wisdom endowed with two factors) is called the insight into the characteristic of passing away because it contemplates the characteristic of dissolution.

746. "Having known the object and reflecting" (ārammaṇañca paṭisaṅkhā) means having known the previous object such as materiality. "And contemplates dissolution" (bhaṅgañca anupassati) means, after seeing the dissolution of that object (materiality, etc.), he contemplates the dissolution of the mind that had that dissolution as its object. "Appearance as void" (suññato upaṭṭhāna) means for that practitioner who thus contemplates dissolution, the appearance as void of self is accomplished, thinking: "Only formations break up; their breaking up is death; there is no one else besides formations who dies or breaks up."

[281] Therefore, the ancient teachers said:
281:
Thus the ancients said:

"Aggregates alone cease; there is no other self. The breaking of the aggregates is called death. The heedful yogi sees the end and destruction of those formations with wise attention, like one piercing a gem with a diamond."

'Higher wisdom insight' (adhipaññā-vipassanā) means the knowledge of the dissolution of the object, the subsequent contemplation of the dissolution of the observing mind, and the appearance [of formations] as void of self. This is called higher wisdom insight because it is an exalted form of insight.

747. 'One who is skilled in the three contemplations' means a monk who is proficient in the three contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). 'And in the four insights' means in the four contemplations beginning with the contemplation of revulsion (nibbidānupassanā). 'Because of being skilled in the three appearances' means because of being proficient in the three modes of appearance: as destruction (khaya), as fall (vaya), and as voidness (suññata). 'Unshaken by various views' means he does not waver due to various types of false views such as the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi).

748. That yogi, being thus unshaken, possesses the attention that 'only the new thing that has not yet ceased, ceases; only the new thing that has not yet broken, breaks.' Just as one sees the breaking of a fragile vessel that is being broken, or the scattering of fine dust that is being scattered, or the popping and bursting of sesame seeds that are being roasted, he abandons the sign of arising, presence, and the continuity and shape of all formations, and sees only their destruction. Just as a man with good sight standing on the bank of a pond or a river might see large bubbles on the surface of the water rising and quickly bursting when it rains heavily, even so, he sees that all formations are breaking, breaking. Indeed, with reference to such a practitioner, the Blessed One said:

"One who looks upon the world as a bubble, and looks upon it as a mirage, is not seen by the King of Death."

749. For him who thus constantly sees that 'all formations are breaking, breaking,' the knowledge of contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā-ñāṇa) reaches its strength, accompanied by eight benefits. These are the eight benefits: (1) abandoning the view of existence (bhava-diṭṭhi/sassata-diṭṭhi), (2) giving up attachment to life, (3) constant application [in meditation], (4) pure livelihood, (5) abandoning anxiety [over worldly matters], (6) fearlessness, (7) gaining patience and delight in the Dhamma, and (8) overcoming dislike and delight.

Note:
1. By the words 'beginning with,' the contemplations of fading away (virāgānupassanā), cessation (nirodhānupassanā), and relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā) are indicated.
2. Connect: 'That yogi... possessing the attention... abandons... and sees only their destruction.'
3. Connect: 'Just as one sees... he sees.'
4. The phrase 'abandons' means that arising, presence, the continuity of mind and matter, and the sign of shape are no longer seen or encountered; it does not mean a deliberate discarding, but rather that they are not found, and only destruction is seen at every moment of contemplation.
5. Connect: 'That yogi... even so... sees.'
282:
(8) The ability to suppress and abandon dislike for the forest and meditation, and delight in the cords of sensual pleasure.

Therefore, the ancients said:

"Seeing these eight supreme qualities, the sage, a contemplator of dissolution, repeatedly applies himself to the destruction of formations for the sake of attaining the Deathless (Nibbāna), like one whose clothes or head are on fire."

## The Knowledge of Contemplation of Dissolution is finished.

## Explanation of the Knowledge of Appearance as Fearful

750. As the yogi practices, develops, and frequently cultivates this knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅga-ñāṇa), which has as its object the end, fall, breaking, and cessation of all formations, the formations that are constantly breaking in all planes of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings appear to him as a great fear. Just as to a fearful man who wishes to live in comfort, things such as lions, tigers, leopards, bears, hyenas, ogres, demons, wild bulls, mad dogs, rutting elephants, poisonous snakes, thunderbolts, cemeteries, battlefields, and pits of glowing embers appear as a great fear, so do formations appear to him. As he sees that 'past formations have ceased, present ones are ceasing, and formations that will arise in the future will likewise cease,' the knowledge called 'appearance as fearful' (bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa) arises in him at that stage.

Here is an analogy: It is said that a certain woman had three sons who had committed crimes against the king. The king ordered them to be beheaded. She went with her sons to the place of execution. Then, having cut off the head of the eldest son, they began to cut off the head of the middle one. Seeing the head of the eldest cut off and the middle one being cut off, she abandoned all attachment and hope for the youngest son, thinking, 'He too will be just like them.' In this analogy, the woman's seeing the cut-off head of the eldest son is like the yogi's seeing the cessation of past formations. Her seeing the head of the middle son being cut off is like seeing the cessation of present formations. Her abandoning attachment for the youngest son, thinking 'He too will be just like them,' is like seeing the cessation of future formations, thinking 'Formations that will arise in the future will also break.' To the yogi who sees thus, the knowledge of appearance as fearful arises at this stage.

There is another analogy: It is said that a certain woman whose children did not survive (putipajā) gave birth to ten children. Nine of them had already died. One was dying in her arms, and another was in her womb.

Note:
1. Just as when one's clothes or head are on fire, one cannot attend to other matters but must quickly extinguish the fire, even so, the yogi endowed with the knowledge of dissolution cannot attend to other matters but repeatedly and constantly contemplates the destruction of formations.
2. This refers to the knowledge of dissolution that contemplates and takes as its object the cessation called the coming to an end, the vanishing, and the breaking [of formations].
3. Connect: 'To that yogi... formations... appear as a great fear.'
4. Connect: 'Just as... to a man... they appear.'
283:
That woman, having seen the nine children who had died and the tenth who was dying, gave up her attachment and expectation for the child in her womb, thinking, "This one too will surely be just like those [ten] children." In this analogy, the yogi's seeing the cessation of past formations (saṅkhāras) is to be understood like that woman's recollection of the death of her nine children; the yogi's seeing the cessation of present formations is to be understood like her seeing the dying state of the child in her hand; and the yogi's seeing the cessation of future formations is to be understood like her giving up attachment and expectation for the child in her womb. To that yogi who sees in this way, at this moment of seeing, the Knowledge of Appearance as Fearful (Bhaya-t-upaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa) arises.

751. Does the Knowledge of Appearance as Fearful itself feel fear or not? It does not feel fear. Indeed, it is merely the investigative reflection: "Past formations have ceased, present formations are ceasing, and future formations will cease." Therefore, for example, just as a man with good sight, looking at three charcoal pits near a city gate, does not himself feel fear; rather, there is only the investigative reflection in him: "All those who fall into these charcoal pits will experience no small suffering."

Or, for example, just as a man with good sight, looking at three spikes—a spike of khadira wood, an iron spike, and a golden spike—placed in a row, does not himself feel fear; rather, there is only the investigative reflection in him: "All those who fall upon these spikes will experience no small suffering." In the same way, the Knowledge of Appearance as Fearful (Bhaya-ñāṇa) does not itself feel fear; rather, there is only the investigative reflection regarding the three realms of existence—which are like the three charcoal pits and the three spikes—that "Past formations have ceased, present formations are ceasing, and future formations will cease." Because formations in all realms of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings appear to that knowledge as ruined and dangerous, it is called "Appearance as Fearful" (Bhaya-t-upaṭṭhāna).

When it appears as fearful in this way, there is this text from the Paṭisambhidāmagga:
"To one contemplating as impermanent (anicca), what appears as fearful? To one contemplating as suffering (dukkha)? To one contemplating as non-self (anatta)? To one contemplating as impermanent, the sign (nimitta) appears as fearful. To one contemplating as suffering, the occurrence (pavatta) appears as fearful. To one contemplating as non-self, both the sign and the occurrence appear as fearful."
284:
To one contemplating as suffering, the occurrence appears as fearful. To one contemplating as non-self, both the sign and the occurrence appear as fearful. This is the Pali text.

In that text, "sign" (nimitta) means the sign of formations. This is a term for the formations of the past, future, and present. Indeed, one contemplating as impermanent sees only the death and destruction of formations; therefore, the sign of formations appears to that yogi as fearful. "Occurrence" (pavatta) means the occurrence of the material and immaterial realms of existence. Indeed, one contemplating as suffering sees only the state of being constantly oppressed even in the occurrence of what is considered happiness; therefore, the occurrence of existence appears to that yogi as fearful. One contemplating as non-self sees both this sign and occurrence as being like an empty village, like a mirage, or like a city of Gandhabba spirits—empty, hollow, void, without an owner, and without a leader. Therefore, both the sign of formations and the occurrence of existence appear to that yogi as fearful. This is how it should be understood.

## The Knowledge of Appearance as Fearful is finished.

## Explanation of the Knowledge of Contemplation of Danger (Ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa)

752. To that yogi who frequents, develops, and cultivates that Knowledge of Appearance as Fearful, in all the three realms of existence, four modes of birth, five destinations, seven stations of consciousness, and nine abodes of beings, no protection appears, no shelter appears, no destination [of safety] appears, and no refuge appears. Among the formations in all realms, births, destinations, stations, and abodes, there is no longer any longing for or misapprehending even a single formation as "I". The three realms of existence appear like charcoal pits full of glowing coals without flames; the four great elements like fierce poisonous snakes; the five aggregates like murderers with raised swords; the six internal bases like an empty village; the six external bases like village-plundering robbers; the seven stations of consciousness and nine abodes of beings like things ablaze, burning, and flaming with the eleven fires. All formations appear as boils, as diseases, as darts, as calamities, as afflictions, being devoid of satisfaction, devoid of essence, and becoming a great mass of danger.

How? Just as to a fearful man who wishes to live happily, a forest thicket, even if beautifully situated, appears as if containing wild beasts; a cave as if containing tigers; water as if containing crocodiles and water-demons; enemies as if with raised swords; food as if with poison; a road as if with robbers; a house as if on fire; and a battlefield as if with an advancing army.
285:
To explain further: Just as that man, having reached the aforementioned forest inhabited by wild beasts, etc., is afraid, terrified, and has his hair standing on end, seeing only the danger all around; in the same way, when all formations appear as terror through the power of the contemplation of dissolution (bhaṅgānupassanā), this yogi sees them as entirely tasteless and joyless, seeing only the danger. To that yogi who sees thus, the knowledge of contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa), also known as the knowledge of danger (ādīnava-ñāṇa), arises. With reference to this knowledge of danger, it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

"How is wisdom in the appearance as terror the knowledge of danger? Wisdom in the appearance as terror is the knowledge of danger in that: arising is terror; occurrence is terror; the sign is terror; accumulation is terror; rebirth-linking is terror; destination is terror; generation is terror; reappearance is terror; birth is terror; aging is terror; sickness is terror; death is terror; sorrow is terror; lamentation is terror; despair is terror. Wisdom in the state of peace is the knowledge of the state of peace (santipada-ñāṇa) in that: non-arising is safety. Non-occurrence... (pe)... non-despair is safety. Wisdom in the state of peace is the knowledge of the state of peace in that: arising is terror, non-arising is safety. Occurrence... (pe)... despair is terror, non-despair is safety.

"Wisdom in the appearance as terror is the knowledge of danger in that: arising is suffering. Occurrence... (pe)... despair is suffering. Wisdom in the state of peace is the knowledge of the state of peace in that: non-arising is happiness. Non-occurrence... (pe)... non-despair is happiness. Wisdom in the state of peace is the knowledge of the state of peace in that: arising is suffering, non-arising is happiness. Occurrence... (pe)... despair is suffering, non-despair is happiness.

"Wisdom in the appearance as terror is the knowledge of danger in that: arising is with bait (sāmisa). Occurrence... (pe)... despair is with bait. Wisdom in the state of peace is the knowledge of the state of peace in that: non-arising is without bait (nirāmisa). Non-occurrence... (pe)... non-despair is without bait. Wisdom in the state of peace is the knowledge of the state of peace in that: arising is with bait, non-arising is without bait. Occurrence... (pe)... despair is with bait, non-despair is without bait."

Notes:
1. The word "even" (in the Pali/Burmese context) indicates that even if a forest, etc., is well-situated in a pleasant manner, if wild beasts are present, that forest appears only as a danger and not as something to delight in. Needless to say, this applies to a forest that is not well-situated.
2. Ādīnava (danger/disadvantage) + Ñāṇa (knowledge) = Ādīnava-ñāṇa (knowledge of danger). Ādīnava + Anupassanā (contemplation) + Ñāṇa = Ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa (knowledge of contemplation of danger).
3. "Occurring in danger" means occurring while seeing and knowing that danger.
4. Santi (peace) + Pada (state/attainment - Nibbāna) + Ñāṇa = Santipada-ñāṇa (knowledge of the state of peace, Nibbāna).
286:
Wisdom in the state of peace is the knowledge of the state of peace in that: non-despair is without bait. (8)

Wisdom in the state of peace is the knowledge of the state of peace in that: arising is with bait, non-arising is without bait. Occurrence... (pe)... despair is with bait, non-despair is without bait. (9)

Wisdom in the appearance as terror is the knowledge of danger in that: arising is formations (saṅkhāra). Occurrence... (pe)... despair is formations. (10)

Wisdom in the state of peace is the knowledge of the state of peace in that: non-arising is peaceful Nibbāna. Non-occurrence... (pe)... non-despair is peaceful Nibbāna. (11)

Wisdom in the state of peace is the knowledge of the state of peace in that: arising is formations, non-arising is peaceful Nibbāna. Occurrence... (pe)... despair is formations, non-despair is peaceful Nibbāna. (12)

"He sees arising, occurrence, the sign, accumulation, and rebirth-linking as suffering; these five knowledges of seeing are the knowledge of danger."

"He sees non-arising, non-occurrence, the signless, non-accumulation, and non-rebirth-linking as happiness; these five knowledges of seeing are the knowledge of the state of peace."

"This knowledge of danger arises in five places; the knowledge of the state of peace arises in five places; (the yogi) knows the ten knowledges. Because of being skilled in these two knowledges (of danger and the state of peace), he is no longer shaken by various wrong views."

That seeing is called 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing; it is called 'wisdom' (paññā) in the sense of understanding in various ways. Therefore, it is said: "Wisdom in the appearance as terror is the knowledge of danger." This is the Pali text.

753. In that text, 'arising' (uppāda) means rebirth in this existence due to past kamma. 

'Occurrence' (pavatta) means the continuous occurrence of the materiality and mentality that have thus arisen. 'Sign' (nimitta) means the sign of all formations. 'Accumulation' (āyūhana) means kamma which is the cause of future rebirth-linking. 'Rebirth-linking' (paṭisandhi) means future arising in a new existence. 'Destination' (gati) means the five destinations where that rebirth-linking occurs. 'Generation' (nibbattī) means the generation of the aggregates (khandha). 'Reappearance' (upapatti) means the continuous occurrence of resultant (vipāka) in the fine-material or immaterial spheres, as stated in the phrase "of one who has attained or one who has reappeared." 'Birth' (jāti) means birth caused by kamma-existence (kammabhava), which is the cause of aging, etc. 'Aging and death' (jarā-maraṇa), etc., are obvious.

Among these fifteen terms starting with arising, only the five primary terms—arising, etc.—are stated as the objects where the knowledge of danger occurs. The remaining ten terms are stated as synonyms or variations of those five primary terms. Indeed, the two terms 'generation' and 'birth' are synonyms for 'arising' and 'rebirth-linking'. The two terms 'destination' and 'reappearance' are synonyms for 'occurrence'. 'Aging', etc., are synonyms for the 'sign'. Therefore, it is said:

"He sees arising, occurrence, the sign, accumulation, and rebirth-linking as suffering; these five knowledges of seeing are the knowledge of danger."

And: "This knowledge of danger arises in five places."
289:
Just as an elephant stuck in a great swamp, [289] a king of Nagas in the mouth of a Garuda, the moon entered into the mouth of Rahu, or a man surrounded by enemies—just as these beings desire only to be freed and wish only to escape from those respective bonds and dangers, so too the mind of that yogi desires to be freed and wishes to escape from the entire mass of formations (saṅkhāra). Then, for that yogi who is thus devoid of attachment to all formations and who desires to be freed from the entire mass of formations, the Knowledge of Desire for Deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa) arises.

## The Knowledge of Desire for Deliverance is concluded.

## Explanation of the Knowledge of Contemplation of Reflection

757. Thus, desiring to be freed from the formations that exist within all three realms of existence (bhava), the four modes of generation (yoni), the five destinations (gati), the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa), and which are constantly perishing (moment by moment), that yogi, in order to be freed from the entire mass of formations, again grasps those same formations by attributing the three characteristics through the Knowledge of Contemplation of Reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa) in the following manner:

That yogi sees all formations as impermanent (anicca) for such reasons as: (1) because they cannot transcend the end of destruction, (2) because they are temporary, (3) because they are bounded by rise and fall, (4) because they are disintegrating, (5) because they are fickle, (6) because they are perishable, (7) because they are unenduring, (8) because they are subject to change, (9) because they are coreless, (10) because they are devoid of prosperity, (11) because they are conditioned, and (12) because they are subject to death.

He sees them as suffering (dukkha) for such reasons as: (1) because they are constantly oppressive, (2) because they are unbearable, (3) because they are the basis of pain, (4) because they are like a disease, (5) because they are like a boil, (6) because they are like a dart, (7) because they are like a calamity, (8) because they are like an affliction, (9) because they are like a danger, (10) because they are like a misfortune, (11) because they are like a fear, (12) because they are like a plague, (13) because they are defenseless, (14) because they are not a shelter, (15) because they are not a refuge, (16) because they are a danger (ādīnava), (17) because they are the root of evil, (18) because they are like a murderer, (19) because they are the objects of taints (āsava), (20) because they are the bait of Mara the killer, (21) because they are subject to birth, (22) because they are subject to aging, (23) because they are subject to sickness, (24) because they are subject to sorrow, (25) because they are subject to lamentation, (26) because they are subject to despair, and (27) because they are the objects of defilements.

He sees them as foul (asubha), which is an attendant of the characteristic of suffering, for such reasons as: (1) because they are unpleasant, (2) because they have a bad odor, (3) because they are loathsome, (4) because they are repulsive,
290:
(5) because their beauty is destroyed by lack of adornment, (6) because they are ugly, and (7) because they are extremely unsightly.1 For such reasons, he sees them as foul (asubha), as an attendant of the characteristic of suffering.

He sees them as non-self (anatta) for such reasons as: (1) because they are alien, (2) because they are devoid of a self, (3) because they are vain, (4) because they are empty of a self, (5) because they have no owner, (6) because they are not subject to control, and (7) because they do not occur according to one's will.

[290] 758. When the yogi sees in this way, the formations are said to have been grasped by attributing the three characteristics. But why does he grasp them in this way? For the purpose of perfecting the means of release. Here, this is the simile:

A man, thinking "I will catch a fish," took a fish-trap and placed it in the water. He thrust his hand into the mouth of the trap and, seizing a snake by the neck in the water, he was glad, thinking, "I have caught a fish." Thinking, "I have indeed caught a large fish," he lifted it up and looked. Seeing the three stripes (on its neck), he recognized it as a snake. He became afraid, seeing the danger, and becoming weary of his grip, he desired to release it. Devising a means of release, he unwound his hand starting from the tail, raised his arm, and after swinging it around his head two or three times to weaken the snake, he let it go, saying, "Go, you evil snake!" He then quickly climbed up the embankment of the pond and stood looking back at the way he had come, thinking, "Oh, I have indeed been freed from the mouth of a great snake!"

In this simile, the time when the man was glad, having seized the snake by the neck thinking it was a fish, should be understood as the time when this yogi was glad at the beginning having obtained this physical body (attabhāva). The man's seeing the three stripes after pulling the snake's head out of the trap's mouth should be understood as this yogi's seeing the three characteristics in formations after breaking down the compact mass (ghana-vinibbhoga). The time when the man was afraid should be understood as this yogi's Knowledge of Appearance as Terror (bhayatūpaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa). Then, his seeing the danger is like the Knowledge of Contemplation of Danger (ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa). His weariness of the grip is like the Knowledge of Contemplation of Dispassion (nibbidānupassanā-ñāṇa). His desire to release the snake is like the Knowledge of Desire for Deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa). His devising a means of release is like the attributing of the three characteristics to formations through the Knowledge of Contemplation of Reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa). Just as that man, having swung the snake to weaken it and rendered it unable to turn back and bite, released it well, so too this yogi, having swung the formations (as it were) by attributing the three characteristics and weakened them so that they are unable to appear again as permanent, pleasant, beautiful, or as a self, releases them well. Therefore, I have said: "He grasps them in this way for the purpose of perfecting the means of release."

759. By this much (of the practice of meditation), it should be understood that the Knowledge of Reflection (paṭisaṅkhā-ñāṇa) has arisen in that yogi. With reference to that Knowledge of Reflection—

Footnote:
1. The word 'vībhatsa' conveys the meanings of loathsome, ugly, and unsightly. Here, to avoid repetition with previous terms, it is translated as "extremely unsightly."
291:
[291] 'For one who attends [to formations] as impermanent, what knowledge of reflection (paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇa) arises? As suffering. For one who attends as not-self, what knowledge of reflection arises? For one who attends as impermanent, knowledge of reflection arises regarding the sign (of formations). For one who attends as suffering, knowledge of reflection arises regarding the continuity (of occurrence). For one who attends as not-self, knowledge of reflection arises regarding both the sign and the continuity.' Thus it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. I, 227).

In this text, 'reflecting on the sign' [1] means having known the sign of formations as 'unstable, temporary' by way of the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa). To explain further: it is not that the knowledge arises only after having known; rather, it is spoken of in this way according to conventional usage, similar to the statement, 'Dependent on the mind-door and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises' [2]. Alternatively, according to the method of unity (ekatta-naya), it should be understood that the preceding reflection and the subsequent arising of knowledge are spoken of as one. In this same way, the meaning of the other two phrases [1] should also be understood.

## The Knowledge of Reflection (paṭisaṅkhā-anupassanā-ñāṇa) is concluded.

## Explanation of the Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa)

760. That meditator, having thus grasped with the knowledge of reflection that 'all formations are empty' [2], again [3] grasps emptiness in two aspects: 'This is empty of self or of what belongs to self' [4]. Having thus grasped, seeing neither a self nor anything belonging to another as an accessory of a self, he again [1] grasps the fourfold emptiness stated in this context: 'I am not anywhere, for anyone, anything [2, 3]; nor is there anywhere, in anything, anything of mine [4, 5]' [6].

How? This meditator, according to the text 'Nāhaṃ kvacani' (I am not anywhere), does not see a self in any place [7]. According to the text 'Kassaci kiñcanatasmmi' (for anyone, anything), he does not see his own self as something to be brought into the state of being 'something' for another. That is, he does not see [himself] as a brother in the place of a brother, a friend in the place of a friend, or an accessory in the place of an accessory. Regarding 'Na ca mama kvacani,' setting aside the word 'mama' (mine) for a moment, 'na ca kvacani' means [he does not see] another's self anywhere...

Notes:
1. Paṭi (again) + Saṅkhā (knowing) = Paṭisaṅkhā (knowing again). This precise meaning is appropriate because although it was known by previous knowledges, it is known again by this knowledge. However, if the meaning is taken only for this single knowledge, the word 'again' is not useful; therefore, in the Commentary, the meaning of 'paṭi' as 'again' is set aside and explained simply as 'jānitvā' (having known).
2. In the phrase 'Dependent on the mind-door and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises,' the preceding action of 'depending' and the subsequent action of 'arising' occur simultaneously. However, in worldly convention, they are spoken of as if they occur at different times. Similarly, in this teaching, 'reflecting on the sign, knowledge arises,' the preceding action of knowing and the subsequent action of arising occur simultaneously, but are taught as if they occur sequentially according to worldly convention.
1 (Other): The other two phrases are 'reflecting on the continuity, knowledge arises' and 'reflecting on both the sign and the continuity, knowledge arises.'
2-3: Connect 'having grasped... again... grasps again.'
4: 'Empty of self' means empty of the qualities of a self as perceived by foolish worldlings, such as 'owner (sāmī) of the house of aggregates, dweller (nivāsī) within the house of aggregates, doer (kāraka), or feeler (vedaka).' Since it is not a part or power of such a self, it is also 'not what belongs to self.' It is empty of both.
1 (Again): Connect 'not seeing... again... grasps again.'
2: I am not the concern of anyone; there is no 'I' that is the concern of anyone.
3: This translation in parentheses is an alternative meaning by splitting the words as 'kiñcana + asmi.'
4: Not my concern; there is no 'other' who is my concern.
5: This translation in parentheses is an alternative meaning by splitting the words as 'kiñcana + atthi.'
6: See the 'Manual of Vipassanā' Vol. 2 for the method of contemplating fourfold emptiness.
7. If one sees 'I am not anywhere,' one no longer sees the self in any place or any phenomenon. This explains the intended meaning, not just the literal grammatical meaning.
292:
One does not see [anything] that should be regarded as a brother in the place of a brother, or as a friend in the place of a friend, or as a requisite in the place of a requisite. This is the intended meaning. In the passage "na ca mama kvacani" (and nowhere is there anything of mine), setting aside the word "mama" (mine), according to the passage "na ca kvacani" (and nowhere is there anything), one does not see another's self anywhere. This is the intended meaning. Now, bringing back the word "mama" (mine) that was set aside, according to the passage "mama kismiñci kiñcanatatthi," one does not see that another's self exists in the state of being something of one's own concern, such as a brother in the place of one's own brother, or as a friend in the place of a friend, or as a requisite in the place of a requisite; thus, in any place, one does not see another's self as something that should or could be regarded as one's own concern. This is the intended meaning.

Note 1: If one sees that no one exists in the state of being a concern—that they are not a concern—then one no longer sees anything that should be regarded or taken as another's concern. Therefore, here too, only the intended meaning is explained, not the grammatical meaning.

Note 2: Regarding how one's own self is not another's concern, the Ṭīkā explains the connection as follows: "This creator is Brahmā, Mahābrahmā, the Overlord, the Unvanquished, the All-Seeing, the Controller, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Most Excellent, the Ordainer, the Master, the Father of those who have been and are to be." Thus, it is said "of anyone" and so forth, to show that one does not see a self-entity that is the concern of someone like Brahmā or an eternal God, as imagined by those outside the Sasana. By the above Ṭīkā, it should be understood that "another" here does not only mean brothers and so on, but also includes the Lord God, the owner of the world, whom those outside the Sasana believe to be the creator.

In this way, this yogi does not see a self-entity in any place, time, or phenomena. He does not see his own self as something that should be regarded as another's concern, nor does he see another's self, nor does he see another's self as something that should be regarded as his own concern. Therefore, this yogi has grasped the emptiness (suññatā) pertaining to the four aspects.

761. Having grasped the emptiness pertaining to the four aspects as described, he again grasps emptiness through six aspects. How? The eye is empty of self, or of what belongs to self, or of permanence, or of stability, or of eternity, or of an unchanging nature... [and so on]... the mind is empty. Forms are empty... [and so on]... mental objects are empty. Eye-consciousness... [and so on]... mind-consciousness. Eye-contact—in this manner, the method should be applied up to aging and death (jarāmaraṇa).

762. Having grasped emptiness through the six aspects as described, he again grasps it through eight aspects. That is to say: form is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence, in terms of the essence of permanence, the essence of stability, the essence of happiness, or the essence of self; or in terms of permanence, stability, eternity, or an unchanging nature. Feeling... perception... mental formations... consciousness... the eye... [and so on]... aging and death are without essence, void of essence, departed from essence, in terms of the essence of permanence, the essence of stability, the essence of happiness, or the essence of self; or in terms of permanence, stability, eternity, or an unchanging nature. Just as a reed is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence; just as a castor oil plant... just as a fig tree... just as a white-barked tree... just as a coral tree... just as a lump of foam... just as a water bubble... just as a mirage... just as a plantain trunk... just as a magical illusion is without essence, void of essence, departed from essence; even so, form... [and so on]... aging and death are without essence, void of essence, departed from essence, in terms of the essence of permanence... [and so on]... or an unchanging nature. (Cūḷaniddesa, Mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 88).
293:
Therefore, it is said that one cannot do as one wishes. In another way, no action can be accomplished by mere wish alone; it can only be completed when causes are in harmony. For this reason also, it is said that one cannot do as one wishes.

3. It means one cannot obtain by wishing: "May my form be only good like this, may it not be bad like this."

4. As stated in the fifth paragraph of page 268: "The cause (kamma) does not exist within the result (vipāka), nor does the result exist within the cause. Kamma and vipāka are empty of each other, yet the result cannot arise without the cause." Just as kamma and vipāka are empty of each other (referring to the reading kammādi viya), or as form is empty of a performing self (referring to the Sinhalese reading kārakādīhi viya), it means form is empty of its own cause and its own result. Indeed, the result does not exist within the cause as if it were pregnant or latent, nor does the cause exist within the result as if it were pregnant or latent. (Commentary)

He sees. He sees feeling... consciousness as void of (essence)... as empty.

764. Having thus grasped emptiness through ten modes, he grasps it again through twelve modes. The manner of grasping is: form is not a being [1], not a life, not a person, not a youth, not a woman, not a man, not a self, not belonging to a self, not "I", not "mine", not another's [2], not anyone's.

Note 1: This does not mean that form is not a "being" in terms of conventional worldly usage. Why? Because the meaning that form is not a being in that conventional sense is already self-evident. Indeed, people do not call form alone a "being". In truth, it means that form is not the "being" called "self" (atta) as imagined by those outside the Dispensation. In seeing it as not a person, not a youth, not a woman, not a man, and not "I", understand that it similarly means there is no "self-entity". (Commentary)

Note 2: In this regard, the Cūḷaniddesa Pāḷi, which is the original source for the Visuddhimagga, contains the reading "na koci—not anyone". The commentaries on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta also have the same. Here, the meaning "not another's property" is included within the mode of seeing "not anyone's property" to be mentioned next; therefore, the reading "na koci—not anyone" is more appropriate.

He sees feeling... consciousness as not a being... not anyone's property.

765. Having thus grasped emptiness through twelve modes, he grasps it again through forty-two modes by virtue of the full understanding of investigation (tīraṇapariññā). The manner of grasping is: he sees form as impermanent [1], as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as an alien, as disintegrating, (10) as a calamity, as a misfortune, as a terror, as a menace, as fickle, as perishable, as unenduring, as no protection, as no shelter, as no refuge, (20) as no resort, as void, as empty, as hollow, as non-self, as not delightful [2], as a danger, as subject to change, as coreless, as the root of misery, (30) as murderous, as without prosperity, as subject to taints, as conditioned, as the bait of Māra, as subject to birth, as subject to aging, as subject to illness, as subject to death, as subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, (40) by way of origin, by way of cessation, by way of gratification, by way of danger [1], and by way of escape. He sees feeling... consciousness as impermanent... by way of escape.

Note 1 (on 765): The term "aniccato" could be translated as "by way of impermanence" or "in the aspect of impermanence"; however, for brevity, it is translated here simply as "impermanent". The same applies to "suffering", "disease", etc.

Note 2 (on 765): The term "anassādato—not delightful" is not in the Pāḷi text. The Commentary states that if this term is included, there would be forty-three modes instead of forty-two. Therefore, this term should be regarded as an interpolation.

Indeed, one who sees the world of the five aggregates as empty by seeing form as impermanent... by way of escape, is said to look upon the world as empty. One who sees feeling... consciousness as impermanent... by way of escape, is said to look upon the world as empty.

"Mogharāja, always mindful, look upon the world as empty (of self); having uprooted the view of self, one may thus overcome death. The King of Death does not see one who looks upon the world in this way." (Sutta Nipāta 1125; Cūḷaniddesa, Mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddesa 88)
294:
He spoke these words: "The King of Death does not see one who looks upon the world in this way (as empty)."

[294] 766. In the manner described, the practitioner (yogi) who views [the world] as empty, applies the Three Characteristics, and comprehends formations, abandons both fear and delight, and becomes indifferent and neutral towards formations. He no longer clings to them as "I" or "mine," just like a man who has let go of his wife.

Notes:
1. Although this aspect of danger (ādinava) was mentioned before, it is stated again here according to the sequence of teaching: (1) arising (samudaya), (2) passing away (atthaṅgama), (3) gratification (assāda), (4) danger (ādinava), and (5) escape (nissaraṇa). Therefore, this danger should be counted together with the previous ones as forty-two aspects.
2. Here, the term 'aniccato' can also be translated as 'by way of impermanence' or 'in the manner of impermanence.'
3. 'Attānudiṭṭhi'—the view that follows the self—is indeed 'sakkāyadiṭṭhi' (personality belief).

For example, a man might have a wife who is desirable, lovely, and pleasing. He would be unable to live without her even for a moment [Note 1], and he would cherish her exceedingly. If he were to see that woman standing, sitting, talking, or laughing with another man, he would be angry and displeased, experiencing intense grief and distress. At a later time, seeing the faults of that woman and desiring to be free from her, he would divorce and abandon her, no longer regarding her as "my wife." From then on, even if he saw her doing anything with any other man, he would not be angry or distressed; instead, he would be indifferent and neutral. In the same way, this practitioner, desiring to be delivered from all formations, comprehends formations through the knowledge of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā). Seeing nothing to be grasped as "I" or "mine," he abandons fear and delight, and remains indifferent and neutral towards all formations.

Note 1: 10 finger-snaps are called 1 khaṇa; 10 khaṇa are 1 laya; 10 laya are 1 khaṇalaya; 10 khaṇalaya are 1 muhutta. In Burmese usage, it is commonly spoken of as "a moment" or "an instant."

For the practitioner who thus knows and thus sees, the mind shrinks, recoils, and rolls back from the three types of existence (bhava), the four modes of birth (yoni), the five destinations (gati), the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), and the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa); it does not stretch out. Either equanimity or repulsiveness becomes well-established.

Just as water drops on a slightly inclined lotus leaf shrink, recoil, and roll back, and do not spread out; so too... [etc.] ...Just as a chicken feather or a piece of sinew thrown into a fire shrinks, recoils, and rolls back, and does not stretch out, so too the mind of that practitioner [shrinks, etc.] from the three types of existence... [etc.] ...it does not stretch out. Either equanimity or repulsiveness becomes well-established. When this occurs, it should be understood that the knowledge known as "Equanimity towards Formations" (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) has arisen in that practitioner.

767. If this knowledge of equanimity towards formations sees Nibbāna, the state of peace, as peaceful, it lets go of the entire occurrence of formations and leaps into Nibbāna. If it does not yet see Nibbāna as peaceful, it continues to occur repeatedly, taking only formations as its object.
295:
(How is this so?) It is like the direction-finding crow of seafaring merchants. It is said that when merchants board a ship to travel the sea, they take with them a so-called direction-finding crow (disākāka).

Note 1: This means it does not rush in with delight in those various objects of formations.
Note 2: This refers to the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) that is mature enough to give rise to the knowledge of conformity (anuloma-ñāṇa), seeing the element of Nibbāna-peace as peaceful.

When the ship is blown to a foreign place by a storm and the shore is not visible or predictable, they release the direction-finding crow. That crow flies from the top of the mast into the sky, travels through all the cardinal and intermediate directions in order, and if it sees the shore, it flies directly towards it. If it does not see the shore, it returns again and again to rest only on the top of the mast. In the same way, if the knowledge of equanimity towards formations sees the element of Nibbāna-peace as peaceful, it abandons the entire flow of formations and rushes only towards the element of Nibbāna-peace. If it does not yet see it, it continues to occur again and again, taking only formations as its object.

This knowledge of equanimity towards formations, occurring delicately like flour being rolled and pressed on a tray [Note 1] or like carded cotton from which seeds have been removed [Note 2], grasps formations in various ways, abandons both fear and delight, and stands neutral in the investigation of formations through the power of the three types of contemplation [Note 3]. Standing thus, it reaches the state of being the three gateways to liberation (vimokkhamukha) and becomes the condition for the classification of the seven types of noble persons (ariya-puggala).

768. In this regard (reaching the state of being the gateways to liberation and being the condition), because this knowledge of equanimity towards formations occurs through the power of the three types of contemplation, it is said to reach the state of being the three gateways to liberation through the power of the predominance of the three faculties (indriya). To elaborate, the three contemplations are called the three gateways to liberation. As it is said:

“These three gateways to liberation lead to the exit from the world: the contemplation of all formations as limited and bounded for the sake of the mind's entering into the signless (animitta) element; the stimulation of the mind regarding all formations for the sake of the mind's entering into the desireless (appaṇihita) element; and the contemplation of all things as foreign for the sake of the mind's entering into the emptiness (suññata) element. These three gateways to liberation lead to the exit from the world.”
(Thus it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga).

Note 1: Just as flour becomes finer and more delicate the more it is pressed on a tray, so too the knowledge of equanimity towards formations becomes subtler and subtler the longer it lasts.
Note 2: Just as cotton becomes finer the more it is carded, so too the knowledge of equanimity towards formations becomes subtler and subtler the longer it lasts.
Note 3: Although explained in detail as the seven contemplations or the eighteen principal insights, they are included within the three contemplations such as the contemplation of impermanence. Therefore, the sub-commentary states that insight reaching its peak stands only through the power of these three contemplations.

In that text, 'as limited and bounded' (pariccheda-parivaṭumato) means by way of rise and fall, both as a limit and as a boundary. Indeed, the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), having limited them by the thought 'before their rise, formations did not exist,' and following their destiny, contemplates them as bounded by the thought 'after their fall, they do not go anywhere; they vanish right here.' 'Stimulating the mind' (manosamuttejanatāya) means [296] for the purpose of making the mind terrified. Indeed, through the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), one makes the mind terrified of formations.
296:
To contemplate well as an external stranger means to contemplate well as non-self in this way: "I am not this, this is not mine." Thus, it should be understood that these three terms are stated by way of the contemplation of impermanence and so on. Therefore, immediately following that, in the explanation of the questions, it is said:

"To one who attends [to formations] as impermanent, formations appear as passing away. To one who attends as suffering, formations appear as a terror. To one who attends as non-self, formations appear as empty."

Notes:
1. By the qualification "by way of power," it makes known that the "limit" is indeed arising and falling away, and the "boundary" is also arising and falling away.
2. In this sentence, by the words "defining as not yet existing before arising," it should be taken that "limit is arising," and by the words "not going beyond falling away," etc., it should be taken that "boundary is falling away."

769. Now, which are those deliverances for which these contemplations are the doors? They are these three: the signless deliverance (animitta-vimokkha), the desireless deliverance (appaṇihita-vimokkha), and the void deliverance (suññata-vimokkha). For it is said:

"One who attends as impermanent, having a predominance of resolution (adhimokkha), acquires the signless deliverance. One who attends as suffering, having a predominance of tranquility (passaddhi), acquires the desireless deliverance. One who attends as non-self, having a predominance of wisdom (veda), acquires the void deliverance."

Herein, "signless deliverance" is the Noble Path that proceeds by making Nibbāna the object through the signless aspect. For that [path] is called signless because it arises in the signless element (Nibbāna), and it is called deliverance because it is liberated from defilements. In this same way, the Noble Path that proceeds by making Nibbāna the object through the desireless aspect¹ is called "desireless." The Noble Path that proceeds by making Nibbāna the object through the void aspect is called "void."

Note:
1. "Aspect of being free from the craving of desire" means the aspect where there is nothing to be desired or no craving to be produced in Nibbāna.

770. However, in the Abhidhamma¹, "At whatever time² he develops supramundane jhana that is an outlet [from the round of rebirths] and leads to the dispersal [of defilements], for the abandoning of wrong views³, for the attainment of the first stage⁴, he enters and dwells in the first jhana... desireless, void." Thus, only two deliverances are mentioned. This is said with reference to the arrival via insight (vipassanā-gamana) in a literal sense.

For although in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, insight knowledge⁵ [is described as]:

"The contemplation of impermanence is the void deliverance because it gives up the adherence to permanence. The contemplation of suffering is the void deliverance because it gives up the adherence to pleasure. The contemplation of non-self is the void deliverance because it gives up the adherence to self." Thus, it is called "void deliverance" by way of giving up adherence.
297:
"The contemplation of impermanence is the signless deliverance because it gives up the sign of formations (appearing) as permanent. The contemplation of suffering is the signless deliverance because it gives up the sign of formations (appearing) as pleasure. The contemplation of non-self is the signless deliverance because it gives up the sign of formations (appearing) as self." Thus, it is called "signless deliverance" by way of giving up the sign of formations.

Notes:
1. In Abhidhamma... only two deliverances are taught—connect this.
2. At whatever time... he develops—connect this.
3-4. For the abandoning... and for the attainment... he develops supramundane jhana—connect this.
5. It is true that insight knowledge is taught as void deliverance, signless deliverance, and desireless deliverance—connect this.

"The contemplation of impermanence is the desireless deliverance because it gives up desire for permanence. The contemplation of suffering is the desireless deliverance because it gives up desire for pleasure. The contemplation of non-self is the desireless deliverance because it gives up desire for self." Thus, it is called "desireless deliverance" by way of giving up desire.

Even so, that insight knowledge is not literally "signless" because it does not abandon the sign of formations¹. But it is literally "void" and "desireless." And the deliverance is extracted at the moment of the Noble Path by way of the arrival of that [insight]. Therefore, it should be understood that only the two deliverances, the desireless and the void, are mentioned in the Abhidhamma. This is the discussion on deliverance here.

771. As to what was said, "It is the cause for the classification of the seven types of Noble Persons," therein: (1) the faith-follower (saddhānusārī), (2) the one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta), (3) the body-witness (kāyasakkhī), (4) the both-ways-liberated (ubhatobhāgavimutta), (5) the Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī), (6) the one attained to vision (diṭṭhippatta), and (7) the one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta)—these are the seven Noble Persons. This knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) is the cause for the classification of these seven Noble Persons.

Note:
1. Insight knowledge occurs only while taking formations as objects and contemplating them; therefore, it is said that it does not abandon the sign of formations.

772. To explain in detail: the person who attends [to formations] as impermanent, having a predominance of resolution (adhimokkha), acquires the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). That person is a "faith-follower" (saddhānusārī) at the moment of the path of Stream-entry. In the remaining seven stages [of paths and fruits], he is "one liberated by faith" (saddhāvimutta).

773. The person who attends as suffering, having a predominance of tranquility (passaddhi), acquires the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya). That person is a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī) in all [eight stages of paths and fruits].

If, after attaining the immaterial jhanas, he reaches the fruit of Arahantship, he is called "both-ways-liberated" (ubhatobhāgavimutta).

774.
298:
774. However, one who contemplates by way of the aspect of non-self (anatta), having a preponderance of wisdom and acquiring the predominant faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), is called a Dhamma-follower (dhammānusārī) at the moment of the Path of Stream-entry. At the six intermediate stages (the three lower fruits and three higher paths), such a person is called one attained to vision (diṭṭhippatta). At the moment of the Fruit of Arahantship, such a person is called one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta).

775. For it is said: 
“For one contemplating by way of impermanence (anicca), the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is predominant. Because the faculty of faith is predominant, one acquires the Path of Stream-entry; therefore, one is called a faith-follower (saddhānusārī).”
Likewise: “For one contemplating by way of impermanence, the faculty of faith is predominant. Because the faculty of faith is predominant, the Fruit of Stream-entry is realized; therefore, one is called one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta),” and so on (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.221).

776. It is further stated:
“One is liberated through faith, thus one is ‘liberated by faith’ (saddhāvimutta). One realizes [Nibbāna] after having touched [the immaterial jhanas], thus one is a ‘body-witness’ (kāyasakkhī). One has reached [the goal] after seeing [Nibbāna], thus one is ‘attained to vision’ (diṭṭhippatta). One is liberated while having faith, thus one is ‘liberated by faith.’ One first touches the contact of jhana and afterwards realizes Nibbāna, the cessation; thus one is a ‘body-witness.’ It is known, seen, understood, realized, and touched through wisdom that ‘formations are suffering, and cessation is bliss’; thus one is ‘attained to vision’” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.221).

777. Regarding the other four terms: one follows faith, or one goes (follows) by means of faith, thus one is a ‘faith-follower’ (saddhānusārī). Similarly, one follows the Dhamma known as wisdom, or one goes by means of the Dhamma; thus one is a ‘Dhamma-follower’ (dhammānusārī). One is liberated by both parts—the immaterial jhana and the Noble Path; thus one is ‘liberated in both ways’ (ubhatobhāgavimutta). One is liberated while knowing; thus one is ‘liberated by wisdom’ (paññāvimutta). In this way, the etymological meanings should be understood.

## Knowledge of Equanimity towards Formations (Saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa)

778. This knowledge of equanimity towards formations is essentially one with the two previous knowledges. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:
“This knowledge of equanimity towards formations, while being a single entity, receives three names:
299:
At the beginning, it is called ‘knowledge of desire for deliverance’ (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa); in the middle, it is called ‘knowledge of contemplation of re-reflection’ (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa); and at the end, it is called ‘knowledge of equanimity towards formations’ (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) which has reached its peak.”

779. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga text, it is also stated:
“How is wisdom that is desire for deliverance, re-reflection, and steadying called knowledge of equanimity towards formations? Wisdom that is desire for deliverance, re-reflection, and steadying regarding arising (uppāda) is knowledge of equanimity towards formations. Wisdom that is desire for deliverance, re-reflection, and steadying regarding occurrence (pavatta)... [etc.]... regarding the sign (nimitta)... [etc.]... regarding despair (upāyāsa) is knowledge of equanimity towards formations.
(Perceiving that) arising is suffering... [etc.]... is a fear... [etc.]... is accompanied by taints... [etc.]... arising is a formation... [etc.]... despair is a formation—wisdom that is desire for deliverance, re-reflection, and steadying is knowledge of equanimity towards formations” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.54).

780. In that text, it is ‘desire for deliverance,’ it is ‘re-reflection,’ and it is ‘steadying’; thus it is called ‘desire for deliverance, re-reflection, and steadying.’ Thus, the desire to abandon arising and so forth in a yogi who has become weary through the knowledge of revulsion (nibbidā-ñāṇa) in the preceding stage is ‘desire for deliverance’ (muñcitukamyatā). Re-reflecting in the middle stage to find the means for deliverance is ‘re-reflection’ (paṭisaṅkhā). Looking on with equanimity at the end after being delivered is ‘steadying’ (santiṭṭhanā). Referring to such steadying, it is said: “Arising is a formation; one looks on those formations with equanimity, thus it is equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā),” and so on. Thus, these three are but a single knowledge.

781. Furthermore, it should be understood as a single entity through the following canonical text: “That which is desire for deliverance, that which is contemplation of re-reflection, and that which is equanimity towards formations—these states are one in meaning, and only the phrasing is different” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.227).

782. For this clansman who has attained equanimity towards formations in this way, his insight reaches its peak and becomes ‘insight leading to emergence’ (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā). Both names—‘insight that has reached its peak’ (sikhāppatta-vipassanā) and ‘insight leading to emergence’—are names for the triad of knowledges starting with equanimity towards formations (Note: The triad refers to equanimity towards formations, conformity knowledge, and change-of-lineage). It is called ‘reached its peak’ because it has reached the summit or the highest state. It is called ‘leading to emergence’ because it goes towards the emergence [of the Path]. The Path is called ‘emergence’ (vuṭṭhāna) because it emerges from the external sign (the object of contemplation) and from the internal occurrence (the flow of defilements and aggregates). It ‘goes towards’ it means it connects with the Noble Path.

783. Herein, this is the matrix (mātikā) for clarifying the fixing [of the mind] and the emergence: Having fixed [the mind] on the internal (ajhätta), one emerges from the internal. Having fixed on the internal, one emerges from the external. Having fixed on the external, one emerges from the external.
300:
One emerges from the external; having inclined towards the external, one emerges from the external. Having inclined towards the external, one emerges from the internal. Having inclined towards materiality, one emerges from materiality. Having inclined towards materiality, one emerges from mentality. Having inclined towards mentality, one emerges from mentality. Having inclined towards mentality, one emerges from materiality. One emerges from the five aggregates simultaneously. Having initially inclined through the aspect of impermanence, one emerges through the aspect of impermanence. Having initially inclined through the aspect of impermanence, one emerges through the aspect of suffering, or through the aspect of non-self. Having initially inclined through the aspect of suffering, one emerges through the aspect of suffering, or through the aspect of impermanence, or through the aspect of non-self. Having initially inclined through the aspect of non-self, one emerges through the aspect of non-self, or through the aspect of impermanence, or through the aspect of suffering.

Notes:
1. The initial application of insight is called 'abhinivesa' (initial inclination). Therefore, 'abhinivisitvā—having initially inclined' is equivalent to 'having initially observed.' The term '(observed)' is shown in parentheses to indicate that 'observed' can be used instead of 'inclined.' In this context, the commentary states that 'abhinivesa'—initial inclination or initial observation—refers to observation at the stage of the 'Definition of Mentality and Materiality' (nāmarūpa-pariccheda).
2. In this specific context, because it is stated 'through the aspect of impermanence,' the phrase 'abhinivisitvā—having initially inclined or initially observed' should be understood as observation at the stage of 'Knowledge of Comprehension' (sammasana-ñāṇa) and so forth.

Having initially inclined through the aspect of non-self, one emerges through the aspect of non-self, or through the aspect of impermanence, or through the aspect of suffering.

784. How? Here, a certain yogi from the very beginning inclines towards (observes) internal formations; having inclined, he sees those formations correctly. However, emergence of the Path does not occur merely by seeing purely internal phenomena; external phenomena must also be seen. Therefore, he sees the aggregates of others and also inanimate formations (anupādinna-saṅkhāra) as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. That yogi at times contemplates the internal, and at times the external. As he contemplates thus, while contemplating the internal, his insight connects with the Noble Path. This is called 'having initially observed the internal, he emerges from the internal.'

If, however, while he is contemplating the external, his insight connects with the Noble Path, this is called 'having initially observed the internal, he emerges from the external.' This same method applies to emerging from the external and the internal after initially observing the external.

785. Another yogi from the very beginning inclines towards materiality; having inclined, he sees the collection of primary materiality (bhūta-rūpa) and derived materiality (upādā-rūpa) as a group. However, emergence does not occur merely by seeing purely materiality; mentality must also be seen. Therefore, taking that materiality as an object, he sees the feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that arise as 'this is mentality.' That yogi at times contemplates materiality, and at times

Notes:
1. An- (not) + upādinna (clung to as 'I' or 'a being') = anupādinna: the collection of inanimate external materiality and formations that are not grasped or clung to as 'I' or 'a being.'

contemplates mentality. As he contemplates thus, while contemplating materiality, his insight connects with the Noble Path. This is called 'having initially observed materiality, he emerges from materiality.'

If, however, while he is contemplating mentality, his insight connects with the Noble Path, this is called 'having initially observed materiality, he emerges from mentality.' This same method applies to emerging from mentality and materiality after initially observing mentality.

786. Having initially inclined thus: 'Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation,' at the time of emergence in this same manner, it is called 'emerging from the five aggregates simultaneously.'

[301] 787. A certain yogi from the very beginning contemplates formations through the aspect of impermanence.
301:
However, emergence (of the Path) does not occur merely by contemplating through the aspect of impermanence; one must also contemplate through the aspect of suffering and the aspect of non-self. Therefore, he contemplates through the aspect of suffering and the aspect of non-self. For that yogi who practices thus, emergence occurs at the time of contemplating through the aspect of impermanence; this is called 'having initially inclined through the aspect of impermanence, he emerges through the aspect of impermanence.'

If, however, emergence occurs for him at the time of contemplating through the aspect of suffering or the aspect of non-self, this is called 'having initially inclined through the aspect of impermanence, he emerges through the aspect of suffering or the aspect of non-self.' This same method applies to emerging through the remaining aspects after initially inclining through the aspect of suffering or the aspect of non-self.

788. Among these persons, whether one has initially inclined through the aspect of impermanence, or through the aspect of suffering, or through the aspect of non-self, if at the time of emergence (by the Path), emergence occurs through the aspect of impermanence, all three types of persons are predominant in resolution (adhimokkha). They acquire the predominant faculty of faith (saddhindriya) and are liberated through the signless liberation (animitta-vimokkha). At the moment of the first path (Stream-entry), they are called 'faith-followers' (saddhānusārī); in the seven subsequent stages (of paths and fruits), they are called 'liberated by faith' (saddhā-vimutta).

If emergence occurs through the aspect of suffering, all three types of persons are predominant in tranquillity (passaddhi). They acquire the predominant faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) and are liberated through the desireless liberation (appaṇihita-vimokkha). In all (eight stages of paths and fruits), they are called 'body-witnesses' (kāyasakkhī). Specifically, among those who emerge through the aspect of suffering, if one has an immaterial absorption (arūpa-jhāna) as a basis, that person is called 'liberated in both ways' (ubhatobhāga-vimutta) at the moment of the highest fruit (Arahantship).

Or, if emergence occurs for those three types of persons through the aspect of non-self, all three types of persons are predominant in wisdom. They acquire the predominant faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) and are liberated through the emptiness liberation (suññata-vimokkha). At the moment of the first path, they are called 'Dhamma-followers' (dhammānusārī). In the six intermediate stages, they are called 'attained to vision' (diṭṭhippatta). At the moment of the highest fruit, they are called 'liberated by wisdom' (paññā-vimutta).

789. Now, in order to clarify this insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā) along with the preceding and succeeding knowledges, twelve similes should be understood. The following verse is the summary of those similes:

## 
Bat, cobra, (flame), and house,
Ox, ogress, (from the path), and child,
Hunger, thirst, cold, and heat,
Darkness (covering at the end), and like poison.

These similes are suitable to be presented starting from the 'Knowledge of Appearance as Terror' (bhaya-ñāṇa) or any other stage of knowledge. However, if presented at this stage (of insight leading to emergence), everything from the Knowledge of Terror up to the Knowledge of Fruition becomes clear. Therefore, it is stated (in the Visuddhimagga) that they should be presented only at this stage.

[302] Regarding the 'Bat': A bat, hoping that 'there will be flowers or fruits in this tree,' perches on a Nyan-si tree (likely a species of tree) that has five branches. It contemplates and examines one branch, but finds no flower or fruit that is worth taking or using on that branch.
302:
Just as with the first branch, [the bat] examined the second, third, fourth, and fifth branches but found nothing. That bat, reflecting, "Alas, this tree is fruitless; there is nothing here worth taking or using," abandoned its attachment to that tree, climbed up by a straight main branch, poked its head out through the fork of the branches, looked upwards, flew up into the sky, and landed on another fruit-bearing tree.

Notes:
1. (Flame) (From the path) These words are added from the detailed explanation to follow, in order to complete the eight-syllable verse.
2. (Behind the last cover) These words in parentheses are also additions made appropriately to complete the eight-syllable verse.

In this simile, the yogi should be understood as the bat. The five aggregates of clinging (pañcupādānakkhandhā) should be understood as the five-branched Madhuka tree. The yogi’s preoccupation with the five aggregates is like the bat’s perching on that tree. The yogi’s examination of the remaining aggregates after examining the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) and seeing nothing worth taking is like the bat’s examination of the remaining branches after examining each branch and seeing nothing worth taking. The three knowledges, such as the knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatāñāṇa), of the weary yogi who wishes to be released by seeing the mark of impermanence (aniccā) etc. in the five aggregates, are like the bat’s abandoning of attachment to the tree upon reflecting, "Alas, this tree is fruitless." The yogi’s conformity knowledge (anulomañāṇa) is like the bat’s climbing upwards by a straight main branch. Change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhūñāṇa) is like poking the head out and looking upwards. Path knowledge (maggañāṇa) is like flying into the sky. Fruition knowledge (phalañāṇa) is like landing on another fruit-bearing tree.

791. The simile of the cobra has already been mentioned in the section on the knowledge of reflection (paṭisaṅkhāñāṇa). However, in the comparison of the similes here, the difference is this: change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhūñāṇa) is like the releasing of the snake; path knowledge (maggañāṇa) is like the position of one who, having released it, stands looking back at the path he came; fruition knowledge (phalañāṇa) is like the standing in a safe place after having gone there.

792. In the simile of the house, it is said that a householder, having eaten in the evening, went to bed and fell asleep, and the house caught fire. That householder, upon waking and seeing the fire, was terrified and looked around, thinking, "It would be good indeed if I could escape without being burnt." Seeing an exit path, he went out and ran with great speed to a safe place and stayed there. In that simile, the worldling’s (bālaputhujjana) grasping of the five aggregates as "I" and "mine" is like the householder’s falling asleep after going to bed and eating. The knowledge of the appearance of terror (bhayatūpaṭṭhānañāṇa), which arises from seeing the three marks while practicing the right path, is like the time of being terrified upon waking and seeing the fire. Like looking for the exit path [303] is the knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatāñāṇa).
303:
Like seeing the exit path is conformity knowledge (anulomañāṇa). Like going out is change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhūñāṇa). Like running with great speed is path knowledge (maggañāṇa). Like staying in a safe place is fruition knowledge (phalañāṇa).

793. In the simile of the ox, while a certain farmer was asleep at night, his oxen broke out of the pen and fled. That farmer, going to the pen at dawn and looking, realized they had fled. Following their tracks, he saw the king’s oxen. Thinking "These are my oxen," he was leading them away when, at daybreak, he realized, "These are not my oxen; they are the king’s oxen." Terrified, thinking, "Before the king’s men seize me as a thief and bring me to ruin, I will flee," he abandoned the oxen and ran with great speed to a safe place and stayed there. In that simile, the worldling’s grasping of the aggregates as "I" and "mine" is like the taking of the king’s oxen as "my oxen." The yogi’s realization of the aggregates as "impermanent, suffering, and non-self" (anicca, dukkha, anatta) by way of the three marks is like the realization at daybreak that they are "the king’s oxen." The knowledge of the appearance of terror (bhayatūpaṭṭhānañāṇa) is like the time of being terrified. The knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatāñāṇa) is like the desire to go after abandoning the oxen. Change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhūñāṇa) is like the abandoning of the oxen. The path (magga) is like the act of fleeing. Fruition (phala) is like staying in a safe place after fleeing.

794. In the simile of the ogress, a man lived with an ogress. At night, thinking "This human is asleep," she went to a cemetery and ate human flesh. That man, following her and wondering "Where is she going?", saw her eating human flesh and realized she was a non-human. Terrified, thinking "Before she eats me, I will flee," he ran with great speed and stayed in a safe place. In that simile, the grasping of the aggregates as "I" and "mine" is like the living together with the ogress. The realization of the aggregates as impermanent etc. by seeing the three marks is like the realization that "This woman is an ogress" upon seeing her eating human flesh in the cemetery. The knowledge of the appearance of terror (bhayatūpaṭṭhānañāṇa) is like the time of being terrified. The knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatāñāṇa) is like the desire to flee. Change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhūñāṇa) is like the abandoning of the cemetery. The path (magga) is like the act of fleeing with great speed. Fruition (phala) is like staying in a safe place.

795. In the simile of the child, there was a woman who was very fond of her son. While sitting in her palace, she heard a child's cry in the street and, thinking "Is someone harming my son?", she went with great speed and, with the perception that it was "her own son," she picked up another person's child.
304:
That woman, realizing 'This child is another's,' became terrified and looked here and there [304]. Thinking, 'Let no one accuse me or say, "This woman is a kidnapper,"' she left the child right there and quickly ascended the palace again and sat down. In this simile, the taking of another's child with the perception of 'one's own son' should be understood as the taking of the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha) as 'I' and 'mine.' The realization that 'This child is another's' should be understood as the realization of 'Not I, not mine' by way of the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa). The state of being terrified should be understood as the knowledge of appearance as terror (bhayatupaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa). Looking here and there should be understood as the knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa). Leaving the child right there on the road should be understood as conformity knowledge (anuloma-ñāṇa). The time of standing in the middle of the road after leaving the child should be understood as change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). Ascending the palace is like the Path (magga). Sitting down after ascending is like the Fruit (phala).

796. These six similes—'Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, darkness, and poison'—are stated to show the state of the yogi established in emergence-leading insight (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā), whose mind is inclined, leaned, and sloped towards the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma). To explain: Just as a man overcome by hunger and very famished desires delicious food, even so, this yogi, afflicted by the hunger of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa), desires the food of mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati), which has the taste of the deathless (amata-rasa).

Just as a thirsty man with a parched throat and mouth desires a drink made of many ingredients, even so, this yogi, afflicted by the thirst of the round of rebirths, desires the drink of the Noble Eightfold Path.

Just as a person afflicted by cold desires heat, even so, this yogi, afflicted by the cold of the moisture of craving (taṇhā-sineha) in the round of rebirths, desires the fire of the Path which burns up the defilements (kilesa).

Just as a person afflicted by heat desires cold, even so, this yogi, scorched by the eleven fires in the round of rebirths, desires Nibbāna, which is the subsiding of the eleven fires.
