1. Connect as: "The conditions... are two."
2. By this qualifying term, it is shown that "In the process of fruit attainment, the gotrabhū does not take Nibbāna as its object, but takes only formations as its object."
3. In the year 236 of the Sasana, the Sasana reached Sri Lanka and the Mahāvihāra monastery was founded; the lineage of teachers residing there is called Mahāvihāravāsī. Between the years 455 and 466 of the Sasana, King Vaṭṭagāmaṇi built and donated the Abhayagiri monastery; the lineage of teachers residing there is called Abhayagirivāsī. Later, those Abhayagirivāsīs also accepted the doctrines of various sects that opposed the views of the Mahāvihāravāsīs, as well as the Mahayana doctrine called Vetulla.

Since this is not possible, that statement [of the Abhayagiri teachers] is not at all [logical]; it has already been rejected by the Pali of the Paṭisambhidāmagga mentioned before. Therefore, that statement should not be accepted. Indeed, only this statement [of ours] should be accepted: "For a trainee also, only the fruit arises, not the path." And regarding his fruit, if that noble disciple had attained the path associated with the first jhāna, only the fruit associated with the first jhāna arises. If he had attained a path associated with the second jhāna or others, only the fruit associated with the second jhāna or others arises. Thus is the attainment of that [fruit].
343:
Only the fruition associated with the first jhāna occurs; if one has attained a path associated with any one of the jhānas such as the second jhāna and so on, then only the fruition associated with that particular jhāna such as the second jhāna and so on occurs. In this way, the entry into the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) takes place.

[343] 864. Furthermore, because of the statement: "Friend, there are three conditions for the persistence of the signless deliverance of mind (animitta-cetovimutti): non-attention to all signs, attention to the signless element, and prior preparation" (M. Ni. 1.458), the persistence of that attainment of fruition occurs through these three factors. Therein, "prior preparation" means the delimitation of the time before reaching the fruition. Indeed, because it is delimited as "I shall emerge from the attainment at such and such a time," the persistence of that attainment of fruition lasts until that delimited time arrives. Thus occurs the persistence of that attainment of fruition.

865. Furthermore, because of the statement: "Friend, there are two conditions for the emergence from the signless deliverance of mind: attention to all signs and non-attention to the signless element" (M. Ni. 1.458), the emergence from that attainment of fruition occurs through these two factors. Therein, "all signs" refers to the signs of materiality, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. To explain further: it is true that one does not attend to all these signs simultaneously; however, this term "all signs" is spoken in an all-inclusive sense. Therefore, when one attends to whatever sign of formations is the object of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), emergence from the attainment of fruition occurs for that person. Thus should the emergence from that attainment of fruition be understood.

866. (e) In the question "What follows fruition, and what does fruition follow?", as for fruition, either fruition itself or the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) follows it. Fruition, however, exists as following the path, following fruition, following change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), and following the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Therein, in the path-process, it follows the path; each subsequent fruition follows each preceding fruition. In the attainments of fruition, the first fruition follows change-of-lineage. To explain further: in this context of the attainment of fruition, "conformity" (anuloma) should be understood by the name "change-of-lineage" (gotrabhū). For it is said in the Paṭṭhāna: "The conformity of an Arahant is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of proximity-condition. The conformity of trainees (sekhas) is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of proximity-condition." The fruition by which there is emergence from cessation (nirodha) follows the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Among those fruitions, excluding the fruition arising in the path-process, all the rest are called fruition occurring by way of the attainment of fruition. Thus, by way of arising in the path-process or in the attainment of fruition:

This supreme fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala), which allays the fever of defilements, which has the Deathless Nibbāna as its object, which is beautiful, which has vomited up the baits of the world, is exceedingly peaceful.

Just as honey is mixed with ambrosia, it is saturated with that pure, nutritious, and blissful fruition-happiness, which is more delightful than the delightful bliss [of jhāna and the path].
344:
Connect this as: "One is moistened by whichever bliss of the fruit... one experiences that bliss of the fruit."

[344] That bliss of the fruit, which is the supreme essence of that very Noble Fruit belonging to the Noble Ones, the wise person experiences by developing the wisdom of insight.

Because of that (experiencing through the development of insight), this experiencing of the essence (of bliss) of the Noble Fruit is called the benefit of the development of wisdom (paññā-bhāvanā) in this context.

## Explanation of the Attainment of Cessation

867. The ability to enter the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is not merely the experiencing of the essence of the Noble Fruit; this ability to enter the attainment of cessation should also be understood as a benefit of this development of wisdom.

In this regard, the following is the set of questions to clarify the attainment of cessation:
(a) What is the attainment of cessation?
(b) Who attains it, and who does not?
(c) Where is it attained?
(d) Why is it attained?
(e) How is it attained?
(f) How is it maintained?
(g) How is it emerged from?
(h) To what does the mind of one who has emerged incline?
(i) What is the difference between one who is dead and one who has entered the attainment?
(j) Is the attainment of cessation conditioned or unconditioned, mundane or supramundane, produced or unproduced?

868. Therein, (a) regarding the question "What is the attainment of cessation?": It is the non-occurrence of consciousness and mental factors through the process of successive cessation.

(b) Regarding the question "Who attains it, and who does not?": All worldlings, Stream-enterers, and Once-returners, as well as dry-insight [1] Non-returners and Arahants, do not attain it. However, Non-returners and those whose taints are destroyed (Arahants) who are attainers of the eight attainments do attain it. For it is said:

"Wisdom consisting in mastery by way of two powers, the subsiding of three formations, sixteen kinds of knowledge-exercise, and nine kinds of concentration-exercise is the knowledge of the attainment of cessation." (Paṭis. I, 34).

This accomplishment does not exist in others except for Non-returners and Arahants who have attained the eight attainments. Therefore,

Notes:
1. Sukkhavipassaka: Dry-insight practitioner. One who practices insight purely without the "moisture" of serenity-concentration (samatha-samādhi) such as access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), and thus becomes a Non-returner or Arahant.
2. The wisdom that is the cause of being one who has mastery is called "wisdom consisting in mastery." Because of this proficient wisdom, such a person is called a master; that wisdom is indeed the wisdom of mastery or proficient wisdom.

only those Non-returners and Arahants who have attained the eight attainments enter it, and no others.

869. Among these two powers and so on, what are the two powers? ... What is mastery? In this matter, there is nothing for us to say. All this has already been explained in the Niddesa (detailed exposition) of this Uddesa (summary). How is it explained?

[345] Regarding "with two powers," the two powers are the power of serenity and the power of insight.
345:
What is the power of serenity? One-pointedness and non-distraction of mind through the power of renunciation (nekkhamma), which is the departure from sensual desire, is the power of serenity. Through the power of non-ill will (abyāpāda). Through the power of the perception of light (ālokasaññā). Through the power of non-distraction (avikkhepa). ... Through the power of inhalation in one who contemplates relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassī). Through the power of exhalation in one who contemplates relinquishment, one-pointedness and non-distraction of mind is the power of serenity.

In what sense is it the power of serenity? It is the power of serenity because it is unshaken by the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) through the first jhāna [Note 1]. It is the power of serenity because it is unshaken by thought and examination (vitakka-vicāra) through the second jhāna. ... It is the power of serenity because it is unshaken by the perception of the sphere of nothingness through the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. It does not shake, does not move, and does not tremble due to restlessness (uddhacca), defilements associated with restlessness, and the aggregates (khandhas); therefore, it is called the power of serenity. This is the power of serenity.

Note 1: If hindrances occur, it is called 'shaking'. For one who is endowed with the first jhāna, hindrances cannot occur; thus, it is said to be 'unshaken by hindrances'. This first jhāna is called the power of serenity because it encourages the absence of shaking caused by these hindrances. Understand the subsequent sections in the same way.

What is the power of insight? Contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is the power of insight. Contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā). ... Contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā). Contemplation of revulsion (nibbidānupassanā). Contemplation of fading away (virāgānupassanā). Contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā). Contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā) is the power of insight. Contemplation of impermanence in form (rūpa). ... Contemplation of relinquishment in form is the power of insight. In feeling (vedanā). In perception (saññā). In formations (saṅkhāra). In consciousness (viññāṇa). In the eye. ... In aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), contemplation of impermanence. ... In aging and death, contemplation of relinquishment is the power of insight.

In what sense is it the power of insight? It is the power of insight because it is unshaken by the perception of permanence (niccasaññā) through the contemplation of impermanence [Note 1]. It is unshaken by the perception of pleasure (sukhasaññā) through the contemplation of suffering. It is unshaken by the perception of self (attasaññā) through the contemplation of non-self. It is unshaken by delight (nandi) through the contemplation of revulsion. It is unshaken by lust (rāga) through the contemplation of fading away. It is unshaken by origination (samudaya) through the contemplation of cessation. It is unshaken by grasping (ādāna) through the contemplation of relinquishment; therefore, it is called the power of insight. It does not shake, does not move, and does not tremble due to ignorance (avijjā), defilements associated with ignorance, and the aggregates; therefore, it is called the power of insight. This is the power of insight.

Regarding 'due to the stilling of the three formations (saṅkhāras)', which three formations are stilled? For one who has attained the second jhāna, verbal formations (vacīsaṅkhāra) consisting of thought and examination [Note 1] are stilled. For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra) consisting of inhalation and exhalation [Note 2] are stilled. For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha), mental formations (cittasaṅkhāra) consisting of perception and feeling [Note 3] are stilled. It is due to the stilling of these three formations.

Note 1: If one perceives as permanent, it is called 'shaking'. For one who sees as impermanent through contemplation of impermanence, such shaking does not exist. Therefore, contemplation of impermanence is called the power of insight. Understand the subsequent sections in the same way.

Note 1 (Verbal Formations): Vacī (speech) + saṅkhāra (formation) = vacīsaṅkhāra. Formations that produce speech—that is, the thought and examination that cause speech. When speaking, one must think and examine; therefore, thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra) are called verbal formations. A person attaining the cessation of perception and feeling enters the jhānas in succession and practices insight. Therefore, when entering the second jhāna, those thoughts and examinations are stilled. This describes that stilling.

Note 2 (Bodily Formations): Kāya (body) + saṅkhāra (formation) = kāyasaṅkhāra. Formations produced by the body, such as the nose and abdomen, namely inhalation and exhalation. These are stilled upon reaching the fourth jhāna. This describes that stilling.

Note 3 (Mental Formations): Citta (mind) + saṅkhāra (formation) = cittasaṅkhāra. Feeling and perception, which are said to be produced by the mind because they occur in association with the mind. These are stilled upon reaching the cessation of perception and feeling. This describes that stilling.

[346] Regarding 'through the sixteen occurrences of knowledge (ñāṇacariyā)', which sixteen occurrences of knowledge? Contemplation of impermanence is an occurrence of knowledge [Note 4]. Contemplation of suffering. Contemplation of non-self. Contemplation of revulsion. Contemplation of fading away. Contemplation of cessation. Contemplation of relinquishment. Contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭānupassanā) is an occurrence of knowledge. The path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga)...

Note 4: The term 'ñāṇacariyā' is translated as the occurrence of knowledge, or it may also be translated as the conduct of knowledge.
346:
The Ṭīkā states that it is the knowledge occurring in the sense-sphere; in the case of the exercise of knowledge (ñāṇacariyā) of the Path and Fruition, it is called 'exercise of knowledge' because knowledge is predominant, or because it is produced by knowledge.

...is the occurrence of knowledge. The attainment of the fruition of Stream-entry is the occurrence of knowledge. The Path of Once-returning... (p)... the attainment of the fruition of Arhatship is the occurrence of knowledge. These are the sixteen exercises of knowledge.

Regarding the nine exercises of concentration (samādhicariyā), what are the nine exercises of concentration? The first jhāna is an exercise of concentration.1 The second jhāna... (p)... the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is an exercise of concentration. For the sake of obtaining the first jhāna, there are initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), zest (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (ekaggatā)... (p)... for the sake of obtaining the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are initial application, sustained application, zest, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind. These are the nine exercises of concentration.

Regarding mastery (vasī), there are five masteries:2 mastery in adverting (āvajjanavasī), mastery in attaining (samāpajjanavasī), mastery in resolving (adhiṭṭhānavasī), mastery in emerging (vuṭṭhānavasī), and mastery in reviewing (paccavekkhaṇavasī). One adverts to the first jhāna wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes; there is no sluggishness in adverting, thus it is called mastery in adverting.

Notes:
1. It is also translated as 'the occurrence of concentration'; it refers specifically to the concentration occurring in the sense-sphere.
2. Connect as: 'The masteries are five.'
3. The word 'āvajjanāya' is also translated as 'of adverting'; however, considering the subsequent words ending in the locative case like 'adhiṭṭhāne' (in resolving) and 'vuṭṭhāne' (in emerging), only the locative sense 'in adverting' is appropriate. Regarding the meaning of this adverting, the Commentaries and Sub-commentaries such as the Visuddhimagga state it is the adverting that reviews the jhāna factors. The Paṭisambhidāmagga Commentary, however, says it is the adverting to enter the jhāna.

One attains the first jhāna wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes; there is no sluggishness in attaining,1 thus it is called mastery in attaining. One resolves (to remain) in the first jhāna wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes;2 there is no sluggishness in (remaining according to) the resolution,3 thus it is called mastery in resolving.4 One emerges from the first jhāna wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes; there is no sluggishness in emerging, thus it is called mastery in emerging. One reviews the first jhāna wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes; there is no sluggishness in reviewing, thus it is called mastery in reviewing. The second jhāna... (p)... one adverts to... (p)... reviews the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception wherever one wishes, whenever one wishes, and for as long as one wishes; there is no sluggishness in reviewing, thus it is called mastery in reviewing.

Notes:
1. Here too, the word 'samāpajjanāya' is translated by some as 'for the sake of attaining', but as shown in Note 3 above, only the locative sense is appropriate.
2. Some translate 'adhiṭṭhāti' as 'places/sets'; the translation 'resolves to remain' is clearer.
3. Since 'adhiṭṭhāne' is in the locative case here, 'āvajjanāya' etc. should also be understood in the locative case.
4. The Commentaries and Sub-commentaries state that mastery is achieved only if one can resolve to stay for a very short time, such as the snap of a finger. However, it seems mastery is achieved if one can remain for as long or as short a time as intended. Only then would it be consistent with the qualifier 'yāvaticchakaṃ' (for as long as one wishes).

"These are the five masteries," He taught.

870. In the above Pali, the phrase "by the sixteen exercises of knowledge" is a superior exposition (ukkaṭṭhaniddesa). For an Anāgāmī, however, (the attainment of cessation) occurs through fourteen exercises of knowledge. If so, why does it not occur for a Sakadāgāmī through twelve exercises of knowledge, or for a Sotāpanna through ten? It does not occur because the lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure, which is an obstacle to concentration,1 has not yet been abandoned. Indeed, the Sotāpanna and Sakadāgāmī have not yet abandoned that sensual lust. Therefore, their power of calm (samatha) is not complete. When that calm is incomplete, they are unable to enter the attainment of cessation, which must be entered by two powers, due to the deficiency of power.
347:
For the Anāgāmī, however, that sensual lust has been abandoned. Therefore, this Anāgāmī possesses complete power; because of possessing complete power, he is able (to enter the attainment of cessation). Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "For one emerging from cessation, the wholesome state of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for fruition attainment by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya)." Indeed, in the Great Book of the Paṭṭhāna, this was taught with reference only to the emergence of an Anāgāmī from cessation.

871. (c) In which realm do they attain it? They attain it in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava), also known as the sensual and fine-material realms. Why? Because of the existence of the sequence of attainments. In the four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava), known as the formless realm,

Note:
1. Connect as: '...sensual lust which is an obstacle.'

there is no occurrence of the first jhāna and so on. Therefore, they are unable to attain it in that formless realm. Some teachers (keci), however, say it is because of the absence of the physical base (vatthu-rūpa).

872. (d) Why do they attain it? Being weary of the arising and passing of formations (saṅkhāra), and becoming mindless even in the present life, they attain it with the intention: "We shall dwell happily, having reached the cessation which is the peace of Nibbāna."1

873. (e) How does the entering of that attainment of cessation occur? In this question, for one who has made efforts by the power of calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), and has performed the preliminary duties, and who brings the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to cessation—by such cessation, the entering of that attainment of cessation occurs. Indeed, one who makes effort only by the power of calm reaches the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and remains there. One who makes effort only by the power of insight reaches fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti) and remains there. But one who makes effort by the power of both calm and insight, performs the preliminary duties, and brings the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to cessation, enters that attainment of cessation. This is the summary here.

874. The detailed explanation is as follows: Here, a monk who wishes to enter the attainment of cessation, having finished his meal and washed his hands and feet, sits down in a secluded place on a well-prepared seat,2 holding his upper body erect, establishing mindfulness directed towards the meditation subject, and sits cross-legged.

Notes:
1. This is a direct and precise translation of the words 'nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ'; it states that cessation itself is the peace of Nibbāna. This should be specially noted.
2. Connect as: '...sits on a seat.'

That monk, having entered the first jhāna and emerged from it, contemplates the formations (saṅkhāra) contained in that first jhāna as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self.

To explain further, this contemplation or insight (vipassanā) is of three kinds: insight for grasping formations, insight for fruition attainment, and insight for the attainment of cessation. Among these, insight for grasping formations, whether it be dull or sharp, is certainly a proximate cause for the Path. Insight for fruition attainment is suitable only when it is sharp, similar to the development of the Path. Insight for the attainment of cessation, however, is suitable when it is neither too dull nor too sharp.
348:
Therefore, this monk contemplates those formations (saṅkhāra) with insight (vipassanā) that is neither too slow nor too sharp.

Then, having entered the second jhāna and emerged from it, he contemplates the formations in that second jhāna in the same way. Then the third jhāna... [pe]... Then, having entered the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) and emerged from it, he contemplates the formations in that sphere in the same way. Then, having entered the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) and emerged from it, he performs the fourfold preliminary duties (pubbakicca): the non-destruction of separate belongings (nānābaddha-avikopana), waiting for the Saṅgha (saṅgha-paṭimānana), the summons of the Teacher (satthu-pakkosana), and the delimitation of the duration (addhāna-pariccheda).

Notes:
1. If insight is slow, the Path is reached slowly; if sharp, it is reached quickly. This is the only difference. The commentary states that insight which reaches the level of characteristics is indeed capable of producing the Path.
2. It means the Path that produces Fruition must be sharp.
3. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga Commentary, it is also stated that "equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā) supports Fruition even if it is slow." For the final decision, see the Manual of Insight (Vipassanā-shunee-kyan), Volume 2 (6th ed. p. 306, 7th ed. p. 332).

875. Among those four, "the non-destruction of separate belongings" is as follows: whatever requisites such as a bowl and robes, a bed and stool, a dwelling place, or any other kind of requisite that is not connected to this monk but exists separately—he should make a determination (adhiṭṭhāna) so that they are not destroyed by fire, water, wind, thieves, rats, and so forth.

The procedure for making this determination is: "May this and that requisite not be burned by fire, not be swept away by water, not be destroyed by wind, not be taken by thieves, and not be bitten by rats within these seven days." When such a determination is made, no danger will befall those requisites for the duration of those seven days.

However, the requisites of a monk who does not make a determination are destroyed by fire and other causes. How? Just like the requisites of the Elder Mahā Nāga. It is said that Elder Mahā Nāga entered a village for alms at the home of a laywoman who was his mother. The laywoman offered him rice gruel and had him sit in the refectory. The Elder sat there having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). While he was sitting, the refectory caught fire, and the other monks took their respective seats and fled. The villagers gathered, and seeing the Elder, they said, "An idle monk." The fire burned the grass, bamboo, and wood, and remained surrounding the Elder. The people brought water in pots, extinguished the fire, cleared away the ashes, prepared the floor (smeared with cow dung), scattered flowers, and stood there worshipping him. The Elder, emerging at the designated time and seeing those people, thought, "I have become famous (for my attainment)," and flew into the air to Piyangu Island. This is what is called "the non-destruction of separate belongings."

Regarding requisites that are connected to the body, such as the inner robe, the outer robe, or the seat-mat, there is no need for a separate act of determination. The power of the attainment itself protects them, as in the case of the Venerable Sañjīva...
349:
By the power of the attainment itself, one is protected and guarded against those [dangers such as fire]. How so? It is said: 'The psychic power through the diffusion of concentration of the Venerable Sañjīva; the psychic power through the diffusion of concentration of the Venerable Sāriputta.'

Note 1: While the Venerable Sañjīva was in the attainment of cessation, cowherds and others, thinking he was dead, piled up grass, wood, and cow dung and set them on fire. Not even a single thread of the Elder's robe was burnt. This lack of burning was due to the majesty and power of serenity-concentration (samatha-samādhi) achieved through the successive attainments. This refers to that psychic power.

Note 2: While the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna at the Kapota Canyon on a moonlit night, a wicked yakkha struck his freshly shaved, shining head with great force. The sound was like a thunderclap. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was in the attainment of cessation. Due to that blow, the Venerable Sāriputta did not feel even the slightest pain. This refers to that psychic power.

876. 'Waiting for the Saṅgha' means the Saṅgha's waiting or expectation. The meaning is: not performing a legal act of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma) until this monk [who is in the attainment of cessation] arrives. To explain further: in this context, the act of waiting itself is not his preliminary duty (pubbakicca); rather, the reflection on the waiting is the preliminary duty. Therefore, one should reflect thus: 'If the Saṅgha wishes to perform any legal act, such as a motion (ñatti) and so on, while I am seated in the attainment of cessation for seven days, I shall emerge [from the attainment] even before any monk comes and calls me.' For one who enters the attainment after having made such a reflection will indeed emerge at that time.

However, if a monk does not make such a reflection, and the Saṅgha, having assembled and not seeing him, asks, 'Where is such-and-such monk?' and is told, 'He is in the attainment of cessation,' the Saṅgha sends a monk, saying, 'Go and call him in the name of the Saṅgha.' Then, as soon as that messenger monk stands within earshot and says, 'Friend, the Saṅgha is waiting for you,' the emergence occurs. Such is the gravity of the Saṅgha's authority. Therefore, one should reflect on that waiting and enter the attainment in such a way that one emerges by oneself.

Note 1: Legal acts decided and carried out by the assembly of the Saṅgha are of four types: Ñattikamma, Ñattidutiyakamma, Ñatticatutthakamma, and Apalokanakamma. Among these, an act that is decided and confirmed merely by a motion (ñatti) to inform the Saṅgha of the intended business is called Ñattikamma. An act that must be completed by announcing the confirmation once along with the motion is called Ñattidutiyakamma; it means an act where the motion is the second [part]. An act that must be completed with three announcements of confirmation along with the motion is called Ñatticatutthakamma; it means an act where the motion is the fourth [part]. An act that is settled by stating the matter and asking for agreement three times is called Apalokanakamma; it means an act of request. These are the acts referred to.

877. 'The Teacher's summons'—in this case too, the reflection on the Teacher's summons is the duty of this monk. Therefore, that too should be reflected upon thus: 'If the Teacher should lay down a training rule (sikkhāpada) because of an incident that has arisen, or should teach the Dhamma due to a similar occurrence while I am seated in the attainment of cessation for seven days, I shall emerge even before any monk comes and calls me.' For one who sits after having made such a reflection will indeed emerge at that time.

However, if a monk does not make such a reflection, and the Teacher, not seeing him when the Saṅgha has assembled, asks, 'Where is such-and-such monk?' and is told, 'He is in the attainment of cessation,' He sends a monk, saying, 'Go and call him in my name.' Then, as soon as that messenger monk stands within earshot and says, 'The Teacher calls the venerable one,' the emergence occurs. Such is the gravity of the Teacher's summons. Therefore, one should reflect on that summons and enter the attainment in such a way that one emerges by oneself.

878. 'Limitation of duration' means the limitation of the life span. This monk [entering cessation] should be very skillful in the limitation of the duration [of life], [thinking] 'Will my life-formations (āyusaṅkhāra) [350] last for seven days?'
350:
One should enter [the attainment] only after reflecting, "Will [the life-formations] continue for seven days or will they not?" The fault is this: if one enters without reflecting on the life-formations that might cease within seven days, that monk's attainment of cessation cannot prevent death. Since there is no death within the attainment of cessation, one would emerge from the attainment prematurely. Therefore, one should enter only after reflecting on this duration of life. Indeed, it is said [in the Commentary]: "While it is acceptable not to reflect on the remaining three tasks, one must certainly reflect on this duration of life."

879. That monk, having entered the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) as described and emerged from it, and having performed these preliminary duties, enters the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). Then, after passing one or two thought-moments, he becomes without mind and reaches cessation. Why do thoughts not continue beyond two thought-moments? Because of the application (payoga) toward cessation. To elaborate: for this monk, making the two states of tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) like a pair yoked together, the ascent through the eight attainments is the application for the gradual cessation of thought, not for the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Because it is an application for cessation, thoughts do not occur beyond two moments.

Note 1: Āyu (life) + saṅkhāra (formation) = āyu-saṅkhāra: the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) which is conditioned and maintained by causes such as kamma.

However, if a monk emerges from the base of nothingness and enters the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception without performing these preliminary duties, he is unable to become mindless afterwards; he turns back and remains only in the base of nothingness. Here, the simile of a man who has never traveled the road before should be told.

The simile is this: A man traveling a road he has never been on before comes across a water-filled ravine or deep mud. Having crossed it, he reaches a stone slab heated intensely by the harsh sun. If he descends into the ravine without adjusting his lower and upper robes, he turns back to this side out of fear that his belongings will get wet. Even after stepping on the stone slab, because his feet are burning, he turns back to this side. In that simile, just as that man, because he did not properly adjust his robes, turns back to this side as soon as he descends into the ravine or as soon as he steps on the hot stone slab, so too the practitioner (yogāvacara), because he has not performed the preliminary duties, turns back as soon as he enters the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and remains in the base of nothingness.
351:
The appropriate simile is this: A man who has traveled that road before, upon reaching that place, wears one cloth firmly and holds another in his hand. Having crossed the ravine and merely stepped on the hot stone slab, he reaches the other side. In the same way, a monk who has performed the preliminary duties, having entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, subsequently becomes mindless and dwells having reached the cessation of mind and mental factors.

880. (f) To the question "How does it persist?", the persistence of that attainment of cessation entered in this way occurs (as intended) by the power of the predetermined duration, and by the absence of the exhaustion of life, the expectation of the Saṅgha, or a summons by the Teacher in the interval.

881. (g) To the question "How does one emerge?", emergence occurs in two ways: by the arising of the fruit of Non-returning for an Anāgāmi, and by the arising of the fruit of Arahantship for an Arahat.

882. (h) To the question "To what is the mind of one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation inclined?", it should be known that it is inclined toward Nibbāna. Indeed, it is said [by the nun Dhammadinnā]: "Friend Visākha, the mind of a monk who has emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling inclines toward seclusion (Nibbāna), leans toward seclusion, slopes toward seclusion."

883. (i) To the question "What is the difference between one who is dead and one who has entered the attainment of cessation?", this meaning is also stated in the Mahāvedalla Sutta. How is it stated?

"Friend, in the case of one who is dead and has passed away, the bodily formations—in-breathing and out-breathing—have ceased and subsided; the verbal formations—applied and sustained thought—have ceased and subsided; the mental formations—perception and feeling—have ceased and subsided; life is exhausted; heat has subsided; and the faculties are broken up. In the case of a monk who has entered the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, the bodily formations have ceased and subsided; the verbal formations have ceased and subsided; the mental formations have ceased and subsided; but life is not exhausted; heat has not subsided; and the faculties are not broken up."

884. (j) To the question "Is the attainment of cessation conditioned (saṅkhata)?", etc., it should not be said that it is conditioned, nor unconditioned, nor mundane, nor supramundane. Why? Because it does not exist in terms of ultimate reality (sabhāva). However, because it is attained by the power of the person entering it, it is called "attained" (samāpanna). Therefore, it is proper to say it is "produced" (nipphanna), not "unproduced" (anipphanna).

Thus, this peaceful attainment, cultivated by the Noble Ones,
Which reaches the designation of Nibbāna in this very life,
The wise, having developed noble wisdom, enter upon it.
Therefore, the ability to enter this attainment
Is called an advantage of wisdom in the Noble Paths.

## Explanation of the Accomplishment of Being Worthy of Offerings, etc.

885. The accomplishment of being worthy of offerings (āhuneyya), etc., brought from afar, is not merely the ability to enter the attainment of cessation (which is the advantage of this development of wisdom).
353:
The development of Noble Wisdom has many benefits as described; therefore, a wise person who possesses foresight should take delight in the development of that Noble Wisdom.

Notes:
1. This refers to being endowed with the six direct knowledges (abhiññā): (1) Iddhividha-abhiññā, the power to perform various supernormal feats; (2) Dibbasota-ñāṇa, the divine ear which can hear all sounds, far and near, large and small; (3) Cetopariya-ñāṇa, the knowledge of others' thoughts, also called paracittavijānana-abhiññā; (4) Pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa, the knowledge of recollecting past lives; (5) Dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa, the divine eye; and (6) Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa, the knowledge of the destruction of taints.
2. See Khandha-niddesa, paragraph 428.
3. Like the Once-returners, Arahants are multiplied by 12 through the doors of the Void (suññata), Signless (animitta), and Desireless (appaṇihita) liberations, and the four modes of progress (paṭipadā). These are further divided into 12 types of those liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta), 12 liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta), 12 with the three knowledges (tevijja), 12 with the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiñña), and 12 who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidāpatta), totaling 60 types. As previously mentioned, there are 48 types of Non-returners, 24 types of Stream-enterers, 12 types of Once-returners, 60 types of Arahants, 1 Paccekabuddha, and 1 Sammāsambuddha. The Commentary (Ṭīkā) shows a total of 146 types of Noble Persons (ariya-puggala). In this context, it should be understood that the 60 types of Arahants, along with the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, are intended.

890. By this sequence of words—
"A man wise, established well in Virtue, developing Consciousness and Wisdom, a bhikkhu ardent and discreet, he can disentangle this tangle."
—In this Visuddhimagga, which is the path of practice leading to Nibbāna taught by way of Virtue (sīla), Concentration (samādhi), and Wisdom (paññā) in this verse, the development of wisdom along with its benefits has been fully illustrated.

This is the twenty-third chapter called the Description of the Benefits of Developing Wisdom (Paññābhāvanānisaṃsa Niddesa) in the section on the Development of Wisdom in the Visuddhimagga, composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.

## The Detailed Explanation of the Benefits of Developing Wisdom Ends.

Notes:
1. Connect "By this sequence of words..." with "...has been fully illustrated."
2. Connect "In this verse... taught... in the Visuddhimagga..."
354:
## Concluding Remarks

[354] 891. By this sequence of words—
Having set forth this verse: "A man wise, established well in Virtue, developing Consciousness and Wisdom, a bhikkhu ardent and discreet, he can disentangle this tangle."
And having promised:
"Now, while explaining the true meaning of this verse taught by the Great Sage, which is divided into Virtue and so on...
Having obtained the very rare monkhood in the Dispensation of the Conqueror, those yogis here who, though desiring purity and striving, do not attain purification because they do not know the true, safe, and straight path of purification consisting of Virtue and so on...
For their gladdening, I shall speak the Visuddhimagga (Path of Purification), which is full of well-purified decisions and based on the method of teaching of the dwellers of the Mahāvihāra;
Let all good people who desire purification listen to me as I speak with care."
—That Visuddhimagga which I promised to speak has now been spoken.

892. In that Visuddhimagga—
The decision regarding those meanings divided into Virtue and so on (taught in the original verse) has been stated according to the method of the Commentaries (Atthakathā) that explain the meaning of the five Nikāyas.
Having collected all that, the meaning has been presented for the most part with decisions, free from the faults of confusing different doctrines.
Therefore, yogis who desire purification and are endowed with pure wisdom should certainly show respect for this Visuddhimagga.

[355] 893. Born in the lineage of the elders of the Mahāvihāra fraternity, who are numerous and are Great Vibhajjavādīs (those who speak after analyzing), and being a wise person capable of clear exposition—

Notes:
1. Connect "By this sequence of words... this Visuddhimagga has been spoken."
2. Connect "Having set forth... we promised."
3. Connect "In that Visuddhimagga... has been presented."
355:
2- This refers to the determination of the meanings of virtue, concentration, and wisdom as taught in the original Pali verse beginning with "Sīle patiṭṭhāya..." and translated into Burmese as "The wise man, established in virtue..."

3- Connect this with: "...has been stated as the decision."

4- Vibhajja (analytical) + vādī (one who speaks). Connect with: "...of the Elders who are the noble Vibhajjavādins."

Venerable Saṅghapāla is endowed with the pure ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) that thin out the defilements; he is also endowed with the virtue of restraint (vāritta-sīla) and the virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla); he constantly exerts himself in the practice (paṭipatti) of concentration and wisdom.

He possesses a heart imbued with qualities such as patience, delight in goodness, and loving-kindness that wishes for the welfare of others. Having accepted the request (of that Venerable Saṅghapāla) and desiring the long-lasting of the True Dhamma, whatever mass of merit I have acquired by composing this Visuddhimagga, by the power of that merit, may all beings attain the three types of happiness (human, celestial, and Nibbāna).

894. Just as this Visuddhimagga has been successfully completed in this Dispensation without obstacles, consisting of Pali text in fifty-eight recitation sections (bhāṇavāra);

Notes:
1. This means having a heart imbued with qualities such as patience, delight in goodness, and loving-kindness.
2. To make the attributes of Venerable Saṅghapāla easier to understand, they are translated as separate sentences; therefore, additional connecting words are added in parentheses to link with the subsequent text.
3. A portion of Pali text that can be recited continuously without stopping is called one bhāṇavāra. It is a collection of Pali text equivalent to about 250 verses, where each verse consists of four feet of eight syllables each (totaling 32 syllables). In Burmese terms, it is understood as one 'round' or 'sitting' of recitation. This work is said to be completed in 58 such bhāṇavāras.

Likewise, may all the heart's desires and intentions of the entire world of beings, which are based on goodness, be quickly and successfully fulfilled without obstacles. (End of two verses)

895. [This Visuddhimagga was composed by the Elder] who is adorned with extremely pure faith, wisdom, and energy; who is the meeting place of the collection of qualities such as the virtue of restraint, the virtue of performance, uprightness, and gentleness; who is capable of penetrating the thicket of his own doctrines and the doctrines of other sects;

Notes:
1. Connect the meaning as: "extremely pure virtue of restraint and performance," or "virtue of restraint adorned with faith, and virtue of performance adorned with wisdom and energy." As stated in the Sīla-niddesa (paragraph 19), "The virtue of Pātimokkha restraint is perfected by faith." Thus, it is said here to be adorned with faith. As also stated there, "The virtue of sense-restraint is perfected by mindfulness; the virtue of livelihood purification is perfected by energy; the virtue regarding requisites is perfected by the wisdom of reflection." Thus, it is said here to be adorned with wisdom and energy. Mentioning adornment by wisdom implies the perfection of adornment by mindfulness as well. In this context, the variant reading "paṭimaṇḍita-sīlācāra..." in the Pali is more appropriate.
2. This term is an attribute of Venerable Buddhaghosa. Connect as: "The Elder named Buddhaghosa, who is the meeting place of all qualities..."
3. The doctrine of the Mahāvihāra residents is called 'saka-samaya' (one's own doctrine); the doctrines of other sects like the Abhayagiri residents are called 'samayantara' (other doctrines). Alternatively, the doctrine within the Dispensation is 'saka-samaya', and the doctrines of those outside (bāhira) are 'samayantara'. The confused, difficult, and profound aspects of these doctrines are called 'gahana' (thicket), meaning they are like a thicket difficult to traverse. This refers to the Elder Buddhaghosa who is endowed with the ability to penetrate such confusion and difficulties.

[The Elder] who is endowed with sharpness of wisdom; who possesses the power of unimpeded knowledge in the Teacher's Dispensation consisting of the various scriptures of the Tipiṭaka together with the Commentaries; who is a great grammarian; who possesses the beauty of sweet and noble speech arising effortlessly from the perfection of the vocal apparatus; who is a speaker of appropriate and free speech; who is the most excellent among those who proclaim doctrines; who is a great poet; who is an ornament to the lineage of the Elders of the Mahāvihāra, who are like lamps to the lineage of Elders, and who possess unimpeded wisdom in the superhuman states (jhāna, path, and fruit) adorned with qualities such as the six higher powers (abhiññā) and the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā);

Notes:
[The note here discusses the grammatical connection of the Pali compound 'samatthapaññāveyyattiyasamannāgatena'].
1. This refers to the Elder Buddhaghosa who is endowed with sharpness of wisdom.
2. Connect as: "...in the Dispensation consisting of various scriptures."
3. These three terms are also attributes of Venerable Buddhaghosa; connect with the term "the Elder."
4. These three terms are also attributes of Venerable Buddhaghosa.
5. Connect as: "...in the superhuman states adorned with qualities..."
6. Connect as: "...of the Elders who possess unimpeded wisdom..."

[The Elder] who is like an ornament to the lineage; who is endowed with vast and pure wisdom; who is called a resident of Moraṇḍa village; who was given the name Buddhaghosa by his teachers and preceptors.

Notes:
1. These three terms are also attributes of Venerable Buddhaghosa. The last term is a translation of 'Moraṇḍakheṭakavattabbena'. In Sanskrit dictionaries, the word 'kheṭa' has three meanings: (1) village, (2) a place for forest-dwellers or farmers, (3) a small town. In South India, a village is still called 'kheḍā'. Therefore, the etymology is: Moraṇḍa + kheṭa = Moraṇḍakheṭa (Peacock Egg Village). One born there is Moraṇḍakheṭaka. One who should be called so is Moraṇḍakheṭakavattabba. This is the meaning translated here.
Where is Moraṇḍa village? In modern times, in the Guntur district of South India, there are places called Kotanemalipuri and Gundalapalli, about 51 miles from Nagarjunakonda and 58 miles from Amaravati. Ancient Buddhist ruins are scattered around that area. In the Telugu language of that region, a peacock is called 'nemali' and an egg is called 'gundalu'. Therefore, scholars of the Archaeological Survey of India believe these two places might be the birthplace of Venerable Buddhaghosa, formerly known as Moraṇḍakheṭa (Peacock Egg Village).

The Elder of such name composed this work called the Visuddhimagga. (This Visuddhimagga...)

[356] 896. As long as even the mere name "Buddha" (the Enlightened One) of the Blessed One—who possessed a pure heart, who possessed the quality of equanimity (tādi) towards the desirable and undesirable, who is the greatest in the three worlds, and who sought the highest qualities such as virtue—remains and exists continuously in the three worlds;

For that long, may it remain without disappearing in the three worlds, showing the method for the purification of virtue and so forth to the sons of good family who seek liberation from the world.

## The Visuddhimagga is Finished.

Notes:
1. A direct translation would be: "The work called Visuddhimagga composed by the Elder..." Because the sentence was too long, it was split. In splitting it, the subject "This Visuddhimagga" was added to connect with the later part: "May this Visuddhimagga... remain... showing..."
2. In the original Pali, this verse is the second, and the other is the first. However, in Burmese, it is customary to state the indefinite (aniyata) clause before the definite (niyata) clause, so the order was swapped in translation.
3. Connect as: "For that long... showing... may it remain."

## Special Conclusion of the Burmese Translation
With the fervent righteous desire that Burmese men and women who are not proficient in the Pali language may easily, accurately, and completely understand the methods of the practice of virtue, concentration, and wisdom as presented in the Visuddhimagga, just like those proficient in Pali, the Most Venerable Mahasi Sayadaw U Sobhana, Aggamahāpaṇḍita, residing at Sāsana Yeiktha, Yangon, began writing this Burmese translation of the Visuddhimagga on the 3rd waxing day of Tabaung, 1323 ME, during available times. The translation from the basic sections of Virtue, Concentration, and Wisdom, through the Diṭṭhivisuddhi-niddesa to the end of the Visuddhimagga, was completed on the 3rd waxing day of Wagaung, 1324 ME.

Just as this Burmese translation of the Visuddhimagga has been successfully completed without dangers or obstacles, may all virtuous monks and laypeople, men and women, who desire the practice, study this Burmese translation of the Visuddhimagga, practice according to the correct method, and quickly realize the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna.

## The Burmese Translation of the Visuddhimagga is Finished.

Notes:
1. The above statement refers to the completion of the first edition. For this second edition, which includes the addition of the Paññābhūmi-niddesa, writing began in the month of Tawthalin, 1331 ME, and was completed on the 1st waxing day of Nadaw.
